en: Record of Investigating the Profundities of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll One.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Fazang of Xisi Monastery in the Wei Kingdom.
Taking refuge in the Ocean of Great Wisdom, the Daśakāya Vairocana.
Pervading the entire realm of phenomena, the unsurpassed Honored One of Great Compassion;
the vast and stainless Dharma, the perfect wheel of liberation;
Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and the rest—the great Bodhisattvas of the ocean-like assembly.
While I remain on the stage of those still bound by afflictions, I long for the Great Dharma Gate.
I pray only that you will show me your compassion, increasing my power of mindfulness and wisdom,
so that this secret and profound treasury may be opened to bring vast benefit to both myself and others.
May it be that the Dharma remains long in the world, so that the lamp may be transmitted and the Buddha’s kindness repaid.

For the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is like empty space—vast and boundless, transcending both sight and hearing; the great ocean of wisdom is profound and limitless, defying thought and deliberation. This subtle and profound, mysterious principle is rarely found through names and words; its boundaries are vast and indistinct.
When one encounters the pure model [of the teachings], one cannot fathom its source.
Yet, because the capacities and responses of beings differ in ten thousand ways, they manifest forms and speech that fill the dharma-realm;
while the mind and its objects are of a single flavor, the subject and object vanish, returning to profound stillness.
Its essence and function are boundless and its perfect fusion is unfathomable; thus, the formless manifests as form, like the rising of the great sun from the eastern valley.
To manifest speech through silence is like the vast ocean pouring into a great abyss.

Therefore, beginning in the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmagarbha-dhātu*), he expounded the inexhaustible profound framework (*gāṅga*) to encompass those of superior attainment and guide them to ascend to the realm of the Buddha. Thereafter, his transformation spread throughout the Sahā world, gradually unfolding the clouds of compassion; he showered subtle moisture to nourish the three capacities and fostered the sprouts of the Way so that all might return to the single principle.
Thus we know that because the conditions of karmic resonance differ, the responses of the Sages vary accordingly;
yet though these responses differ, they are one in their inconceivability.

The Avataṃsaka Sūtra is the sublime discourse gathered from the ocean-like assembly and the ultimate teaching that illuminates the King of Mountains; its principle and wisdom are vast and far-reaching, exhausting the entire Dharma-realm and extending to the very source of truth.
The profound and subtle words are as vast as empty space, yet they pervade even the most minute lands.
Thus, there is no deficiency between the great and the small; the immense realms silently enter the tip of a single hair.
Without altering the scale of the vast or the fine, the ultimate infinitesimal is harmonized to encompass the entire Dharma-realm.

Thus, through the Indra-net of interreflecting shadows, the realms are layered upon one another; like lamps of crystal light, they shine faintly across the ten directions. The one is many without obstruction, and the many are one in perfect penetration. The nine periods of time are subsumed within a single kṣaṇa, and a single thought-moment is extended to encompass eternal kalpas. With the ultimate, firm seeds of the three births as the cause, and the manifestation of universal virtues through the perfected path of the ten stages as the fruit, the fruit is no different from the cause, branching out through the five positions to distinguish their paths;
the cause is no different from the fruit, unifying the ten bodies to reach the same destination.
Therefore, the Mother of Awakening attended to the capacities of beings in the Eastern City, clarifying her ten eyes through six thousand commentaries;
while the Youth inquired of his friends in the Southern Land, achieving the hundred-and-ten perfections within a single lifetime.
Thus, without even passing beyond the King of Trees, the six heavens were reached;
how could it be that the Flower Treasury was moved, for the ten lands were already empty and harmonious?
Within the midst of dust, he manifested the precious verses, their brilliance equaling that of the eight assemblies.
The King of Pearls is revealed within the inherent virtue, its seven aspects perfectly manifest.
Vast and resonant, it stands far beyond the reach of thought and deliberation;
lofty and brilliant, it transcends the sight and hearing of the deaf and blind.
Therefore, Samantabhadra first fashioned [this teaching] through the Ocean-Seal Samādhi, and it first arose at dawn on the second week;
Nāgārjuna finally surveyed it from the Palace of the Dragons, and it was only after six hundred years that it became manifest.

Now, "Great" (Mahā) takes inclusion as its meaning; "Square" (Pra) takes providing a model as its function. "Vast" (Viśva) signifies that the essence is ultimate and the functions are all-pervasive; "Buddha" refers to the perfection of the fruit and the fulfillment of enlightenment. "Flower" (Puṣpa) is a metaphor for the blossoming of the myriad practices; "Adornment" (Maṇḍa) is a metaphor for embellishing this fundamental essence. "Sūtra" (Sūtra) means to string together and stitch; it refers to the teaching capable of expressing [the truth] which is inscribed therein.
Taking the Dharma to illustrate the person through metaphor, it is called the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Pure Eye of the World": since the three types of vessels and so forth shine forth at the proper time, and their brilliant illumination is even more so for a pure eye, the Dharma and the metaphor are raised together; hence it is called the "Pure Eye of the World."
Language is unified in principle, and categories follow one another;

therefore, they are called "chapters" (*pin*). This sutra contains thirty-four chapters; as this chapter is established at the beginning, it is called the first. Thus, it is titled: *The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra, Chapter One: The World-Purifying Eye*.
The remaining meanings are as explained below. To expound this sutra, ten topical sections will be briefly opened:

first, clarifying the origins of the teaching's emergence; second, clarifying its inclusion within the Pitakas and schools; third, revealing the distinctions among the established teachings; fourth, distinguishing the capacities of the sentient beings for whom the teaching is intended; fifth, identifying the essence of the expressive teaching; sixth, clarifying the fundamental tenets and purport of what is expressed; seventh, providing a detailed commentary on the title of the sutra; eighth, clarifying its textual category and history of translation; ninth, distinguishing the scope of the text’s meaning; and tenth, explaining the text section by section.
Regarding the origins from which the initial teaching arose, there is first a general exposition followed by a specific clarification.

As for the general account: since the causes and conditions for the emergence of the Great Teaching are immeasurable, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* provides an extensive analysis of the causes and conditions for the arising of the Prajñā teachings at its very beginning.

Just as Mount Sumeru cannot be moved by the absence of cause or by minor conditions, so too is the Buddha: he speaks only on account of great causes and conditions, namely, so that the Prajñāpāramitā may circulate in the world and bring vast benefit to all classes of beings.

The *Lotus Sūtra* also states: "The Tathāgata appears in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition, namely, to open, show, awaken, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
This sutra further states: "The nature-arising of the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is inconceivable.
Why is this? It is not through minor causes and conditions that one attains Samyaksaṃbodhi and appears in the world."
Through ten kinds of immeasurable, innumerable, hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya causes and conditions, one attains equal and perfect enlightenment and appears in the world. What are these ten?
First, to give rise to the immeasurable mind of bodhi and not abandon any sentient being.
Thus it should be understood, as explained at length in such passages.
Next, to specifically clarify [the inexhaustibility], ten points are briefly presented to illustrate its endless nature. What are these ten?

That is to say: by way of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), by the power of vows, by the resonance of capacity, as the fundamental basis, for the purpose of manifesting virtues, for the purpose of manifesting stages, for the purpose of development, through seeing and hearing, for the purpose of accomplishing practice, and for the purpose of attaining the fruit.

Regarding the phrase "because it is the primordial nature of phenomena": it is the primordial nature of all Buddhas that they constantly turn this inexhaustible wheel of Dharma throughout all inexhaustible worlds; it is like the eternal rule of a great king’s highway, which proceeds without stopping or rest until the very end of the future.
Therefore, the subsequent "Inconceivable" chapter states: "The entire dharma-realm and worlds as vast as space are all measured exhaustively with the tip of a single hair."

Upon each and every tip of a hair, in every moment of thought, they manifest bodies as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, continuing thus until the end of all future kalpas.

Each and every transformed Buddha has as many heads as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields; each head has as many tongues as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields; from each tongue issue as many sounds as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields; each sound proclaims as many sūtras as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields; each sūtra explains as many dharmas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields; and within each dharma, there are explained as many word-bodies and flavor-bodies as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.

Furthermore, for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, he speaks diverse bodies of phrases and bodies of flavors, such that his voice fills the entire Dharma-realm, and there is not a single sentient being who does not hear it.
"Throughout all future kalpas, the Wheel of Dharma is constantly turned; the Tathāgata’s voice is without distinction, uninterrupted, and inexhaustible.
The commentary explains:

According to this scriptural passage, within the space of a single hair-tip and in the span of a single thought-moment, such karmic functions as described above are manifested; it is likewise so in every subsequent thought-moment.

Just as within the space of a single hair-tip there is such inexhaustible karmic activity from moment to moment, so too, throughout every other hair-tip, extending in succession across all worlds equal to the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm, each is likewise inexhaustible and inexhaustible.

This means that spatially, a single hair-tip encompasses the entire Dharma-realm; temporally, a single kṣaṇa exhausts an ocean of kalpas. This indicates that the activity of arising occurs instantaneously in this space, and that the activity of arising occurs eternally in this time; furthermore, this does not depend on causes and conditions, for such is the natural law of all Buddhas.
All that is explained in the subsequent sections of this sutra is likewise so.
Question:
If this is the case, why is it that the locations consist of only eight assemblies, while the times are restricted to two sets of seven?
Answer: The *Vairocana-parivarta* states: "Within each and every atom, oceans of Buddha-lands dwell in peace; clouds of Buddhas pervade and protect with mindfulness, encompassing and covering all."
It further states: "Within a single pore, there are immeasurable Buddha-fields, adorned and pure, dwelling in vast tranquility.
In every one of those places, Vairocana Buddha expounds the True Dharma amidst oceans of assemblies."
The commentary explains:
How much more so, then, could the eight assemblies not encompass the ten directions and the Dharma-realm?
Furthermore, the "Chapter on Arousing the Mind" states: "Know that immeasurable kalpas are but a single thought-moment, and a single thought-moment is itself immeasurable kalpas."
The commentary explains:
How much more so, then, at the time of the second seven-day period, does it not encompass oceans of immeasurable kalpas?

The "Inconceivable Chapter" states: "All Buddhas universally manifest all Buddha-lands of the three periods of time within a single atom; they universally manifest the sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas of the three periods of time within a single atom; they universally manifest all sentient beings of the three periods of time within a single atom; and they universally manifest the Buddha-deeds of all Buddhas of the three periods of time within a single atom."
The commentary explains:

Here, "the three periods within the realm of phenomena" comprehensively encompasses all kalpas of the past and future limits; this is because it is said that the dharmas of all Buddhas are thus always taught.
Regarding "secondly, by the power of vows": this means that by the power of the Tathāgata’s original vows, this teaching is manifested in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.

Therefore, the "Vairocana Chapter" states: "Within the lands of the ten directions, throughout all oceans of worlds, through the sovereign power of the Buddha’s vows, the wheel of Dharma is universally turned."
It further states: "By the spiritual power of Vairocana Buddha, the turning of the wheel of Dharma occurs within all lands; the vow-sounds of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva pervade all oceans of worlds."
The commentary explains:

This refers to those who, throughout the ten directions, within the void of the Dharma-realm, across all worlds and within every atom, simultaneously preach this sutra; all such instances are brought about by the power of the Original Teacher’s vows.
Therefore, at the beginning of each of the subsequent assemblies, it is stated: "By the power of the original vows of Vairocana Buddha.

Furthermore, a verse in the "Cloud Assembly Chapter" says: "Throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons, this Dharma is extremely difficult to encounter; should anyone hear it, know that it is through the power of the original vows."
The commentary explains:
This means that it is through the power of the Buddha’s vows that the assembly is enabled to hear [this teaching].
It further states: "Though the Tathāgata does not appear in the world, nor is there any parinirvāṇa, by the power of his original great vow, he manifests the sovereign Dharma."

Regarding "because of the resonance with the three types of capacities": the Tathāgata is impartial and undergoes no change; he manifests his body and preaches the Dharma in accordance with the needs of sentient beings.
This has three meanings:

first, taking the pure merits of the Buddha’s physical form and voice as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), he responds to their resonance to accomplish the gathering and transformation of beings.

The verse from the *Cloud Assembly* (*Meghasamudgata*) says: "Just as one with eyes and sunlight can see even the most subtle forms, so too, by virtue of the most supreme spiritual power, those with pure minds behold all Buddhas; this refers to the manifestation of their bodies."

Furthermore, the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" states: "The Buddha, through his practices in the past, attained a single, subtle, and wondrous voice; though he has no mind regarding self or other, he is able to respond to all and thus preach this Dharma."

"The two fruits of Buddhahood possess no coarse characteristics of form or sound; they manifest only through the power of the supreme vows of equalizing wisdom and reason, appearing in forms and speech in accordance with the resonance of sentient beings' capacities."

The verse from the *Cloud Assembly* (*Meghasamudgata*) says: "The Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are entirely pure; according to those who are to be transformed, they universally manifest wondrous form-bodies."
It is further said: "All Tathāgatas have no teaching of the Buddha-dharma; rather, they expound the Dharma according to those who are to be transformed.
This third point integrates the two preceding meanings of existence and non-existence without obstruction, because it accords with the unobstructed nature of the Dharma-realm.

The "Chapter on Śāntamati" states: "The Buddha-body pervades the entire Dharma-realm and manifests universally before all sentient beings; filling every vessel capable of being transformed, the Buddha therefore dwells here beneath this Bodhi tree."

Within as many pores as there are atoms in all Buddha-fields, Buddhas sit, each surrounded by immeasurable assemblies of Bodhisattvas, for whom they individually and fully expound the conduct of Samantabhadra.
The commentary explains:
This refers precisely to the scope described in this sutra.

Regarding the phrase "because the four are the basis," it means that since one intends to gradually bestow the derivative teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings, it is appropriate to first demonstrate the fundamental Dharma at the outset.

Because it is clear that the branches arise based on this root, for this reason, he first taught the Dharma of this sutra, and only thereafter did he gradually teach the secondary, branch-level teachings of the Hīnayāna and so forth at places such as the Deer Park.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" (*Xingqi pin*) states: "Just as when the sun rises, it first illuminates the high mountains," and so forth, as cited below in the section on the establishment of the teaching.
Fifth, regarding "because of manifesting virtues": this means to manifest the sublime virtues of the Buddha-fruit, causing all bodhisattvas to have faith in, incline toward, and realize them.
This is of two kinds:
first, the fruit of reliance, which refers to the Lotus Treasury Adorned World-Ocean;
second, the direct fruit, which refers to the ten bodies of the Tathāgata as they pervade the three worlds and so forth.
Both are as explained below.
These two types of non-obstruction consist of four propositions:
first, the manifestation based on the internal, such as the manifestation of oceans of lands within a single atom.
Second, the manifestation of the primary within the internal; for example, Buddhas manifesting from within pores.
Third, the manifestation of the basis within the internal; for example, lands manifesting from within pores.
Fourth, the manifestation of the primary within the basis; for example, Buddhas manifesting within a single atom.
Therefore, by citing any single gateway, all [teachings] are subsumed without exception, as will be explained below.
It is for the purpose of manifesting these fruits of merit that this sutra is preached.

Regarding "the sixth, because it reveals the stages": this is to reveal that the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the causes of Buddhahood proceeds from the single path to the fruit through five distinct stages.
This also has two aspects:

first, the sequential and distributed gate (*krama-vyūha-mukha*), which refers to the ten faiths, ten understandings, ten practices, ten dedications, and the ten stages; only after these are completed does one reach the Buddha-stage, proceeding through a gradual succession of levels from the subtle to the manifest.

Second is the gate of mutual inclusion through perfect interfusion: this means that within a single stage, all preceding and succeeding stages are subsumed; therefore, each and every stage, when fulfilled, reaches the stage of Buddhahood.
These two [powers] are unimpeded, as explained extensively in the various assemblies of the subsequent chapters.

Regarding "the seventh, because it brings forth": this is for the purpose of bringing forth the Tathāgata-garbha-nature and its arising merits within the minds of sentient beings, so that all Bodhisattvas may rely upon this to practice and learn, thereby breaking the shell of ignorance to manifest the virtues of their nature.
This also has two aspects:
first, to manifest it through verbal expression so that one may know it exists;
second, to instruct in its practice so that it may be made manifest.
This is as explained in detail in the following passages, such as "Breaking the Microdust to Reveal the Sutra Scroll.

Regarding the eighth point, "because of seeing and hearing," this demonstrates that while this inexhaustible and sovereign Dharma-gate is the domain solely of Bodhisattvas at the ultimate stage, it causes sentient beings of lower stages to likewise see and hear it, so that they may attain the indestructible and inexhaustible seeds of the Vajra, ensuring they shall eventually reach the ultimate stage.
It is also as explained in the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature.
Regarding the phrase "because it brings about the fulfillment of practice," this means that by manifesting this universal Dharma, it causes all bodhisattvas to fulfill the practices of Samantabhadra.
"A single practice is all practices; at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta, one attains perfect enlightenment, fully endowed with the body of wisdom, realized not through another.
It further states: "If a bodhisattva upholds this Dharma, they will achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* swiftly by employing only slight skillful means," and so forth.
This also has two types:
first, the instantaneous accomplishment of multiple practices; second, the universal accomplishment of all practices, both of which are explained below.
Regarding "because of attaining the ten fruits": it means causing one to attain the fruit of wisdom and the abandonment of afflictions at the stage of Buddhahood.
There are also two kinds:

first, the fruit of abandonment, which refers to the removal of hindrances. This is illustrated in the "Universal Good Chapter" (Samantabhadra-parivarta), where one hindrance is shown to be all hindrances, and in the "Minor Marks Chapter" (Lakṣaṇānuvyañjana-parivarta), where one abandonment is shown to be the abandonment of all; these are explained in detail as stated below.

The second is the fruit of wisdom, which refers to the perfection of virtues; thus, one is fully endowed with the ten bodies, attaining mastery over the three worlds in both their adverse and favorable aspects, and achieving non-obstruction between the environment and its inhabitants, as described in the "Inconceivable" chapter and elsewhere.
The above has been a brief exposition based on these ten points to demonstrate how this scriptural teaching arose.
Second, regarding the clarification of the inclusion [of the teachings] within the Piṭakas (Tripiṭaka), ten points are briefly presented to explain this subsumption:

first, clarifying the three Piṭakas; second, revealing what is included; third, distinguishing the two Piṭakas; fourth, resolving contradictions; fifth, opening up the categories; sixth, determining what is included; seventh, inclusion within one section; eighth, inclusion within three sections; ninth, the ninefold division; and tenth, the complete twelvefold division.

First, regarding the explanation of the Three Piṭakas: the first is called Sūtra, or alternatively Sūtranta, or Sūtra; this is translated as "Sūtra" (Kie-king). The term "Sūtra" (Kie) has two meanings:
it accords with the principle (dharma), and it accords with the capacity of the audience (yoga).
The Sūtra also has two meanings: namely, because it penetrates the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and because it sustains those to be converted.
Regarding "penetration," Vasubandhu’s commentary states:
it is called *sūtra* because it is able to penetrate the basis (*āśraya*), the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the phenomena (*dharma*), and the meaning (*artha*).
That is to say, the locus wherein something is spoken of for this purpose and by means of this is called the "basis" (*āśraya*).
The characteristics of the ultimate and conventional truths are called the "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*).
The ten types of skillful dharmas and so forth are called the "dharmas" (*dharma*).
To explain all phenomena according to their underlying intention (*samdhāya*) and so forth is termed "meaning" (*artha*).
Furthermore, Asvabhāva explains it as "piercing through" or "sewing together.
The commentary states:
"Piercing through" (*pratisaṃdhi*) has the sense of "entering," while "sewing together" (*saṃdhāna*) has the sense of "harmonizing.

This means that by piercing through the principles with the words of the Noble Ones, one prevents them from being lost or obscured; by sewing them together and joining them, one brings about their expression and ensures they endure for a long time.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because it can penetrate and encompass, it is called a sūtra (*sūtra*).
Since the Buddha’s holy teaching penetrates and sustains both the meanings that ought to be explained and the sentient beings who are to be converted, it is termed a 'Discourse' (*sūtra*)."
“A sūtra that accords with the principle is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound;
‘sūtra’ as ‘scriptural collection’ is explained by the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Furthermore, there are five meanings [of sūtra] in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*:
First, the spring; second, the source; third, the manifestation; fourth, the measuring line; fifth, the garland.
The direct translation of the term is "thread" (*sūtra*); for what reason is it called "scripture" (*jing*)?
This means that just as thread can string together flowers and warp-thread can support the weft, their functional significance is similar.

However, because this region values the name "sūtra" (warp) and does not prize the term for "thread," the translation follows what is valued here: the term for "thread" is discarded and "sūtra" is retained, establishing the name based on the analogy.
The second is *vinaya*, here translated as "discipline" (*tiaofu*).

"Discipline" (*tiao*) means to harmonize and guide; "discipline" (*fu*) means to restrain and extinguish. This refers to harmonizing and controlling the karmas of body and speech, thereby restraining and eliminating all unwholesome conduct.
This is the practice that is expressed, namely, the treasury of discipline (*vinaya*).
Alternatively, it may be translated as "extinction" (*nirodha*); extinction has three meanings:
first, the extinction of unwholesome karma; second, the extinction of afflictions (*kleśa*); and third, the attainment of the fruit of extinction.
Some call it *śīla*, which means "coolness. The transgressions of the three karmas are like a blazing fire; because the precepts can extinguish them, it is called "coolness.
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is termed "natural goodness," or "keeping one's word," because one is truly able to maintain what was previously received.

Some say it is *prātimokṣa*, which here means "conducive to liberation" (*anuloma-vimukti*); because one attains liberation by following [the path] through the observance of the precepts, it is also called "individual liberation" (*prātimokṣa*).
The three are the Abhidharma Piṭaka. *Dharma* means "phenomenon" (*dharma*). *Abhi* has seven meanings;
one is "counter-phenomenon" (*abhidharma*), which has two senses:
first, it is "confronting," meaning that through wisdom one proceeds toward the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
The second is "confronting observation" (*pratimukha-samādhi*), which refers to the observation of the fruit-intelligence (*phala-jñāna*) that realizes the extinction of *nirvāṇa*.
Although causal intelligence (*hetu-jñāna*) also possesses confronting observation, it is termed merely "facing toward" because it involves looking upward in progressive cultivation.

Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "This Dharma is directed toward non-abiding nirvāṇa, for it can expound the various sublime gateways such as the truths and the factors of enlightenment."
This is explained in terms of causal knowledge (*hetu-jñāna*), and it refers exclusively to that which is signified (*abhidheya*).

Second is the category of "enumerated phenomena" (*saṃkhyeya-dharma*). The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya) translated during the Liang dynasty explains: "Among all phenomena, a single phenomenon is repeatedly manifested—whether by its name-characteristic (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or its general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)—and is thus called an 'enumerated phenomenon'."

Regarding the third name, "Subduer of Doctrines" (*vādavin), that treatise states: "This doctrine can subdue all [opposing] teachings through the dual capacities of establishing and refuting, by means of skillful methods such as correct exposition and reliance; therefore, it is called 'subduing'."
The fourth is called "penetrating the Dharma" (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), because it is able to penetrate and explain the meaning of the sūtras.

The sūtras are referred to as "Dharma," and since this [Abhidharma] can penetrate them, it is the penetration of the Dharma; the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (She lun) calls this "understanding the Dharma," because through Abhidharma, the meaning of the Sūtra becomes easy to understand.

The fifth is called the incomparable dharma (*anupama-dharma*), the sixth is called the great dharma (*mahā-dharma*), and the seventh is called the analytical dharma (*pravicaya-dharma*); these three refer exclusively to that which is expressed.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Alternatively, the sūtra is called *dharma*, while the treatise, which is capable of definitive discernment, is called *abhidharma*."
This refers to matching teaching with teaching, as in the aforementioned general dharma.
Alternatively, it is called *mātṛkā*, which means "matrix" (*benmu*); it is so named because the teachings and their meanings serve as its basis and source.
It is also called "Discriminative Liberation" (*vibhaṅga-vimukti*).
Alternatively, it is called *upadeśa*, which means "Exegesis" (*lunyi*); in the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, it is termed "Explanation.

These three aforementioned types—Sūtra and so forth—all encompass the meanings and principles that are expounded and from which they arise; thus, they are collectively designated as "Pitakas" (*piṭaka*).
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, chapter four, states: "Why are those three and these two called 'pits' (*pitaka*)?
Answer: Because they include; that is to say, they include all objects of knowledge."
"The first two Piṭakas [the Sūtra and Vinaya] are designated by both *karmadhāraya* (appositional) and *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds;
the latter two Piṭakas [the Abhidharma and Śāstra] are designated solely by *tatpuruṣa* compounds, because their names are derived from what they express (*abhidheya*).
Regarding other matters such as the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the various classifications, these are explained extensively elsewhere."
Second, regarding the manifestation of what is subsumed: under which collection (*piṭaka*) is this sūtra subsumed?
It is subsumed either solely under the Sūtra collection, because it is not the other two;
or it is subsumed under two collections, because its definitive analytical meaning is included within the Abhidharma.
Alternatively, it may be subsumed under the three categories, as the subsequent text also reveals various modes of ethical conduct (*śīla-caryā*).
This is explained according to the *tongjiao* (common teaching).

Alternatively, it may be subsumed under the ten treasuries (*daśa-kośa*) mentioned in the subsequent text, because the principal and its associates are fully present, thereby manifesting inexhaustibility.
This is based on the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao).
Question:
The Three Baskets (San-zang) are established according to the teachings, while the Ten Baskets (Shi-zang) are defined by their meanings; how can one say that meanings encompass the teachings?
Answer: In the case of the Hīnayāna, neither the teachings nor the meanings are integrated;
in the case of the Triyāna, the meanings are integrated but the teachings are not.
In the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), both teaching and meaning are integrated; therefore, it is able to encompass [all].
For instance, such things as the inclusion within the teaching of the non-conceptual contemplation of the *yathābhūta-vākya* already exist within the Three Vehicles, let alone in the One Vehicle.
However, that which merely indicates and represents belongs to the category of the Teaching (*śāsana*); this can be seen by reflecting upon it.
Third, regarding the distinction between the two Piṭakas: these are the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
First, the Tripitaka Teaching is established based on the small faculties of the śrāvakas; it elucidates the principles, practices, and fruits of the śrāvakas, and is thus called the Śrāvaka Piṭaka.

Second, the Tripitaka Teaching is established based on the great faculties of the bodhisattvas; it elucidates the dharmas practiced by bodhisattvas and so forth, and is thus called the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.

The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Treatise on Ornamentation), chapter four, states: "These three baskets, due to the distinction between the higher and lower vehicles, are further described as the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka."
Regarding the fourth point, the resolution of contradictions:
Question—The sūtras also state, "For those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha, one teaches the twelve links of dependent origination. Why, then, is this not called the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka?
Answer:

Because Pratyekabuddhas likewise only sever the grasping at a self and only realize the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā), their attainment of the fruit of Arhatship and entry into nirvāṇa are no different; when compared with Bodhisattvas, they both belong to the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna), and therefore they are not mentioned separately.
Question:
Since all [three vehicles] are equally inferior, why is only this one called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka? Answer:
Because Pratyekabuddhas also appear in worlds where no Buddha exists and thus lack an instructor,
whereas Śrāvakas are not like this, they alone receive this specific designation.
Question:
Question: Since the teachings of the Hīnayāna also contain explanations of the Bodhisattva vehicle, why are they not also called the "Bodhisattva Piṭaka"? Answer:
Because in those schools, the bodhisattvas' objects of abandonment, their realizations, and the nirvāṇa they enter are no different from those of the two vehicles.
Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva is unique and not manifold, it is also not mentioned.
Question:

If this is so, why do the *Samantābhibhū-samādhi-sūtra*, in its "Three Collections" chapter, and the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* state that those three vehicles constitute the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka)?
First, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; second, the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka; third, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Answer:
In those sūtras and śāstras, it is stated that these three piṭakas exist within the Mahāyāna; therefore, they do not refer to the Hīnayāna.
Question: Based on this very text, how should one reconcile the statement that pratyekabuddhas possess a *garbha* with the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*? Answer:

The former is based on the principle that the fruit is not different [from the Buddha], and thus they are combined; the latter is based on the fact that there are slight differences in their teaching and practice, and thus they are distinguished. Therefore, these two explanations do not contradict one another.
Fifth, regarding the classification by way of types: within the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, according to various sūtras and śāstras, it is further divided into three types:

first, the Controversial Śrāvaka-piṭaka. This refers to the four Āgamas of the Sūtra-piṭaka, the five sections of the Vinaya-piṭaka, and the twenty treatises of the Abhidharma-piṭaka. Because these texts contradict one another and their expositions differ, yet do not obstruct the attainment of the fruits of sainthood, they are collectively termed the "Controversial Piṭaka."

Second is the Collection of Śrāvakas that Accords with Reality (*yathārtha-śrāvaka-piṭaka*). This refers to works such as the "Śrāvaka-bhūmi" and the "Śrāvaka-viniścaya" of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, which elucidate the practices, stages, and fruits of the śrāvakas; these all accord with reality and correspond to reason. They differ from the *Mahāvibhāṣā* and various heterodox treatises, because what is taught by one who is to become a Buddha cannot be contested by heterodox doctrines. Therefore, they are collectively termed the Collection of Śrāvakas that Accords with Reality.
Question:
Since what is explained here differs from the various schools of the Hīnayāna, are there then two kinds of śrāvakas?
Answer:

In this context of the teaching, the Śrāvaka Dharma is divided into two because while the teaching is exhausted, the principle is not; it does not mean that there are internal distinctions among the Śrāvakas themselves.

Third, the provisional establishment of the Śrāvaka Piṭaka: as in the Mahāyāna sūtras, for the purpose of attracting Śrāvakas to turn their minds [toward the Great Vehicle], the established dharma-gates are taught using terminology identical to that of the Śrāvakas, such as the four noble truths of non-action (anabhisaṃskāra) and the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).
As it is taught in various Mahāyāna sūtras, I shall not cite them here at length.
Since these are not the studies of bodhisattvas, they are therefore designated as the "provisionally established Śrāvaka Piṭaka."
Question:
Although the names used here are the same as those in the Hīnayāna, their meaning is actually that of the Mahāyāna; how can they be collectively referred to as the Śrāvaka Piṭaka? Answer:
It is solely for this reason that it is termed a "provisional establishment" (prajñapti).
Question:

Since the training of those śrāvakas who have matured faculties and turned their minds [toward enlightenment] is subsumed within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, what is the use of this provisionally established piṭaka in relation to them?
Answer: There are two types of Śrāvakas who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]: the superior and the inferior.
The superior ones enter the Great Vehicle directly and do not rely on this treasury (the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*).

Those of inferior capacity are still fearful of the vast; therefore, as a skillful means, he employs the same terminology and enumerations as they are accustomed to, so that they may easily believe and accept it—this is why this gateway was established.
Within the second category, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, there are likewise three types according to various sacred teachings:

first, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka within the Hīnayāna, which explains how a bodhisattva attains buddhahood through the sequential stages of thirty-four mental states and so forth, yet does not discuss the ten bhūmi stages or positions, and remains distinct from the śrāvakas and others.

As explained in the *Mahāvibhāṣā* and the *Abhidharmakośa*, within the second category—the Bodhisattvapiṭaka among the shared teachings of the Mahāyāna—it elucidates the sequential stages of the bodhisattva’s practice. Although it speaks of differences between those who "turn their minds" (*cittavivartana*) and those who "proceed directly," both rely upon the gradual progression through the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) to reach the fruit of Buddhahood, as taught in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and various other Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras.

Within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka of the Three Unshared Teachings, it is elucidated that the five stages of the bodhisattva’s reliance upon the practices of Samantabhadra are perfectly integrated. This means that one stage is all stages, and one practice is all practices; they are perfectly consummate within the Dharma-realm, unimpeded and sovereign, with beginning and end being equal throughout. When each individual stage is fulfilled, the ten Buddhas are realized with their complete retinues of principal and attendant figures.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are two kinds of Prajñāpāramitā:
the first is the shared [Prajñāpāramitā], which refers to this *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and other Vaipulya sūtras that are taught in common with the śrāvakas."
"Second is the uncommon [teaching], namely the *Acintya-sūtra*, because it is not taught in common with the śrāvakas.
The commentary explains:

"Among these, the 'small' that is shared with the 'great' does not refer to those of dull faculties; the 'great' that is shared with the 'small' does not refer to the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddha). Therefore, there are three Bodhisattva-piṭakas."
Question:
Since the two collections (piṭaka) of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas are distinct, those two types of persons each attain their respective fruits separately.
Now that the Bodhisattva collection is divided into three stages, should it not follow that these three types of Bodhisattvas each become Buddhas individually?

Answer: Buddhahood is but one; however, because the capacities of sentient beings vary in depth, the teachings speak of three types. This does not mean that the essence of Buddhahood actually consists of three.
What is presented here follows the distinctions made within the teachings, rather than being based on the actual nature of the Buddha-body.
Question:
If all three explanations accord with reason, then the essence of the Buddha would also become threefold;
if the principle of attaining Buddhahood is one, then two of the explanations must be false.
Answer: Regarding the attainment of Buddhahood by a single individual, there are generally three meanings.
First, from the perspective of the fundamental following the derivative, as taught in the Hīnayāna, because [the Buddha] is identical to the śrāvakas.

Second is the gate of the beginning being distinct while the end is identical, as taught in the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), because it distinguishes [the Mahāyāna] in contrast to the Śrāvakas.

Third is the gate of the end being exhausted and only the beginning remaining, as taught in the Unshared Teaching (*asādhāraṇa-yāna*), because the followers of the Two Vehicles are like the deaf and blind, having no one to contrast with them.

The Buddha-body is perfectly interfused and fully possesses these three meanings; therefore, while the three explanations differ from one another, the Buddha himself is not manifold. For this reason, there are these three categories within the present Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

Regarding its inclusion within the sixth dhyāna and its classification among the scriptural collections (piṭaka): it is not included in the first three Śrāvaka-piṭakas; rather, among the latter three Bodhisattva-piṭakas, it is correctly included only in the last one, because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* specifically identifies this sūtra as being "unshared" (asādhāraṇa).
Alternatively, among the three categories, one excludes only the first and includes both of the latter two, because this sutra contains both the universal and the specific.
Or, it may also be subsumed under the provisionally established Śrāvaka Piṭaka, since the sutra also elucidates the Four Noble Truths and so forth.

Alternatively, they may be understood as collectively encompassing both Piṭakas, because the teachings of the Śrāvaka Piṭaka likewise flow from the Dharma-dhātu of the One Vehicle, and thus their flavor is not distinct.

Regarding the seventh category, within the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it is comprised solely of the Vaipulya division; for the Abhidharma treatises state that it is the basis for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, and because it proclaims the vast and profound Dharma, it is called Vaipulya.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the Śrāvaka-piṭaka does not contain the Vaipulya [class], or because the title of this scripture has already made it manifest.
As for the eighth triad of categories, these are the Vyākaraṇa (Prophecies), the Udāna (Inspired Utterances), and the Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings).
Because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that the other nine divisions are of the Hīnayāna, this sūtra is not among them; therefore, it is subsumed solely within the [remaining] three.

As for the ninth division being subsumed within the ninefold classification, this refers to excluding the *nidāna*, *avadāna*, and *upadeśa*, because the third chapter of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states that those who protect the Mahāyāna uphold the nine divisions while excluding the first three.

Regarding the tenth [category], which possesses twelve [aspects]: the first is subsumed under the *sūtra*, because the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that everything from "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) up to "so it was practiced" (*tathānuṣṭhitam*) constitutes a *sūtra*.
Second is *geya* (verses in response), because the subsequent text contains repeated verses (*geya*).
Third is *vyākaraṇa* (prophecy), because the subsequent text contains prophecies regarding the attainment of Buddhahood and so forth.
Fourth is *gāthā* (stanzas), because the subsequent text contains direct prose followed by verses and the like.
Fifth, the self-explanations (*udāna*), such as when [the Buddha] emerges from meditative concentration and immediately speaks the "Fundamental Section" (*mūla-bhāga*) and so forth.
Sixth, the dependent originations (*nidāna*), such as when [the Buddha] speaks in response to a request, as in the following text.
Seventh, the parables (*avadāna*), such as when the parables are explained at length, as in the following text.
Eighth, the *Vastu* (Basis of Past Events), as explained below, because it concerns the fundamental events experienced by Vairocana and others, as well as Samantabhadra, in their past lives.
Ninth, the *Jātaka* (Birth Stories), as explained below, because it describes the characteristics of the previous births of Vairocana and others.
The vastness of the ten directions can be understood through a single gateway.

As for the eleven rare phenomena, they are as described in the subsequent text, such as the preaching of the Dharma from a pore, the emergence of various jeweled pillars from a seat, and the manifestation of Buddhas, and so forth.

Regarding the twelve types of doctrinal treatises (*mātṛkā*), as explained in the eighty-first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, they refer to the systematic investigation and analysis of various sūtras.

All sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) are termed *mātṛkā*, because in these instances the Blessed One himself extensively analyzes the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), as is explained in the "Chapter on Clarifying Difficulties" (*Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*) and elsewhere in the text.
Therefore, this sutra is fully comprised within the twelve divisions [of the canon].
Other meanings will be explained below in the section on the twelve divisions of the scriptures. The classification according to the Piṭakas and divisions is concluded.
Third, regarding the clarification of the distinctions in the establishment of the teachings, there are briefly ten categories:

first, recounting ancient expositions; second, distinguishing right from wrong; third, describing the traditions of the Western Regions; fourth, reconciling contradictions; fifth, clarifying what is currently transmitted; sixth, determining the provisional and the ultimate; seventh, revealing the expansions and contractions [of the teachings]; eighth, the chronological sequence of the teachings; ninth, classifying the teachings according to their meaning; and tenth, opening up the schools through principle.

Regarding the beginning and middle [of this treatise], the various virtuous masters of antiquity have established numerous systems of teaching that are difficult to fully manifest; I shall briefly describe ten schools to serve as a mirror for reflection.

First, Bodhiruci of the Later Wei established the doctrine of the "Single-Sound Teaching" (*ekasvara-dharma*), asserting that all sacred teachings are solely the Tathāgata’s single, perfect sound-teaching (*ekasvara-saṃbhoga-dharma*). It is only because of the differences in the faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings that it is divided into various types, as in the sūtra passage concerning "the moisture of a single rain," and so forth.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind," and so forth.

Second, during the Chen dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha and others established the two teachings of Gradual and Sudden. They maintained that for those with the capacity for gradual enlightenment, the Great [Vehicle] arises from the Small; because the teachings provided therein fully encompass the Three Vehicles, they are called "Gradual," such as the *Nirvāṇa* and other sutras.

If one considers those of direct and sudden capacity, the Great Vehicle does not proceed by way of the Small; the teaching provided is exclusively that of the Bodhisattva Vehicle, and is therefore termed "Sudden," namely the *Avataṃsaka* and other such sutras.
Later, Dharma Master Daoyuan and others also maintained this same view.

Thirdly, during the Later Wei dynasty, Vinaya Master Guangtong, following the teachings of Buddhayaśas and Paramārtha, established three types of teaching: namely, the gradual, the sudden, and the perfect.
Master Guang’s interpretation of the meaning is as follows:

first, for those whose faculties are not yet mature, one first teaches impermanence and subsequently teaches permanence, or first teaches emptiness and subsequently teaches non-emptiness; such gradual progression is termed the "Gradual Teaching."

The second is for those whose faculties are matured; for them, all Buddha-dharmas are fully expounded within a single Dharma-gate—namely, the constant and the impermanent, the empty and the non-empty, and so forth—all are explained together without further recourse to gradual stages; therefore, it is called "sudden."

Third, for those who have reached the higher stages and are approaching the realm of the Buddha, he expounds the secret, sovereign dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s ultimate fruit-virtue of unimpeded liberation; therefore, it is called "Perfect" (Yuan).
Thus, this sutra is subsumed under the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun) teachings.
Later, masters such as Zhuntong of the Guangtong lineage also followed and upheld this tradition, agreeing with this interpretation.
Fourth, during the Qi dynasty, Master Dayan and others established the fourfold system of religious teachings (sijiao):
First is the school of substantial causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-vāda*), which refers to the Sarvāstivāda and other such Hīnayāna sects.
Second is the school of provisional names (*prajñapti-saṃjñā-vāda*), which refers to the teachings of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) and the Sautrāntika school.
Third is the non-true school (*asatya-yāna*), referring to the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, which teach the principle of emptiness and clarify that all phenomena are not real, and so forth.

Fourth is the true school (*satya-yāna*), referring to the *Avataṃsaka* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras, because they elucidate the true principle of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).

The Five Protectors of the Dharma and others established five religious schools. That is to say, within the aforementioned fourth school, they opened up the true Buddha-nature to constitute the True School (*zhēn zōng*), which refers to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other such scriptures;
the fifth is named the Dharma-realm School (*fǎjiè zōng*), referring to the *Avataṃsaka*, which elucidates the dharma-gate of the sovereign and unimpeded nature of the Dharma-realm.
Sixth, the masters Chan Master Si of Nan Yue and Chan Master Zhi-zhe of the Chen dynasty established the Fourfold Teaching (*caturvidha-śāsana*):
first, the Tripitaka Teaching, also called the Hīnayāna Teaching, as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "One must not associate with those who study the Tripitaka of the Hīnayāna."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Hīnayāna is called the Tripiṭaka, while the Mahāyāna is termed the Mahāyāna-piṭaka.

Both are known as the "Shared Teaching" (*sāmānya-dharma*) and also as the "Gradual Teaching" (*anupūrva-dharma*), meaning that within the Mahāyāna sūtras, the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are taught in common and are intended for practitioners of all three capacities (*indriya*).
Furthermore, it is as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, where the ten stages such as Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) are common to the three vehicles;

this is the third [category], called the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), also known as the Sudden Teaching (*dunjiao*). This refers to the principles of the Dharma gates taught in various Mahāyāna sūtras that do not apply to the Hīnayāna and other [lower vehicles].

The fourth is called the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), also known as the Esoteric Teaching (Mimijiao). This refers to the unimpeded dharma-gate in which the Dharma-realm is sovereign, complete, and perfect, such that the one is all and the all is one; it is also exemplified by the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other such texts.
Seventh, during the Tang Dynasty, the Dharma Master Wonhyo of Silla in the Land of the Eastern Sea composed a commentary on this sūtra, in which he also established four teachings:
first, the distinct teaching of the Three Vehicles, such as the teaching of the Four Noble Truths, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, and others.
Second, the teachings common to the three vehicles, such as the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*.
Third, the teachings specific to the one vehicle, such as the *Śrīgarbha Sūtra* and the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
Fourth is the teaching of the fulfillment of the One Vehicle, namely the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the teachings of Samantabhadra.
The detailed explanations of these four are as found in their respective commentaries.
Eighth, the Dharma Master Jizang of the Tang established three types of teachings as the Three Wheels of the Dharma:
First is the fundamental wheel of Dharma, namely the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which was taught at the very beginning.
Second is the secondary and derivative wheel of Dharma, namely the Hīnayāna and other teachings, which were taught subsequently.

The third is the Dharma-wheel that subsumes the branches back into the root, namely the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which was taught forty years later as the teaching that returns the three vehicles into the one vehicle.
A detailed explanation is provided therein.

During the Liang dynasty, Master Yun of Guangzhai Monastery established the doctrine of the four vehicles (*catuṣ-yāna*). He maintained that, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the three carts provided at the gate constitute the three vehicles, while the great white ox-cart bestowed upon the child at the crossroads constitutes the fourth vehicle; this is because the cart at the gate is identical to the sheep and deer carts in that neither can actually be obtained.

If it were not so, then when the elder led his sons out from within the house, he would have said, "These three vehicles are already outside the gate," and the sons should have obtained the vehicles immediately upon leaving the house.
How could it be that after emerging, one reaches the place where the chariot originally pointed out and yet, not finding it there, seeks it again later?
Therefore, we know that this is a provisional [expedient] identical to those of the sheep and the deer.
This is because it is taught through the provisional methods of the skillful means within the Mahāyāna;
a detailed explanation may be found in the *Fahua Shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).
Tenth, the Dharma Master Yin and the Dharma Master Min of Jiangnan during the Tang dynasty established two teachings:

First, the Sūtras of Śākyamuni are called the "Teachings of Adaptation," because they follow the capacities and dispositions of beings to break their attachments according to their conceptual reckonings, such as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and others.

Second, the Sūtras of Vairocana are called the "Teachings of Equality," because they are taught with sovereign freedom according to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and others.
That master explains these two teachings as having four brief distinctions:
first, a difference in the principal [teacher], meaning that the former was spoken by the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) of Śākyamuni, while this was spoken by the ten bodies of Vairocana.

Second, the difference in location: that [text] states he was on a seat of wood, trees, and grass in the Sahā world, while this [text] states he was on a golden seat beneath jeweled trees in the Lotus Treasury World.
Third, there is a difference in the assembly: that [teaching] was spoken for śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, whereas this is spoken exclusively for bodhisattvas at the ultimate stage.
Fourth, there is a difference in the mode of exposition: that is merely taught in one direction, while this is necessarily taught universally throughout the ten directions.
An extensive explanation may be found in the aforementioned *Huayan Shu*.

Second, regarding the discernment of right and wrong: these ten masters who established the teachings were all Dharma generals of their time, possessing peerless brilliance and insight, such as Master Zhiyi and Master Zhiyan. Their spiritual wonders and responsive communications reached the highest levels; having heard the Dharma on Vulture Peak, they remain present in our memory today.

Dharma Master Yun followed this principle to establish his school and lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, moving the heavens to rain down flowers and other such wonders, all as revealed in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).

Furthermore, how could these virtuous masters have divided the holy teachings out of a desire for eccentricity? It was simply because their understanding encompassed the myriad scriptures and they presented different approaches according to the capacities of their listeners; constrained by the necessity of expression, they established distinct schools and provided separate exegeses, striving to ensure that each of the Buddha’s teachings accorded with what was appropriate for its audience.
Question:
Among these ten preceding statements, which is correct and which is incorrect? Answer:

According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the Buddha spoke the words "internal," "external," and "intermediate," and immediately entered meditative concentration; at that time, five hundred arhats each offered their own interpretation of these words.
After the Buddha emerged from meditative absorption, they all asked the World-Honored One,
"Who has grasped the Buddha's intention?
The Buddha said:
"It was not my intention.
The people asked the Buddha,
"If it was not in accordance with the Buddha's intention, will we not incur an offense?"
The Buddha said:
"Although these are not my own views, each accords with correct principle and is fit to serve as sacred teaching;
they bring merit and are free from fault. Moreover, since each of these various explanations has some measure of sacred teaching as its evidence, they must not be entirely rejected or discarded."
Third, regarding the accounts from the Western Regions: the three wheels of Paramārtha, the four teachings of Jñānagupta, and the five expositions of Amoghavajra are all as explained elsewhere.

Furthermore, in the first year of the Wénmíng era, Fǎzàng was fortunate enough to meet the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra from Central India—whose name means "Sunshine" (Rìzhào) in the language of Táng—at the Tàiyuán Monastery west of the capital, where he was translating sūtras and śāstras.
At that time, I personally asked:
"Regarding the holy teachings of a single lifetime, have the virtuous masters of the Western Regions made any discernment between the provisional and the ultimate?
The Tripitaka Master replied:
"In the Nālandā Monastery of India during the recent era, there were two great virtuous masters of debate at the same time:

one named Śīlabhadra and the other known as Jñānaprabha. Both possessed spiritual insights that transcended their peers and enjoyed high renown throughout the Five Indias; the various heterodoxies bowed their heads in submission and the different schools returned to them with sincerity. Students of the Mahāyāna looked up to them as they do to the sun and moon; they were each the sole peerless figure in all of India."

Because the lineages they inherited differed, their established teachings were distinct. Specifically, Śīlabhadra directly inherited from Maitreya and Asaṅga and followed closely upon Dharmapāla and Nanda; relying on sūtras such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi*, he established three types of teaching. He held that when the Buddha first preached the Hīnayāna at the Deer Park, although he spoke of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), he had not yet taught the ultimate truth of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); therefore, these were not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), referring specifically to the four *Āgamas* and similar sūtras.

During the second period, although the emptiness of all phenomena was taught in reliance upon the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the principle of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) had not yet been explained; therefore, these teachings—namely those of the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and others—are also not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

In the third period, the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) was established by fully explaining the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the three absences of nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*), and the two truths of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) in accordance with the correct principles of the Mahāyāna; these include such sūtras as the *Saṃdhinirmocana*.
Furthermore, each of these three stages is explained by means of three meanings:
first, gathering sentient beings; second, teaching the doctrine; and third, revealing the principle.
Now, the first stage gathers only śrāvakas, teaches only the Hīnayāna, and reveals only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
The second exclusively gathers bodhisattvas, teaches only the Mahāyāna, and reveals only the two kinds of emptiness.
The third universally gathers all capacities, explains all vehicles, and fully reveals both emptiness and existence.
Therefore, the first two [teachings] each lack something in their respective capacities to gather sentient beings (*sattva*), their doctrines (*dharma*), and their principles (*naya*);

thus, they are not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). The latter one, however, leaves no capacity unengaged, no doctrine incomplete, and no principle imperfect; therefore, it is of definitive meaning.

"The second, Master Jñānaprabha, inherited the lineage distantly from Mañjuśrī and Nāgārjuna, and more recently from Āryadeva and Bhāviveka; relying upon sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and treatises such as the *Madhyamaka*, he also established three teachings. He maintained that when the Buddha was first at the Deer Park, he taught the Hīnayāna for those of inferior faculties, clarifying that both mind and objects exist."

During the second period, for those of middling faculties, he taught the Dharma-characteristics Mahāyāna, clarifying the principle that objects are empty while the mind exists as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). Because their faculties were still inferior, he was unable to lead them into the equality of true emptiness; therefore, he made such a statement.

In the third period, for those of superior faculties, he taught the signless Mahāyāna, elucidating that both mind and objects are empty, equal, and of a single flavor; this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Furthermore, these three periods may also be explained through three meanings.
First, regarding the gathering of those with the capacity (*yogyatā*): during the first period, he gathered only those with the capacity of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

The second [classification] encompasses both the Great and Small Vehicles, as this school maintains that one portion of the followers of the Two Vehicles does not proceed toward the fruit of Buddhahood.

The third [classification] encompasses only Bodhisattvas, including both gradual and sudden approaches, because all followers of the Two Vehicles ultimately proceed toward the fruit of Buddhahood, as there is no alternative path.
Second, regarding the classification by teaching: first, only the Hīnayāna is taught; second, all three vehicles are taught; and finally, only the One Vehicle is taught.

Third, regarding the revelation of principles: because the first [period] refutes the *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) and so forth of non-Buddhists, it teaches that dharmas produced through conditions are definitively substantially existent.

Next, one gradually breaks their attachment to the view that the dependent origination of the two vehicles is truly existent, teaching that this dependent origination is merely "semblance existence. Because they fear this true emptiness, one provisionally maintains the concept of "conventional existence" to guide them.

Only at a later time, when finally reaching the ultimate Mahāyāna, does it teach that this dependent origination is itself emptiness of intrinsic nature, equal and of a single flavor, and non-obstructive to the two truths; therefore, the Dharma-characteristics (dharmalakṣaṇa) Mahāyāna, with its notions of "attainment" and so forth, belongs to the second teaching and is not the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

The sequence of these three teachings is fully cited from the *Sujñānamahāyānasūtra*—here translated as the *Mahāyāna-sūtra of Sublime Wisdom*—in the commentary on the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra* by the master Jñānaprabha; this [text] was previously unheard of.
Regarding the contradiction in the fourth assembly:
Question—Since these two teachings are each mutually contradictory as sacred scriptures, it is not known whether they can be reconciled or not.
Answer: There is neither meeting nor non-meeting.
As for the initial absence of meeting: since both are in accord with the sacred teachings and benefit sentient beings according to conditions, what need is there to wait for a formal meeting?

This refers to the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta* (the standpoint of teaching according to the individual) among the four types of *siddhānta* in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and it also corresponds to the *sattvāśaya-abhiprāya* (the intention regarding the inclinations of sentient beings) among the four intentions in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. Because [the Buddha] may either praise or disparage a single dharma depending on these factors, there is no need to force a reconciliation between these two explanations.
Regarding the second point, "there are none who do not understand," there are two gates:
first, teaching according to the capacity of the recipient; second, the recipient receiving the teaching according to their capacity.
Within the former, concerning the Buddhist gate of what is understood and what is not understood, there are four positions:

First, regarding the breadth or narrowness of the beings included; second, regarding the completeness or deficiency of the verbal teaching; third, regarding the magnitude of the benefit to sentient beings; and fourth, regarding the depth or shallowness of the revealed principle. As for the first:

if it includes only the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) without encompassing the bodhisattvas, or if it includes only the bodhisattvas without encompassing the two vehicles, then because the scope of beings included is narrow, it is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Only when it broadly includes all three types of practitioners in their entirety is it of definitive meaning.

Second, if one speaks only of the Hīnayāna without including the Mahāyāna, or speaks only of the Mahāyāna without including the teachings of the Hīnayāna, such statements are each deficient and thus not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); however, if one speaks so as to encompass both the Great and Small Vehicles and fully possess the three vehicles (*triyāna*), only then is it of definitive meaning.
Based on the two aforementioned approaches, the judgment of Śīlabhadra as found in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other texts is likewise reasonable.

Third, regarding the magnitude of benefit for sentient beings: if one causes all sentient beings to obtain the benefit of the Hīnayāna, or causes all sentient beings to obtain the benefit of the Mahāyāna, yet some obtain only minor benefit and cannot be made to attain ultimate benefit, these are both not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Only if one can cause all those sentient beings, as well as the two vehicles who have entered into quiescence, to all equally attain the benefit of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), is it then considered definitive.

Fourth, regarding the manifestation of the depth and shallowness of the principles: if one regards dependent origination as substantially existent according to conventional discourse, or even if one refutes substantial existence yet still maintains conventional existence, then because the phenomenal marks have not been fully integrated and the principle has not been fully manifested, it is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

However, if one teaches that what arises dependently is itself emptiness of intrinsic nature, such that it does not obstruct dependent origination and the two are harmonized as non-dual, then because the integration of conditions is complete and the rational nature is perfectly revealed, it is only then considered definitive meaning.
The *Sūtra of Sublime Wisdom* relies upon the two aforementioned gates; thus, Jñānaprabha’s judgment is highly reasonable.
Therefore, these two explanations each rely on a distinct gate and do not contradict one another; how could there be any contradiction?
Second, regarding the reception of the teachings according to the capacities [of the audience]: Question:
In both accounts, the three teachings each begin with the teaching of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). How should one interpret the initial teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*? Answer:
The various virtuous masters offer three interpretations.
The first states:
These three wheels of Dharma are taught in relation to those with gradual realization, whereas the *Avataṃsaka* was initially taught in relation to those with sudden realization.
If that is so, regarding the *Guhyakapada-sūtra*, which initially expounds the Dharma of the three vehicles in their entirety—is this to be categorized as gradual or sudden?

If it belongs to the gradual teaching, it should have expounded only the Small Vehicle; if it belongs to the sudden teaching, it should have expounded only the Great Vehicle. Since it contains all three, it clearly contradicts [the definitions of both], and therefore this interpretation is also difficult to accept.
One says: If one relies on the gate of explicit manifestation (*vyakta-mukha*), there is the aforementioned sequence of the three dharmas;
if one refers to the gate of secrecy (*guhya-mukha*), then all these teachings are simultaneous.
If that were so, then at the initial stage, the manifest would be small while the esoteric would be great; why then is the manifest not made great while the esoteric is made small?
Furthermore, from which sacred teaching is this distinction between the manifest and the esoteric determined?
Since the principles are inconsistent and there is no further authoritative teaching, it is difficult to rely upon them for practice.

Regarding these two preceding interpretations, these three wheels of Dharma do not exhaustively encompass all teachings: the first is gradual rather than sudden, and the last is explicit rather than esoteric.
One explanation states:

It is simply that when the Tathāgata’s perfect voice is uttered once, beings of different categories understand it accordingly; thus, in the Small Vehicle compilation, only the Small Vehicle was taught; in the Great Vehicle compilation, only the Great Vehicle was taught; and in the Universal compilation, all three vehicles were fully expounded.
If this is so, since each of the councils lacks both a predecessor and a successor, how could there be such a sequential order of these three teachings?
Now, resolving this difficulty, we shall reconcile the two explanations.
Generally speaking, there are two major categories for the Tathāgata’s teaching through his perfect voice:
first, teaching for those whose faculties are fixed in this life; second, teaching for those whose faculties are not fixed in this life.
The first three sections are as follows:

First, there may be sentient beings whose faculties for the Hīnayāna are fixed in this life; they perceive that from beginning to end the Buddha taught only the Hīnayāna, just as in the various schools of the Hīnayāna, where the Tripiṭaka was compiled without any Mahāyāna at all.

Second, there are some sentient beings whose faculties for the three vehicles have matured in this life; seeing that the Buddha taught only the three vehicles from beginning to end, as in the *Guhyapada-malla-sūtra*.

When the Buddha first preached the Dharma at the Deer Park, immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of Arhatship; immeasurable sentient beings realized the path of Pratyekabuddhahood; and immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and dwelt in the first bhūmi and so forth. This is explained in detail, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* also speak in the same way.
By analogy with this principle, all that is taught hereafter universally encompasses these three vehicles, as described in various Mahāyāna sūtras.

Third, there may be sentient beings whose faculties for the Single Vehicle (ekayāna) ripen in this very life; such individuals first behold the Buddha beneath the King of Trees within the Flower Treasury World (Puṣpaka-dhātu), where, relying on the Ocean Seal Samādhi (sāgaramudrā-samādhi), the Buddha expounds exclusively for bodhisattvas the inexhaustible, perfect, sovereign, and unimpeded Dharma-gates, complete with their primary and auxiliary elements. This remains the case even until the ultimate end, for this Dharma universally subsumes the nine periods of time, encompassing both the preceding and the succeeding.
Regarding the second, those with indeterminate faculties, there are two stages:

first, because their faculties for the Hīnayāna in this life are indeterminate, they are capable of entering the stage of the Three Vehicles; that is, upon first hearing only the Small Vehicle, they do not yet understand it; subsequently, hearing only the Great Vehicle, they likewise do not understand it; and finally, hearing both together, they realize them as being of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* explains this according to the faculties (*indriya*).

Second, because the faculties of those in this world who follow the Hīnayāna are indeterminate, there are those capable of entering the stage of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Specifically, first, it is taught that the teaching of the Hīnayāna alone is not definitive (*neyārtha*); second, the teaching that encompasses both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna is likewise not definitive; and finally, by reconciling the three vehicles into one, the teaching of the One Vehicle alone is established as definitive (*nītārtha*).
The *Sūtra on Sublime Wisdom* intends this very point.
Since the faculties are not fixed, there are these two approaches; therefore, each of the two masters expounds one approach, and thus they do not contradict one another.

Because the faculties of beings in this world are thus either determinate or indeterminate, it follows that the teachings may appear either with a sequential order or without one; this can be understood by applying the same principle to the interpretation.
Fifth, regarding the clarification of the extant tradition: among the virtuous masters of the present day, there are two views concerning the Mahāyāna.

First, some establish a Mahāyāna consisting of three vehicles (*triyāna*), on the grounds that this school maintains that those of the two vehicles who have entered the state of quiescence will certainly not attain Buddhahood; therefore, they explain the three vehicles in full according to the distinctions among the five natures (*pañcagotra*).

Second, the establishment of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) Mahāyāna: because this school maintains that even those of the two vehicles who have entered into quiescence will eventually attain Buddhahood, it speaks of the One Vehicle alone on the basis of the universal presence of this Buddha-nature.
The former masters cite scriptural authority to establish this point, stating:

"As it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 590: 'If there are classes of sentient beings whose nature is determined for the Śrāvaka Vehicle, having heard this Dharma, they will swiftly be able to realize their own stage of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*)."
Those whose lineage is fixed in the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, having heard this Dharma, will swiftly attain liberation by relying on their own vehicle.
Those whose lineage is fixed in the Unsurpassed Vehicle, having heard this Dharma, will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If there are classes of sentient beings who, though they have not yet entered the state of correct determination free from outflows, are of indeterminate lineage regarding the three vehicles, upon hearing this Dharma, they shall all resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, the second chapter of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "He further expounded the essential points of the Dharma, namely, the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*) and the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of the ultimate (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*). Even those sentient beings belonging to the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle correctly attain unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa by means of this path and this practice."
All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas share this same wondrous path of purification; they all equally attain this same ultimate purity, and there is no second.
