It is based on this that I have spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) of there being only a single vehicle; it is not that within the entire realm of sentient beings there are no various types of spiritual lineages (*gotra*), nor the distinctions among sentient beings of dull faculties, middling faculties, or sharp faculties.
The commentary explains:

This is because the three vehicles share the same object of observation—the path of non-substantiality (niḥsvabhāva); thus, with this intentional meaning (saṃdhāya-bhāṣita), it is called the "One Vehicle. In reality, however, each of the three vehicles realizes its own nirvāṇa, and they are not one.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle thirty-seven, states: "Regarding individuals who achieve [their goal], briefly stated there are four types:
those with the lineage of the śrāvaka, who achieve it by means of the Śrāvaka-yāna;
those with the lineage of the pratyekabuddha, who achieve it by means of the Pratyekabuddha-yāna;"
"Those who possess the Buddha-lineage are brought to fulfillment by means of the Unsurpassed Vehicle;
those without the lineage are brought to fulfillment by means of the happy realms.
Both the *Śīla-sūtra* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* state this in the same way.

Furthermore, the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "An individual belonging to the lineage of a śrāvaka who is exclusively oriented toward tranquility cannot, even if they receive the various skillful means of courageous application established by the Buddhas for their guidance, ever be made to sit at the site of enlightenment and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening."
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* also speaks in this same way.
The ninth fascicle of the *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha-sūtra* likewise states that the three vehicles each have fixed distinctions.

Passages such as these are not of the Hīnayāna; rather, within the Mahāyāna, they acknowledge the distinction between the three [vehicles]. Therefore, each constitutes a Mahāyāna teaching for the three vehicles.

Second, the latter master cites those teachings of the One Vehicle Mahāyāna; the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle thirty-three, states: "All sentient beings equally possess Buddha-nature; they are all of one vehicle, one liberation, one cause, and one fruit, sharing the same nectar of immortality. All shall attain the eternal, blissful, self, and pure—this is called the single flavor."

Furthermore, the first chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third, except for what is taught by the Buddha as an expedient means."
Furthermore, it says: "First, one guides sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, and only thereafter does one deliver and liberate them solely by means of the Great Vehicle.

Moreover, the third [chapter] states: "After my parinirvāṇa, there will again be disciples who have not heard this sutra; they do not know and do not perceive the conduct of bodhisattvas, yet they give rise to the notion of parinirvāṇa regarding the merits they have attained and enter into nirvana."

In other lands I shall become a Buddha under different names; although these people harbor the thought that they have attained extinction and enter into nirvana, they will seek the wisdom of a Buddha in those lands.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 95, also states this.

Furthermore, regarding the four śrāvakas mentioned in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-upadeśa*—namely, those who have regressed from the bodhicitta and those who are transformational beings—the Buddha bestows predictions upon these two types of śrāvakas because their faculties are not yet mature; as for the other two, the determined and the arrogant, the Bodhisattva bestows predictions upon them as a skillful means to cause them to resolve their minds toward enlightenment.
The commentary states:
Since it is merely said that they are "not yet mature" and not said that they lack the root [of liberation], we know that they will certainly attain the Bodhi of a Buddha.
Furthermore, the statement that one uses "expedient means to cause them to resolve their minds" refers precisely to the arousal of the bodhicitta.

Furthermore, the second, fourth, and seventh chapters of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* all state in the same way that the two vehicles possess no real nirvāṇa; rather, they merely abide through the power of samādhi and will inevitably attain unsurpassed bodhi in the future.
The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states: "As for the fourth person, it is because they employ skillful means to lead them into the city of nirvāṇa.
The city of nirvāṇa refers to the city of the various dhyānas and samādhis."
"Having passed beyond that city, cause them to enter the city of Great Parinirvāṇa.
This is similar to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, where one dwells in the bliss of samādhi; because they have transcended the segmented [birth-and-death], it is metaphorically called "nirvāṇa."
In reality, however, there exists that body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*), and it is through this that one practices the bodhisattva path in the Pure Land.
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "To say that those of the two vehicles attain nirvāṇa is the Buddha’s skillful means; only the Tathāgata attains parinirvāṇa."

Furthermore, this sutra, as well as the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra*, the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, and the *Buddhadhātuśāstra*, all state that the two vehicles who have entered parinirvāṇa receive a transformation body (*nairmāṇikakāya*) outside the three realms.
Furthermore, in the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*, it is stated that for those of the two vehicles, there is absolutely no such thing as the permanent extinction of the "ash-like" cessation (nirvāṇa).

Such passages as these also belong to the Mahāyāna; they do not admit of a fixed distinction between the three vehicles, and for this reason, they are termed the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Regarding the sixth point, the provisional and the ultimate, some say:

"The One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is provisional and the Three Vehicles are ultimate. This is because, according to the first period of teaching in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, it was taught solely for those setting out on the Śrāvaka Vehicle; thus, there is no attainment of Buddhahood at all [for them].
The teaching of the second period was expounded solely for those who have set out to practice the Mahāyāna; that is, it generally asserts that there is no one who will not attain Buddhahood.
Since these two [teachings] are either excessive or deficient, neither is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
It is better to regard the teachings of the third period as definitive (nītārtha), wherein those with the spiritual lineage (gotra) attain realization while those without it do not.

Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* belongs to the second period of teaching, it is a provisional teaching given with intentional ambiguity (saṃdhābhāṣya). Therefore, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* treats the One Vehicle (ekayāna) as a skillful means; thus, in reality, the One Vehicle is taught only with reference to those of indeterminate lineage.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, and other treatises all provide this same explanation.

Furthermore, regarding the passage in the third chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* concerning those who conceive the thought of extinction and enter into nirvāṇa, according to the eighty-first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, these are all manifestations of transformation śrāvakas entering extinction.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* both provide interpretations consistent with this assembly.

Treatises such as the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra* and the *Ratnagotravibhāga* all refer to those of the two vehicles who are not yet fixed and are turning toward Bodhi; they undergo transformation through the prolongation of their lifespan, rather than entering extinction only to arise again and receive a new body.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that regarding the fourfold permutation of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*)—namely, both being accomplished, one being accomplished while the other is not, the former being unaccomplished while the latter is, and both being unaccomplished—the fourth case, where both are unaccomplished, refers to the time when Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas enter the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
Furthermore, the *Eighty Fascicle [Avataṃsaka]* states: "In the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder, there is only the pure *dharmadhātu* of true suchness (*tathatā*).

Based on such passages, once one has entered nirvāṇa, both body and wisdom are extinguished, and the sense faculties and consciousnesses are forever non-existent; how, then, could there be further transformation and practice to achieve Buddhahood?
Therefore, the teaching that there is only one vehicle (ekayāna) is not the ultimate definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

In the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the third turning of the wheel was taught for the sake of those who have set out upon all vehicles; it is designated as definitive meaning. Thus, one should know that the three vehicles are the teachings that exhaustively accord with the principle of reality.

Furthermore, both the second and fourth chapters of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* state that the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is taught with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*); thus, we know it is provisional. Some say:

"The One Vehicle is real and the Three Vehicles are provisional. This means that while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* teaches only the Single Buddha Vehicle, the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* speaks of the Three Vehicles after [the former], asserting that those of fixed nature among the Two Vehicles are extinguished and no longer exist; therefore, the Three were taught as a skillful means (*upāya*), whereas in reality there is only one.

If it is argued that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is a teaching of the second period, taught to lead those of indeterminate disposition among the two vehicles by declaring that all shall attain Buddhahood, yet is not definitive because it still does not state that those of determinate nature do not attain it—then, if that were so, at the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the existence of śrāvakas of determinate nature had not yet been taught; for what reason, then, does that treatise establish four types of śrāvakas?
From what source is that statement regarding "fixed nature" derived?
If there were a fixed nature, how could [all things] collectively be established?
If one grants that they are collectively established, how can they be called "fixed in nature"?

Therefore, we know that the statement regarding "fixed nature" reiterates what was taught previously in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, whereas the subsequent *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies that all beings will ultimately and completely attain Buddhahood. Consequently, that treatise follows the textual sequence of this sūtra, reconciling the earlier provisional teachings with the later ultimate teaching; thus, we know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was certainly taught after the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.

In the *Miaozhi lun* (Treatise on Wondrous Wisdom), the One Vehicle of the Three Teachings follows after the Three Vehicles; likewise, in the Liang dynasty’s *Lun* (Treatise), which establishes the three categories of the True Dharma, the One Vehicle is also placed last—both works agree with this explanation.

To explain passages in the *Lotus Sūtra* such as "conceiving the thought of extinction and entering nirvāṇa" as referring to the manifestation of a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) nirvāṇa is utterly contrary to both scripture and reason.

As for the contradiction with scripture: if these were transformation śrāvakas, they would in reality be Buddhas and bodhisattvas; how could they be so deluded regarding the nirvāṇa they themselves manifested that they would give rise to the thought of attaining extinction?
If one were to provide such an interpretation, it would mean that one has never even read the sutras.

As for its contradiction of reason: if entering nirvana were a state of permanent cessation, then when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest nirvana before those to be converted—if those to be converted possess an indeterminate lineage and are courageous, capable of not fearing birth and death and being able to cultivate sublime practices—[this manifestation would be meaningless].

If there is a certain class of people who are by nature timid and weak, who fear birth and death while training as a Buddha or Bodhisattva, and who first enter nirvāṇa with the intention of later practicing the bodhisattva path;
Since your school asserts that upon entering extinction there is no further arising, does this not mislead a certain class of sentient beings?
To thus mislead sentient beings—how can this constitute guidance?

Moreover, this text is not irrelevant; furthermore, you have failed to grasp the intent of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, yet you have arbitrarily concluded that the One Vehicle is merely a provisional teaching (*upāya*).
That sutra states: "If the Tathāgata teaches through skillful means according to their inclinations—referring to the two vehicles—it is in fact the One Vehicle, for there are no two vehicles.
The two vehicles enter into the One Vehicle; the One Vehicle is the vehicle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-yāna*).

Furthermore, in that sutra, it extensively refutes the two vehicles by stating that there is no nirvana; it also says: "This sutra cuts off all doubts, definitively establishes the ultimate meaning, and leads one into the path of the One Vehicle."
Could it be that the One Vehicle was taught as a mere expedient?

As for the statement in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* that the One Vehicle is of intentional meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣya*), this was spoken before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* had been taught; however, when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was later taught, it was revealed that the three vehicles previously presented were all expedient means.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains the transformation and simultaneous extinction of the basis; the *Vyākhyāyukti* (or *Prakaraṇāryavācā*) explains the One Vehicle through six meanings; and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains the One Vehicle through ten meanings—all of these accord with the interpretation of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, because these treatises were composed in accordance with that sūtra.

The *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fa-hua lun) states that even those of the two vehicles who have attained certainty receive predictions of enlightenment; this is because it was composed in accordance with this root sūtra.

If one does not believe in the One Vehicle and clings to the provisional while deviating from the ultimate, such a person is truly to be pitied. Thus, the second volume of the *Śata-upamāna-sūtra* (*Bai yu jing*) says: "Once there was a village located five *yojanas* from the royal capital, where the water was excellent and delicious."
The king commanded the villagers to provide him with fine water every day. The villagers became exhausted and distressed, and all wished to move away from this village.
At that time, the village headman said to the people: "Do not go."
"I shall petition the King on your behalf to reduce the distance from five *yojanas* to three *yojanas*, so that you may be closer and not grow weary on your journeys.
He then went to inform the King, who reduced it to three *yojanas*. When the people heard this, they were filled with great joy.
Someone said to him, "This is indeed the original five yojanas; there is no difference at all.
Although he heard these words, because he trusted the king’s speech, he ultimately refused to abandon his position.

The people of the world are likewise thus: practicing the True Dharma to cross over the five realms of existence toward the city of Nirvana, they become weary in heart and wish to abandon it, halting their carriage within birth and death and unable to proceed further.

The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, possesses great skillful means; within the One Vehicle Dharma, he distinguishes and teaches three vehicles. Those of the Lesser Vehicle, upon hearing this, rejoice, considering it easy to practice; they cultivate goodness, advance in virtue, and seek deliverance from birth and death.

Later, hearing others say that there are no three vehicles and therefore it is but a single vehicle, he would never be willing to abandon his faith in the Buddha’s words; the man from the village was just like this.
The commentary explains:
This sutra is the excellent definitive judgment from the Buddha’s own mouth; its provisional and ultimate meanings are clearly revealed, so that all other interpretations may be brought to rest.
Seventh, regarding the manifestation of opening and closing: indeed, each of these three vehicles and the one vehicle possesses two aspects.
Regarding the three vehicles, there are two types:
first, the three vehicles at different times, as in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, where in the first period there was only the Hīnayāna, and in the second period only the Mahāyāna;
second, the three vehicles simultaneously, as in the third period, when [the teaching] is universally intended for those setting out on all vehicles and so forth.

Within this teaching, the characteristics of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) are concealed while the characteristics of the Three Vehicles (triyāna) are manifest; therefore, based on what is manifest, it is collectively termed the "Three Vehicles.
Regarding the One Vehicle, there are two aspects:

first, refuting multiplicity to clarify unity. This is as in the *Lotus Sūtra*, which refutes the reality of the two [vehicles] to establish extinction, and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which refutes the absence of Buddha-nature; both of these speak of the One Vehicle by means of refuting provisional teachings through specific assemblies.
The two direct bodies manifest as one, as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where there is nothing to be refuted because it does not address the two vehicles;
rather, it directly reveals the dharma-realm for the sake of the great bodhisattvas as the ritual for attaining buddhahood.

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* was taught first as having no provisional means with which to harmonize it; the *Nirvāṇa* was taught last to harmonize all the preceding provisional means. Thus, it is not the case that the reality can be revealed without exhausting the provisional; both are termed the One Vehicle.
Furthermore, each of these is further divided into three types.
Regarding the first set of three concerning the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*):

the first refers to "initial difference and final identity" (*ādi-bheda-paryanta-samatā*). This means that initially, the practices differ—such as the cultivation of the Four Noble Truths, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*)—but finally, upon attaining the fruit, the bodies and wisdoms of those of the three vehicles are identical in their cessation. As explained in the *Abhidharmakośa* and other texts, this refers to the teachings of the Hīnayāna at the initial stage.

Second, they are identical at the beginning but divergent at the end; that is to say, having equally heard the Prajñāpāramitā and equally contemplated the absence of intrinsic nature, those of the three vehicles each attain their own respective fruits, as previously cited in the scriptures.

If one considers the differences between the Noble Truths, Dependent Origination, and the practice of the Six Perfections, these may also be termed as having distinct beginnings and ends; this refers to the teachings of the second and third periods.

The three [vehicles] are different in their proximity but identical in their distance; that is to say, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other such sutras, they first use the skillful means of the three vehicles to entice and lead [beings], and later cause them all equally to attain liberation through the Mahāyāna.
The three aspects of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) are:
first, preserving one among the three, as taught in the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other sūtras;
second, negating one among the three, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other sūtras.
The first [type] consists of the three manifestations alone, as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and others.
Therefore, it is generally explained that there are four propositions:
first, some cases have only the three and not the one, as in the *Abhidharmakośa* and others.
Second, there are two [teachings] or only one, with no third, as in the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras.
Third, there are both one and three; this has two positions:
first, the initial [teaching] is substantially one but expediently [manifested as three], as in the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other sutras.
The latter consists of one reality and three expedients, as seen in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other texts.
Alternatively, it may be neither one nor three, because from the perspective of ultimate principle (*tattva*), it transcends all verbal expression.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Śāriputra asks Subhūti:
“The Tathāgata has bestowed predictions upon these sons of the gods; among the three vehicles, by which vehicle do they receive their prediction?
Subhūti replied, “Within the characteristics of dharmas, there is neither one nor three. How, then, can you ask by which vehicle they receive their prediction?”
Therefore, regarding the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles, there are both their existence and their sublation, and various explanations differ.
Some, hearing that only the Two Vehicles are refuted, claim this refers exclusively to those of indeterminate lineage;
others, hearing that neither two nor three exist, claim that even the Mahāyāna’s ultimate teaching is refuted.
Alternatively, one might hear that the Mahāyāna is not sublated and thus conclude that the provisional teachings of the Mahāyāna also persist.

Now, there are two levels of explanation: first, from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*), it refutes the notion that the two vehicles undergo actual extinction; [the second level refutes their extinction from the perspective of principle].
Second, regarding the teaching, this also accords with the provisional teachings of the Mahāyāna.
This is because the provisional Mahāyāna teachings permit entry into quiescence, whereas the two vehicles do not achieve Buddhahood.
However, profoundly refuting the two vehicles is itself the refutation of the three; therefore, the refutation of the two and the refutation of the three are not mutually contradictory.

Regarding the eighth [section], the sequence of the teachings: we shall now discern the entirety of what was taught by the Tathāgata throughout his lifetime, clarifying the teachings according to their chronological order.

In general, there are four major categories: first, the gate of the distinction between the root and the branches; second, the gate of the arising of the branches based on the root; third, the gate of subsuming the branches back into the root; and fourth, the gate of the non-obstruction between the root and the branches.
From beginning to end, from root to branch, these are simultaneous; from start to finish, they are of one kind, with no differing teachings. Nevertheless, there are three stages:

first, within the Hīnayāna, he initially delivered [the Dharma] to Kauṇḍinya and others, and finally delivered it to Subhadra; in between, he likewise taught only the Hīnayāna and benefited only those of Hīnayāna capacity, as stated in the four *Āgamas*, the five-part Vinaya, the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (or *Upadeśa*), and other such texts.

Second, if categorized according to the three vehicles, from beginning to end they all teach the three vehicles to universally benefit the three types of capacities. As previously cited in various Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Malla-sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, although there are differences therein between the provisional and the ultimate, all of them possess the three vehicles.

Third, if categorized according to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), from the beginning until the ultimate stage, it is taught for great Bodhisattvas alone that there is only the One Vehicle. For example, when the *Avataṃsaka* and other such sutras were first preached, they did not admit of the Two Vehicles; furthermore, they encompass the nine periods of time, including both the preceding and the succeeding. Therefore, at the ultimate stage, there is no further divergent teaching.

However, since these three categories are explained based on the faculties and the specific stage of this world, they are mutually consistent across all teachings from beginning to end, with no actual sequence of priority.
Second, regarding the classification according to the principle of the fundamental giving rise to the derivative, there are four types:
first, it refers to teaching the Mahāyāna to great bodhisattvas at the outset, followed by the teaching of the Middle Vehicle, then the Small Vehicle, and finally the teachings for humans and devas.

As it is said in the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" (*Xingqi pin*) later in this sutra: "For example, when the sun rises, it first illuminates all the great kings of mountains, next it illuminates all the great mountains, then it illuminates the diamond jewel mountains, and finally it shines universally upon the entire earth."

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise: having accomplished the sun-wheel of wisdom of the immeasurable and boundless Dharma-realm, he constantly radiates the immeasurable and unimpeded light of wisdom. First, it illuminates the great mountain-kings that are the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; next, it illuminates the Pratyekabuddhas; next, it illuminates the Śrāvakas; next, it illuminates those sentient beings with resolute roots of goodness, according to their capacity for transformation. Thereafter, it illuminates all sentient beings, even those of the fixed-in-wrongness (mithyātva-niyata), acting as a cause and condition for their future benefit.

Furthermore, in this chapter: "Just as when the trichiliocosm is first formed, first the palaces of the various devas of the form realm (rūpadhātu) are formed, next the palaces of the various devas of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are formed, and finally the human abodes and the dwellings of other sentient beings are formed."

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is likewise: first he gives rise to the wisdom of the various practices of a bodhisattva, and subsequently he gives rise to the roots of goodness of pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and all other sentient beings.

Based on these passages, it is clarified that the Buddha first taught the Mahāyāna and later gradually taught the Hīnayāna; this is explained in terms of the Dharma as the arising of the derivative from the fundamental, rather than in terms of the capacities of the practitioners, because there is no case of one who first studied the Mahāyāna and subsequently studied the Hīnayāna.
Question:
Are the dharmas not distinct? Answer:
Because the teachings of the Hīnayāna necessarily flow forth from the Mahāyāna, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"The eighteen schools and the two original ones all emerge from the Mahāyāna."
The intent of the *Samantabhadrotsāha-samādhi-sūtra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* is likewise the same.

Regarding the third section, "The Gate of Subsuming the Branches into the Root," according to the *Anantārtha-sūtra*, at the first stage he taught the Hīnayāna, at the next stage he taught the Madhyamayāna, and at the final stage he taught the Mahāyāna.

According to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, during the first period there was only the Hīnayāna; during the second period, only the Mahāyāna; and during the third period, all three vehicles were present.

According to the *Sujñāna-sūtra*, during the first period there was only the Hīnayāna; in the subsequent period, all three vehicles were present; and in the final period, there was only the One Vehicle (*Ekayāna*).

This refers to the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (Wuliangyi jing), which combines the Great [Vehicle] while opening up the Small; and the *Saṃdhinirmocana* (Shenmi jing) and others, which combine the Small while opening up the Great—meaning that within the Mahāyāna, they open up both the provisional and the ultimate.

However, since both the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and the *Jñānālokālaṃkāra* are each sacred scriptures, one cannot accept one while rejecting the other; therefore, these two sūtras are combined here into four general sections:
first, the Hīnayāna of the initial period, which both sūtras describe in common;
second, the Mahāyāna of the middle period, which is described exclusively in the *Saṃdhinirmocana*.
The third period possesses the three vehicles; this is the second chapter, "Excellence of Wisdom," from the third section of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*.
The fourth period consists of the single vehicle; this is taught exclusively in the third section of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*.
Therefore, one should know that the *Sūtra of Sublime Wisdom* (*Suvarṇaprabhāsa*) was preached after the *Saṃdhinirmocana*.

If one claims that the *Sūtra of Sublime Wisdom* has not been translated in this land and thus does not believe it, consider that since the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* belongs to the teachings of the third period, yet it maintains that those of fixed nature among the two vehicles and sentient beings lacking the [Buddha] nature do not attain Buddhahood—thereby possessing the three vehicles while calling them "all vehicles"—then the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* must have been preached after the *Saṃdhinirmocana*.

However, since those of the two vehicles with fixed natures as well as the icchantikas devoid of nature all attain Buddhahood, one should know that this is precisely the teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) from the fourth period; therefore, it accords perfectly with the *Sūtra of Sublime Wisdom* without any doubt.

Furthermore, regarding the initial teachings of the Hīnayāna, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other sources, they were preached during the three weeks following the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment.

According to the *Record of Tripitaka Master Paramārtha*, it is said: "Seven years after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he preached the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras; this is the teaching of the second period."
Furthermore, it is said: "Thirty-eight years later, he preached the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, which constitutes the third period of teaching.

However, according to both the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Anantamukha-sūtra*, it is stated that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other sūtras were preached forty years later; therefore, we know that this [teaching] was spoken after the *Saṃdhinirmocana*.
Paramārtha: This teaching must certainly be based on the sacred scriptures (āgama); if there were no sacred scriptures, how could one arbitrarily establish a number of years?
If you do not believe this, then the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*—which stands at the very end—is beyond doubt.

Nevertheless, in all four of these periods, the provisional precedes the real and the latter accords with the former; thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* sūtras harmonize the three vehicles of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, leading them back to the ultimate One Vehicle—the meaning of which is definitive.
Therefore, these four [sections] proceed from the shallow to the deep, clarifying the gradual process of subsuming the branches and returning to the root.

Regarding the fourth, the Gate of the Non-obstruction between Root and Branches: this means that first, by citing the teaching of the "Illuminating Mountain King," it clarifies that there can be no arising of the branches without the root;
subsequently, by revealing the various currents that flow back to the great ocean, it clarifies that there can be no returning to the root without the exhaustion of the branches.

This constitutes the mutual illumination of the root and the branches, and the reciprocal support of bestowal and withdrawal; only thus does one possess the skillful means for gathering and sustaining living beings.
Therefore, in general discussion, there are five stages in total:
first, the fundamental One Vehicle teaching, as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;

Second, the teachings of the Hīnayāna with intentional meaning; third, the teachings of the Mahāyāna with intentional meaning; fourth, the explicit teachings of the three vehicles—these first three are as explained in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*;
fifth, the teachings that refute the notion of a separate [Hīnayāna] and establish the One Vehicle, as explained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, and others.

Since these four preceding gates are thus perfectly penetrating and unobstructed, that which is prior and posterior is itself without priority or posteriority; and that which is without priority or posteriority is itself prior and posterior—all are entirely free from hindrance. One should reflect upon this accordingly.
The ninth [classification] divides the teachings according to their meaning.
There are five categories of teaching; this classification is based on meaning rather than historical events.
First, the Hīnayāna teaching; second, the Initial Mahāyāna teaching; third, the Final teaching; fourth, the Sudden teaching; and fifth, the Perfect teaching.
The first, the Hīnayāna, can be understood as previously explained.

Regarding the second, the Initial Teaching (Śākyamuni’s provisional teachings): because the second and third periods of teaching in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* both agree that those of fixed nature among the two vehicles will not attain Buddhahood, these are now combined and treated as a single teaching.
Since this does not yet exhaust the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma, it is established as the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna.

Third, as for the Final Teaching: because those of fixed nature among the two vehicles and the icchantikas who lack the Buddha-nature are all destined to attain Buddhahood, it fully exhausts the most ultimate discourse of the Mahāyāna and is thus established as the Final Teaching.
However, the former two teachings both rely on the gradual cultivation and accomplishment of the stages and positions, and are thus collectively termed "Gradual Teachings.

As for the fourth, the Sudden Teaching, it holds that the mere non-arising of a single thought is itself called Buddhahood; because it is not taught according to the sequence of stages and positions, it is established as "Sudden."
As the *Saṃcayagāthā* states: "One who has attained the true nature of all dharmas does not proceed from one stage to another.
The *Laṅkāvatāra* says: "The first stage is itself the eighth stage; even up to the realm of nothingness, what sequential order can there be?"
Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Grounds" (*bhūmi-paṭala*) below, it is said that the ten grounds are like the tracks of birds in the sky; how could any distinction be found?
This is explained in detail in such works as the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra*.

Regarding the fifth, the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): it clarifies that one stage is all stages and all stages are one stage. Therefore, the fulfillment of the mind of the ten faiths (*shixin manxin*) subsumes the five stages of attaining perfect enlightenment and so forth. Because it relies on the *Indra’s Net* of the Samantabhadra Dharma-realm, wherein the principal and its attendants are fully present in infinite layers, it is called the Perfect Teaching; this is as taught in scriptures such as this [Avataṃsaka Sūtra].

If one considers the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the dharmas as taught, in the initial Dharma of the Hīnayāna there are seventy-five dharmas and consciousnesses are only six; thus, the original nature of dharmas is not fully explained, leading to many divergent disputes, as described in the various sūtras and śāstras of the Hīnayāna schools.

Within the second, the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*), the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena) is extensively expounded while the true nature (*tathatā*) is briefly discussed. Because the established One Hundred Dharmas (*śata-dharma*) provide clear and decisive analysis, there is no contradiction or dispute. The eight consciousnesses taught therein consist solely of the characteristics of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-lakṣaṇa*); their names and categories largely coincide with those of the Hīnayāna. Thus, they are certainly not the ultimate or profound teachings, as explained in such works as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

Third, within the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*), the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are briefly explained while the true nature (*tathatā*) is extensively expounded, because it brings phenomena into accord with principle.

The eight consciousnesses established therein are understood as being the Tathāgatagarbha that arises in accordance with conditions, possessing both the aspects of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing. Furthermore, it does not discuss the enumerations of the hundred dharmas in detail, nor is it like the Hīnayāna; yet it is not as manifold in its approaches as [the teachings in] scriptures such as the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and treatises such as the *Ratnagotravibhāga*.

Within the fourth, the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao), no characteristics of phenomena (lakṣaṇa) are taught at all; rather, it exclusively elucidates true nature (bhūtatathatā). Furthermore, there are no differentiated characteristics of the eight consciousnesses (vijñāna); everything that exists is merely deluded thought (parikalpita). All dharmas are in reality beyond words. It involves reviling the teachings and encouraging detachment, destroying appearances and extinguishing the mind. To give rise to the mind is delusion; not giving rise to it is Buddhahood. Moreover, there is neither Buddha nor non-Buddha, neither arising nor non-arising. This is the intended meaning of such examples as Vimalakīrti’s silence, which manifests the non-duality (advaya) of dharmas.

Within the Fivefold Perfect Teaching (*pañca-pūrṇa-yāna*), that which is taught is exclusively the inexhaustible Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Its nature-ocean is perfectly interfused, and its dependent origination is unimpeded; phenomena are mutually identical and mutually inclusive. Like Indra’s net, they are infinitely layered and boundless, with subtle intercontainment such that leaders and associates are inexhaustible. Each of the ten-times-ten Dharma-gates accords with the Dharma-realm, as will be explained in detail below.
However, these five teachings involve both opening and closing, and they also comprise five layers:
first, they may be taken as a single whole, meaning that they are solely the great skillful means of the Tathāgata for gathering and transforming sentient beings.
Secondly, these may be divided into two: namely, the teachings of the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles.

Although within the former teachings there are differences—some preserving the three and some merging the two—they all provide access for those entering via the Three Vehicles; thus, they are called the "Three Vehicle Teachings.

The latter directly reveals the fundamental Dharma and does not accommodate the Two Vehicles; therefore, it is exclusively the One, which is termed the "Common Teaching" and the "Uncommon Teaching" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
This is also the same as the two teachings established by the masters of the seal-seal school (*mudrācārya*) and others.
Thirdly, they may be divided into three, namely: the teachings of the Hīnayāna, the Triyāna, and the Ekayāna.
Since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* treats this sutra as not being shared with the two vehicles, it is termed "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*), which is precisely the One Vehicle.

Because the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others allow for the same contemplation to yield benefits for all three vehicles, they are termed "shared," which is precisely the Three Vehicles.
By inference from the four *Āgama* scriptures, that which is not shared with bodhisattvas is also called "unshared," and this refers to the Hīnayāna.
Based on these three stages, the eighth fascicle of the *Liang Translation of the Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states: "The Tathāgata establishes the True Dharma in three ways:
first, establishing the Hīnayāna; second, establishing the Mahāyāna (some texts read 'three vehicles'); and third, establishing the One Vehicle."
"Because it is the third and most excellent, it is called 'well-established.
This is also stated in the *Sūtra of Sublime Wisdom* (*Jñānottara-sūtra*).
Furthermore, the second fascicle of the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha’s *Commentary on the Different Tenets of the Schools* (*Samayabhedoparacanacakra-ṭīkā*) also states this in the same way.
Fourth, it may be divided into four, which has two meanings:

first, within the aforementioned common teachings, there are four because they consist of three that are preserved and two that are merged, while opening up two distinct doctrines: (1) the distinct teaching of the Hīnayāna;
and (2) the common teaching of the Three Vehicles, such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and others.
Third is the One Vehicle of the Common Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-ekayāna*), such as the *Lotus Sūtra* and others;
fourth is the One Vehicle of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-ekayāna*), such as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and others.
These four are established by distinguishing between the gradual and sudden teachings based on whether they involve traversing stages or being beyond stages.
First, the Hīnayāna teaching; second, the gradual teaching; third, the sudden teaching; and fourth, the perfect teaching.
Alternatively, these may be divided into five by further subdividing the aforementioned gradual teaching into two: the initial and the final teachings.
The five teachings mentioned above are not restricted to specific sutras, but are discussed by way of general categories.
As indicated above, this applies to all sutras and treatises, which can be understood accordingly.
The tenth [teaching] establishes the school through principle; this school comprises ten aspects:

First is the school that maintains the coexistence of both phenomena and a self (pudgala), namely the followers of the Vātsīputrīya and other sects within the Human and Deva realms, as well as among the Hīnayāna.
They establish three categories of phenomena:
first, conditioned phenomena; second, unconditioned phenomena; and third, that which belongs to neither category.
That is, the first two are dharmas, while the latter one is the self (*ātman*).
Furthermore, he establishes five dharma-treasuries:
first, the past; [and so forth].
1. The future; 2. the present;
3. the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); 4. [the past].
The fifth is the "inexpressible" (avaktavya), which is precisely this self, because the inexpressible is both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Second is the school that asserts the existence of a self and the non-existence of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), namely the Sarvāstivādins and others.
He explains that all phenomena are subsumed under two categories:
first, name; second, form.
Alternatively, they are subsumed under four categories, namely: the three time periods and the unconditioned.
Alternatively, five categories of phenomena are established:
first, mind; second, mental factors; third, form; fourth, non-associated formations; and fifth, unconditioned phenomena.
This implies that there are only these phenomena and no separate self.
The school that maintains that three dharmas have no past or future is the Mahāsāṃghika and others.
They assert that only the present and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas exist, because the substance and function of past and future dharmas are both non-existent.
Fourth are the schools that maintain both the conventional and the real regarding the supernormal powers (abhijñā), namely the Prajñaptivādins and others.

They assert that the two time periods of the past and future do not exist; within present phenomena, those that reside in the aggregates (skandha) are real, while those that reside in the elements (dhātu) and bases (āyatana) are conventional. Thus, the conventional or real status of various phenomena is indeterminate according to their respective natures. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* and certain teachers of the Sautrāntika school also belong to this same category.
The fifth is the school that asserts the conventional is false while the ultimate is real;
this refers to the Lokottaravāda and others. They maintain that conventional phenomena are provisional because they are false, whereas supramundane phenomena are real because they are not false.
Sixth, the school that maintains all phenomena are merely names refers to the Ekavyāvahārikas and others.
They assert that all persons and phenomena exist only as provisional designations and possess no substantial reality whatsoever.
This view also extends to the initial stage of the Initial Teaching (Āgama).
The seventh is the school that all things are empty, which refers to the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna.

It asserts that all phenomena are entirely empty of intrinsic nature, transcending the realm of conceptualization because they are free from discrimination; this is as explained in detail in such texts as the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

The eighth is the school of the Non-emptiness of the Eightfold True Virtues (*aṣṭavidha-tattva-guṇa-amogha-naya*), which refers to what is taught in the various sutras of the Final Teaching (*paryanta-deśanā*).
It holds that all phenomena are solely *tathatā* (suchness), because they are subsumed within the actual virtues of the *tathāgatagarbha*;
thus, the true essence is not empty, as it is endowed with the virtues of its nature.

The ninth is the school of the simultaneous severance of all conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*), which refers to the principle beyond words revealed by the sudden teaching (*tongjiao*), wherein both principle and phenomena are extinguished in a state of equality free from thought.

The tenth is the school of perfect luminosity and complete virtue, which refers to the dharma-gates revealed by the distinct teaching (*biejiao*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), wherein the principal and its attendants are fully present in inexhaustible sovereignty.

The preceding sections have categorized the teachings and established the fundamental tenets, providing a general outline and extensively citing scriptural principles to clarify the characteristics of their meanings as explained in the separate records.

Fourth, regarding the capacities of those for whom these teachings are intended, there are generally ten levels; among these, the first five distinguish those who are not suitable vessels, while the latter five correctly manifest the intended recipients.
Regarding the five types of individuals who are unsuitable as recipients [of this teaching] mentioned previously: first, those who contradict the truth and are not fit vessels.

This refers to those who do not resolve to attain bodhicitta nor seek liberation, but instead rely upon this sutra to seek fame and profit, using it to adorn their notions of self and personhood. Since the sutra is not a condition for such persons, they are not fit vessels.
The text below states: "To preach the Dharma for the sake of fame and profit is the work of Māra.
Furthermore, it mentions such things as preaching with impure intentions, which leads to falling into evil realms.
Second, those who turn their backs on the correct [Dharma] are not suitable vessels.

That is to say, they feign a great resolve and falsely cultivate perverse goodness; though they may temporarily attain rebirth among devas or humans and ultimately claim to achieve Buddhahood, they fear falling into the Avīci Hell to suffer for many kalpas.
Just as Devadatta was the pinnacle of the icchantikas, and just as the eight great virtuous persons were destined to become non-virtuous;
the former can be known by their initial state, while this [latter case] is revealed only at the final stage.
The text below states: "To cultivate various roots of goodness while forgetting the bodhicitta is the work of Māra.
Since the sutra does not have this as its objective, such a person is likewise not a suitable vessel.
Third, one who deviates from reality is not a vessel.

This means that although they are not crafty or deceitful, they nevertheless grasp the scriptural texts according to their own biased views; consequently, the supreme teachings that transcend ordinary intellect fail to enter their hearts, and thus they become unfit vessels.
The *Dilun* states: "If one hears and forms an understanding based on what is heard, one cannot be said to have truly heard.
This is also like the five kinds of faults incurred by grasping at meaning according to the sound [of the words].
These three aforementioned stages all belong to the realm of ordinary, ignorant sentient beings.
The text below states: "This sutra shall not fall into the hands of any sentient beings, with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas.
This is because this sutra is not a condition for the transmigration of sentient beings; therefore, it does not enter their hands.
Fourth, those who are narrow-minded and inferior are not suitable vessels;
that is to say, all followers of the two vehicles lack the vast mind and are likewise not such vessels.
As the text below states: "All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not even hear this sutra, let alone receive and uphold it."
Furthermore, Śāriputra and the other five hundred śrāvakas were all like those who are deaf and blind; they neither heard nor saw.
This is because those who guard the provisional [teachings] are not vessels for this.

Specifically, the bodhisattvas of the common teaching of the three vehicles, whose practice within their own respective systems has not yet fulfilled the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, are likewise not such vessels.

The following text states: "Although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may practice the six pāramitās and cultivate the roots of goodness of the factors of enlightenment for immeasurable billions of nayutas of kalpas, if they have not heard this sutra, or though they have heard it, do not believe, accept, uphold, or accord with it, such individuals are still merely 'provisional' bodhisattvas."

Question: According to the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* and other texts, one fulfills the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) after practicing for ten thousand kalpas; why is it that here, immeasurable billions of people do not believe in this sūtra?
Answer:

Because they practice faith and the other [five roots of goodness] only during the stage of sequential cultivation (*xingbu*), and have not yet heard or believed in this perfect fusion (*yuanrong*) wherein the ten faiths of Samantabhadra encompass all within one; by this, one knows the distinction between the two schools.
If it were not so, having already spent such vast eons practicing the path, yet lacking faith in this sutra—how could one be called a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva?
This concludes the exclusion of those who are not suitable vessels.
Regarding the second section, which clarifies those for whom [the teaching] is intended, there are five points.

First, the primary intended recipients: these are the bodhisattvas of universal capacity within the uncommon teaching of the One Vehicle; they are precisely the vessels for whom this sutra is intended.
The subsequent text states: "Such sutras as these are taught solely for the sake of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who ride the inconceivable vehicle, and not for others.
The commentary explains:
"Vehicle" (yāna) has the meaning of "transporting" or "carrying forward."

If one follows the distinct gate, first proceeding from the initial stage to the Ten Faiths, and subsequently advancing through the Ten Abidings up to the fruit of Buddhahood, ascending step by step like a chariot to reach the other shore, this is called "conceivable."
If one relies on the Universal Gate (Samantamukha), because a single stage is all stages, and likewise a single progression is all progressions, it is called the Inconceivable Vehicle.
One who rides this vehicle attains the six stages immediately upon fulfilling the mind of the ten faiths, as explained in the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*) and other texts.
Furthermore, the stages such as the Ten Abodes are all likewise so, as explained in the various assemblies of the subsequent chapters.
Moreover, it is like Sudhana’s attainment of the five stages within a single lifetime; this is because all are mutually inclusive within the characteristics of the Universal Dharma (Pūrvavidhi).
Furthermore, the "Chapter on Samantabhadra" states: "It is not known by the spheres of others; through the skillful means of Samantabhadra, all may enter it.
Moreover, Samantabhadra exhorted the assembly, saying:
"The sphere of the Universal Eye and the pure body—I shall now expound them; you, sirs, listen attentively."
Thus it should be understood.
Question:
Why is this dharma not the domain of others?

Answer: Because Vairocana pervades all directions of the dust-world and universally responds to the various capacities of all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, those with distinct capacities perceive only according to their own faculties;
each sees only what they themselves see and hears only what they themselves hear, without seeing what others see or hearing what others hear.

This "Universal Good Mechanism" perceives all that is seen and hears all that is heard; since these are entirely within the scope of Vairocana’s capacity for transformation, it is called the "Object of the Universal Eye."
Therefore, one should know that the two types of capacities—the universal and the particular—elicit two corresponding types of teachings—the universal and the particular—each of which is distinct.

Regarding those who are "dual-capable," this refers to those within the period of the Bequeathed Dharma who see, hear, believe in, and incline toward this inexhaustible Dharma; they become seeds of the diamond-like nature and shall certainly attain this universally interfused, all-encompassing Dharma.

As in the subsequent passages concerning the swallowing of the vajra-like [wisdom], the metaphor of a small fire burning extensively, and the case of the Tuṣita deva-son who, emerging from hell, attained the tenth stage and the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), benefiting others in an inexhaustible succession—all of these result from having previously heard this Dharma as their fundamental cause.
Furthermore, the subsequent passage states: "Even while in the great ocean or amidst the fires at the end of a kalpa, one who possesses decisive faith without doubt will certainly hear this sutra.

Third, regarding those who are led [to this stage], it refers to those bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching who, as previously mentioned, have for a long time nurtured a profound understanding within that teaching and have thoroughly mastered the source of the *xingbu* (extensive) teachings; such individuals shall immediately attain this Dharma-realm of Samantabhadra.

Since it is stated that they will not believe this sutra for immeasurable billions of nayutas of kalpas, we know that they must certainly believe and accept it after these kalpas have passed; for there is no other path to attain Buddhahood apart from this universal Dharma, and the sutra does not say that they would still fail to believe even after these kalpas have elapsed.
Question:

If those prior to that stage must have faith and acceptance after passing through those kalpas, then one knows that the two schools on the stages (bhūmi) are not distinct. How could it be that what they believe lacks the ten stages?

Answer: Within that teaching, there is the sequential progression through the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) up to the fruit of Buddhahood; this is intended to nurture the faculties and capacities of beings so as to bring them to maturity. Even for those who progress most slowly, they will certainly attain faith and entry by the end of these kalpas.
As for those who are swift, their time is not fixed, which can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the "fourfold transformation": because those of the two vehicles have dull faculties, they must first turn back and enter the common Mahāyāna teachings, relinquishing their status as followers of the two vehicles to receive the title of Bodhisattva; only thereafter do they enter this Dharma of Samantabhadra. Therefore, it is said that this sutra is intended solely for Bodhisattvas and does not include those of the two vehicles.
If this were not the case, other Mahāyāna sūtras also have śrāvaka assemblies as their intended audience and likewise lead those of the two vehicles to enter the Great Vehicle.

Yet, in this sūtra alone, the assembly lacks the capacity of śrāvakas and the text contains no discourse on turning back from the Lesser Vehicle; how, then, could it be established as a definitive, profound, and extensive scripture?

If there were śrāvakas present at the eighth assembly, it was for the purpose of providing a contrast to manifest the Dharma; they were like those who are deaf or blind, not the intended recipients of the teaching. As for the six thousand bhikṣus, they were not arhats; therefore, there is no contradiction.
Therefore, one should know that, in general, none of those of the two vehicles can enter the Dharma-realm of Samantabhadra instantaneously.

According to the ultimate teaching, there is no follower of the two vehicles who does not turn back to enter the common bodhisattva path; and there is no such bodhisattva who does not enter this Dharma of Samantabhadra. Thus, in succession, there is none who is not a vessel for this Dharma.

Regarding those who are distant for five reasons: this refers to all ordinary people, the foolish, non-Buddhists, and icchantikas, all of whom possess Buddha-nature; because their obstructions are heavy, they shall also enter this Dharma after a long period of time.

As both the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* and the *Ratnagotravibhāga* state, it is because icchantikas slander the Mahāyāna that they are said to lack buddha-nature for immeasurable periods; this does not mean they ultimately lack the nature of purity.

Furthermore, it is like the great tree of the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, which does not sprout its seeds in either of two places—the followers of the Two Vehicles or the icchantikas—yet does not abandon the nature of birth; it is also like the analogy of the sun shining upon one born blind, and so forth.

Therefore, one should know that there are no sentient beings whatsoever who ultimately do not enter this Dharma, because all sentient beings possess this universal Dharma. As the subsequent text states:
"The Bodhisattva knows that within the bodies of all sentient beings there is the *tathāgata-bodhi*," and so forth.
Question:

If that is so, why do treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi* state that those of the two vehicles with fixed natures and sentient beings without the potential for enlightenment will certainly not become Buddhas?
Answer:
These various explanations exist because the teaching vehicles differ in their degree of clarity;
according to the Hīnayāna, all sentient beings collectively lack the nature of great bodhi, as stated in the Minor Treatises.

If one follows the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna, there is a distinction between five natures (*pañca-gotra*), such that one portion possesses the nature [for enlightenment] while another portion lacks it, as in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts.
If one relies on the final teaching, all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, as in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and other scriptures, as well as the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* and other treatises.

If one relies on the Sudden Teaching, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is of a single flavor and a single characteristic; it cannot be said to exist and cannot be described as non-existent. It transcends words and cuts off all thought, as taught in such texts as the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra*.

If one relies on the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is endowed with both cause and fruit, and possesses both essence and attributes; it is perfectly luminous and replete with virtues, as explained in the section on the Tathāgata’s Bodhi in the "Nature-Arising" (Xingqi) Chapter.
Fifth, regarding the essence of the teaching as the expressive medium (*vācaka*), a general discussion of its essence—from the shallowest to the deepest—comprises briefly ten gates:

first, the gate of defining the essence through verbal expression; second, the gate of universally encompassing that which is expressed (*vācya*); third, the gate of pervasively including all phenomena; fourth, the gate of dependent origination as mind-only; fifth, the gate of integrating conditions to enter reality; sixth, the gate of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena; seventh, the gate of the mutual inclusion and fusion of phenomena; eighth, the gate of the infinite interpenetration like Indra’s net; ninth, the gate of the clear manifestation like a sea-seal; and tenth, the gate of the perfect completeness of the principal and its attendants.
The first section consists of two parts:
first, the analysis of the Hīnayāna, and second, the revelation of the Mahāyāna.
Within the former, there are three explanations by various masters based on the Sarvāstivāda school.
One school says:
Only the bodies of names (nāma-kāya), phrases (pada-kāya), and phonemes (vyañjana-kāya) constitute the essence of the teaching.
Therefore, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* asks: "What is the intrinsic nature of the twelve divisions of the scriptures?"
Answer: "The name-body, phrase-body, and phoneme-body abiding in succession, etc. One says:

Because sound is virtuous, it constitutes the essence of the Buddha’s teaching; whereas names (*nāman*) and so forth, being indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), constitute the functional activity of the teaching.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 126, states: "What is the Buddha’s teaching?"

Answer: It refers to the Buddha’s speech, utterances, discourses, vocal sounds, vocal paths, and vocal intimation; this is the Buddha’s teaching, which, in brief, has the vocal karma of the speaker as its essence.
"What phenomena does the Buddha’s word refer to? Answer:

"It refers to the collection of names (*nāmakāya*), the collection of phrases (*padakāya*), and the collection of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*), arranged in sequence, distributed in sequence, and joined in sequence; this collectively reveals the functional activity of the Buddha's teaching."
The commentary explains:
According to the correct interpretation of the *Vibhāṣā* masters, sound is their essence.

Since the Sautrāntika school also maintains that sound constitutes their nature, the fourteenth fascicle of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* refutes the Sautrāntikas by stating: "You should not establish that the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and syllables (*vyañjanakāya*) have sound as their very essence."

Furthermore, Asvabhāva’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* refutes that [position], stating: "To claim that the phrases and words of the various sūtras constitute its intrinsic nature is unreasonable; for the former [the sūtra] belongs to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), while the latter [the words] belong to the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*)."
Furthermore, based on the two preceding explanations, the virtuous masters collectively take [the phonemes] as the essence of the teaching; the rest is as stated there.
Within the Mahāyāna school, there are four propositions:

first, subsuming the provisional under the real, where sound alone is the essence, because names and so forth are merely provisionally established through the modification of sound and possess no separate essence.
Wu-xing’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* states: "The term 'bodhisattva' is established based on the great vow.
The *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* states: "'Derived from accomplishment' refers to the speech of the noble ones (*ārya*)."
The two categories [of names and phrases] are conventionally distinct from the reality [of sound], because they take names and so forth as their intrinsic nature.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle 2, states: "If names, phrases, and so forth were not distinct from sound, then there would be no difference between the objects of the unimpeded knowledges of dharmas and of expression."
Third, the combined discussion of the provisional and the real, including both sounds and names, and so forth.
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "There are those who perform the Buddha-work through sounds, speech, and written characters."
In the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is said that the speaker speaks by means of two things, and the listener hears by means of two things, namely: sound and names.
Question:
According to this school, sound manifests good and evil, yet sound itself is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, since names, phrases, and syllables are by nature indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), how can that which is indeterminate constitute the substance of the Noble Teaching?
Answer: If they are transformations of a contaminated mind (*sāsrava-citta*), they may indeed be indeterminate; however—
If the teachings are spoken by a Buddha or Bodhisattva through subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), they are all subsumed under the category of the wholesome.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Upon what basis do they rely? It refers to vocal sounds and virtuous syllables."
The fourfold combination of the provisional and the real is simultaneously extinguished; it is neither sound nor name, because it is identical with emptiness and because speech is itself non-speech.
As the *Vimalakīrti* says: "The nature of letters is detached; this is liberation."

In the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, wind is used as a metaphor for sound and painting as a metaphor for names; just as the wind moving through tree leaves or a painting on a wall can be perceived, the wind in the sky and a painting in the air cannot both be perceived.
One should know that the names of the Mahāyāna sounds are likewise so; they are all ungraspable because their characteristics are exhausted.
These four preceding lines constitute a single teaching-essence; therefore, the non-obstruction of emptiness and existence is called the Mahāyāna Dharma.
This means that emptiness is not different from existence; this existence is illusory existence, and while illusory existence is manifest, its entire substance is emptiness.
Existence is not different from emptiness; this emptiness is true emptiness, and while true emptiness is serene, its entire substance is existence.
Therefore, there is not even a hair’s breadth of distinction between emptiness and existence.
Thus, the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states: "If any phenomenon were not empty by even as much as a hair-tip, then no Buddhas would appear in the world."
Furthermore, it says below: "All phenomena are ultimately empty; not even the slightest mark exists. There are many such instances.

Second, regarding the gate of comprehensively encompassing the signified meaning: this does not merely involve taking up the teaching as the signifier as described before, but also gradually and comprehensively takes up the signified meanings, because both are dharmas that are to be known and understood.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 81, states: "The essence of all sūtras is briefly of two kinds:
first, the letter; second, the meaning.
The letter is that which is relied upon; the meaning is that which relies upon it."
"These two types are collectively termed the 'entirety of the objects of all that is knowable.
The commentary explains:
"This is because the meaning is made manifest by relying upon the text."
Regarding the third cycle, which encompasses all dharma-gates: this means that all dharmas constitute the essence of the teaching.
This is also of two kinds:
first, conditioned dharmas; second, unconditioned dharmas, because that which is unconditioned cannot bring about the arising of awakening.

As stated below, the jeweled ground, fragrant trees, cloud-palaces, and the Dharma-gates of the Dharma-realm—such as the Flower Garland—are all none other than Buddha-activities. Just as the Bodhisattva Supreme Sound and the lotus flower upon which he sits encompass the person, the Dharma, the teaching, the meaning, the practice, the stages, cause and effect, and principle and phenomenon, they are collectively capable of generating resolute understanding and conduct; therefore, they are all the substance of the teaching.
This can be understood through reflection.

Regarding the fourth gate, the Dependent Origination as Mind-Only: all these aforementioned differentiated teachings are, without exception, manifestations of mind-only; therefore, they all take consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) as their essence.
However, there are two meanings:
first, the mutual correspondence between the original and its reflection; second, the complete inclusion of both speaker and listener.
Regarding the first, which generally elucidates all teachings, there are four propositions in total:

First, there is the position that only the fundamental [consciousness] exists and there are no images (*nimitta*), as in the teachings of the Hīnayāna; because it does not accept the manifestation through the transformation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), many masters such as Dharmatrāta have established this doctrine.

The second is both the original and the reflection, as in the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna: outside the minds of sentient beings, the Buddha possesses subtle and wondrous dharmas such as form and sound; through the power of the superior conditions of the listener’s roots of goodness striking the Buddha’s altruistic activities as the cause, mental images of words and meanings arise within the Buddha’s wisdom, constituting the teaching of the original nature and characteristics.

By the power of this teaching of the Buddha acting as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), it strikes the seeds of wholesome roots—both outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*)—of those who hear the Dharma; thus, for the consciousness of the listener, the aspects of word and meaning arise as the aspect of an image (*pratibimba*). This is the teaching of the "aspect of the image."
The *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Through the successive power of mutual predominance, the two consciousnesses become determinate.
Masters such as Dharmapāla all establish this principle.

Third, there are cases where there are only reflections and no original substance, as in the Final Teaching of the Mahāyāna. Apart from the minds of sentient beings, the Buddha-fruit possesses no material body, nor any speech, activities, or marks of merit; it consists only of suchness (*tathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*). With great compassion and great vows acting as dominant conditions, they cause the manifestations of the Buddha’s form and voice preaching the Dharma to appear within the minds of those disciples whose faculties have matured. Therefore, the holy teachings are solely the images within the minds of sentient beings.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "All Tathāgatas have no teaching of the Buddha-dharma; yet, according to those who are to be transformed, they expound the Dharma for them.

It further says: "The Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is inconceivable—without form, without marks, and without peer—but it manifests physical forms for the sake of sentient beings, so that throughout the ten directions, there is none who undergoes transformation and does not see it."
It is not only this that is so; masters such as Nāgārjuna and Sthiramati have all established this same principle.

The fourth [case] is neither the original nor the reflection. As in the Sudden Teaching (tun-jiao), it is not simply that there are no Buddha-forms outside of the mind; rather, the Buddhas manifested within the minds of sentient beings are likewise empty of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnya*). This is because they are merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) and lack any separate reflections; because the nature of form and so forth is detached from existence and non-existence; and because all things are beyond words, and even "beyond words" is itself non-existent. Therefore, the sacred teaching is precisely the teaching of no-teaching.
As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, nor is there any parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* clarifies that the Buddha is eternally present within the dharmadhātu, such that there is no time when he does not appear in the world.
The schools of Nāgārjuna and others frequently establish this principle.

These four preceding explanations constitute a single teaching; they are perfectly integrated and unimpeded, such that none obstructs another, because each sacred teaching encompasses sentient beings by proceeding from the shallow to the profound.
This can be seen through reflection.
Regarding the second point—that both teaching and hearing are fully subsumed—there are likewise four propositions:
first, apart from the Buddha-mind, there are no sentient beings to be transformed, much less the teachings spoken; therefore, these are manifested solely by the Buddha-mind.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that sentient beings have no separate self-substance; rather, they are formed by grasping the *tathāgatagarbha* to constitute themselves as sentient beings.

Since this *tathāgatagarbha* is realized as the very self-substance of the Buddha’s wisdom, therefore the entire being of every sentient being is wholly contained within the mind of the Buddha’s wisdom.
The subsequent text states: "All Buddhas fully understand that everything evolves from the mind.

It further says: "Within the Bodhi-body of the Tathāgata, one sees all sentient beings giving rise to the bodhicitta, practicing the bodhisattva path, and attaining equal and perfect enlightenment; even seeing all sentient beings enter the quiescence of nirvana is likewise so."
"All are of a single nature, because they lack inherent nature.

It further says: "All kalpas of the three periods of time, all Buddha-fields and all phenomena, all sense faculties, minds, and mental factors—all these illusory phenomena are fully manifested within the body of a single Buddha."

Furthermore, the second chapter of the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, the "Tathāgatagarbha" chapter, states: "All sentient beings are entirely within the wisdom of the Tathāgata; therefore, they are called a 'garbha' (store)."

Because the wisdom of suchness accords with the object of suchness, no sentient being whatsoever can ever transcend the realm of suchness; since all are sustained by the Tathāgata, sentient beings who are thus contained are called the *tathāgatagarbha* (the womb/embryo of the Tathāgata).
Therefore, apart from the Buddha’s mind of wisdom, not a single dharma can be found.
Second, [the Buddha's qualities] are collectively present within the minds of sentient beings, because there are no distinct Buddha-qualities apart from the minds of sentient beings.
What is the meaning of this?

The Buddha realizes Buddhahood by attesting to the *tathatā* (suchness) within the minds of sentient beings; furthermore, because initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) is identical to fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), it is therefore entirely present within the minds of sentient beings as the arising of function from the essence. At the time of the response-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) and transformation-body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*), this is precisely the great function of the *tathatā* within the minds of sentient beings, and there is no separate Buddha apart from this.
This meaning is extensively elucidated in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
Furthermore, the text below states: "If one wishes to seek knowledge of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should contemplate in this way: the mind creates all Tathāgatas."
"According to any one of the three scriptural authorities, the entirety [of the teaching] consists of only two minds, because the former two explanations are inseparable.

That is to say: within the mind of a sentient being, the Buddha preaches the Dharma for the sake of the sentient beings within his own mind; within the Buddha’s mind, the sentient beings listen as the Buddha of the sentient beings' minds preaches the Dharma. In this way, the preaching and listening are fully encompassed without obstruction; this is called the profound principle of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only)."

Fourth, both that holy teaching and those two minds are neither [existent nor non-existent], because they mutually cancel each other out and do not manifest simultaneously; and because when the two positions are fused as a pair, there is nothing that is not subsumed.

This means that in the Buddha-mind there is no listener among sentient beings, and in the sentient-being-mind there is no speaker who is the Buddha; thus both are doubly subsumed, for the two characteristics are exhausted.
The Sūtra says: "Now, as for those who preach the Dharma, there is neither preaching nor demonstration; likewise, as for those who listen to the Dharma, there is neither hearing nor attainment.
Furthermore, the subsequent passage states: "That which sentient beings are born is not truly birth, nor is there any transmigrating within the cycle of birth and death."
Furthermore, a sutra states: "The Tathāgata does not preach the Dharma, nor does he deliver sentient beings.
Such passages as these demonstrate that these four [principles] are perfectly integrated and unimpeded within a single holy teaching; only then do they constitute the ultimate truth.
Regarding the fifth section, the "Gate of Entering Reality by Harmonizing Conditions," there are also two meanings:
first, subsuming the derivative within the fundamental; second, harmonizing appearances to reveal the nature.
In the first of these, since all sacred teachings flow from the Truth, they are eternally not different from the true nature, just as the tides arising from the ocean do not lose their salty flavor.

In the treatises, these are termed the twelvefold teaching flowing from True Suchness (*tathatā*), and it is also said that they are the teachings that flow equally from the most pure Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, when the root subsumes the branches, it is solely True Suchness.

Regarding the second point, the mutual manifestation of characteristics revealing the nature: it means that all those various differentiated teachings arise from conditions; because they arise from conditions, they necessarily lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because they lack intrinsic nature, they are precisely suchness (*tathatā*).
