From the third chapter, "On Names and Titles," down to the eighth assembly, it is called the Section on Revealing the Path and Encouraging Practice;
fourth, the verses spoken by Samantabhadra at the very end are called the Section on Entrustment and Circulation.
Now, further examining the subsequent text, it is divided into five general sections:
first, the "Section on the Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching";
second, within the "Śāṇa Chapter," a complete cycle of question and answer titled the "Section on Presenting the Fruit to Encourage Joyful Faith."
Third, the cycle of questions and answers from the second assembly to the sixth assembly is called the Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generating Understanding;
fourth, the cycle of questions and answers within the seventh assembly is called the Section on Entrusting Oneself to the Dharma to Advance in Practice and Accomplish Conduct;
fifth, the cycle of questions and answers within the eighth assembly is called the Section on Relying on Persons to Enter Realization and Accomplish Virtue.
The presence or absence of the [five] sections has been explained above.

These five parts all arise from the preceding to initiate the succeeding; their textual sequence generates one another, and their principles and meanings are complete and sufficient. Therefore, there is neither addition nor subtraction.
Within the initial introductory section, there are two parts:
first, the exposition of the introductory section within this land; second, the exposition of the introductory sections throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions.
The beginning consists of three parts:
first, there are four characters that serve solely as the "testimony of faith";
second, from the words "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) onwards, it serves both as the introductory sequence.
3. From "The Earth Trembles" onwards, it refers exclusively to the arousal [of the mind].
If one considers it in relation to what follows, there can be four possibilities:
either only the realization and faith belong to the beginning; or only the arousal belongs to the end; or both belong to the middle; or neither belongs to the main body of the teaching at the end.

Furthermore, the first four characters have a universal meaning but a restricted textual application; because they appear at the very beginning of the text, their meaning extends throughout all eight assemblies.

From "At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) onwards, the textual application is universal but the meaning is restricted; since the subsequent assemblies all contain phrases such as "at that time," the textual application is universal;
however, as this [phrase] is restricted to the beginning, its meaning is restricted.
Furthermore, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, this is divided into five parts:

first, a general indication that [the teaching] has been heard; second, the time when the teaching arose; third, the manifestation of the Teacher; fourth, the place where the teaching arose; and fifth, the capacity of the audience for whom the teaching was intended.
According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* and other sources, there are six introductory elements (nidāna):
first, faith; second, hearing; third, time; fourth, the teacher; fifth, the location; and sixth, the assembly.
Now, in explaining this meaning, I shall briefly establish four sections:

first, clarifying the reasons for the establishment of these six meanings; second, distinguishing the direct transmission of what was heard; third, identifying the person who transmitted the Dharma; and fourth, explaining the text itself.
The reason these six propositions are established at the beginning consists of six points.
First is the establishment by the Buddha's teaching.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, as the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, he addressed Ānanda:
"The twelve divisions of the scriptures, you shall propagate and circulate.
He further addressed Upāli:
"All the precepts and rules of discipline, you shall receive and uphold."
He addressed Aniruddha, saying:
"You have attained the divine eye; you shall constantly guard the relics and exhort others to make offerings.
He then addressed the great assembly:
"Even if I were to remain for an eon, or slightly less than an eon, I would eventually have to pass away.
Having said this, he lay down with his head toward the north beneath the twin śāla trees, intending to enter parinirvāṇa.
Ānanda’s love for his kinsmen was not yet extinguished, and his mind was submerged in an ocean of grief. Aniruddha said to Ānanda,
“Although the World-Honored One is present today, tomorrow he will no longer be.”
"You should inquire of him regarding matters of future importance; for what reason have you fainted like these foolish people?
Ānanda immediately rose and asked, "I do not know what matter I should now request to ask."
The *Loudou jiao* states:
"There are four essential matters:

first, [the question of] those who personally received the teachings from the Tathāgata while he was in the world, all of whom accepted them with faith; second, after the extinction of the Tathāgata, what words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras?"

The second question asks: while the Tathāgata is in the world, the bhikṣus take the Buddha as their teacher; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, whom shall they take as their teacher? The third question asks:
while the Buddha was in the world, the bhikṣus dwelt in reliance upon the Buddha; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, in reliance upon whom shall they dwell?
The fourth question was: "When the Tathāgata was in the world, he disciplined the ill-natured Chandaka himself; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how shall we dwell together with him?
Ānanda questioned according to these instructions.
The World-Honored One replied:
"At the beginning of the sūtra, one should place these six phrases.
Second, he said:
The bhikṣus all take the Prātimokṣa as their teacher.
Thirdly, it is said:
they all abide in reliance upon the four foundations of mindfulness.
The four types of monks of evil character are to be disciplined through *brahmadaṇḍa*.

This is called "silent exclusion. If their minds become supple and submissive, they are to be taught the *Kātyāyanāvavāda-sūtra*, which is here called the "Sūtra on Departing from Existence and Non-existence," in order to destroy their prideful mind.
Furthermore, in the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Ānanda requested the Buddha:
"How should the Dharma-eye be compiled?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, a bhikṣu of great virtue should ask:
'In what place did the World-Honored One preach the Mahā-Apadāna and other such sūtras?
You should answer him thus:"
Thus have I heard.

At one time, while residing in the kingdom of Magadha, he first attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree and preached the Dharma; [the text continues] until it says he preached the Dharma between the twin śāla trees.

In this manner, the sūtras spoken in more than twenty such locations were personally entrusted by the Buddha to Ānanda for compilation; therefore, these six phrases constitute the established teaching of the Buddha.
The second reason for establishing these six phrases is to eliminate doubts.
As the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha stated:

"According to the *Sūkṣma-vinaya*, when Ānanda ascended the high seat to compile the Dharma-piṭaka, his body was like that of the Buddha, complete with the primary and secondary marks; when he descended from the seat, he returned to his original form."
When the assembly saw this auspicious omen, they again gave rise to three doubts:
first, they doubted that the Great Teacher, the Buddha, out of compassion had arisen from *nirvāṇa* to preach the Dharma once more for the sake of the multitude;
second, they doubted that the Buddha-Sage had come from another direction.
There are three doubts concerning Ānanda’s transformation into a Buddha.
Now, in order to eliminate these three doubts, six phrases have been established.

Therefore, when Ānanda himself declares, "Such a Dharma as this I have heard from the Buddha," it is clearly understood that this was not the Buddha speaking again, nor did a Buddha from another direction come, nor did Ānanda himself become a Buddha; rather, it is simply because the power of the Dharma has caused him to resemble the Buddha.
Third, it is for the sake of generating faith in those of the future.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The reason why time, direction, persons, and so forth are placed at the beginning of all sūtras is that one wishes to cause faith to arise."
Fourth, it is because it avoids the faults of addition and subtraction.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "One should know that the statement 'Thus have I heard' is intended to avoid the faults of addition, subtraction, and heterogeneity."

This means that such teachings were heard by me directly from the Buddha, not received through successive intermediaries; this demonstrates that the listener is capable, and that all that has been heard is free from the faults of exaggeration, underestimation, or deviation from the truth.
It is not as with the foolish who lack capability, who, upon hearing anything, may fail to avoid additions, omissions, or distortions.

When the teachings were being compiled, those who transmitted the Buddha’s instructions uttered these words at the outset of the discourse in order to inspire reverence, faith, and acceptance among sentient beings: "Such a Dharma I have heard from the Buddha. Thus, the words and their meanings are definitive, without any addition or omission. Therefore, those who hear it should, after listening correctly, reflect upon it according to reason, and should be encouraged to practice and study it.
Fifth, it is for the purpose of ceasing all disputes.
If one were to compose [the treatise] oneself, disputes would arise; therefore, it is not so.
This is explained according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Sixth, because it differs from the non-Buddhist paths.
Those non-Buddhist scriptures and treatises were either said to have been obtained when a stone cliff collapsed or brought by a blue magpie; therefore, they are not to be trusted.
Therefore, I shall now fully set forth these details to clarify that the Dharma is not erroneous, so that people may believe and accept it.
Second, regarding the distinction between what was heard directly and what was heard by tradition as exemplified by Ānanda and others, there are two explanations according to the Hīnayāna:

first, it is said that since Ānanda was born on the very night the Buddha attained enlightenment, he became a disciple of the Buddha at the age of twenty; thus, the sūtras from those twenty years onward were heard directly by him, while those prior to that were heard by tradition.
Therefore, the *Dharmacakrapravartana-sūtra* states: "At the time of Ānanda’s compilation [of the teachings], he himself spoke this verse:
'When the Buddha first preached the Dharma, at that time I was not present; thus I heard it through successive transmission.'"

The Buddha traveled to Vārāṇasī and turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths for the assembly of five bhikṣus; therefore, it is known that prior to this, [the teachings] were not heard directly from him.
A second view holds that all [teachings] were heard directly from him.
Therefore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "When Ānanda served as the Buddha’s attendant, he made this vow:
'I pray that you will teach me every single sutra spoken by the Buddha during the twenty years [of his ministry].'"
The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* also states this. Thus, it is known that [the Buddha] heard these teachings directly from him in all cases.

According to the Mahāyāna, there are two senses in which "all were heard directly": 1. [The Buddha] heard them directly from the Buddhas of the ten directions. 2. [The Buddha] heard them directly from Śākyamuni Buddha himself.
The Buddha spoke it again for him, as in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and other texts; the Buddha returned to his original location and spoke it once more for Ānanda.
Furthermore, as in the aforementioned *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke it in its entirety once more; therefore, this was heard directly from him.
Second, because Ānanda has constantly heard [the teachings].
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The learned Ānanda, whether present or absent, is naturally able to understand the meaning of the permanent and the impermanent."
Furthermore, it is said: "Ānanda attained the *bodhyaṅga-samādhi*, and thus he constantly heard the sūtras spoken by the Buddha, whether near or far.
Regarding the one who transmits the Dharma through the three concentrations, a question is raised:
At the time this sūtra was being preached, those of the two vehicles were as if deaf and blind; how could Ānanda have claimed, "I have heard"?
Answer: There are two points.
First, even if it were Ānanda, there would be no fault in this.
Why is this? According to the *Aśokarāja-saṃvarta-sūtra*, there are three kinds of Ānanda:
the first is Ānanda, here translated as "Joyful Celebration" (Qingxi), who upholds the Dharma-piṭaka of the śrāvakas and, according to his capacity and portion, serves the two higher vehicles.

The second was named Ānandabhadra, which translates as "Joyous and Virtuous. He upheld the Dharma-treasury of the Middle Vehicle; regarding the higher Mahāyāna, he practiced according to his strength and capacity, while for the lower Hīnayāna, he maintained it with ample leisure.
The third is Ānanda Sāgara, here translated as "Ocean of Joy"; this Bodhisattva upholds the Dharma-treasury of the Mahāyāna, while also comfortably maintaining the two lower vehicles.
According to this scriptural passage, it is logically consistent that Ānanda-sāgara is a great bodhisattva capable of upholding the Great Dharma.

However, according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), since these individuals who transmit the Dharma are all manifested within the Sea-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi) of Vairocana Buddha, they are, in fact, the Buddha himself.
The second [position] states that it was not transmitted by Ānanda; this is also logically uncontradicted.
Why? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "There are two types of teaching: first, the manifest teaching; second, the secret teaching."
"This *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is a teaching of explicit revelation; therefore, it was entrusted to Ānanda.
Just as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is a teaching of secret mystery, it was entrusted to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra," and so forth.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The sūtras not yet heard by Ānanda shall be propagated and circulated by the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha.
According to this, it is the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha who utters the formula "Thus have I heard."

Furthermore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is Mañjuśrī who utters "Thus have I heard," for that treatise states: "Mañjuśrī and Ānanda compiled the Mahāyāna Piṭaka in another pure location."

Furthermore, in the *Mañjuśrīparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is stated that four hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Mañjuśrī was still present in the world; therefore, we know that he transmitted this Dharma.
Fourth, the explanation of the text.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, "tathā" (如) means "conformity";
"ā" (是) means "faith," and it also means "seal."
Thus, [the Buddha] was immediately accepted with faith by Indra, and therefore it is said, "Thus" (*evam*).
This term "Thus" summarizes the textual meaning of the entire work; that is, it refers to the Dharma he himself heard, and thus it is called "Thus."
According to the Tripitaka Master Dīrghaśroṇa, the explanation is given in terms of the Three Jewels:
first, regarding the Buddha, it means that what the Buddha has spoken is what I have heard, and what I have heard is what the Buddha has spoken.
Second, regarding the Dharma: "What I have heard is a discourse that accords with principle; what I have transmitted is a teaching that accords with principle.

Third, regarding the Saṃgha: "What I have heard is that which has been heard in common by all these Bodhisattvas; what I have transmitted is that which has been heard in common by all those Bodhisattvas."
According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, it is said that those who transmit the Buddha’s teachings state: "Such a matter I have heard in the past.
This general statement functions according to four meanings:
first, based on analogy; second, based on instruction; third, based on question and answer; and fourth, based on authorization. A detailed explanation is as found in that treatise.
The "self within" refers to the provisional entity consisting of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Generally speaking, there are four kinds of self:
first, the true self, which refers to the permanence, bliss, self, and purity within True Suchness (*tathatā*), having True Suchness as its intrinsic nature.
Second is the self as a sovereign, which refers to the eight types of sovereign selves and so forth, having wisdom as their nature;
third is the conventional self, which refers to the provisional entity of the five aggregates, having that which appears as a master and so forth—manifested by consciousness-only—as its nature;
fourth is the grasped self, which has that which is grasped by both conceptual and innate [ignorance] as its nature.
Furthermore, there are also four types of minds that take me as their object:
first, the view [of a self], which refers to ordinary worldlings;
second, pride, which refers to those in training (śaikṣas).
The third [type] is that of practice, referring to those beyond training (aśaikṣa);
the fourth is that which conforms to worldly convention, referring to the Buddhas.
Among these four types of "self," the first three are all applicable.
Judging according to the provisional teachings, among the latter four [teachings], it is unique to the first; however, it may also be applied to the latter three—contemplate this accordingly.
Why is it that "no-self" is not mentioned, yet "self" is spoken of?

This is said for the sake of manifesting direct hearing, for the sake of linguistic convenience, in accordance with worldly convention, and to manifest non-self; all as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Question:
Why does the transmitter of the Dharma not refer to himself by name, but instead uses the pronoun "I"?
Answer: Because there would be the fault of confusing it with other things that share the same name.
Question:
"Am I not proficient? Answer:
Since 'I' has already been mentioned, it necessarily refers to oneself and serves to distinguish one from others."
Question:
Why does it not say "heard by the ear"? Answer:
This is because the general encompasses the particular.
Question:
The ear merely hears sounds; how can it possibly understand them?
Answer: The ear hears the sound, while the mind understands the meaning and so forth; these are combined as non-dual, and thus it is said that "hearing" occurs through their conjunction.

According to the Sarvāstivāda, the sense organ hears; according to the *Tattvasiddhi*, consciousness hears; according to the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, hearing occurs through their conjunction—this is precisely emptiness and non-action.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Hearing occurs due to the conjunction of four conditions:

first, the faculty of hearing is unimpaired; second, the sound is within the range of audibility; third, there is no obstruction between them; and fourth, there is the desire to hear. Because of these, one hears."
Therefore, this hearing is "not-hearing-hearing. Furthermore, it possesses ten conditions:

first, the foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as the fundamental support; second, the seeds of the auditory consciousness as the causal condition support; third, the manas as the defiled support; fourth, the mental consciousness as the discriminative support; fifth, its own kind of auditory consciousness as the immediately preceding support; sixth, the unimpaired faculty of hearing as the support of the same object; seventh, the attention (*manaskāra*) with the desire to hear; eighth, the presence of an object as the objective condition; ninth, the absence of obstacles in the interval; and tenth, the proximity of the object such that it is within the range of hearing, which also applies to other factors being unobstructed, and so forth.
Therefore, this "hearing" is the non-hearing of hearing because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the teaching, this should be distinguished accordingly.
From "At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) onwards applies to both prefaces; that is, the latter four phrases within the six phrases.
Among these, the first three are explained together—namely, the time, the teacher, and the location;
the last one is explained separately—namely, the assembly of fellow listeners.
This should also be understood as corresponding to the three worlds.
The preceding section also has two parts:
first, a general indication of the three characteristics; second, a detailed explanation of the three meanings starting from "Just attained perfect enlightenment.
Why are there these two sections?
This means that with respect to the locus (*sthāna*), the former passage mentions both the defiled and the pure in general, while the latter specifically reveals the characteristics of the pure.
Furthermore, the former relies upon the defiled as a point of reference, while the latter specifically distinguishes the pure.

Moreover, because there is a beginning and an end in time, defilement and purity in locus, and shallowness and depth in the Buddha, it is necessary to provide this repeated analysis and clarification.

The first of the three [sections] within the preceding [part]: regarding "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*), according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, it refers either to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) or to a long succession [of moments]; however, it is taken to mean the completion of both the preaching and the listening. Therefore, it is collectively designated as a conventional construct, "one time."
In the Hīnayāna, this refers to actual time; in the Mahāyāna, it is a provisional designation.
To explain it separately, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* of the Liang dynasty, "one time" has three meanings:
first, the time of equality, meaning there is no sinking or floating, nor any inversion.
Second, at the time of their conjunction, it means causing the hearing, the capacity for hearing, and correct hearing;
third, at the time of turning the wheel of Dharma, it means correct preaching and correct reception.
Regarding the two aspects of "Buddha," it has the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*), and there are two types: original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) and initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*).
Furthermore, the treatise states: "It is like the blooming of a lotus flower, like awakening from sleep," and so forth.
This refers to first awakening to what is known, and subsequently awakening from afflictions.
Alternatively, there are three types of awakening, namely: [awakening] for oneself, for others, and to fulfillment; one who possesses such awakening is called an "awakened one" (buddha).
Alternatively, he is named Bhagavat, which has four meanings as explained in the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
first, "possessing virtue," because *bhaga* means virtue and *vat* means to possess;
second, "skillful discrimination," because *bhaga* means discrimination and *vat* means skillful.
The third is named Yaśas, where "Ya" signifies existence and "Śas" signifies renown;
the fourth is named Vighuṣṭa, where "Vi" signifies the ability to destroy and "Ghuṣṭa" signifies lust, anger, and so forth. Thus, "Vighuṣṭa" means one who can destroy lust, anger, and ignorance.
Among these four, the first is general and the latter three are specific.
Within the specific ones, the first refers to the quality of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), the second to the quality of merit (*puṇya-guṇa*), and the last to the quality of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* provides an explanation based on six meanings; its verse states: "Sovereignty, brilliance, and physical excellence, renown, auspiciousness, and nobility."
"Because it possesses these six kinds of distinct meanings, it is collectively designated as 'Bhagavat'.
The detailed explanation is as found therein.

Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, citing the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, provides an explanation based on ten meanings, stating that "Buddha" means awakening, supreme, the celestial drum, and so forth.
Regarding the "three locations," the country is general while the site is specific.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "He attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the village of Uruvilvā on the banks of the Nairañjanā River in the kingdom of Magadha," and so forth.
This is called the "Land of Non-Harming," because within this country, those who commit offenses are subject only to banishment and punishment, and there is no execution.
This serves as a representation of the characteristics of the Great Dharma’s compassionate salvation.
It is also called the Land of Good Victory (Suśāsanā).
Or it is called Magadha; this is the name of a lunar mansion, here translated as "Not Evil," which presides over the twelfth month.
*Dha* means "place."
It is called the Land of No Evil and also the Land of Star-Abodes.
There are four meanings of "quiescence" (*śānti*):
first, the cessation of hindrances, which refers to both natural cessation and cessation through antidotes.
Second, because it realizes the principle of cessation.
Third, because it manifests the virtue of cessation, namely by revealing the ten bodies of the Buddha as well as the dharmas of Samantabhadra and others.
As the Sūtra says: "The Great Parinirvāṇa is able to establish the great meaning."
It can be understood that because the four benefits of aiding sentient beings bring about cessation,
there are likewise four aspects to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*): first, the physical location;
Second, the practice, as in the sutra passage: "Generosity is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)," and so forth;
third, the principle, as in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "All phenomena are the site of enlightenment, because one knows all phenomena to be empty," and so forth;

fourth, its pervasion of all phenomena—meaning that all things, such as persons and so on, are analogously understood as being called "sites of enlightenment" because they are places where the Path is attained, according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analysis.
It is also like a worldly threshing floor, where chaff and filth are winnowed away to select the genuine grain.

Here, too, it is the same: by extinguishing delusions and accomplishing virtues, one attains the Path; thus, the Path itself is the "field," and the term is applied according to its functional identity (*karmadhāraya*).

Regarding the "site of practice" (*kṣetra*), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "In the center of Jambudvīpa, a diamond throne (*vajrāsana*) rises from the diamond ground, extending through the earth of Jambudvīpa to its upper limit; therein all bodhisattvas cultivate the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*)."
Why is this? Because there is no other basis or capacity capable of receiving this samādhi.
"All bodhisattvas" refers to the thousand bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Below the section "Beginning the Attainment of Perfect Enlightenment," the second part provides a detailed analysis of the three preceding meanings.
First, it analyzes the time; second, the locations; and third, the principal figures.
Within the analysis of time, there are provisionally five sections:
There are five parts: first, defining the scope; second, subsuming what precedes and follows; third, revealing distinctions; fourth, indicating the doctrine;
and fifth, explaining the main text. Regarding the first, defining the scope, Bodhiruci states:

"Among the eight assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka*, the first five assemblies were preached during the first seven days after the Buddha’s enlightenment; the sixth assembly and those following were preached during the second seven days, because the beginning of the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* refers to the 'second seven days.'"
Furthermore, some say that the eighth assembly was preached at a later time, because in that text there are Śāriputra and the other five hundred śrāvakas, all of whom were ordained at a later time.
These interpretations likely do not accord with the text, for it is certain that no Dharma was preached during the first seven days.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "For what reason was nothing preached during the first seven days?"
"Because one contemplates the practice of dependent origination.
Since it says "contemplates," it is clearly known that this does not refer to the teaching of the Dharma.
Suppose there is a defense stating:
If one merely says that the ten stages are not being taught, yet does not say that other dharmas are not being taught, then it cannot be said that there is contemplation.
Furthermore, the subsequent treatise explains: "It is for the sake of manifesting the joy in one's own dharma that [the Buddha] does not speak [of them]."
Thus, we know for certain that the first seven assemblies certainly do not refer to the *Śrāvaka-piṭaka*.

Furthermore, the eighth assembly cannot belong to a later period; how could it be that half of one collection of sūtras was spoken first, the remaining sūtras were spoken in the middle, and only later was the sequence resumed?
How could it be that the Buddha lacks the power of *dhāraṇī*, such that he cannot expound all dharmas in a single thought-moment?
Jeta Grove and Śāriputra both involve the mutual interpenetration of the nine periods of time; as the subsequent text states: "All past kalpas are placed within the future and the present."
"All kalpas of the future are placed within the past.
It also says, "Within a single thought-moment, one establishes all the Buddha-activities of the three periods of time," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Such passages exist everywhere throughout the scriptures; how could the Śāriputra and the Jetavana used here not belong to this same category?
Thus, we know that this sutra was certainly preached during the second seven-day period.
Regarding the second point, the inclusion of what precedes and follows, there are three layers:
first, it is held that during these two periods of seven days, the eight assemblies were taught simultaneously.
If this is so, why would there be a sequence of before and after?
Answer: It is like the inscription on a seal; when one reads it, the sequence of before and after [in the mind] occurs simultaneously with the impression upon the paper.
Question:
If that is so, how can their repeated meeting be established? Answer:
Their repetition also occurs simultaneously because they are unimpeded, just as the light of lamps interpenetrates one another.
The remaining points, such as immovability and ascending to heaven, can be understood by following this explanation.
Second, at this very moment, all the immeasurable eons preceding and following it are entirely subsumed and exhausted, because this is the time of inconceivable liberation.
Third, regarding the inclusion within the infinitely layered eons and thoughts: this is because they are gathered and contained within one another like Indra’s net.

Third, regarding the manifestation of distinctions: according to the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*, during the second seven-day period at the Deer Park, he turned the Wheel of the Four Truths three times for those five men; this is the Hīnayāna.

According to the *Guhyakapuruṣa-sūtra*, on the second week, when the Deer Park was being used to turn the Wheel of Dharma for an immeasurable great assembly, there were those who attained the paths of Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva; these constitute the Three Vehicles.

According to this sutra, during the second seven-day period, beneath the King of Trees, he turned the inexhaustible wheel of Dharma for the assembly of bodhisattvas of the ocean-like multitude, clarifying that this is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Regarding the statement that "the three above are simultaneous": from the perspective of the Dharma, it signifies that the fundamental and the derivative are simultaneous; from the perspective of persons, it reveals that the capacities and responses of sentient beings differ.
According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it was twenty-one days;
according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it was six or seven days;
and according to the *Udāna-varga* (or *Qǐxìng xíng jīng*), it was forty-nine days.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it was eight weeks;
according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fifty-seven days;
and according to the *Dvādaśayātra-sūtra*, it was said to be one year.

These differences arise because the capacities of those to be trained (*vineya*) vary in the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*), such that they each require distinct instructions; thus, the teachings differ.
In the fundamental teaching (*mūla-śāsana*), the capacity of the trainees is fixed, and therefore there are only two [weeks] times seven [days].
Regarding the four [aspects] representing the Dharma, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Because it displays excellence through the comparison of time, place, and so forth."
"Because this Dharma is supreme, it is taught at the initial time and in the superior location.
This has three meanings:
first, this sutra refers to the initial time to indicate that the fundamental Dharma is supreme.
Second, the teaching of the end is likewise the same, because the manifestation of the end does not depart from the root.
Third, it reveals that the root is not the end; for while the time of the end is indeterminate, the time of the root is determinate.
The duration of the root is fixed at two weeks, with no other explanation.
Fifth, regarding the explanation of the text: "Attaining Perfect Enlightenment for the First Time" signifies the meaning of the very beginning.
Furthermore, there are two aspects:
first, the initial seven days, which mark the beginning of his present existence; second, the second seven days, which mark the beginning of his preaching the Dharma.
In this context, it has been seven days since he attained perfect enlightenment; therefore, it is said that he "has just attained perfect enlightenment.
Generally, there are five meanings:

first, according to the Hīnayāna, the *janmakāya* Buddha attained perfect enlightenment for the first time beneath this tree through thirty-four moments of mind; like the various arhats, this is a true attainment rather than a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Second, regarding the Mahāyāna, it refers to the manifestation of the eightfold transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), wherein he first attains perfect enlightenment.

Third, regarding the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*), it refers to the moment when the practices of the ten stages are fulfilled; following the path of non-interruption (*ānantaryamārga*), the fruit manifests with perfect clarity, which is termed "first attaining perfect enlightenment."
Fourth, regarding the Dharma-body: it is said to be "initially accomplished" because it first manifests in its perfect entirety as the newly attained efficient cause.
In the Mahāyāna above this, there is no beginning to a beginning.

Fifth, regarding the ten Buddhas: this refers to the fact that throughout all the infinite worlds of Indra’s net, in every single thought-moment, each attains initial Buddhahood, complete with principal and retinue, encompassing the entirety of the three worlds. Therefore, this includes the beginnings of immeasurable kalpas, both preceding and following.
Among these, the fifth alone is primary, while it also subsumes the preceding four; this may be understood by analogy.
This is because these five aspects are mutually inseparable and because they encompass the preparatory means (*upāya*).
"Regarding 'Its ground is vajra,'" the second section provides a detailed analysis of the location.
This is also divided into five gates:
first, determining the location; second, identifying its inclusion; third, clarifying its distinctions; fourth, representing the dharma; and fifth, explaining the original text.
Regarding the initial location: Question—
Is the place where this sutra was preached a pure land,
or is it a defiled realm?
If that were the case, what fault would there be? Both positions possess errors. Why?

If this is a pure land, why does the preceding passage refer to it as "the kingdom of Magadha," and the subsequent passage further refer to it as "Jambudvīpa among these four continents," and so forth?
From this, one should know that it is not a defiled land.

If it were a defiled land, why would the subsequent passage state, "This Lotus Treasury World-Ocean shook in six ways and eighteen modes," and so forth? This clearly demonstrates that this sutra was not preached in a defiled land.
Since these appear contradictory, how can they be definitively established? Answer:
Based solely on this sutra, the two lands of defilement and purity are fused and mutually inclusive, forming four propositions:
Alternatively, it may be only the Sahā world, because the root follows from the branch;
or it may be only the Flower Treasury World, because the branch follows from the root.
These two cases have been explained above.

Alternatively, they may appear as a pair, because the Saṃbhava-kṣetra (the Flower Treasury World) possesses the dual aspects of defilement and purity within the Sahā world; this is because the derivative depends upon the fundamental.
As the subsequent text states: "The Sahā world within the Flower Treasury realm"—this is what that refers to.
Alternatively, both defilement and purity may be transcended, for the ocean of fruition is ineffable.
These four preceding gates are combined into a single land; they are fused and unimpeded, such that any of them may be spoken of according to the occasion.
Second, regarding the clarification of inclusion within [the assembly], first, to explain the integration and inclusion, there are also three levels:
first, this awakening beneath the tree itself includes the eight assemblies among humans and devas; therefore, it is said in all cases that they do not depart from here.
Second, it encompasses the ten directions such that all lands without exception do not lie outside the shade of this king of trees.
Third, it encompasses the infinitely layered lands within a single speck of dust on the tip of a hair, like the net of Indra, for they are all contained within this Lotus Treasury World-realm.
Second, regarding integration, there are also three types, meaning that this tree of awakening is integrated into the locations subsumed within the preceding three layers.
Third, concerning the manifestation of distinctions: there are three kinds of places where the Buddha preached the sutras.

The first consists solely of the sixteen great kingdoms within the realm, which are the locations where the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) taught; these pertain to both the Hīnayāna and the teachings of the Three Vehicles.

The second refers exclusively to the locations where the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha teaches within the eighteen perfect and replete lands of the wondrous pure realms outside the [three] realms (*dhātu*), as described in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and other texts.

These wondrous pure realms are not subsumed within the three realms, yet they are not separate from them, because they pervade all places; this teaching applies to both the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle.

The third is the realm of the Lotus Treasury, where defilement and purity are perfectly interfused like an infinite Indra’s net, and which is the locus for the teachings of the ten Buddhas; therein, the primary and secondary worlds are fused together, encompassing the threefold world—this is exclusively the locus for the teaching of the Distinct Teaching of the One Vehicle.
What is now being analyzed refers strictly to the last one, while simultaneously encompassing the first two, because their root and branches are inseparable.
Regarding the fourth, the representation of phenomena: by relying on these superior bases, one represents the superiority of phenomena.
The *Dilun* states: "Because this Dharma is supreme, it is taught in a supreme location.
However, there are three levels of significance:

first, because he attained bodhi beneath this tree, he did not preach this teaching elsewhere; this clarifies that what is taught corresponds exactly to what was realized, for it does not change according to the varying capacities of different beings, as was the case with the teachings at the Deer Park and other locations.
Second, it relies upon the perfectly interfused Lotus Treasury World (*padmagarbha-dhātu*) to signify that what is taught is the blossoming of a perfect and sublime nature.

Third, it relies upon this locus of the multilayered Indra’s net (*indrājāla*) to signify that what is taught is likewise multilayered and inexhaustible, such as the inconceivable liberations (*acintya-vimokṣa*).
The remaining meanings are as explained in the "Chapter on the World.
Regarding the fifth [section], the explanation of the main text, there are three parts:

first, clarifying the site of the path; second, the Bodhi tree atop the ground; and third, the lion throne beneath the tree. Herein, the ground serves as the fundamental basis for practice, the tree represents the establishment of the virtues of practice, and the throne signifies the function of practice in gathering and benefiting others. Thus, like the nature of dependent origination, each element is entirely and completely integrated, encompassing all phenomena without exception.
However, these three stages are each analyzed through ten topical gates in the text.
Within the initial explanation of the site of the practice, there is a thesis, an exposition, and a conclusion.
In the thesis, the phrase "the ground is adamantine" indicates the essential nature of the ground, meaning that its substance is entirely unyielding.
The passage below stating that "the adamantine thick earth is indestructible" refers to this.

"Complete adornment and purity" characterizes the virtues of that ground; it means there is no aspect that is not adorned, as indicated in the subsequent text: "Within the ground of the Lotus Treasury World, the wind-circle is fully encompassed, with fragrant oceans, lotus kings, and so forth serving as its adornments and purities."
"The ground is endowed with wonderful jewel-luminous fragrant rivers and nets of trees.
Thus, because its pure virtues are perfectly complete above and below, it is said to be "endowed" (*paripūrṇa*).
Here, the absence of any impurity whatsoever is called "pure" (*śuddha*), and the absence of any virtue that is not fulfilled is called "adorned" (*vyūhita*).
Within the second section, the detailed explanation, ten phrases reveal ten kinds of pure adornments:

first, the pure adornment of jewel flowers; second, the pure adornment of jewel wheels; third, the pure adornment of exquisite colors; fourth, the pure adornment of banners and so forth; fifth, the pure adornment of fragrant garlands; sixth, the pure adornment of jewel nets; seventh, the pure adornment of raining jewels; eighth, the pure adornment of flowering trees; ninth, the pure adornment of the Buddha’s power; and tenth, the pure adornment of wonders.
Possessing these ten kinds, it is said to be "fully endowed with adornment and purity.
First, regarding the "adornment and purity of jewel-flowers," this refers to the various flowers made of many jewels possessing four meanings:
first, the meaning of subtlety; second, the meaning of blossoming; third, the meaning of producing fruit; and fourth, the meaning of adornment and purity.
The text below states: "Precious flowers cover all lands, fully able to nurture the merits of the Buddha.
Regarding the adornment and purity of the two precious wheels, it means that these precious wheels possess five meanings:
first, the meaning of perfection, because they are free from deficiency or diminution; [and so forth].
Second, the meaning of encompassing virtues, because it is complete with spokes, rims, and so forth;
third, the meaning of revolving motion, because it moves from this toward that;
fourth, the meaning of crushing delusions, because it is like grinding them to pieces.
The fifth meaning is "subjugation," because it is like the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) of a noble universal monarch (*cakravartin*).

Furthermore, "treasure" (*ratna*) carries the sense of being precious; as the subsequent text states: "Treasure-flowers of wondrous color form a radiant wheel, adorning and filling all dharma-realms, pervading everywhere throughout the ten directions."
"The three colors are adorned with purity; that is to say, this wondrous color possesses four meanings.
First is the meaning of brilliant manifestation, because it possesses both shape and color.
Second is the meaning of emptiness, because it stands while containing the void."
Third, it has the sense of being endowed with merit, because it encompasses all things;
fourth, it has the sense of being useful, because sentient beings obtain superior benefits upon seeing or hearing it.
As these categories are manifold, they are said to be "immeasurable."
Because there is nothing that is not adorned, it is called "majestic adornment" (*vyūha*).
This means that this ocean-receptacle is both deep and vast; it accumulates virtues and encompasses them to provide boundless benefit and nourishment, and is therefore said to be "like the ocean."
The ten characteristics of the great ocean should be analyzed here; the name "World-Ocean" (*lokadhātusāgara*) used in the subsequent text is established based on these.
Regarding the "pure adornments of the four banners" and so forth, this refers to the distinct meanings of the four items: banners, streamers, canopies, and light.
The banner (*dhvaja*) has two meanings:
first, to rise high; second, to subjugate, as in the banner of Śakra.
The pennant (*patākā*) has two meanings:
First, as a banner; second, as that which follows conditions.
This likewise has two meanings:
first, to manifest excellence; second, to provide cover and concealment.
Light also has two meanings:
first, the removal of darkness; second, the illumination and manifestation of things.
As the subsequent text states: "Within the precious banner there is radiance, adorned by hanging jeweled flags and streamers."

The five fragrant garlands are pure and adorned; that is to say, "exquisite fragrance" means being aromatic, "exquisite flowers" means being in full bloom, and "exquisite garlands" means being strung together. These three things are spread all around to constitute the offering.
Furthermore, one should string exquisite fragrant flowers together to form garlands and hang them from the four sides as banners to create adornment.
As the subsequent text states: "Suspend various flower garlands to serve as adornment."
The six kinds of jewel nets are pure and adorned; these nets provide a shimmering and magnificent embellishment.
As the subsequent text states: "Jewel-wheel lattices cover it from above.

According to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (The Sutra Praising the Pure Land), the seven jewels are: first, gold; second, silver; third, vaidūrya; fourth, sphatika; fifth, red pearl; sixth, aśmagarbha; and seventh, musāragalva.

The seventh is the "Rain of Jewels Adorned and Purified," meaning that what is rained down is vast and abundant, such that there is nothing that does not become functional for the Dharma-gates; thus it is called "sovereign," which refers precisely to manifesting the body and preaching the Dharma.
The eight precious trees are adorned and pure, which signifies the meaning of the establishment of manifold virtues.
As the subsequent text states: "Adorned by clouds of pure precious trees, they are universally able to illuminate all bodies."
Thus, "light" (*ābhā*) means flourishing.

Regarding the phrase "the nine Buddha-powers are solemnly pure," the expression "due to the Buddha’s spiritual power" cites the cause, while "causing these [qualities] to arise" distinguishes what is accomplished: first, the expansion of the essence; second, the adornment of the marks; and third, the illumination of the function.
The following text states: "In all world-oceans there are immeasurable jewel-wheels of adornment, produced by the spiritual power of the Tathāgata of Boundless Colors.
Regarding the ten marvelous and pure adornments, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three kinds of jewels:
first, the jewel of persons, such as the precious jewel of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), which has the function of raining down material goods; [the other two are omitted here].
Second is the treasure of the devas, meaning that all things belonging to the various devas are capable of being summoned at will;
third is the treasure of the bodhisattvas, who are capable of preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.

Now, this treasure of the bodhisattvas is already a most extraordinary treasure when compared to those of humans and devas; how much more so is the treasure born from the inexhaustible roots of goodness possessed by the Tathāgata, which is both a dharma-gate and a material treasure? Thus, it is exceedingly extraordinary.
The following sentence provides a summary:
Because the roots of goodness are immeasurable, and because the produced ornaments are likewise immeasurable, it is said that "immeasurable roots of goodness adorn the site of enlightenment."

Furthermore, these roots of goodness are also used for adornment, as stated in the following passage: "Ten million billion clouds of pāramitās and clouds of roots of goodness, and so forth, adorn the precious throne."
The present case is likewise the same as that.

Regarding "immeasurable," the subsequent text states: "The past practices of Vairocana Buddha have caused the oceans of Buddha-fields to be exceedingly pure; immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless, he exercises sovereign mastery throughout them all."
The remaining meanings will be explained in detail in a later chapter.

Within this context, there are also the six characteristics—totality, particularity, sameness, difference, formation, and disintegration—which may be understood by analogy with the general principles.
The section on the site concludes.
In the second [section], "Awakening under the Tree," there are also ten phrases.
The first is the general phrase.
There are three explanations for "Bodhi Tree" (bodhivṛkṣa): namely, the *upapada* (dependent), the *tatpuruṣa* (possessive), and the *karmadhāraya* (appositional).

Because in the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*) the non-obstruction between the environment and its inhabitants, and between person and phenomena, is thus realized, the attainment of Bodhi is itself the tree.
It rises above the six heavens and radiates brilliance throughout the ten directions; therefore, it is called "extraordinary.
This is the general statement.
Below, nine phrases specifically elucidate this extraordinariness:

First, the excellence of the trunk: this signifies that the body of the tree is luminous, pure, and firm; therefore, it is described as "pure lapis lazuli" and so forth. Second, the excellence of the branches:

this signifies that the spreading branches represent the differentiation of skillful means according to the capacities of sentient beings; therefore, they are described as "jeweled branches" and so forth.

The "three leaves" are extraordinary; that is to say, the branches, twigs, and terminal leaves represent the meaning of providing shade, support, and benefit, which is why they are called "precious leaves" and so forth.
The word "cloud" (yún) is pronounced with the second tone when it signifies the palate and gums; furthermore, when pronounced with the first tone, it signifies the gathering and massing of clouds.

The four extraordinary flowers signify the meaning of the exquisite adornment of various practices; because they are the practices accomplished through benefit, they are described as "variegated colors" and so forth.
The five extraordinary fruits signify the meaning of the fruition attained when practices are perfected.

As for "wishing-fulfilling" (cintāmaṇi): first, it is like the mind of the transformer, because it saves all equally; second, it is like the minds of those being transformed, because they obtain whatever they seek.
"Maṇi" is the general name for precious jewels; to distinguish this specific type from others, it is called the "wishing-fulfilling maṇi."

Furthermore, these five preceding phrases constitute the essence of a single tree: the pure dharma-realm is like the earth; the manifestation of the Buddha-body is like a tree growing from the earth; the differences perceived according to the capacities of beings are like the branching of the tree; the fact that there is nothing seen that does not benefit is like the leaves providing shade; the accomplishment of practice through such benefit is like the blossoming of the tree's flowers; and the attainment of the fruit upon the fulfillment of practice is like the tree bearing fruit.
This refers to manifesting at the Bodhi tree to initiate transformations and gather in sentient beings.

Another interpretation states: the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is like the earth; the bodhisattva lineage within that consciousness is like the seed of a tree; the arousal of the bodhicitta is like the sprouting of a tree; the cultivation and increase of correct practice is like the growth of the tree’s trunk; and the performance of cultivation according to the stages is like the branching out of the tree.
This refers to one's own practice.

Protecting and benefiting others is like the shade of tree leaves; the two practices of self and other adorning each other are like flowers; and the perfection of causes resulting in the manifestation of the fruit is like a tree bearing fruit.
This explains how one becomes a Buddha-tree through the sequence of spiritual practice.
The five preceding lines clarify that the substance of the tree encompasses all virtues;
the following four lines clarify the sovereign and wondrous function of this tree of awakening.
The sixth phrase reveals the excellence of the light, meaning that the function of the light reaches everywhere.

The seventh reveals the excellence of the manifested transformations: wherever it goes, it manifests and performs Buddha-work; because it is boundless, it cannot be surpassed—this refers to all places;
because it never ceases, it cannot be exhausted—this refers to all times.

There are eight extraordinary qualities: namely, performing various Buddha-activities in all places, universally manifesting the Mahāyāna path of the Bodhisattvas, and being able to manifest the Dharma through the light of this Āgama.
Furthermore, these three preceding phrases correspond, in their respective order, to the inclusion within the three types of action: bodily, mental, and vocal.
Ninth is the extraordinary power of the Buddha, which refers to the manifestation of sound through the empowerment of the Buddha’s power to praise his virtues.
If the tree itself did not spontaneously emit sounds to offer praise, there would be no one in the world capable of knowing the Tathāgata’s supreme merits.
Within these ten phrases, the six characteristics—general and specific—may be understood by analogy.
The section on the Tree of Awakening is concluded.
The third, the "Excellence of the Precious Seat," also contains ten phrases.

The first is the general statement; according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the Buddha is the lion among men, and thus any place where the Buddha sits—whether a couch or the ground—is called a "lion’s seat" (*siṃhāsana*), as is the case with the seat of a king.
Furthermore, because one sits upon this seat to preach the Dharma of the fearless lion’s roar, it is also called the Lion Seat (*siṃhāsana*).
In the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*), among the ten kinds of seats explained, the Lion Seat is specifically analyzed and its profound meaning is expounded.
All of the above are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds;
alternatively, they may also be understood as *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds, because the basis [the seat] and the supported [the Buddha] are fused into one.

Furthermore, because this seat encompasses the entire Dharma-realm—including all phenomena of persons, dharmas, teachings, and meanings, as well as the profound, vast, and extraordinary worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions—it is called "inconceivable," like the great ocean.
Below, nine phrases are used to specifically manifest the inconceivable:
first, the inconceivability of adornment, meaning that the essence encompasses all virtues; thus it is said, "various wonderful jewel flowers," and so forth.
Second is the inconceivable radiance of light, meaning that its wondrous function is without fixed direction, like clouds pervading everywhere; hence it is called "radiating light" and so forth.
Third is the inconceivable inclusion, meaning that it internally contains the great ocean of countless bodhisattvas; hence it is called a "treasury."
The fourth is the inconceivability of vocal action (*vākkarman*), meaning that his great voice resounds afar and accomplishes immeasurable benefit; thus it is called "inconceivable.
Furthermore, these aforementioned three phrases correspond respectively to the functional applications of the three types of action: body, mind, and speech.

The fifth is the inconceivable empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which means that although the light from this seat shines everywhere, the Buddha’s radiance further and more extensively covers it, thereby manifesting its supreme excellence.

The light of a *maṇi* jewel can illuminate and cover a wheel-turning king’s palace for forty *yojanas*, but the Buddha’s radiance now pervades the entire dharma-realm and completely covers this seat, surpassing that measure; therefore, it is said to "exceed the *maṇi* jewel," and so forth.
Sixth is the inconceivability of transformation, which refers to the transformative function that awakens beings; thus it is called "performing Buddha-work.

Seventh is the inconceivability of responding to capacities, which means that all those throughout the ten directions whose faculties have matured behold [the Buddha] simultaneously, as he universally responds from a single seat without any obstruction.
Eighth is "swift and inconceivable," which means that "a single thought-moment" refers to the extreme brevity of time;
"all transformations" refers to the vast number of manifestations;
and "pervading the dharma-realm" refers to its ultimate depth and breadth.
To be able to manifest a single transformation in a single thought-moment is already rare; how much more so to manifest all [transformations]?
To be able to manifest all things in a single thought-moment is already exceedingly rare; how much more so when each and every manifestation is profound and vast, filling the entire Dharma-realm?
In a single moment of thought, this boundless great function swiftly arises; all other moments of thought are likewise to be understood accordingly.
Ninth is the inconceivable true nature: because the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha is all-pervasive, it causes the aforementioned sublime functions to be swiftly accomplished without obstruction.
Furthermore, these four preceding lines clarify the sequential relationship of the functions of this seat:
first, what its characteristics are; second, how it should be applied; third, how it is expedient; and fourth, by what means it is accomplished.
It should be understood that the four questions are answered by the four lines in their respective order.
The final line provides a summary.
Because explaining each in detail would be too exhaustive, it concludes with the phrase "immeasurable various jewels," and so forth.
Because the seat is high and prominent, it is also called a "platform" (*tāla*).
Question:
What is the underlying principle by which this Lion Throne is termed "inconceivable"?
Answer: Since it is called "inconceivable," its meaning is truly inexhaustible.
Briefly stated, there are ten kinds: first, it is inconceivable as having parts, because it is identical to the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
It cannot be contemplated as being without parts, for it manifests according to the capacities of beings;
it cannot be contemplated through abstract principle, for the adornments of precious flowers constitute its reality;
it cannot be contemplated as being identical to phenomena, for it is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
It cannot be conceived through the retributive environment (*niśraya-vipāka*), for it is accomplished by Bodhisattvas and others;
it cannot be conceived through the primary retribution (*mukhya-vipāka*), for it is the fruit of the Buddha’s support (*niśraya-phala*);
it cannot be conceived through the person (*pudgala*), for it is subsumed within the Dharma that serves as its support.
It cannot be conceived in terms of the Dharma, for it possesses the three karmas that function for the sake of sentient beings;
it cannot be conceived in terms of the fruit, for it possesses all bodhisattvas at the stage of the cause;
and it cannot be conceived in terms of the cause, for it is the possession of the Buddha-fruit itself.

These ten meanings above are characterized by unimpeded mutual identity: namely, the single seat is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); the ten meanings are the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); that they are all equally the meaning of "seat" is the common characteristic (*sabhāga-lakṣaṇa*); that the ten meanings do not intermingle is the distinct characteristic (*asabhāga-lakṣaṇa*); that these ten meanings cause the dharma of the seat to arise is the productive characteristic (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa*); and that each abides in its own dharma is the disintegrating characteristic (*bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa*).
Question:
Since it is said that [the Buddha] manifests for the sake of sentient beings, he is not without measure; however, we do not yet know what the extent of that measure is. Answer:
Nevertheless, this is difficult to know; it can only be discerned through analogy.
As stated in the "Chapter on the Grounds":
"The circumference of the seat of a Bodhisattva of the tenth ground is equal in measure to ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems."

To compare the measure of this seat with that of the Tathāgata’s seat is like comparing a handful of soil the size of a bean to the great trichiliocosm; such is the extreme difficulty of measuring the extent of the Tathāgata’s seat.
The preceding three sections have collectively completed the explanation of the perfection of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
From here on, the third section explains the perfection of the world of the wise and perfectly awakened ones (*vidyā-sambuddha-loka*).
Within this, there is a brief analysis organized into five gates:
First, defining the Buddha-body; second, clarifying the integration and inclusion; third, revealing the distinctions; fourth, representing the Dharma; fifth, explaining the main text.
Regarding the first, defining the Buddha-body: Question:
What kind of body is the Buddha of these eight assemblies?

Answer: Some commentators explain that this is the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha, because the attainment of the eightfold path under the Bodhi tree is the Nirmāṇakāya; because not departing from the ascent to heaven constitutes a "repeated transformation" (punar-nirmāṇa); and because Vairocana is merely another name for Śākyamuni and is not a separate vipākakāya (retribution body).
Furthermore, another interpretation states:
"The Buddha who preached this sutra is the true recompense body (*sambhogakāya*), because he is the Dharmadhātu-body of Vairocana and because he dwells within the pure land of the Lotus Treasury."
In the first part of the seventh assembly below, there is a praise of the Buddha’s twenty-one kinds of sublime merits; this is the true retribution body (*vipākaphala-kāya*).
However, because it does not depart from the transformative manifestation (*nirmāṇa*), it encompasses this [teaching] beneath the tree, yet it is not the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Now, the explanation:

this Buddha, according to the subsequent text, is the body of the ten Buddhas, encompassing the three worlds; it is that which is seen prior to the stages of the Ten Faiths and the Three Sages, and is not the actual retribution-body.
However, because dwelling in the Flower Treasury (Huazang) is not restricted to a single transformation;
because the lands, bodies, and so forth are not limited to the previous two [categories];
because they fully encompass the previous two through the mutual interpenetration of their nature; and because they are complete with primary and attendant elements like a net of Indra.
Therefore, these are exclusively the bodies of the ten Buddhas that pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
Regarding the second [aspect], "fusing and subsuming," there are two points:
first, it directly subsumes all three worlds without exception, because one becomes a Buddha only upon possessing these three matters.

The three bodies and two bodies are subsumed within the wisdom of perfect enlightenment among these three; likewise, the wondrous pure land and the body born together with others are all without exception subsumed herein.

Furthermore, both the primary retribution of the pores and the secondary retribution within the atoms each encompass all phenomena, such as the three worlds, in a layer upon layer manner, appearing like Indra’s net; this can be understood by reflecting accordingly.

Third, regarding the manifestation of distinctions: this single body of Śākyamuni appears in various forms according to the diverse capacities of sentient beings. Sometimes it appears as something ordinary rather than noble, such as when it is seen as the body and feet of a three-footed black elephant or as the body of a tree spirit; these appearances occur within the realms of humans and devas.
Alternatively, they are noble but not ordinary, because they share the same physical form as the noble bodies of Arhats.
Alternatively, they are both ordinary and noble: they are ordinary because they possess the actual retribution body born of father and mother, which is composed of the four great elements;
yet they are noble because they are endowed with the fivefold Dharma-body and have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).
Alternatively, it is neither ordinary nor noble, because it is subsumed within the three bodies (*trikāya*) of this Mahāyāna, and thus differs from the noble arhats of the Hīnayāna.

Or, it is transformation (*nirmāṇa*) and not dharma or recompense (*vipāka*), because it possesses the eight phases [of a Buddha] while remaining in Jambudvīpa, whereas the true recompense is established separately at the peak of the form realm (*rūpāvacara-agra*). As stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and other texts, this refers to the initial teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).

Alternatively, it is the retribution for the transformation of the non-Dharma; that is, this very body is endowed with twenty-one kinds of sublime merits because it is a body of enjoyment (*saṃbhoga-kāya*), as stated at the beginning of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*. This refers to the Final Teaching (*paryanta-yāna*).

Alternatively, there may be dharmas that are neither retribution nor transformation, because form (*rūpa*) is itself suchness (*tathatā*). As the Sūtra says: "This body of mine now is itself the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
This refers to the sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*).
Alternatively, they are both Dharma-bodies and both reward and transformation bodies, as previously explained in the threefold classification.

Alternatively, they are neither Dharma-bodies nor reward and transformation bodies, because these are the ten Buddhas, because they pervade the three worlds, and because they are fully endowed with primary figures and their retinues; this is as stated in the latter part of this sutra, which refers to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Therefore, this body of Śākyamuni is perfectly interfused, unimpeded, and utterly inconceivable.
Fourth, regarding the representation of the Dharma: there are, in total, four types of Buddhas who preach the Dharma.
The first is the body of an Arhat, which represents the preaching of the Hīnayāna teachings.
Second, the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha represents the teaching of the Three Vehicles, explaining extensively that which precedes the stages (*bhūmi*) and briefly that which pertains to the stages themselves.
Third, the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha represents the teaching of the Three Vehicles, explaining extensively that which pertains to the stages themselves and briefly that which precedes the stages.
The forty bodies of the Buddha represent the Dharma of the One Vehicle, taught simultaneously across six stages.
Because these teachings are complete with their primary and attendant aspects in an inexhaustible manner, the Buddha likewise possesses these ten bodies in an inexhaustible way.
Fifth, regarding the explanation of the text: within the text, the meaning of this wisdom of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is explained by means of ten sections;
the first is general, while the remaining nine are specific.
Within the general section, the Tathāgata first takes his place upon the precious throne, hence the passage beginning with "The Tathāgata dwells here," and so forth.
Subsequent wisdom accords with the true source; therefore, it is said that one "attains supreme perfect enlightenment regarding all dharmas.

Furthermore, regarding the term "Tathāgata," the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because what is expressed through speech does not deviate from the *tathatā* (suchness), he is called the Tathāgata."

Furthermore, the *Dharmacakrapravartana-śāstra* states: "The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called 'suchness' (*tathatā*), and perfect awakening is called 'coming' (*āgata*). Because one has perfectly awakened to the ultimate truth, one is called a Tathāgata."
Furthermore, a sutra states: "One attains perfect enlightenment by riding upon the six pāramitās; therefore, one is called the Tathāgata.
Moreover, a śāstra states: "One attains perfect enlightenment by riding upon the path of suchness."
Question: Since this [Tathāgata] is designated as such because he has emerged from obstructions, why is he not designated as "Thus-Gone" (Tathāgata) while still entangled in them? Answer:
There is indeed this meaning; thus the Sūtra says, "The Dharmakāya circulating through the five destinies is called 'sentient beings'.
Since it speaks of "circulating," one should know that there is going.
Alternatively, there is also no going, because although it remains within the entanglements (*saṃyojana*), it does not move.
Question:
If that is so, then since it does not move when emerging from the obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), there should likewise be no coming.
Answer: Pure dharmas accord with reality and arise from reality; therefore, they can "come.
Defiled dharmas contradict principle and are false dharmas; therefore, they cannot "go."
Alternatively, there is no coming, because initial awakening (ādikṣaya-bodhi) is identical to fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi).
Since there is no distinction between initial and fundamental awakening, there is therefore no coming.
Thus, a sutra says: "The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata."
Furthermore, "all dharmas" refers to the two truths that are to be realized.
"Supreme Perfect Enlightenment" (Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) refers to the sublime wisdom capable of realizing them.

Although Bodhisattvas also possess a partial realization of the truth, their stage is not yet ultimate; thus, they cannot be called "supreme. Here, the term "Supreme Perfect Enlightenment" is used in reference to the state of ultimate perfection.

Below, nine sections are used to specifically elucidate the meaning of the Tathāgata’s attainment of perfect enlightenment; that is to say, within the Tathāgata’s single dharma-realm body, there are three layers of the three karmas manifested in accordance with conditions.
The first section has three gates, clarifying how the mastery over the three equal karmas encompasses the transformation of sentient beings.
The second section, from "His body pervades beneath his seat" onwards, clarifies that the benefits produced by the three karmas in transforming sentient beings are not in vain.
From "The three [bodies] are all able to manifest universally" onwards, it clarifies the accomplishment and benefit of the three karmas, which are then returned to suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding the first of these, the physical karma (*kāyakarman*) is clarified first; herein there are two parts:
the first phrase clarifies the impartial physical karma, while the section beginning with "universally entering" distinguishes the physical karma that gathers in and nurtures sentient beings.
Furthermore, the preceding phrase reveals profundity, while the subsequent phrase clarifies vastness.
Moreover, the former clarifies that [the dharmadhātu] is not identical to the three periods of time, hence it is called "equality";
the latter distinguishes that it is not separate from the three periods of time, hence it is called "universal entry."
Furthermore, the former signifies the meaning of immutability, while the latter signifies the meaning of following conditions.
Moreover, the former refers to the essence, while the latter refers to the function.
Furthermore, "clarity" (liao) means illuminative awareness.
The "dharmas of the three periods" refers to all dharmas mentioned previously.
"Equality" means that one realizes the past and future to be equal to the present; thus it is called equality, which is explained here in terms of the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*).

Second, one thoroughly understands that the phenomena of the three periods of time are in a state of flux, yet they ultimately dissolve into the single reality, devoid of any distinction between the three; thus it is called "equality. This refers to the realm of ultimate truth.

The meaning of the text lies herein: this refers to not abiding in phenomena (*dharma*) but entering into principle (*li*). "Universally entering" and so forth refers to not abiding in principle but following phenomena. Thereafter, it does not deviate from principle while following phenomena, nor do phenomena contradict principle.
Principle and phenomena are fused and integrated; they are two yet non-dual, without obstruction or hindrance.
These two phrases reveal the meaning of this body as being the basis for all other virtues.
Next, the speech-karma of equality is explained.

Regarding "the wondrous voice pervading everywhere": this clarifies that the Tathāgata’s perfect voice, like the nature of dependent origination, pervades all places while nevertheless not destroying distinct individual expressions.
If one loses the melodic contours through universal pervasiveness, then universality is not sound;
if the melodic contours deviate from universal pervasiveness, then sound is not universal.

Now, without destroying the contours to achieve universal pervasiveness, and without moving from universal pervasiveness to produce distinct melodies—this is called the Tathāgata’s perfect sound, which is not a realm of mental consciousness or discursive thought.
Just as space possesses five meanings, it serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s perfect voice because they resemble one another.

First is the meaning of pervasiveness: the Buddha’s perfect voice pervades the Dharma-realm, reaching everywhere without exception; it is like Maudgalyāyana seeking the Buddha’s voice from afar and being unable to find its limit.
Second is the meaning of equality: although emptiness is all-pervasive, its essence is eternally non-dual; how much more so is the Buddha’s perfect voice, which is equal and of a single flavor.

Third is the meaning of non-obstruction: just as this empty space is without any obstruction, so too the Buddha’s perfect voice encounters no hindrance whether it is heard or not, according to the maturity of the faculties of sentient beings.

Fourth, regarding the meaning of appearing before [others]: all sentient beings each perceive that space is facing them, yet space does not actually appear before anyone; the perfect sound is likewise, for while it is heard individually by various capacities according to their differences, the sound itself has no duality of "this" or "that."

The fifth meaning is "containing and receiving" (*saṃgraha*): this means that because this space encompasses and receives all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), the perfect sound (*pariśuddha-svara*) is likewise so, for it contains and subsumes the meanings of all the phenomena it expresses.
The remaining meanings are as explained below in the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" (*Xingqi pin*).
Within the section on mental karma (*manaskarma*), there are two parts:
first, the clarification of impartial mental karma; second, from the term "equal mind" (*samacitta*) onwards, the clarification of the mental karma of gathering beings.
Furthermore, first is principle and subsequently is valid cognition;
first is wisdom and subsequently is compassion.
Moreover, because the two benefits lack abiding conditions and are fused into a non-dual characteristic, they are mutually integrated.
Furthermore, the characteristic of the equality of phenomena is precisely that which the Buddha’s wisdom traverses; therefore, it is called the "sphere of practice.
The phrase "like space" serves as a metaphor for this dharma of equal practice.

Furthermore, because the characteristics of object and wisdom are identical, and both subject and object are extinguished—being like space, unimpeded, of a single flavor, all-pervasive, inclusive, and functional.
Furthermore, one should reflect upon this by considering whether it is only the object that is like space, or only the wisdom, or both, or neither.
Another explanation states:
because the merits of the Buddha-fruit, such as ethical discipline and so forth, are said to be identical to the true nature (*dharmatā*), they are called "equal."
It is known only by the Buddha’s wisdom; therefore, it is called the "sphere of wisdom.
Yet, because it has no limits or boundaries, it is like space.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle four, states: "As a sūtra says:"
Even all the metaphors and similes employed to illustrate the merits of the Tathāgatas are in fact slanders of the Tathāgatas;
with the single exception of the metaphor of space, for the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata’s ethical discipline and so forth are identical to space.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding the phrase in the latter line, "the equal mind that accords with sentient beings," there are four meanings:
