Regarding the concluding summary at the end, there are two meanings: first, it concludes the preceding assembly of the multitude by showing that it extends throughout the ten directions; second, since this summary occurs after the demonstration of the Dharma, one knows that the demonstration of the Dharma likewise extends throughout the ten directions.
The section on the demonstration by the Dharma Lord is concluded.
Third, the section on the Dharma Lord entering meditative absorption.
This contains two parts:
First, there are four preliminary considerations regarding the various assemblies:
first, as for presence and absence, only the second assembly lacks [the specific teaching] because the stage of the dharma it symbolizes has not yet been established;
in the other assemblies, the stages of the dharma they symbolize have been established.

Regarding the second point, "emerging and not emerging": only the eighth [consciousness] does not emerge, because it symbolizes the realization of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as being without retrogression;
the others symbolize the arising of transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*).

Regarding the third point, "cause and fruit": the first, seventh, and eighth are fixed as fruits, because the first explains the fruit, the seventh involves profound practice, and the eighth involves the realization of the profound mystery.
Others all explain it as being due to the cause; furthermore,
it is explained that the seventh [ground] also possesses the meaning of "having a cause," because in the *Avataṃsaka*, it is formed by the adornment of causal practice.
If judged in this manner, there are four permutations:
either only the fruit, namely the first and the eighth;
or only the cause, namely the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth.
Some are both cause and effect, namely the seventh;
some are neither cause nor effect, namely the second, which is entirely non-existent.

Regarding the four types of persons who can enter [the stages]: only the eighth, the Buddha, enters by himself, because the liberation through mastery over the Dharma-realm is exhausted only in the Buddha.
Although the fruit was initially mentioned, it was for the purpose of inspiring faith in sentient beings.
Although the seven practices are profound, they are nonetheless the practices of persons who are on the path.
Second, regarding the explanation of the text, there are two parts:
First, this land is described, and subsequently, the universal application is established.
Regarding the initial section: those who sit before the Buddha manifest that cause and effect are inseparable.
For what reason do they enter meditative concentration?
It is revealed that [the Buddha] does not speak because he has not yet realized [the fruit], in order to receive empowerment, and to remove the doubts of the assembly.
Why does he enter the meditative absorption of the fruit?
It is in order to teach the dharmas of the fruit.
Why is it entered by means of the person? Because it is for the sake of the person who enters.
Purity has four meanings:
There are four kinds of purity: first, natural purity; second, purity through the subduing of afflictions; third, purity of the roots of goodness; and fourth, purity of beneficial function.
The term "store" (*garbha*) has four meanings:
first, inclusion; second, accumulation; third, production; and fourth, inexhaustibility.
Samādhi is here translated as "equipoise" (samāhita), because it is free from sinking and agitation.
It is called "equal" (samā) because concentration and wisdom are balanced;
it is called "holding" (hita) because the mind is not distracted and remains fixed upon a single object.
To internalize the Dharma within the mind is called "right reception" (*samādhi*).
Within this, purity is the treasury; purity itself is the treasury.
The Tathāgata’s pure treasury is such that the Tathāgata himself is the pure treasury.
The samādhi of Pure Treasury (Vimalagarbha) is itself Pure Treasury;
both interpretations are possible, which can be seen by reflecting upon them.
The subsequent explanation clarifies their meaning: the first phrase explains "Tathāgata," and the second phrase explains "Pure Treasury."
Freedom from defilement is purity;
fulfillment is the treasury;
and space is a metaphor for the former two.
Regarding "tying together and penetrating" (jiētōng): throughout this sutra, all sections are explained as forming a single whole, meaning that one part is itself all parts.

For now, we shall take up matters from within one such section; fearing that its original context might be severed, we repeatedly draw out the concluding ties at the end of each passage to establish the original whole, thereby clarifying its inexhaustibility.
Therefore, to briefly clarify the distinctions in the scope of the samādhis entered, there are ten stages:

first, regarding the unimpeded nature of all concentrations, it is stated in the section on "Arising" that "Samantabhadra Bodhisattva arises from those samādhis; he arises from as many samādhis as there are atoms in a world-system."
The commentary states:

This has two meanings: first, because this samādhi contains and encompasses many samādhis; second, because this samādhi universally enters into many samādhis. Therefore, this samādhi is itself the ocean of samādhis such as the "Dust" (rajas) samādhi.

Second, regarding being unimpeded in all places, as this text states: "When the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra enters right samādhi in this world, it is likewise in all Buddha-lands throughout the entirety of the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space."
This also has two meanings: first, because this samādhi encompasses the lands of the ten directions; second, because this samādhi pervades all paths of sensory objects.
Third, it is unimpeded throughout all time, as stated in the section on "Arising": "Samantabhadra arises from the samādhi of all three periods of time," and so forth.
This also has two meanings: namely, that it definitively encompasses the three periods of time and universally enters the three temporal limits.

Fourthly, these three successive layers are fused and integrated into one; this is because Samantabhadra’s samādhi is unimpeded and sovereign, and because these three explanations are definitive and inseparable from one another.

Fifth, within the ocean of samādhis such as the *dhūpa-rajas* (incense-dust) and others, each single one possesses all meditative concentrations, for each individually encompasses the ten directions and the entirety of the three periods of time.
Sixth, as it is with one samādhi, so it is with all.
Seventh, within a single atom, one immediately perceives Samantabhadra’s Samādhi of Perfect Clarity, which encompasses all ten directions and exhausts the three periods of time.
Eighth, as it is within a single atom, so it is within every atom and every path.

Within each single thought-moment, there are the Samādhis of Samantabhadra entering into the dust-motes and so forth, each encompassing the paths of the dust-motes, extending throughout all lands of the ten directions and exhausting the nine and ten eons.
Just as it is within a single thought-moment, so it is in all other thought-moments throughout the entire ocean of kalpas extending across the past and future limits.
Taking these ten layers as the standard, one should apply this principle accordingly to all other stages, as well as to the teachings, meanings, principles, and phenomena.
The section on entering meditative concentration is concluded.
Within the fourth section, "The Empowerment by All Buddhas," there are two parts;
first, the analysis of the various assemblies, which has two sub-sections:

Regarding the initial presence or absence [of the empowerment]: it is absent in the second, seventh, eighth, and third assemblies because the two stages have not yet been established and there is no entry into meditative concentration; in the seventh assembly, the practice follows the Dharma without differing from what preceded; and in the eighth assembly, the Buddha enters concentration himself without relying on external assistance.
Other assemblies are not like these, and therefore the empowerment exists in all of them.
The two Buddhas differ in terms of distance, number, and names, all of which should be understood according to the text.
There are three parts to the explanation of the passage:
first, the oral empowerment and its purpose; second, the mental empowerment; and third, the physical empowerment.
Furthermore, first he exhorted and instructed him to increase his eloquence; next, he invisibly influenced him to increase his wisdom; finally, he touched the crown of his head to awaken him.
Regarding the mutual accomplishment of empowerment and praise, there are four permutations:
first, empowerment without praise, such as the two empowerments of the Buddha’s intention and body.
Second, praise without empowerment, such as the verses of praise by various bodhisattvas;
third, both empowerment and praise, such as the verbal karma of the Buddha;
fourth, neither empowerment nor praise, such as other textual passages.
The section on the mouth has two parts:
first, explaining the additional praise; second, explaining the purpose.
Within the first part, there are three sections:

First, it clarifies that the Buddhas manifest their bodies here without departing from their original lands; this is to show that "the other" is "this" without destroying "the other," and "the distant" is "the near" without destroying "the distant"—as is known through the nature of dependent origination.
Second, it praises the attainment of profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Third, it clarifies the causes of this concentration: first, the power of others; second, one's own power.
Furthermore, it is the synthesis of the power of the fruit, the power of the cause, and dependent origination.
Moreover, regarding the Buddha’s original vow: it clarifies that the Buddha, having previously witnessed these matters in the past, immediately made a vow, which is now being fulfilled.
Regarding the explanation of what is being done: for what purpose is this addition made?
It is for the sake of expounding this Dharma.
Within this, there are ten phrases:
The first is the general [meaning], which refers to the initial turning of the wheel of the One Vehicle (ekayāna); because this is the wheel of the fruit (*phala-dharmacakra*), it is called "Buddha.
Within the specific [meanings] there are nine:
first, the meaning of that which is turned, which is the essence of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
"Opening" (kai) means manifestation.
The second [turning], which skillfully transforms and exhausts the source, is the characteristic of the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra).
"Reaching the ten directions" is the point where the connection is established.
Third, the wondrous removal of the obstacles of delusion is the function of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
Fourth, its simultaneous turning in the ten directions is the locus of the Wheel of Dharma; furthermore, it exhausts the oceans of lands.
Fifth, the turning from cause into fruition is the scope of the Wheel of Dharma.
The sixth door, which subsumes all fruits, is the virtue of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
The seventh, skillfully bringing about the fruit of joy, is the objective realm of the Wheel of Dharma.
The eighth, skillfully conforming to worldly conventions, is the expedient means (*upāya*) of the Wheel of Dharma.

The ninth, "Examining the Faculties and Bestowing the Dharma," refers to those who are the recipients of the Wheel of Dharma; their similarities and differences, as well as their formation and destruction, should be understood by analogy.
Regarding the second [section], "Mental Application" (*manasikāra*), there are two parts: first, the application itself, and second, its explanation.
Regarding the beginning and middle [of the text], the first is general while the rest are specific.
Within the specific section: first is the wisdom of attaining the Dharma, meaning that the wisdom of the five oceans is not one, hence it is called "boundless" and so forth;
second is the wisdom of the limit of exhaustion, meaning it exhaustively reaches the five oceans and encompasses the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Third is the wisdom of formation and destruction, which refers to the five seas of accumulation and dispersal; this is also the sea of worlds.
Fourth is the wisdom of those to be transformed, which refers to the five seas in terms of defilement; this is also the sea of sentient beings.
Fifth is the wisdom of principle, which refers to the five seas all being profound; this is also the sea of the dharma-realm.
Sixth is the wisdom of the three samādhis, meaning that the five oceans are all objects of meditative concentration;

seventh is the wisdom of the faculties and desires; eighth is the wisdom of eloquence in speech; ninth is the wisdom of the pervasive body; and tenth is the wisdom of the perfect voice—all of these pertain to the five oceans and so forth, as may be inferred accordingly.
This is largely the same as the ten knowledges discussed below.
In the commentary, there is first an inquiry and then an explanation.
Question:
The Buddhas possess both power and compassion; for what reason do they bestow their grace only upon Samantabhadra and not upon others? Answer:

Because he is the eldest son, because he is the leader of the assembly, because he has reached the bottom of the Buddhas' vows, because of his original vow, because he is endowed with universal virtues, because he has attained the dharmas of meditative concentration, and because these are not attained by others.

Furthermore, wherever such a fixed locus exists, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) for all Buddhas to gather there, just as it is the natural law of the ocean to collect all its tributary streams; thus it is called "Dharma.

This principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is precisely how things are; therefore, the wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) of all Buddhas can likewise be transmitted to others.
Question:
Why did the Buddha not speak of this himself? Answer:
There are two intentions [behind this]:
first, since that which is taught is profound and mysterious, there is a fear that the opportunity for others to attain it might be severed.
If this is so, why do other people not teach it?
This is for the sake of expounding the Universal Dharma (Samantabhadra-dharma).
Second, it clarifies that whenever this dharma is taught, it must necessarily be the teaching shared by all Buddhas.
If a Buddha were to teach it alone, there would be no principle for joint transmission, which would contradict the nature of a shared teaching.
Therefore, a single teaching by Samantabhadra is the teaching of all Buddhas.
Within the empowerment of the three bodies, why is it called "mo"?
It is because it causes awakening and causes one to be endowed with the majestic power and virtue of a Buddha.

In this regard, it need not be that the Buddha’s body actually comes here, nor that his outstretched hand is physically extended; it need not be that each person is touched on the crown of their head without mutual interference, nor that all are stroked simultaneously without temporal sequence. All of these are the unimpeded mastery of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda); one should understand this through reflection.
The section on empowerment is concluded.
Within the fifth section, "The Universal Request by the Great Assembly," there are two parts:
first, the prose passage expressing wonder that [the Buddha] did not speak immediately, thereby giving rise to a subsequent request.
This also involves the invitation of both bodily and mental karma: namely, reverence, which is bodily;
and observation, which is mental.
Both being focused together constitutes single-mindedness.
Regarding the subsequent invitation for right speech and action, how does it differ from the previous invitation?
It is said that this differs because it specifically invites Samantabhadra and because he is known to be the master of the Dharma discourse.
Furthermore, as this assembly includes both the new and the old congregations, it is not the same as the former.
The Dharma being requested is no different from what preceded it; therefore, it is not listed separately.
The ten verses are divided into three parts:

first, eight verses praising the Master of the Dharma and requesting [the teaching]; second, one verse citing the subject matter to be taught and requesting [it]; and finally, one verse praising the assembly’s delight in hearing and requesting [the teaching].
The first two [sections] consist of five verses that generally praise the virtues of Samantabhadra;
the latter three specifically praise his virtue of preaching the Dharma.
This also means that the preceding section praises the causes for having teachings, while the subsequent section praises the fruits of having teachings.
Within the preceding section, the ten kinds of merit of Samantabhadra are briefly revealed:
first, the fulfillment of causal practices and vows; second, the equality of resultant virtues. The first of these is manifested by the initial verse.
The first verse reveals that the three bodies are omnipresent and the four aspects of merit and wisdom are profound and vast;
the second verse reveals the fivefold universal vision of the ocean of Buddhas and the sixth capacity to manifest within every atom and land;
the fourth verse reveals the seventh quality of pervading all times and places and the eighth quality of constant manifestation through deep meditative concentration.
Ninth, its essence fills the Dharma-realm; tenth, its function pervades the ocean of sentient beings. These also represent wisdom first and compassion last, as manifested in the fifth verse.
Furthermore, these ten virtues are subsumed into five pairs:
first, cause and effect; second, body and wisdom; third, vision and manifestation; fourth, profundity and vastness; and fifth, essence and function.

Within the section on the specific praise of qualities, the first verse praises realization and abandonment as causes. It is explained extensively and universally: that is, the first line praises the realization of principle, the second line praises the abandonment of hindrances, the third line praises universal pervasiveness, and the fourth line provides the extensive explanation.

The two verses and one line praise the internal and external causes that are able to benefit the sublime teaching: the first line praises Samantabhadra’s internal realization, which gives birth to the ocean of all Buddha-virtues;
the second line praises his external ability to universally radiate clouds of light of the Dharma-teaching;
and the third line praises his ability to benefit sentient beings by strengthening their pure conduct.
The latter phrase means that, for this reason, one is able to skillfully expound the realm of the Buddha.
The third verse praises profound practice as the cause, which enables one to rain down the teaching of the Dharma.
Within these three [aspects] above, if distinguished by the capacity to teach, there are: first, extensive exposition; second, skillful exposition; and third, instantaneous exposition.
If categorized according to what is taught, there are three: first, the Buddha’s Dharma; second, the Buddha’s realm; and third, the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The following verse clarifies the Dharma that is taught: the first line provides a general summary of the "Flower Treasury World" (*Huazangjie*) and so forth mentioned below;
the next line cites the "Buddha’s acts of adornment and purification" mentioned below.

In the second line, "entering" refers to the ocean of the Buddhas and the ocean of the Dharma-realm; "that which is entered" refers to the ocean of sentient beings and the ocean of their faculties and desires.
The third line concludes the request;
the final verse praises the assembly for possessing two qualities that qualify them to hear [the teaching]:
First, aspiration; second, the faculty.
Within the former, there are also two:
first, because the body is free from pride and indolence, it is called "reverence"; [the second is...]
Because the two minds are free from divergent thoughts, it is said that one contemplates Samantabhadra.
Although within the two faculties there may be a single mind that delights in hearing, if wisdom is lacking, one cannot receive and comprehend [the teaching].
This also has two aspects:
first, profound wisdom that penetrates the profound principle; second, extensive wisdom that discerns extensive phenomena.
The following phrase concludes the request for the teaching to be expounded.
The section on the shared invitation is concluded.
Within the sixth dhyāna, the fundamental section is briefly explained in two parts:
first, the contemplation of the five oceans; second, the exposition of the ten knowledges.
Furthermore, the former is the object of contemplation and the latter is the wisdom that contemplates;
moreover, the former is the basis for realization and the latter is the basis for teaching.
For what reason, then, does he speak without emerging from meditative concentration?
This refers to: because the function of clarity and concentration is unimpeded; because it is used as a locus to manifest the profundity of the Dharma; and because they operate in tandem.
Regarding the first two [of these], there are two parts:
first, it clarifies that because the ocean of objects is profound, contemplation is not achieved through one's own power alone.
Regarding the second [section], the correct contemplation of the five oceans of dharmas, there is a brief presentation in ten gates:
first, the differentiation of their meanings and characteristics. This refers to the differentiation of these five meanings within the inexhaustible, perfectly luminous ocean-treasury of nature:
the first is the meaning of the basis (*āśraya*), which applies universally to all [the others].
Second, the sense of sprouting; also, the sense of accumulation;
third, the sense of functional application;
fourth, the sense of skillful differentiation and the sense of classification.
The meaning of the perfection of the five awakenings:
these five are each identical to and inclusive of the other four; as they are all profoundly vast and inexhaustible, possessing inconceivable virtues, they are thus called the ocean.
Second, regarding the distinction between defilement and purity, there are two types:
first, the specific, which is either exclusively pure, such as the ocean of Buddhas;
or exclusively defiled, such as the ocean of sentient beings.
In some cases they are both [pure], namely the world-sphere (*dhātu*) and the sense-faculties (*indriya*), as well as desire;
in other cases they are not both, namely the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*).
Regarding the two that are pervasive: in some cases they are both pure, because sentient beings and so forth also flow back toward the source and are fundamentally pure.
Alternatively, they may be defiled, because even Buddhas and others follow conditions;
or they may both be so or not be so—reflect upon this accordingly.
Thirdly, regarding the integration of principle and phenomena, there are likewise four propositions, which can be understood through their complete inclusion.
Fourth, regarding the classification by person and dharma, there are two types:

first, the specific classification, wherein sentient beings and Buddhas are persons; the dharma-realm is the root of dharmas and desires; that which is both person and dharma; and the world-realm, which is neither person nor dharma.
Second, the general classification, which likewise possesses four permutations (catuṣkoṭi), to be understood as encompassing all categories in their entirety.
Fifth, regarding cause and effect, there are also two [categories].
Within the specific [analysis], there is the case where the world-realm is simultaneous while the dharma-realm is not; the other two phrases may be understood accordingly.
Within the general [analysis], there are likewise four phrases, which should be inferred by reflection.

Sixth, regarding the three worlds; seventh, regarding the object and wisdom; eighth, regarding the dependent and the primary [receptacle]; ninth, regarding the Three Jewels. One should reflect upon these four preceding sections, noting that each contains both general and specific statements.
Tenth, regarding the integration through fusion, there are two aspects.
First, regarding the ocean: this means that the world is identical to sentient beings, as in the case where the forms of sentient beings constitute the world;
and the world is identical to the dharma-realm, as in the case of the Dharma-realm Indestructible Lotus World-Ocean.
The ocean of worlds is precisely the faculties and desires; as the mind creates the world, so too is the world the Buddha, like the body of the land.

Second, regarding sentient beings as the world—as previously explained—they are also the dharma-realm, as the sutra states: "This very dharma-realm, circulating through the five destinies, is called 'sentient beings'."
This is also the root desire, as it is said that "the mind and its activities are one.
Furthermore, the Buddha is the sentient-being body among the ten bodies, and because sentient beings are themselves the Truth (Tathatā).
Regarding the latter three oceans, each one individually possesses the others; all can be understood through reflection.
Second, within the context of wisdom (*jñāna*), there are also two parts:
first, the initial three distinct wisdoms are the wisdoms of the first three oceans, while the subsequent seven wisdoms are the wisdoms of the latter two oceans.
Regarding the two types of penetration: it means that within one wisdom there are five oceans, and within one ocean there are ten wisdoms, which are fused and integrated through contemplation.
The five oceans are profound and mysterious; they are expressed by means of the number five so that people may find it easier to believe.
The ten wisdoms are somewhat coarse; they are expressed by means of the number ten so that their fundamental nature may be realized.
Therefore, while the object and the wisdom are not distinct, the coarse and the subtle are always differentiated; this is according to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Furthermore, as the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "The conduct of the Tathāgata and the realm of the Tathāgata—what is the difference between these?"
The Buddha said:
"That which the Tathāgata practices is called 'all modes' (*sarvākāra*). It is the pure buddha-field adorned by the immeasurable multitude of qualities common to all Tathāgatas.

The domain of the Tathāgata consists of the distinctions among the five realms in all their modes: namely, the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), the realm of worlds (*lokadhātu*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the realm of those to be disciplined (*vineyadhātu*), and the realm of the means of discipline (*vinayopāyadhātu*)."
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and the *Yogācārabhūmi* also name these five the "five immeasurables" (*pañcāpramāṇa*).

Since these five constitute the domain of the Tathāgata, they are subsequently referred to as "wisdom" (*jñāna*) and termed "retroactive wisdom" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); this is explained in terms of the Three Vehicles.
Question:
Since one is contemplating the ocean, why is it that the ocean is not described, but wisdom is? Answer:
Because the ocean is an object of realization (*pratyakṣa*), when one intends to speak of that realization, one is in fact speaking of the wisdom (*jñāna*).

It is like a person who goes to a temple and contemplates a stūpa until its image is impressed upon their own mind; later, returning home, they describe the stūpa, yet they are actually describing the mental impression, not the stūpa itself.
Question:
Since it is said that [the teaching] is attained while in meditative concentration, why must it be brought forth afterwards? Answer:
This is for the sake of entrusting the Dharma. Why?
It refers to contemplating the ocean while in meditative concentration; this is the most subtle state within the mind.
Although the contemplation of the ocean by the ten knowledges occurs within meditative absorption, it is expressed through words; therefore, it is subtler than the following.
The section on exposition is the coarsest, as it is directed toward sentient beings and thus involves manifesting [the teaching] upon emerging from absorption.

This explains that exposition takes wisdom as its basis, and wisdom takes the ocean [of the Dharma] as its basis; for exposition is established by relying on wisdom, and wisdom arises by relying on principle.
The text consists of three parts:
first, the reliance upon wisdom; second, the granting of the exposition; third, the clarification of the intent of the exposition.
In this context, there are five meanings of "Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*), as set forth in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*:

first, the aspiration for the Mahāyāna serves as the seed; second, Prajñā serves as the mother; third, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) serves as the womb; fourth, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) serves as the nursemaid; and fifth, all Buddhas serve as the father.
Furthermore, there are ten meanings, as explained below in the section on Maitreya’s Knowledge.
Regarding the ten types of knowledge: first, because success is immediately followed by failure, success is pure; failure is likewise so.
Because it thereby possesses the other nine [attributes] and so forth, it is called "inconceivable.
This term "inconceivable" applies throughout the following nine phrases.

Within these two [categories], it is inconceivable because the emptiness and existence of sentient beings are non-dual; because their types are numerous; because their characteristics are mutually identical; because their characteristics are mutually inclusive; because they encompass all dharmas; and because their faculties and natures are manifold. Thus, they are also inconceivable.
Furthermore, the *dhātu* is the *tathāgatagarbha*; it is designated as "sentient beings" according to conditions, which is its arising.
Moreover, this arising exists within wisdom.

Among these three [categories], the first pertains to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the second to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the third to both; the fourth pertains to neither. Each of these applies to both the defiled and the pure—reflect upon this accordingly.
The faculties and desires are subsumed within the latter two knowledges and also within the former seven, as distinguished in the preceding inquiry.
The latter seven clarify the Buddha’s ocean because they consist of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Fifth, because they are bestowed according to the faculties and desires [of beings] and because they universally transform;

sixth, because they manifest virtues; seventh, because of light and sound; eighth, because of the inclusion of the three wheels; ninth, because of profound meditative concentration. Thus, both the characteristics and the identity of essence and function remain undestroyed.
The tenth [point] summarizes the specific sections.
This concludes the "Original Section.
Within the seventh section, "Emerging from Samādhi and Accomplishing Benefit," there are two parts:

First, one enters the meditative absorption of the primary and its attendants (*saparivāra-samādhi*). Since the preceding section clarified that meditative concentration does not obstruct functional activity, it spoke of the "ten knowledges" (*daśajñāna*);
here, it clarifies that functional activity does not obstruct meditative concentration, hence it is called "unimpaired," meaning that those concentrations remain unimpaired.
How is it non-disintegrating?
It is explained and revealed by means of the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
Within the two [sections on] arising benefit, there are two [parts]:
First, regarding the internal benefit, there are also two parts;
first, benefiting this assembly, which has four aspects:
first, realizing the essence of the Dharma;
Second, based on realization, one gives rise to skillful wisdom;
third, based on wisdom, one gives rise to sublime eloquence;
fourth, one speaks without interruption, which is due to the power of one's vows.
Second, the two [sections] generally connect and manifest the perfection.
Regarding the second [section], the external benefit, there are three parts;
first, the movement.
The two benefits are as follows: first, it causes fear during movement, whereas by reversing this, there is joy;
second, it bestows the fruit of bliss upon the cause of peace and goodness.
Furthermore, it causes destruction during movement, whereas by reversing this, there is the adornment of jewels.
The three rains of jewels refer to this Dharma-gate.
Because ten were reduced by these [three], ten is indicated while seven are listed.
Section Eight, "The Chapter on Praising Virtues with the Light from the Hairs," has two parts:
First, the pores and radiance of all Tathāgatas represent the supreme empowerment of the Buddhas.
This praises the virtues of Samantabhadra and manifests his teaching endowed with all virtues, so that the assembly may develop reverence and yearning.
This is the wisdom of the sound of praise for the supreme radiance.
Within the twenty-four verses, there are two parts:
the first eight verses praise the vastness of Samantabhadra’s three karmas, which exhaustively reach the very source and depths of the Buddhas.
Among these, the first three constitute the body;
the next half constitutes speech;

and the subsequent two and a half constitute the mind. Within these, the first half is concentration (*samādhi*) and the latter is wisdom (*prajñā*); the following two exhaust the very source and depths of Buddhahood.

The latter six verses praise the universal and unimpeded nature of the essence and function [of the Tathāgata] as it responds to capacities. Among them, the first praises the universality of the essence: that is, the body of Samantabhadra sits within this assembly, yet he is seen in each and every one of the infinite worlds throughout the ten directions; he is always present in those very places, yet his body is fundamentally not divided from its original location, nor does it come or go.
It is likewise so within all atoms and within the bodies of all sentient beings; because sentient beings are themselves suchness, they are Samantabhadra.

In reality, the One Vehicle Buddha-land is also identical to the perfect pervasiveness of Samantabhadra. However, because it is easier to understand by way of the superior [aspect], the land is distinguished and the principle is emphasized, manifesting the One Vehicle by means of the Three Vehicles—this can be seen through reflection.
The functions of the latter five sciences are:
first, manifesting the body; second, manifesting the Dharma; third, purifying vows; fourth, [benefiting] sentient beings; and fifth, manifesting wisdom.
Within the ninth section, "Granting Permission to Speak and Causing Joy," there are also two parts:

First, the prose section indicates the underlying intent: having already experienced joy upon hearing the "Section on the Original Nature" (*mūlaparivarta*), one now experiences further joy because the "Section on the Exposition" (*deśanāparivarta*) is permitted to be taught; hence, it is called "repeated joy.
Second, the verses reveal the matter of this joy. Among these, there are ten verses, divided into three parts:
the first two and a half verses present the Buddha’s transformative virtues as transcending ordinary perception and being unfathomable.

Within this, the first [section] concerns the teaching of the Dharma through profound wisdom; the second, the adornment of the lands and the harmonizing of sentient beings; and the latter half generally concludes by showing that the capacity of the transformer and the transformed is inexhaustible and unfathomable.
The second [section] consists of five and a half verses, which admonish the assembly to purify themselves so as to become fit vessels for the Dharma.
Within this, the first half [of the verse] excludes those incapable of hearing [the teaching].
"Those who delight in evil" refers to those who create the causes for the miserable realms (*durgati*).
"Those attached to existence" refers to those who, even if they perform virtuous deeds, do not seek liberation (*niḥsaraṇa*).
The latter line concludes the refutation, stating "unable to comprehend" and so forth, which reveals that [such persons] are not suitable vessels.
The following verse clarifies that only those possessing three powers are fit to be vessels:
first, the power of past roots of goodness; second, the power of proximity to virtuous friends; and third, the power of the Buddha’s protective mindfulness.
The concluding phrase of the preceding line states: "These sentient beings are able to attain superior wisdom.
The subsequent verse sets forth seven mental qualities that must be present to be fit for hearing the Dharma:
first, a straightforward mind, because it is free from flattery and crookedness;
Second is the pure mind, because it is free from seeking faults and the like;
third is the mind of loving-kindness, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;
fourth is the mind of compassion, for the sake of saving sentient beings.
Fifth is the mind of profound resolve, for the sake of practice;
sixth is the mind of faith, for the sake of receiving the profound Dharma;
seventh is the mind of insatiability, because the thirsting mind knows no fullness.
The concluding phrase of the latter line states: "Upon hearing this Dharma, they rejoice immeasurably.
Thus far, two stanzas and ten sections have generally identified all those who are suitable vessels for hearing the teaching; next, two stanzas specifically cite this particular assembly.
The first line clarifies that one who possesses four virtues is capable of knowing the Buddha’s realm:

first, dwelling on the stage of Samantabhadra; second, possessing the vows of Samantabhadra; third, practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra; and fourth, realizing the emptiness of the *dharmadhātu*. The subsequent line concludes this by stating that such a person knows the Buddha’s realm.
The next verse praises this great assembly for attaining two benefits in the present:
first, the direct vision of the Buddha; second, the attainment of Samantabhadra’s skillful means.
The final verse serves as a general conclusion, stating that all sentient beings who hear the Buddha-dharma do so solely through the power of the Buddha.
The third section consists of two verses, which cite the teaching and grant permission to explain it, while exhorting the audience to contemplate and find joy therein.

The first verse cites the teaching and exhorts contemplation: because the Buddha and his buddha-field are within one’s own body, it exhorts the assembly to contemplate them within the pores of their skin.

The final [verse] clarifies that one must possess the Universal Eye (*samantacakṣus*) in order to behold this Dharma; the subsequent line, which permits the teaching and exhorts the listener, may be understood accordingly.
Among the ten eyes mentioned below, the tenth is the Universal Eye, because it perceives the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) through the gateway of equality.
If discussed generally, the ten eyes taken together are called "universal" (*p'u*).

In the tenth section, which specifically presents the divisions of the ocean of Dharma, it first clarifies that the speakers in the various assemblies differ: only the two chapters on the *Saṃghīti* and the *Lakṣaṇa* were spoken by the Buddha, while all others were spoken by Bodhisattvas; the significance of this is as explained below.
Furthermore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are five types of discourse:
first, those spoken by the Buddha; second, those spoken by his disciples; third, those spoken by immortals (ṛṣis); fourth, those spoken by devas; and fifth, those spoken through transformation.
This is based on the production of sounds, phrases, and sentences;
if considered in terms of being bestowed, it encompasses both sentient and insentient beings, according to the Three Vehicles.
Furthermore, there are five explanations, as stated below: "The Buddha speaks, Bodhisattvas speak, lands speak, sentient beings speak, and all things of the three periods of time speak."
"This penetrates all phenomena equal to the three worlds, according to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
The text consists of two parts:
first, an extensive analysis of the world-oceans, which answers the previous question regarding the fruit."
The second section, from "In the distant past" onwards, answers the previous question regarding the cause.
This section consists of two parts:
first, a detailed exposition of the world-system; second, a summary in verse.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, a general discussion of the ten worlds;

second, a specific analysis of the Flower Treasury World-realm (*Kusumatalagarbhadhatu*), which also serves as an explanation of the tenth world-realm’s destruction, since formation is itself destruction.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, the presentation and enumeration of the topical headings; second, the detailed explanation according to those headings.
Within the first part, there are three sections:
First, a general introduction citing scriptural evidence; second, the formal listing of the ten names; third, concluding on their inexhaustibility.
Regarding these ten, the first has four meanings:

first, because the substance of the land transcends all marks and is only established through speech, it is called "explaining worlds," as is established in the *Catuḥpratisaṃvid-sūtra*, and as explained below in the section on dependent origination regarding the contemplation of bondage and so forth.
Second, because lands manifest through the perfuming of consciousness by names and phrases, it is called "expounding";
third, because of the sounds and speech within those lands, as explained in the verse below;
fourth, because the establishment of names differs across worlds, it is called "expounding."
The first statement refers to the world (*loka*), while the latter three refer to its realm (*dhātu*);
the second involves the grasping of the realm of conditions;
and the third is due to its reliance [on that], whereby it endures for a long time.
Fourth, the external appearance is well-proportioned;
fifth, the internal body is full and robust;
sixth, the marks of virtue are magnificent and beautiful.
Seventh, purification through the removal of defilements;
eighth, the arising of Buddhas when the vessel [of sentient beings] is pure;
ninth, the duration of time for the sūtras.
The ten conditions, the ten dispersions, and the ten formations are all manifold and profound; they are collectively termed "oceans.
Every single world-system possesses these ten.
Now, to provide a general explanation of the various oceans of worlds, I shall briefly set forth ten gates:

First, categories; second, inhabitants; third, names and entities; fourth, defilement and purity; fifth, outflows and non-outflows; sixth, common and uncommon; seventh, the mundane and nirvana; eighth, the primary and secondary supports; ninth, persons and dharmas; tenth, non-obstruction.
First, regarding the clarification of categories: in the Hīnayāna, there is only one category, such as the Sahā world-system, and no distinct pure lands. Within the Triyāna, there are two types;
the first concerns the Buddha’s own dwelling place, which has three aspects: [The text continues with the three aspects of the Buddha’s dwelling place.]
First, the land of the dharma-nature;
second, the land of actual virtues, referring to sublime conduct and so forth;
third, the land of physical characteristics, referring to supreme jewels and so forth.
The latter two constitute the land of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
Since these three are not places for gathering and transforming others (*parasaṃgrahavastu*), they are not analyzed here.
Second, regarding the places where Buddhas gather and transform others, there are also three:
First, the land of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya-bhūmi*), which has two types:
first, the defiled, referring to this Sahā world and others, which pertains to Śākyamuni;
second, the pure, referring to the transformation lands in other directions, which pertains to other Buddhas.
Second is the transformed defiled land, referring to such acts as pressing the earth with the toes.
Third is the land of others' enjoyment, referring to the eighteen perfections and so forth.
Regarding the first two, there are two parts:
If one relies on the Initial Teaching (Shijiao), there are only ten billion Jambudvīpas and ten billion Śākyamunis as the scope of their conversion and guidance.

If one relies on the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, a trichiliocosm is taken as a single unit; counting such units up to the number of grains of sand in the Ganges constitutes a single "world-nature" (*lokadhātu-vibhāga*); counting these natures up to the number of grains of sand in the Ganges constitutes a single "world-ocean" (*lokadhātu-samudra*); counting these oceans up to the number of grains of sand in the Ganges constitutes a single "world-lineage" (*lokadhātu-gotra*); and counting these lineages up to an immeasurable number of grains of sand in the Ganges constitutes a single Buddha-world.

Regarding the scope of those to be converted and their lands of enjoyment: according to the Initial Teaching (śīkṣā), it is located at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu-śikhara*), because it is taught as being within the same realm to lead in those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

According to the Final Teaching (*paryantavāda*), it does not reside within the three realms; as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Thirty-two Ganges-sands of Buddha-lands to the west of here, there is a world named Unsurpassed (*Anabhibhūta*); this is the true retribution pure land (*vipākaviśuddhakṣetra*) of Śākyamuni Buddha."
Furthermore, amidst all the peripheral regions of the Sumeru worlds, there are occasionally found pure buddha-fields; these are proclaimed as transformations to attract sentient beings.
Third, regarding reliance on the One Vehicle, there are two aspects:

first, in terms of the fruit, it divides the ocean of the ten Buddhas’ own bodies and lands; this is ineffable, yet for the sake of providing a basis for discourse, ten are taught as in the Second Assembly.
Second, in terms of the spheres of gathering and transforming beings, there are three categories:
First, from the realm of Mount Sumeru and the tree-shaped worlds, extending to the world-oceans of the forms of all sentient beings, constitutes the first category.
Second, beyond the trichiliocosm, there are ten distinct types of worlds:

1) world-nature, 2) world-ocean, 3) world-wheel, 4) world-perfection, 5) world-differentiation, 6) world-spiral, 7) world-turning, 8) world-lotus, 9) world-Sumeru, and 10) world-appearance; these, which were previously described as the domain of the Wheel-Turning Kings for the ten thousand sons, constitute the second category.
Third, the ten Lotus Treasury Adorned World-Oceans, complete with their primary and attendant features like Indra’s net and so forth, constitute the realm of the Buddha; this is the third category.
These three aforementioned categories collectively comprise ten matters that, as their primary elements, constitute the world-systems:

first, the ocean of world-systems; second, the ocean of world-systems arising from causal conditions; third, the ocean of world-systems abiding; fourth, the ocean of world-systems in shape; fifth, the ocean of world-systems in substance; sixth, the ocean of world-systems in adornment; seventh, the ocean of world-systems in purity; eighth, the ocean of world-systems where Tathāgatas appear in the world; ninth, the ocean of world-systems in kalpas; and tenth, the ocean of world-systems in the methods of destruction.

Regarding the inhabitants of these two [realms]: in the case of the Hīnayāna, they consist only of noble beings who still possess a remainder of support (*sopadhiśeṣa-ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

In the case of the Three Vehicles, the first two of the three [realms] are inhabited by ordinary beings, followers of the Two Vehicles, bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), and the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Buddhas;
the latter one is inhabited by bodhisattvas from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) onward and the reward bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*) of Buddhas.

Regarding the statement in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* that Bodhisattvas of the third bhūmi are born into the pure lands of the Buddhas, this is explained in terms of the seventh bhūmi; thus, the first bhūmi corresponds to that third [bhūmi].

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the *Awakening of Faith* that bodhisattvas prior to the [first] bhūmi perceive the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya), this refers to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*), based on perception through samādhi.
Within the One Vehicle, this is discussed primarily in terms of three stages:
first, the stage of seeing and hearing; second, the stage of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*); and third, the stage directed toward the fruition.
This can be understood through general principle: the Buddha-bodies in these three locations are identical to the ten Buddhas.

Regarding the names and their essence: "world" (*loka*) refers to time, and "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to a specific limit or boundary; thus, they are manifested within the limits of time and are named according to their characteristics.
Abounding, profound, and vast beyond measure, it is likewise called the "Ocean.
The term "world-ocean" (*lokadhātu-samudra*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound, where the world itself is the ocean, following the metaphorical usage.

According to the Hīnayāna, its substance consists of the seven atoms (the mother and six sons), the four objective particles such as form, and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which are substantial matter (*dravyarūpa*).
Within the Three Vehicles, for ordinary beings and those prior to the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, all take the ālayavijñāna as their essence.

Regarding the two meanings [of the stages] from the first stage upward, in the retribution land (*vipākabhūmi*), they likewise take the ālayavijñāna as their essence; however, that which is manifested by the two wisdoms takes the wisdom of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) as its essence.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The consciousness-only wisdom of Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas, up to its manifestation as the substance of the pure land.
According to the Final Teaching (Zhōngjiào), both take the Tathāgatagarbha and True Suchness (Tathatā) as their substance.

If it is the One Vehicle, then by means of the inexhaustible dharma-realm, the various modes of activity—such as the three worlds, persons, dharmas, principle, and phenomena—are mutually the very substance of one another; this may be understood through reflection.
Regarding the fourfold classification of defiled and pure: in the Hīnayāna, there is only the defiled.
In the Three Vehicles, there are two [classifications]:
first, according to stages (*avasthā*), and second, according to phenomena (*dharma*).
At the beginning and middle [of this section], there are four pairs that clarify its defilement and purity:

first, regarding cause and effect. This means that the abodes of Bodhisattvas from the stage of the Vajra [mind] downward are called "lands of retribution" (*vipākabhūmi*) and are not called "pure lands" (*śuddhakṣetra*), because their afflictions have not yet been exhausted.

Only the Buddha alone has caused all habitual tendencies to vanish; thus, his dwelling is called "pure. Therefore, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* says: "The three levels of worthies and the ten stages of sages dwell in the land of retribution; only the Buddha alone dwells in the pure land."

Second, regarding the distinction between the exclusively uniform and the non-uniform: the lands inhabited by Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward are called "Pure Lands" because they exclusively transcend the three realms (*tridhātu*). This is because they possess the meaning of the four "exclusively uniform" attributes: exclusively pure, exclusively blissful, exclusively free from faults, and exclusively sovereign.
The stages from the seventh downward are not yet called "Pure Land," because they do not exclusively transcend the three realms;

even if one were to transcend them through the power of vows, the four aspects would not be fully perfected, meaning that the untainted wisdom of contemplation (*nirāsrava-vipaśyanā-jñāna*) is still subject to interruption, and thus it is not free from faults and so forth—this is explained according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

Third, regarding the distinction between the pure and the mixed: places where ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles dwell together are not called "pure lands," whereas the birthplaces of bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi) are called "pure. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Worlds are immeasurable and are of two kinds: namely, pure and impure."

In a pure world, there are no hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts, nor are there the realms of desire, form, or formlessness; it is inhabited solely by a multitude of bodhisattvas dwelling therein, and for this reason it is called a "pure world."

A bodhisattva who has already entered the third stage takes rebirth there by the power of their vows; among them, there are no ordinary beings, nor are there śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, whether they be those still subject to birth or those beyond it.
The commentary explains:
Since this third stage is named "Pure Intention" (*śuddhāśaya*), it is identical to the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), as this is distinguished according to the seven stages.

Fourth, regarding falling back or not: from the point of entering the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) onwards, the birthplaces of Bodhisattvas in the three levels of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*) who have reached the stage of non-retrogression are called "Pure Lands. Within these, there are also those of the four fruits and the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*), just as in the land of Amitābha; those born there all abide in the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Once they have become capable [of rebirth], they return to the lower status of light-furred beings; such places where the three groups of sentient beings coexist are not called "Pure Lands.

Among these four pairs of eight meanings, the first concerns the fruit as being exclusively pure, the last concerns regression as being exclusively defiled, and those in between, when compared with one another, pertain to both the defiled and the pure.

Second, regarding the fourfold categorization by way of phenomena (*dharma*), there is that which is "only pure": this refers to taking the aspect of purity within the aforementioned four gates, as well as the fact that the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the stage where one abides during the state of regression is pure.

Alternatively, it may be exclusively defiled, because within the four gates, one grasps the defiled by way of mutual comparison, and because the Buddha-fruit is explained in accordance with conditions based on the capacities of sentient beings; thus, in the *Awakening of Faith*, it is termed "that which is produced by the illusory karma of following defilement."
Or they may both be [present], because the two preceding meanings are not mutually exclusive.
Or they may be neither, because the two meanings are mutually integrated rather than fixed as one, and because the two characteristics are exhausted.
The One Vehicle is also twofold:
first, regarding categories, the first category is defiled, the latter category is pure, and the middle category is common to both.
Second, regarding dharmas, they may both be pure, because they are identical with the Buddha.
Alternatively, they may both be defiled, because they are sentient beings;
alternatively, they may possess both [aspects], because the two preceding meanings are inseparable;
or alternatively, they may not be simultaneous, because the two characteristics merge and the two characteristics are exhausted.
Within each of the three aforementioned categories, all four permutations are present; this should be understood by applying the same principle.
As for the fifth category, the outflowing and non-outflowing, according to the Hīnayāna, it consists exclusively of the outflowing.
The Three Vehicles have two gates:
first, the gate of following characteristics; second, the gate of mutual integration.
Within the first, there are four propositions:
First, those that are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*), namely the lands manifested by ordinary beings and those on the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi;
second, those that are exclusively without outflows (*anāsrava*), namely the lands manifested by Buddhas;

third, those that are both, namely the lands manifested by the two types of wisdom of Bodhisattvas on the bhūmis as well as those manifested by the *ālayavijñāna*. Although these two are subsumed under the two truths of suffering and the path, they do not possess separate ontological entities; they are merely subsumed differently according to their specific meanings.
The fourth is "neither," meaning that all are immediately empty and do not fall into numerical categories.
This above is according to the Initial Teaching (Śākyaputrīya-yāna).
Second, within the Teaching of Interfusion, there are likewise four propositions:
Either one or all [of these] are untainted (*anāsrava*); this remains the case even at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), because they are by nature free from the outflows (*āsrava*).
As the Sūtra says: "Form is untainted and unbound; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are untainted and unbound," and so forth, as explained at length.
Second, all [dharmas], including even the Buddhas, possess outflows (*sāsrava*), because they do not depart from the nature of dharmas that have outflows.
As the Sūtra says: "The Buddhas dwell within the midst of the three poisons, the four inversions, the five desires, and so forth, and thereby attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," and so on at length.
The first phrase is the outflow-free within the non-differentiation of the outflowing; therefore, it is itself outflow-free.
The second phrase is the outflowing within the non-differentiation of the outflow-free; therefore, the outflow-free is itself its outflowing.
Three are both [bound and liberated], because the two preceding meanings are not mutually exclusive.
Four are neither, because they are all devoid of the nature of being bound or liberated.
As the Sūtra says: "Form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated," and so forth, as extensively explained.

Within the One Vehicle, as with the dharma-realm of dependent origination, if there were not "one," then "all" would not be established; their mutual fusion and non-obstruction likewise possess the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi), which can be understood through total inclusion—reflect upon this.
Regarding the sixth point, the common and the uncommon, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the boundaries; second, revealing the characteristics of the meaning.

In the first part, every single world consists of sentient beings; that is to say, through the power of the maturation of common seeds, the *vipākavijñāna* (retributive consciousness) transforms into the appearance of the material world (*bhājanaloka*), such as form and so forth.
Question:
How many sentient beings’ ripening consciousnesses (*vipākavijñāna*) undergo transformation within a single world-system? Answer:
In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are three masters' explanations.
The first master says:
"All sentient beings [arise] because the sūtras state that they are 'collectively produced by the sovereign power of the karma of all sentient beings.'"
Next, the Master refutes this, saying:
"If that were so, then all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would truly transform this defiled land into [a pure land];
and all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) would truly transform other realms and this world-system into various pure and wondrous lands."
Furthermore, when noble ones who are weary of the realm of form are born into the formless realm, they certainly do not descend again; what use would there be for them to transform into this land?
Because these three great faults exist, it is clear that [this power] cannot reach all sentient beings.

It should be stated that this refers to those currently residing [in this realm] and those who are to be born there; their ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) transforms into this world-system. The sūtra uses the term "all" based on a partial reference, because all those with a common karma collectively transform it together.
Later, the Master further refutes the second [position], saying:

"If that were so, when the receptacle world is about to perish, since there would be neither those currently dwelling therein nor those about to be born there, whose ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) would transform into this world?"
Furthermore, ordinary beings who are weary of the realm of form and are born into the formless realm manifest formless bodies; what use would it be for them to transform [the world] into earth?

Moreover, if a physical body were to exist in a different plane from the environment of that realm, they would be so vastly separated in terms of coarseness and subtlety that they could not support one another; even if such a body were transformed into that [environment], what benefit would there be?
It is also due to these three kinds of great faults that those currently residing and those about to be born are both unable to undergo transformation.
That is to say: first, when the receptacle world is about to be destroyed, both those about to be born and those currently residing lack any objects of enjoyment;
second, if one were to receive a body in the formless realm while currently residing here, there would be no sense of enjoyment within this land.
Third, even if there were a body in the form realm that differed from this [desire realm] in terms of coarseness or subtlety, it would likewise lack the functions of support and enjoyment.
Therefore, these three [realms] all lack the sense of transformation.
If that is so, what is it that undergoes transformation?
Zhengyi should say:
"In general, all transformed lands serve as the support for and the object of enjoyment for the physical body (*rūpakāya*).

If they can serve as such supports and objects of enjoyment for the body, then even if one is born in another region, the consciousnesses of that [body] would likewise be able to transform this land."
Therefore, when the receptacle world is about to be destroyed or first formed, although sentient beings are absent, the land still appears.
This point is analyzed in accordance with the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Second, regarding the manifestation of the characteristics of the common and the uncommon: if, according to the Hīnayāna, [the world] is composed of atoms that are common to all, then it is exclusively common.
Within the context of the three vehicles, there are four propositions:

the first is that [the realm] may be exclusively common. This means that although the environment and its resources do not exist apart from consciousness, the consciousnesses are distinct while the characteristics of the land are one; this is because they are collectively manifested from the seeds of common characteristics within those respective consciousnesses.

Just as when the four elements are gathered together they form a single pillar, the characteristic of that pillar is not separate from the four elements, yet there are not four pillars corresponding to the four elements; one should know that the principle herein is likewise.

If one considers the land of self-enjoyment, the Buddhas share a single land with all other Buddhas; this is because, just as the *dharmakāya* is the common basis for all Buddhas, so too is this land of the same *dharmatā*.
If it is a land of enjoyment for others, it is likewise shared by both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, just as a king and his ministers share a single kingdom.
Furthermore, all lands of defilement are manifestations of the collective karma of sentient beings; therefore, there is no distinction between them.
Second, such supports and fruits are all non-common (*asādhāraṇa*), because each manifests within its own foundational consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

The treatise states: "Both are the maturation-consciousnesses (*vipākavijñāna*) of sentient beings, each transforming [its own object]. They appear in the same location as similar [images] without mutual obstruction, like the light of many lamps or the dreams of many people. While the causes are distinct, the characteristics of the fruits are similar; since there is no difference in their location, they are conventionally termed 'common,' yet in reality, each is distinct."

"The pure lands of all Buddhas are likewise; the transformations of their respective consciousnesses all pervade the dharma-realm, and because they are similar in the same location, they are said to be 'common'.
The commentary explains:

"If there were even one land that did not follow the differentiation of individual consciousnesses, then there would be dharmas external to the mind, and the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) would not be established."
The treatise states: "I say that the objects of consciousness are merely manifestations of consciousness.
From this, one should know that all things are transformations of one's own consciousness; therefore, they are each distinct.
Regarding "the third is both common and uncommon," this is because the two preceding explanations are not mutually exclusive.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "External objects and so forth arise either through the cause of uncommon conceptualization, or again through the cause of common conceptualization."

If it arises through common conceptualization, then even though that conceptualization itself is absent, [the object] does not perish forever because it is sustained by the conceptualizations of others.
Otherwise, the conceptualizations of others would be without their fruit.
Although they do not cease, those who have attained purity possess pure right view regarding that object.
For example, among many practitioners of meditation, various and immeasurable differences in views can be observed regarding a single object due to their respective concentrated mental states.
"That is also like this.
The commentary explains:

This statement concerns how the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment) follows from common conceptualization; its non-common conceptualization is the same as that of the second [category] mentioned previously. Therefore, it is established that all external receptacle worlds possess these two meanings accordingly, and thus both are preserved.
Regarding the fourth point—that which is neither common nor uncommon—there are two meanings:
first, because the previous two explanations mutually negate one another; second, because it is impossible to definitively select either one. Therefore, they are both "neither."

Secondly, because the characteristics of the land and its supporting consciousness are exhausted, and because consciousness arises from conditions and lacks intrinsic nature, it is therefore inexpressible, being free from both common and uncommon characteristics.
Regarding these, if they are explained as being transformations of the *ālayavijñāna* as the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), this belongs to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).
If, however, they are explained as manifestations of the *tathāgatagarbha* within the *ālaya*, this belongs to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*).
If all marks are exhausted, such that there is only a single pure mind, perfectly equal and impartial, beyond words and transcending thought, it belongs to the Sudden Teaching (*dun jiao*).
If one relies on the Perfect Teaching (*yuan jiao*), there are two senses:

first, as explained in the preceding teachings, it is identical to the inexhaustible dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) with its infinitely layered Indra’s net, wherein one enters the unimpeded and complete state of principal and attendant factors; this belongs to this [Perfect Teaching].
Second, seeking by way of meaning, there are also four propositions:
first, some are exclusively common, because they share the same dharma-realm and their characteristics are identical;
second, some are exclusively uncommon, because their dependent origination is distinct and their characteristics do not intermingle.
Third, they may both be so, because the two aforementioned meanings are inseparable and because their total essence is mutually identical without being destroyed;
fourth, they may both be neither, because the two characteristics are extinguished and all forms and negations are exhausted.
The seventh section, the Gate of Worldly Nirvāṇa, has two parts:
first, following the characteristics; second, mutual integration.
Within the first part, there are four statements:
First, there is that which is exclusively mundane, referring to the abodes of those prior to the stages [of the bodhisattva path] and ordinary beings.

Second, there is that which is exclusively nirvana, referring to the nirvana in which the Buddhas abide at the stage of fruition; even their own *svasaṃbhogakāya* lands are likewise subsumed within that great nirvana.

Third, it is both mundane and nirvanic; according to treatises such as the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, one should know that within the untainted dharmadhātu there are three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*).
Because it is produced by untainted wholesome roots, it is called "worldly";
yet because it is not produced by tainted karma or afflictions, it is also called "nirvāṇa."
Based on this meaning, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states: "World-Honored One, there is the conditioned world and the unconditioned world; there is conditioned nirvana and unconditioned nirvana."
The commentary explains:
conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) belong to the mundane level of ordinary beings, while unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) belong to the fruit of Buddhahood, which is nirvāṇa.
Conditioned nirvāṇa and unconditioned saṃsāra constitute the transformation-rebirth (*pariṇāma-vaipākika*), and because their respective expectations differ, they are assigned to the "both" category.
The four meanings, by analogy with the pure dharma-dhātu of all Buddhas, are neither mundane nor nirvāṇa; for it is not the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles, nor is it the nirvāṇa at the twin śāla trees.
Second, regarding their mutual integration, there are also four propositions:
first, "sometimes only the mundane," meaning that even the pure lands of Buddhas are entirely subsumed within the receptacle world;
second, "sometimes only nirvana," meaning that even the defiled lands of sentient beings are identical in nature once their characteristics are exhausted.
Third, both may be present together because of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena; as the Treatise states: "There is not the slightest difference between the world and nirvana.
Because there is no distinction, they are non-dual yet dual, manifesting simultaneously.
Fourth, because there is not even a hair’s breadth of discrimination, duality is non-dual; as form and negation are both exhausted, both are negated.
As the Sūtra says: “The Tathāgata does not perceive birth-and-death, nor does he perceive nirvāṇa.”
Furthermore, this sutra states: "Both the world and nirvana are unobtainable. This is what that refers to.
Regarding the eighth point, the gate of the basis and its manifestations: according to the Hīnayāna, this refers exclusively to the environmental retribution (*pariṇāmanavipāka*).

Within the Three Vehicles, although the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) is manifested by the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) and the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), it is categorized solely as the *niṣyanda-vidhāna* (retributive environment).

However, according to the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*), it encompasses all three worlds. This is because the Śākyamuni Buddha possesses a "land-body" (*kṣetra-kāya*) and so forth; thus, the entire world is the Buddha’s body. Furthermore, because there are "worlds in the form of sentient beings" and so forth, sentient beings are themselves the world. This is because the phenomenal and the noumenal (*nimitta-nimittin*) are interpenetrated and unimpeded, and their mutual identity is sovereign.
Regarding the ninth category, the Dharma-gate of persons: in the Hīnayāna, there is no such meaning of a Dharma-gate of persons.
In the Triyāna, this meaning of a Dharma-gate of persons may exist.
In the Ekayāna, it is fully present; because this refers to the Buddhas, Samantabhadra, and all sentient beings alike, it pertains exclusively to persons.
Alternatively, because all worlds are themselves Dharma-gates, as the text states: "The pure and wondrous forms enter into the gates of immeasurable True Dharma.
This clarifies that worlds and so forth are entirely Dharma-gates.

Regarding the tenth gate of non-obstruction: in the world of the Hīnayāna, there are only phenomenal characteristics; above these, there exist only principles such as suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self.
Within the Three Vehicles, in the Dharma-nature Land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*), only the principle (*li*) exists, while all else is phenomena (*shi*).
However, in the two higher schools, principle and phenomena are neither identical nor different; this is termed "unimpeded" (*asaṅga*).
Within the One Vehicle, there are briefly ten levels:
first, the non-obstruction between phenomena and mental states. This means that while phenomena manifest in accordance with mental states, those phenomena transcend the realm of mental states.
As the text says: "They are like illusions, having no fixed location, all arising from deluded thoughts."

Second is the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*), which means that while being entirely identical to the true nature (*tathatā*), the characteristics of the lands (*kṣetra-lakṣaṇa*) remain distinct and clear.
As the text says: "The Lotus World-Ocean of the Dharma-realm, which is indestructible," and so forth.

The third aspect is the entry into non-obstruction, as the text says: "To fill the ten directions with a single buddha-land, and for the ten directions to enter into one without remainder," and so forth.
The fourth aspect is that the aspects themselves are non-obstructive, as the text says: "Immeasurable worlds are a single world," and so forth.

The fivefold manifestation of non-obstruction means that within a single atom one sees all lands, and likewise within the atoms of those lands one sees lands; thus, they are layered upon one another like Indra’s net.
Sixth, the non-obstruction between the principal and its retinue: in any single world-system, there must necessarily be all others as its retinue.

Seventh, the non-obstruction between essence and function: this means that within a single ocean of lands, there must necessarily be great functions that respond to the capacities of beings by preaching the Dharma.

Eighth is the unimpededness of concealment and manifestation: this refers to the concealment and manifestation of the defiled and the pure, the concealment and manifestation of different categories, and so forth, which can be understood by determining them according to conditions.

Ninth is the unimpededness of time and place: this refers to, for example, manifesting three periods of kalpas within a single kṣaṇa, or manifesting immeasurable lands within a single thought-moment; such is unimpededness.

Tenth is the unimpeded nature of formation and destruction; that is to say, formation is itself destruction, and destruction is itself formation, and so forth. These manifest without obstruction with such sovereign mastery that they are difficult to comprehend and transcend all conceptual deliberation.
These ten non-obstructions are simultaneously and fully possessed; they should be harmonized and integrated through the skillful means of the six characteristics (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*).
The meaning of the ten worlds has been briefly elucidated in this manner; all other aspects of meaning shall be revealed according to the text.

Within the second section, the "Detailed Explanation by Chapter," there are ten internal sub-sections; the first is not explained individually because its explanation is already contained within the explanation of the remaining nine.
In this text, the first eight are explained initially, and the tenth is explained last.
Regarding the preceding section, there are two parts for each of the first seven: namely, the prose and the verse.
The initial text contains no verse.
Within the prose of the first part, there are four sections:
First, the heading; second, the establishment; third, the analysis;
fourth, the conclusion. "All world-oceans" refers to the fact that each of those three categories is not singular.

Regarding the phrase "already accomplished" (*siddha*) and so forth: first, these various conditions collectively accomplish all worlds throughout the three periods of time, yet these worlds differ in being already accomplished or not yet accomplished.
Second, the accomplishment of a single world is itself pervasive throughout the three periods of time.
Reflect upon this: the former [set of] conditions encompasses the distinction of the realms (*dhātu*), while the latter realm encompasses the distinction of the conditions (*pratyaya*).
This is according to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Among the eight conditions, the first is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Second, the natural law of dependent origination;
third, the karmic power of those to be converted;
fourth, when a bodhisattva’s practice is perfected and he is destined to attain buddhahood in that realm, then by this power that realm is brought into existence.
Fifth, the universal cause is accomplished;

sixth, because Bodhisattvas cultivate vows and practices in order to adorn and purify all lands without exception, those lands are able to contain and sustain them through the unimpeded power of those vows and practices, and are thus called "liberation and mastery";
seventh, the primary cause of Great Enlightenment.
These eight are accomplished through universal vows.
Among these eight, the first four are accomplished through expedient means; because they are coarse in character, they also pertain to the defiled.

The latter four are accomplished in terms of reality; because they are subtle in character, they are exclusively pure, as the sutra states: "This land of mine is eternally peaceful and secure," and so forth.
This is because a single world-system inherently possesses both the coarse and the subtle.
