Among these ten concentrations, the first five are for accomplishing the benefit of others: first, possessing the dharmas of fruition; second, entering universal skillfulness; third, skillfully perfecting the vessel of adornment; fourth, correctly benefiting those with the capacity; and fifth, the limits of such benefit.

The latter five are for accomplishing one's own benefit: first, accomplishing the preparatory application; second, entering correct realization; third, expanding subsequent knowledge; fourth, conforming to nirvāṇa; and fifth, conforming to bodhi.
Furthermore, the first [verse] is general while the remaining nine are specific; this brief explanation makes it clear.
Within the second section on the universal exhortation, the first part consists of the verses, and the latter part concerns the prosodic divisions of those verses.

Within the verses: the first four praise the Buddha’s virtues as difficult to encounter; the next three clarify the superior benefits realized upon encountering him; and the final one concludes with an exhortation to offer worship.
Regarding the three kings' joyful verses in the announcement, there are two parts:
first, the king’s joy upon hearing [the news];
second, the decree issued in verse, which contains three sections:
The first [week] was for announcing the proclamation; the next seven [weeks] were for preparing excellent offerings; and the final [week] was for inspiring the thought of approaching the Buddha.
All four [groups] went together to the Buddha: first, the King and his inner retinue; and last, the eight classes of outer retinues.
Regarding the second section, the benefits gained from hearing the sutra, there are three parts.
First, explaining the title of the sutra: it means that practice can manifest the fruit; because the fruit is cited to indicate the cause, it is called "Manifesting" (*Pratyutpanna*) and so forth.
If one follows this meaning, it refers exclusively to the cause.
Furthermore, this assembly of Buddhas is manifested as such, which constitutes exclusively the fruit.
Within this, the three times are the three present moments; therefore, it encompasses nine and ten times.
It is not so; since the past and future do not exist, how could one speak of the present?
This is because it is the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), and thus it merely includes its retinue.
Within the section on the two youths obtaining benefit, there are two parts:
First is attaining meditative concentration for one's own benefit; second is benefiting others by teaching verses. Within the first, there are four concentrations:

first, the dharma that universally encompasses all objects; second, gathering [the mind] and returning it to the heart; third, attuning to the dharma with fearlessness; and fourth, the perfect clarity of the eye of wisdom.
Regarding the two aspects of benefiting others, there are two parts:
first, the presentation of the verses; second, the benefits obtained.
Within the verses, there are three sections:
The first verse is general: its first half refers to the aforementioned concentration of the Dharma-eye, while its second half summarizes what is seen by that eye.
The next seven verses specifically distinguish the Buddha’s past lives (*jātaka*), which are seen through the Buddha;
the final two verses specifically describe seeing various Buddhas and cultivating the causes for the sake of sentient beings.
The benefits obtained can be known. Within the nine verses of the Tathāgata’s praise, there are five sections:

first, one verse in general praising the youth; second, two verses specifically recording his primary retribution (*vipāka*); third, two verses specifically recording his secondary environment (*niśraya-phala*); fourth, two verses praising his ascetic practices; and finally, two verses summarily recording both his environment and primary retribution.
The fourth major section, "Achieving Superior Progress," has two parts.
First, the Buddha is raised as the objective condition for practice.
Within this, the distinction between the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and the period when a Buddha appears is made because the conditions for practice differ in each case.
That the youth’s life remains is due to the continuity of his practice.
Second, the benefit of practice established through conditions.
This section has two parts:
Upon first seeing the Buddha, one attains the four dhyānas as the beginning of superior progress.
First, regarding "recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānusmṛti*), the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Just as the Buddha has attained it, so shall I also attain it."
First, it is for the sake of mindfulness of the Buddha;
second, one enters the Universal Gate to exhaustively explore this oceanic treasury;
third, wisdom-holding serves as the agent of transformation, while the Wheel of Dharma of Wisdom is correctly established as that which is transformed.
Fourth, because these profound dharmas gladden the spirit.
Second, attaining meditative concentration upon hearing the sutra constitutes the culmination of superior progress.
As for the title of the sutra: it is called "Stainless" (*vimala*) because the intrinsic nature of the *dharmadhātu* is pure.
Because it possesses merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is called "adornment.

While the preceding sutra focused on the characteristics of the fruit (*phala-lakṣaṇa*), this section concerns the essence of the fruit (*phala-svabhāva*), because it represents a progressively deeper state of self-mastery and advancement.
Regarding the two concentrations, the former pertains to self-benefit and the latter to the benefit of others.
Furthermore, as for the stage at which the youth in this context attains the Dharma:
according to the meaning of the preceding and following passages of the sutra, there are three ways of attaining Buddhahood.

First, regarding the stages: by means of the six aspects of skillful means, at the very end of the stage of the ten faiths, immediately following the stage of superior progress, one enters the initial stage of the ten understandings and attains Buddhahood; for this is the stage of non-retrogression according to the Final Teaching of the Three Vehicles.
Through the One Vehicle, the six aspects are harmoniously integrated, thereby encompassing all stages up to the fruit of Buddhahood.

Therefore, within this context, the child’s vision of the first Buddha constitutes the stage of self-maintenance (*svabhāga*) of the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), while hearing the first sutra constitutes the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*) of the stage of faith.

Seeing the subsequent Buddhas explains the initial stage of the "self-nature" (svabhāva-bhūmi); hearing the subsequent sutras explains the initial "superior progress" (viśeṣa-gamana), because all stages are thereby fully encompassed.

Second, regarding practice, one does not rely on the sequence of stages in general; rather, through the culmination of self-nature and superior progress, one immediately reaches the fruit of Buddhahood.

Third, from the perspective of principle (*li*), all sentient beings have already attained completion and are no longer newly perfected, because all residual characteristics have been exhausted and the virtues of their nature (*xingde*) are fundamentally full.

Following this, there should have been a concluding summary (*pratisaṃdhi*), stating that "the boy was now such-and-such a person by name," as well as accounts of the earth shaking, flowers raining down, and the arrival of witnesses from other directions; furthermore, there should have been a unification with the ten directions and a restatement in verse (*gāthā*). However, because the transmission of the sutra is incomplete, these elements do not yet exist.
Question:
Now that this assembly has concluded, why is it that no one among the multitude has attained benefit? Answer:
Briefly stated, there is no separate benefit for this reason due to four points.

First, among the three preceding meanings, it is because of the first two meanings that the characteristics of the benefit for the youth are explained; it is because of the final meaning that there is no separate benefit obtained within the assembly.
Second, Guangtong’s commentary states:

"This sutra was preached by the Buddha shortly after his initial attainment of enlightenment; it merely reveals that the essence of the Dharma-wheel of the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle is the foundation of all teachings, and that the beneficial aspects of all other teachings derive their benefit from this [One Vehicle]. Therefore, they are not distinguished here."
Third, there are two types of teaching:
first, the teaching that adapts to the capacities [of beings].
This teaching encompasses all phenomena according to their capacities; as capacities progress, it provides benefit according to their respective discernment.

Second, regarding the teaching that pursues the Dharma: it encompasses sentient beings in accordance with the Dharma; since the Dharma itself neither increases nor decreases, there is no distinct benefit [for any particular group].
Fourth, this sutra is like the rising sun, which first illuminates the high mountains.
Since there were no capacities of middling or inferior grade, there was consequently no benefit corresponding to such [lesser] portions.
All subsequent assemblies mentioned in the text below should be understood according to this principle.
The explanation of the first assembly is concluded.
*An Investigation into the Profundities of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Three;

*An Investigation into the Profundities of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Four. This was composed by the Śramaṇa Fazang of Xisi Monastery in the Wei State, from the beginning of the second assembly until the conclusion of this assembly.
Chapter Three: On the Names and Epithets (Nāmanirdeśa-parivarta).
This chapter is also analyzed according to four sections:
first, the explanation of the title; second, the purpose of its inclusion; third, the essential doctrine and its scope; and fourth, the word-by-word commentary.
The first three sections:
First, regarding the title of the division—this section below clarifies the second part, titled "The Division on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Result and Giving Rise to Understanding.

This refers to the portion from here up to the sixth assembly, which explains the perfect causes of the five stages of cultivation and the fulfillment of the result of the ten bodies, enabling all bodhisattvas to understand these meanings and characteristics; therefore, it is given this name.
Regarding the name of the second assembly, it is called the "Assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance" (Pǔguāng Fǎtáng Huì).
There are five meanings for this explanation:
first, in terms of the factual event (*vastu*), because the Buddha emitted light from within the hall that shone everywhere, this hall is named "Universal Radiance."
The Dharma is preached therein, and it is also called the "Dharma Hall" (*dharmasabhā*); this is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative determinative compound). Second, regarding the Dharma itself:

that which is far-reaching and all-pervasive is termed "Universal" (*samanta*); that which is illuminated and penetrated by wondrous wisdom is termed "Light" (*prabha*); and the profound track of object and wisdom is termed "Dharma. Thus, this Universal Light is itself the Dharma.
Furthermore, regarding the designation "Hall of Universal Radiance" (*Puguang*): when this is spoken of within the hall, it is named after its governing subject (*yishu*).
This term "Dharma" admits of two interpretations, whereas "hall" is strictly a governing subject.
Thirdly, in terms of the object (*jing*): "universal" refers to the essence (*ti*), while "radiance" refers to the function (*yong*); "Dharma" encompasses both teaching (*jiao*) and meaning (*yi*).
The fourth is based solely on wisdom, which is explained in the same manner as the objects.

The fifth is based on reality: that is to say, within the unimpeded Dharma-realm, even a single atom or a single practice manifests throughout the Indra-net in infinite layers; therefore, it is called "universal."
Because it is universally perfect, luminous, and brilliantly radiant, it is further called "light" (*ābhāsa*).
Because there is nothing that does not accord with the correct path, it is also called "Dharma.
Thus, the Dharma responds to conditions, forming the aggregates (*skandha*) which constitute the hall.
All [these terms] are *karmadhāraya* (attributive) compounds; examples such as "taking the three emptinesses as the gate" can be understood by analogy.

Furthermore, faith is called "universal" (*pu*) because it encompasses all six stages; it is "light" (*guang*) because it extinguishes delusions and reveals principle; and it is a "hall" (*tang*) because it accommodates the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings.
Regarding the names of the three categories: "Tathāgata" is a name, interpreted according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
Alternatively, "Tathāgata" is itself the name, because among the ten epithets, Tathāgata constitutes one.
Among these, "name" (*nāman*) refers to specific designations such as Śākyamuni, while "title" (*abhidhāna*) refers to the ten epithets, which are the universal names of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, that which invokes the essence is called a "name," whereas that which indicates qualities is called a "title."
Furthermore, the names and titles are no different, as explained within the text.
There are also three reasons for the sequence of these two [sections].

First, regarding the reason for the division: since the preceding section cited the fruit to encourage the arising of faith and delight, this section now clarifies the causes by which that fruit can be attained, so as to give rise to correct understanding; therefore, it follows next.
Regarding those who come for the second assembly: because faith is the foremost among the causes cultivated, they come next.

Furthermore, it is said that while the previous assembly clarified the objects of faith, this one distinguishes the practice of the one who has faith; thus, it follows according to the sequence of meaning.
Question:
Do the three factors, beginning with the name, belong to that which is capable of faith? Answer:
To establish faith, we shall discuss this together in this assembly.
Question:
Was faith not already established previously?
Answer: Generally, faith arises in dependence upon an object.
This object has two meanings:
First, by indicating the objective realm of phenomena, it clarifies where they reside; second, by subsuming them within the mind, it brings about faithful practice.
The previous assembly relied on the former meaning, while this section concerns the latter meaning.
Furthermore, in the previous assembly, the fruit was extensive while the cause was brief; thus, both were categorized as belonging to the fruit.
In this assembly, the cause is extensive while the fruit is brief; thus, both are categorized as belonging to the cause.
Question:
Since both are resultant phenomena (*phala-dharma*), why was the reliance [on external conditions] clarified in the previous assembly, while the primary [retribution] is explained here? Answer:

The reliance on external retribution (*bāhya-upabhoga*) is coarse, manifest, and easy to perceive, and thus was distinguished first; the primary retribution (*mukhya-upabhoga*) is subtle, hidden, and difficult to know, and thus is explained later.
Furthermore, if we consider the Buddha, one must first establish the pure land as a dwelling place, and only afterwards determine the primary retribution (the physical body).
Moreover, these two may exist interchangeably; either may be cited as appropriate.
Question:
Regarding the cultivation of causes, why is it that this assembly and the sixth assembly both possess the dharmas of fruition, whereas the assemblies in between do not follow this pattern?
Answer: This assembly marks the beginning of the cultivation of causes; yet it is joined with the fruition, and the fruition occurs at the very start of the assembly.
The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth represent the culmination of the causal process, yet they also coincide with the fruit, though the fruit itself follows this coincidence.

These [stages] manifest how the perfect cause arises based upon the ocean of the fruit; once the cause is fulfilled, it returns to merge back into the perfect fruit. This is the grand theme and the hallmark of the beginning and end of this text.
Regarding the three categories [of causes] that arise, there are two interpretations.
The first states:
the preceding category clarifies the *niṣyanda-phala* (fruit of outflow), while this one clarifies the *vipāka-phala* (fruit of maturation).

Among the primary retributions, there are no more than the three karmas. This chapter clarifies that the bodily karma is universally pervasive, because names and titles are established based upon the body; the "Chapter on the Four Truths" clarifies that the Buddha’s vocal karma is all-encompassing; and the "Chapter on Radiance and Enlightenment" clarifies that the Buddha’s mental karma is universally awakened.
The subduing of the three wheels all constitutes direct retribution; however, because the bodily karma is the coarsest, it is distinguished first.
A second explanation states:
this is according to the question and answer that follows.

Furthermore, this chapter elucidates the meaning of the "ocean of lands. Since the preceding chapter distinguished the "ocean of worlds," it clarified how the substance follows conditions to manifest its resultant characteristics; now, by means of conditions, it conversely clarifies the resultant substance itself.
It follows next because it distinguishes the reality upon which the characteristics depend;
this can be seen by reflecting that each [world-system] pervades the three worlds.
Furthermore, while the previous assembly was based on the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*), this one is based on the Endurance World (*Sahā*).
There are various opinions on this matter.
Regarding the threefold essence and purpose of the *Samdhinirmocana*, there are likewise three points:
first, clarifying the division of the schools. From the beginning up until the sixth assembly, it constitutes a single sequence of question and answer; therefore, they must be analyzed together.

This refers to two cycles of cause and effect: the first is the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) and the latter is the essence (svabhāva); the former is causal dependent origination (hetu-pratyaya-utpāda), while the latter is the ultimate reality (tattva).
These two are also joined in pairs, namely: person (pudgala) and phenomena (dharma).
There are also two aspects of the person: that which is believed and that which believes.
Within the object of belief, the transformation lord takes internal realization of the ocean of lands as its essence and seven days of contemplation as its characteristic.

Furthermore, taking the image itself as its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it is additionally described as having "function" (*vṛtti*); moreover, supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and illumination are its function.

Within the context of assisting in transformation, Mañjuśrī takes sublime wisdom within faith as his essence and auspicious, supreme virtues as his characteristic; furthermore, pervading all places is his characteristic, while the benefit of sentient beings through speech—such as the recitation of verses—is his function.
Regarding the second [category], the capacity for faith, there are likewise two aspects:

first, with respect to the cause, its essence is the purity of realization (*pratisaṃvid*), its characteristic is the possession of virtuous qualities, and its function is its sublime meritorious activities; all of these are as explained in the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*), which one should examine in detail.

Second, with respect to the fruit, its essence is the inexhaustible Dharma-realm manifested within faith, its characteristic is the supreme virtues of the ten bodies (*daśakāya*), and its function is the benefit of sentient beings through transformation according to their capacities; this is also as explained in the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader."
The Dharma also has two aspects:

first, in terms of its objective realm (*viṣaya*), it takes the ocean of lands of equality within faith as its essence; it is said to be tenfold according to the capacities of sentient beings, with supreme virtues as its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and its function (*karman*) being to correspond with practice and teaching.

Second, in terms of practice (*caryā*), it takes internal realization within the stage of faith as its essence; its characteristic is the harmonious integration of all stages, and its function is the attainment of Buddhahood for the benefit of others.
Question:
It is not yet known at what stage this Śākyamuni Buddha resides.
Answer:
If one says that faith in the Dharma is itself faith in the Buddha of Middle Capacity, the same applies to the other stages; reflect upon this.
Third, regarding the categories, there are also two:
first, concerning the characteristics, the thesis is that the body of the Tathāgata is named "Universal Response" because it extensively benefits all sentient beings.
Second, regarding the actual substance, it takes the ocean of ten Buddha-lands as its primary theme.

Fourth, concerning the explanation of the text: within this single section of questions and answers concerning the cultivation of causes to accord with the fruit and the arising of understanding, there are three long divisions:
first, the introductory division; second, the division of the request; and third, the division of the exposition.
Within this, the introductory sequence also extends from the sixth assembly onward, and the same applies to the requests for instruction.
At the beginning, there are three parts:
first, by indicating where the Buddha resides, the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) is clarified;
Second, from "skillfully awakening and knowing" onwards, there is the praise of the Buddha’s merit, which is the clear wisdom that correctly awakens to the world;
third, from "bestowing ten buddha-lands" onwards, there is the praise of the bodhisattvas’ merit, which distinguishes the world of sentient beings.
According to tradition from the beginning:

The Hall of Universal Radiance (Puguang Tang) is located approximately three li southeast of the Bodhi tree, within a bend of the River Sītā. When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, the nāgas saw him sitting exposed beneath the tree and consequently constructed this Dharma hall for him; this was because the nāgas primarily provide offerings by providing shade.
Furthermore, because the hall is near the tree, it is raised together with the altar.
Moreover, according to this sutra, the Bodhi tree is taken as the foundation; all other locations do not deviate from this.
Furthermore, regarding the "initial attainment" mentioned herein, it is distinguished in terms of faith in the Dharma.
As for the "Lotus Treasury," it refers to the blossoming of the practice of faith, the departure from defilement, and the gathering of virtues; this is to be understood by analogy with the Dharma.
Furthermore, because the Bodhisattvas in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* have attained the Lotus Dhāraṇī, there is always a lotus seat wherever they preach the Dharma.
All other meanings are identical to the previous explanation.
Second, from "The Wisdom of Excellent Awakening" (*sujñāna*) onwards, the text explains the superiority of the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) over the world.

Among these, there are ten phrases; the text is identical to the first ten of the twenty-one kinds of superior merits of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. As will be seen below at the beginning of the seventh assembly, all twenty-one phrases are fully present.
Now, based on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, these ten phrases will be explained.
The first is general, while the remaining nine are specific.

Regarding the "virtuous awakening and wisdom" within the general category, it is termed "Perfect Awakening" (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). This means that one who possesses the latter nine virtues is called "virtuously awakened. Because it accords with principle and is free from error, it is termed "correct" (*samyak*) and "virtuous" (*kuśala*); because it illuminates and discerns, it is termed "awakening" (*bodhi*) and "wisdom" (*jñāna*).

Regarding "initially having no two thoughts within the distinction," this refers to the merit of being exclusively unobstructed; that is, because one is free from the two obscurations and distinct from ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

Furthermore, it is because there is no manifestation of the two—either knowing or not knowing—with respect to distant time, space, or vast objects. Therefore, by virtue of having no two thoughts, it is called "excellent awakening wisdom" (*sujñāna*).

Second, regarding "thoroughly penetrating the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*), the treatise calls this "entering the signless dharma. This is the merit of being able to enter non-duality; it is also called the merit of the skillful means of training and transforming others, because one is both able to personally enter the pure *tathatā* that is free from the signs of existence and non-existence, and is also able to lead others to enter it.

Regarding "the third dwelling, the dwelling of the Buddhas": this refers to the merit of observing those to be trained and transformed. It means that because one dwells in great compassion and constantly observes the world; because it is the merit of spontaneously and effortlessly benefiting sentient beings with joy and bliss without ceasing; and because one abides securely in the noble, celestial, and Brahma-dwellings.

The "Tathāgata of the Fourfold Equality" refers to the attainment of the merits of activities similar to those of all Buddhas; within the *dharmakāya*, there is no distinction among the basis, the intention, and the activity, which is to say that the three factors of wisdom, principle, and the benefiting of others are non-dual.

Regarding the fifth, the "unimpeded destination" (*anāvaraṇagati*), it is the merit of having permanently severed that which is to be countered; that is to say, because one has already reached the state of reliance upon the place where all obstacles are liberated, through the actualization and accomplishment of the path that serves as the antidote to the two hindrances.

The sixth, being endowed with the qualities of non-retrogression, is the merit of subduing non-Buddhists; that is to say, having realized the Dharma teachings, others cannot turn them back, for one has subdued them by manifesting the Dharma of one’s own true path.

The seventh, the state of being unbreakable, is the merit of subduing the enmity of Māra; that is to say, amidst circumstances of opposition or compliance, the mind cannot be obstructed, and though dwelling in the world, one is not defiled by the eight worldly dharmas. Since worldly objects that disturb the mind and hinder virtue are called "Māra," this state consists in overcoming them.

The eighth is "abiding in the inconceivable," which is the merit of establishing the teaching; this means that the sublime teaching thus expounded transcends the domain of all discursive thought (*vitarka*).

The ninth is "equally penetrating the three times," which is the merit of prophesying the three times; this means that the past and future are prophesied as being just like the present, clearly and without distinction, and is therefore called "equal penetration."
Possessing these nine distinctions, the first general statement is established.
The points regarding similarity and difference, as well as formation and destruction, may be understood by applying this principle accordingly.
Third, in the explanation of the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), there are two parts:
First, the individuals are identified; second, their actual virtues are praised.
Regarding the first part, there are four sections:
first, distinguishing the many from the few, meaning they are as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-lands.
Second, distinguishing the great from the small, meaning they are great bodhisattvas;
third, distinguishing the end from the beginning, meaning they are those in their final birth before buddhahood;
fourth, distinguishing the new from the old, meaning they have gathered here from other directions.
However, regarding these four stages, one may understand by analogy that each subsequent stage is increasingly marvelous when compared to the preceding one.
Among the three [types of birth], the first—birth as a human—has three meanings:

first, in relation to humans; second, in relation to the heavens; and third, in relation to the body of one born in the lower realms; this is explained according to the conventional appearance (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*).

If we speak in terms of actual retribution, among the four kinds of transformational rebirths (*pariṇāmikī-vipāka*), only the final stage—wherein birth and death no longer exist—remains; therefore, it is called "one life."
The intent of this sutra is explained according to the preceding meaning.
Within the section praising his virtues, there are eight phrases and seven pairs of meanings. The first two phrases constitute the pair of "medicine and disease":

the first phrase refers to his thorough understanding of the capacities and dispositions (*gotra*) of sentient beings, while the latter phrase refers to his profound realization of the *dharmadhātu* as it is transmitted to them.

Second is the pair concerning defilement and purity through constant and skillful reflection, as explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*: based upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), its imagined defiled aspect is termed saṃsāra, while its perfected pure aspect is termed nirvāṇa; because these two aspects are not different, they are called the single dependent nature.
If one perceives one part, the nature of the remaining parts is not different.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata does not see saṃsāra, nor does he see nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Between the world and nirvāṇa, there is not even a hair’s breadth of difference."
This is called the non-obstruction between defilement and purity.

Through the integration of the four propositions, one may view it as following from the fundamental to the derivative, which is exclusively the mundane; or conversely, as exclusively nirvāṇa; or as both appearing simultaneously through mutual fusion; or as both vanishing through mutual negation. Skillfully contemplating this principle is called "skillful reflection," and contemplating it incessantly is called "constant reflection."

Third, the pair of cause and fruit: this refers to the various distinctions among the karmic causes and retributive fruits of all sentient beings; it is clearly understood that these are all established in dependence upon the mental activities of the various consciousnesses of sentient beings.

The first pair of the Fourfold Teachings refers to "meaning" (yi) and "flavor" (wei). "Meaning" refers to the meanings of all dharmas that are to be explained; "flavor" refers to the teachings that explain all dharmas, namely the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables.

The first pair is that of the five fetters and liberation: because one contemplates the characteristics of that world as being emptiness itself, it is called "transcending worldly dharmas," which does not depend upon the destruction of the world.

The second pair is that of principle and phenomena: dharmas arising from conditions are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*), while the truth of the absence of intrinsic nature is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
To realize that conditions are themselves the truth without destroying dependent origination is called the ultimate differentiation of the unconditioned;
to dissolve principle so as to manifest only phenomena without losing sight of principle is called the ultimate differentiation of the conditioned.
The subsequent text states: "One emerges from the conditioned realm into the unconditioned realm, yet does not destroy the conditioned realm.
The same applies to the unconditioned; one may reflect upon this accordingly.

The seven [intervals] and the three times form one pair; that is to say, knowing that each of the three present moments encompasses the past and future and enters into them through mutual identity constitutes the ten times.
"Mi" (靡) means "without" (猶無).
"Penetrating" (guàn) means to pass through.
There is nothing throughout these three periods of time that one does not thoroughly comprehend.
The preceding section on the introduction is now concluded.
The second section is the Request for the Distribution.
Within this, the texts of the subsequent five assemblies are requested collectively; herein there are three parts:
first, the recollection of the request; second, the recollection of the inquiry; and third, the recollection of the manifestation.

In the section on questions, Dharma Masters such as Yu and Fan divided them into one hundred and twenty-four questions: namely, the first ten questions concern the practice of the essence of the Dharmakāya; the intermediate one hundred questions concern the practice of cultivation arising from the Saṃbhogakāya; and the final fourteen questions concern the practice of equality of the Nirmāṇakāya.
Furthermore, if the ninety intermediate questions are combined into nine, there are then forty-three questions in total.
Master Guangtong combines the questions on the mind of sympathetic joy and so forth into one, resulting in thirty-four questions:

the first ten concern the Buddha-dharma of the past limit (*pūrvānta*), the next ten concern the Buddha-dharma of the middle limit (*madhyānta*), and the final fourteen concern the Buddha-dharma of the future limit (*aparānta*). These will be answered in the sixth assembly below.
Now, based on this commentary, the text is divided into three general sections:

first, ten questions concerning the basis upon which causes depend for their results; second, ten questions concerning the causes from which results arise; and third, fourteen questions concerning the results obtained through causes.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharmakāya, and there is nothing that does not return to realize this Dharmakāya.
This is intended to clarify that the cause depends upon the fruit for its completion, yet the cause can also produce the fruit;
the fruit can descend into the cause, and thus the fruit is realized by means of the cause.
Cause and effect are mutually established, yet dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature.

Because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is the true *dharmadhātu* which is itself without nature; thus, its essence does not obstruct dependent origination, and so the true *dharmadhātu* does not destroy cause and effect.
The principle of the reality of cause, effect, and dependent origination is established based on this.
Furthermore, regarding the first ten questions, they are answered collectively within the first three chapters of this assembly.

If categorized separately: the *Catuḥsatya-parivarta* answers the first question concerning the teaching of the Dharma; the *Prabhāsa-bodhi-parivarta* answers the second and third questions concerning power and perfect enlightenment; and this present chapter answers the remaining questions.

The general response follows the text; however, from the "Explanation of Difficulties" (*Mingnan*) onwards, the three subsequent chapters each have their own specific questions. Because the stage of faith (*śraddhā*) does not constitute a formal rank (*bhūmi*), there are no anticipatory questions regarding the "ten faiths," which distinguishes it from the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) and other such stages.

These first ten questions have two explanations: first, they are categorized according to the two fruits of the environment (*āśraya*) and the primary reward (*sambhoga*). Specifically: (1) the first question generally asks about the environmental support (*pratyaya*) of the Pure Land; (2) the second generally asks about the primary reward of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); (3) the third asks about the adornments of the land; (4) the fourth asks about what is realized by the Dharma-body; (5) the fifth asks about the land’s freedom from defilement; (6) the sixth asks about preaching the Dharma after realization; (7) the seventh asks about the essence of the aforementioned land; (8) the eighth asks about the light-halo of the primary reward; (9) the ninth asks about the arising of lands in response to conditions; and (10) the tenth asks about such matters as the manifestation of the eight aspects of perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).

The second [section] asks exclusively about the ocean of lands; this is because, according to the subsequent text and the *Ratnakaranda-śrī-vyūha-sūtra*, this assembly elucidates the meaning of the ocean of lands.

Within these ten [points], the first five clarify that the lands are fully endowed with various virtues, while the latter five clarify that the substance and function of the lands are perfectly complete.
Furthermore, the first is the general [category], while the remaining nine are the specific ones.
Within the specific ones, there are nine meanings regarding the "land" (*kṣetra*):
first, the meaning of distinct abiding, referring to the red lotus and so forth, as explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Second is the meaning of being endowed with virtue, which refers to the fact that principles, practices, and so forth each possess their own refinements.
Third is the meaning of maintaining the path, which refers to the differences in what is attained through scripture, inference, analogy, and direct realization.
Fourth is the meaning of detachment from defilement (*virāga*), which refers to the purity of intrinsic nature, characteristics, and function.
Fifth is the meaning of establishing the teaching (*śāsana*), which refers to manifesting the land through words, such as when speaking of the world-system (*loka-dhātu*) and so forth.
Sixth is the meaning of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which means that wisdom, consciousness, and phenomena all possess an intrinsic nature.
Seventh is the meaning of sublime function (*prabhāva*), which refers to such things as subduing others through majestic radiance.
Eighth is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), which means that Buddha-fields arise in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
Furthermore, it causes the causal practices to arise in accordance with each buddha-field;
furthermore, because Buddhas appear in accordance with each field, it is also said to "arise"—this follows the *Tuṣita-sūtra* (Dōsha jīng);
furthermore, a field arises in accordance with the completion of causes and conditions, as in the case of the arising of worlds through the completion of causes and conditions.

Ninth is the meaning of manifest awakening, which refers to the manifestation of the path to perfect enlightenment within all oceans of lands, because there is no obstruction between the environment and its inhabitants.
The remaining meanings should be understood by referring to the answers provided below.
Next, regarding the ten questions within the causal stage (*hetu*), the answers are provided from the chapter "Ascending Mount Sumeru" down to "The Abodes of Bodhisattvas.

Of these, the first nine questions concern the practice of self-cultivation according to the stages, while the subsequent question beginning with "Rejoicing" concerns the practice of transforming sentient beings in accordance with conditions.
Regarding the ten *piṭakas* of the beginning and middle [sections], why is the question placed after the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), while the answer is placed before it?
This is because the *piṭaka* has two meanings:
first, the sense of "giving birth" (*janana*). Therefore, it is placed after the dedication, because it gives birth to the realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*) of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Second is the sense of "gathering" (*saṃgraha*), which is why it occurs prior to "dedication" (*pariṇāmana*); for it gathers all practices so that they may be transformed into dedication.
By virtue of these two senses, the two locations mutually clarify one another, and thus there is no contradiction.
The ten vows are answered within the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
The ten concentrations (*daśa samādhayaḥ*) are answered in the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences" (*Daśakṣānti-parivarta*).

Taking the contemplation of the mind to internalize principle constitutes patience (*kṣānti*), while the non-diffusion of the mind through quiescence constitutes concentration (*samādhi*); because quiescence and contemplation are unimpeded and constitute but a single mind, each of these two locations manifests a distinct meaning.
This is because all bodhisattvas, when taking the ultimate and conventional truths as their objects, possess two characteristics:
first, non-perversion; second, non-distraction—as explained in detail in the Liang Dynasty treatise.

Regarding the ten masteries (*daśavaśitā*), they are answered in the "Chapter on the Ten Clarities" (*Daśavidyādhikaraṇa*). Because their functions and clarifications are explained in detail, two names are established.
This is because when translated separately as the *Bodhisattva-mūla-karma-sūtra*, they are also called the "Ten Clarities" within its questions.
In the *Duṣa* (Tousha), these are called the Ten Methods of Flight (*daśa-uddhāna*).

Furthermore, as no separate explanation is found for the Ten Summits (*daśa-mūrdhan*), some ancients have attempted to correlate them with the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*; however, this is likely an error, and it is difficult to rely upon for practice.
Now, examining that sūtra which expounds the Dharma in eleven locations, six of these are identical to this [text].
That sūtra states that in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, ten dhyāna-concentrations are taught;
specifically, it teaches ten adamantine minds (*vajracitta*) for the first dhyāna.
In the second dhyāna, the ten vows were taught;
in the third dhyāna, the ten patiences were taught;

and in the fourth dhyāna, within the palace of Maheśvara, the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground was taught, without mentioning a second assembly at the Universal Radiance Hall or the multi-storied pavilion of Jetavana.
Furthermore, this question shares both similarities and differences with that [previous one], and thus it is difficult to apply [the same answer].
Some say that there is an answer in the "Inconceivable Chapter" (*Acintya-parivarta*).
However, since the "Chapter on Non-Thought" (*Acintya-parivarta*) and others answer questions regarding subsequent fruits, they cannot be subsumed under this category.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Saṃghāṭi" elucidates the ten great numbers; because these represent the ultimate limit of numerical calculation within the stage of causes, they may also be referred to as the "Ten Summits."
However, since there is a separate inquiry at the beginning of this chapter, it is also difficult to assign [the title] here.

Within the "Chapter on Lifespan," ten successive layers of Buddha-lands reach their ultimate limit; because the Buddha-field of Worthy Leader (*Bhadramukha*) is the most extreme boundary, it is called the "Pinnacle. Yet, as there are ten such layers, it is termed the "Ten Pinnacles" (*daśa-mūrdhan*), which is likewise unobjectionable.
Since there was no separate question at the beginning of that chapter, it serves as the answer.
Here, the question is posed in relation to those who are superior and more exalted below, while the answer is given in terms of the continuity within the present context.
Furthermore, if there is a separate question in the subsequent text of this very sutra, it means that there was no question at this point;
conversely, if there is an exposition below without a preceding question, it constitutes the answer to that [prior] question.
Therefore, one must understand this.

The section following "the mind of sympathetic joy" clarifies how bodhisattvas initiate practices in accordance with conditions; this is answered in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Abodes," because that text explains how bodhisattvas universally respond to various circumstances by initiating sublime practices in all places according to the needs of sentient beings.
This question is posed in terms of the action that depends [upon a basis], while the following answer is given in terms of the place where that action resides.
Judging by this, it is also extremely clear how the questions and answers are interconnected within the Middle Period of the Buddha’s teaching.
In the section clarifying the transformation of others through following conditions, first is seeing the minor virtues of others and rejoicing in them with one's heart;
second is transforming sentient beings so that they may perpetuate the Buddha-seed, which refers to sowing the seeds of the Buddha within the field of sentient beings and so forth.
These two constitute the mind that transforms others.
Below, the practice of transforming others is clarified: how is it that one does not abandon them?
Because of the intent to rescue and deliver them.
Wherein is one saved?
Within the midst of afflictions and delusive thoughts.
How is one saved?
Because one knows the faculties and their modes of activity. How is this resolved?
By understanding the medicinal teachings of the Dharma.
How is deliverance accomplished?

It should be understood through the following four phrases in order: causing one to leave behind the defilements of accumulation, to transcend suffering and hardship, to resolve doubts regarding the path, and to realize the extinction of craving.
Regarding the fourteen questions concerning the future limit, they are answered collectively from the "Inconceivable" chapter through the "Samantabhadra" chapter.
Among these, the "superior dharma" refers to the superior dharma of bodhi, as explained in the preceding text.
"Immovable and non-reverting" refers to the absence of effortful application (*anābhoga*).
Other meanings are for the most part the same as those explained in the preceding assemblies.
Within the third section on "The Exposition," the response to the previous questions is provided throughout the subsequent five assemblies.
This section is divided into three parts:

first, within this assembly, answering the ten initial questions concerning the Buddha-dharma of the past; second, from the third assembly downward, answering the Buddha-dharma of the present; and third, from the "Inconceivable Chapter" downward, answering the Buddha-dharma of the future.
Regarding the first [of the two parts], there are two sections:
first, assembling the assembly to manifest the perfection [of the teaching]; second, the formal exposition in response to specific conditions.
Within the former, there are two [subsections]:
First, the capacity for accumulation is clarified; second, that which is accumulated is clarified.
Within the first [section], there are two intentions:
first, looking back, it serves as a response to questions; second, looking forward, it serves to assemble the multitude.
"In the preceding thought," "knowing the mental state," refers to acknowledging the question.
Furthermore, it raises the capacity of the mind as a vessel for receiving the Dharma.
"Manifesting spiritual powers according to their forms" refers to answering by manifesting images, thereby filling that vessel.

That is to say, regarding the one hundred and twenty-four questions as previously contemplated, and the Dharma-gates taught from here down through the sixth assembly that answer these questions—all of them appear instantaneously and with perfect clarity within the Tathāgata’s body of the Dharma-realm. Therefore, although the subsequent five assemblies are unfolded, there is no protraction; and although a single body appears instantaneously, there is no contraction.
Furthermore, that the six positions are clearly distinct yet not different, and that they are perfectly interfused and mutually inclusive without being impaired, is precisely due to this.
To cause all beings to behold this and thereby moisten their empty minds—this is my answer.
Because he made the aspiration, "May you manifest for me," it has now been manifested.
As the subsequent scripture states: "Within the pure Dharma-body, there is no image that does not appear."

Furthermore, regarding "images" (liangxiang): they are formed through the conditions of the assembly and signify non-obstruction. These images are produced by imprinting the Buddha-body upon the capacity of the sentient being's mind; alternatively, the Buddha-body manifests these images in response to the capacities of beings. Each possesses the dual meaning of emptiness and existence, as well as the meanings of power and lack of power. Contemplate how these four propositions are harmoniously integrated within the sense of non-discrimination.
Furthermore, the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*) consists in the capacity to manifest forms according to the needs of beings and to attract them through movement.
Second, regarding "assembling the multitude," the World-Honored One raised his hand to gather the assembly.
"Knowing the thoughts of the mind" means discerning the causes from which the assembly has gathered.
"According to their likeness" clarifies that the teaching accords with the capacities of the listeners.
"Manifesting supernormal powers" correctly clarifies the summoning of the assembly to gather.

Furthermore, as previously described, he manifests supernatural powers through these images, causing bodhisattvas from other regions to see this light of supernormal power, whereby they know that a certain Dharma is being taught and they gather here;
likewise, he causes this assembly to see these images of the Buddha, whereby they know for certain that the Dharma I have asked about is being taught, and they abide in joy.
How is this known?
Because the light of the Tathāgata’s body is of two kinds:
first, it is subtle and thus difficult to know; second, it is manifest and thus causes it to be known.

Within that which causes [beings] to know, according to what dharma he intends to preach for each individual as appropriate, the light from the Buddha’s body first manifests that image, so that when the assembly sees it, they already know that a certain dharma is being preached.

As it is said that when the *Prajñāpāramitā* was preached, one should consult the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and as it is similarly stated for the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and so forth, it is therefore said that he manifested supernatural powers according to their respective forms.
Regarding the second section on the assembly, it should be understood that within each of the ten directions, there are three worlds.

Furthermore, each possesses eight aspects: first, distance; second, the name of the land; third, the title of the Buddha; fourth, the presiding Bodhisattva; fifth, the inclusion of the retinue; sixth, coming here to pay homage; seventh, manifesting a seat; and eighth, sitting according to their original direction.
The world being named "Form" (rūpa) signifies that the dharmic characteristics of the stage of faith (śraddhā-bhūmi) are coarse and manifest.
The Buddha being named "Wisdom" (jñāna) signifies that the initial awakening within the stage of faith arises from original awakening (mūla-awakening).
The fact that Bodhisattvas share the same name "Śūra" (Hero) signifies that faith is the beginning of the causal path.
Regarding the meaning of the name Mañjuśrī, five interpretations will be briefly set forth:
first, his name is *Mañjuśrī*, also transcribed as *Śrī* or *Mañjuṣrī*; it is translated as "Worshipful Head," "Universal Head," "Gentle Head," "Sublime Virtue," or "Sublime Auspiciousness."
Regarding these ten bodhisattvas, according to the Sanskrit original they all share the name Śrī; in the *Dousha jing* (Tathāgatotpattisambhava-nirdeśa), they are likewise named Śiri.

Furthermore, in the Sanskrit language, the word for "head" is *śiri*, and terms such as "auspiciousness" (*śrī*) and "virtue" (*guṇa*) are also rendered as *śiri*; thus, differences have arisen in their translation.

Regarding his place of origin: according to the *Mañjuśrī-parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, he was born into a Brahmin family in this land; four hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he entered parinirvāṇa atop Mount Gandhamādana.
According to this sutra, these are bodhisattvas from the eastern direction who currently reside at Mount Qingliang.

The *Sutra of the Silent and Harmonious Sound* (*Śāntasvararāja-sūtra*) also states: "Ten thousand Buddha-worlds to the east of here is a land named Ratnāvāsā; the Buddha there is named Ratnalakṣaṇa. These are the bodhisattvas of that realm."
Regarding the "Threefold Knowledge (Traividya) Master and Disciple," according to the *Pātrāvadāna Sūtra*, he was formerly the teacher of Śākyamuni.
This sūtra states: "He is the mother of all Buddhas of the three periods of time and the teacher of all Bodhisattvas."

Regarding the four clarifications of the stage: if considered from the perspective of the cause, these are bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), because they constantly abide in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
If considered from the perspective of the fruit, according to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, they attain buddhahood in the world-system of Equality in the south, with the name Dragon Seed (*Nāgabīja*).
Regarding the five functions of manifesting brilliance: according to the *Māyopama-samādhi-sūtra*, subduing the field of Māra and so forth constitute the power of taming sentient beings.
According to the *Pratibhāsa-ratnagarbha-sūtra*, Kāśyapa’s expulsion and other such acts constitute the power of supreme supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).
From the certainty of emptiness, no debate or refutation can prevail; this is the power of wisdom, which pertains to the Three Vehicles.
As in the "Chapter on Radiant Enlightenment" (*Prabhāsa-bodhi-parivarta*) regarding all places and so forth, this refers to the One Vehicle (*Ekayāna*).
Regarding the bodhisattvas from all directions who all prostrate with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, the meaning of prostrating to the Buddha is briefly presented in three sections:
first, the number of prostrations; second, the respectful etiquette; and third, the realization of the fruits.
Regarding the threefold prostration performed at the beginning, middle, and end, there are two intentions:
first, because there are three locations for the prostration; second, to manifest that the Buddha possesses the divine eye, the divine ear, and the knowledge of others' minds.
Second, regarding the seven modes of respectful demeanor,
as stated in the *Kongmu* and so forth. Third,
regarding those who have attained the fruits, there are two types:
First, one attains the five fruits in the near term, and so forth;
second, one attains the fruit of Buddhahood in the distant term, as explained in the "Chapter on the Worthy Head" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*), and so forth.

Regarding sitting according to rank: according to the twelfth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, non-Buddhists sit according to their other teachings because they disparage the Buddha; laypeople sit like guests; and all members of the fivefold assembly stand because their body and mind belong to the Buddha.
If a Great Arhat who has accomplished his task is permitted to sit, the others of the three remaining fruits are not allowed to sit, because their great tasks are as yet unfinished.
It is like when a king’s high ministers are seated, while all others must remain standing.
Since all of these are great bodhisattvas, they sit here for that reason.
Within the second pair, the "Correct Exposition Based on Conditions," there are two parts:
the first three chapters provide a direct response to the preceding questions, while the latter three chapters address specific inquiries and provide individual answers as the discussion unfolds.
Another explanation:
the first three are the conditions for initiating practice, while the latter three are the characteristics of that which is initiated.
Another explanation:
The former is the objective realm that is the fruit of what is perceived, while the latter is the causal activity of the perceiving subject.
Since this practice of faith is the expedient means for abiding and does not constitute a distinct stage in itself, there is no question regarding it at the outset.
Within the first three chapters, there are five sections: first, praising the rarity of the assembly;

second, restating the questions and providing a general outline; third, interrogating the outline to reveal the essence; fourth, interrogating the essence to distinguish its characteristics; and fifth, interrogating the characteristics to clarify their functions.
Why, at the beginning, does Mañjuśrī answer the Buddha’s question?

It is because he possesses wisdom identical to that of the Buddha; because his auspicious and wondrous wisdom has mastered the ocean of lands; and because it increases the hearts of all bodhisattvas with leaping joy.
Why do they not enter meditative concentration?
Because faith has no fixed locus.
In the previous assembly, could there possibly have been such a locus?
Because these fruits and virtues are profound and subtle,
could there not be dharmas that constitute the fruit within them?
They exist because they serve as the causes for [further] fruition and because they universally possess extensive causes.
The praise of its rarity is briefly based on two meanings:
first, because this single assembly is itself the assembly of all places throughout the void of the dharma-realm;
second, because this is itself the dharma-gate, as explained in the "Chapter on the Radiance of Enlightenment."
The second part, "Summarizing the Questions within," refers back to the two preceding questions (the seventh and eighth).

"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" summarizes the previous demonstration of attaining perfect enlightenment; alternatively, "the Buddha’s emergence" summarizes the demonstration of attaining perfect enlightenment.
The two preceding questions (the seventh and eighth) are not summarized here in brief.
"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" (Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment) serves as the general conclusion; the remaining phrases may be understood as being the same as those previously explained.
As for the initial phrase "inconceivable" (acintya), it runs through all the subsequent phrases; therefore, the conclusion states that "all are inconceivable."
Regarding the "inconceivable," the general meaning herein is that the principle of the single-flavor Dharma-realm is divided into two:
first, the ocean of lands that can adapt; second, the conditions of the sentient beings who are adapted to. These two are non-dual, harmoniously integrated, and unobstructed.
If one follows from the essence through conditions, then the characteristics are immediately perfectly interfused and without distinction, beyond the reach of verbal expression.
If one follows from the essence through conditions, then it is again confirmed as the arising of distinct phenomena through conditions.
By means of these various forms of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the text conversely reveals that the essence of the land (*kṣetrasvabhāva*) is wondrously and supremely inconceivable;
this is its intended meaning. For this reason, there are three aspects to the sense of "inconceivability":

first, by using the expression of conditioned phenomena as a provisional support, it conversely reveals the meaning of the land's essence being utterly beyond all conditions. This is what is meant by saying that while the words reside within conditions, the intended meaning dwells outside of them; hence, it is called "inconceivable."

Second, since the lands are manifested in dependence upon conditions, and because the dust-particles of the objects of perception are calculated by means of dependent origination, the essence of the lands is caused to be established as distinct through these conditions. This clarifies that the lands possess a distinction within non-distinction, and are non-distinct despite being distinct; therefore, they are inconceivable.

The three conditions have no separate conditions, for their essence is itself the condition; therefore, the differentiated dependent origination is precisely the profound ocean of lands. This means that the principle is extremely close yet difficult to recognize, and is thus inconceivable—contemplate this.
Within the section on the third [topic], the investigation of the marks that reveal the essence, first the investigation and marking is stated:
"How is it known that [it is] inconceivable? Subsequently, the revelation of the essence is stated:
This is because the dharmas of all Buddhas accord with the dharma-realm of those to be converted, because the two gates are fused as a pair, and because they are without limit or boundary.
This is a brief explanation based on their essential nature (*tattva*).
Within the fourth section, "Investigating the Substance and Distinguishing the Characteristics," first the substance is investigated as follows:
"How is it known that the distinctions are boundless?
Because they are equal to the dharma-realm."
The subsequent explanation of their characteristics states:
"Without yet discussing the entirety of the worlds throughout the ten directions,
we shall briefly distinguish ten types based on this single Sahā world in order to manifest their inexhaustibility."
The other boundless realms should be understood by analogy with this.

Regarding these various bodies and so forth, some commentators explain them as being the Buddha’s bodies; therefore, the subsequent discussion of the differences in their names and titles serves to explain the various designations.
Now, if one carefully examines this passage and consults the *Tuṣita-sūtra*, it refers to the sentient beings who are to be transformed, not the Buddha who performs the transformation.

Because this sentence is long, it follows the linguistic conventions of the Western Regions (India); it should be read as a single phrase: "transforming and teaching all various bodies and so forth, up to sentient beings of different kinds," and "the objects perceived are also diverse" should be treated as a separate phrase. In this way, the meaning becomes clear.

However, because the Buddha-lands are equal and without distinction that could be differentiated, one relies upon the distinctions among the sentient beings to be transformed to discern the characteristics of the differences within the ocean of lands.
Among these ten statements, the first generally enumerates the distinctions of the body consisting of the five aggregates;
the second concerns the different ways names are established based on the body;
and the third concerns the body being present in all places.
Fourth, there are various forms and colors according to their respective locations, such as white, black, and so forth;
fifth, there is length or brevity according to the existence of a body and life;
sixth, consciousness is able to apprehend all objects, or it is the sphere of realization attained through cultivation.
Seventh, regarding the nature of the objects entering the faculties: either wisdom enters the phenomena (*dharma*), or there are differences in the gates of awakening and entry;

eighth, briefly there are only the six faculties, while extensively there are twenty-two faculties—whether these be the five faculties such as faith, or those categorized by sharpness and dullness, or birth and maturity—as explained below in the ninth dedication, "The Ocean of All Faculties";
ninth, the distinctions among the various realms of existence, such as the four modes of birth and the five destinies, as in the "Dense Forest of Birth and Action," and so forth.
The ten karmas yield diverse retributions, as in the "Dense Forest of Karmic Actions" and other such texts.

According to the Sanskrit original and the *Tuṣita-sūtra*, each of these phrases originally contained various expressions; they appear thus because of abbreviation. Therefore, it concludes by stating that sentient beings are of various different kinds.

That what is seen is also different means that not only are the distinctions between the retributions of karma regarding the primary and secondary realms boundless, but the views and aspirations harbored within their minds are each distinct.
In the *Duṣa-sūtra*, this is called "each having heard the voice of the Buddha."

Furthermore, the first nine phrases distinguish the differences in retribution (*vipāka*), while the tenth clarifies the differences in karma (*karman*); this reveals the distinctions in perception (*darśana*).

Moreover, regarding the statement that the specific boundaries of these sentient beings constitute the characteristics of the ocean of lands (*kṣetra-samudra-lakṣaṇa*), there are three interpretations, as explained above in the section on the "Inconceivable" (*acintya*) within the headings; one should reflect upon them accordingly.
Within the section distinguishing the functions through the fifth investigation of characteristics, the initial inquiry regarding these characteristics states:
"While it may be so that there are distinctions among the faculties (indriya) which are followed, how can the distinctions among those that follow them be perceived?"
Master Shi Yong said:
"The manifestations of the seal [of reality] appear according to diverse capacities; the teachings of the Buddha are manifold and difficult to explain in their entirety.
Regarding these diversities, there are three points of discussion:"

First is the body named "Universal Application," second is the teaching named "Pervasive Application," and third is the light-wheel named "Exhaustive Illumination Application"; these together serve as the standard for what follows.
Alternatively, they may be divided into two:
first, the Buddha; second, the Dharma.
Within the Buddha there are also two:
first, the body; second, the name.
Within the Dharma there are also two:
There are two aspects: the one reality and the two expedients.
Among these, the distinctions between the Buddha-body and the teaching of reality are difficult to clarify, as they are discussed together in the "Chapter on Radiant Enlightenment.
The distinctions between the names of Buddhas and the teaching of expedients are easy to discern, and thus these two aspects are treated separately in these two chapters.
Furthermore, another explanation is as follows: In these first two chapters, Mañjuśrī answers by citing principles to respond to the preceding questions;

in the final chapter, the Tathāgata answers by citing concrete instances to explain and establish those principles. Therefore, within the first two chapters, the two dharmas of name and teaching are distinguished.
Since these distinctions have been raised as asked above, the distinctions in the meanings of Buddha-fields and so forth are inconceivable.
The intention here is that they are equal to the *dharmadhātu*; this constitutes the comprehensive answer.
Regarding the first [section], the differentiation of names, there are two parts:
first, the manifestation of the distinct names; second, from "These are all... onwards, the explanation of the reasons for these distinctions.
Within the former, there are two [subdivisions]:
First the inquiry, followed by the explanation.
Within the explanation, there are three parts:
first, the analysis of this realm; second, the realms of the ten directions; third, the exhaustive penetration of the entire dharma-realm.
Question:
In this context, does the name refer exclusively to Śākyamuni Buddha,
or does it apply to other Buddhas as well?
Answer:

If one speaks according to the Three Vehicles, only these ten billion worlds within this realm are named Śākyamuni; in all other worlds throughout the ten directions, they are the names of distinct Buddhas.
If one speaks according to the One Vehicle, the entire Dharma-realm is, in its totality, the name of Śākyamuni.
Question:
If that is so, why does the preceding text state that the Buddhas of the ten directions preach the Dharma and know the mental activities and so forth of others? Answer:
All these are places transformed by this Buddha; therefore, there is no separate Buddha.
Furthermore, as they manifest within the Ocean-Seal Samādhi of Śākyamuni, there is no separate Buddha.
Another explanation states:
Just as the name of one Buddha pervades the ten directions, so too do all other Buddhas of the ten directions each likewise pervade the ten directions.

Furthermore, if there are those with the capacities of the three vehicles, they will each hear the name of the Buddha in their respective location throughout the various four-continent worlds, yet they may not necessarily know the names of the Buddhas in other locations.
If there is a capacity for the One Vehicle, it can instantaneously receive all names at once, so as to respond to the names for all capacities.
That a single capacity is able to receive them is because it is the capacity of Samantabhadra; for a single capacity is itself all capacities.
Furthermore, regarding these names and titles: according to the Hīnayāna, they are real names;

in the initial teaching of the Triyāna, they are names that are both provisional and empty; in the Final Teaching, these names are identical to the equality of True Suchness, as the Sūtra says: "The nature of names is detached; this is called liberation.
In the Sudden Teaching, all are transcended, such that both name and non-name are left behind.
The Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) likewise transcends both, for it is not obstructed by names.

Now, a single name is all names, and all names enter into a single name; yet they are neither destroyed nor obstructed, encompassing the entirety of the Dharma-realm—this is the "Indra’s Net" of names.
Question:

Regarding this great trichiliocosm, according to other sutras and treatises, there are ten billion sets of four continents within the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains; it is not possible for there to be further sets of four continents above or below.

If both upper and lower [realms] exist, then each of the four continents must likewise have its own upper and lower realms; thus, there ought to be three hundred billion [worlds]. Why, then, do you still say there are only one hundred billion?
Answer: If one refers to the actual locus of the Hīnayāna, there is no principle by which it could be altered.
If one refers to the three vehicles, although they consist of emptiness, true suchness, and so forth, these do not obstruct phenomena; therefore, the original phenomena are not destroyed.
If this is the One Vehicle, then phenomena are unimpeded, fused, and sovereignly transformative.
Therefore, the locations clarified herein are perfectly integrated according to the teachings, manifesting inexhaustibility through the number ten.
In this single realm of Sahā, there are two kinds of integration (*yōng*):

first, taking the place where the Dharma is preached as the center, in order to establish the relationship of principal and attendant, one integrates those ten billion [worlds] so that they have upper and lower positions, thereby making them complete;

thus, there are not three hundred [realms]. Second, even if one were to take a single *cāturdvīpaka* world at the very eastern edge of the Cakravāḍa mountains as the location of the Dharma-preacher, this itself constitutes the center; by integrating the remaining four *cāturdvīpakas*, the retinues of the ten directions are likewise made complete. Since all *cāturdvīpakas* are attendants in relation to others and principals in relation to themselves, the Cakravāḍa mountains also shift and change accordingly. The principle of such integration applies equally to the other realms of the ten directions; this is according to the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
If one were to rely on the perspective of the Three Vehicles, it would not be as described here, as explained in other sutras and treatises.
*Sahā* is translated here as "Endurance" (*Kanshin*).
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The beings therein possess faults such as greed, anger, and ignorance; because the Brahma King endures these, it is named after him."
The *Pātrāvadāna-sūtra* states, and so forth: "Subhūti" means "Good Reality.
"Hani" may mean "renunciation" or "arising and ceasing," as the original term is difficult to determine definitively.
"Bhagavān" has six meanings, and so forth.
"Erapattra" is translated here as "King’s Grove" (Wánglín); it is so named because the Buddha was born in this grove when he was still a prince.
In the second section, the explanation of the specific reasons, there are three parts:
first, citing the capacity [of the audience]; second, the bestowal of transformation; and third, the intent of the transformation.
Within the first part, there are two points:

First interpretation: These names and titles pervade the Dharma-realm because, based on the Buddha's own capacity to transform sentient beings with whom he has a karmic affinity, such distinctions exist; it does not mean that they apply to everyone.
Second interpretation: How could these specific capacities have a karmic affinity with the Buddha?

This means that because the Buddha, while practicing over many kalpas in the past, had seen, heard, and rejoiced in [the Dharma], he possesses the necessary conditions (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, regarding the various instances of opposition and compliance, and so forth, they are recorded as in a separate account.
Within the two types of transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*), there are five phrases:

first, a general statement on the skillful means of gathering and transforming beings through the three wheels; second, the skillful means of verbal action (*vāk-karman*); third, the skillful means of physical action (*kāya-karman*); fourth, the skillful means of mental action (*manas-karman*); and fifth, the manifestation of gifts according to the faculties [of beings].
Another explanation is as follows:
the first phrase refers to manifesting physical deportment to gather in sentient beings, hence it says "various skillful means";
the second refers to vocal karma, such as the Brahma-voice and so forth.

The three kinds of teachings spoken refer to: teaching the retribution of karma and so forth for humans and devas; teaching the provisional path for those of the two vehicles and so forth, which is precisely the Four Noble Truths.

The three intentions behind these transformations refer to the intent with which the teachings for humans, devas, and the two vehicles are spoken, desiring to cause them to know the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Chapter Four: The Four Noble Truths. The four introductory sections are the same as before.
First, regarding the explanation of the name: "Four" (catvāri) is a number. "Truths" (satyāni) is the meaning;

that is to say, because they are real and factual, they can produce non-erroneous understanding. Therefore, both are called *satya* (truths), which is an explanation based on the inclusion of the number (*saṃkhyā-sahita-vyutpatti*).
This chapter does not explain the meaning of the Four Noble Truths; rather, it clarifies that the names of the Four Noble Truths differ, and is therefore titled "The Chapter on the Four Noble Truths.
Second, regarding the purpose of its inclusion, there are five points:
first, to provide an exegesis that establishes the meaning of the provisional path at the end of the preceding chapter.
Second, because speech-action (*vākkarman*) is distinguished immediately following body-action (*kāyakarman*);
third, because whereas previously the different names of the person who speaks were clarified, here the different names of the Dharma that is spoken are clarified;
fourth, because it answers the question within the preceding inquiry regarding the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.

Fifth, this section follows because it explains and establishes the distinct characteristics of the provisional teachings within the differentiated dharmas that were previously validated by the capacities of the audience.
Third, regarding the essential purport (*piṇḍārtha*): it takes the boundless and profoundly deep ocean of truths as its essence, as well as the ocean of the aforementioned buddha-land.
The meaning of the Four Noble Truths is briefly set forth in five sections:
first, the explanation of names; second, the discernment of characteristics; third, the essential nature; fourth, the functional activity; and fifth, the classification of types and timing.
The commentary on the text has three parts:

first, clarifying the names of the truths in this land; second, distinguishing the names of the truths in the ten worlds outside of Sahā; third, revealing the names of the truths in all worlds throughout the entirety of space beyond those ten realms.
Regarding the beginning and middle [of the teaching], within each of the Four Noble Truths there are three parts:
first, the enumeration of names; second, the summation of their number; and third, the clarification of their intent.
These names are established in order to subdue sentient beings according to their specific capacities.

"Harmonizing" means to bring into harmony; "subduing" means to restrain and subdue. This refers to harmonizing and controlling the karmas of body, speech, and mind, thereby restraining and eliminating all unwholesome conduct.
For what reason did Mañjuśrī speak thus?
This is because one of clear and wondrous wisdom has skillfully mastered the meaning of the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, for what reason are only the distinctions of the Four Noble Truths revealed?
It is because these provisional teachings are easy to understand through their distinctions.
Furthermore, this is done to entrust and manifest the Dharma. Why?

It means that since even these limited teachings of the Hīnayāna possess such distinctions throughout the entirety of the world-system, one can know without doubt that the distinctions of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), which encompasses all directions, are boundless in principle.
Furthermore, it serves to dismantle conceptual attachments and guide the mechanism [of the mind]. Why is this?

It is because it expounds those limited teachings of the Hīnayāna so that they become universal, thereby causing them to lose their fundamental attachments and manifesting the boundless Dharma-realm of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), leading them to enter therein.
Furthermore, because this is based on the common teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and encompasses those of lower stages, it is explained as follows:
