Sixth, with the perfection of pure wisdom, he answers questions concerning the ability to avoid the evil realms and so forth.
The sixth stage, "Supreme," signifies the complete fulfillment of practice and cultivation.

Through the power of wisdom in the seventh stage, the sequential skillful means, it answers the sixfold names of the various stages and so forth, wherein all virtues are perfectly complete: first, the grounds; second, the perfections; third, meditative concentration; fourth, the superknowledges; fifth, the branches of enlightenment; and sixth, the fearlessnesses.

The preceding section on the perfection of causes concludes with the eighth point, the power of the eight pure dharmas, which answers the Buddha’s questions regarding the three karmas of the support (the environment) and the supported (the Buddha).
The ninth point, the wisdom that discriminates and swiftly understands all phenomena and so forth, answers the questions concerning the attainment of the Buddha’s ten powers and other qualities.

The preceding phrase clarifies the fruit of the primary body, the environment, and the marks and signs; this phrase clarifies the fruit of the differentiation of merits. These two together clarify the fulfillment of the fruit.
Thus far, the section on self-benefit is complete.
The tenth is the power of vows, the power of spiritual transformations, and the power of wisdom, answering questions regarding their respective Buddha-fields.
The eleventh is responding according to those who are ready for transformation and so forth, answering questions regarding the maturation of sentient beings and so forth.
The twelfth section, beginning with "Thus the bodhisattvas practice," answers the question regarding the practice that leads to buddhahood.
The thirteenth section, beginning with "In immeasurable lands," answers the question regarding the protection and upholding of the treasury of the Dharma.
Fourteen, the accomplishment of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and so forth, answers the question concerning detailed exposition.

Fifteen, being fearless amidst the great assembly and so forth, restates the question; possessing the perfection of superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), this answers the question concerning how Māra cannot destroy one.
16. From "the sixteen successive distinctions" onwards, he answers the question regarding the inexhaustible upholding of the True Dharma.
17. From "endowed with great compassion" onwards, he answers the question regarding the ability to expound [the Dharma] throughout all worlds.
The eighteen kings of the ten directions respectfully protected [the Buddha], so there is no need for a brief response.
Furthermore, as this refers to the fruit of practice, there is no response.
Moreover, the statement that "none other than the Buddha is faultless" and so forth is also a general response.
Question:

After the completion of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), only a Bodhisattva who has received their office (*abhiṣeka*) can be said to be "incapable of being surpassed by anyone other than the Tathāgata. Why, then, is this statement made here regarding a stage that belongs to the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) prior to the [ten] stages?
Answer:
This is the dharani method of the marks of Samantabhadra’s stage within the Perfect Teaching; therefore, at the point where a single stage is perfected, all stages are fully subsumed.

Just as in the case of the bhikṣu Sāgaramati, where the Buddha preached the Dharma upon his head, he attained the state of a Buddha as a successor immediately after completing the ten abodes; the fact that he is not mentioned again as entering the ten practices and so forth is explained in the same manner.

This is stated with reference to the initial stage; as in the "Chapter on Minor Characteristics" (*Kṣudrakalakṣaṇa-paṭala*), it is said that upon emerging from the hells, one immediately attains the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Regarding the stages from after the realization of Non-arising Patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) up to before the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement (*vimala-samādhi*), those are explained with reference to the final stage.
The positions of the two intermediate answers can be understood by analogy.

19. Regarding "all the worlds pay homage" and so forth, there is likewise no separate answer; because they share the same fruit of practice (*pratipatti-phala*), they may also be understood as being included within the subsequent section.

20. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the question concerning the increase of the power of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-bala*) and the attainment of the white dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) is answered. Within this, first there is a general presentation, followed by an explanation.

Regarding the preceding section: first is the excellence of physical action (*kāyakarman*); next, from "with a mind of loving-kindness" (*maitracitta*) onwards, is the excellence of mental action (*manaskarman*); and finally, from "endowed with eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) onwards, is the excellence of verbal action (*vākkarman*).

The following explanation consists of eleven points: the first six constitute the qualities of the cause of self-perfection; the seventh constitutes the purity of realized wisdom; the eighth is skillful exposition in accordance with realization; the ninth is the ability to mindfully retain the teachings; the tenth is skillful exposition in accordance with what has been mindfully retained; the eleventh is the ability to investigate dharmas not yet attained.
The final five constitute the fruits of superior progress: first, attaining the Buddha’s external power and function;
second, attaining the Buddha’s internal, ultimate wisdom;
third, attaining the Buddha’s wisdom of skillful exposition; [and so forth].
Fourth, correctly teaching the profound Dharma;
fifth, attaining the supreme wisdom of a Buddha, which refers to possessing the means of valid cognition (*yukti-pramāṇa*), the bodhisattva’s vow-wisdom (*praṇidhijñāna*), and so forth.

In the second verse section, there are twenty verses: the first thirteen verses praise the eleven types of practice in the preceding first section, while the final seven verses praise the virtues accomplished through the eighteen types of practice in the subsequent section.

Regarding the preceding section, the first four verses praise the initial two segments; specifically, the first one and a half verses praise the progressive excellence of what is cultivated, referring to the stage of "Initial Resolve" (*prathamacittotpāda*) as the "First Ground" (*prathamabhūmi*).
Having already attained the treasury of merit from generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), it is said that one "nurtures" it.

The next line praises the cessation of negligence; the following line praises the departure from the darkness of delusion; the next two lines praise the non-forgetfulness of the *bodhicitta* and so forth; and the final two lines praise the joy of the Tathāgatas.

The next verse reiterates the cultivation of excellence. The first three lines reiterate non-retrogression; the final line reiterates being free from both householders and ordinary worldlings among those who have left the home life; the remainder is omitted and not reiterated.
The final verse reiterates the Buddha’s joy, which is easily understood.

Following this, there are two verses that correspond to the next three sections: specifically, the first five lines anticipate the fourth section on pure conduct, while the subsequent line, "endowed with all stages," retroactively corresponds to the third section on the abodes.
The second half of the verse on "merit" fulfills the fifth great vow; the next half-verse [fulfills] the sixth, the attainment of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
and the subsequent one and a half verses fulfill the seventh, transforming and delivering beings according to their respective needs.
The next verse praises the eighth [quality], not abandoning the various pāramitās.
The next verse praises the ninth, delivering all sentient beings according to their requests.
The next verse praises the tenth, causing the Three Jewels to flourish.
The next two verses concern the non-futility of what the Bodhisattva undertakes.

From here below, seven verses praise the virtues accomplished through practice; among these, the first one and a half verses praise the text concerning the fulfillment of the cause and the perfection of the fruit within the first nine of the eighteen phrases.
The next two and a half verses praise the preservation of the True Dharma and its extensive exposition.

The following three verses praise the passage on the benefits of the three types of action (karma) in the eighteenth [chapter], specifically praising the aforementioned act of preaching the Dharma with a composed, majestic, firm, and profound manner within the great assembly in order to eliminate delusions.
The following clarifies that what was taught accords with the principle, and thus the Tathāgata rejoices in it;
what was taught accords with the capacities of the audience, and thus the great assembly practices it.
This concludes the third assembly.
Record of Investigating the Profundities of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Five;
Record of Investigating the Profundities of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Six.
This concludes the fourth assembly, composed by the Śramaṇa Fazang of Xisi Monastery in the Wei Kingdom.
15. Chapter Fifteen: The Sovereign Ascent of the Buddha to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven.
Regarding the initial explanation of the title, there are two aspects:
first, the name of the assembly is designated according to its location, thus it is called the "Assembly in the Yāma Heaven."
Regarding the summary of the dharma, it is called the "Assembly of the Ten Practices," which can be understood according to the explanation provided.

As for the names of the two chapters: the Buddha is the principal teacher of transformation; relying on his essence to give rise to function, he "ascends" in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
Where should one expect to be reborn?
It is said to be Yāma.

Regarding Yāma, if the full term is used, it is Suyāma; "su" means "good" (śubha) in this language, and "yāma" means "time" (kāla). This is because in that heaven there are no sun or moon by which the passage of time could be known.
Therefore, the *Mahāsāṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "The blooming of red lotuses signifies day; the blooming of blue lotuses signifies night.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains the name of this heaven as the Heaven of Singing Delight (*Gītanirghoṣa*), also known as the Heaven of Many Playful Delights (*Bahudeva*).
"Deva" (Heaven) signifies purity and radiance.

Yet, those in this heaven are so attached to pleasure that they do not think of goodness at all; it is only thanks to the Bodhisattva Peacock King and the Lord of Devas named Mucilinda who constantly guide them.
Either it was a real deva who lost his companion and wept as he informed the King, or it was a manifested deva who fell into the water;
this was done to inspire weariness with [samsaric] existence through the arousal of fear.
Question:

Since both the preceding and succeeding [categories] ascend without departing [from their respective realms], they should all equally be named "Masters" (*vaśavartin*). Why, then, is this assembly alone designated as "Masters"? Answer:
Because they ascend and travel without moving [from their place], these space-dwelling devas surpass the previous earth-dwelling ones; therefore, they are called "Masters."
The abode of Akaniṣṭha is established differently from Tuṣita; therefore, it alone is singled out for its name.
Furthermore, because one enters the profound through practice and surpasses the previous stage of understanding, it is designated by the term "sovereignty" (vaśavartin).

Furthermore, because they connect through the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), they proceed from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the Yāma Heaven; both are internal ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) unlike those previously mentioned who abide in faith. Because their fruition is manifested here as the practice of detachment from signs, they arrive at this celestial realm of emptiness.
Second, regarding the purpose of the second assembly, there are also two points:

first, as for the reason for its arrival, it is because practice arises based on understanding, and because it answers the ten previous questions concerning practice; for these reasons, it has arrived.

Regarding the arrival of the two chapters: it means that the "Clarifying Dharma" (*vidyā-dharma*) was the culmination reached in the previous assembly, while "Ascending to Heaven" (*deva-loka-gamana*) is the result achieved in this assembly; as they follow one another in immediate succession, it is necessary for [the latter] to come.
Furthermore, it clarifies that through the understanding of the Dharma, profound realization arises, and one enters into practice; for this reason, one ascends to heaven and must therefore return.
This is an analysis according to the Dharma.
Within the three categories of the ultimate goal (*paryavasāna*), there are likewise two:
Regarding the initial unification of the schools: in terms of persons, this refers to the principal teacher of transformation and those who assist in transformation;

in terms of the Dharma, it refers to the matters of teaching and their underlying principles. In all cases, essence, characteristic, and function are mutually integrated and unimpeded; these should be understood according to what was previously explained, differing only in their application to practice.
Regarding the two chapters on the assembly: the first concerns the invitation to the Buddha at the site of adornment, wherein the Tathāgata responds to the call;

this is what is elucidated here. Regarding the fourfold explanation of the text: this assembly contains four chapters of scripture; the first two are the introduction, and the latter two are the formal exposition.
The preceding section has two parts:
the first is the introduction consisting of the invitation to the Buddha, and the second is the introduction consisting of the praise of the Buddha.

Furthermore, the former concerns his ascent to heaven, while the latter concerns the assembly of the bodhisattvas; since the Buddha is the principal teacher, he is mentioned first, and as the bodhisattvas are his companions, they follow next.
Furthermore, the former is the fruit and the latter is the cause; the former is that which can transform, and the latter is that which is transformed.
Regarding the initial section of the text:
first, the explanation is the same as that stated at the beginning of the preceding assembly.

Another explanation states there are seven [aspects]: first, the Dharma Kings under the Bodhi trees in the ten directions appear simultaneously; second, the Buddhas of the ten directions each ascend to the Yāma Heaven; third, the celestial kings of the ten directions each adorn their seats and invite the Buddhas; fourth, the Buddhas of the ten directions accept the invitations and ascend to the palaces; fifth, the celestial kings of the ten directions obtain benefits and praise the Buddhas; sixth, the Buddhas of the ten directions together ascend to the sublime thrones; seventh, the jewel palaces of the ten directions are each vast and expansive.
Why are they all expounded identically throughout the ten directions?

Because the Dharma-gate of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) pervades the entire Dharma-realm; whenever a single dharma arises, it necessarily manifests everywhere. Therefore, when about to expound this Dharma, its principle is not partial or localized, which is why there is an inexhaustible simultaneous exposition throughout the ten directions—namely, that one exposition is all expositions, and so forth.
Within this, there are three kinds of non-obstruction:
first, because the one is precisely the many, the Buddha beneath a single tree is the Buddha beneath all trees;
second, because movement is precisely stillness, the Buddha beneath the tree is the same as the one ascending to heaven.
Because the three—movement and stillness—are one and many, one ascends to heaven without moving from any location whatsoever.
This is the mark of the ten Buddhas’ unimpeded, perfectly interfused endowment of virtues; it is not what other schools can discern, so reflect upon this accordingly.
Regarding the first two sections of the text, they are explained in the same manner as the preceding assembly.
Within the third section, "The Adornment of the Request," there are three parts:
first, beholding the superior conditions from afar; second, adorning the seat to manifest the faculties; and third, requesting the Buddha to manifest his intention.
Regarding the array of the assembly, there is first the general description and subsequently the specific details.
That the first assembly numbered ten thousand while this one numbers one hundred thousand signifies the characteristic of increasing stages.
Furthermore, that the previous hall was not adorned with jewels while this one is adorned with jewels reveals the characteristic of practice being noble and endowed with virtue.
There are twenty-three phrases in this separate section:
the first seven distinguish the adornments of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*);
the subsequent seven phrases, beginning with "one hundred thousand devaputras," reveal the adornments of the sentient-being-world (*sattva-loka*).

The subsequent nine phrases, beginning with "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions," constitute the adornment of the world of the Wisdom-Perfectly-Awakened One. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
the first seven [phrases] are the adornment of external objects; the next six are the adornment of internal retribution; and the final ten are the adornment of the Dharma-gates.

In the "Exalted" section, the first phrase concerns the characteristic of cause; the second, the characteristic of fruit; the third, the characteristic of merit; the fourth, the characteristic of concentration; the fifth, the characteristic of vow; the sixth, the characteristic of excellence; the seventh, the characteristic of dharma; the eighth, the characteristic of function; the ninth, the characteristic of subtlety; and the tenth, the characteristic of teaching.
Among the three requests made to the Buddha, the first summarizes what preceded and the latter constitutes the formal request.

In the fourth section, where he accepts the invitation and ascends the hall, it is shown that the spiritual capacity and the teaching are in accord; this first clarifies the situation in this land and subsequently classifies other regions accordingly.
Within the section on the benefits obtained by the Fifth Heavenly King, this realm is first distinguished and the other directions are subsequently categorized by analogy.
Within the former, the benefit of attaining meditative concentration is first presented, followed by the benefit of generating wisdom.
In the midst of wisdom, [the Buddha] first recalls his own roots of goodness and subsequently praises the ten Buddhas of the past to manifest the excellence of the present stage.

In truth, all Buddhas of the past have likewise taught these ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi-dharma*); however, because it is now intended to demonstrate that the characteristics of the stages gradually increase, he praises the ten Buddhas—beginning with the Buddha named *Candrasūryapradīpa*—by citing them in sequence from the previous assembly. This does not mean that the other Buddhas prior to Kāśyapa and the others did not also previously teach these ten stages of practice in this very place.
The sixth, the Ascending the Seat, and the seventh, the Expansive Hall, may both be understood according to the preceding sections.

Chapter Sixteen: The Bodhisattva’s Discourse in Verse. Regarding the initial explanation of the title: its essential nature is a wondrous cause; through the accumulation of practice, the patterns of the text emerge, and the teaching is thus clearly manifested. Hence, it is called "The Bodhisattva’s Discourse in Verse."
The remaining meanings, as well as the purpose and the thesis, are all explained as before.
Regarding the fourth section, the explanation of the text, three points are the same as before.
Within the initial gathering of the assembly, first this realm is addressed, and subsequently the categories are applied universally.

In the preceding section, the first part reveals the place from which [the assembly] comes, while the latter part, beginning with "By the Buddha’s spiritual power," clarifies the gathering of the bodhisattvas.
Within the former, the initial description of the distance and dimensions serves to manifest the gradual increase in their rank.
The preceding hundred and these one hundred thousand, etc., have their remaining boundaries determined by analogy with the above.
Second, the actual manifestation of the characteristics of the three worlds in their primary location:
as for the worlds being given the same name "Wisdom" (*prajñā*), it is because the previously explained wisdom serves as the basis for practice.

The Buddhas share the name "Equal to the Eye" because it signifies that their practice and mind perceive the Dharma with clarity; furthermore, it signifies that they practice the various *pāramitās* to guide the world.

The Bodhisattvas share the name "Forest" because it signifies that they practice the conduct of the *dharmadhātu* to accomplish the virtues of the *dharmadhātu*; when virtue is lofty, it is like a tree, and when practice is vast, it is called a forest.
The ten paramitas are loftily cultivated together, and the myriad practices emerge in dense array; because their dharma-characteristics are similar, they are called a "forest.
The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
In the second section on the emission of light, the toes of the feet are the source from which the light issues.

However, the big toe possesses two powers: those of walking and standing. The former [section] manifested standing, while this [section] reveals walking; thus, they are distinct. The remainder is explained as before.

Within the third verse of praise, the ten bodhisattva verses constitute ten sections: the first provides a general account of the events and principles of this assembly, while the subsequent nine specifically manifest the gates of meaning regarding the Buddha’s virtues.
"The forest of former masters" (pūrvācārya-vana) identifies the specific speakers; as they are the presiding masters of this assembly, they are mentioned first.
"Receiving the Buddha's spiritual power" (buddhānubhāva) indicates the basis upon which the praise and exposition are delivered.
Regarding "universally observing the ten directions," there are four intentions:
first, as the *Dilun* states, "to manifest the absence of self-conceit and the absence of partiality";
second, to manifest that the Dharma being taught pervades the ten directions.
Thirty: because of the transformation through the Vaipulya [sūtras].
Forty: because the Yāma gods in the four directions all share this teaching, speaking it simultaneously in assembly.
The eleven verses are divided into two parts:
The first seven [verses] summarize the events within the assembly, while the latter four praise the Buddha’s virtues of sovereign mastery.
Within the former section, the first verse describes the emission of light in this chapter; it is presented first because it is proximate.

The subsequent two verses concern the matters of the preceding chapter: therein, the first half-verse refers to this world-system, and the second half-verse refers by analogy to the other ten directions.
The next three verses summarize the contents of this chapter, displaying them through a general reference to the ten directions;

the subsequent verse concerns the passage from "not departing from the Bodhi tree" to "reaching the Yāma heaven" and so forth. Here, "among humans" refers to each of the aforementioned Jambudvīpas, and the "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) refers to beneath the aforementioned Bodhi tree.
In the latter four verses praising the Buddha’s virtues, the first praises the profundity and vastness of his virtues, each being revealed by half a verse.
The following two explain the aforementioned vastness of his activity: the first concerns responding to the world while remaining detached from it, also each revealed by half a verse;

the second concerns the non-obstruction between the one and the many—the first half indicates this, and the second half explains it—this refers to manifesting the single body of Vairocana, which is what is meant by "all the kings of trees" and so forth below.
The latter [verse] explains the profound virtue of the former; it should be understood that the first half provides the heading and the second half provides the explanation.
Second, because one awakens to the benefit of cause and effect, it is named "Forest of Wisdom" (Huilin).
The ten verses are divided into two parts:
the first verse establishes the headings. Specifically, the first half cites the Buddha’s qualities as difficult to encounter, clarifying that meeting him is a cause for celebration;
the second half cites the rarity of encountering the assembly, demonstrating that meeting them is a cause for joy.
The "stainless great being" is this bodhisattva.

Among the nine subsequent explanations, the first explains why the assembly of bodhisattvas is so difficult to encounter: the first half of the verse reveals the clarity of their own wisdom, while the second half distinguishes their excellence in benefiting sentient beings.

The latter eight verses explain the reasons why the Buddha’s virtues are difficult to assail. Among them, the first six correctly manifest the Buddha’s virtues, while the final two provide a comparative analysis based on understanding.
Within the former group, the first clarifies that the Buddha acts as a lamp to dispel darkness;
the second [verse] concerns the perfect illumination of the six perfections.
Third, the three supreme virtues transcend the realm of ordinary emotion;
fourth, quiescence and activity benefit all living beings;
fifth, those who see or hear [the Buddha] obtain benefit.

6. Regarding the section "The cause is deep and the fruit is thick," the following clarifies the benefits of understanding and realization (*jñāna-darśana*). Within this, the first [comparison] relies upon the offering to the Buddha to evaluate the benefit of realization, while the last relies upon extensive giving to manifest the loss caused by delusion.
The third [section] is named "Victorious Forest" (*Vana-vijaya*) because it realizes the sublime Dharma.
The ten verses are divided into two parts:
the first four praise the profundity and vastness of the Buddha’s light, while the latter six clarify the realization of the Truth through illumination.
In the preceding section, the first two lines present analogies and the latter two provide the doctrinal explanation.
Within the former, there are eight phrases:
the first phrase is an analogy for the time when the Buddha attained enlightenment.
The second metaphor illustrates that the Buddha’s mind is free from all defilements and obscurations;
the third metaphor illustrates the Buddha’s body emitting pure light—meaning the sun serves as the metaphor for the Buddha’s body;
and the fourth metaphor illustrates the universal illumination of that light.
The fifth simile illustrates its vastness and abundance;
the sixth illustrates that its limits cannot be known;
the seventh illustrates that even wisdom cannot fully comprehend it.
If this is so even for these eight similes, how much more so for those who are ignorant and deluded?
In the subsequent explanation by way of the Dharma, the first [simile] reveals the vastness of the light,
while the last reveals its profound depth, as it is identical to the *dharmatā*.
Within the latter six [sections], the first three eliminate characteristics, the next one eliminates nature, and the final two resolve doubts.
Within the former [three], the first eliminates the characteristics of the three periods of time, and the second eliminates the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
The second half clarifies the benefits of contemplation; all subsequent verses follow this pattern.
Third, one is free from all signs (*nimitta*).

Next, one is free from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because things are merely provisional constructs arising from conditions, they lack intrinsic nature, and because they lack intrinsic nature, there is nothing to be understood.
The next two [verses] resolve doubts to demonstrate non-arising.
The doubt is as follows:
"If dependent origination lacks intrinsic nature, by what cause does arising occur?"
The commentary states:

Because there is that which is produced, "that which is produced" refers to deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*); it is called "produced" because deluded conceptualization arises in dependence upon conditions.
Due to this grasping at deluded conceptualization, one speaks of "arising," yet in reality, there is no arising.
This is according to the nature of what is grasped (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Another interpretation states:
that which is produced is the effect; it is in dependence upon this effect that the cause is said to be "able to produce" the effect.
Since that which is dependent on others is non-arising and its cause likewise has no dependence, it does not arise.
This is explained in terms of the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Furthermore, another interpretation states:
What is called "having birth" clarifies the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha* following conditions (*pratyaya*).
Because that which is produced is perfumed by the perfumer, it therefore follows conditions.
Since that which perfumes is already empty, that which is perfumed remains unmoved;
therefore, it likewise has no arising. Because that which perfumes is also produced by the mind, it is termed "that which is produced."
This refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

This verse negates the producer by depending upon that which is produced; the subsequent verse likewise dispels the producer by means of that which is produced. Therefore, it is said that "the contemplation of that which is produced is also like this."
The fourth [section] is called the Forest of Fearlessness because, through faith and delight in the profound principle, one does not fear the evil destinies.
The ten verses are divided into five parts;
the first two clarify the benefits of hearing and having faith in the Dharma taught by this Buddha.
First, let us distinguish that which is heard.
"This place" refers to this Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu).
Furthermore, it is the place where this Buddha preaches the Dharma.
The first two lines reveal its vastness; the next line distinguishes its accordance with conditions; the final line reveals its unchanging nature.
The subsequent verse reveals the benefits of hearing and believing this Dharma.
The second section consists of two verses clarifying that hearing the Buddha-dharma in other regions is beneficial.

First, it clarifies what is heard: the first half-verse reveals the vastness of the place from which it is heard; the next line reveals the profundity of what is heard; and the final line reveals that what is heard is not forgotten.

The subsequent verse reveals the benefits: the first half restates what was previously heard; the next line employs that [hearing] to seek Buddhahood; and the final line clarifies that seeking will inevitably result in attainment, hence the phrase "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*) and so forth.

The three verses on the two realms clarify that hearing and believing the Buddha-dharma of the past is beneficial; in each verse, the first half sets forth what is believed, while the second half makes it known that the benefit of such faith is evident.

There are two verses concerning the four [aspects]. Hearing and believing the Buddha-dharma of the present is beneficial; therein, the first line concerns the ability to believe, the next two lines concern the Buddha who is believed in, and the final line concerns the Dharma that is believed in.
The subsequent verse reveals the benefit, because it concerns the attainment of hearing what is difficult to encounter. Furthermore, another interpretation states:

the first half of the preceding verse clearly explains the manifestation of the Buddha through faith, while the second half clearly explains the benefit of faith—namely, that by means of this faith, one realizes perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and so forth.
The subsequent verse reveals that this Dharma is supreme and difficult to hear.
The five verses consist of two verses that summarize all the aforementioned Buddha-dharmas and exhort one to practice and study them.

Within these, the first verse exhorts one to uphold and to proclaim the teaching; the first line restates the aforementioned Dharma, the second line exhorts one to uphold it, the third line exhorts one to proclaim it, and the final line praises its excellence to further encourage such action.
The subsequent verse exhorts both upholding and practice. The first half exhorts practice, for by exhorting the cultivation of practice, one accomplishes the two adornments (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*).

The next line exhorts upholding; its distinction from the preceding part is that while previously it was through upholding that one was able to teach, here it is through upholding that one is able to practice.
The final line clarifies the benefit of such practice, namely, the attainment of *bodhi*.
The fifth [section] is called the Forest of Shame and Remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya-vana*) because it is free from the discrimination of non-gradualism.
The ten verses are divided into two parts:
the first nine separately praise the Buddha-dharma, and the final one concludes both of the preceding sections.
Regarding the preceding section, the first [verse] praises the Dharma realized by the Buddha: the first half praises the excellence of the Dharma, while the second half praises the benefit of faith.
The subsequent eight [verses] praise the wisdom capable of realizing [the Dharma], which is twofold:

the first clarifies that the realization of the Dharma is all-encompassing; the first half clarifies that all Buddhas speak of what they themselves have realized, while the next line clarifies that the wisdom of a single Buddha realizes everything without exception, and is therefore inconceivable.

The latter seven clarify that non-evidence serves as evidence; among them, the first establishes the heading, wherein the first half constitutes "non-evidence" and the second half constitutes "evidence.
Within the first half, there are five points:

first, the explanation in terms of wisdom (*jñāna*), which states that this direct realization of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) does not arise from worldly conceptual wisdom, nor does it arise from ignorance or from form (*rūpa*) and other phenomena.

Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "This wisdom is neither wisdom nor non-wisdom; it is not wisdom in the sense of conceptualizing wisdom, nor is it non-wisdom in the sense of being a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*)."
In this context, "not wisdom" refers to ignorance (*moha*).
Second, it is explained in terms of its object: the realized wisdom of principle (*li-zhi*) serves only as a cause of understanding (*jñāna-hetu*), not as a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*).
Since ignorance lacks wisdom, it is neither a productive nor an understanding cause; therefore, both are said to be "non-arising."

Third, the correct interpretation based on the object and the wisdom: because wisdom conforms to the object, it is not [merely] wisdom; because the object conforms to wisdom, it is not the absence of wisdom.

Fourth, the interpretation based on quiescence and illumination: because wisdom is itself quiescent, it is not [merely] wisdom; because it does not lose its illumination, it is not the absence of wisdom.

The fifth is an explanation by way of absolute transcendence (*anapekṣā*): because the characteristics of cognition are exhausted, it is not "cognition"; because there is no cognition to be depended upon, it is not "non-cognition.
In the second half [of the verse], it is shown that only such a wisdom of non-cognition can illuminate phenomena and extinguish darkness; thus, it serves as the proof.
Among the six subsequent verses, the first five explain the first half of the chapter, while the last one explains the second half.
Within these five, each verse presents a simile in its first half and applies it to the Dharma in its second half.

First, the analogy of the distinct natures of the ignorant and the wise; second, the analogy of equally accomplishing the unreal; third, the analogy of the mutual incompatibility of the two natures; fourth, the analogy of the separation between the conditions of the ignorant and the wise; fifth, the analogy of the non-substantial accomplishment of function. These five all manifest the distinction between the affairs of the ignorant and the wise, as both are ultimately not real.
Delusion and awakening are thus severed, and the marks of cognition are exhausted.
In the subsequent explanation of the supreme function of wondrous wisdom, the first half provides an analogy.
*Gāthā* here means "efficacious medicine," signifying that which can eliminate all poisons.
The correspondence of the lower half of the verse may be understood accordingly.

In the subsequent pair of verses regarding the "knots," the first half-knot signifies the superiority of the Buddha’s wisdom, while the second half-knot signifies the superiority of the sublime Dharma.
The sixth [verse] is called the Forest of Diligence because it involves ardent contemplation of both principle and phenomena without conceptual discrimination.
These ten verses collectively praise the Buddha’s non-discriminative wisdom of illumination; the first verse is general, while the remaining nine are specific.

Within the former, the meaning that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are without distinction can only be known by a Buddha; however, to know them in full detail is called "discriminative knowledge" (*vibhaktajñāna*).
The subsequent line refers to "comprehensive knowledge."
The latter phrase is deeply understood.
Within the section on differentiation, each instance first presents a metaphor followed by the corresponding principle (*dharma*).
The first is a metaphor for the mutual penetration of the true and the false; it means that the false arises based on the true, just as gold manifests in various forms.
Unrighteousness is false and is thus likened to gold-colored [deception].
Since it lacks substantiality, it is identical to the True; therefore, their natures are not distinct.
Furthermore, the true mind follows conditions to manifest as either righteousness or unrighteousness, yet the essence of the mind remains no different; therefore, their natures are not distinct.
Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra* says: "The Tathāgatagarbha acts as the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "When it coexists with the unwholesome, it is called ignorance; when it coexists with wholesome dharmas, it is described as clarity."
This refers to the statement: "The nature of clarity and ignorance is non-dual; this non-dual nature is itself the true nature.
Furthermore, the entire "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality" in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* conveys this same meaning.
Second, both lack a real analogy: sentient beings, in terms of their internal retribution, are analogous to the Dharma;
non-sentient beings, in terms of the external vessel-world, are analogous to non-Dharma.
Both lack a fixed nature and neither exists [ultimately].
Another interpretation:
Because sentient beings are themselves non-self, sentient beings are not real.
Because non-self does not obstruct sentient beings, that which is not a sentient being is likewise not real.
Because principle and phenomena mutually negate one another, neither is truly real.
As the Sūtra says: "That which is both self and non-self, and free from duality—this is the meaning of non-self.
Furthermore, because sentient beings are themselves non-existent, even the characteristic of non-existence is transcended.
Therefore, all are not real. This can be understood through the application of the Dharma.
Regarding the analogy for the three births being without the characteristic of cessation: it means that the dharma of birth is itself non-birth, just like the characteristic of non-cessation.
Furthermore, these future characteristics will be non-existent at the very moment they arise, just as the future lacks the characteristics of the past.
The analogy for the four types of cessation being without the characteristic of arising is that a dharma which has arisen is itself non-arising, just like a dharma that has already ceased.
Furthermore, that which has transcended faults is itself faultless, just as the present and future do not exist [as substantial entities].
The five dharmas are devoid of grasping when used as metaphors; that is to say, because nirvāṇa is free from characteristics, it cannot be grasped.

In terms of karmic retribution, the "remainderless" and "with remainder" are spoken of based on the locus where afflictions are extinguished; however, in reality, there is no distinction in the principle of extinction.
Regarding the metaphor for the lack of distinction among the six natures: it means that numerical categories are not different, and phenomena are identical to emptiness.

The seventh [type] is the "differentiation according to conditions," which serves as a counter-example; that is, taking the number ten as the basis, it increases beyond ten, and wisdom forms conceptions of hundreds, thousands, and so forth upon it; therefore, it is called "differentiation."
However, since all those numbers are multiples of ten, it is said that they are all fundamental numbers.
Moreover, while that ultimate truth manifests as diversity according to conditions, if one seeks those diverse phenomena, they do not differ from the single True Reality.
Briefly stated, there is no convergence with the [preceding] dharmas.
The eighth is the analogy of being firm and indestructible in essence; that is to say, although they are equally conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they are eternally and profoundly tranquil.
The ninth is the analogy of clinging to difference and opposing sameness, which can be understood [by the preceding].

The seventh is the Forest of Accomplishing Power through the Name of Worldly Emptiness. The meaning of these verses clarifies the convergence of defilement and purity within emptiness, extolling the true Buddha.
The ten verses are divided into two parts:
the first nine clarify the objective realm, and the final one establishes practice.

Regarding the preceding section, the first six [verses] reveal non-arising by way of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), while the latter three reveal signlessness (*animitta*) by way of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Within the former group, the first four reveal the non-arising of worldly phenomena (*laukika-dharma*), and the latter two analogously reveal the supramundane (*lokottara*).
Regarding the preceding section: the first two [verses] establish the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), while the latter two establish the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Within the former, the first one and a half verses deduce the derivative back to the fundamental, while the latter half reveals the derivative by means of the fundamental.

This means that the mind undergoes transformation according to its habitual perfumation to become sentient beings; since the mind is like an illusion and lacks reality, how could the sentient beings who are that very mind possibly possess substantial existence?
Regarding the latter two [ignorances]: the first is because one does not know that the world is empty, and thus one continues to revolve within this empty world;
the second is because one does not know that the world is suffering, and thus one constantly transmigrates within this world of suffering.
In this context, the mundane world is neither self-created nor created by another; it has four aspects, the first of which concerns the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and so forth.
Regarding the two subsequent categories within the supramundane, the first provides the definition: that which is the reverse of this mundane world is called the supramundane.
Since the mundane world is empty, how could there be a supramundane reality that can be grasped?
Therefore, it is said that both are not real.
The first half [of the verse] concerns the actual principle; the second half concerns deluded sentiment.
In the commentary on the subsequent verse, the first three lines explain that the world is empty;
the final line states that because there is no "world" to contrast with, the supramundane is likewise not real.
Furthermore, according to this text, it merely negates the designation "world" as being transcendent, without providing any separate positive representation; therefore, it too is empty.
Second, regarding the signlessness (*animitta*) within the absence of what is grasped (*parikalpita*), there are also two parts:
the first two concern worldly emptiness, while the latter one pertains to a category of supramundane [emptiness].
Within the former, the first interrogates conventional sentiment, and the second reveals the principle.
In the preceding section, the first line interrogates the essence, the second line interrogates the characteristics, and the final two lines clarify the delusions of ordinary beings.
In the subsequent verse, the first half clarifies that emotional attachments are non-existent, while the second half clarifies that the rational nature is manifest.

In the subsequent section on "Transcending the World," both the Buddha and the Dharma are transcendent; yet, according to conceptual calculations based on emotional attachments, neither exists as a substantial entity.

The following clarifies the accomplishment of practice: the first half [of the verse] shows the extinction of false views and the manifestation of the Real, while the second half clarifies that the Dharma-Buddha is eternally manifest.
The eighth [section] illuminates the Buddha’s Dharma-body; it is named "The Forest of Solidity," praising the quiescence of the Dharma-body of the Buddha.
The ten verses are divided into two parts:
the first seven reveal the Dharma, and the latter three establish contemplation.

Regarding the preceding section, the first two [lines] indicate the two chapters of subject and object. First, it reveals that the essence of what is praised is quiescent: although grasses and trees grow from the earth, one cannot find the seeds or fruits of those grasses and trees within the earth itself. This is a metaphor for how the Buddha manifests distinctions according to the capacities of sentient beings, yet within the Buddha, no distinct intention can be found; thus, it is said below that "the immeasurable bodies are not the Buddha," and so forth. Subsequently, it reveals the equality of the praising subject, which is evident.
Within the extensive explanation of the latter five [verses], the first three verses explain the aforementioned praise of emptiness: first, it clarifies that karma does not exist;
second, by analogy with karma, it shows that the body also does not exist;
third, by analogy with both karma and the body, it shows that consciousness also does not exist.

The final two verses explain the previously praised state of "non-existence within existence": first, they clarify the great function that responds to capacities; second, they clarify that the essence is not manifold. The following three [verses] clarify the benefits of practice:
first, the benefit of realizing and seeing the Dharmakāya; second, the destruction of marks to return to the True; third, the realization of the Truth and detachment from marks.
The ninth [stage] is called the Forest of Tathāgatas because it involves contemplating the *tathatā* (suchness) of the mind.
The ten verses are divided into two parts:
the first six clarify how the mind creates ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and the latter four clarify how the mind gives rise to the noble ones (*ārya*).
In the preceding section, the first four and a half verses present analogies, while the final half-verse provides the application to the Dharma.
Within the former, the first two verses use the analogy of a painter creating a painting to illustrate how false phenomena depend upon the True;
the next two clarify the analogy of the mind as painter creating the painting to illustrate how the false depends upon the mind.
The second half clarifies the analogy of a painter who does not know his own mind, which serves as a metaphor for the ignorance inherent in dependent origination.

The intended meaning here is that all sentient beings rely upon true dependent origination; the mind of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is perfumed by the branches of existence, such as names-and-words and the view of self, whereby the bodies of the six realms manifest.
Dependent origination is illusory; it does not obstruct non-existence nor destroy existence. Therefore, there are two gates for its comprehensive integration:
if one integrates conditions to follow reality, then all differentiated marks are exhausted, leaving only True Suchness;
if one subsumes the branches to return to the root, then the diverse forms of the six realms revolve solely within the mind.
From the perspective of the former, dependent origination does not exist, for it is the gate of True Suchness;
from the perspective of the latter, dependent origination is not destroyed, for it is the gate of arising and ceasing.
Therefore, existence and destruction are non-dual, being but a single dependent origination.
The two gates are unimpeded and are but a single mind.

Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Based on the dharma of the one mind, there are two gates: first, the gate of the suchness of the one mind; second, the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind."
"However, these two gates each comprehensively encompass all phenomena.
This is what that means.
Now, within this text, "picturing" (or "depicting") also carries two meanings:
First, because it relies upon a wall, it is only flat;
second, because it relies upon the skillful mind of the painter, it appears as if there were height and depth.

The first two verses clarify the first gate: that is, the first half-verse of the initial stanza uses the metaphor of the differences in the distribution of perfuming; the next line reveals that these differences exist only within deluded perception; and the final line shows that when appearances are exhausted, they are identical to the Truth.
The four great elements (mahābhūta) are a metaphor for the true mind.
The colors are a metaphor for the illusory appearances arising from conditions.

The first half of the subsequent verse clarifies that the true and the deluded are not identical; the first line clarifies the metaphor of the creator being distinct from the created: the true reality that subsumes delusion is not identical to delusion, because its nature is truly real.
The second phrase clarifies that the created is not the creator, using the analogy that the delusion which relies upon the Real is not identical to the Real, because its nature is empty.

The latter half clarifies that the delusive does not depart from the Real; it means that by means of emptiness one penetrates the Real, and when emptiness is exhausted, the Real manifests—hence it is said they do not depart.
Therefore, contemplate that they are neither separate, nor different, nor identical.

The following two verses clarify how a painted image depends upon the mind that paints it; this serves as a metaphor for the subsequent gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*). Here, the painter’s mind is a metaphor for the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) and other transforming minds, while the colors of the painting are a metaphor for the retributive bodies of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) produced by those transformations.

The first half clarifies that the subject and object are not identical, while the second half reveals that the fundamental and the derivative are not separate; that is to say, because the mind is the fundamental and its manifestations are the derivative, they are not identical, yet because the mind transforms into retribution, they are not separate.

This clarifies that the mind is able to transform objects; while the essence of the mind is not the object, the object arises from the transformation of the mind, and the phenomenal aspect of the object is not the mind itself.
Because it arises from the mind, the object is not separate from the mind;
because it transforms the object, the mind is not separate from the object.
Therefore, although they are neither identical nor separate, they must be consciousness alone and not merely objects.
Question:

The preceding verse only clarifies that the colors are not separate from the four great elements, but does not clarify that the four great elements are not separate from the colors; why is this different?

Answer: The preceding passage clarified that the True [Nature] is unchanging while the delusory is subject to transformation; this [passage], however, reveals how the mind transforms into objects, and thus they are not the same.

The first half of the subsequent verse clarifies that the painter’s skillful mind is a metaphor for the transforming consciousness, which takes non-abiding as its basis; therefore, it is inconceivable.

The second half [of the verse] reveals that the colors of the painted images manifested therein serve as a metaphor for the various transformed appearances (nimitta) that each manifest from the mind, being known as having no substantial essence.

The latter half [of the commentary] states that the painter does not know that these paintings all manifest from the mind; this serves as a metaphor for how sentient beings are deluded regarding the measure of their own minds (svacittamātra).
The following one and a half verses provide the doctrinal correspondence, which may be understood accordingly.

Second, regarding the clarification that the Buddha arises from the mind: "As is the mind, so too is the Buddha. This compares ordinary beings to the Buddha; just as the mind creates ordinary beings, the creation of a Buddha is likewise, for both arise entirely from the mind.
Just as it is with the Buddha and sentient beings, the Buddha is used as a category to represent ordinary people.
The following two lines bring them together to reveal their identity: the mind creates the Buddha, yet there is no distinction between the mind and the Buddha;
the mind creates the ordinary person, yet there is no distinction between the mind and the ordinary person.
Because the subject and its basis are identical, it is said that there is no distinction. Furthermore, another explanation states:
this is the first verse within the second section on the exhortation to practice and study, which integrates and resolves the beginning and the end.
There are three aspects to the fundamental and the derivative:
first, the fundamental alone, which refers to the ultimate truth as it accords with the purity of nature; herein, original enlightenment is termed "Buddha.
Second, the derivative alone, which refers to sentient beings who are manifestations thereof.
The three are simultaneous, meaning the mind that undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*), because it relies upon the true capacity for transformation.

These three aspects of dependent origination are interpenetrating and unimpeded; since each one fully encompasses the others and their natures do not differ, they are said to be "without distinction."
Next, one section provides further exhortation for practice: the first half clarifies that the Buddha already knows [the benefits], citing what is above to exhort those below;
the next line exhorts those below to emulate those above;
and the final line concludes by clarifying the knowledge of these benefits.

The next verse clarifies that body and mind are neither identical nor separate: the first half shows they are not identical because their characteristics are distinct; the second half shows they are not separate because the body manifests in dependence upon the mind.
The following verse provides an exhortation to practice: the first half sets forth that which is sought, while the second half exhorts one to contemplate according to principle.
This means that when this gathered mind enters into reality, it is the Tathāgata; conversely, to depart from this is to go astray.
Another explanation is that it is also because the Buddha’s marks manifest as transformations of the mind.
The tenth is called the Forest of Wisdom (*jñānaketu*) because it knows the profound and vast essence and function of the Buddha.
The ten verses are divided into three parts:

the first three praise the Buddha’s Dharma-body as being free from marks; the next one clarifies that the praising Buddha has attained great merit; and the final six praise the Buddha’s manifested forms and sounds.

In the preceding section, the first part clarifies the separation from the characteristics of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Specifically, the first phrase indicates separation from the three objects of fragrance, taste, and touch; therefore, it is said to be "ungraspable.
The second phrase indicates separation from the object of form (*rūpa*); the third phrase indicates separation from the object of sound (*śabda*).
The next phrase is free from the dust of dharmas.

The following one is free from the marks of the measurable and the immeasurable; "immeasurable" refers to the many and "measurable" to the few, both of which are false conceptualizations and neither should be grasped.
Next, regarding the first point—being free from the characteristics of verbal expression—there are two meanings:
First, it refers to cases such as speaking when one should not speak during the eight improper times, which brings no benefit to oneself or others.

Second, it refers to failing to recognize that the Dharmakāya is not an object of verbal expression, yet asserting that it can be explained to others according to words; this leads to falling into the four types of false views, such as existence and non-existence, thereby deceiving both oneself and others, as exemplified by the five faults of grasping at meaning according to the sound of the words.
The two preceding verses clarify that the mind, body, and activities of the Dharma have ceased; this verse clarifies that the path of language is cut off, and is therefore inconceivable.
The second single verse clarifies the praise of the merits attained by the Buddha, which may be understood accordingly.
The third section praises the Buddha’s virtue of manifesting his appearance; it consists of six verses divided into two parts:
the first three clarify the characteristics of the Buddha’s body—namely, that he manifests a body while being bodiless, and that his body is itself bodiless;
the latter three clarify the characteristics of the Buddha’s speech—namely, that he manifests sound while being voiceless, and that his voice is itself voiceless.

Regarding the first [of the two points] concerning the preceding section: the example of the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) is not a true analogy. This is because when it is reflected upon by a yellow garment, it appears as yellow.
This involves two meanings:
first, the gem is not yellow, yet it manifests as yellow; second, the yellow that is manifested is not actual yellow.
The Buddha’s body is likewise: it appears in response to the capacity of those who encounter it.

Since these two meanings share the same analogy, the subsequent line answers by stating, “The Buddha is also thus. One should understand that this analogy is explained in detail in the *Jñānālaṃkāra-sūtra*.

Second is the analogy of manifesting while remaining apart from visibility: just as forms appear based on space, yet space itself is not visible, so too the Buddha manifests forms according to the capacities of sentient beings, yet the Buddha is not form and cannot be seen.
The next section explains the analogy of the "single lifting," which refers to the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*).
Great wisdom has two meanings: first, the meaning of perfect luminosity, which was illustrated by the preceding metaphor; [the second is the meaning of great function].
Second is the meaning of being free from marks (*animitta*), which is illustrated by the subsequent analogy.
In all cases, they manifest forms in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, yet these are not [substantial] form; therefore, it is said that "none can behold them.
According to this text, it is clear that the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) lacks such coarse attributes as physical form.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states as follows.

Second, regarding the voice of the Buddha’s speech, the first part clarifies that it is neither sound nor non-sound, as revealed by two half-verses. Because one must rely on the conventional expression (*vyavahāra*) to realize the ultimate reality (*tattva*), it is said: "One does not know [it] apart from sound."

Next, one verse praises the profundity [of the teaching] and exhorts study, clarifying the benefit of adorning the unsurpassed path to approach reality and the benefit of distancing oneself from all delusions to abandon the false.
The final verse clarifies that it is neither spoken nor unspoken; each half-verse reveals this, as can be understood.
Furthermore, it is clear that even in the Buddha-ground there is no teaching; teaching occurs only in accordance with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings.

Chapter Seventeen: The Ten Practices of the Bodhisattva Puṇyapuṣpakūṭa. First, regarding the explanation of the title: the essence of the ten perfections’ benefit and nourishment is called "merit" (*puṇya*). It possesses the power of adornment and elicitation, like a flower that bears fruit; the various practices intermingle and embellish one another, like a cluster of flowers.

Furthermore, "virtue" (guṇa) is the essence of the practice, "flower" (puṣpa) is its function, "collection" (saṃcaya) is its characteristic, and "bodhisattva" is the person. Since that person possesses those virtues, it is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound).
This is an alternative name for Guṇakanda (Forest of Merit), similar to what occurs below in the "Chapter on the Vajradhvaja Dedication.
The ten practices are the dharmas of the stages; thus, their names are established by incorporating numerical designations.
The ten practices of the Bodhisattva are also designated by their primary referent (*yǒuzhǔshòu*), with both person and dharma serving as the headings of the chapters.
Regarding the two purposes for this section: since the preceding introduction has already been clarified, the main body of the teaching (*zhèngzōng*) ought now to be revealed.
Furthermore, since the preceding assembly has already gathered, the formal exposition and transmission follow; thus, it comes next.
Regarding the third point, the essential purport, there are three parts:

first, clarifying the dharma of provisional stations according to the Three Vehicles; second, clarifying the dharma of distinct practices; and third, the dharma of the stages and positions of Samantabhadra’s practice in the One Vehicle.
In the various early and intermediate holy teachings, this is explained through many approaches; when summarized, there are ten:
first, among the two types of *pāramitās*, it belongs to the stage of the causal *pāramitā*;
second, among the seven *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, it is subsumed within the second *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa of the stage prior to the [ten] grounds, specifically the stage of "Vigor" (*vīrya*).
In the four practices prior to the third stage, one accomplishes the practice of the *ākāśagarbha-samādhi*;
within the discerning cause (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*) of the four virtues of the Dharma-body in the fourth [stage], one accomplishes the seed of the discerning cause for the virtue of bliss;
and among the four types of persons in the preparatory stage prior to the fifth stage, this is the thirtieth type of practitioner.
The above points are all as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (She lun) of the Liang dynasty and other texts.
Among the six sets of six types of wisdom (*prajñā*), this is the second stage, that of wisdom through reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);
among the seven sets of six types of patience (*kṣānti*), it is the stage of practicing patience (*anuvartana-kṣānti*).
Among the eight kinds of *gotra*, this is subsumed under the *prakṛti-gotra*.
The above points are all as explained in the *Mūlaprakṛti-sūtra* and other texts.

Among the three types of upholding (*dhāraṇī*), this is subsumed under the upholding of the practice of skillful means (*upāya-prayoga-dhāraṇī*), as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.

Among the four obstacles eliminated prior to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), this is the third: subduing and eliminating the fear of suffering characteristic of the Śrāvakas, thereby attaining the retribution of a silver-wheel-turning king (*rājā cakravartin*) who rules over the three continents.

Second, to clarify its specific practice: according to the second stage of the "nature of the lineage" (*gotrabhūmi*) in the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayaguhya Sūtra* (the *Renwang jing*), there are ten mental states, namely: contemplating the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena; and contemplating impurity, suffering, impermanence, and non-self.
The three roots of goodness are generosity, loving-kindness, and wisdom.
The three foundations of mindfulness refer to patience regarding past causes, patience regarding present causes and effects, and patience regarding future effects.
It has already transcended the knowledge and views of self and person, as well as the notion of sentient beings, and cannot be destroyed by the inverted notions of non-Buddhists.
The *Benye jing* (Sutra on Original Acts) is also the same.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of practice:
first, the general, which refers to the ten practices such as faith;
second, the specific, which refers to these ten perfections (*pāramitās*). Here, it is the specific that is elucidated, not the general.
Within the latter, there are again two parts:
first, the cause;
second, the fruit. Herein, the perfection of the cause is elucidated.
These [preceding stages] are all explained according to the teachings of the Three Vehicles, wherein practices are manifested by means of provisional dharmas.

As for the third [section], which clarifies the practice of Samantabhadra according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the ten practices herein fully encompass all practices of the preceding and succeeding stages, exhausting them entirely. Therefore, when this stage reaches its fulfillment, one arrives at the ultimate stage.

As it says in the tenth stage of fulfillment: "Entering the Indra-net Dharma-realm, one achieves mastery over the Tathāgata’s unimpeded liberation; becoming a hero among men, one lets out the great lion's roar and, as a Wheel-Turning King of the Dharma, turns the unimpeded wheel of the Dharma," and so forth.
The commentary states:
This refers to the bodhisattva at the stage of ultimate perfection; yet they are still not yet a Buddha, because the aspect of the fruition remains ultimately ineffable.
Regarding the fourth section, the explanation of the text: within this formal exposition, there are two chapters.
The first chapter clarifies what is practiced, while the subsequent chapters reveal what is accomplished.
Furthermore, the former concerns practice according to the successive stages of the path, whereas the latter concerns practice throughout its general beginning and end.

Furthermore, the former refers to the state (*avasthā*) and the latter to the practice (*caryā*). Moreover, the former refers to the stage of self-perfection (*svabhāga*) and the latter to the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*).

Within the first category, seven divisions are the same as before: (1) the division on samādhi, (2) the division on the [divine] powers, (3) the division on emergence, (4) the division on the fundamental [nature], (5) the division on exposition, (6) the division on the realization of the fruit, and (7) the division on verses.

Why is this so? It is because the teaching arises based upon realization; therefore, one first enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*). To manifest the excellence of the Dharma, the Buddhas collectively bestow their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). As the time for the teaching is approaching, one emerges from concentration. Since words cannot be manifested all at once, the fundamental section (*mūla-bhāga*) is briefly indicated. Because brevity alone cannot provide full detail, it is subsequently explained extensively. To show that what is taught is comprehensive, the conclusion and verification (*pramāṇa*) are finalized. Furthermore, so that the taught Dharma may be easily received and maintained, there is the section of verses (*gāthā-bhāga*).
Regarding the question of why one enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*) at the beginning and middle [of the path], there are six points, explained as before.

Among these, three first present the person who enters concentration: their practice has achieved merit that is like a forest; because ten [qualities] are taught, they are not different [from the previous explanation], and this is called "entering."
Second, it reveals that this is not through one's own power; that is, by attributing the transformation to the Buddha, it is said that "one relies upon his power.
Third, it correctly clarifies the attainment of meditative concentration; that is, by the spirit becoming submerged in realization and attaining resonance, it is said that "one enters."

"Bodhisattva" designates a person distinct from [other] dharmas and distinguishes them from the fruit of Buddhahood. "One who has subdued through settled goodness" cites the capacity [to do so] to manifest their distinction. Goodness has two meanings: [1] that which is inherently good, and [2] that which is good by virtue of being associated with it. Here, it refers to the latter. "Settled" (niyata) means fixed; it indicates that this goodness is not subject to regression. "Subdued" (vinīta) means tamed; it indicates that the afflictions have been suppressed. This is because the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfections is superior to that of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, "settled" means that the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfections is certain to reach its ultimate limit. "Subdued" means that the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfections is capable of suppressing all afflictions. Thus, the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfections is both superior and certain. Therefore, it is called "settled goodness. Because they possess such goodness, they are called "those who have subdued through settled goodness. This is what is meant by "Bodhisattvas who have subdued through settled goodness. As for "who have attained the stage of non-retrogression," this refers to those who have attained the stage of non-retrogression in the Mahāyāna. It is said that there are five types of non-retrogression: first, non-retrogression regarding the roots of goodness; second, non-retrogression regarding the stage; third, non-retrogression regarding the path; fourth, non-retrogression regarding birth; and fifth, non-retrogression regarding the certainty of enlightenment. Among these, non-retrogression regarding the roots of goodness means that one does not lose the roots of goodness already cultivated. Non-retrogression regarding the stage means that one does not fall back from the stages already attained. Non-retrogression regarding the path means that one does not abandon the path already entered. Non-retrogression regarding birth means that one will not be reborn in evil destinies after this life. Non-retrogression regarding the certainty of enlightenment means that one will never again turn back from the state of certain enlightenment. Here, it refers to the last. This is because the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfections is certain to lead to supreme, perfect enlightenment. Therefore, it is called "non-retrogression. Because they have attained such non-retrogression, they are called "those who have attained the stage of non-retrogression. This is what is meant by "Bodhisattvas who have subdued through settled goodness and have attained the stage of non-retrogression. As for "who dwell in the great vehicle," this refers to those who dwell in the Mahāyāna. It is said that there are three types of dwelling in the great vehicle: first, dwelling in the great vehicle by way of aspiration; second, dwelling in the great vehicle by way of practice; and third, dwelling in the great vehicle by way of realization. Among these, dwelling in the great vehicle by way of aspiration means that one aspires to the Mahāyāna. Dwelling in the great vehicle by way of practice means that one practices the Mahāyāna. Dwelling in the great vehicle by way of realization means that one realizes the Mahāyāna. Here, it refers to the last. This is because the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfections is the very realization of the Mahāyāna. Therefore, it is called "dwelling in the great vehicle. Because they dwell in such a great vehicle, they are called "those who dwell in the great vehicle. This is what is meant by "Bodhisattvas who have subdued through settled goodness, who have attained the stage of non-retrogression, and who dwell in the great vehicle. As for "who, having heard this profound Dharma," this refers to those who have heard this profound Dharma. It is said that there are two kinds of profundity: first, profundity of meaning, and second, profundity of expression. Here, it refers to both. Profundity of meaning refers to the fact that the Dharma is difficult to understand. Profundity of expression refers to the fact that the words are difficult to comprehend. Here, it refers to the former. This is because the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfections is difficult to understand. Therefore, it is called "profound. Because they have heard such a profound Dharma, they are called "those who, having heard this profound Dharma. As for "gave rise to a mind of great joy," this refers to the arising of a mind of great joy. It is said that there are two kinds of joy: first, joy of hearing, and second, joy of practice. Here, it refers to both. Joy of hearing refers to the joy felt upon hearing the Dharma. Joy of practice refers to the joy felt while practicing the Dharma. Here, it refers to the former. This is because the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfections is joyful to hear. Therefore, it is called "great joy. Because they gave rise to such great joy, they are called "those who gave rise to a mind of great joy. This is what is meant by "Bodhisattvas who have subdued through settled goodness, who have attained the stage of non-retrogression, who dwell in the great vehicle, and who, having heard this profound Dharma, gave rise to a mind of great joy. As for "and who have planted roots of goodness under many Buddhas," this refers to those who have planted roots of goodness under many Buddhas. It is said that there are two kinds of planting roots of goodness: first, planting roots of goodness through giving, and second, planting roots of goodness through wisdom. Here, it refers to both. Planting roots of goodness through giving refers to making offerings to the Buddhas. Planting roots of goodness through wisdom refers to hearing and upholding the Dharma. Here, it refers to the latter. This is because the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfections is rooted in wisdom. Therefore, it is called "planting roots of goodness. Because they have planted such roots of goodness under many Buddhas, they are called "those who have planted roots of goodness under many Buddhas. This is what is meant by "Bodhisattvas who have subdued through settled goodness, who have attained the stage of non-retrogression, who dwell in the great vehicle, who, having heard this profound Dharma, gave rise to a mind of great joy, and who have planted roots of goodness under many Buddhas. As for "who, having heard this sutra, were able to believe and accept it," this refers to those who, having heard this sutra, were able to believe and accept it. It is said that there are two kinds of believing and accepting: first, believing and accepting through faith, and second, believing and accepting through understanding. Here, it refers to both. Believing and accepting through faith refers to the acceptance based on trust. Believing and accepting through understanding refers to the acceptance based on comprehension. Here, it refers to the latter. This is because the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfections is difficult to comprehend. Therefore, it is called "believing and accepting. Because they were able to believe and accept such a sutra, they are called "those who, having heard this sutra, were able to believe and accept it. This is what is meant by "Bodhisattvas who have subdued through settled goodness, who have attained the stage of non-retrogression, who dwell in the great vehicle, who, having heard this profound Dharma, gave rise to a mind of great joy, who have planted roots of goodness under many Buddhas, and who, having heard this sutra, were able to believe and accept it. As for "the World-Honored One then praised them, saying: 'Excellent, excellent! Sons of good family, you have well spoken,' this refers to the World-Honored One praising them. It is said that there are two kinds of praise: first, praise of the person, and second, praise of the dharma. Here, it refers to both. Praise of the person refers to praising their capacity. Praise of the dharma refers to praising their teaching. Here, it refers to the latter. This is because the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfections is a sublime dharma. Therefore, it is called "well spoken. Because they spoke such well-spoken words, they are called "those who have well spoken. This is what is meant by "the World-Honored One then praised them, saying: 'Excellent, excellent! Sons of good family, you have well spoken. As for "if there are good men or good women who wish to quickly attain supreme, perfect enlightenment," this refers to those who wish to quickly attain supreme, perfect enlightenment. It is said that there are two kinds of wishing to attain: first, wishing to attain through aspiration, and second, wishing to attain through practice. Here, it refers to both. Wishing to attain through aspiration refers to the aspiration to seek enlightenment. Wishing to attain through practice refers to the practice of seeking enlightenment. Here, it refers to the latter.
