The following two [verses] concern the desire to know the great dharmas of the Buddha-fruit: first, knowing the Buddha’s virtue of inexhaustible supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
second, knowing the Buddha’s virtue of provisional and ultimate wisdom, wherein "expedient means" (*upāya*) refers to the provisional.
The final phrase refers to knowing the Buddha’s Dharma.

Furthermore, the first four [phrases] may be understood as referring to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the next two to the fundamental stage (*maula*), and the last three to the subsequently attained stage (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*).
Moreover, among these twenty phrases, the first three concern self-benefit (*svārtha*), while the remainder concern the benefit of others (*parārtha*).

Regarding altruism: it should be understood that among these, the first seven [verses] concern knowing the vessels to be converted; the next nine concern knowing the dharma-medicine for conversion; and the final one concerns correctly bestowing the Dharma upon those with the appropriate capacity.
Second, the difficulty of practice regarding conditions is manifested through the firmness of the practice, which contains two parts:
first, the practice is manifested by posing essential questions based on hypothetical heavy sufferings, consisting of two initial questions followed by two answers.
Second, by employing the "ocean of objects" (dust-sea) to make the enumeration manifest, there is likewise first a question and then an answer.
Within the answer, there are two parts:
first, the benefit of causing others to escape suffering; second, the benefit of achieving the fruition for both self and others.
The above is also the "durable diligence" (*durjayavīrya*) from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the "insatiable diligence" (*atṛptivīrya*) from the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
The fifth, the practice of being free from delusion and confusion, is the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), which is also treated through four gates.

First, it takes meditative concentration (*samādhi*) from among the object-determining mental states as its essence, such as the knowledge of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) mentioned in the *Awakening of Faith*.
Second, regarding its types, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are also three kinds:
first, the dhyāna of dwelling in happiness in the present life, which refers to the eight meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth;

Second is the meditative concentration that benefits sentient beings, which refers to relying on this [concentration] to employ the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather sentient beings and so forth;
third is the meditative concentration that brings forth supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which refers to being able to bring forth the eighteen transformations and so forth.
Furthermore, there are ten types mentioned below to demonstrate inexhaustibility.
Regarding the three secrets, the *Sārthavāha-sūtra* states: “Mañjuśrī said:
‘I have a distracted mind.’”
Why is this? For one whose mind is distracted has no place of abiding.
Because I have attained liberation within the minds of the noble ones and have brought all sentient beings to fulfillment, I have no place of abiding.
"For this reason, I call myself one with a distracted mind.
(4) Explanation of the Text:
This explains that through internal cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one becomes free from the habituation to delusion and brings distraction to rest.
The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states: "In all stages, bodhisattvas constantly cultivate two practices:
first, non-perversion; second, non-distraction.
This refers to these very practices.
The text consists of three parts:
first, the dhyāna of dwelling in happiness in the present life;
second, from "This bodhisattva accomplishes tranquility" onwards, the dhyāna that draws forth meritorious qualities.
Third, "When the bodhisattva hears this" and below concerns the dhyāna for benefiting sentient beings.
This section has two parts:
first, the general; second, the specific.
The first part consists of eleven phrases:
the first two phrases set forth two headings—namely, the first phrase sets forth the departure from confusion, and the latter phrase sets forth the departure from delusion.
The subsequent eight phrases provide a comprehensive analysis by traversing various phenomena, which, when grouped according to their characteristics, form four sections:

The first [of these three] refers to that which is received and maintained; the next two refer to the succession of receiving bodies through transmigration. Because this involves intentionally retaining delusions (*kleśa*) out of compassionate vows to take on a body, there is no confusion or delusion. Regarding the six lower stages, it is said that death is of two kinds: 1. Death at the end of one's lifespan (*āyuṣ-kṣaya-maraṇa*). 2. Death due to the exhaustion of merit (*puṇya-kṣaya-maraṇa*). In the case of Bodhisattvas, because they have mastery over their births, they do not experience death due to the exhaustion of merit. However, for those who have not yet attained mastery over birth, both types of death may occur. Furthermore, regarding the manner of death, there are two types: 1. Natural death (*prakṛti-maraṇa*), which occurs when the life-force is exhausted. 2. Forced death (*upakrama-maraṇa*), which occurs when the life-force is cut short by external conditions such as weapons, poison, or fire. Among these, Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery over birth do not undergo forced death. As for natural death, it is said that Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery over birth can voluntarily relinquish their life-force at will. This is because they possess the power to sustain their life-force for as long as they desire. Furthermore, regarding the manner of death, there are two types: 1. Gradual death (*krama-maraṇa*), where the faculties cease sequentially starting from the feet. 2. Sudden death (*sakṛt-maraṇa*), where the faculties cease all at once. Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery over birth generally undergo sudden death, as they can relinquish their life-force instantaneously. However, for those who have not yet attained mastery over birth, both gradual and sudden death may occur. Finally, regarding the state of mind at the time of death, there are two types: 1. Death with a distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta-maraṇa*). 2. Death with an undistracted mind (*avikṣipta-citta-maraṇa*). Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery over birth die with an undistracted mind, as they maintain mindfulness and clear comprehension (*smṛti-samprajanya*) until the very end. For those who have not yet attained mastery over birth, both states of death may occur. Thus, it is explained that while ordinary beings are subject to various forms of death, Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery over birth transcend these limitations through their superior power.
The statement that "because of ignorance, one causes the continuity of future births" is spoken with reference to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "When an ordinary worldling undergoes conception, a male conceives desire for the mother and a female conceives desire for the father; therefore, they enter the womb in a state of deluded confusion."
Furthermore, while within the womb, the consciousness is clear and distinct, but upon emerging, one is suddenly overwhelmed by the pain of birth and thus becomes confused.
The Bodhisattva differs from this; both upon entering and leaving [the womb], he is free from delusion and confusion.
Furthermore, the second fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that there are four ways of entering the womb:
first, entering with full awareness but remaining and emerging without full awareness, which refers to a Wheel-Turning King;
second, entering and remaining with full awareness but emerging without full awareness, which refers to a Pratyekabuddha.
In three cases, one is fully aware, namely the Bodhisattva; in four cases, one is not fully aware, namely other sentient beings.
The subsequent three [cases] may be understood as referring to the arising of practice through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

The latter two [sections] concern awakening and the elimination of demonic activities; for when practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one is frequently disturbed by demons, heterodox spirits, ghosts, and the like, and thus these matters are analyzed, as explained at length in the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*.
The following phrase concludes the practice cultivated over many kalpas.
In the second section, which provides a detailed analysis, there are two parts:
first, clarifying freedom from delusion; second, clarifying freedom from distraction.
In the preceding section, the first part restates what has gone before;

from "Regarding 'non-existence'" onwards, it reveals what follows. Within this latter part, first, by being free from the darkness of delusion, one hears the Dharma and does not forget it; second, from "For what reason" onwards, it provides an explanatory proof.
The preceding section has three parts:
first, the general summary; second, the specific details, beginning with "That is to say" (*tadyathā*); and third, the conclusion, beginning with "When the Bodhisattva hears this.
Within the specific details, there are seventeen phrases of Dharma:
First, the profoundness of essence; second, the wondrousness of characteristics—these two are the dharmas of principle (*dharmatā*).
Third, the possession of virtues; fourth, the abundance of virtues—these two are the dharmas of practice (*pratipatti*).

Fifth, the dharma of teaching; sixth, the dharma of cause; seventh, the dharma of fruit; eighth, the dharma of aspiration; ninth, the dharma of remaining unstained while dwelling in the world; tenth, the skillful discernment of worldly dharmas—these two are the dharmas of wisdom (*jñāna*).

11. The universal nature of the objects of knowledge is called the "vast dharma"; 12. the manifold gateways of the objects of knowledge are called "immeasurable"; 13. the clear analysis of dharmas; 14. the truly pervasive is called "common"; 15. the conventional and distinct is "uncommon"; 16. the dharmas of limited measure known at the stage of the cause; 17. the dharmas without boundaries known at the stage of the fruit.
Regarding the lower section on "bondage": because one is free from the darkness of delusion, although one hears many teachings, one does not forget them even after a long time.
In the lower explanation, there is first a question and then an explanation.
There are four propositions:

First, the concentration of not disturbing others; second, constantly guarding the true Dharma; third, cultivating goodness without ceasing; and fourth, because wisdom is constantly practiced, there is no forgetting.
Regarding the second [section], the explanation of "not being distracted," there are two parts:
first, hearing many sounds—because one lacks past obstructions, one is therefore not distracted; [the second part follows].
Regarding the section following "In this way, etc.," one hears a vast sound; because of skillful observation, there is no distraction.
Within the preceding middle section, there are three parts: first, hearing the six sounds; second, clarifying the twelve ways of non-distraction; and third, the absence of the four obstacles.
Regarding the explanation of the twelve [factors], the first eight concern non-distraction in one’s own practice, while the latter four concern non-distraction in benefiting others.
Within the former group, the first is that because one knows the essence of sound is empty, mindfulness is not distracted.

Nevertheless, the bodhisattva is able to remain entirely undisturbed amidst the objects of the six sense-fields; because loud and high-pitched sounds are the most powerful among those that cause agitation, they are singled out for mention.
Second, one does not abandon right concentration.
Third, no error regarding the object of focus;
fourth, no error regarding entry into the principle;
fifth, the constant practice of generosity and the other perfections.
Sixth, the six fundamental minds are never forgotten, which refers to practicing the vow for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Seventh is the meditative concentration on the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*). Eighth, from "realizing the true principle" (*tattvārtha-prativedha*) onwards, it clarifies altruistic action:

First, the wisdom that initiates transformation; second, the actual accomplishment of the work of transformation; third, the benefit accomplished through that transformation; and fourth, the contemplation of the emptiness of the transformative work.
Although one hears those sounds, one does not abandon these practices which have been one's constant conduct from the beginning; therefore, it is said that they are "unconfused."

In the section explaining the reasons for this, it is stated that because there are no four obstructions—namely, the two aforementioned obstructions of afflictions and karma being inactive, and the two subsequent ones consisting of venerable persons and revered teachings—one attains such a state and is not disturbed.
Second, regarding the section on how the broad voice cannot be disturbed, there are two parts:
first, a general explanation that the broad voice cannot cause disturbance;
second, an explanation of the reasons for this lack of disturbance, which has three points.

First, the contemplation through the investigation of skillful means (*upāya-paryeṣaṇā*): first, one contemplates that the characteristics of sound arise and perish without ceasing; next, one contemplates that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is likewise unattainable; finally, one contemplates that the assembly of conditions for hearing constitutes "hearing," yet there is no hearer.
Second, from "Hearing the good and the bad" onwards, it clarifies the contemplation of reality as it is, free from defilement (*yathābhūta-virāga-darśana*).
Third, from "Knowing all" onwards, it clarifies the contemplation of the direct realization of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-sākṣāt-kriyā-darśana*).
Within this, first the exhaustion of characteristics is clarified as being identical to the dharma-nature;

subsequently, the nature itself is clarified to show that these sounds do not merely fail to disrupt or disturb the bodhisattva’s right mindfulness, but rather serve the bodhisattva as an entry point into the realm of dharma-nature, becoming instead a favorable condition for the long path rather than a state of mental distraction.

In the *Māyopama-samādhi-sūtra*, it is said that even if one were to strike a drum for an entire kalpa using the great earth as the drum and Mount Sumeru as the mallet right by the ear of Subhūti, it would not be able to disturb his mind with even a subtle thought.
Why is this? Because they have entered the meditative concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Regarding the second [section], the citation of meritorious qualities, it cites the gradual increase of six kinds of meritorious qualities.

First, clarifying the attainment of concentration through the departure from distraction; second, the induction of wisdom through the departure from delusion; third, the increase of concentration through the gathering of its associates; fourth, the growth of wisdom through the increase of compassion; fifth, the perfection of concentration through uninterrupted practice; and sixth, the fulfillment of wisdom as the actualization of the fruit.
Within the third [section], the concentration for benefiting sentient beings, there are three parts:

first, benefiting them by causing them to leave behind disorder; second, from "In all... onwards, benefiting them by causing them to leave behind delusion, which serves as the cause; and third, from "Ultimately... onwards, benefiting them by causing them to attain the fruit.
The sixth is the practice of excellence (*sādhumatī*), which is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
First, its intrinsic nature consists of the factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) among the object-specific mental states (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*).
Second, regarding its types, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states that there are three:
First, the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena; second, the wisdom of the emptiness of dharmas; third, the wisdom of the emptiness of both.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also presents three types:
preparatory, fundamental, and subsequently attained.
Furthermore, there are four types of wisdom:
first, the wisdom that realizes [the truth]; second, subsequently attained wisdom; third, wisdom for the benefit of others; and fourth, innate wisdom (*sahaja-prajñā*).
The ten types of wisdom mentioned in the subsequent text are intended to manifest its inexhaustibility; they should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If there is no prajñā, the five perfections are like the blind.
Therefore, it is through the guidance of the eye of wisdom that the others are enabled to become pāramitās.
Regarding the three secrets, the *Sārthavāha-sūtra* states: "Mañjuśrī said:
'I am without wisdom. Why is this?'"
Those who lack wisdom do not fear birth and death, nor do they seek to escape afflictions; they dwell and take pleasure together with deluded sentient beings.

I, too, neither fear nor seek to escape within birth, death, and afflictions; I dwell together with deluded sentient beings in one place, sharing their pleasures for the sake of bringing them to accomplishment.
"Therefore, I am said to have no wisdom.
Regarding the fourth section, the explanation of the text, there are three parts within it:

first, citing the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, from "having nothing to rely upon" onwards, correctly clarifying the characteristics of the practice; third, from "this bodhisattva abiding in this" onwards, manifesting the benefits and functions of the practice.

The first four lines consist of two parts: the first two lines present the combined thesis, stating that the substance of the three karmas is empty because there is nothing to manifest, and thus the function of the three karmas is empty.

The latter two lines provide the exposition, meaning they distinguish between defilement and purity: the emptiness of defilement is the absence of bondage, and the emptiness of purity is the absence of liberation; this explains the aforementioned emptiness of substance.
The final line provides the exposition of the emptiness of function.
Because both the substance and function of these [three karmas] are empty of both defilement and purity, they are termed the "quiescent karma of body, speech, and mind.
Since one wishes to rely upon this to give rise to contemplative insight and penetrate the profound principle, it is first cited and set forth.
Regarding the second section, "Manifesting Practice," there are four parts:
first, clarifying the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*), which involves inferring the characteristics [of reality] to enter the contemplation of the ultimate;

second, from "neither arising nor ceasing" onwards, clarifying the wisdom of the fundamental essence (*mūla-jñāna*), which involves the exhaustion of characteristics to realize the contemplation of the ultimate.

3. From "The Bodhisattva forms this thought" onwards, the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) is clarified; it is the unimpeded contemplation of appearances arising based upon reality.

4. Through the contemplation that accords with appearances by means of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to gather and transform beings, because these are appearances that are identical to reality, there is no fault even in taking them as mere appearances.

In the preceding section, the first three phrases clarify the contemplation of consciousness-only without marks (*vijñaptimātra-nirnimitta-vipaśyanā*); that is, one contemplates the emptiness of the marks of the grasped (*grāhya*), such that in the beginning there is nothing upon which to rely and in the end there is nothing in which to abide.
How is it known that objects are empty and have no basis for abiding?
Because they abide in accordance with the mind.
This clarifies the correct abiding in the contemplation of consciousness-only; this is precisely relying on consciousness to dispel delusive objects.
The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states: "Based on the apprehension of consciousness, the non-apprehension of objects arises.
The older commentary states: "Because one relies upon consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), the principle that objects lack intrinsic substance is established."
This is what is meant by that.
Next, the contemplation on the non-arising nature of consciousness is clarified.

Regarding "the immeasurable minds and so forth," one contemplates the nature of the apprehending mind as being identical to the nature of all apprehended phenomena, and identical to the characteristic of the absence of intrinsic nature.
"Equal" (等) means "the same" (同).
This refers to the negation of consciousness by relying on the non-existence of objects (*anartha*).
The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states: "Based on the non-apprehension of the object, the non-apprehension of consciousness arises."
The *Old Treatise* states: "Because objects do not exist, the fundamental consciousness does not arise.
This is precisely what that means.
To manifest the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*) is to seal the emptiness of the previously grasped [objects], because the characteristic of signlessness manifests before one.
Regarding "bottomless depth": the seal is able to realize that consciousness is empty; taking the emptiness of consciousness as the foundation, it is "bottomless" because consciousness is exhausted.
Regarding "the nature of suchness": the seal simultaneously realizes the two kinds of emptiness—namely, the suchness of mind and the suchness of objects—which are one and the same true nature.
Although within suchness there is no characteristic that can arise, it is called "being free from karmic retribution.
Nevertheless, because this preparatory application (*prayoga*) can give rise to correct realization, it is said that "skillful means gives birth to the transcendence of birth."

"Detachment from arising" refers to the stage of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-avasthā*); that is, it summarizes the preceding preparatory practices (*prayoga*) which possess the functional capacity for realization.

Below this, the second section clarifies the wisdom of actual realization: the principle of the identity between the object and its cognition is not subject to the transitions of arising and ceasing, and is thus called "non-arising and non-ceasing";
because it merges with the ultimate truth, it is called "nirvāṇa," and so forth.
This clarifies that it does not exist; that which does not exist is precisely not non-existent. Therefore, it is said that "though non-existent, it is spoken of as existent.
Since existence and non-existence are both transcended, speech cannot arise; therefore, it is said that "the path of language is cut off."

This briefly demonstrates the distinction from inference: whereas worldly wisdom has a basis upon which it rests, this [wisdom] has no such dependence; therefore, it is said to be "detached from all [dharmas]," and so forth.
From here below, the benefits of realization are revealed in five phrases: first, the benefit of increasing wholesome qualities.
Because one realizes the truth, the wholesome qualities previously generated are made to increase manifold; therefore, it is said to be "nurturing," and so forth.
When the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) first arises at the initial moment, it is further perfumed and thereby increased.

Second, to clarify the benefit of abandoning hindrances: "entering" (*praveśa*) refers to conforming to realization; "leaving" (*niḥsaraṇa*) refers to abandoning delusion; "being unbound" (*abaddha*) refers to severing the seeds of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*); and "being unattached" (*asaṅga*) refers to destroying the seeds of the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Third is the benefit of realizing truth, which means realizing the true principle that was previously unrealized.
Fourth is the benefit of transcending stages, which means surpassing the mundane world.
Fifth is the benefit of generating wisdom, which means that by virtue of this realization of the principle, one is able to give rise to subsequent wisdom to discern worldly phenomena.
The third section, clarifying subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), has two parts:
first, clarifying the skillful means of seeking by reconciling principle with phenomena;
second, from "The Bodhisattva understands thus" onwards, clarifying the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena to manifest authentic realization as it truly is.
First a general overview, followed by a detailed analysis.
Within the detailed analysis, there are eight phrases:
the first explains the quiescence of the world, knowing that the substance of delusion is empty.
Second, they understand the Buddha’s profound Dharma and know that reality is free from marks;
third, because defilement and purity are mutually integrated, they are equal and without distinction;
fourth, within defilement there is constant purity, such that the mundane world enters the Buddha-dharma.
Fifth, being unstained yet stained, the Buddha-dharma enters the world;

sixth, because the gates of defilement and purity are distinct, they do not intermingle—meaning that while the whole substance is purity, it does not lose its defilement, and while the entire form is defilement, it does not lose its purity; this is called "the non-duality of defilement and purity, yet their duality. Seventh, explaining the meaning of non-intermixture:

because worldly dharmas are empty, they do not require destruction and do not obstruct persistence; because they do not require destruction, they have never not been identical with the Buddha-dharma; because they do not obstruct persistence, they have never been mixed with the Buddha-dharma; therefore, it is said that "worldly dharmas are not destroyed."

Eighth, because the Buddha-dharma is true, it cannot be destroyed and is not obstructed by following [worldly conditions]. Because it is not obstructed by following [worldly conditions], it has never failed to conform to worldly dharmas; because it cannot be destroyed, it has never been mixed with worldly dharmas. Therefore, it is said that the Buddha-dharma is truly real, and so forth.
Another explanation:
Although the Buddha-dharma enters the world, it is not destroyed by worldly dharmas. Why is this?
Because the true *dharmadhātu* is indestructible.
Question:
If that is so, why not say that worldly phenomena enter into the Buddha-dharma, for worldly phenomena are likewise indestructible?
Answer: Because worldly dharmas enter into the Buddha-dharma, they may be subject to destruction and exhaustion; therefore, they are not discussed here.
This is because the true and the delusory are not of the same order.

The reason for thus trampling upon and blending the defiled and the pure is that one desires to constantly gather and transform sentient beings within the world while remaining eternally abiding in nirvana.
That which allows one to embrace living beings through great compassion without contradicting the contemplation of ultimate principle is precisely this Dharma.
The fourth, the contemplation of great compassion, has five parts:
first, abiding in the equality of the three periods of time, clarifying how compassion arises based on principle;
second, establishing the resolve to gather in and deliver sentient beings.
Third, to take pity on others with one's own mind;
fourth, to admonish oneself not to abandon them;
fifth, to provide correct rescue in response to conditions.
The second section contains five points:
first, "I am not established; who is it that is established?"—this transforms beings so they may achieve goodness;
second, "subduing and departing from evil karma."
Third, the quiescence of afflictions;
fourth, the joyful attainment of the fulfillment of causes;
fifth, the pure attainment of the perfection of results.
Third, regarding "taking pity on beings with oneself," the first phrase reveals what one understands;
the subsequent section, "properly taking pity on the suffering of beings," has two parts:
first, clarifying that they possess various heavy sufferings; second, from "not free from the three obstructions" onwards, showing that they lack the bliss of liberation.
In the preceding section, there are the dharma, the analogy, and the application.
Within the dharma: seeing birth and undergoing suffering is present suffering; treading upon dangerous paths is future suffering; these constitute the fruit of suffering.
The entanglements of afflictions are the cause of suffering.
Within the context of conforming to the Dharma, the bonds of affection are the cause of suffering, while remaining within birth-and-death and so forth constitutes the fruit of suffering.
These are the meanings of the four evil destinies, and so on.
Regarding King Yama, according to various sacred teachings, there are five categories:
first, he is subsumed under the realm of hell-beings (*naraka-gati*), as stated in the second fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*;

second, he is subsumed under the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*), as stated in the "Bodhisattvabhūmi" section of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, though further scriptural passages have yet to be seen.
Third, it is not subsumed under the two destinies (*gati*), because according to this scriptural passage, there is a separate destiny of King Yama;
fourth, it is a transformational creation (*nirmāṇa*), as stated in the fifth chapter of the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* and in the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, among others;
fifth, it is created by Bodhisattvas, as the seventy-seventh fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "Yama is named the Dharma King."
"Regarding whether one brings benefit or harm, it should be said that they only bring benefit.
Thus, we know this is a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, King Yama speaks a verse to the sinners:
"You have obtained a human body yet failed to cultivate the Path; you are like one who reaches a place of great treasure and returns empty-handed.
Now that you have created this for yourself, you must experience its consequences; what is the use of crying out in suffering?"
Question: Does this king sever beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava),
or does he sever beings in the state of existence at birth (upapattibhava)?
Answer: This refers to severing the existence of beings in their fundamental state (*mūlabhava*), because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) does not exist within the hells.

Regarding the absence of the bliss of liberation, the first part clarifies that there are obstacles—namely, being inseparable from afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering—which constitute the three obstacles; the latter part clarifies that there is no escape.
The text contains three pairs of concepts:
First, the absence of the cause for liberation, meaning that the darkness of delusion constitutes an obstruction and the failure to perceive true illumination constitutes a lack of remedy;
second, the absence of the fruit of liberation, meaning that the endless cycle of birth and death constitutes an obstruction and the failure to attain release likewise constitutes a lack of remedy.

The first two of the three [stages] prior to attainment refer to: first, clarifying that there are obstacles which prevent one from seeing the right path; and second, clarifying the absence of remedies.

Within the fourth stage, the self-exhortation, it is stated that since sentient beings endure such heavy suffering, it would be unreasonable not to transform them first before attaining [enlightenment] oneself.
Within the fifth section on "Correctly Gathering Beings," there are three phrases: establishing them in goodness, taming those who are evil, and delivering them to liberation.
This constitutes the third major section on the benefits of practice.
Because this practice of *prajñā* excels all other practices, none of the preceding practices possess these benefits; this may be understood from the text itself.
The seventh is the practice of non-attachment, which gathers all roots of goodness with a mind that dwells nowhere.
Furthermore, through the mutual guidance of compassion and wisdom, it skillfully practices the conduct of non-attachment by dwelling neither in attachment nor in non-attachment.
Non-attachment is practice; it is the skillful means of deliverance (*upāya-pāramitā*), having the wisdom attained subsequently (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and compassion as its essence.
As for its types, there are two:
the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states, "First, the skillful means of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-upāya*); second, the skillful means of rescue."
The subsequent text contains ten points which may be understood.
Regarding the commentary, there are three sections:
first, within the practice of one's own level, the cultivation of the practice of non-attachment;
2. From "The bodhisattva in all Buddha-lands" onwards, [the text] explains cultivation within the stage of superior progress;
3. From "In a single thought-moment" onwards, it clarifies cultivation within the stage of perfected accomplishment.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, it clarifies the practice of great wisdom, manifesting non-attachment in self-benefit;
second, from "The Bodhisattva thus contemplates reality" onwards, it clarifies the practice of great compassion, revealing non-attachment in benefiting others.
The preceding section has three parts:
first, seeing purity without being stained; second, beholding impurity without revulsion; third, explaining both of the preceding two together.
Within the first of these, there are two sub-sections:
First is the individual explanation, followed by the summary and conclusion beginning with "This bodhisattva.
Within the former section, there are fourteen phrases:
the first four constitute the practice for purifying the buddha-field; in every thought-moment, this constitutes uninterrupted cultivation.
Among these, first is non-attachment in contemplating the adornment of the buddha-field;
second is non-attachment in approaching the Buddha to make offerings;
third is non-attachment in the skillful cultivation of practice—meaning that the absence of any objective activity is itself non-attachment.

Fourth, the karma accomplished is non-attachment; that is, volition (*cetanā*) is the essence of karma, which, when extinguished and enters into the truth, is called "abiding in the dharma of no-thought," and this is non-attachment.
Second, the ten phrases beginning with "In every thought-moment" clarify the practice of the Dharma-body.
Among these, the first three constitute non-attachment to the Buddha Jewel;
the next two constitute non-attachment to the Dharma Jewel—the first being the place where the Dharma is heard, and the second being the actual hearing of the Dharma;

the final three constitute non-attachment to the Sangha Jewel—the first being the sight of the Sangha, the second being the sight of the Śrāvaka Sangha, and the third being the sight of the Bodhisattva Sangha.
The first eight [verses] cultivate the practice of non-attachment toward the objects of the Three Jewels;

the latter two cultivate the practice of non-attachment toward one’s own conduct: the first within the practice of gathering the Dharma, and the second within the practice of cultivating correct conduct.
The second section, the summary and conclusion, has two parts:
first, the summary of the preceding practice of the Pure Land; second, from "seeing the Buddha" onwards, the summary of the preceding practice of the Dharma-body.
The subsequent conclusion establishes the adornment, meaning that these dharmas adorn that Pure Land. This concludes the specific details to form a general whole, thereby clarifying the first phrase.

Regarding the second point, concerning non-attachment to defilement, there is only a single phrase; because pure phenomena are easily craved when pursued and difficult to relinquish, they are explained through many approaches.
Third, in the explanation, there is first a formal inquiry.
All worldly people love purity and loathe impurity; why is it that Bodhisattvas do not act in this way?
In the following explanation, first there is a general response to the question: because they contemplate that defiled and pure phenomena are quiescent and equal.

Regarding "Absence of Hatred and Attachment," the following section specifically elucidates six pairs of dharmas that are mutually dependent and mutually subsuming; since each lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one neither hates nor attaches.

In the second [section], the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), first there is a recapitulation of the preceding [stage] to introduce the subsequent one: that is, by means of the aforementioned contemplation of the wisdom of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one accordingly enters into the nature of sentient beings; because their natures are identical, one thus transforms and delivers sentient beings while remaining eternally unattached.
The following explicitly reveals the characteristics, which are sevenfold:
first, non-attachment toward those to be converted;
second, non-attachment toward the methods of conversion.
Third is non-attachment to the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*), which means that through great compassion one shares the same fruit as [the Buddha] and dwells where the Buddhas dwell;
fourth is non-attachment to the teaching of transformation, which means that because it follows the differences in local dialects, it is called "various languages" and so forth;

fifth is non-attachment to the place of transformation, which refers to the six destinies (*ṣadgati*) and so on as the dwelling places of sentient beings; furthermore, this is non-attachment to the practice of transformation, which refers to the two vehicles (*dvyāyāna*) and so on as the spheres of practice for those being transformed, and thus they are called "paths" (*mārga*).
Sixth is non-attachment regarding the basis for manifesting emanations, meaning that one relies on samādhi to perform deeds of transforming others;
seventh is non-attachment regarding wandering through buddha-fields—these involve causing wisdom to revolve perfectly and without obstruction throughout all conditioned phenomena and activities.
The second, the superior progression, has three parts:
first, accomplishing the superior practice oneself;
second, from "Having received the prediction" onwards, the gathering and transformation through great compassion; [and third, the conclusion].
III. "Non-attachment to the body" and below: Great wisdom illuminates the principle to manifest non-attachment.
In the first section, there are nine phrases:
the first is awakening to the True Teaching.

First, because one has understood the Buddha’s teaching that exhausts all principles with a mind free from attachment regarding the various Buddha-lands previously visited, it is called the "Teaching of Reality" (shijiao);
second, because one has sought the teaching and attained its essential meaning, one is unimpeded in the Way;
third, because one establishes practice based upon the teaching, it is said that "one has already established oneself in the Dharma."
Because the four causes are accomplished through practice, it is said that one "possesses the bodhisattva practices";
because the five practices are accomplished as immovable, it is said that one "abides in the bodhisattva mind";
because virtues are accomplished by relying on the mind, it is said that one "achieves tranquil liberation."
The seventh virtue is the perfection of detachment from signs, hence it is said that one does not dwell upon or cling to what is practiced;
the eighth is the entry into realization through detachment from signs, hence it is said that one abides in the pure path;
the ninth is the attainment of realization and the inclusion of the fruit, hence it is said that one receives the prediction of enlightenment.
The meaning of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is explained in detail below in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*).
Regarding the two aspects of the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), there are first:
mindfulness that sentient beings possess no merit but have faults; and second, from the passage beginning "At that time, the bodhisattva," the arousal of compassion to provide salvation.
Furthermore, the former [verse] concerns the increase of great compassion, while the latter concerns the persistence of great compassion.
Within the former, there are two parts:

first, it clarifies how one transmigrates through birth and death due to delusion and craving—namely, not knowing suffering, having no vision of cessation, being shrouded in darkness and lacking faith, and not severing the origin [of suffering].
One whose mind is not true is far removed from the Path;
this is the fault of delusion (*moha*).
To constantly engage in defilement is the fault of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Regarding "transmigration": because of the accumulation of karma through prior ignorance and craving, the fruits of suffering continue in succession.
Second, from the passage "not seeing the Buddha" onwards, it clarifies that various sufferings are experienced due to wrong views and pride.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, due to obstacles, one does not encounter true persons or the True Dharma, and thus gives rise to false views;
second, from the passage beginning "does not seek," it clarifies that due to pride, one slanders true persons and the True Dharma, entering the realm of Māra’s evil.

Among these, first is not seeking a virtuous friend; second is rejecting the hearing of the True Dharma due to fear arising from hearing about emptiness; third is slandering it because of improper reflection; and fourth is abandoning [the teachings] and practicing erroneously.
The first part clarifies how, due to this false pride (*mithyā-māna*), one clings to existence and undergoes suffering.
The second part, beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva saw," concludes that his compassionate mind has increased, such that he does not cling to his own virtues.
Within the section on being followed by great compassion, there are three parts:
first, the arising of the mind of transformation; second, the manifestation of non-attachment; and third, the accomplishment of transformative practice.

Regarding the first, the initial part generally clarifies the intention: that for the sake of many sentient beings, [the Bodhisattva] undergoes many kalpas individually, never for a moment becoming separated from them.
It does not depart even as far as the tip of a hair; this clarifies that the mind of great compassion follows sentient beings like a calf follows its mother.

Second, it specifically reveals the depth of compassion: this means that for the sake of transforming a single being, one acts in many places for many periods of time, and the same applies to many beings.
"Thought after thought without interruption" clarifies uninterrupted cultivation (*nirantara-bhāvanā*).
"In each and every minute particle there is equality" clarifies the practice of manifesting emanations; this is long-term cultivation.

Regarding the third [section], great wisdom illuminates the principle to clarify the reason for non-attachment. Within this, first ten phrases directly distinguish non-attachment, followed by the section beginning with "Why is this? which explains the underlying reasons.
In the commentary, first there is the inquiry: for what reason is the bodhisattva unattached to anything?
In the subsequent explanation, this is clarified by means of eight similes;
the first serves as a general explanation.
"By contemplating all dependently originated phenomena as the dharma-realm—neither existent nor non-existent, being like an illusion—one does not cling.
The following section sequentially dispels doubts.
A doubt arises:
"The illusory fire of the world cannot serve the function of burning.
Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world to extensively benefit sentient beings, how could he be the same as that [illusory fire]?"
The commentary states:
Just as lightning also possesses functions such as illuminating darkness, how could it be substantially existent?
Nevertheless, lightning has three meanings:
First, the meaning of sudden appearance; second, the meaning of illuminating darkness; third, the meaning of swift cessation.
Regarding the three meanings of the Buddha-fruit:
first, arising from stillness through function is the meaning of sudden appearance.
Second, the quiescence of activity itself is the meaning of "swift cessation";
third, the unimpeded and vast benefit to sentient beings through the activity of quiescence is the meaning of "illuminating darkness.
This demonstrates that the aforementioned [qualities] do not cling to the Buddha.
The third doubt says:
If the Buddha is like lightning, why do Bodhisattvas initiate practice and go forth to seek him?
If the cause is not false, how could the fruit not be real?
The commentary states:
The practices of a bodhisattva are like a dream; how could they be real?
Furthermore, a dream also possesses three meanings:
First, the meaning of being of one essence;
second, the meaning of manifest reality, because it causes the dreamer to perceive existence;
third, the meaning of functional utility, because it serves as a condition for the waking state.
It is like being startled awake from a dream because of running within it; upon looking back, there was no one who came and no running, and one realizes that one’s own body was originally unmoving.

Since a bodhisattva has not yet attained Buddhahood, they have not yet reached the ultimate awakening regarding the great dream of their own mind. Therefore, their practice also possesses three meanings:
first, emptiness because of the realization of principle; second, reality because ignorance is not yet exhausted; and third, function because of the capacity to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

This means that within the dream of ignorance, through diligent effort over many kalpas, one suddenly attains great awakening and the fruit of Buddhahood manifests before them. Looking back at the dream, they realize there was nothing actually accomplished; yet when turning toward their own fundamental nature, its inherent virtues remain perfectly intact. This is to be understood through the analogy of crossing a river in a dream, as found in the eighth bhūmi below.
By means of this explanation, the four doubts regarding non-attachment to the bodhisattva practices mentioned above are addressed:
"If the bodhisattva practices are like dreams and non-existent, why does the sutra state, 'This is a bodhisattva practice' and 'This is a practice of the two vehicles'?"
The commentary states:
"The Dharma that is heard is like an echo.
An echo also has three meanings:

First, the meaning is established through conditions such as sound and the valley; second, the meaning is without a fundamental basis; third, the meaning is expressed through verbal designation. The sacred teaching also has three aspects:

first, the sentient being’s resonance and the Buddha’s response; second, the essence itself is without a fundamental basis; third, the expression is revealed in accordance with the faculties [of beings]. Therefore, this teaching is "non-speaking speaking."
Regarding these explanations above concerning non-attachment in one's own practice, five doubts may arise:
"The fruit, practice, and so forth previously discussed can be considered narrow and thus empty; however, worldly affairs are vast, and these ought to be real."
The commentary states:
"It is like a transformation. There are also three meanings of "transformation": [insert the three meanings here].
First, it is sustained and manifested by supernatural power; second, it is not included among the category of sentient beings;

third, it serves the functions of sentient beings. The world is likewise: first, it arises as a transformation of one's own consciousness; second, its nature and characteristics lack substantial reality; third, it contains and sustains sentient beings.
This clarifies that in the preceding passage, the mind has no attachment when contemplating pure and impure lands.
A sixth doubt asks:
"If the lands are like transformations and do not truly exist, why are there distinctions between good and evil regarding their causes?"
The commentary states:
"The arising of karmic retribution is like the transformation body of Mañjuśrī.
An ancient master explained it as follows:

This is called the "repeated transformation body" (*punar-nirmāṇa-kāya*), meaning that a further transformation is produced upon a previous transformation; thus, both cause and effect are transformations.
Now, let us further question the Tripiṭaka Master:
*manomaya*, which here means "mind-born" or "mind-made," refers to the mind-born body (*manomaya-kāya*).
Because that body further gives rise to transformations, it is also called the "transformation body" (*nirmāṇakāya*).
This also has three meanings:
first, both transformations are not substantially existent; second, the two aspects appear with perfect clarity; third, there is the functional utility of producing effects and responding to causes.
The three meanings regarding karma and its fruit should be understood accordingly; therefore, it is that which both exists and does not exist.
The seventh doubt asks:
If both karma and its fruit are empty, by what means are the various types of retribution for sentient beings differentiated?
The commentary states:
"Because it is drawn by the mind.
There are also three meanings for a painted image:
First, the meaning of uniform leveling, because it is the same as the wall;
second, the meaning of having high and low, because the painter does not lose his skill;
third, the meaning of non-obstruction, because the level and the high do not obstruct one another.
Sentient beings are likewise: upon the flat wall of *tathatā* (suchness), they paint images with their minds.
First is the meaning of emptiness, because [the mind] merges into identity with suchness;
second is the meaning of existence, because karmic fruits are not lost and the mind undergoes transformation according to its habitual perfuming.
The meaning of the three non-obstructions refers to the non-obstruction between emptiness and existence.
This is the aspect of total emptiness and the aspect of manifest appearance; it reveals that nothing exists, and for this reason, the gathering and transforming of beings is not abandoned.
Because there is always nothing to be transformed, one does not become attached.
An eighth doubt asks:
"If sentient beings are thus, for what reason do Bodhisattvas respond to their capacities and preach the Dharma?"
The commentary states:

"The Dharma taught is like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)," meaning that these very words are always identical to the limit of reality; it does not mean that only silence constitutes such identity.
Thus far, the four gates have explained the sense of non-attachment within the aforementioned practice of benefiting others.
Third, regarding the absence of attachment within the practice of ultimate fulfillment, there are three parts:
first, one's own practice; second, the transformation of others; and third, the explanation of their accomplishment.
The preceding section has three parts:
first, practicing for a single thought-moment with extensive scope—this is the swiftness of time;
second, filling the ten directions—this is the extensiveness of place.
Third, it is great;
fourth, like the dharma-realm, it reveals the excellence of practice;
fifth, like space, it manifests the vastness of practice.
That is to say, by illuminating and seeing the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one accomplishes this practice that accords with that nature.
Second is the breadth of understanding, which refers to the thorough comprehension of all the skillful means (*upāya*) through which the Buddhas have realized the definitive principle.

The third section explains and establishes the preceding two to manifest non-attachment. This means that by realizing one’s own mind can pervade the worlds of the ten directions in a single, swift thought-moment, one suddenly accomplishes the practice of understanding (解行) as previously achieved;

furthermore, knowing that the nature of one’s own mind arises according to conditions yet is itself without arising, and that principle and phenomena are unimpeded such that it does not abide fixedly, it is said to be "swiftly revolving. By virtue of this, one is able to give rise to great conduct in accordance with the Dharma.

Within the second [section], the practice of benefiting others through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), there is first the preliminary practice, followed by the section beginning with "even unto" which clarifies non-attachment.
Within the former, there are five phrases:
first, seeing the superior [state] gives rise to joy;
Second, from "arousing great compassion" downward, [the text shows] that he does not grieve for himself or others;
third, from "not yet accomplished" downward, it indicates his intention for transformation—namely, to perfect the good and harmonize the evil;
fourth, from "far removed" downward, it clarifies the initiation of his transformative practices.

5. "If one hears" refers to the correct transformation (*samyak-pariṇāmana*) existing within the realm of existence (*bhava*). This is explained by ten points: first, the diversity of vocal expressions; second, the distinctness of the karma created; third, the designations and conventions of various methods; fourth, the gathering of the assembly, termed "harmony"; fifth, the divergence of destinations, termed "transmigration" (*saṃsāra*); sixth, the individuality of what is cultivated, termed "various practices" (*saṃskāra*); seventh, the distinctions in the limits of attainment, which are also the objects of focus (*ālambana*); eighth, the differences in the positions attained; ninth, the inequality of the fruits reached; and tenth, the correct transformation arising from the vow, beginning with "I shall... and so forth.
The explanation of the three pairs can be understood.
The eighth is the practice of respect (*gaurava-caryā*), which is established through five sections.
First is the explanation of the name: it is so named because the bodhisattva’s vows and practices are profound, vast, lofty, supreme, and worthy of honor.

Regarding the second, its essential nature: it takes great vows as the substance of its practice; however, because this is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 49, states: "The excellence of the wisdom of each successive stage that one aspires to is called the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*)."
Furthermore, it has as its nature the three factors of faith (*śraddhā*), aspiration (*chanda*), and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Moreover, the *Awakening of Faith* (Qixin lun) states...
[and so forth]. Regarding the three types, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* says: "Aspiration is of two kinds:"
"First, the vow to seek bodhi; second, the vow to benefit and bring happiness to others.
Alternatively, there are the four great vows and five vows as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Or there are ten vows, as explained below.
Regarding the four functions: because this great vow pervades all practices and, through its support, causes them to become sublime, these functions are called "venerable practices.
Fifth, within the "Explanation of the Text and Analysis of Characteristics," there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the practice of self-maintenance; second, from the words "That bodhisattva... onwards, the manifestation of the practice of superior progress.
The preceding section has three parts.
First, it clarifies the basis upon which conduct arises, namely the various roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
"Good" (*kuśala*) carries the meaning of being in accord with principle; "root" (*mūla*) carries the meanings of being preeminent and of growth and development.
Among these, there are nine phrases: the first is general, while the remaining eight are specific.

Within the specific section: (1) the resolve to practice is firm; (2) it eminently transcends the realm of ordinary beings; (3) its course is profound and difficult to fathom; (4) the virtues it engenders are vast and manifold; (5) having realized tranquility, it is imperturbable; (6) its practice is sublime and without peer; (7) the mind of grasping and rejecting has ceased; and (8) its extensive conduct is equal to that of a Buddha. Because it possesses all these meanings, it is called "venerable."
The second part correctly reveals the aspects of practice, which consists of four points:
first, firmness of mind, meaning the arousal of the two types of mindfulness—of aspiration and application;
second, excellence of external conditions, meaning both adverse and favorable conditions, wherein even Māra as an adverse condition can bring about the accomplishment of practice.
The three practices achieve respect, namely the two practices of purity and the alleviation of suffering;
the four vows achieve non-retrogression.
From the third section, "This Bodhisattva," onwards, it clarifies how the accomplishment of these practices brings about benefit.
"Having established oneself in the practice of reverence therein" means that the completion of this practice of one's own portion has been achieved.

From "moment by moment" (*kṣaṇe kṣaṇe*) onwards, the text correctly clarifies the two benefits; first, regarding self-benefit, there is a turning away from faults and a turning toward the increase of virtues. In principle, this actually applies to the universal increase of all practices and vows.
Regarding the manifestation through vows, it is because this constitutes the stage of the perfection of vows (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
Below, the benefit of others is clarified; by virtue of this, the Bodhisattva internally possesses actual merit, ensuring that all external seeing and hearing are not in vain.
The second, the superior progression, has three parts:

first, cultivating the practice of respect for the mind; second, based on the mind, cultivating the practice of respect for wisdom; and third, based on wisdom, cultivating the practice of respect for compassion.
The beginning and middle also consist of three parts:
first, clarifying the practice of the unimpeded mind;
second, from "The bodhisattva thus... onwards, clarifying the practice of the inexhaustible mind.
Third, from "And the bodhisattva" onwards, there is a double conclusion of the two practices.
This section has two parts:

first, based on principle, the arising of transformation clarifies the practice of non-obstruction; second, from "Among the number of sentient beings" onwards, it clarifies the practice of the unobstructed fusion of principle and phenomena.
In the beginning, middle, and end, there are the dharma, the analogy, and the application.
Question:

Since one neither proceeds toward saṃsāra nor proceeds toward nirvāṇa, one should say that one does not abide within the current of these two; why then do you speak specifically of not abiding within the current of saṃsāra?
Answer: Master Yuan’s commentary states:
“The previous ‘not tending toward the two places’ refers to being detached from existence (*bhava*).”
"Not dwelling in the middle" means being free from non-existence.

This refers to the absence of a place for birth and death, which is termed "cutting off the middle current"; because one does not dwell in this non-existence, it is called "not dwelling in the middle current."
Now, let this be further explained:

It is like a river flowing eastward, which does not abide on the southern bank nor abide on the northern bank; yet it can still be said that the flow between the banks is not severed, because there is no separate entity in the middle—it is merely designated in relation to the two banks.
If that is so, then the southern bank could also be attained; why, then, is it not said that nirvāṇa is the middle stream?
Explanation:
Because the sentient beings to be saved are on this shore, the discussion is therefore focused specifically on saṃsāra.
By approximation, that too may be obtained.
Question:
Why is there no separate "middle" apart from the shore?
Answer:

For all sentient beings, the Tathāgatagarbha, which is like water, is the far shore; the deluded mind, which is like waves, is this shore. Because the water that constitutes the waves is not in motion, the far shore is not this shore;
because the waves that constitute the water are not still, this shore is not the far shore.
For this reason, both banks exist simultaneously.
Furthermore, because water that is not moving is precisely the wave, that [water] is not the "other bank";
and because a wave that is not still is precisely the water, this [wave] is not the "this bank."
Neither this nor that is called the Middle Way.
Therefore, when Bodhisattvas abide in the middle, they never fail to conform to it; when ordinary beings and those of small capacity remain on the banks, they never fail to aspire toward the middle.
Based on this meaning, the Bodhisattva is the transformer, yet ultimately there is no transforming;
sentient beings are the transformed, yet ultimately there is no being transformed.
Contemplate this through the mutual identity of the middle and the extremes, and the unimpeded, perfect fusion of subject and object.
Within the integration of principle and phenomena, two interpretations are offered:
first, from the perspective of appearances; second, regarding reality.
Regarding the former, the initial phrase is general, applying to all things.
Regarding the section "The mind is without attachment," which specifically elucidates the middle [truth], there is first a direct exposition consisting of five pairs of ten phrases:

First, as for what was stated above regarding "non-attachment," it does not mean that one is unattached toward a single sentient being while remaining attached to all others, nor does it mean that many are detached from one; rather, it is because [the mind] is unattached to all things collectively.

Second, benefiting others by increasing their cultivation of the wholesome and transforming them to eliminate the unwholesome; this is spoken with reference to the stage of the cause where results have not yet been achieved.

Third, the arising of the fruit of perfected goodness does not occur, while the afflictive obstructions are eternally exhausted and do not cease; furthermore, the fulfillment of the fruit of merit does not arise, yet one abides in great *nirvāṇa* and does not cease; this is spoken with reference to the initial attainment of the fruit.

The four vertical [categories] all achieve the fruit; yet the realms of sentient beings are not exhausted, nor do those in the state of fruition increase. This is said in reference to what occurs after the fruit has already been attained.
Although the fifth, as previously stated, involves no increase or decrease and so forth, these transformative deeds nevertheless accomplish benefit without fail.
Although these transformative deeds are unfailing, they do not contradict what was stated before; thus, there is no duality. This concludes the preceding discussion.
The subsequent explanation has two parts; first, the inquiry:
"Since the manifestation and transformation of sentient beings involve both increase and decrease, why do you say there are no two?"
Commentary:
Because the realm of birth is identical to the dharma-realm, there is no increase or decrease in that which arises.
Since extinction and so forth are without dependence or attachment, this explains the previous statement regarding non-attachment to the one, the many, and so on.
In the subsequent explanation, first comes the inquiry:
"If they are identical with the dharma-dhātu, how can they not be non-dual? The explanation follows:
Because the *dharmadhātu* is non-dual, it causes the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) to likewise be without increase or decrease;

this is the second point. Regarding the explanation based on the ultimate reality: the first phrase reveals that the Bodhisattva’s own mind is undefiled, for wisdom characterized by attachment cannot illuminate this unimpeded Dharma;
the subsequent phrases reveal the characteristic of non-obstruction.
The first five pairs are divided into three sections;

the first two constitute one section, which integrates phenomena to make them harmonious, such that the one and the many are without obstruction. The first part provides the heading and the latter part provides the explanation.
"To place" (*zhu*) means to set; it refers to placing many sentient beings within a single sentient being, such that there is no increase in the one and no decrease in the many.
The principle of "placing one within many" may be understood by reversing the above.
As for the realm of sentient beings, it is the Tathāgatagarbha.
Because its nature is pervasive and its characteristics are harmoniously integrated, phenomena accord with principle without obstruction.

The next two [phrases] are taken as one to clarify that once the phenomena (*dharma*) are understood, their principle (*li*) arises and ceases without obstruction; this can be understood through one heading and one explanation.

The final pair concludes the preceding two, clarifying the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*dharmatā*): it is called "not empty" because while conforming to true reality (*tattva*), it does not lose its phenomenal character; and it is "non-dual" because while manifesting the characteristics of phenomena, it is immediately the truth itself.
The subsequent explanation consists of two parts:
first, explaining that phenomena are identical to principle; second, explaining how phenomena are subsumed by principle.
The *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The realm of sentient beings and the dharma-realm are non-dual and without distinction."
It is this very *dharmakāya* that, because it is defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*), transmigrates through the five destinies and is called a "sentient being" (*sattva*).
Furthermore, it is said: "The *dharmakāya* is the sentient being, and the sentient being is the *dharmakāya*; the *dharmakāya* and the sentient being are one in meaning but different in name."
Furthermore, it says: "If there were anyone who claimed that the realm of sentient beings and the dharma-realm are two distinct things, I would call such a person an icchantika.
Second, from the passage beginning "The bodhisattva thus," onwards, [the text] explains the cultivation of inexhaustible virtues based on the inexhaustible mind.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a direct exposition; second, an explanatory establishment.
In the former, there is first the arising of practice based on principle.
Later, regarding "adorned by supreme virtues," the first part reveals the excellence of merit; the section beginning with "skillfully able to discern" clarifies the profundity of wisdom.
Because it illuminates the ultimate limit of phenomena, it is called "reaching the other shore."

Second, from "thoroughly discerning" (*sarva-vibhakta*) onwards, it clarifies the universal response through external transformation. First, the bodily activity (*kāyakarman*) universally manifests; next, the mental activity (*manaskarman*) is untainted; finally, the vocal activity (*vākkarman*) provides extensive exposition.
In the second section, the establishment through explanation, there are three parts:

the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*). Regarding the principle: although one is detached from all desires within the realm of all phenomena, one does not sever the path of self-cultivation nor abandon the practice of transforming others. Therefore, by relying on quiescence to give rise to activity, the virtues of such practice are inexhaustible, causing the two types of benefit for self and others to become exceptionally sublime.
To say that "merit is inexhaustible" means that virtue is vast.
To "enter the pure dharma-realm" means that realization is profound.
The two benefits for self and others within these [phrases] can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the "three pairs of fetters," this refers to the fusion of the two preceding minds into a single practice; thus, by their mutual negation, both characteristics vanish.
Within this, there are five pairs and ten phrases:

the first pair concerns the cultivation of practice. This means that what is ultimately an unimpeded mental activity is not ultimate because it involves entering into principle while ceasing all seeking.
This is the practice of the inexhaustible mind, because the arising of virtue is infinite.

By the arising of virtue, one enters into principle; by entering into principle, one constantly gives rise to virtue. Therefore, both are negated; the following cases are all to be understood accordingly.
Second, regarding the severance of delusions: this means that by illuminating the emptiness of the nature of delusions, there is nothing to be severed or abandoned;
yet because it is distinct from the illumination of the root and its branches, it is not the case that one does not abandon them.

Third, regarding the realization of principle: this means that because principle is without marks, it is not something to be relied upon; thus, by illuminating this principle of non-reliance, it causes wisdom to become perfectly clear and bright, yet it is not the case that one does not rely upon it.

Fourth, in terms of what is accomplished: at the time of realizing the principle, because there is nothing to be discarded regarding the emptiness of defilement, it is not mundane; and because purity does not exist therein, it is not the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, there is no defilement to be loathed and no purity to be delighted in.
Fifth, regarding the stages, these are not those of ordinary beings or novices; that is to say, they are the attainment of the fruits of the two vehicles, such as the four fruits and so forth.
This concludes the first section. Second, based on the mind, one cultivates and accomplishes the practice of venerated wisdom.
Among these, the first phrase cites what precedes to introduce what follows; that is, "accomplishing the resolute mind" cites the preceding mind.
"Practicing the bodhisattva path" precisely clarifies practicing the conduct of wisdom based upon that preceding [mind].
Within this, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the wisdom that enters the principle through practice; second, from "For example, like space," onwards, the wisdom of the dual fusion of principle and practice.
In the former, first is the clarification that transformative practice is without teaching, and second is self-practice without conceptual thought.
Regarding the preceding section, the first five pairs of ten phrases clearly manifest the meaning, which can be understood;
the second part, beginning with "For what reason," provides the explanation.
Within this, "no receiving and no turning away" means there is no true Dharma to be received, and no false delusion to be turned away and extinguished.
Furthermore, because one does not admit extraneous conditions, there is no "reception" (āvedha); because right practice is firmly established, there is no "transformation" (parāvṛtti).

Moreover, regarding the aforementioned five pairs of dharmas associated with the Two Vehicles and so forth, one is able to remain without reception; regarding the principles of correct teaching that have not been explicitly taught, one is able to remain without transformation. Because one initiates practice in accordance with reason without retreat or cessation, it is called "non-retrogression" (avaivartika).
Regarding the second section, "One's Own Practice within Non-Conceptuality," there are two parts:
first, the actual exposition; second, the establishment through explanation.
As for the phrase "the practice herein is the time of quiescence," this restates what was previously mentioned.
The phrase "not dwelling on thoughts" (*bùniàn*) explicitly reveals the state of non-thought (*wúniàn*). This is identical to the effortless practice (*wúgōngyòng xíng*) of the eighth stage;

therefore, it is called non-thought. One does not allow the mind to be moved by ten factors: namely, the three periods of time, the three categories, and the three stages. Within these, that which is internal constitutes the primary retribution (*zhèngbào*), while that which is external constitutes the secondary retribution (*yībào*); thus, both types of retribution are fully present within the internal and external.
Furthermore, the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness may also be attained.
The latter one is concluded by way of its stage, for within this stage, although one cultivates great vows, there is nonetheless no conceptualization.
The subsequent explanation has two parts:

To first explain why there is no recollection (*asmṛti*): because within the equality of all phenomena, one thoroughly realizes that there is no cognitive activity capable of proceeding toward an object or achieving its realization; therefore, there is no recollection.

Regarding the subsequent explanation of why there is no "orientation" (*mukha*): because the orienting subject and the object oriented toward are non-dual, and because even this non-duality is transcended, it is said that there is "no non-duality.
Furthermore, this also serves to explain what precedes while initiating what follows: the statement that principle and practice are non-dual explains the preceding;

yet, although they are unified and without duality, the capacity [of the subject] and the object [oriented toward] remain distinct, hence it is said there is "no non-duality," which initiates the subsequent text.
Regarding the second section, "The Wisdom in Which Principle and Practice are Mutually Integrated," there are two parts:

first, the explicit clarification that principle and practice are unimpeded; second, from "This Bodhisattva" onwards, the clarification of the establishment of merit and virtue once [practice] is perfected.
The preceding section has two parts.
First, the presentation through both dharma and analogy: "without distinction" indicates that practice is identical to principle, for the aspects of practice have dissolved;
"not non-attainment," etc., clarifies that principle is identical to practice, for the efficacy of practice remains. These two constitute a single practice.

Just as in the analogy, it is not that this undifferentiated space does not exist, nor is it meant that there is some other substance; likewise, within the Dharma, it is not that this undifferentiated perfect enlightenment is not established.

This does not mean that there is no distinction between "equality" established by way of principle and "equality" established by way of practice; rather, it clarifies that non-attainment is used as the means of attainment—reflect on this.
In the subsequent explanation, first the practice of non-practice is explained, and subsequently the identity of practice and non-practice is explained.
Furthermore, the first part clarifies that principle does not contradict practice, and practice encompasses principle to achieve fulfillment;
the latter part clarifies that practice does not contradict principle, and principle merges with practice to return to quiescence.

First, I shall explain the initial meaning: although the practice that encompasses principle consists of the myriad practices, it is eternally quiescent; this is the practice of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
Among these, the first line correctly demonstrates that ultimate truth does not contradict correct practice.
The subsequent portion reveals the aspects of practice that are identical with that truth: first, the practice for one's own benefit;
second, beginning with "subduing," the practice for the benefit of others.
Not destroying cause and effect constitutes two aspects of practice: namely, because it does not obstruct existence and because it does not depend upon destruction.
The following explanation clarifies that these practices do not contradict principle; this may be understood accordingly.
Second, clarifying that "merit is perfected and virtue is established" has two parts.

First, regarding equality with the Buddhas: this means that the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have all equally accomplished these unimpeded practices, and now [the practitioner] has likewise attained them; therefore, they are equal. This is the general statement.
The following provides a detailed analysis: first, because it reveals the fundamental intrinsic awakening within, it is said that "the Buddha-nature is not severed";
second, although practice is identical to principle, its cultivation is constantly initiated, and thus it is said that "the True Dharma is not destroyed"; for these reasons, one is equal to a Buddha.
Second, regarding the ability to produce [teachings] concerning the Dharma:
the first phrase provides a general summary, while "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) and what follows provide a detailed exposition in three parts;
first, the eloquence that produces the Dharma is untainted.
Second, from "abiding securely" onwards, it clarifies the fearlessness of the wisdom that promotes the Dharma;
third, from "not abandoning" onwards, it clarifies the non-attachment of the practice that promotes the Dharma.
Regarding the third [section], which relies on wisdom to cultivate the practice of honoring compassion, herein, first, it clarifies the connection between the preceding and the subsequent sections.
"When a bodhisattva thus achieves the wisdom of veneration" refers back to the profound wisdom previously accomplished.
"Practicing the bodhisattva path" means relying on that [wisdom] to cultivate this practice of great compassion.
The second part, which correctly elucidates the middle [section], consists of two sections:

first, a general statement on the intent of the practice of compassion, which means first transforming beings to emerge from obstacles through the maturation of their education, and subsequently transforming them to abide in the Path.
Furthermore, the former [instruction] causes one to emerge from evil calamities, thereby attaining the benefit of human and celestial realms;
the latter causes one to emerge from birth and death, thereby attaining the benefit of liberation.
Second, from the passage "Thus instructing" onwards, the compassionate practice is manifested by examining the mind through its actual effects.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, clarifying that the mind has no other seeking; second, from "merely wishing to subdue" onwards, clarifying that it is solely for the benefit of others.
Regarding the former, there is first a direct exposition, followed by an explanation.
Regarding the preceding section, first come the evil persons and later the virtuous persons.
