The speech emerging from the Ground of Clarity (Prabhākari-bhūmi) is not to be grasped as having the nature of mere sound.
It is not that there is no ground-knowledge of the bodies of phrases, names, and syllables; rather, this accords with the third alternative, manifesting that meaning is not non-existent.
It is not that there is no wisdom regarding the stages (*bhūmi*), for there are dharmas that are expressed and free from signs.
It is not that there are no names, phrases, or syllables, for there is the teaching that expresses them.
Why, then, is it said that there is this teaching?
Because he intends to proclaim it.
Why is it said that the stages (*bhūmi*) are devoid of characteristics?
It is so that they are not grasped according to the literal expression.
For what reason have I spoken this again?
You should not grasp the meaning merely according to the sound of the words.
This is the principle of the treatise; it is spoken as the words of Vajragarbha to admonish the assembly to remain free from attachment.
Among the five faults, the first two are faults of contradicting practice; the next two are faults of contradicting the person; and the last one is a fault of contradicting the Dharma.
This means that although the meaning of what was said does not exist at all, one claims it truly exists; therefore, it is not right faith.
Second, being unable to rouse the mind to abandon appearances and seek reality is called "retreating from valor.
Third, although the nature of phenomena is not thus, one proclaims to others that the Dharma is exactly so; therefore, it is said to be "deceiving others."
Since these four statements were spoken by the Buddha, to say otherwise is to slander the Buddha.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s intention lies precisely in the meaning of transcending words; yet you claim that the Buddha’s wisdom takes the grasped marks as its object, and thus you also slander him.
The fifth refers to the Dharma being shallow and superficial, similar to worldly matters of conventional designation; therefore, it is said that the Dharma is treated lightly.
Furthermore, the purport of the Buddha’s teaching indicates meanings that transcend verbal expression, enabling all sentient beings to transcend the mundane and become sages.
If we now accept what they say at face value, it is merely worldly discourse; it cannot cause people to transcend the mundane and attain the sacred.
Thus, the transgression of slighting the Dharma is indeed grave.
The extensive explanation of the meaning is concluded.
From here below is the second section, which clarifies the extensiveness of its exposition.
This consists of six verses divided into five parts:
The first verse has three lines clarifying the scope of what is taught;
the second has three lines demonstrating that [the author] is free from fault and admonishing the assembly to eliminate deficiencies;
the third consists of one and a half verses revealing that what is taught is concise rather than extensive.
The fourth section consists of one verse which exhorts the assembly to listen with respect, thereby manifesting that [the teaching] has been well-spoken;
the fifth section consists of one verse which demonstrates that [the Buddha] has attained power, in order to inspire faith in sentient beings.
Within the former [section], the first phrase is a general statement.
Regarding the phrase "although this matter is difficult," "this matter" refers to the aforementioned point concerning the great nature of the dharmas.
"Although" (*sui*) is an indefinite term;
it means that while these dharmas of this stage consist of two parts, and although the resultant part (*phala-bhāga*) cannot be described, the causal part (*hetu-bhāga*) can be described.
Therefore, the treatise on the sūtra states: "I have spoken only of one part," meaning that the causal portion is one part in relation to the fruit.
Regarding the meaning of these two parts, various explanations differ.
Some say that the teaching which expresses [the meaning] constitutes the causal portion, while the meaning expressed constitutes the resultant portion.
This explanation is quite superficial.
Some say: "The causal practices prior to the stages (bhūmi) constitute the causal portion, while the realized wisdom from the stages onward constitutes the resultant portion.
But does this chapter not speak of the dharmas prior to the stages?
Therefore, one knows that this is not the case.

If one were to take the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of the various stages as the cause and the actual realization (*samyag-adhigama*) as the fruit, this would also hold true to a limited extent. Some say:

The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) have two aspects: first, from the perspective of gradual increase, they are termed the "causal aspect" (*hetubhāga*); in this sense, the ten stages can be described because they possess distinct limits, just as the waxing moon can be described in terms of its differences.

Second, from the perspective of the time of perfection, they are termed the "fruition aspect" (*phalabhāga*); in this sense, the ten stages are indescribable because they lack distinct limits, just as there is no differentiation when the moon is full.
Therefore, these twenty stages have no difference in their essential nature; they are merely provisionally established as two divisions based on the degree of partial fulfillment versus completion.

This, however, is not yet correct. How could it be that the stage of Joy (*pramuditā*) can be described even before reaching the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), while it cannot be described until the ten [perfections] are fully realized?

If it were the case that the preceding serves as the cause for the arising of the succeeding, and the succeeding arises in dependence upon the preceding as its effect, this might be partially acceptable; yet it still does not accord with the intended meaning of the text. Some say:

"The ten stages (daśabhūmi) have two aspects: first, the dharma-gate of the ten stages established by the teaching, which appears as if it were an external object upon the consciousness of the listener, and is termed the 'causal portion' (*hetubhāga*), because it indicates that ultimate meaning which transcends words."

Second, the entry into the correct practice of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) through the transcendence of all verbal designations is called the "resultant portion" (*phalāṃśa*), because it is that which is manifested by the causal portion (*hetvaṃśa*).
Therefore, while the causal aspect (*hetu-bhāga*) can be explained, the resultant aspect (*phala-bhāga*) cannot.
This explanation accords slightly with the literal meaning of the text, yet it is still not entirely correct.
My current interpretation consists of two levels:

First, these ten stages have two parts: first, the ten stages in their ultimate reality, which are known only by a Buddha and traversed only by a Buddha’s wisdom; this is called the "fruition part" (*phala-bhāga*).
As the aforementioned treatise states: "By whom is this wisdom realized?"
The verse states: "Because it is the sphere of activity of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Furthermore, the preceding text says: "Wisdom arises as the Buddha’s realm.

Additionally, in the section on the "Additional Merits" (*guṇavibhāga*), it speaks of the inconceivable Buddha-dharma; and as with the tracks of birds, which depend upon the great void, [the Buddha's qualities] constitute the ocean of fruition.
The ten stages (bhūmi) according to their secondary characteristics, which are what the bodhisattva knows and what the bodhisattva practices, are called the causal portion (hetubhāga).

This is precisely the fruit portion (phalabhāga), which is profoundly transcendent and ultimately ineffable; however, the causal portion can be explained by way of accommodation to the capacities of sentient beings.
This meaning applies to the general purport throughout this entire section of the sutra.
Question:
If that is so, can the realized wisdom of a bodhisattva be described?
Answer: It refers to what is taught as the fulfillment of cultivation within the practice, and so forth.
Regarding the two terms, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) have two divisions:

First, with respect to wondrous wisdom: because the wisdom of direct realization is identical to its object, and because it is free from characteristics and free from verbal expression, it is termed the "resultant portion" (*phalāṃśa*). It is thus ineffable, just as the tracks of a bird in the sky are identical to space and cannot be described.

Second, regarding the skillful means (*upāya*), the distinctions between the stages (*bhūmi*) are manifested by relying on the dharmas, as in the subsequent text where the first three stages are identical to the mundane world, while the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages are identical to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and so forth.

Furthermore, by relying on the factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*), the categories of the path (*mārgapada*), the truths (*satya*), and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to reveal the distinctions between the stages (*bhūmi*), it causes sentient beings to understand the meaning of the stages through these means; therefore, it is called the "causal portion" (*hetubhāga*). This is like the tracks in the sky: when distinguished according to the bird, they are called the causal portion, but since they are equally non-different from the sky itself, they are called the resultant portion (*phalabhāga*).
The single trace encompasses both [aspects], and thus it is divided into two parts.
Question:
Since the traces of both the bird and the sky are devoid of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), why is there that which can be spoken of and that which cannot be spoken of?
Answer: Although the tracks are devoid of characteristics, they are described in terms of the bird;
yet, in being described in terms of the bird, that which is described remains eternally detached [from characteristics].
The traces are identical to empty space, and their principle is ineffable; by analogy, the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi*) can be understood in this same way.
This explanation is restricted to the present "Chapter on the Stages," which is why it says: "Although it is difficult [to explain], it is nonetheless but one part."
This is the general statement.
Below, there are six phrases that specifically elucidate the three greatnesses (*mahattva*):

the first phrase clarifies the greatness of the accomplishment of the cause; the next phrase clarifies the greatness of the gradual accomplishment of the cause; and the remaining four phrases clarify the greatness of the accomplishment of cultivation through the teaching and exposition.
To explain these three greatnesses, we shall briefly establish four sections.
First, regarding the explanation of their names: the compassionate vow permeating the mind serves as the foundation for initiating practice; thus, it is called "accomplishment of the cause.
Because it is extracted from within the discourse on the [three] greatnesses, it is designated as "greatness" (*mahat*).
Second, because hearing, reflection, and cultivation can sequentially give rise to supramundane realized wisdom, it is called the gradual accomplishment of the cause.
Third, because true wisdom realizes the ultimate reality which cannot be directly pointed out, but is manifested through the provisional use of words, the teaching speaks of cultivation.
Question:
Since these three all emerge from within the "Exposition of the Great," why are the first two not called "Teachings"?
Furthermore, since they all emerge from within the "Section on Causes," why is the last one not called a "Cause"?
Answer: Because the capacities produced by the former two manifest in the latter, they are both designated as "causes.
However, since their essence is not profound or subtle, there is no need for verbal qualification, nor are they termed "teachings" (śāsana).

The latter, the wisdom of realization, is profound and subtle; as it might be confused with the stage of fruition, it is distinguished by means of words, being described as "cultivation" through verbal teaching.
Second, defining it according to its locus, there are two parts:
first, concerning the provisional locus.
It is metaphorically established as being present in the stage of the lineage prior to the grounds (*pṛthagjanabhūmi-gotra-avasthā*), because its seeds as causes have been accomplished.

It is gradually metaphorically established as being present in the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-avasthā*), because one initiates practices such as hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*) in order to proceed toward the realization of truth.
It is said that cultivation is situated from the first bhūmi upward, because wisdom realizes the truth.
Second, regarding the actual stages:

these three all reside on the bhūmis; however, prior to the first bhūmi, during the cultivation of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), compassion, vows, and so forth are termed "accomplishment through causes," while hearing, reflection, and cultivation are termed "gradual progress through causes. Once the direct realization has been attained, it is termed "cultivation through the teaching."
Third, regarding the determination based on the text: within the sections explained below, these three are present throughout all the stages (*bhūmi*).
Why is this? For instance, by what cause does a bodhisattva seek this wisdom?
There are two causes:
first, to save sentient beings; second, to seek bodhi.
Because one seeks bodhi above and saves sentient beings below, one is called a Bodhisattva; thus it is said, "the vow of compassion."
Since these two internally possess this cause and one seeks to advance toward the various stages (*bhūmi*), what is the gradual sequence?
It is said that by practicing and studying the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*), one gradually enters the various stages.
These two are both contained within the wisdom of preparatory application (*prayoga-jñāna*).
Once the wisdom of application (prayoga-jñāna) has concluded, one must necessarily manifest conformity with ultimate reality.
The first two aspects are coarse and can be directly presented; therefore, they are not entrusted to other phenomena.
The essence of the stage of realized wisdom (sākṣātkāra-jñāna-bhūmi) cannot be directly shown, and thus it is entrusted to distinct phenomena.
This is used for manifest expression.

For example, as it is taught that the ten wholesome actions and so forth are explained in the main stage of the second bhūmi; the four dhyānas and so forth are explained in the main stage of the third bhūmi; and the factors of the path (mārga-pakṣa-dharma) and so forth are explained in the main stage of the fourth bhūmi—all such teachings constitute the cultivation and integration [of practice].
Regarding the fourfold explanation of the text: the first phrase, "compassion," refers to the practice of benefiting others, while "arousing the vow" refers to the practice of benefiting oneself.
The explanation of these two passages should be understood as presented in the treatise.

Regarding "attainment through gradual development," as the verse states, "gradually fulfilling all the stages," this means that the three types of wisdom arise in succession to produce supramundane knowledge; because they are the causes for that [knowledge], it is called "fulfilling all the stages."
Regarding the teaching on cultivation, there are two types:

cultivation for fulfillment refers to the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*), which can only serve as causes for supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*) but cannot fulfill that stage of knowledge (*jñāna-bhūmi*). It is only through the supramundane pure mind that one can fulfill it; therefore, it is said to be "attainable by the wise."
The following clarifies the practice of contemplative cultivation. Within this, the phrase "those who practice these stages" refers to the practitioners of the stages (*bhūmi*).
The expression "subtle and extremely difficult to see" clarifies that the object of contemplation cannot be perceived by any other state of mind.
"That which cannot be known by the mind" means it cannot be known by a defiled mind; as the treatise states, "It can be known through the purity of one's own mind.
Herein, cultivation for fulfillment relies upon fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while contemplative cultivation pertains to subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Conversely, when observing internally, both are inexpressible; therefore, this is called "cultivation as taught by the scriptures.
The following three phrases constitute the second section, which clarifies that [the teaching] has been well-expounded and exhorts the assembly to eliminate faults.
First, it is shown that he is already free from two faults:
first, being free from the fault of the Buddha not rejoicing [in his teaching], as indicated by the statement, "one should speak by relying on the Buddha's power";
second, being free from the fault of speaking with partiality, as indicated by the statement, "all listen."
Second, he admonishes the assembly to avoid two faults:
first, a lack of respect toward the speaker.
To eliminate this error, he says, "You all should show reverence."
Second, regarding disputes over the Dharma:
because one is free from these faults, it is said that "all listen with a single mind.
From here on, for one and a half verses, the third point clarifies that what is taught is concise rather than extensive.
The first two phrases cite the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*); because these are what wisdom penetrates, they are called "conformable.
Since this wisdom enters into the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of those various stages, it is called "the practice of the mutual entry of the characteristics of the stages."
The treatise states: "Regarding 'cultivation according to practice,' this refers to entering through the cultivation of preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Regarding 'fulfillment of cultivation according to practice,' because one enters realization through preparatory application and accords with the principle in its perfection, it is called 'entry through the full appropriation according to reality.'"
The practice of entering this wisdom is immeasurable and boundless; therefore, it is said that even if one were to explain it for immeasurable billions of kalpas, one could never exhaust it.
That which is now briefly explained is the essential summary, and thus it is called "according to reality."
Although this is a brief exposition, it fully encompasses the extensive meaning; therefore, it is said that "its meaning is without remainder.
From the following verse on, the fourth section exhorts the assembly to listen with respect, demonstrating the excellence of his own teaching.
Regarding "waiting with single-minded reverence," there are two aspects:
first, physical reverence.
"Abiding in majestic deportment" explains this reverence.
"One who is capable of receiving the teaching" explains "waiting for.
Second, there is "reverence of mind.
Because one requests a resolution and seeks the Dharma with a determined intent, it is said that "the mind is resolved as intended"; this explains "reverence of mind."
"Capable of recollecting and maintaining" explains "maintaining.
The former refers to being able to receive [the teaching] through physical reverence; this refers to being able to maintain it through mental respect.
The statement that he now speaks by the power of the Buddha serves to show that it is not by his own power, thereby eliminating any conceit of superiority (*adhimāna*).
The second half clarifies that which is taught: "By what means" refers to the proclamation through celestial sounds;
"What is the subject matter" refers to the presentation of reasons and examples;
and "In reliance upon what" refers to relying on virtuous syllables, as they do not contradict the meaning.
As for what is manifested: it is the manifestation of the meaning of the stages (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, another explanation states:
the great voice proclaims the cause by means of analogies, speaking in accordance with the principle of logical proof (*upapattisādhana-yukti*).
The meaning is called "non-contradiction," as it is explained according to the principle of the nature of things (*dharmatā-yukti*);
this may be understood.
In the treatise, the word "skillful" (*kuśala*) is a term for "expertise," and thus it possesses two meanings:
First, skillfulness in matching the voices of others; second, the thoroughness with which meaning is expressed—these should be understood as explained in the treatise.
From here on, the following verse is the fifth [section], which manifests the attainment of power by oneself, thereby inspiring faith in sentient beings.
The first two lines clarify that although the vast and manifold collection of the buddhas' spiritual powers has been gathered within my own body;
the latter two lines show that what I have now manifested is but a single drop from an ocean, while that which remains unspoken is like the great ocean itself.
How much more so, lacking the power of the Buddha, could one not even explain a single drop?
Thus concludes the preceding section on the Request.
Below this begins the seventh section, clarifying the Exposition, which is divided into four gates.
First, regarding the explanation of the title: it is called the "Section on Exposition" (*vibhāga*) because it elaborates upon and proclaims the distinctions between the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Second, regarding the intent of its inclusion: since the request for fulfillment has already been made and Vajragarbha has informed the assembly that he intends to explain one portion, this section follows to formally expound the dharmas of the stages.

Regarding the meaning of the threefold explanation: in the previous section on the "Request for the Ground," the essence of the ground (*bhūmi-tattva*) was already explained to enable those of superior capacity to awaken to and understand its profound principle.

Now, by discerning the characteristics of the ground (*bhūmi-lakṣaṇa*), those of middling and inferior capacities are enabled to achieve understanding in accordance with these characteristics; therefore, it is explained clearly.

Furthermore, while the preceding section has briefly demonstrated how to generate correct understanding, this section now extensively sets forth how to initiate practical cultivation; therefore, it is explained in detail.
Regarding the fourfold explanation of the text, the exposition of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is divided into ten sections.
Regarding the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), there are briefly seven sections:

first, the explanation of the name; second, the purpose of its inclusion; third, the abandonment of hindrances; fourth, the realization of principle; fifth, the accomplishment of practice; sixth, the attainment of the fruit; and seventh, the commentary on the text.

First, regarding the explanation of the names: only the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states: "The first is the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); because for the first time one attains the nature of the noble ones (*āryatva*), fully realizes the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), and is able to benefit oneself and others, giving rise to great joy."
The commentary explains:

There are three meanings here—first, attaining the stage; second, realizing the principle; and third, accomplishing the practice. Since all of these are obtained for the first time, one gives rise to joy.

Because the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains the meaning of "accomplishing practice" solely based on the third [stage], both Asvabhāva and Vasubandhu state in their respective seventh fascicles: "Because, by means of this, one first attains the superior capacity to accomplish the welfare of oneself and others."

This means that when a bodhisattva enters the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they attain the supreme capacity to accomplish the welfare of both themselves and others, giving rise to extreme joy.

This is not the case for śrāvakas and others who enter clear realization; they attain only the capacity to accomplish their own welfare and do not give rise to such joy. Therefore, that stage is not called the "Extremely Joyful Ground" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
According to the *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra*, this is explained solely in terms of realizing the principle.
That treatise states: "Having first attained the flavor of the Dharma, one gives rise to great joy.
According to the seventy-eighth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the fourth chapter of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, it is explained by means of two meanings.
He says: "Because one accomplishes the great purpose, attains the unprecedented supramundane mind, and gives rise to great joy.
The commentary explains:
"Great purpose" refers to the accomplishment of the practices for the dual benefit [of self and others].

The supramundane mind is the attainment of the noble stage (*āryabhūmi*); this is equivalent to the "attainment of the two practices" and the "attainment of the noble stage" as explained in the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*, as interpreted in the section on the fundamental divisions (*maulabhāga*).
The remaining meanings are as explained below in the "Analysis of Names.
Second, regarding the sequence: for what reason is this stage elucidated first?

It is because the power of the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) prior to the stage gives rise, without interval, to the innate (*prakṛti*) uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) capacity, causing it to manifest in actuality.
At the outset, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) realizes and perceives the true reality (*tattva*), thereby extinguishing delusions and establishing practice; therefore, this is explained first.

Regarding the three things to be abandoned, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle nine, states: "First is the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*). This refers to that which arises from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) within the two obstacles, because the nature of an ordinary person is established based upon those seeds."
When the path of seeing of the two vehicles manifests, one attains the nature of an noble being by severing only one type [of affliction];
when the path of seeing of a bodhisattva manifests, one attains the nature of an noble being by severing both types.
The commentary explains:
"Ordinary beings" (pṛthagjana) are so called because they arise by adhering to divergent views; this is the old term for "worldlings.
"Nature" (prakṛti) refers to the two obstacles of conceptual discrimination.

A non-associated dharma is provisionally established upon those seeds; because this nature is established based upon those seeds, those seeds themselves are called the "obstruction of the state of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*).
This is the obstruction of an ordinary person, analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.

The *Mahāyāna-saṃgraha* (Liang-lun) names this "the nature of ordinary beings' ignorance," while the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Shi-di-lun) names it "the obstacle of the ordinary being's mark of self.
The commentary explains:
since both refer to the mark of self (*ātma-nimitta*) as a general term for the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*), there is no contradiction between them.

Furthermore, although this state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is established on the basis of seeds, the manifest conceptualization prior to the Path of Seeing is also subsumed under this obstruction; thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that "the delusion of clinging to self and phenomena" is precisely this obstruction. Therefore, it is known that this obstruction extends to both the manifest and the latent.
Question:
If the two obstacles are analyzed as having both manifest and seed forms as their essence, why are the two delusions only manifest and not seeds? Answer:
Because the hindrances are broad and ignorance is narrow, they do not contradict one another.

Furthermore, although this state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) encompasses both the fundamental and derivative afflictions, as well as their manifest and latent seeds, it is nonetheless induced by clinging; therefore, greed, hatred, and so forth are subsumed under the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).
Question:

Since the state of a noble one (*ārya*) is the opposite of that of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), why is the nature of a noble one in the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) established solely on the basis of seeds (*bīja*)? Answer:
Because their manifestation is intermittent, they do not constitute the nature of an ārya.
Question:
If that is so, since the seeds of uncontaminated innate knowledge (*dharmatā-jñāna*) already exist prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), why is the nature of an ārya not established for them?
Answer: Because there would be the fault of the two natures—ordinary and noble—existing simultaneously in contradiction with one another.

Although the seeds exist, they do not constitute the noble nature; for example, when the "subtle-subtle" mind is provisionally established based on the seeds of the cessation of mind (nirodhasamāpatti), although those seeds are present, it is not the cessation attainment itself, because the meanings of "having mind" and "being without mind" are mutually contradictory.
This case is the same as that.
Furthermore, it is explained:

because those uncontaminated seeds do not yet exist prior to the stages of the path (bhūmi), one does not possess the nature of an Ārya; for the existence of innate seeds (dharmatā-bīja) is not admitted [in this system].
Question:

Since the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) is subsumed under the category of non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), and since the nature of an noble one (*āryatva*) is the opposite of that of an ordinary being, why is it not established as a non-associated formation? Answer:

According to the Mahāyāna school, the noble nature (*āryatva*) is also subsumed under the category of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*); specifically, it is that which is among the twenty-four [factors], namely non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
This is because the Mahāyāna school allows this to be untainted (*anāsrava*), unlike the Hīnayāna school, for which it is not untainted.
Another explanation:

Because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are inferior, the dissociated [factors] are established separately; because the power of the Noble Ones (*ārya*) is superior, they are not established separately—thus there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Although [these factors] are abandoned at the first stage (*bhūmi*), they actually pertain to both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*)."

Furthermore, regarding the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), the mental apprehension of the objects of knowledge is obstructed; thus, it is said that the ten types of ignorance are non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*). Therefore, ignorance itself constitutes the delusion (*moha*) belonging to the category of the ten obstructions.
The foregoing has been explained by way of the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*).

In reality, the first bhūmi also eliminates the karmic fruits and so forth of the miserable destinies; therefore, it is necessary to state that it completely abandons two types of delusion along with their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*):
first, the delusion of clinging to a self and phenomena, which is the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva-vibandha*);

second, the delusion of the afflictions of the miserable destinies, which refers to the various karmas and fruits of those destinies. It should be understood that these categories of delusion are collectively termed "delusion."
The commentary explains:

This clarifies that the two aforementioned delusions are not merely ignorance (*avidyā*). The delusion present at the time of grasping at a self and phenomena, along with the factors arising simultaneously with it, are designated as the first delusion.

Regarding the category of delusion, the karma and its fruits of the miserable realms—though their essential nature is not itself delusion—are collectively termed "delusion" because they are the karma issued forth by delusion and the fruits it has induced.

That treatise further states: "The ignorance that arises simultaneously with both the sharp and dull categories of hindrances constitutes two types of delusion. Specifically, the ignorance that arises at the same time as the sharp category of the five views is called the first delusion; that which arises simultaneously with the dull category of greed and so forth is called the latter delusion."
Regarding the term "dysfunction" (*dausthulya*), that treatise provides two explanations.

The treatise states: "The mention of 'dysfunction' here indicates either those two types [of afflictions and secondary afflictions] themselves, or the unserviceability (*akarmanyatā*) arising from those two."
The commentary explains:
This first interpretation identifies the *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness) as the seeds of the two delusions (*moha*).
It is called "coarse" because it is evil, and "heavy" because it denotes a state of sinking; thus, we know that the two delusions refer exclusively to their active manifestations (*samudācāra*).

The subsequent explanation states that these two types of delusion induce a state of non-pliability within body and mind; because they are coarse and further heavy, they are termed "coarse heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya*), which is neither manifest nor a seed.
According to this principle, these two delusions also include their seeds. Furthermore, according to the analysis:
these two delusions may be divided into three, namely: affliction (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and retribution (*vipāka*).
Alternatively, they may be divided into four by adding *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness);
or they may be divided into five, because within the afflictions (*kleśa*), two types of obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) are distinguished.
All of these are what is excluded in this context.
Generally speaking, there are three types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*):

first, abandonment by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*), which refers to the permanent severance of the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and their associated mental states (*citta-caitta*), as well as all defiled phenomena—whether unwholesome (*akuśala*) or obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*)—that arise through the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Among these, the mind-king (the universal mind), the universal mental factors, and the specific-object mental factors are not defiled and are not dharmas subject to abandonment; yet, because they are associated with afflictions, they are termed "associated bonds. Furthermore, because the afflictions are abandoned, they are also said to be abandoned.

Second is abandonment through detachment from bondage (*visaṃyoga-prahāṇa*). This refers to wholesome states associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) and non-obscured neutral states (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) pertaining to both form and mind, which do not directly oppose the Path and whose nature is not inherently abandonable; they are said to be abandoned because the afflictions that take them as objects within the six consciousnesses are abandoned.

Third is non-arising abandonment: this means that once the afflictions of views have been abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one relinquishes the body of an outsider; since the basis for rebirth no longer exists, both the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) and the retribution of non-conception (*asaṃjñivipāka*) will never arise again.
Furthermore, the total retributive karma that draws one toward the three evil realms is entirely non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is also termed "non-arising" (*anutpāda*).
The retribution of the three evil realms, the absence of sexual organs, the presence of two sexual organs, birth in Uttarakuru, and so forth, are likewise all cases of non-arising.
In the case of animals and hungry ghosts, there is no basis for the fruits of distinct retributive good karma, nor do they arise.
This explanation above has been given according to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*).

If one speaks according to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-śāsana*), even at the first stage (*bhūmi*) one abandons the segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*) of the triple world along with its afflictions, karma, and suffering; from the stages onward, one only severs the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the transformational retribution (*nirmāṇa-vaipākika-vedanīya*).
Regarding the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), they are gradually suppressed prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*) and completely severed at the first stage.

Regarding the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one also trains in suppressing them prior to the stages; a portion is severed at the first stage, while the remainder is severed portion by portion throughout the subsequent stages, being exhausted only at the stage of Buddhahood.
This is as explained in the Liang dynasty treatises, the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, and other works.
Regarding the fourth, the "object realized," it refers to the meaning of the dharmadhātu-tathatā as being universally pervasive (*sarvatraga*).

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "First is the universally pervasive tathatā; this means that this tathatā is revealed by the two kinds of emptiness, and there is not a single dharma that does not abide within it."
The commentary explains:
"Formations" refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is revealed by the emptiness of both self and phenomena, pervades all conditioned formations; therefore, it is called "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*).
In the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty, it is termed "pervasive" (*vyāpin*), because it pervades all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Vasubandhu’s *She lun*, in its seventh fascicle, states: "Because there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is not selfless, it is called 'all-pervading' (*sarvatraga*)."
The seventh fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* also states: "Because there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is not empty, it is called 'pervasive' (*sarvatraga*).
In reality, the two kinds of emptiness extend through the other nine stages; however, because they are first realized at this initial stage, it is so named.
There are briefly four types of practice accomplished through cultivation (*bhāvanā-sādhyā-caryā*):

first, the practice of giving accomplished through cultivation by way of its preeminence; second, the arising of the ten great vows based on what has been accomplished; third, the ten practices such as faith and so forth, which refer to that which is accomplished through cultivation; and fourth, the practice of actualization, which refers to the cultivation of all practices without exception, such as the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*).
The remaining practices to be cultivated are evident from the explanation of the text itself.
Regarding the sixth point, the fruits obtained, there are briefly four kinds:
first, the attainment of the four fruits, such as pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) at the time of completion in that particular stage, which should be understood as explained below.
Second, one attains the fruits such as great wealth produced by the perfection of the practice of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Third, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, one penetrates the meaning of the emptiness of obstacles and attains the fruit of the extinction of all obstacles.

The fourfold penetration attains the wisdom and insight (*jñāna*) of the three natures and the three absences of nature within the consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) doctrine, as well as the fruits of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
The remainder is as explained in the text.
Regarding the seventh section, the explanation of the text, there are two distinct parts within this stage:
first, the prose (long-form), and second, the verse (stotra).
Within the former, there are four sections:

First, the section on the initial abiding stage; second, the section explaining the names of the stages; third, the section on abiding securely in the stages; fourth, the section on the comparative excellence [of the stages].
Within the first section, the author of the treatise divides it into four parts:
first, "by means of what body," which refers to the body as a basis consisting of the thickly accumulated roots of goodness;
Second, as for its purpose: it is to seek the fruit of Buddhahood.
Third, as for its cause: it takes great compassion as its cause. Fourth, as for its characteristics:
its characteristic is to transcend the state of an ordinary person and attain the state of a sage.
Each of these four [points] is individually analyzed through ten gates, which is termed "the bodhisattva’s initial abiding in the first stage.

Furthermore, these four meanings correspond to the four characteristics of the bodhisattva’s production of the mind (*cittotpāda*) within the "Abiding" chapter (Chapter 48) of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, specifically regarding the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*); while the texts are identical, the phrasing differs slightly, and their correspondence can be understood by reflecting on their meaning.

He asked: "First, what are the characteristics of a bodhisattva’s generation of the mind? Second, upon what does the generation of the mind focus? Third, what are the manifestations and signs of the generation of the mind? Fourth, what are the benefits of the generation of the mind?"
That treatise, relying on this scriptural passage, provides a brief commentary that is not exhaustive.
Regarding the first [section], "Based upon what body," there are three parts:

first, a summary recapitulation; second, the actual manifestation of the characteristics of practice; and third, from the words "Such sentient beings" onwards, the conclusion regarding entering the stage through practice.

Within the explicit exposition of the practice, the first phrase is general; it refers to the accumulation of superior roots of goodness over one great *kalpa*, hence it is called "thickly accumulated.
As for "if there are sentient beings," these are sentient beings who have newly entered the stages (*bhūmi*), not those prior to the stages.

Some judge that these ten phrases belong to the stage of generating the mind prior to the first bhūmi, only entering the first bhūmi thereafter; this does not accord with the text. How could that which belongs to the stage prior to the bhūmis be subsumed under the first bhūmi?
Since this passage explains the first stage (*bhūmi*) and does not mention the stages prior to it,
one should understand that this refers to the location of the first dwelling (*vihāra*), wherein the characteristics of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) upon which it relies are described.
Within the separate analysis, this accumulation consists of nine types:
first, the accumulation of practice, which constitutes the retinue of wholesome deeds.

For one who upholds the precepts, wisdom is the primary factor, while the precepts serve as its accompanying support; thus they are called a "retinue. As the Sūtra states, "by cultivating various wholesome practices," it means that the three clusters [of training] are not singular, hence the term "various wholesome practices."

Second is the accumulation of meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃbhāra*), which refers to concentration that assists the path of wisdom; it is called the "concentration with well-perfected retinue.
As the Sūtra says: "Because of having well accumulated the factors that assist the path."

Third is the accumulation through association, which refers to associating with the Buddhas, making offerings and showing them respect, and cultivating the wisdom of hearing; as the sutra says, "Because of making offerings to the Buddhas."

The fourth is "accumulation" (*saṃbhāra*), which refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) that is well able to deliberate upon and accumulate the various perfections (*pāramitā*); thus it is called "accumulation. As the sutra states, "because of gathering all pure and white dharmas," the six perfections counteract defilements and are therefore termed "pure and white."

The fifth is the collection of protection (*ārakṣā-saṃbhāra*): this refers to the practice of wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) which, by following virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), serves as a means of gathering and protecting [the practitioner].
Because one is able to enter into the supramundane true realization through cultivation, it is called the "cultivation of actual realization" (*bhāvanā-satyābhisamaya*).
Because one practices and realizes [the truth], and because one is instructed, guided, and protected by those virtuous friends, it is said that "one is protected by spiritual friends.
Sixth is "extensive gathering," which means extensively benefiting all sentient beings through a mind of profound compassion.
Seventh is the assembly of the mind of faith, which refers to the resolute faith, delight, and seeking of the Great Dharma.

Eighth is the present assembly, which refers to the fact that according to the accumulation of roots of goodness, one directs them mostly toward benefiting others; thus it is said that the mind is largely directed toward compassion.

Among these, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is based on the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) because the practice of loving-kindness is coarse;
compassion (*karuṇā*) is based on the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) because it is understood as being subtle.
Question:
The preceding text stated that loving-kindness bestows happiness and compassion removes suffering; why, then, is this different?
Answer: These two have both general and specific aspects.

The distinctions are as previously explained. Regarding the general discussion of bestowing happiness (*sukha*) together [with compassion], it is as described in the third stage: when compassion is "vast," "immeasurable," and "limitless," it bestows happiness. Specifically, "vast" refers to bestowing the happiness of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); "great" refers to bestowing the joy and happiness common to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); and "immeasurable" refers to bestowing the joy and happiness not common to the form realm. The same applies to pity (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); thus, one should know that they all equally bestow happiness.
Furthermore, as in the case of the third stage, one enters into compassion for the sake of suffering sentient beings; thus, it is known that they share the same extraction of suffering.
This passage is also like this, and therefore their sameness is known.

The ninth is the seeking of accumulation (*saṃbhāra-paryeṣaṇā*), which refers to seeking the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) for the sake of sentient beings; thus it is said, "eagerly seeking the Buddha’s wisdom.
According to the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*, this phrase is subsumed within the eighth stage, the concentration of faith (*śraddhā-saṃbhāra*).
There is a separate sixth collection, the pure mind, which refers to the supramundane mind of true realization that is free from defilement; thus it is called "wholesome" because it is a pure mind.

Furthermore, among these nine, the first five protect against the activity of afflictions, namely: first, the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*); second, the training in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The remaining three trainings in wisdom are the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
there are four according to the treatise, with the addition of the pure mind, because it gathers supramundane knowledge.

The latter four protect the practices of the two vehicles; among them, the first two protect the minds of the two vehicles, namely, extensively protecting a narrow mind and protecting a small mind through faith.
The latter two protect the practices of the two vehicles, namely, protecting against narrow-minded practice through compassion and protecting against seeking small-scale practice.
Furthermore, among these ten, the first one is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), as it encompasses all practices into a single, thick accumulation;
the remaining nine are all intermediate manifestations within that accumulation, and are thus specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).

Within these nine, the presence of the meaning of "accumulation" (saṃcaya) constitutes their common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa), while the distinctions such as precept and concentration constitute their specific characteristics (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa).
Their formation and dissolution are to be understood as before.
It is by relying on this body, which is the accumulation of all such accumulations, that one is able to give rise to this mind of true realization and abide in the first stage (prathamā bhūmiḥ).
All these collections are subsumed within the "Ground" (*bhūmi*), as they are included in its initial section.

As for the statement that "sentient beings such as these are able to give rise to the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* mind," this mind is precisely the well-determined vow within the "Original Section" (*mūla-bhāga*); the aforementioned text refers to this.

Regarding the second point, as for the meaning for which such a mind is generated, it is as the Sūtra states: "For the sake of attaining all-aspect wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). This reveals that the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom is fully endowed with the ultimate perfection of knowledge, abandonment, realization, and cultivation; therefore, this serves as the general statement.
The Buddha’s wisdom, activity, and function benefit sentient beings; there are nine distinctions, and it is for the sake of seeking these that such a mind is generated.
First is the power of Buddha-wisdom, which is capable of performing the activity of answering questions.

This is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*), by which he is able to provide definitive explanations regarding the meaning of cause and effect and other such matters according to the questions of sentient beings.
This meaning is explained in detail as it is taught in other sūtras; therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] acts "for the sake of attaining the ten powers."
The two forms of fearlessness represent the thorough realization of Buddha-knowledge, enabling the performance of the work of refuting heterodoxy.
Because one uses the four forms of fearlessness to refute the doctrines of non-Buddhists, it is said that this is for the sake of attaining great fearlessness.
The third is the Buddha-wisdom of equality, which is able to perform the activity of instruction.

This means that having attained the two kinds of emptiness and being fully endowed with the Buddha-dharmas, one teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to likewise realize and enter [the truth]; therefore, it is said, "for the sake of attaining the fullness of the Buddha-dharmas."
The fourth is the Buddha-wisdom of rescue, which is capable of performing the activity of salvation.
This means that by skillfully transforming sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), it is said to be "for the sake of rescuing all the world."
The five pure Buddha-wisdoms can perform the causal activity of providing rescue and protection.
Because great compassion serves as the cause for rescuing sentient beings, it is said: "for the sake of purifying the mind of great compassion."
The sixth is the knowledge of non-remainder, which is the Buddha-knowledge capable of performing the activity of universal observation.

This means that one constantly uses the Buddha-eye to universally observe the sentient beings of the worlds in the ten directions without exception; therefore, it is said to be for the sake of the knowledge of non-remainder and non-obstruction directed toward the ten directions.
The seventh is the undefiled Buddha-wisdom, which has the function of adorning the lands and gathering in sentient beings.

This means it adorns all worlds so that they are free from obstructions and defilements; without requiring further effort, it accords with the capacities of beings through these lands, causing them to give rise to faith and enter the Dharma. Therefore, it is said to be "for the purpose of purifying all Buddha-lands so that none remain."

Regarding the "unimpeded wisdom and mind" mentioned in the treatise: unimpeded wisdom (jñānāsaṅga) manifests the absence of obstacles previously mentioned, while unimpeded mind (cittāsaṅga) manifests the absence of defilements previously mentioned.
Furthermore, this is because the former refers to liberation through wisdom (prajñāvimukti) and the latter refers to liberation of the mind (cetovimukti).

The eightfold awakening of Buddha-wisdom is able to suddenly awaken to the mental activities of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time in a single thought-moment as its functional operation; therefore, it is said that within a single thought-moment, one knows the affairs of the three periods of time.

The Buddha’s wisdom of the ninefold turning of the wheel of Dharma has the function of skillfully bringing all sentient beings to liberation; therefore, it is said that he turns [the wheel] with mastery, up to and including by means of the Buddha’s spiritual power.
One who gives rise to such a mind is precisely one who has previously generated the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The treatise asks: Why does it speak only of "generating the mind" (*citta-utpāda*) and not of "generating wisdom" (*jñāna-utpāda*)?
The first question concerns the mind alone;
the second question concerns the other mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), such as mindfulness (*smṛti*) and concentration (*samādhi*).
In reality, at this time, all these qualities arise together; why then speak of the mind alone?
The commentary states:

"Mind" is the sovereign master; by mentioning this, all mental factors such as wisdom are subsumed. Therefore, it says that within the mind, knowing, abandoning, realizing, and cultivating are all subsumed—this answers the first question.
Furthermore, because it also subsumes all factors conducive to the path, this answers the subsequent question.
Third, as for the cause by which such a bodhicitta is generated, it is as the sutra states: "Because this mind has great compassion as its foremost [quality].

While the previous explanation revealed the fruit sought within the context of "for what purpose," the present passage reveals the causal capacity through the question: "By what cause does one seek great enlightenment? Thus, it is by means of this cause that one seeks great bodhi.
Because one seeks this bodhi for the sake of saving sentient beings with great compassion as the foremost priority, it is not for one's own peace. Why is this?
Because without such a Dharma of Great Bodhi, there is no means to ultimately save sentient beings; therefore, all practices take great compassion as the foremost.
This great compassion has nine types:
first, the preeminence of wisdom.
Because it gives rise to superior wisdom by taking subtle suffering as its object, it is called the "preeminence of wisdom."

Regarding the explanation of the distinction between *jñāna* (knowledge) and *prajñā* (wisdom): this wisdom has both general and specific aspects. Generally speaking, there is no difference in the objects of knowledge; however, when distinguished, there are two gates:

first, *jñāna* cognizes conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while *prajñā* illuminates ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This is as in the Ten Perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*), where the sixth is named *prajñā* because it illuminates principle, and the tenth is named *jñāna* because it mirrors phenomena.

The two types of wisdom can decisively determine the distinctions between cause and effect, the favorable and the adverse, and the defiled and the pure; while discernment (*prajñā*) can illuminate and penetrate the conventional and substantial nature, as well as the existence and non-existence of all phenomena.
Herein, the explanation is based on the latter meaning.

Furthermore, when observing the twelve links of dependent origination among sentient beings, that which precedes can give rise to what follows, and all such instances are termed "causes"; that which follows arises in dependence upon what precedes it, and all such instances are termed "effects.
Whether observed in direct or reverse order, there is both defilement and purity.

Regarding the defiled dependent origination in direct and reverse order: from ignorance as the condition for volitional formations, up to old age and death, this is called the direct contemplation (*anuloma*).
From "By what condition does old age and death arise?"—namely, by birth—and so on back to ignorance, this is called the reverse contemplation (*pratiloma*).
Regarding the purification of the forward and reverse sequences: because ignorance ceases, formations cease, and so on up to old age and death; this is called the forward contemplation (*anuloma*).
For what reason do old age and death cease?
Because birth ceases, and so on back to ignorance; this is called the reverse contemplation (*pratiloma*).
This contemplation is called "wisdom" because it has the sense of decisive discernment.
To contemplate all phenomena as being merely names without substantial reality is called the "contemplation of specific characteristics";
to contemplate all phenomena as the single flavor of *tathatā* (suchness) is called the "contemplation of common characteristics."
This contemplation is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*), because its function is to illuminate and discern. Second is "inclusion by means" (*upāya-saṃgraha*).

This means that since one has already understood suffering as described above, one now employs the skillful means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to rescue sentient beings from suffering; therefore, it is said to be "included by means."
"Third is 'purity and ultimate reach.
'Purity' (chun) refers to being profound and sincere; 'ultimate reach' (zhi) refers to reaching the limit. Because compassion is predominant, it is called 'purity and ultimate reach.
There are two types of purity and ultimate reach:"

First is the purity of the straightforward mind (*ṛjukacitta*): this refers to the initial generation of the resolve to bring benefit to the entire realm of sentient beings, as that mind remains consistently unchanging.

Second is the purity of the profound mind (*gambhīracitta*): this refers to the sentiment of compassion for suffering that penetrates to the furthest limits of time; thus it is said, "because of the purity of the straightforward mind and the profound mind."

Furthermore, the straightforward mind leads to the realization of principle, while the profound mind leads to the accumulation of goodness; thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "The straightforward mind consists in correctly recollecting the dharma of True Suchness."
"The profound mind" refers to the delight in accumulating all virtuous practices.
Regarding the "immeasurability of the four immeasurables":
it means that by embracing the Tathāgata’s immeasurable spiritual powers and inspiring faith in sentient beings, their measure is said to be equal to the power of the Buddha.
The fifth is the greatness of certainty.

Regarding "the supreme certainty of faith and profound wisdom as the excellent antidote": it means having the certain conviction that the profound wisdom of all Buddhas is capable of being bestowed upon sentient beings to serve as the function of the most excellent antidote. Therefore, it is said: "By the power of well-ascertained sentient beings and the power of the Buddhas."
This means that by employing the power of the Buddha’s wisdom to bestow it upon sentient beings and thereby augment their own intellectual power, it is called "the power of sentient beings.
Sixth is "conformity" (*anuloma*).
This means conforming to *bodhi* so as to attain perfect enlightenment; thus it is said: "Because one proceeds toward unimpeded wisdom and conforms to spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*)."
Seventh is the greatness of correct reception (*samyak-samādāna*).

This means that one is able to receive the great and supreme teachings of all Buddhas and transmit them to sentient beings; thus it is said that one can receive all Buddha-dharmas, because one teaches and transforms others through wisdom.
Eighth is the greatness of supreme excellence, because it encompasses superior, wondrous, and impartial merit; thus it is said to be "vast as the dharma-realm.
Ninth is the greatness of abiding in exhaustion.

This means that abiding in this state is the cause for the impermanent fruit of craving, whereas its exhaustion is the cause for the eternal fruit of nirvana; therefore, it is said to be ultimately like space, extending to the end of the future.

The fourth point clarifies what characteristics arise when this mind is generated. As the Sūtra states: "As soon as the Bodhisattva generates such a mind, he immediately transcends the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*). This is because this mind is itself the supramundane path, and at this moment, one abandons the nature of an ordinary being;
furthermore, it is because one has newly attained the rank of an Ārya, thereby surpassing the stages of the internal ordinary beings (*adhimukticaryā*) prior to the [ten] stages.
This is the general statement.
There are eight types of faults regarding the meaning of "transgression," which will be explained individually below.

First is the fault of entering the stage (*avasthā-praveśa-doṣa*): at this time, one first accomplishes the supramundane mind; because it is analogous to a worldly person first dwelling in the womb, it is called "entering the Bodhisattva stage."
This phrase refers to the [spiritual] stage; thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its "Chapter on Abiding," names it "entering the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth.

The tenth fascicle of the Liang dynasty’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "First, entering the bodhisattva’s stage of right determination, because one enters the bodhisattva’s first untainted stage (*anāsrava-bhūmi*)."
Regarding the faults of the two families: because they have attained a portion of the *dharmadhātu* realized by the Buddha, it is said that they are "born into the family of the Buddha.

The second volume of the *Liang-lun* states: "Being born into the family of the Buddha is like the various Bodhisattvas being born into the royal family of the Dharma; it is because they are fully endowed with supreme excellence."
The commentary explains:

Although he previously resided in the womb, there would have been no fault in being born into a lowly family; rather, it was essential that he take birth in a royal household so as to manifest his excellence.
This phrase refers to "family" in terms of attaining the Dharma.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the "Chapter on Abiding," states: "Born into the family of the Tathāgata.
Because one transcends the three [inferior] castes through the establishment of great practice and is capable of succeeding to the lineage of the Buddha, it is called "noble caste."
Regarding the point that there is nothing to be censured or disparaged, the *Liang* commentary states: "Because they surpass the lineage of the two vehicles as well as that of the mundane world.
The explanation says:
This is truly because the followers of the two vehicles also attain the dharma-realm of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), yet they are unable to succeed to the stage of Buddhahood.
For example, although one may be born into a royal family, if they are merely a servant or slave to the king, they are not considered noble;
however, when one obtains the very substance of the king and succeeds to the throne, they are truly like a son. Thus, it is similar to the case of a son.
The four paths transcend [the mundane] because they are not of the nature of outflows (*āsrava*); thus, they are not subsumed under the worldly path.
Because they are without outflows, they are subsumed under the supramundane path; therefore, it is said that they "transcend all" up to the supramundane path.
Although one may have attained the Mahāyāna, it is not considered superior if it does not prevail in the world.

For example, even if one belongs to the royal caste, if they are merely a king of ghosts and spirits, they are not to be esteemed; it is only when one is a king of humans and devas that their excellence becomes manifest. Therefore, it is said: "Because there is a similar dharma arising from a different path."
The *Liang-lun* states: "Fourth, having already transformed all worldly activities, because one is determined not to commit wrong actions such as killing.

Fifth is the excellence of the essence of the dharma (*dharmatā*), meaning that the Bodhisattva takes great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as his very essence; since performing the affairs of others is identical to performing his own, this is considered a dharma analogous to his own self-nature. Therefore, it is said that he "dwells within the Bodhisattva-dharma."
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Suppose someone were to ask:
'What is the essence of a bodhisattva?
How should one answer?"
One should answer correctly by saying:
"Its essence is great compassion.
This is what that means.

Although his path was previously superior, if his own person were impaired or deficient, he would not be truly superior; therefore, by citing great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), his essential nature is revealed and established.
Regarding the six abodes: because he does not abandon the world, he does not dwell in nirvāṇa;
because his skillful means (*upāya*) are undefiled, he does not dwell in the world.
Skillfully departing from the two extremes and dwelling in non-dwelling, they are said to "be counted among the ranks of bodhisattvas.
The treatise explains that this refers to the sūtra’s statement that they "dwell in the proper station of bodhisattvas."
Just as a prince who possesses all his faculties is not considered superior simply because his dwelling is inferior,
so too a bodhisattva, despite possessing great compassion, is not yet considered superior if they remain attached to the two extremes.

Having transcended the karmic transgressions of the seven births, one enters the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the three periods of time through the wisdom of the noble ones that accords with emptiness; because this manifests the characteristic of being without end or limit, and because life is thus analogous [to suchness], it is said that one "equally enters the suchness of the three periods."
In the treatise on the *Sūtra of the True Suchness of the Three Times*,
it should be understood that the character "like" (*ru*) is employed in two senses here.
Just as that prince, though superior in both his physical form and his correct conduct, would not be considered truly superior if his lifespan were short.

The eight points concerning the certainty of transcendence consist of the certainty of the cause, which is the non-interruption of the Buddha-lineage, and the certainty of the result, which is ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the accomplishment of similarity: although a prince may excel by relying on a legitimate livelihood, if his resolve is not established, his undertakings will not be accomplished, and he will be incapable of succession. Therefore, it is said that within the lineage of the Tathāgata, one is certain to ultimately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The phrase "dwelling in such dharmas" serves as a summary by restating what has preceded.

That is to say, within the four preceding meanings: first, the internal body upon which one relies is clarified; second, the external fruit sought is distinguished; third, the causes for seeking that fruit are revealed—these three clarify the origins from which the resolve is generated;

fourth, the actual characteristics of the generated resolve are revealed, which constitutes the characteristic of the first dwelling-ground (*bhūmi*). Therefore, it is said that "dwelling in such dharmas is called dwelling in the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*)," because it is a state of immovable dharma.

Regarding the "unshakable dharma" (*akopyadharman*), this explains the meaning of "abiding": first, because once one has realized the true reality, it is never lost; second, because one cannot be moved by the divergent paths of the two vehicles.
The explanation of the meaning of abiding is hereby concluded.
The second section, the Analysis of Names, has three parts:

first, ten phrases clarifying abundant joy; next, ten phrases on the joy arising from mindfulness of what is to be attained in the future; and finally, ten phrases on the joy arising from mindfulness of what is being attained in the present.
Another explanation:
Among these three, the first clarifies the distinction of joy (*prīti*), while the latter two clarify the distinction of the causes of joy.

Furthermore, the former is precisely the joy that constitutes the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of this stage, whereas the latter two clarify that joy arises only when one directs the mind toward the objects of focus within this stage.
Furthermore, regarding the first pair: for what kind of body does joy arise? It arises because one has attained this stage through the thick accumulation of roots of goodness.
Regarding the second pair: for what purpose does joy arise? It arises because the sought-after fruit of Buddhahood will certainly be attained.
Regarding the third pair: with what kind of manifestation does joy arise? It arises because one presently leaves the state of an ordinary person and attains the stage of an Arya.
For what reason is joy (*muditā*) not explicitly distinguished within the [causal] factors?
It is because the compassionate mind is so deeply moved that the characteristic of joy is obscured.
Regarding the statement at the beginning that there is "much joy," it means that the experiences of satisfaction and delight are manifold.
In the treatise, there are three kinds:
first, mental joy (*citta-prīti*), which is the mind entering meditative observation, because the mind is then at ease and delighted;
second, essential joy (*tattva-prīti*), which is the joy upon emerging from observation, because it is associated with feeling (*vedanā*).

Regarding the three faculties of joy (*prīti*): because the preceding mental substance is joyful, it causes the physical sense-faculties (*rūpindriya*) upon which it relies to become harmonious, supple, tranquil, and pleasant; thus, it is said that "joy is predominant."
This is the general statement.
Specifically, there are nine kinds:

first, reverence and joy, because one attains unshakable faith (*aveccappasāda*) within the Triple Gem, because it is called "abundant faith," and because this is similar to the attainment of unshakable purity (*aveccappasāda*) upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the Hīnayāna.

Second is "loving joy" (*preman*), because one contemplates the *tathatā* (suchness) that is free from defilement, because it is said to be "abundantly pure," and because the Sūtra refers to it as "abundant affection.
The former two are mental joy.

Third is the joy of rejoicing (*prāmodya*), so called because one realizes for oneself that what has been attained is superior to the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*) and because of the great exultation it inspires.
Fourth is the joy of flexibility (*praśrabdhi-prāmodya*), so called because physical and mental well-being is universally enhanced.
In the fifth chapter of the *Śāstra*, there is "joyful exultation," which is omitted here for brevity.
Fifth is "capacity for joy," because one perceives that awakening (*bodhi*) is near and because one is said to be highly capable of receiving it.
How does this differ from "anticipating future attainment"?
Anticipating future attainment refers to rejoicing in advance at the fruit;
here, rejoicing refers to being able to experience the cause itself.
The preceding section explains joy through one's own practice; the following three clarify joy through transforming others.

Regarding the sixth, "unbreakable joy": because one has already previously tamed one's own mind, whether when explaining one's own doctrine in response to another's argument or when another explains their own doctrine, the mind remains tamed and free from contention. This is because it is devoid of all agitation and, as it is said, does not delight in strife or quarreling.

Seventh is non-affliction and joy: because one possesses a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, and body and speech are harmonious and gentle, even if one encounters an evil person, one gradually transforms them through the Way; this is because one does not afflict others and because it is said that one does not like to disturb or trouble sentient beings.

Eighth is non-anger and non-delight: this refers to seeing sentient beings whose minds deviate from the Dharma by not acting according to what they profess, and whose physical conduct is improper by violating the Way; because one feels compassion upon seeing them, endures them without anger, and thus does not harbor ill will or resentment.
The first two phrases refer to not vexing or harming others; this phrase refers to being able to endure the vexation of others.
Furthermore, the former two prevent others from being vexed, while this phrase ensures that one does not give rise to anger oneself.

Regarding the second thought, one should give rise to joy because [the fruit] will be attained; while the first phrase was general, here the intention is to clarify the meaning of what has already been attained and what is yet to be attained. Why, then, does one bring to mind other Buddhas?
Commentary:
Thinking, "Just as the Buddha has attained it, so shall I also attain it," one gives rise to joy in the mind because of such mindfulness.
This is precisely mindfulness of others' accomplishment.
There are another nine kinds:

first, "recalling the Buddha-dharma" is in fact the recollection of the Dharma itself; however, because the general encompasses the particular, these other nine are derived from the gateway of recollecting the Buddha. Therefore, all nine kinds are termed "recollecting the Buddha."

This refers to the dharmas attained through the recollection of the Buddha and the dharmas he has taught; since these have already been realized and will likewise be accomplished, it is said that "the mind of joy arises from the recollection of the Buddha's dharmas.
Second is the recollection of the Bodhisattvas.
Some commentators explain it thus:
"When this Buddha was a bodhisattva in the past, I also shared that same state; therefore, joy arises. Now, the present interpretation is as follows:
The meaning of the text is this: since those who attain the Way through mindfulness of the Buddha have bodhisattvas as their retinue, I too shall have them;
therefore, I give rise to joy. This is why it says, "mindfulness of all bodhisattvas," and so forth.

Regarding the third, "recollection of the practice of the Buddha": herein, this specifically refers to the recollection of the bodhisattva practices. Why is it called "recollection of the practice of the Buddha"?
Explanation:
It is because the various practices of the bodhisattvas are the practices performed by the Buddha, and because they originate from the Buddha.

Fourth is the purity of mindfulness of the Buddha, which refers to mindfulness of all the perfections (*pāramitās*) of the Buddha because they are free from defilement; it is called "mindfulness of the purity of the various *pāramitās*.

Fifth is the excellence of mindfulness of the Buddha, which refers to mindfulness that the Bodhisattvas are superior to other beings; it is called "mindfulness of the various Bodhisattvas as being distinctively superior to the [other] assemblies."
Sixth is the power of non-retrogression through mindfulness of the Buddha; thus it is called "indestructible.
Seventh is mindfulness of the Dharma by which the Buddha transforms and teaches sentient beings.
Eighth is mindfulness of the Buddha’s ability to extensively benefit sentient beings.
The ninth is the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha through which one enters, namely, the gate of skillful wisdom.
Question:

Looking at these ten phrases, only the first phrase concerns mindfulness of the Buddha, while the others concern other matters; why does the author of the treatise refer to them all collectively as "mindfulness of the Buddha"?
Answer:

This is established based on the unimpeded characteristics of the inexhaustible dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), wherein within each and every condition (*pratyaya*), all conditions are fully subsumed.
Because the Master of the Treatise relies on this principle, he brings the nine [recollections] back into the one, collectively naming them "recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānusmṛti*).

Just as the first phrase encompasses nine, so it is for each of the remaining phrases; thus, beneath every single phrase there is inexhaustibility, for these dharmas of this stage are the dharmas of *dhāraṇī*.
This is the meaning illustrated by the aforementioned example of the *siddham* syllabary.
Following this principle, the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) constitute the general category, while everything from the ten stages (*bhūmi*) up to Buddhahood constitutes the specific categories.
Subsuming the particulars into the general, there is nothing that is not fully present within faith; the same applies to the other stages—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, regarding these ten phrases, the Master of the Treatise provides another round of explanation.

The Treatise states: "Regarding the first two moments among these, they are 'common recollections of the Buddha,' meaning that within the ten [recollections], the first two moments are common, as both are objects of recollection.
Now, these are again divided into two, namely, the recollection of the Buddha and the recollection of the Buddha-dharma; thus it is said, "because there are two: the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma."
The intention here is to establish the Three Jewels through exclusion.

Regarding the mention of "recollection of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas," it is by means of the recollection of the Buddha that one distinguishes between the recollection of the Buddha and the recollection of the Bodhisattvas; thus, there are two.

Because the statement "contemplating all bodhisattvas" directly mentions bodhisattvas, and because the preceding section on the "Dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu) has already clarified the distinction [of the Dharma], the Buddha thus fully embodies the Three Jewels.
