Because we observe through direct perception that without the preceding member, the subsequent member does not exist.
This demonstrates that there is no fruit apart from the seed; therefore, it is said that the fruit is the "fruit of the seed.
Regarding the statement that "the three do not depart from ignorance and thus constitute the practitioner," this is an explanatory interpretation.
Because the fruit is not separate from the seed-ignorance, it is called "not departing."

Third, the section beginning with "If not separate" explains the meaning of non-identity (*ananyatva*). First, it reveals two faults; subsequently, it cites a verse from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* to establish the argument.
Regarding the statement that [the effect] is not identical to the cause: this is because [the effect] is that which is produced, whereas [the cause] is not the producer.
Regarding "the cause is not different": because that which is capable of producing gives rise to that which is produced.
Since the effect does not conform to the cause, the effect is neither annihilated nor is the cause eternal.
Because the fruit is not different from the cause, the fruit is not eternal and the cause is not interrupted.
Furthermore, because they are not identical, both cause and fruit are not interrupted; because they are not different, both cause and fruit are not eternal.
Furthermore, consider this by reversing the argument.
Since "that which is" is not separate from "that which is not," it follows that what is not eternal is also not discontinuous; this can likewise be seen through reflection.
Fourth, the concluding summary from "arising from self" onwards can be understood by analogy with the preceding sections.

Third, regarding the classification based on great compassion: sentient beings with false views who cling to inverted causes—such as the god Īśvara as the cause of sentient beings—are truly to be pitied.
In this present passage, because it reveals that ignorance produces formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, it serves as the contemplation of causes in order to counteract those attachments.

Fourth, regarding the analysis according to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it corresponds to the fourth contemplation of the characteristics of causes and conditions (*hetupratyaya*).

Regarding the phrase "because the members of existence (bhavāṅga) lack activity": this clarifies that these members of existence do not simply follow one after another based on their predecessors; rather, it clarifies the absence of intrinsic nature in the subsequent members. Furthermore, while the preceding member acts as the efficient cause for the subsequent one, the preceding member itself also lacks activity. Therefore, the various links of dependent origination are the domain of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Fifth, regarding the non-interruption of the three paths, the four gates are the same as before.
First, concerning the non-interruption of the three paths according to the sūtra:
afflictions are of two kinds, namely, those that incite and those that moisten.

Although all afflictions are capable of activating and moistening [karma], ignorance is predominant in the stage of activating karma, while craving and grasping are superior in their power to moisten karma for rebirth; therefore, they are mentioned specifically.
Because it does not arise repeatedly, a single ignorance (avidyā) is established;
because it irrigates again and again, craving (tṛṣṇā) and grasping (upādāna) are distinguished.
Karma also has two aspects: that which is unmoistened and that which is already moistened.

When karma exists as the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and has not yet been moistened by craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*), its initial formation and manifestation are termed "formative forces" (*saṃskāra*).

When karma exists as the productive cause (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*) and has already been moistened by craving and grasping, such that it is about to produce the future fruit, it is established as "existence" (*bhava*).
This is explained in terms of the existence of karma alone.
Suffering also has two aspects: that which exists in the state of cause and that which exists in the state of fruit.

Among them, the five factors beginning with consciousness are exclusively causes of retribution, while the two stages beginning with birth are exclusively fruits of retribution. Because the specific characteristics of the causal stage—which is what is projected—are difficult to discern, the five members are distinguished based on their status as the future fruit. That is to say, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the characteristic of consciousness as a cause becomes manifest.
Next, when the faculties are not yet matured, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) increases;
next, when the faculties are matured, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) become clear and flourishing;
based on these, contact (sparśa) arises, and from contact, sensation (vedanā) arises; at that time, it is called the culmination of the fruit of sensation.
Based on these stages, the causes are established as five members.
Because the characteristics of the distinctions in the resultant stage are easy to understand, two members are established in total to manifest the three types of suffering.
However, if the resulting fruit is yet to come in the future, "birth, old age, and death" are taught in order to engender revulsion toward it.
If one arrives at the present, the five [factors] beginning with consciousness are taught in order to bring about a thorough understanding of the arising of the various stages;
this is explained in detail as it appears in the eighth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Furthermore, these three—afflictions, karma, and suffering—constitute the characteristics of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). As stated in the verse from the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra* composed by the Bodhisattva Viśeṣacinti: "The afflictions are the first, eighth, and ninth; karma is the second and the tenth; the remaining seven are said to be suffering. These three encompass the twelve factors."
From the three, two arise; from the two, seven arise; from the seven, again three arise. Thus, it revolves like a wheel.
All worldly phenomena consist solely of cause and effect and lack a person; merely from empty dharmas do empty dharmas arise in turn.
The commentary explains:
This distinguishes the mutual arising of the three paths to manifest the two kinds of selflessness, as explained at length in that [text].
Second, regarding the analysis based on revulsion for the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the treatise names this "the contemplation that subsumes faults" (*ādīnavānudarśana*).
This refers to the three paths that encompass the causes and fruits of suffering, due to a profound sense of weary detachment.
Thirdly, regarding the classification by means of great compassion, the treatise names them "seeking liberation through divergent paths."

The internal counteragent to the cause of asceticism refers to the fact that false asceticism is merely a cause for afflictions, karma, and deluded conceptualization, and is not a cause for happiness; as stated in the Sūtra: "Within this, there is ignorance, craving, and so forth."
Fourth, regarding the analysis according to great wisdom (*mahājñāna*), the treatise calls this "entering the contemplation of the truths" (*satyadarśana*).
Since the three paths constitute the truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), they are the phenomena known by great wisdom.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it asks: "How many members are subsumed under the truth of suffering, and which constitute suffering in the present life? Answer:
Two, namely birth and old age and death."
Question:
How many factors of the Truth of Suffering (duḥkhasatya) are comprised within that which constitutes suffering? Answer:
The five [links] refer to the nature of the seeds from consciousness through feeling.
Question:
How many links are subsumed under the truth of origination (samudaya-satya)?
Answer: "The remaining factors. Explanation:

When the five causes and two fruits are both subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), the five factors consisting of afflictions and karma are subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).

Furthermore, the eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "All are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering, because they have the nature of the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*)."
"The five [links] are subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), because they are of the nature of karma and afflictions.
The commentary explains:

"This means that twelve [links] are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), as they are of the nature of the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*); it should be understood that only five [links] are subsumed under the Truth of Origination."
The sixth section, "Discriminating the Prior and Subsequent Limits," also has four gates identical to those above.

First, regarding the discrimination of the prior and subsequent limits according to the Sūtra: among these twelve links, the first two are the "projectors" (ākṣepaka), the next five are the "projected" (ākṣipta), the next three are the "producers" (abhinirvartaka), and the final two are the "produced" (abhinirvṛtta).
Regarding the differentiation of the three time periods (*traiyadhvika*) therein, there are briefly three explanations in the various sacred teachings:

First, according to this sutra, the "projecting" (*ākṣepaka*) and the "projected" (*ākṣipta*) are distinguished; the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) and the middle limit (*madhyānta*) are divided, while the "produced" (*abhinirvartaka*) and the "produced" (*abhinirvṛtta*) are combined into the posterior limit (*aparānta*). This is because the projecting [karma] is distant and thus divided, whereas the producing [karma] is proximate and thus combined.
Secondly, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the productive [causes] and the produced [results] are separated, while the inducing [causes] and the induced [results] are combined.
Therefore, the first ten belong to the present and the latter two to the future, because the ten causes and two results are divided between the two time periods.

The three lives are introduced together; according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, "the first two are past, the next eight are present, and the final two are future, thus constituting the three periods of time."

In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other treatises, it is established that the ten causes and two fruits necessarily belong to different time periods; among the causes, the first seven and the following three may be either simultaneous or non-simultaneous, whereas the second, third, and seventh are each determined to be simultaneous.
Thus, these twelve links of single-layered cause and effect are sufficient to manifest cyclic existence and to eliminate the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
Furthermore, through this cycle of cause and effect across the three time periods, the two types of self—the self of persons and the self of phenomena—are eternally non-existent.

Second, regarding the renunciation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the treatise calls this the "contemplation for guarding against faults. This refers to the three types of faults raised by opponents against this principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*):
first, that all bodies arise simultaneously; this is the enumeration of the names of the faults.
As for the question "Why?", the opponent asks this to investigate the reason for establishing the fault.
"Because there is no distinct cause" explains the nature of the established fault.
Since there is no distinct cause such as a self (*ātman*), why would it not be possible for bodies in the five destinies to be born simultaneously?
The names listed in the second [section] can be understood through their respective definitions.
Regarding the phrase "because there is no agent," this explains the characteristics of the established fault.
If there is no self that performs actions, who will experience the retribution of the future?
The points of inquiry can be understood from the enumeration within the three [sections].
In the explanation, since there is no self, who would maintain this karma and cause it to reach its fruit?
Therefore, [the karma] would necessarily perish.
The statement that "the former does not receive retribution" is made by looking back from the former toward the latter;
the statement here that "one loses the practice" is made by looking forward from the latter toward the former.
The phrase "these three" below serves as a general summary to clarify the protection.
This refers to past and present causes, which are specifically termed "distinct causes" (*anyathā-hetu*).
Because this answers the three preceding objections, it is called an "answer.
It also extends to include the subsequent phrase.
Since the present and the future are distinct, and this distinction arises from their respective causes, how could there be the fault of [all things] arising simultaneously?
Furthermore, since specific causes yield specific retributions, how can you say that there is no experiencing of retribution?
Since the retribution of distinctions arises from diverse causes, how could there be the fault of losing one's station?
In the subsequent commentary, the internal [causes] of the past are first explained.
Regarding the phrase "ignorance conditions volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*), which refers to the past, this is a citation of the scriptural text.
The explanation below consists of two parts:
first, clarifying that past causes can produce the present; second, showing that present effects arise from past causes.
It is taught that the present consciousnesses and so forth serve as the basis for what is to come.
In this context, it would suffice to speak only of past causes; why then is it necessary to further state that the present serves as their future?
This is done in order to prevent three faults by means of the mutual connection between cause and effect.
The phrase "this is seeing" concludes the previous explanation by summarizing that the past is the meaning of cause.
Within the second explanation concerning the present, the statement "from consciousness up to feeling, one sees the present" restates the scriptural text.
The commentary explains two phrases:

first, it clarifies that the present fruit arises from past causes; second, from the phrase "furthermore, it can" onwards, it clarifies that past causes obtain the present fruit. Since the present is the future of that past, it is said that one obtains the future fruit.
Third, regarding the section below "craving and grasping" which explains the future [existence], first the text is cited.
The phrase "furthermore there is birth" explains that from craving, grasping, and so forth, there arises existence and birth-and-death; this is termed "there is birth."
Question:
In the previous explanation, both the past and present were treated as relative to one another across two time periods; why is it that the future is not explained in this same way now? Answer:
Because those [factors] of the past and present are themselves divided into two groups within the Sūtras, they must be linked together to establish the protection against faults.

As for craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), the Sūtra itself states that there are three types; since these are categorized as the future from the perspective of their results, they do not require the Master’s linking, and thus are not discussed here.
Regarding the phrase "provisionally fixed" (*yīwǎng dìng*), it serves to conclude and distinguish the preceding text.
What has been elucidated above is a single unity; dividing this across the three periods of time is termed "provisional.
Such is the nature of the principle and its numerical sequence, and thus it is called "fixed."

The following section explains how births arise from one another across the three periods of time in an inexhaustible succession; thus it says, "Furthermore, there is the turning of subsequent births. Regarding the question, "What is the meaning of this?
the following section explains that the previous defense against the fault [of infinite regress] has three points:

first, a general clarification that karma does not necessarily yield its fruit; second, citing the sūtra to clarify that it does yield fruit; and third, concluding both the attainment and non-attainment of the result.
Regarding the preceding section, first there is a general enumeration: due to three reasons, past karma cannot produce its retribution.

First, "there may be that which has not yet been performed": with respect to craving, grasping, and becoming sought in the past, because these were not yet performed at that time, the fruits of birth, aging, and death cannot arise in the present.
Question:

Considering the meaning of this passage, it seems to state that past ignorance has not yet produced volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); for what reason, then, does it say that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth have not yet been produced? Answer:
If ignorance has not yet produced karma, for what reason is it said that there is past karma?
Due to three reasons, one does not receive retribution.

As for the statement that "some karma has already been performed but its retribution not yet obtained," this refers to seeking craving, grasping, becoming, and so forth in the present; although the action has already been completed, because it has not yet matured, the fruits of birth, aging, and death are not obtained in the present.
Regarding "obtaining an antidote": if karma that has already been moistened is ripe, it should logically result in the future attainment of the fruits of birth, aging, and death.

Alternatively, if one attains the fruit of an Arya in this very life, because craving and grasping are severed, the karma that had already matured is rendered scorched and extinguished, such that it cannot yield its retribution.
Second, from the passage "In this regard, ignorance... onwards, it clarifies that one receives retribution by virtue of three meanings presented in the sutra.

That is to say, since there was already ignorance as a condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) in the past, it is known that [the karma] has already been performed; this is not the same as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and the other links.
Since the five fruits, such as consciousness and so forth, are now obtained, it is clearly known that karma has already yielded its fruit.
Because craving and grasping in the present are not severed by the Noble Path, they cause the succession of future birth and death to continue without interruption.

Third, in the section beginning with "Therefore," which provides a dual conclusion: that which has already been performed constitutes the *saṃskāra* (formative) link; that which has not yet been performed constitutes the *bhava* (existence) link; that which has already attained its fruit constitutes the *vijñāna* (consciousness) link and so forth; and that which has not yet attained its fruit constitutes the *jāti* (birth) link and so forth.
"Since the Noble Ones have severed what ordinary persons have not yet severed," this concludes the section on the protection of karma.
Given such distinctions, how could there be the fault of the entire body experiencing [sensation] simultaneously?
If there is that which has been performed and that which has not yet been performed, by what cause would they be simultaneous?
If there is that which has received retribution and that which has not yet received it, how could they be simultaneous?
If there is that which has been severed and that which has not yet been severed, how could they be simultaneous?
The phrase "If that were so" below reiterates and clarifies the point:
that which is not to be experienced as all karma has already been abandoned;
nor is it that which is not to be experienced at all, for that has not yet been abandoned.
"Nor is it simultaneous" clarifies that what was previously done and not yet done,
as well as what has been attained and not yet attained, can be known.
The passage beginning with "If one acts for oneself" guards against the second fault of not receiving retribution, meaning that one acts for oneself and must receive the results oneself.
Why not accept [the alternative] that it is received by another? Because that other does not perform [the action].

Third, regarding the fault of losing the third type of action through the protection [of abstaining] from those three things: since one does not acquire [the action] by abstaining from the first three types, there is no fault of losing an action; thus, no actions fail to yield their results.
The subsequent summary can be understood accordingly.

Third, regarding the classification by means of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*): when a bodhisattva sees various non-Buddhists practicing heterodox paths in their quest for liberation while reckoning [the cause] as being without cause (*ahetu*) and so forth, they give rise to a mind of great compassion; observing this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they rescue them from those false attachments.

The treatise states that "the causes of the prior and middle periods" refers to the two members of the past being the prior period, as they serve as the cause for the consciousness and other factors of the present middle period.
It further states "and the causes of the middle and subsequent periods," meaning that craving, grasping, and becoming of the middle period serve as the cause for the future subsequent period.

Regarding the statement that it refers to the middle limit and the two limits before and after: within the middle limit, the five results such as internal consciousness belong to the prior limit, while the three causes such as craving belong to the subsequent limit.

Since these causes exist, how can one say they do not? Therefore, the conclusion states: "If such causal matters did not exist, then the various resultant matters of sentient beings would likewise not exist."
Fourth, regarding the classification according to great wisdom (*mahājñāna*), the treatise names this "the contemplation based on the entry of faith through [discerning] power and lack of power.

The two past links possess power relative to the present but lack power relative to the subsequent links; the three links beginning with craving (*tṛṣṇā*) possess power relative to what follows but lack power relative to what precedes them.
Another explanation is as follows:

the two preceding [moments] are powerful while the five present ones are powerless; the three present ones are powerful while the two subsequent ones are powerless. This is because that which is capable of producing is "powerful," while that which is produced is "powerless."
The Bodhisattva raises up these transformed beings, causing them to leave the false and enter the correct; therefore, it is called "entrance through faith.
Because they rely on the illumination of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom, it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).

Regarding the statement that the transformations of the beginning, middle, and end are superior, this is a reiterated explanation establishing that the sequence of beginning, middle, and end constitutes the "powerful and powerless," while the superiority of the transformation constitutes "entrance through faith."
This means illuminating the three periods of time to transform sentient beings for the sake of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*).
Within the seventh section on the differentiation of the three types of suffering, there are also four gates.

First, the sutra clarifies that these links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) are all aggregates of suffering; it then proceeds to explain the causes of the three sufferings by analyzing the discrimination associated with sensation (*vedanā*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "How many are associated with pleasant feeling?
It refers to all except for two.
The commentary explains:

Excluding feeling and old age and death, the remaining ten possess pleasant feeling, because feeling does not coexist with itself, and because there is generally no pleasant feeling in the state of old age and death.
"How many [factors] are associated with painful feeling?"
This means that among those [twelve links] and those excluded, one [link] is included.
The commentary explains:
"Excluding only the link of sensation (vedanā), the remaining eleven are suffering-sensation (duḥkhavedanā)."
"How many are associated with equanimity?
As was explained regarding pleasant feeling:
because in the state of old age and death, adventitious equanimity is mostly absent."
"How many do not coexist with feeling (*vedanā*)?
It refers to one among those excluded, namely the limb of feeling itself, because feeling does not coexist with feeling.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) is likewise.
Next, regarding the analysis of the three types of suffering, there are two approaches:
first, the approach of actual principle which applies universally, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: "How many members are subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*)?
They are those members associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā-sahagata*), as well as a portion of those not associated with feeling."
How many are comprised within suffering?
They are the factors associated with painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā-sahagata*), as well as a portion of the factors not associated with feeling (*vedanā-asahagata*).
How many factors are comprised within the category of suffering?
This means that all factors of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) and the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) are also factors of the suffering of formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).

Alternatively, there are factors subsumed under the suffering of formations that do not belong to the other two types of suffering; these are the factors associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā-sahagata*), as well as a portion of the factors not associated with feeling (*avedanā-sahagata*).
The suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) comprises the ten links in their entirety as well as a portion of the link of feeling (*vedanā*), namely pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).

Excluding the painful feeling within the link of feeling and the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) comprises the eleven links in their entirety as well as a portion of the link of feeling, namely painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*).
The suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) subsumes both the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);

all of these are the suffering of conditioned existence. Alternatively, there may be suffering of conditioned existence that is not subsumed by those two categories, namely, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*).
Therefore, the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā) universally subsumes all twelve [links].
The eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states this in the same way.
Second is the gate of manifesting according to the increase of characteristics, as explained in this sutra.
This means that because the characteristics of flux appear in the first five branches, they are called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

As for the two types, contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*), because contact gives rise to suffering through its encounter [with objects], it is called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Regarding the remaining [branches] being termed the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), it is simply that the destruction of pleasure is named the suffering of change.

Since the factors of old age and death possess no pleasure that could be destroyed, why are they called the suffering of change? Explanation: There are two types of the suffering of change: [the suffering of change due to the transformation of conditioned phenomena, and the suffering of change due to the separation from what is pleasant].
First, pleasure becomes suffering through its destruction; this is explained from the perspective of that which is destroyed.
Second, because destruction itself is suffering, it is called "suffering due to change" (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*).
Since this factor of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) can destroy birth (*jāti*), it is categorized under suffering due to change.
The remaining text may be understood.

Second, regarding detachment from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), among the six types of contemplation according to the Master [Vasubandhu], this corresponds to the fifth, called the "contemplation of neither-detachment-nor-non-detachment."

This means that while ordinary beings do not feel weary [of suffering], Bodhisattvas are able to feel weary of it; thus it is said, "not wearying of what is not wearying," which refers to coarse suffering.

Furthermore, while those of the Two Vehicles do not feel weary [of suffering], Bodhisattvas are able to feel weary of it; this refers to subtle suffering, hence the phrase "various minute sufferings," because they discern all such things as being suffering.
Regarding the phrase "and being weary of various coarse sufferings": that which is to be abandoned by the followers of the Two Vehicles is also to be abandoned by Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, the aforementioned subtle [suffering] is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), while this coarse [suffering] constitutes the other two types of suffering for them.

Third, regarding the classification according to the conformity of great compassion: [the Buddha] takes pity on those non-Buddhists who do not realize the true principle and seek a divergent liberation.
There are four kinds of true liberation; by presenting the correct, the false is revealed.
First, the characteristic of being free from all suffering is the quality of bliss (*sukha*).
Second, the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the quality of permanence (*nitya*).
Third, the characteristic of being free from defilement is the quality of purity (*śubha*).
The four supramundane characteristics are my virtues.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "To be sovereignly detached from worldly dharmas is called 'self'."
The statement, "Those conditioned phenomena are suffering," serves to distinguish the erroneous from the correct.
In the four subsequent sections of the sutra, each is assigned a specific meaning; this present section corresponds to the first.

Regarding the statement that "suffering follows one even unto the bonds of the formless realm," this refers to these three types of suffering. It demonstrates that those non-Buddhists who seek the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi*) and so forth as *nirvāṇa* are, when observed by a Bodhisattva, all subject to the twelve links of dependent origination and the nature of the three sufferings. How, then, could there be any meaning of the blissful qualities of *nirvāṇa* therein?

Therefore, compassion arises accordingly. Fourth, regarding the classification by means of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*): this refers to the seventh case, concerning those who enter contemplation with either prideful or non-prideful faith. Śrāvakas do not perceive subtle suffering and thus claim they have no suffering; this is called prideful conceit (*abhimāna*). However, when they perceive gross suffering, it is not prideful conceit. By citing this, one causes those of the two vehicles to gain faith and entry into the subtle suffering of dependent origination within the Mahāyāna.
Because the Bodhisattva illuminates this, it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).
The phrase "not knowing according to reality" and following explains the characteristics of pride (*māna*).

This section, while previously addressed the conversion of non-Buddhists through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), now addresses the gathering of those of the two vehicles through great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*).
This is because the text contains multiple meanings, which the author of the treatise skillfully extracts.
Regarding the eighth [point], the dependent origination of formations (*saṃskāra*), there are also four sections.

First, concerning the Sūtra: in reality, ignorance (*avidyā*) has no causal condition (*pratyaya*) in relation to formations; yet, when it is said that "formations arise through conditions," there are two meanings:
First, with one's own seeds as the cause and ignorance as the condition, these are spoken of together as "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
However, because the immediate seeds are concealed and this predominant condition is highlighted, it is called "ignorance as the causal condition."

Secondly, because that dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), when viewed in relation to its own dominant fruit, is still a direct cause, ignorance is said to be the causal condition for formations (*saṃskāra*).
The same applies to the others as well.

To clarify that effects do not arise of themselves but must proceed from causes and conditions, and that these causes and conditions, being mutually dependent and devoid of intrinsic nature, are therefore said to be "arisen from causes and conditions" precisely to manifest their non-arising—this is still the perspective of progressive contemplation (*anuloma*).
By observing in reverse, all is extinguished; thus it can be known that there is neither arising nor non-arising.

Second, regarding the contemplation of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) within the context of wearying detachment from the conditioned, among the six gates, this is the sixth, called "Profound Contemplation."
Within this profound contemplation, the latter three gates are subsumed to form four propositions:
first, not arising from self; second, not arising from another; third, not arising from both; and fourth, not arising without a cause.
Regarding the explanation of these four lines, various treatises differ, presenting five general interpretations:

first, concerning the refutation of non-Buddhist schools, it means that all phenomena do not arise from the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) or *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature), hence they are said to be "not self-born";
second, they do not arise from Brahmā, Maheśvara, or other such deities, hence they are said to be "not other-born."
Third, it is not produced by the combination of atoms and the great elements; therefore, it is said that they do not arise together.
Fourth, it does not arise spontaneously without a cause; therefore, it is said that it does not arise without a cause.
Second, regarding the refutation of the Two Vehicles:
first, it is said that all phenomena do not arise from themselves because they do not invariably arise from their own homogeneous causes;
second, it is said that they do not arise from others because they do not invariably arise from those heterogeneous ripening causes.
Third, it is also not produced by those [factors] as simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), and thus it is said that they do not arise together;

fourth, within the Hīnayāna it is accepted that the factor of ignorance (*avidyā*) arises based on improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) directed toward the void, appearing as if it were causeless, yet now it is not so, and therefore it is free from being causeless.
Third, the emptiness [of phenomena] is revealed by means of the dharmas:
first, the fruit does not arise from itself, which is called "not arising from self";
second, since the self is not established, against what could "other" be distinguished?
Furthermore, since both "self" and "other" are individually unestablished, how could there be production from another?
Therefore, it is said that there is no production from another.
Since the three cases—self, other, and cause-and-effect—are each unestablished, it is said that there is no co-production.
Fourth, because there is no resultant phenomenon apart from causes and conditions, it is said that things do not arise without a cause.
These three preceding points are as explained in the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, and other such works.

Fourth, regarding the negation by way of causes and conditions, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "Because it exists from its own seeds, it does not arise from another; because it depends on various conditions, it is not self-made; because it lacks [independent] activity, it does not arise through co-origination; and because it possesses functional capacity, it is not without cause."

Generally speaking, when even a single pair of propositions regarding dependent origination is negated, it is already profoundly deep; how much more so when all four propositions are negated? Therefore, dependent origination is the ultimate in profundity.
Fifth, regarding the gate of unimpeded dependent origination, results arise solely from causes and conditions.
When causes and conditions are examined in relation to one another, each possesses two meanings:
first, being entirely powerful; second, being entirely powerless.

This means: first, because the cause, in relation to the fruit, may not produce it at all while the condition necessarily produces it entirely, it is said that "the cause does not produce, but the condition produces";

second, because the condition, in relation to the fruit, may also not produce it at all while the cause necessarily produces it entirely, it is said that "the condition does not produce, but its own cause produces";
third, because the two powers do not operate simultaneously, they do not produce [the fruit] together.
Because the four conditions and the two powers are neither simultaneous nor absent, there is no arising without a cause.
This section contains two meanings:

first, based on the principle that power may be present or absent, they are made to interpenetrate; that is to say, when the cause possesses power, the conditions must be powerless. Therefore, because the cause possesses power, it can encompass others, and because the conditions are powerless, they can enter into others.
The power of those conditions ultimately converges into the power of the cause; this is termed "not arising from another.
Although it is said "not from another," this conversely reveals "arising from self.
When the power of the cause converges into the conditions, "not from self" is likewise so; reflect upon this by reversing the previous [analysis].
Because the two powers and the two lack of power do not coexist, there is no mutual non-penetration between them;
because one power and one lack of power mutually accord with one another, they are constantly in mutual penetration.
Since they do not obstruct one another and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is expansive, there are no phenomena whatsoever that do not penetrate one another.

The "Chapter on the Ten Patiences" states: "The Bodhisattva skillfully contemplates the dharma of dependent origination; within a single dharma, they understand manifold dharmas, and within manifold dharmas, they understand a single dharma."
It is precisely because of this gate that such is the case.

Second, based on the essence (*tattva*), there is the sense of being both empty and non-empty; therefore, there is mutual identity (*paraspara-saṃbheda*). This means that it is not merely that the power of the cause returns to the conditions to clarify their mutual inclusion; rather, through the essence, the conditions manifest the emptiness of the causal nature, thereby subsuming the cause within the conditions.
Why is this? It means that if there were no conditions (*pratyaya*), there would be no cause (*hetu*); therefore, a cause is so named because it produces an effect.

When there are no conditions and the effect does not arise, at that time it is not called a cause. Clearly, this demonstrates that the cause ultimately depends upon those conditions and does not arise of itself. Thus, conditions possess the quality of existence; what is non-existent cannot be subsumed [within them].
Because of this meaning of emptiness, there is nothing that is not subsumed.
Because it is subsumed by reception (*vedanā*), the cause is discarded and becomes identical with the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);
because the condition is able to subsume, the cause is subsumed and becomes identical with itself.
The remaining causes that subsume conditions such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth may be understood by analogy with volition (*cetanā*).
For this reason, the characteristics of all phenomena are mutually identical and without obstruction.
What was stated in the preceding text—“knowing that one is many, and many is one,” and so forth—all refers to this very meaning.
Therefore, the inexhaustible and great Dharma of dependent origination, characterized by unimpeded mastery, all manifests through this gateway.

Regarding the statement herein that "conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise," the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra* state that "conditioned by the causal factor of ignorance, formations arise. This demonstrates that the cause gives rise to the fruit and clarifies that it is not produced by another.
To say that "conditions can produce volitional formations" clarifies that effects arise from causes and demonstrates that they are not self-created.
Furthermore, because ignorance is the specific cause of volitional formations, they are not created by another.
Furthermore, the substance of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) does not previously exist within ignorance, yet later volitional formations arise from it; therefore, they are not self-made.
The same applies to the other [links]; this may be understood by analogy.

Within this section, the author of the treatise expands [the analysis] into two propositions: "not by oneself" and "not by another. Third, regarding the distinction based on great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*):

it clarifies that among the various non-Buddhists who seek a distinct liberation, they mistake the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception and other such realms for *nirvāṇa*. The Bodhisattva observes that these are merely phenomena produced through the dependent origination of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), and are not the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) *nirvāṇa* characterized by permanence. For this reason, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion accordingly.

Regarding the fourth [classification], which analyzes the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*): within the nine gates, the eighth and ninth gates are combined into one, namely the "contemplation of beginninglessness.
Master Yuan said, "This is the contemplation of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)."
"Because one perceives that the conditioned origination of phenomena has no inherent nature, it is called 'beginningless'.
Now, this means that the dharmas of dependent origination have no fundamental source from which they first arise; therefore, they are said to be beginningless.
The statement in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, "All dharmas are established based on the root of non-abiding," shares this same meaning.

Regarding the phrase "because there is arising in the middle limit, there is arising in the subsequent limit," this is an exposition that cites a phenomenon to establish the principle: it means that this dependent origination is itself non-arising; therefore, it is called "beginningless. This is the dharma known by great wisdom.
The ninth explanation concerning the bondage of causes and conditions also consists of four sections.
The first is based on the Sūtra:

"That which is bound by the arising of causes and conditions" means that these dependent originations bind one another such that they cannot arise; because they are thus bound, they furthermore do not cease.

By means of the single syllable *ba*, the essence of this dharma is sealed; it is free from all conceptual discrimination. However, because even the mark of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is itself free [from such discrimination], it is expressed through words for the sake of manifestation, and thus it is called the "teaching of bondage."

This is to clarify that these bonds exist only within the realm of verbal expression; this section reveals the phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) of dependent origination, as it approaches the exhaustion of rationality and is about to manifest the most subtle and profound state.
The treatise states: "To follow and contemplate the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is to enter the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya); this is the present section.
The explanation of the text is self-evident.
Second, regarding the four gates of profound contemplation based on revulsion toward the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), this is the third, the "unshared activity" (*asādhāraṇa-karman*).

Regarding the statement that "neither of the two acts as the agent": either the cause is taken as self and the conditions as other, or the effect is taken as self and the causes and conditions as other; since neither of these two—self and other—acts [as the agent], it is so stated.
If neither self nor other acts as the agent, how can there be dependent origination?
To resolve this doubt, it is said that "it merely accords with arising," meaning that while arising is spoken of in accordance with conventional truth, in reality there is no arising.

Regarding the phrase "because there is no knower": Master Yuǎn explains that this is a specific refutation of [the view] that it is caused by another, because there is no self as a knower who can perform the action.

Regarding "not abiding at the time of acting," this is a specific refutation of [the view] that it is caused by itself; it clarifies that when ignorance performs the formations, those formations lack an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that abides during that act, and thus, while performing that act, they give rise to subsequent formations. Therefore, it is said that "at the time of acting, they do not abide."
Now, this shall be further explained:
because when the cause possesses power, the condition must necessarily lack power;
since they cannot mutually cognize one another, it is said that there is no "cognizer."
This is called the "time of action" when the non-common fruit arises from causes and conditions;
because there is no dwelling upon either cause or condition, it is said to be "non-dwelling."
This refers to the unique nature of cause and effect.

At the very moment it is producing its effect, this activity does not abide in the cause, does not abide in the conditions, nor does it abide in the effect; therefore, it is said that "at the time of acting, it does not abide."
This meaning should be understood as precisely the sense of "bondage" within the sūtras.

Third, regarding the classification of those who conform to great compassion: this refers to various non-Buddhists who seek a distinct liberation, taking the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and so forth to be nirvāṇa.

The Bodhisattva contemplates this and sees that it consists merely of the links of existence; it is not free from the bonds of defilement and thus loses the truly pure virtue of nirvāṇa. Therefore, he gives rise to great compassion, and thus it is said: "In this way, further defilement gives rise to bondage."
Fourth, regarding the internal differentiation of all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is called "conformity to bondage" within the contemplation of beginninglessness.
This means that arising and ceasing are merely bondage, for they conform to that which is without a fundamental basis.
The tenth [section], the contemplation on the exhaustion of non-existence (*akiṃcana-kṣaya-vipaśyanā*), also consists of four gates.

First, according to the sūtra: it clarifies that once the illusory characteristics of these links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) are exhausted, one accords with non-existence and penetrates to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

This demonstrates that while conventional reality is not destroyed, it is eternally true; thus it is said that "conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise," which is to say they accord with non-existence (*anupalabdhi*).
Question:
Since the arising of formations from ignorance accords with existence (*upalabdhi*), why is it said here that they accord with non-existence?
Answer:

Following the sequence of the preceding sections, we arrive here to demonstrate that when ignorance (*avidyā*) actually gives rise to formations (*saṃskāra*), one accordingly enters into principle by way of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Such is the intended meaning of the sutra.
Question:
Since the forward contemplation is thus, what is the reverse? Answer:

Since birth is already the exhaustion of intrinsic nature, one is then detached from both existence and non-existence; therefore, it is said that this is taught as the contemplation of the exhaustion of non-existence in accordance with reality.
The meaning of the teaching is the same as before; one should reflect upon and grasp its intent.
Secondly, regarding the renunciation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is called the fourth [truth] because it is not produced without a cause; for it accords with existence (*bhava*).
Why, then, is it "accordant with non-existence" in the Sūtra, yet called "accordant with existence" in the Śāstra?
Explanation:

The intent of the Sūtra is to explain by returning conditions to principle, while the intent of the Śāstra is to explain by following nature through its characteristics; each manifests a distinct meaning, and thus this statement is made. Furthermore, another explanation states:
In this treatise, the term "conforming to existence" (sanniveśa) is intended to reveal non-arising; therefore, its meaning does not differ from that of the Sūtra.
Below, the argument specifically refutes causelessness.
First is the reductio ad absurdum (*prasanga*), which states that [if there were no cause], things would arise eternally.
Second is refutation by subversion, meaning that [the teaching] never arises;
third is refutation by censure and interrogation, beginning with "This is not the Buddha's Dharma," meaning that it propounds causelessness, which is the greatest of false views.
The section beginning with "If so" concludes that [the teaching] is not without cause.
The section beginning with "This is called" explains and summarizes the discourse.

Regarding the term "truth of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇasatya*): "characteristics" refers to the characteristics of the previously established answers, while "truth" refers to the distinction between the two previously mentioned truths.
Third, regarding the classification according to those who conform to [the pursuit of] great compassion: this refers to various non-Buddhists who seek a distinct liberation as their nirvana.

The Bodhisattva observes that these are merely the phenomena of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) consisting of the twelve links of dependent origination; they follow along with the pursuit of existence and falsely grasp the formless realm as liberation. Thus, they lose the quality of the self (*ātman-guṇa*) of supramundane nirvana. Out of pity for them, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion.

Fourth, regarding the classification according to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*): this is the ninth, called "various observations" (*nānāvidhadarśana*). This refers to the fact that the characteristics of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) are distinct and each possesses many types of forms; hence it is called "various."
"Conforming to" (anuloma) below explains by manifesting its characteristics.
This is the mundane realm of the three realms of existence; because great wisdom illuminates this, it serves as a gateway.
The separate explanations of the ten gateways are now complete.
Second, the section beginning with "Thus, in reverse and direct order" summarizes the ten chapters.
Since it speaks of ten types of reverse and direct order, it is clear that within each of the preceding ten sections, both reverse and direct orders are present.
Regarding the absence of reverse contemplation (*anuloma-pratyavekṣā*) in the preceding text, it is because that section was abbreviated.

The ten points—1) the arrangement of the branches of existence, 2) their subsumption within the single mind, 3) the mutual generation of their functional powers, 4) their sequential interconnection, 5) the revolving wheel of the three paths, 6) the cause and effect across the three periods of time, 7) the faults of the three types of suffering, 8) the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) arising from causes, 9) appearing as existent yet being non-existent, and 10) their dissolution into equality—are all clearly visible when correlated with and concluded by the preceding ten sections of the text.
The explanation of the practice of the non-abiding path is concluded.
Within the third major section, "The Excellence of its Fruit," there are two distinct parts:
first, the fruit of the practice; second, the fruit of the stages.
Regarding the preceding section, the treatise is divided into five parts:
first, attaining the practice of remedies and the removal of obstacles, which is the fruit of the previously mentioned remedy for superior pride;
second, attaining the excellence of cultivation, which is the fruit of the previously mentioned practice of the non-abiding path.

Regarding the third attainment of samādhi: it is explained as the fruit by virtue of its superior counteractive power compared to what preceded it. That is to say, while the previous cultivation of the three liberations was explained as the counteractive treatment itself, when that counteraction further increases, it is termed the "superiority of samādhi."

Regarding the four unbreakable minds (*catur-akṣaya-citta*): they are described as the fruit in contrast to the preceding stage of abandoning hindrances. Because the hindrances have been extinguished, the mind of samādhi cannot be destroyed; thus it is called the "unbreakable mind."

Regarding the five powers of mastery (*vaśitā-bala*): these are explained as the fruits resulting from the preceding practices; that is to say, the unimpeded progress based upon those prior practices is termed the power of mastery.
In the subsequent detailed explanation, these five are treated in five separate sections.
Regarding the first section of the text, there are two parts:
first, the clarification of the excellence of the practice; second, the manifestation of the removal of obstacles.
Within the former, the meaning of the three gates of liberation is explained through five brief headings:
First is the essence, second is the aspect, third is the remedy for hindrances, fourth is the inclusion of practices, and fifth is the differentiation, as explained separately.

The passage beginning with "This bodhisattva follows the twelve links of dependent origination" correctly demonstrates that within the ten preceding gates, each link of existence possesses these three gates of the contemplation of emptiness.
First, the gateway of emptiness is clarified, which is divided into three parts within the treatise:
first, seeing that sentient beings lack self;
second, regarding the emptiness of intrinsic nature, seeing that phenomena lack self—this phrase is omitted in the sutra.
Third, those two [actions] do not exist, because no agent is perceived.

That is to say, the first two phrases reveal that the substance of the two selves is empty, while the final phrase manifests that the function of the two selves is empty; this also means that the former is "no-self" (anātman) and the latter is "no-belonging-to-self" (anātmīya).
The phrase "Thus" and what follows below constitutes the conclusion, which may be understood accordingly.
Second, regarding the passage beginning with "extinguishing this matter," the gate of signlessness (*animitta*) is also explained through three meanings.

First, as for "extinguishing obstacles": because one contemplates that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) is extinguished, it is said that "this matter is extinguished."
Question:
What is the difference between this and the previously mentioned selflessness (*anātman*)? Answer:
Previously, the absence of self was elucidated by means of all phenomena; here, however, the intention is to eliminate the mind that grasps at characteristics, and thus it is not the same.
Second, regarding the attainment of the antidote: "constant liberation is manifest," though this phrase is omitted in the sutra.

Regarding "the three aspects of mindfulness do not function": because one sees that in the locus of causes and conditions there is not even the slightest dharma-characteristic capable of arising, it is said that "the others do not continue.
Master Huiyuan stated: "Among these three, the first, 'extinguishing hindrances,' means that the grasping nature of the mind perishes;
the second, 'attaining principle as the antidote'..."
Third, the mind that grasps at signs ceases, and not even the slightest phenomenon is seen to arise; thus, one is free from the discriminating mind that grasps at signs.
The previous cessation of grasping at intrinsic nature differs from that of ordinary beings, while the present freedom from grasping at signs differs from that of the two vehicles.
3. Regarding the section beginning with "Knowing these two," this clarifies the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), which also has three parts:
first, the preceding two are the basis for wishlessness; therefore, it says "relying upon."
Second, "not delighting in existence" reveals the essence of wishlessness; therefore, it is called "essential nature.
Third, "only great compassion and so forth" surpasses the two vehicles; therefore, it is called "superior."

Second, from "The Bodhisattva’s Practice" onwards, the excellence of being free from hindrances is clarified: first, being free from that self and so forth is what is abandoned by the gate of emptiness;
second, being free from those with signs is what is abandoned by signlessness;
third, being free from those without signs is what is abandoned by wishlessness; therefore, it is said to be "free from the signs of existence and non-existence."

Because one does not grasp at signlessness (*animitta*), it is called wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); as other sūtras state, "because of signlessness, there is nothing to be wished for or sought"—this is what that means.
Such is the sequence in the treatise.
The passage beginning with "In the fifth stage" cites the inferior to reveal the superior.
First, it cites the fifth stage to reveal the superiority of this gate of emptiness in being free from the self.

This text is inverted; if it were correct, it should state that "by means of the ten kinds of profound and pure minds of equality, one becomes detached," thereby becoming detached from the pride of bodily purity in the fourth stage.
Now, by means of profound emptiness, those two types of self are extinguished; therefore, this is superior.
Second, regarding the abandonment of obstacles in the fourth stage, within this text, the superiority of abandoning activity and reception is manifested.

Third, regarding these six stages and so forth: by citing the ten equalities at the beginning of this stage to refute existence and non-existence, it reveals that the present stage is perfected in signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Since existence and non-existence are all utterly eliminated and dispelled, it is called "superior."
Second, under "Compassionate Mind," the excellence of practice is clarified; this has two parts:
first, the actual practice, and second, the manifestation of the excellence of that practice.
Within the former, there are also two parts:
The first, "the practitioner who initiates courageous cultivation," refers to the initial cultivation that resolutely severs [delusions].
The second, from "the Bodhisattva knows thus" onwards, clarifies the cultivation of one with the resolve of a great man; this refers to the completion of cultivation through decisive resolution.
The preceding section also has two parts.

First is the cultivation of the mind: this refers to contemplating those links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) through the three types of emptiness; because one takes pity on all sentient beings who dwell therein without awakening, it is said that "the mind of compassion increases further. This increase of compassion constitutes the mind of benefiting others.
"Not yet having fulfilled bodhi, etc. refers to the mind of self-benefit.
Below, the excellence of practice is clarified, which consists of two parts:
first, cultivating wisdom without attachment to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); [the second part follows].
Following this, from "transforming sentient beings" onwards, one cultivates compassion and does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Within the former [section], there are also two parts:
first, knowledge; second, revulsion.
Regarding the knowledge of these [phenomena], afflictions, karma, and birth undergo combination and separation, presence and absence, increase and decrease.

Once one realizes that these phenomena possess such defects, one gives rise to weary detachment and understands that they should not be allowed to combine; thus it is said, "I know conditioned things," and so forth.
Therefore, the treatise states: "Knowing that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) have many faults, one distances oneself from the karma and afflictions of birth," and so forth.
It can be understood that what follows concerns the cultivation of compassion to transform sentient beings.
The two types of persons who possess both aspiration and practice are also twofold:
first, wisdom; second, compassion.
Regarding wisdom, that which is called "contemplation of the antidote" (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*) in the treatises takes the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) as its "antidote."
"Seeing more faults than [seeing] views" is a further explanation for establishing [the point].
"The cessation of opposites" clarifies that the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) ceases; hence it is called "the equality of non-existence" (*abhāva-samatā*), and so forth.
"Equal to great compassion" clarifies that the cultivation of pity (*karuṇā*) is likewise to be understood.
Second, from "Then one attains non-obstruction" onwards, it clarifies the excellence of cultivation.
This section has two parts:

first, the manifestation of superior signs. Regarding the treatise’s statement, "Wisdom and great compassion are the superior conformities," this refers back to how each of the two preceding practices contains both compassion and wisdom, which are capable of ascending in conformity [with the ultimate].

Regarding "the unimpeded *prajñā* of the non-abiding path appearing before one": this clarifies that by relying on the aforementioned path of non-abiding compassion and wisdom, the light of the unimpeded knowledge of the Buddha-ground is made to appear before one.
To know that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and nirvāṇa are equal is to understand why wisdom and compassion do not abide [in either].
"Not dwelling together" explains the meaning of non-abiding; it means that wisdom does not coexist with conditioned phenomena, which is why it is said that one "does not abide therein," and so forth.
Furthermore, because compassion abides in the unique unconditioned dharmas (*asādhāraṇa-asamskṛta-dharma*), it is said that "it also does not abide therein," and so forth.
The phrase "because those practices conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-caryā*) are not yet fulfilled" explains the purpose for not abiding.

To fulfill the aids to the path of wisdom, one does not abide in the conditioned; to fulfill the aids to the path of merit, one does not abide in the unconditioned. Therefore, it says, "desiring to be fully endowed with," and so forth.
Third, from "The Bodhisattva abides in the Stage of Presence" onwards, the excellence of the samādhis is elucidated.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the elucidation of the concentration on emptiness; second, the elucidation of the remaining two.
In the former, first the ten types of emptiness are presented as the primary examples, followed by a summary of the many gateways.
Among these, the ten thousand [instances] are referred to as "hundreds of thousands of myriads" in the treatise and the sūtra.
Within the preceding ten emptinesses, the treatise subsumes them into four:
first, contemplation, which refers to the understanding through contemplation;
Second, non-negligence is so named because it gives rise to practice based on understanding and remains free from faults;
third, the attainment of superiority refers to the achievement of virtues through cultivation and the acquisition of supreme qualities;
fourth, acting according to circumstances refers to the arising of function based upon those virtues.
Samādhi is the foundation of great function; therefore, it is called the "cause" (hetu).

Regarding the initial stage, excluding the fourth samādhi, the remaining five are termed "contemplations" (vipaśyanā): first, the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā); second, the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā).
Third, combining and taking the two emptinesses is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Fourth, observing based on the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), within the two kinds of Tathāgata-garbha, this is the empty Tathāgata-garbha; therefore, it is called "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*).

Fifth, observing the seven evolving consciousnesses, they arise in conjunction with the Tathāgata-garbha and lack any self-nature; therefore, it is called "Emptiness through Conjunction" (*saṃyoga-śūnyatā*).
The *Laṅkāvatāra* says: "The seven consciousnesses are likewise; they arise in conjunction with the mind.
It also says: "There are eight non-disintegrating marks, yet even these marks are markless."
This is what is meant by that.
Regarding the two forms of non-negligence: the thorough cultivation of discernment is the "one's own portion" (svabhāga);
tireless application in practice is "superior progress" (viśeṣagamana).
Second, because cultivation is perfected, it is called "ultimate.
Third, regarding the attainment of superior merit: since these excellent qualities arise and manifest based upon emptiness, it is called "arising from emptiness."
Regarding the four matters of causal conditions: these refer to the other three samādhis.

First, by relying on this concentration of emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi), one causes the cognitive hindrances (jñeyāvaraṇa) to be purified; because of this matter, it is called "departing from delusion according to reality."
Second, based on emptiness, one gives rise to compassion and does not abandon sentient beings; therefore, the treatise and the sūtra refer to this as "not abandoning emptiness.

Third, based on the samādhi of emptiness, one vows to remain within the various realms of existence while distancing oneself from defiled attachment, which is called "freedom from conceptualization"; yet, while conforming to existence, one remains free from such non-conceptualization.
The remaining text may be understood.
The fourth section, beginning with "This bodhisattva abides in the presence," clarifies the attainment of the fruit of the indestructible mind.
Among the ten statements, the first one is general.
The profound mind (*adhyāśaya*) is deep-penetrating and immovable; it refers to a mind that remains unshaken when discussing or studying the sūtras, being firm and non-retrogressive.
The remaining nine [aspects] are distinct:
the first is faith-contemplation regarding the principle (*tattva*).
Second, they are capable of being trained through practice;
third, they are not terrified by profound and secret matters;
fourth, they do not lose their own portion [of realization].
Fifth, advancing toward excellence without ceasing;
sixth, not envying the virtues of others and not violating one's own precepts—because these two practices are universally pure, it is called "vast mind";
seventh, generating benefit for all through universal compassion.
Eighth, seeking the wisdom of higher stages;
ninth, skillfully transforming sentient beings.
The fifth section, "Such minds as these," and following, clarify the excellence of the power of mastery.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the general; second, the specific; and third, the conclusion.
In the general section, "such minds as these" refers to the attainment of *prajñā*.
"Superior growth" refers to the excellence of the power of practice.
"Conforming to Bodhi" means being able to penetrate deeply.
There are nine types of superior power; these are categorized into general and specific divisions:

1. The power of subduing [the afflictions], 2. the power of superior understanding, 3. the power of relinquishing the small [vehicle], 4. the power of deep faith, 5. the power of crushing Māra, 6. the power of treating delusions, 7. the power of universal treatment, 8. the power of skillful transformation, and 9. the power of treating obstacles; these are all as explained in the treatise.
Third, the section beginning with "This bodhisattva" concludes the meaning, which is understandable.
Second, the section beginning with "The bodhisattva abides in the manifest" clarifies the fruits of the stage; herein, the three fruits are the same as those mentioned previously.
Regarding the three aspects of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*):
first, the practice of pliancy consists of inwardly hearing and receiving the true Dharma.
One who practices according to the teaching attains the light of wisdom through samādhi by means of the treatises and sūtras.
Commentary:
By means of the retention of meaning (*arthadhāraṇī*), one is able to practice according to what has been taught.
"Because of that matter" refers to the matter of that retention of meaning; for this reason, this is stated.
Relying on the supreme samādhi, one attains śamatha; this is the aforementioned samādhi of suchness.
Vipassanā is the aforementioned excellence of the light of wisdom.
Regarding "having practiced and maintained each practice," this means being able to uphold those practices.

As for the statement that such a person is "refined and pure" up to "luminously pure" within the context of refinement and purity (*parikarma-viśuddhi*), it refers to liberation from those obstacles; thus, it explains refinement and purity.
Because it realizes that meaning, it is explained as "knowing the treasury of the Buddha's Dharma.
Within the explanation of the metaphor, the phrase "predominance of supramundane wisdom" reveals the purity of the essence of realized knowledge (*adhigama-jñāna*).
Regarding "the radiance becomes increasingly superior," this demonstrates that the excellence of its function reveals its essence.
By means of the superiority of the light of the wisdom of teaching, it is shown that the wisdom of realization also increases.
The phrase "up to the wisdom of skillful means" and so forth explains the text concerning the combined metaphors.
Unimpeded *prajñā* is the light of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Skillful means (*upāya*) is the wisdom of the non-abiding path mentioned previously.

Regarding the two explanations of the purity of the knowledge of the teachings: in the previous stage, the metaphor of the lunar disk was used and is thus small; in this stage, the metaphor of moonlight is used and is therefore vast and great, making it superior to the former.
To follow along with the four currents is the conduct of Māra; therefore, it is called the "path of Māra.
This is termed the "evil Māra," which is that path of Māra.
Third, the section beginning with "This is called" concludes the explanation of its characteristics.
The summary of the maturation of karma and the wisdom of vows may both be understood by reference to what preceded.
Within the third major section, the Section of Repeated Verses, there are thirty-nine verses divided into five parts;
the first three verses concern the superior pride regarding the ten equal dharmas as an antidote.

The second [section] consists of twenty verses concerning the excellence of the practice of the path of non-abiding; therein, the first verse provides a general contemplation of dependent origination regarding the mind of the preceding first stage;
the next five verses provide a sequential contemplation of the initial section on causes and conditions;
and the following two verses provide a contemplation subsumed within a single mind.
The fourth has two verses on self-assistance and accomplishment;
the fifth has one verse on non-separation;
the sixth has one verse on the uninterruptedness of the three paths.
Verse 71 distinguishes the three time periods;
verse 81 distinguishes the three types of suffering;
and verse 91 is a transitional verse that contemplates the fetters of the ninth birth.
Eleven verses summarize the eighth [section], the contemplation on dependent origination;
one verse and a half summarize the tenth, the contemplation on the exhaustion of existence;
and two and a half verses in the twelfth [section] summarize the names of the ten gates.

3. From "The Bodhisattva thus" onwards, six and a half verses praise the excellence of that fruition. Among these, the first three verses praise the excellence of the antidotes; the next one and a half verses praise the excellence of practice; the next half verse praises the excellence of samādhi; the next half verse praises the excellence of the indestructible mind; and the final verse praises the excellence of sovereign power.

4. Regarding the "Offerings" section below, the eight and a half verses concern the fruits of the stages. Among these, the first four and a half verses concern the fruit of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), while the subsequent four verses concern the fruit of karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
The fruit of the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) is omitted from the verse summary.
The final verse of the five concludes the exposition on the profound connection.
This completes the explanation of the sixth stage.
Regarding the seventh stage, the Dūraṃgamā (Far-Reaching), there are three parts to its explanation:
First, regarding the final stage of effortful application (*prayoga*), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Because one has reached the very end of the stage of effortful application.

Vasubandhu’s commentary explains: "This means that within this stage, one attains the ultimate limit of effortful application; although one cannot be shaken by any mental images (*nimitta*), one is still said to possess 'application' (*sa-prayoga*) with respect to the signless (*animitta*)."
Second, regarding the two meanings, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:

"Because one is able to far-reachingly realize and enter into the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that is signless (*animitta*), flawless, and uninterrupted, and because it is in close proximity to the pure stages (*viśuddhabhūmi*), it is called 'Far-Going' (*dūraṅgama*)."
The commentary explains:
"Without deficiency and without interruption" means it is distant from the preceding six stages and adjacent to the Pure Ground (śuddhāvāsabhūmi), being proximate to the subsequent eighth stage.
These three [phrases] are applied according to these three meanings.

In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, because one reaches the final limit of the stage of effort (*prayoga*) within the dwelling of signlessness (*animitta-vihāra*), thereby transcending the paths of the two vehicles of the world, it is called the "Far-Reaching Ground" (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).
This is consistent with the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "Because one has practiced for a long time the outflow-free, uninterrupted, signless mental application, and the samādhi of liberation, this stage is pure, unobstructed, and unhindered; it is therefore called the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi (The Far-Reaching Stage)."
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states: "In the seventh stage, the bodhisattva draws near to the path of the One Vehicle; this is called 'Far-Going' (*dūraṅgama*).
Question:
Who is it that goes far?"
Answer:
Because the application of effort reaches its ultimate consummation, one can travel far; since one travels far by means of this, it is called the "Far-Going Stage" (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Because it is distant from the three realms and near to the station of the Dharma King, it is called the 'Stage of Distant Body' (*dūraṅgama-bhūmi*)."
The *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) is titled "Reaching the Distant Ground.
Regarding the second reason for its arrival, there are also three meanings:

first, since the preceding [sections] relied upon the two vehicles to collectively manifest the successive and increasingly superior stages of the bodhisattva, it was necessary for this [sūtra] to arrive.

Second, in the stage prior to the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*), [the practice] was not yet pure; now, entering this stage, it becomes purely signless, and for this reason one must come here.
Third, the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) was not yet fulfilled in the previous stage, whereas it is fulfilled within this stage; therefore, one comes here.

Regarding the third, the obstacles to be abandoned: according to the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), this refers to abandoning the obstacle of the habitual tendencies toward subtle marks (*sūkṣma-nimitta-vāsanā-āvaraṇa*).
The commentary explains:

because the sixth stage involves a slight degree of contemplation with marks (*animittābhiniveśa*), it is termed a "subtle mark-obstruction"; since the seventh stage consists of purely markless contemplation (*animitta-bhāvanā*), this [sixth-stage state] constitutes an obstacle to it.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The obstacle of the manifestation of subtle characteristics refers to a portion of the innate aspect (*sahaja*) within the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that clings to the manifestation of subtle characteristics involving arising and ceasing; this obstructs the sublime path of non-characteristics in the seventh stage, and upon entering the seventh stage, it can be permanently severed."
For this reason, it is said that on the seventh stage one abandons two delusions along with their coarse residues (*dausthulya*):

first, the delusion of the manifestation of subtle signs, which refers here to the grasping at the existence of arising because one still apprehends the subtle signs of birth within the flow of saṃsāra;

second, the delusion of purely intentional seeking for the signless, which refers here to the grasping at the existence of cessation because one still apprehends the process of returning to extinction.

"Because the subtle marks of cessation have been extinguished, one diligently seeks through exclusive attention to the signless (*animitta-manasikāra*), yet has not yet been able to give rise to superior practice within emptiness (*śūnyatā*) regarding existence.
The commentary explains:
