to reckon the phenomenal aspects produced by the former two natures as real is countered by the absence of characteristics.

Regarding the reality of the "subsequent limit" (*paścimānta*): it refers to the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood at the subsequent limit, which is free from entanglements. To counteract this [misconception], it is established that there is no [intrinsic] accomplishment.

Furthermore, among these four [aspects of Buddha-nature], the first is the Buddha-nature abiding in its own nature (*prakṛtistha-gotra*); the next two are the Buddha-nature brought forth (*samudānīta-gotra*); and the last one is the Buddha-nature that attains the fruit (*phalaprāpta-gotra*).

Furthermore, the first path pertains to the stage prior to the path—that is, the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); the next one pertains to the stage of the three types of worthy ones (*tri-śaikṣa*); the next one pertains to the stages of the noble ones (*bhūmi*); and the last one pertains to the stage subsequent to the path.
This can be understood through general inference.
Furthermore, these four points may be understood as successive clarifications of doubts.

Regarding the fifth point, "the reality of the prior limit": in contrast to the "subsequent limit" of the Buddha-fruit, it is said that the defilement of ordinary beings constitutes the prior limit. To counteract this, it is stated that there is "no destruction," clarifying that afflictions are themselves empty and thus indestructible.
This is because within the minds of sentient beings there are two aspects:
first, the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is called the pure aspect; thus, as previously stated, the pure aspect is non-arising.
Second, the storehouse of afflictions (*kleśagarbha*), which is called the defiled aspect; thus, as here stated, the defiled aspect is non-arising.

Sixth, regarding "the reality of the defiled and pure portions": this refers to the stage of cultivation when one turns away from defilement and moves toward purity; because this is countered [by the realization of emptiness], there is no coming.

Seventh, regarding "the reality of the exhaustion of all sentient beings": sentient beings move toward Nirvana; because this is countered, it is said that there is no going—the sūtra and the treatise refer to this as "non-exhaustion."
The second [point], that the intrinsic nature is unarisen, is omitted in this sutra.
The treatise states: "That the intrinsic nature is unarisen means that phenomena lack selfhood (*dharmanairātmya*).
Because those phenomena lack selfhood, they have no inherent essence (*svabhāva*); as the sutra says, 'because there is no existence of an essence.'"

Regarding the phrase "he contemplates the objects," this clarifies that the principle is not non-existent; that is to say, because the objects contemplated in the preceding stages are also the dharmas accepted in this stage, one cannot say they do not exist.

The following clarifies that principle is non-dual; that is, because principle does not exist apart from phenomena, it is called "non-dual. This is identical to the previous passage’s statement that there is "neither duality nor exhaustion.

Third, the section beginning with "no beginning and no middle" clarifies that numerical distinctions are unarisen, because within the three periods of time, defiled and pure phenomena neither increase nor decrease.

This means that the prior limit is defiled, the subsequent limit is pure, and the middle limit is both defiled and pure; because these three limits are non-arising, there is neither increase nor decrease.
Fourth, from "Entering the Tathāgata" onwards, it clarifies that activity is non-arising, because within True Suchness (tathatā) there is the pure, non-conceptual Buddha-wisdom.
The section beginning with "In this way" concludes the preceding explanation.
Next, the section beginning with "Manifesting" explains the purity of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Regarding the phrase "all mind, thought, and consciousness," there are two types of "all": [1] all that is internal, and [2] all that is external.
In the first stage, one is free from the conceptualization and discrimination of the mind that experiences retribution; therefore, it is said that one "practices detachment" and so forth.

In the second stage, one is free from the conceptualization and discrimination of the mind of skillful means; therefore, it is said that one "appropriates the conceptualization of the nature of differentiation."
Regarding "perception" (*saṃjñā*): it is the perception that is free from obstructive phenomena.
The phrase "not the absence of the perception of remedial phenomena" is used to exclude ambiguity.
That perception of the remedy possesses three kinds of excellence within the lower stages:

First, because it proceeds spontaneously without effort, it is said to be "without attachment," meaning that regarding the supreme fruit of Buddhahood, one acts with effortless spontaneity without needing to give rise to craving or seeking.
Second, regarding the characteristic of pervading all phenomena (*sarvadharma-lakṣaṇa*): because it manifests as a broad antidote, it is said that "all phenomena are like space.
Third, regarding entering into the immovable natural progression of *tathatā*: this reveals the profundity of the antidote.
It should be understood that the phrase "like space" functions across two lines [of verse].
Third, from "entering immovability" (*aniñjya*) onwards, the section explaining the attainment of superior practice (*viśeṣa-caryā*) is clarified.
This contains two parts:
First, the excellence of profound practice, which means manifesting transcendence in contrast to what precedes;
second, the excellence of arousal [of bodhicitta], which reveals entry in contrast to what follows.
Within the former, there are two parts:
First, the profound practice is explained in general, meaning that one enters this stage and practices what is mysterious and profound.
Below, there are seven distinct sections, which are grouped into three parts:

the first three sections clarify the distinct excellence of the objects within this stage; the next two sections clarify the vastness of the correct practice within this stage; and the final two sections clarify the quiescent cessation resulting from the removal of hindrances within this stage.
There are three metaphors here, which illustrate these three divisions from the last back to the first.
Among the seven [types of bodhisattvas], the first is called a "Bodhisattva of Profound Practice" because their practice is difficult to enter and is profound.

The second is the "Bodhisattva of Shared Practice," so called because they share the same [practice] as those on the pure stages (*śuddhabhūmi*); that is to say, the stage of purely untainted (*anāsrava*) states is termed the "pure stages."
Because he is identical to those in this stage, it is said that "the world cannot fathom him.
That he cannot be fathomed is like a grain of barley within a heap of barley; its distinction cannot be discerned.
The treatise states that the name of the sūtra is "Incapable of Conceptual Differentiation.
Because the three spheres are profound and neither the grasper nor the grasped appear before one, it is said to be "free from all marks" (*sarvanimittāpagata*).
As for the phrase "protecting against all conceptualizations of obstacles," this refers to guarding against all conceptualizations of obstructive phenomena.
To distinguish it from the notion of a method for treatment, it is called "freedom from attachment.
Fourth, its practice is profound because the practices for benefiting oneself and others are vast;
this is omitted in this sutra.

Fifth is the profundity of non-retrogression (*avivartya-gāmbhīrya*): this means that those of the two vehicles cannot displace or destroy its excellence; hence it says, "all śrāvakas and so forth. Sixth is the profundity of being free from hindrances (*vighna-vigama-gāmbhīrya*):
this means being free from the hindrance of effortful application (*prayoga-āvaraṇa*); hence it says, "profoundly and greatly transcending."
Seventh is the profundity of the manifestation of the remedies (*pratipakṣa*). This means that the practices which serve as remedies are constantly present; hence it is said they "manifest.
In the sutra, this is termed the "manifestation of tranquility" (*śānti*), which refers to the tranquility of *tathatā* (suchness) rather than the tranquility of mundane phenomena.
The following explains the three metaphors as illustrations of what was previously stated.
"The metaphor of cessation" indicates those formations.
"Because it is quiescent" explains the intended meaning of the present metaphor.

In the explanation of the analogy, the phrase "because there is no basis for them" clarifies that in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the primary mind (*cittarāja*) does not function; since mental factors such as perception (*saṃjñā*) have nothing upon which to rely, they likewise do not function.
"Because one has attained effortless spontaneity" explains the diligent application of means (*upāya*), wherein the activities of the three karmas have been stilled and extinguished.
Regarding the phrase "the practice of retribution is accomplished," there are two interpretations:
first, from the perspective of the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*), it is said that "one has attained those factors contrary [to the afflictions]."
Secondly, with respect to the path of realization, it is said that one "abides well within the true suchness (tathatā) of the ālayavijñāna.
However, the fundamental consciousness has two aspects:
during the state of ordinary beings, one abides only in the aspect of deluded defilement; now, in this state, one abides in the aspect of true purity.
If one reaches the stage of Buddhahood, one dwells solely in *tathatā* (suchness), and it is not called the *ālaya-tathatā*.
Since there is still the suffering of the retributive existence of transformation (*pariṇāmi-vaipākika-duḥkha*) at this present stage, both are mentioned together.
Regarding the phrase "abiding in great seclusion," this refers to abiding in the accomplishment of the practice of maturation (*vipākacaryā*) within this treatise.
In the explanation of the second analogy of waking from sleep, it demonstrates how, within this practice, one guards against the perception of those faults.

Regarding those who possess the perception of correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna-saṃjñā*): it is like awakening from a dream; although the dream-image is absent, there is the perception of having awakened. The case in question is just like this:
although one abandons the perceptions of false cultivation belonging to the preceding stage, it is not that the perception of the correct wisdom of this present stage is absent.

Regarding the statement "this practice is quiescent," it reveals that this correct wisdom is itself eternally quiescent; thus, it differs from what preceded, as it reveals the profundity of this practice.
The section beginning with "In this regard" provides a further analysis based on purity.
Regarding "the two minds of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa do not function": this explains the non-functioning of the two minds mentioned in the sutra.

It is like crossing a river in a dream, where this shore symbolizes saṃsāra and the far shore symbolizes nirvāṇa; once one has awakened, both this and that vanish. This is called relying on purity, and thus it is said that the two minds do not function.

Regarding the statement that "the mental engagement with the recollection of objects of experience does not function," this explains that various remembered thoughts no longer manifest before one; that is to say, even within a dream, the mental representations of experiencing objects such as boats or rafts no longer appear.
In the explanation of the third analogy regarding birth in the Brahma-heaven, the passage beginning with "just as being born in the Form Realm" concludes that [the mind] does not function.
This stage is such that the minds of the lower stages do not function at all; it is described as "emerging" in relation to those below.
Regarding "attaining the stage of retribution" (*vipākabhūmi*), this is stated here to clarify its attainment.
This explanation illustrates the meaning of the metaphor by means of being free from superior fetters (*saṃyojana*).

In the subsequent detailed classification, that which follows [the flow] is the mundane mind (*laukikacitta*) and that which does not follow [the flow] is the supramundane mind (*lokottaracitta*); therefore, it is called the "two divisions."
"Mind and so forth" refers to taking up the mind along with thought (*manas*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), as well as recollection and conceptualization; these constitute "conformable activity.
"Buddha and so forth" refers to taking up the Buddha along with *bodhi* (enlightenment), *nirvāṇa*, and so on; these constitute "non-conformable activity."

Below, within the section on the "Non-conforming Practice," three further gates are opened. While the Sūtra addresses only the Mahāyāna, the Master of the Treatise (Śāstrakāra) provides a comparative analysis of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Regarding the first point, "distinction" (*viśeṣa*): it is not that the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ in kind that constitutes a distinction; rather, the distinction refers to the difference between the two—phenomena (*dharma*) and birth (*janman*)—within the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.

Regarding the second point, concerning the distinction between sentient beings and phenomena within the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna: this "distinction" does not mean that sentient beings and phenomena are inherently different; rather, it clarifies that within these two vehicles, the various modes of arising are themselves distinct, and the various phenomena are themselves separate.

Regarding the third point, the distinction between those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*): this is a differentiation of persons made within the context of the Hīnayāna; it does not mean that the difference between "training" and "beyond training" itself constitutes a distinction. Rather, it clarifies the difference between various types of those in training, and the same applies to those beyond training.
The preceding section concludes the opening of the gates.

Regarding the explanation of the distinctions between the Buddha and others in terms of *nirvāṇa*, this is presented by citing the sūtra for comparative clarity: one should know that "the Buddha" corresponds to the first phrase, "the Buddha’s mind and so forth" encompasses the middle two phrases, and "nirvāṇa" corresponds to the fourth phrase.
Why is it that no distinction is made among worldly practices, yet this differentiation is established within supramundane practices?
Because the supramundane is what great beings seek, there is a fear of defiled grasping; therefore, it is explained in detail so that they may be free from it.
In the subsequent explanation clarifying the intermediate section, the explanation of "conformable practice" can be understood first.
Regarding the subsequent explanation of "non-conformable practice," the phrase "distinctions between great and small" serves as a general summary.

In the following specific details, within the Mahāyāna, the Buddha and Bodhisattvas are the persons and *nirvāṇa* is the dharma; within the Hīnayāna, *nirvāṇa* is the dharma and the Arhats and others are the persons.
Second, regarding the distinctions between persons and dharmas, these may be understood from the commentary of the *Śāstra*.

As for the distinctions among Śrāvaka Arhats of the Hīnayāna, as set forth in the *Abhidharma*, there are six types of difference: namely, those subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*), those who attain through reflection (*cetanādharman*), those who attain through protection (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), those who abide [in their state] (*sthitākampya*), those who excel (*prativedhanādharman*), and those who are immovable (*akopyadharman*).
The *Tattvasiddhi* contains nine [chapters], all of which are explained extensively therein;
the remaining passages may be understood accordingly.
Second, from the words "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, it clarifies the initiation of superior practice.
Within this, there are two parts:

first, clarifying that through the power of his original vows he abides [in this state] and is exhorted by all Buddhas; second, from "If [the Buddhas] do not bestow... onwards, clarifying the benefits of such exhortation.
Within the former, there are also two parts:
First is the dwelling of the original vow; second, from "Furthermore, all Buddhas" onwards, clarifies the encouragement to resolve.
Within the former, "conforming to this stage" is the meaning of "dwelling" (*vihāra*) in the sūtra upon which this treatise is based.

"By means of the original vow" explains the basis for abiding; that is to say, having come from the preceding stage, seeking together with others the gate of non-arising forbearance (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) of this very stage is called the "original vow."
Having attained it, one abides by means of the breath; therefore, it is called "abiding.
Regarding the meaning of this abiding, there are two ways of explanation:
first, the explicit meaning, and second, the intended purpose.
The first part clarifies that various bodhisattvas abide or do not abide; generally, there are four explanations:
first, the analysis of entry through contemplation, which means not abiding at the beginning but delighting in abiding at the end.
Previously, while on the stages, one sought to advance toward non-arising; because this had not yet been attained, one did not abide.
Now that this has been attained, one abides because of delighting in tranquility.
Second, regarding the discrimination of the arising of practice: at the beginning one delights in abiding, but in the end one does not abide.
Now, within this stage, one first attains non-arising and dwells therein because of delighting in tranquility;
later, through the Buddha’s exhortation, one initiates superior practice and therefore does not dwell [in that state].

Thirdly, regarding the distinction of abiding in tranquility: from beginning to end there is constant abiding, meaning that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas never for a moment abandon what they have realized and entered.
Regarding the fourth, the discrimination of the arising of activity: all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not abide anywhere, yet they constantly follow along with the world to benefit sentient beings.
In this present passage, the explanation is based on the first two [types of discrimination].
Second, to clarify the intention behind the teaching on "abiding," there are also four meanings:
first, because bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment have a habitual affinity for tranquility, it is said that they abide by the power of their original vows.

Second, in order to lead those of fixed nature among the two vehicles, it is clarified that even this stage of the bodhisattva is a place of great quiescence where movement and arising still occur; how much more so, then, could what they have attained be considered ultimate?
Third, it is to manifest that this stage is profoundly deep and mysterious, and thus one dwells there because it is difficult to abandon.
Fourth, wherever this profound stream of Dharma exists, the Buddhas will invariably construct the bridge of the seven exhortations; therefore, not a single person shall fall away.
The following section on "Exhortation to Practice" consists of three parts:
first, a general exhortation; second, a specific exhortation beginning with "All Buddhas"; and third, a concluding exhortation beginning with "This bodhisattva."

At the beginning and middle [of this practice], the "Flowing Water" refers to one who abides in the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), performing practices spontaneously without exerting effort, and proceeding toward the fruit of Buddhahood.
This is like a great river that flows toward the vast ocean without depending on human labor.
Why is it not bestowed in the preceding stages?
Because the realization of the Dharma has not yet become profound.
Why is it not bestowed in the subsequent stages?
Because one relies on this to encourage the cultivation of non-abiding,
why is it associated with wisdom?
In reality, it extends to other practices as well, because wisdom is the sovereign of practice.
Why is it given at this stage?
It is because this gate of patience (*kṣānti*) encompasses the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*).
As the subsequent text states: "Furthermore, do not abandon this gate of patience; by relying on its power, one is able to accomplish the great practice."
"Why is the wisdom of the Tathāgata bestowed?
Because it is spoken of in terms of the fruit.

Regarding the creation of causes and conditions, the treatise states: "This bestows the power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom in order to transform that mind which delights in and is satisfied with profound practices."
In the subsequent section on specific exhortations, first he praises what has been attained as being supreme, which is the "higher dharma";
subsequently, from the words "I have," he reveals what has not yet been attained and exhorts them to practice it.
Among these, the seven exhortations are subsumed into two categories:
the first six cite many instances of what has not yet been done to turn back the mind that remains stationary;
the last one clarifies that even a small amount of practice can achieve success to increase the mind that moves forward.
Such is the general method of exhortation regarding the Dharma.
Within the first six [verses], they are subsumed into three pairs:

in the first pair concerning self-benefit and benefiting others, the first clarifies that one's own virtues are not yet perfected, while the latter clarifies that those to be converted have not yet emerged [from suffering].
In the second pair, the former indicates that his transformative vows are not yet fulfilled, while the latter indicates that his own virtues are not yet supreme;
in the third pair, the former clarifies that his transformative activities are not yet extensive, while the latter clarifies that his realization of the Dharma is not yet exhaustive.
The first section contains three distinct parts:
first, the mention of powers and so forth to indicate what has not yet been attained;
second, from "In order to attain" onwards, the formal exhortation to practice and cultivation.
The treatise states: "Because one cannot practice the instructions.
The commentary explains:
"Cannot" is an explanation of the preceding phrase.
The phrase "cultivating the teachings" explains this [preceding] sentence.
The passage "the three should also not be abandoned," etc., clarifies the basis for initiating practice.
The *Śāstra* states, "If one does not abandon these," which is clearly an explanatory reversal that makes the meaning intelligible.
The phrase "relying on that power, one is able to act" is an exegesis in accordance with [the text].
Within the second exhortation, the passage "although you have attained these" clarifies what has been personally realized.
The section beginning with "all ordinary beings" clarifies that others have not yet emerged [from suffering]; herein there are also three parts:
First, there is a general exhortation for ordinary beings, which is called "relying on those sentient beings regarding matters that do not benefit them.
Second, its faults are revealed:
the manifestation of afflictions is unwholesome.
The messenger abandons the tranquility of liberation;
householders possess afflictions, while those who have left the home life possess applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Regarding the three [sections] beginning with "You should," the exhortation for them to exercise compassion can be understood.
In the third exhortation, "you should recollect your original vow" is the general exhortation.
The subsequent section, "recollecting the great vows originally propagated," consists of two specific phrases:
first, "desiring to benefit sentient beings" refers to the expansive mind, which is the vow to transform sentient beings below.
Second, those who wish to attain inconceivable wisdom possess a great mind, aspiring to seek the Buddha-wisdom above.
In the treatise, the preceding phrase is explained based on the aspiration to transform sentient beings, while the subsequent phrase is extensively explained through the practice of wisdom.
Regarding "the ability to transform," this refers to exhorting transformation based on the two preceding meanings; it is called "transforming by relying on names" because it relies on names.
In the fourth exhortation, there are three phrases:
the first, "the nature of all dharmas is such," cites the fact that the attained *dharmatā* is naturally so, thereby preventing the arising of attachment.

Second, the passage beginning with "All Tathāgatas" clarifies that those above have not yet attained equality with the Buddha; it means that the Buddha possesses great function (*mahopāya*) and is not merely one who abides in quiescence.

Third, the passage beginning with "Śrāvakas" clarifies that those below are equal to the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*); it means that even those of fixed nature among the two vehicles abide in quiescence and abandon transformation [of others]. These are words of suppression and discouragement.
The "unshared meaning" (*asādhāraṇārtha*) in the treatise explains the second phrase.
"Fatigue from meritorious practice" (*prayogakheda*) explains the third phrase.
Possessing these two faults is termed "their defilement" (*tad-mala*).
Based on this exhortation to turn [the wheel], it is called "turning according to names.
Within the fifth exhortation, there are two parts;
first, "you should observe us," which cites the Buddha’s six kinds of transformative activities (*nirmāṇakarma*).
Second, from "You now" onwards, the exhortation to initiate cultivation is concluded.
In the treatise, the activity of transformation is explained first.
Regarding the phrase "immeasurable bodies" and so forth, this cites the scriptural text.

Regarding those who have achieved power through the Buddha-dharma: when they cultivate and perfect the Buddha-dharma within their own bodies and so forth, it is understood that they possess the power to transform sentient beings.
As for the statement "manifesting based on benefiting sentient beings," this defines their practice; that is to say, these six are all taught in reliance upon altruism.
Next, from the passage "This matter of benefiting sentient beings" onwards, there is an extensive explanation that all six types [of activities] are for the purpose of transforming sentient beings.
Among these, regarding "subduing and gathering": those who are virtuous are gathered through light;
those who are evil are subdued by means of the wheel—referring to the three wheels.
Second, the section beginning with "The Tathāgata performs the immeasurable" explains the concluding exhortation to initiate practice.
Within this sixth exhortation, there are also two parts:
first, the passage beginning with "You have now just attained," clarifies that what has been attained is not yet extensive.
Second, from "We... onwards, the text cites what has not yet been attained to exhort [the practitioner] to arouse it.

Within the treatise: first, there is the entry into this dharma-gate; second, there is the performance of the functional activity of this dharma-gate; third, there is the uninterrupted continuation of this functional activity.
The remainder of the text is self-evident.
In the seventh exhortation, it clarifies that one should do little by way of increasing the resolve for renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-citta*).
Within this, three kinds of immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are first set forth.
"You should" [indicates] the exhortation to exhaustively attain thorough penetration.
Regarding the statement "only a few remain" in the treatise, it means that for those who have not yet attained it, the fruit of Buddhahood is not far off; hence, it says "only a few remain.
The phrase "according to what is seen," etc., explains the three immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
Brief contemplation achieves success; this explains "thorough penetration as it truly is.
Because this increases the resolve for departure (*niṣkrama-citta*), it is called "turning.
Second, from "This bodhisattva" onwards, the summary exhortation is clear.
The second section, beginning with "O Sons of the Buddha," clarifies the benefits achieved through the encouragement [to remain].
This section has two parts:

first, it contrasts the aforementioned abiding in the original vows to demonstrate the loss incurred by not being encouraged; specifically, the commentary explains those who would otherwise enter *nirvāṇa* as being those for whom wisdom is manifested. This interpretation of the sūtra’s intent means that the mention of this cessation is intended to reveal the Buddha and his wisdom.

Second, from "By means of all Buddhas" onwards, there is an exhortation directed toward the aforementioned Buddhas, which reveals the benefits of such exhortation. Within this section, there are the Dharma, the analogy, and the application.
In the Dharma portion, there are also three parts:

first, clarifying that the Buddhas bestow wisdom upon those who enter the gate [of practice]. The *Śāstra* explains that among the causes for gathering merit within those practices, the one that is most excellent is the basis for bestowing wisdom; that is to say, within the practices initiated therein, the cause for gathering merit subsumed by the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena) is the most preeminent, and therefore the Buddhas bestow wisdom.
"Teaching together" refers to correct understanding and wisdom.
The fact that all Buddhas collectively exhort [the practitioner] is termed "teaching together.
In the section beginning with "In a single thought-moment," it clarifies that because of this exhortation, the arousal of practice is swift; this can be understood from the commentary.
3. From "Why is this so? onwards is the section of questions and answers providing an analytical explanation.
It asks: why is it that the practices cultivated during the two preceding great *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas do not equal the practice generated in this single thought-moment?
In the subsequent explanation, first, by means of "one body" and so forth, it is shown that the former does not equal the present.
This "immeasurable" [state] distinguishes this as surpassing what preceded it.
Question:
Question: Since there were a hundred bodies in the first stage (*bhūmi*) and a thousand in the second, why is it said here that there is "one"? Answer:
In reality, the retribution-body (*vipākaphala-kāya*) is one, while the transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) number a hundred and so forth; therefore, they are not different.
Within this, there are eleven phrases.

Regarding the first, "immeasurable body," the commentary explains that it is because one resolves upon the bodies of all bodhisattvas as being identical to one's own body. By the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one causes one's own body to become identical to the bodies of all bodhisattvas; therefore, whatever is cultivated by others is cultivated by oneself. This is due to the power of the wisdom of identity (*samatā-jñāna*).
This is not the intended meaning of the text. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
by the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one causes one's own body to become immeasurable, equal in number to all bodhisattvas; is this not, indeed, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)?
Commentary:
This means that because this Bodhisattva does not emerge from contemplation, he immediately manifests clouds of bodies in accordance with the Dharma-realm; these are actual virtues, not emanations.
This is the meaning of the text.
The arising of sounds and so forth should be understood by analogy with the body.
Regarding these ten phrases,
those based on the first six— which concern the teaching and transformation of sentient beings— are for the benefit of others.
Second, regarding those who rely on the aids to the path, the next two phrases refer to practices for one's own benefit.
Third, regarding those who rely on the purification of obstacles, it should be understood that this clarifies the purity of the qualities and functions of the final two phrases.
These ten phrases possess these three meanings, which will be explained individually below.

"Acting according to the body" refers to the immeasurable body; that is, manifesting whatever body is appropriate for the dharma in which one dwells, such as Avalokiteśvara dwelling in the body of great compassion, and so forth.
Second, "conformity with speech" refers to immeasurable sound; that is, in accordance with the teachings expounded, the vocal sounds are likewise immeasurable.
Third, "conformity with the knowledge of the basis" refers to immeasurable wisdom, because it conforms to that which is known.

Fourth, regarding "arising according to what is grasped": this refers to the various different forms and types across immeasurable places of birth; it is the spontaneously born body (*upapāduka-kāya*) that arises together with its species, being free from volitional effort.
Fifth, regarding "according to which land": this refers to immeasurable pure lands.
Sixth, regarding "attaining the transformation of sentient beings," this refers to the immeasurable transformation of sentient beings.
Next, in explaining the two phrases concerning self-cultivation: first, making offerings to the Buddhas to accumulate merit; second, following the Buddhas to accumulate wisdom.

The latter two phrases clarify the purity of the functions of wisdom: first, the purity of the obstacles to supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); second, the purity of the obstacles to manifesting perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) within immeasurable great assemblies.

Because one knows the faculties of beings within these assemblies and teaches the Dharma accordingly, it is said that in all such places, there is conformity with immeasurable physical, verbal, and mental actions.
This explains the concluding passage.
"Uninterrupted and unceasing" explains the meaning of "immovable.
Regarding the two explanations of the metaphors, it should be understood that the metaphor of the ship illustrates swift progress.

Regarding "superiority of cause," this reveals the basis for the swiftness of practice; since the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is the superior cause of practice, it causes practice to be swift.
The section beginning with "well-accumulated" (*susaṃbhṛta*) below explains the combined text.

"Skillfully gathering [merit and wisdom]," and so forth, refers to the various practices cultivated during the preceding seven stages which assist in bringing this [eighth stage] forth; therefore, they are called "provisions" (*sambhāra*).
The remainder of the text is understandable.
Within the fourth section, "Purifying the Buddha-field," there are three types of mastery:
First, mastery over the vessel-world; second, mastery over the world of sentient beings; third, mastery over the world of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
The first is the locus of transformation, the second is that which is transformed, and the last is the transformer.
Only when one possesses the latter two purities is it called a "Pure Land.
Because one gives rise to unimpeded transformations regarding these three dharmas, it is termed "mastery" (*vaśitā*).
Within the first category—mastery over the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*)—there are two parts:
The first part provides a general heading, which means it first restates what preceded.

The subsequent phrase, "contemplating the Buddha’s power of wisdom," correctly defines its characteristics; that is, because one is able to fully comprehend the characteristics of all worlds, it is called the "power of wisdom."
The following provides a detailed exposition, which consists of five distinct sections:

First, regarding "according to what one desires in one's own mind," it means that within this world, one knows immediately whatever one wishes to know according to one's own mind, and furthermore, one knows immediately whatever one wishes to know according to the minds of other sentient beings.
This is the mastery of knowledge (*jñāna-vaśitā*).
That which can manifest or not manifest is the mastery of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vaśitā*).
Manifestation is formation (*bhava*), and non-manifestation is destruction (*vibhava*).
Another explanation:
that which can manifest formation and destruction does not manifest the opposite.

In the section beginning with "knowing by what karma," it clarifies that whatever one desires, one can manifest it; that is, according to whichever karma brings about formation or whichever karma brings about destruction, if one wishes to know, one knows it immediately.
The ability to manifest [forms] is as previously described.
Because karma accumulates, things are formed; because karma is exhausted, they perish. Since wisdom can know this, it is called the "knowledge of the exhaustion of the accumulation of karma.
Regarding the third point, "according to the duration one desires," this phrase is omitted in the abbreviated version.
4. Regarding the passage beginning with "This bodhisattva knows the stages," which explains how one can manifest [realms] according to their desired extent, there are two parts.
First, it clarifies the distinctions among the four great elements.
As for the phrase "not fixed stages" (*na niyata-bhūmi*) and so forth, it clarifies that because the objects of knowledge in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are narrow, they are termed "small."
The two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the stages (*bhūmi*), etc., are called "great" because the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) in the higher realms are vast.
The Buddha's knowledge is called "immeasurable" because it is limitless.
These three are all termed "objects" (*viṣaya*) as they refer to the scope of what is known.
The wisdom that knows this is therefore called "object-wisdom" (viṣaya-jñāna). Next, the wisdom of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-jñāna) is revealed:
the subduing of the essential nature of the four great elements is termed their "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa).
That which exists above, such as emptiness, non-self, and so forth, is called "common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
The difference between these two is called "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*).
Regarding the knowledge of the subtle and coarse aspects of atoms (*paramāṇu*) below, it should be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Second, from "In a single world-system" onwards, it clearly explains the quantity of the aggregation and dispersal of atoms.
Within this section, first is the general understanding; second, from "This single world-system" onwards, is the specific understanding.
Within this, there are four further points:

first, knowing the quantity of the gross elements (*mahābhūta*) of external objects; second, knowing the quantity of the sensory particles (*rajas*) within the bodies of sentient beings; third, knowing the quantity of material particles in the objects of previous worlds; and fourth, knowing the quantity of the differentiated sensory particles within the bodies of previous sentient beings across the three realms and six destinies.

In this context, "large body" and "small body" are termed "coarse body" (*audārika-kāya*) and "subtle body" (*sūkṣma-kāya*) in the treatise and the sūtra; these represent the distinctions of the three realms.
The treatise states that regarding the coarseness or subtlety of the body: the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) is coarse, while the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) is subtle.
Among forms (*rūpa*), those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are coarse and those of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are subtle.
Therefore, it is said that they follow this sequence; by this one should understand [the point].
According to the Mahāyāna school, even within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) there are atoms (*paramāṇu*), which are forms produced through the mastery of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Next, regarding the knowledge that the bodies of the six realms of existence are composed of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), one analyzes them with awakened wisdom (*jñāna*) to reveal that these atoms do not possess a real, inherent nature.
The fifth section, beginning with "This bodhisattva enters thus," clarifies the extent of their aspiration.
Within this, there are three parts:

first, knowing the formation and destruction of the triple world; second, knowing their characteristics such as magnitude and so forth; and third, knowing how sentient beings appear through transformation in accordance with them. The treatise explains the latter two.

The Treatise states: "Regarding the wisdom of the characteristics of the objects of knowledge such as the desire realm, it also opens two gates: taking 'desire' and so forth to include the form and formless realms, knowing the limits of phenomena within these three realms is called 'wisdom of objects';
knowing the limits of dharmas is called 'wisdom of characteristics.'"
Next, the objects and wisdom are explained in detail.
Among those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), humans are small and the devas are large.

In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) in the first dhyāna; from the second dhyāna upward, there is no applied thought. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the Buddha’s Dharma is taught in order to distinguish it from the false graspings of non-Buddhists who take [those states] to be *nirvāṇa*.
Ordinary beings, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas constitute the noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
Above these, the categories of "Great" and "Small" are distinguished according to the breadth or narrowness of their respective objects of knowledge.

Thus far, only the Great and Small have been explained; the characteristics of the "Immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) have not yet been addressed. Now, this [section] explains them together: the objects known by all Tathāgatas throughout the three realms are vast, expansive, and boundless; therefore, they are said to possess the characteristic of being immeasurable.
Third, from "This is called a bodhisattva" onwards, it clearly explains how he manifests transformations in accordance with sentient beings.
This section has three parts:
first, knowing sentient beings; second, manifesting transformations in accordance with that knowledge; and third, attaining mastery over such manifestations.
The treatise states: "At the beginning, first the text is cited.
'Skillfully knowing that bodies are not identical' provides a general explanation of the sentient beings who are the objects of knowledge.
'Expedient means,' and so forth, explains the skillful manifestation of transformations that accord with the births of those beings."
Regarding the distinction between "different beings" and "beings of the same kind," this refers to the manifested bodies of similar types.

As for the passage beginning with "the lands of all Buddhas," which describes the manifestation of physical bodies throughout various locations, it explains the mastery over emanations, such as the body pervading the trichiliocosm and so forth.

The application of the principle (*dharma*), the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the synthesis (*upanaya*) may be understood accordingly. Second, from "according to the bodies of sentient beings" onwards, it clarifies the sovereign practice regarding the world of sentient beings.
This section contains three parts:

First, a general explanation of mastery; second, a detailed manifestation of mastery from the passage beginning "If, regarding a śramaṇa... onwards; third, a summary of mastery from the passage beginning "Inexpressible... onwards.

In the commentary, the phrase "his mastery in taming sentient beings" provides a general explanation of its characteristics; because this bodhisattva attains mastery within the process of taming sentient beings, he is able to manifest in various ways.

Regarding the statement "he travels to transform sentient beings," this explains that within the sutra, it is said that he appears before great assemblies according to the faith of sentient beings; because he manifests his presence everywhere, it is called "traveling to transform sentient beings."

Regarding the phrase "body and mind performing the same service (*samānārthatā*)": this explains the specific passage within the text concerning transforming oneself to accord with the bodies of others.
That is to say, the Bodhisattva’s own body conforms to the minds of sentient beings, manifesting in a form identical to their own; therefore, it is said that "body and mind perform the same service."
Regarding the phrase "manifesting with an equal portion of body and mind," this commentary explains that the transformation [body] of the Bodhisattva accords with the minds of sentient beings.

The Bodhisattva’s own body appears according to the specific requirements of sentient beings; this is called "manifesting with an equal portion," meaning appearing in the form of a Śrāvaka or other such bodies as appropriate.
The remainder of the text may be understood.
Third, from "In reality, however, he is far removed" onwards, it elucidates the practice of the World-Honored One’s Perfect Enlightenment and Sovereignty.
Within this, there are two types of knowledge regarding the Two Truths:
First, the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*) is clarified, as it is the foundation.
Regarding the statement "to be far removed from the distinctions of bodily characteristics," this explains the relinquishing of all conceptual discriminations concerning bodily characteristics.
Regarding the statement "constant abiding in equality," it means not discriminating between one's own body and the bodies of others.
That is to say, although one regards one's own body as "self" and the ten bodies as "others," they are not discriminated because they share the same rational nature (*dharmatā*).
For what reason is this taught?
It is because one wishes to reveal the causes and conditions for the manifestation of the various bodily marks.
Second, from the passage beginning "This bodhisattva" onwards, there are three parts clarifying the wisdom of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
First, the ten bodies of the objects of knowledge are enumerated; second, the characteristics and functions of these various bodies are clarified; third, the meaning of the ten bodies is explained.

Within the initial enumeration of the ten bodies, the first three belong to the defiled portion (*saṃkleśabhāga*), the next six belong to the pure portion (*vyavadānabhāga*), and the final one belongs to the non-dual portion (*advayabhāga*).
Regarding the "respective portions," this is because they are derived from the single, great principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, within the other-dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the aspect free from defilement is termed the "imagined" (*parikalpita*), the pure aspect is termed the "perfected" (*pariniṣpanna*), and the non-dual aspect is termed the "other-dependent."
Therefore, if one perceives a single part, the nature of all other parts is no different; they are all interpenetrating and fully encompassed within this.
As for the non-dual division, it is spoken of in terms of the exhaustion of all characteristics; thus, it is symbolized by the body of empty space.
Within the treatise, the internal world is further analyzed, wherein the two primary bodies—the sentient world and the receptacle world—are presented first.

That which serves as the cause for the arising of those two—namely karma and afflictions—is the third, the body of karmic retribution (*vipākakāya*). This clarifies that when the former two types arise, they are termed "retribution" because they are caused by afflictions and karma.
Regarding the statement "these are the defiled portions," this refers to the three [aspects] mentioned above.
Next, the pure portions are clarified.
Regarding the statement "the purity of the Three Vehicles," this refers to the four bodies of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and Tathāgata.
"Whichever of the three vehicles [is practiced] by whichever wise one" refers to the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*).
"Whichever phenomenon [is engaged]" refers to the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
These are that which knows and the phenomena that are known.
Regarding "that which clearly manifests purity": the six types mentioned above constitute the category of purity (*śuddha-bhāga*).
Space is not known through the characteristics of the former two; this is termed the "non-dual category" (*advaya-bhāga*). From the passage "This bodhisattva...

onwards, it clarifies the manifestation of the various bodily forms (*kāya-lakṣaṇa*) within the process of formation. Generally, there are ten [forms] for one's own body, and each individual body also possesses ten; thus, through the formation of these marks, one hundred and ten bodies are produced, all of which manifest with unimpeded mastery.
In this passage, three layers are briefly distinguished:
first, taking the body of sentient beings as the primary focus, one forms ten [bodies] such as one's own body and so forth;
second, taking the body of the land as the primary focus, one forms [the bodies].
Third, it should be understood that in this manner, up to the tenth [category], one takes one's own body as the primary basis to manifest those ten bodies.
Regarding the question of how these various bodies attain such characteristics and perform their functions, there are many causes; here, three types are briefly discussed:

first, from the perspective of the gate of the interpenetration of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), for which reason this text first speaks of the equality of one's own and others' bodies and the absence of discrimination, and so forth.

Secondly, regarding the gate of mutual dependence within dependent origination, as stated in the following verse: "The Bodhisattva possesses mastery over the harmony of causes and conditions, such that he can even manifest the body of a Buddha according to his will. Thus it is said.

Third, regarding the Bodhisattva’s power of mastery and wisdom: because within this stage one has long since mastered the principles of non-obstruction in the two preceding gates, one is thus able to act.
The commentary explains that "making the bodies of sentient beings one's own body" refers to the practice of appropriation performed within that mastery.
"Various manifestations" refers to the performance of deeds for the sake of gathering others within the sovereign mastery of perfect wisdom.
The creation of various bodily forms is called "various manifestations," all of which appear in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
3. From "This Bodhisattva" onwards, the ten bodies are extensively revealed.
First, the five phrases within the explanation of the sentient-being body are:

1) karma; 2) birth, which is retribution; 3) the distinctions of afflictions and delusive thoughts; 4) the form realm; and 5) the distinctions of the formless realm. The latter two are opened out from the perspective of retribution.

Second, regarding the ten characteristics of the body of the land, the passage concerning the "small thousand" and so forth explains the first three characteristics: namely, one small thousand-world system, two medium thousand-world systems, and three immeasurable thousand-world systems.
The mention of "a thousand" and so forth refers to taking the latter two [stages]; therefore, it says "one should know.
The distinction between the pure and the impure explains the characteristics of defilement and purity.
"Extensive" and so forth explain the remaining characteristics, indicating that they are the same as those of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).

Regarding the next four [categories], the distinctions of conventional designations (*prajñapti-saṃjñā*): the treatise explains the distinctions between specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), because conventional designations differentiate [beings] as being without self (*anātman*) or person (*pudgala*).
That is to say, the fact that each body is distinct is called its specific characteristic; the fact that the meaning of the conventional designation is uniform is termed its common characteristic.
If one speaks of "provisionality" (prajñapti) in reference to human beings, why is it not spoken of in the context of the Buddha’s body?
It is because the Buddha’s supreme virtues transcend those of all other persons.
Regarding the seventh [point], within the body of the Tathāgata there are naturally ten bodies.
First is the *bodhi-kāya*, because it demonstrates the attainment of perfect enlightenment;
second is the *praṇidhāna-kāya*, because it is the vow to be born in Tuṣita;
third is the *nirmāṇa-kāya*, because it comprises all the Buddha’s emanations and transformations.
Fourth is the body that sustains [the teachings], because it sustains the śarīra of one's own body.
Fifth is the body adorned with the marks and signs, because it is the body of true retribution produced by meritorious karma.
The sixth is the body of sovereign power (*vaśitā-kāya*), because its radiance subdues and gathers sentient beings.

The seventh is the body of mastery over the如意 (*yathākāmāvakrānti-kāya*), because it attains liberation through mastery over all minds—both similar and dissimilar, mundane and supramundane. It is called "similar" because it manifests births at will to appear identical to the world; it is called "dissimilar" because, in reality, it is supramundane.
The following explains the reason:

because he has attained sovereign liberation regarding the supramundane, he is able to manifest conformity; because he has attained sovereign liberation regarding the mundane, he is able to demonstrate non-conformity.

Regarding the eighth, the body of merit: because it possesses the uncommon capacity to act as the cause for vast benefit, its merit is clarified as "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) in order to distinguish it from that of ordinary beings. Thus, it is termed the "uncommon cause."
This great merit extensively manifests the signs of immeasurable bodies, wealth, and so forth, broadly gathering in sentient beings.
As for the nine wisdom-bodies, because they possess unobstructed wisdom, this wisdom is able to perform all tasks and can fully know the distinctions among those tasks.
This means that it can perform all functions; this explains the sense of being unimpeded.
The phrase "those matters" below concludes the discussion on the capacity for knowledge.
As for the ten dharma-bodies, they constitute the entire untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) of all Tathāgatas.

This refers to the quality of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) of all Buddhas, which is called the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*); it is precisely what is termed the Buddha of Nirvāṇa among the ten types of Buddhas.
Furthermore, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) internally realized by the Tathāgata is called the untainted realm.
Regarding the eight explanations for knowing the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*), there are eight explanations in the treatise on the sūtra:
the first two lines distinguish the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*). First, "deliberation" refers to the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*);
second, "skillful observation of the true nature" refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*).
Regarding "subsumed under the practice for the three fruits": that which is obtained through the differentiation of cause and fruit is called the "fruit," while its cause is called "practice.
Regarding "mundane and supramundane": this is a differentiation according to stages; that prior to the Path is called "mundane," and from the Path of Seeing onwards is called "supramundane."
Fifth, regarding the three vehicles, they are distinguished by the Great and the Small.
Sixth, regarding the shared and unshared, they are distinguished by the coarse and the subtle; the coarse refers to what is practiced in common, while the subtle exists only in the Great Vehicle.

Regarding the "seven vehicles and non-vehicles," this is a distinction based on spiritual lineage (*gotra*): those who have already cultivated the seeds of the three vehicles are called "vehicles," while those who have not yet cultivated them are "non-vehicles.

Regarding the "learners and those beyond learning" (*śaikṣa-aśaikṣa*), this is a distinction based on the stages of cultivation: practicing with the aim of seeking is called "learning," while reaching the ultimate fruit is "beyond learning."
Ninth, regarding the explanation of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the treatise cites five phrases from the sūtra:
first, the characteristic of equality, because the immeasurable dharma-gates clarify that they are all equal within the single Dharma-body.
This means that because the Buddha’s immeasurable dharmas are clarified as being one and the same Dharma-body, they are called "equal.
This is the dharma of principle (*li-fa*).
Second, regarding the "unbreakable characteristic," it is so called because [the Dharma] is grasped as it is heard.
This is the definitive teaching within the Buddha's dispensation; because it is spoken in accordance with reality, it is said to be "as it was heard.

Regarding the provisional distinctions of the three turnings: they are taught according to the differences in time, corresponding to the capacities and dispositions of the sentient beings to be converted.
This refers to teaching according to the specific capacities of those to be converted at the time their faculties have matured; such is the provisional teaching.

Regarding the four categories of sentient beings and non-sentient beings: sentient beings possess the six sense organs and so forth as their primary and secondary retributions (*āśraya-vipāka*); that which is insentient is termed "non-faculties" (*anindriya*), and this constitutes defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*).
Regarding the five knowledges of the Three Jewels, they know the foremost characteristic, which refers to the preeminence of the Three Jewels.
The tenth [section] explains six phrases within the "Body of Space":
first, "immeasurable" means being vast and inexhaustible to the ultimate limit.
Second, it is all-pervasive, encompassing all forms and images;
third, it is formless, because it cannot be seen;
fourth, it is non-different, as it lacks the characteristics of obstruction, unlike material phenomena which are subject to limitation and hindrance.
The five boundlessnesses (*anantya*) have the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because they lack the boundaries of beginning, arising, end, and exhaustion;

as for the sixth, the differentiation of the manifest form-body (*rūpakāya*), it is able to universally contain and receive the characteristics of form; by means of form, those distinctions are made, and one is able to know all forms, thereby understanding their differences.
The fifth section, beginning with "This bodhisattva well knows how to give rise to such [states]," clarifies the stage of mastery (*vaśitā*).
Regarding these ten masteries, there are briefly four sections:
first, defining their characteristics; second, overcoming obstacles; third, identifying their causes; and fourth, attaining their respective stages.
First, regarding the analysis of characteristics, it is fully elucidated as presented in the treatise and the sūtra.

Second, regarding the remediation of hindrances, it counteracts ten obstacles as fully elucidated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; since the present treatise shares this with that work, there is no need to record it here.
Regarding the three causes of emergence, according to the tenth chapter on "Excellence" in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the six perfections serve as the causes.

The first three take giving (*dāna*) as their cause: by giving at all times, one attains mastery over life; by giving in all places, one attains mastery over the mind; and by giving all things, one attains mastery over wealth.

The next two take ethical discipline (*śīla*) as their cause: through discipline, one trains body and speech to accomplish superior karma, and furthermore, through the purity of discipline, one takes birth according to one's wish.

Patience is the cause for mastery over resolute belief (*adhimukti*), because when one practices patience, one accords with the intentions of sentient beings; thus, everything comes to function according to one's mind—meaning that such things as transforming earth into gold all proceed in accordance with one’s superior resolve (*adhimukti*).
Diligence is the cause for vows, because by exerting oneself in one's tasks without slackness or abandonment, it causes whatever is vowed to be accomplished according to one's wish.

Dhyāna is the cause for supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), which is termed mastery over spiritual power (*śakti-vaśitā*); because by relying on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one gives rise to supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*) that are accomplished according to one's will.

Prajñā serves as the cause for the latter two [mastery]: that which is called "mastery over knowledge" (jñāna-vaśitā) refers to internal illumination; that which is called "mastery over the Dharma" (dharma-vaśitā) refers to teaching in accordance with the faculties [of beings].

Regarding the attainment of the stage [of mastery] in the fourth [verse], the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains what is attained at the Buddha-ground in terms of the fruit—that is, its inclusion within the "pure dharmas" among the five aspects of the Dharmakāya. Here, however, it is explained in terms of the cause, specifically what is attained from the eighth ground onward; this is taught according to the perspective of the entire progression from beginning to end.
The ten masteries (*vaśitā*) in the lower section, the "Chapter on Transcending the World," are explained as penetrating all stages by way of the stage of Samantabhadra.

Furthermore, the passage in the upper section, the "Chapter on the Wise Leader" (*Bhadramukha*), which speaks of the ten kinds of power of mastery in the ten stages (*bhūmi*), is explained according to the Separate Teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
The sixth section, "This Bodhisattva attains ten masteries," is the Part on Great Superiority (*mahāviśeṣa-bhāga*), which has three parts: first, the greatness of wisdom (*jñāna-mahattva*);
second, the greatness of activity (*karma-mahattva*); and third, the greatness of the qualities in which those two abide (*tad-ubhaya-pratiṣṭhita-guṇa-mahattva*).

Regarding the first of the four great knowledges (*jñānamahattva*), "inconceivable knowledge" means not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa; its clarity and quiescence are difficult to fathom—this is the general statement.
Below, three types are specifically revealed:
first, "immeasurable knowledge," which refers to the depth of realizing the principle through the ultimate perfection of cultivation.
Second is the wisdom of vastness, which is inconceivable in its knowing, for it illuminates objects extensively;
third is the wisdom of non-destruction, which is inconceivable in its removal of hindrances, for it reaches the ultimate in breaking through appearances.
Second, regarding the section beginning with "The Bodhisattva follows thus," which clarifies the greatness of activity (*karma-mahātmya*), the first part reiterates what preceded.
When the *Śāstra* states, "Thus... as previously explained," it refers back to the attainment of mastery (*vaśitā*) that was already described.
Regarding the phrase "the accomplishment of such wisdom is also as previously explained," this refers back to the previously mentioned inconceivable wisdom.
The twelve phrases following the term "ultimate" (atyanta) correctly manifest the greatness of its activity.
Among these, the first three phrases clarify the purity of the three types of action (*karma*), which constitutes the essential nature of action;
the subsequent nine phrases distinguish action according to its cultivation, subsuming them into four categories:

first, that which arises, that which causes it to arise, and that which arises simultaneously. This means that the aforementioned three types of action are "that which arises"; wisdom's causing those actions to arise is called "that which causes it to arise"; and once those actions have arisen, their proceeding together with wisdom is termed "simultaneous. Therefore, it is said that "bodily action proceeds in accordance with wisdom," and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "the two wisdoms encompass non-defiled activity for benefiting sentient beings," this refers to the pairing of wisdom and compassion; thus it is said that "prajñā is predominant and great compassion is primary."

Regarding the three causes that encompass the causes for one’s own practice and the practice of others: this consists of a pair of the "capable of producing" (the cause) and the "produced" (the result). That is to say, initiating great vows is termed "one's own practice. Because this own practice serves as the cause for the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the practices of other Buddhas, it is termed the "cause for the practice of others," and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "Skillfully initiating vows and skillfully receiving the protection of the Buddhas."

Regarding "sustained by the performance of activities": this means that the accomplishment of the three types of action is called "sustenance" because it is indestructible. Within this, there are three phrases:

the first two concern the accomplishment of benefiting others. First, because teaching the Dharma benefits sentient beings, it is said that one "constantly does not abandon the benefit of living beings."
Second, regarding the transformation through supernatural powers in the Pure Land, it says, "knowing all boundless [realms]," and so forth.
Next is the practice for oneself, which refers to the accomplishment of all Buddha-dharmas; thus it says, "summarizing the essential words," and so forth.

3. From "This bodhisattva dwells in this stage" onwards, the greatness of the merits of those two dwellings is clarified; therein, the first ten phrases provide the direct explanation, while the final three phrases form the conclusion.
Regarding the preceding section, the treatise subsumes it into seven [categories]:
the first four constitute one unit, which, being the essence of the qualities of abiding, is called the "merit of abiding well on the path.
The latter six each constitute one unit, which refers to the qualities distinguished by means of cultivation.
Regarding the four phrases in the preceding section:

the first two concern one's own practice—first, purifying the mind to eliminate hindrances; second, gathering wholesome qualities through a profound resolve so as not to depart from the Path, which is termed "firmness in counteraction.
The latter two concern benefiting others—namely, not abandoning them through compassion and loving-kindness, but rather rescuing them.
The following section concerns the cultivation and realization of virtues: second, the virtue of non-forgetfulness is the virtue of dhāraṇī regarding mental action;
third, the virtue of eloquent exposition is the accomplishment of verbal action;
fourth, mastery over the concentrated mind is the virtue of physical action, because supernormal powers are manifested based upon meditative concentration.
Fifth, initiating practice based on the power of aspiration;
sixth, the accomplishment of cultivation, which is the dharma of the accumulation of the powers of knowledge and conduct;
seventh, bestowing wisdom upon the practitioner, whereby they achieve realization and enter the Buddha-realm—this is called "the Buddha bestows wisdom."
3. From "This bodhisattva, in this way" onwards is the conclusion.

Regarding "power of wisdom," this restates the previously mentioned greatness of wisdom; it means attaining freedom from hatred and love, and not discriminating between sentient beings who are afflicted and those who are not.
"Manifesting all that is to be done" refers to the greatness of the prior activity, meaning that it is the activity of equality.

"Being without fault" refers to the greatness of the merit of those two dwellings, because one has attained the seven kinds of merit mentioned previously and thus remains free from error in all practical activities.
The seventh section, "O Sons of the Buddha, regarding this stage of the Bodhisattva," clarifies the analysis of the name and has two parts:
first, the analysis of the name according to the Dharma to manifest the stages;
second, the analysis of the name according to persons to distinguish their virtues.

Regarding the ten phrases in the preceding section, the treatise subsumes them into six: namely, the third and eighth phrases each constitute one category, while the remaining eight phrases are combined two by two into four categories; thus, there are six in total.

The first two [stages] are antidotes to defilement; the first counteracts the functional activities of the lower stages, while the Small Vehicle counters the various demonic activities, and thus it is named "Immovable" (*āniñjya*).
The second counteracts the activity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions, and is thus named "Non-retrogressive" (*anivartana*), for it is through wisdom that these are countered.
Second, because one is able to attain the profound non-arising that is so difficult to attain, it is called "that which all worlds cannot fathom," and so forth.
Third, the two lines [of verse] are termed the purity of practice (*pratipatti-śuddhi*):

first, the purity of aspiration (*utpāda-śuddhi*), which means that at the time of generating the cultivation, one is free from the fault of effortful exertion, just as a prince does not worry about the hardships of domestic farming.
The Bodhisattva is likewise; because he is born into this family, he is free from the fault of effortlessness, and thus it is said that he has no fault regarding his lineage.
Here, the analogy of a child who is without desire illustrates being purely without outflows (*anāsrava*), free from the fault of the defilement of delusion.

Second is the purity of conduct (*caryā-viśuddhi*): this refers to the stage where, at the time of practicing correctly, one is free from the fault of non-attainment and dwells in the ground of birth; because one achieves mastery over all desired matters, it is called the "ground of mastery" (*vaśitā-bhūmi*).

Four times two lines constitute one verse. There are mundane and supramundane forms of conditioned purity and excellence. That which is called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) refers to that which arises through cultivation on the path of instruction; this "conditioned" is termed "accomplishment. Merit is termed "mundane," while wisdom is termed "supramundane. Because supramundane wisdom possesses definitive knowledge, it is termed "ultimate."
The fifth is the superiority of non-action purity (*anabhisaṃskāra-viśuddhi*), meaning that the realization of the truth of the path is not something produced by cultivation.
Because the Sanskrit term for *nirvāṇa* is phonetically close to *nirmāṇa* (transformation), two different translations have resulted.
Because its activity arises from vows and is not accompanied by quiescence, it is called "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*).
The two phrases following the sixth [stage] are named the "excellence of the Bodhisattva grounds," meaning that their respective stages surpass those preceding them.
Regarding "one who abides": in the treatise, this is called *kṣetrajñā*, which means empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
This "surpassing the sixth stage" refers to the initiation of sublime practice, meaning that it is revealed to be superior to what preceded it.

When other matters cause the mind to waver, it is revealed that the former is inferior to this; specifically, in the sixth stage, one contemplates emptiness, yet is moved from that contemplation of emptiness by regarding existence as "other. Now, however, it is not so, and is therefore superior.
Regarding the second point, "previously cultivating goodness is called the stage of effortlessness," this clarifies that it surpasses the [first] seven stages.
"With effort" indicates that the former is inferior to this;
"the goodness arising equally in this stage" demonstrates that this is superior to those.
The remaining text is self-evident.
Second, from "The Bodhisattva attains such [a state]" onwards, the wise explain the name.
That is to say, for what reason is one called an "immovable" (*akṣobhya*) bodhisattva?
There are two meanings:
first, immovability in the absolute sense, meaning that one’s practice proceeds in accordance with the higher [stages];
second, immovability in the sense of a single essence, meaning that one shares the same essence as the practices of all bodhisattvas.
In the preceding section, the first four lines clarify the meaning of "exclusive" (*ekāntika*).

The initial phrase, "entering the Buddha-realm," is termed "entering the Buddha-nature" (*buddhadhātu*) in the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra*; it refers to entering the rational nature (*dharmatā*) of the *dharmakāya*, which is the fruit of Buddhahood.
It is also the realm realized by the Buddha’s wisdom; therefore, it is called "the excellence of the fulfillment of the fruit," which refers to the nature of Śākyamuni.
Śākyamuni is called "Full Excellence" (Pūrṇaśākyamuni) because his fruition is perfect.
Regarding "conformity with the cause," this indicates the latter three phrases, which refer to conformity with the causes of Buddhahood.

Second, "the illumination of the Buddha’s virtues" refers to the inclusion of meritorious qualities; because it carries the sense of being well-purified, it clarifies that the understanding of contemplation includes these virtues.
Third, "following the Buddha’s majestic demeanor" is called right practice (*samyak-pratipatti*); thus, based on understanding, one gives rise to cultivation.

Fourth, "tending toward the Buddha-dharma"—which the treatise calls "the manifestation of the Buddha's sphere"—is because one draws near to the Buddha's sphere; thus, based on practice, one approaches the fruit.
The next ten phrases explain "immovability":
the first one is general.
Regarding "always protected by the power of the Buddha," this is because the higher fruit is bestowed upon the lower [stages].
The remaining nine are distinct; the treatise subsumes them into five, namely: each of the first four constitutes one [category], while the latter five constitute one.

Regarding the first of these, the statement that "one constantly serves as a Caturmahārājika king and so forth" refers to the merit of making offerings, clarifying that this results in receiving the offerings of devas.
Regarding "the two, Guhyapada and others," this refers to the merit of protection: previously they protected in secret, whereas from now on they protect by manifesting their forms.
Regarding "the three, Suvrata and others," this refers to the merit of reliance, as these virtues are accomplished by relying upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The fourth is the ability to manifest immeasurable bodies, which refers to the merit of the purity of the buddha-field; this is the differentiation of manifested bodies within the preceding section on the pure land.
Next, five items constitute one category: the merit of transforming sentient beings.
First, "regarding all bodies" and so forth, means that by vowing to take birth in all realms of existence, one clarifies the benefit of transformation through bodily action (*kāyakarman*).

Second, regarding "attaining great fruits and so forth": this refers to the power of the faculties, the mind, and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), which clarifies the transformation of mental action (*manas-karman*); it signifies being able to know the faculties, desires, and dispositions of sentient beings. Third, regarding "boundless samādhis and so forth":

because immeasurable dharma-power turns the wheel of Dharma, this clarifies the transformation of verbal action (*vāk-karman*). The realization of the Dharma by relying on meditative concentration is called "dharma-power"; because one is able to turn the wheel of Dharma through this dharma-power, it is termed verbal action. Fourth, being worthy of receiving predictions from many Buddhas.
Fifth, the manifestation of attaining Buddhahood, preaching the Dharma, and delivering sentient beings.
Second, from the passage "This bodhisattva enters such wisdom, etc. onwards, it clarifies the immovability of the single essence.

Regarding the phrase "enters such wisdom," the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra* refer to this as "entering the number of the Mahāyāna assembly"; that is, because one shares the same great wisdom as the bodhisattvas in this stage who are free from effort (*anābhoga*), it is called "indestructible" (*asaṃhārya*).
This is the general statement;
the remaining nine are the particulars.
First, "one who has thoroughly mastered the Dharma" refers to indestructible wisdom, because one has personally realized the reality of the Dharma.
"Second, 'constantly emitting [light]' and so forth refers to the indestructibility of speech, because it is spoken based on realization.
Third, 'the three unhindered [powers]' and so forth refers to the indestructibility of liberation, because of the sovereign mastery over the functional activity of the unobstructed *dharmadhātu*."

Regarding "the four [knowledges] such as skillfully knowing the worlds": because the Buddha-lands are pure and indestructible, and because he possesses sovereign mastery and unimpededness regarding all Buddha-lands, it is said that he "skillfully knows" them.
Fifth, "able to manifest all things equally" means that having entered the indestructible Mahāyāna, one is able to manifest through the mental faculty (*manas-karman*) by entering into the Dharma.
Sixth, "sovereignty according to will" refers to the indestructibility of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which is the physical faculty (*kāya-karman*).
Seventh, regarding "skillfully understanding the sequence of before and after," etc.: being able to explain meanings without impairment is the activity of speech (*vākkarman*).

Eighth, regarding "the wisdom that can enter and transform the paths of Māra": remaining unshakable while seated at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), which refers to subduing the enemies that are the Māras.
Regarding the phrase "the nine entrances are equal to the Tathāgata," it means that the Perfectly Awakened One is indestructible because he is able to manifest as a Buddha and preach the Dharma.

The subsequent passage beginning with "able [to act] within the boundless" is a summary; because his practice is unobstructed and uninterrupted, he is called a Bodhisattva who has attained the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
