In the section beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," which clarifies the fruits of the stages (*bhūmi*), the three fruits are the same as before.

Within the explanation of the Dharma of "pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*), the phrase "receiving from the Buddha the distinctions of the world-realms, etc. includes, by the term "etc.," the wisdom regarding the world of sentient beings and perfect enlightenment.

Because these three serve as the basis for initiating the activity of manifesting immeasurable pure lands, they are termed "Dharma-illumination" (*dharmāloka*); therefore, it is said that what is received constitutes their causal characteristic.

In the analogy, superiority is revealed by way of the person: that is, having attained the pure stage, because body and mind are superior, one is purely immaculate and free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
"Manifesting the even more brilliant and pure radiance of the roots of goodness" explains the purity of the wisdom of the teaching.
The remaining text may be understood accordingly.
In the third section, the verse summary consists of forty-four lines, divided into nine parts:
The first three verses constitute the section on the preliminary application (*pūrvaprayoga*) and the stage of accumulation (*sambhāra-bhūmi*).
The second consists of three verses on the stage of pure patience (*śuddha-kṣānti*).
The third consists of fifteen verses on the stage of superior practice (*viśeṣa-caryā*), among which the first five verses concern superior practice itself.
The subsequent ten verses constitute the "Initiation," namely the seven exhortations and so forth.

The section on "Purifying the Buddha-fields" consists of twelve verses; therein, the first four verses concern the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), and the following five concern the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*).
The latter three [chapters] concern the Perfect Enlightenment in the World;
the fifth has one verse on the Section on Mastery;
and the sixth has two verses on the Section on Great Excellence.
The seventh [section] consists of two verses on the analysis of the names;
the eighth consists of five verses on the section on the fruits of the stages;
and the ninth is the final single verse on the section on the limits of the exposition.
The *Acālā-bhūmi* (Immovable Ground) concludes.
Regarding the ninth, the *Sādhumatī-bhūmi* (Ground of Excellent Intelligence), there are seven sections as before.
First, to explain its name, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Because one has attained the most supreme unimpeded knowledge (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*)."

Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Because it is the wisdom of the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), it is called 'wisdom' (*prajñā*); because this wisdom is most excellent, it is called 'excellent wisdom' (*su-prajñā*).

Asaṅga’s commentary states: "That is to say, one attains the four supreme unimpeded analytical knowledges; among all forms of wisdom, the wisdom of the unimpeded analytical knowledges is the most distinguished."
Wisdom (*jñāna*) is itself discernment (*prajñā*), and is therefore called "excellent discernment" (*su-prajñā*).
Regarding the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), they are: phenomena (*dharma*), meaning (*artha*), expression (*nirukti*), and eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena, one attains mastery in knowing all names and phrases.
Through unimpededness regarding meaning, one freely and thoroughly penetrates all principles and meanings.
Through unimpededness regarding expression, one freely and analytically distinguishes all words and phrases.
Through unimpededness regarding eloquence, one freely and eloquently expounds throughout the ten directions as is appropriate for each case.
Because one initially realizes the previously unattained knowledge of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) within this stage, it is called "Excellent Intelligence" (*sādhumatī*).
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states: "Among the nine stages, the four analytical knowledges are most preeminent."

In a single instant, when all humans, devas, and various other beings within the three thousandfold world-system pose questions in diverse voices and with diverse meanings, this bodhisattva is able to answer all these questions universally with a single voice, completely severing all doubts.
For this reason, it is said that he is named "Excellent Wisdom" (Sudhī).
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "Because he possesses mastery in preaching the Dharma and is free from affliction and entanglement, his wisdom increases, becoming sovereign and unimpeded."
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "Because he has attained mastery in teaching the Dharma in all its aspects and has acquired vast, faultless wisdom, he is named Sādhumati."

The *Yogācārabhūmi*, in the "Chapter on Abiding," states: "Because within this stage the intention for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings is purified, one attains the bodhisattva’s unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*)."
"Because one is thereby able to skillfully proclaim the True Dharma, this stage is named the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*).
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "When that wisdom becomes increasingly luminous, supple, and superior, it is called the Stage of Excellent Intelligence."

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Because one has accomplished the four subtle and wondrous analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and is able to skillfully preach the Dharma throughout the ten directions.
In the *Renyō kyō* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra), this is called the Stage of Wisdom-Light (*Prajñābhā-bhūmi*).
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this is called the Stage of Excellent Characteristics (*sukhalakṣaṇa-bhūmi*).
Regarding the second point, the purpose for its inclusion, there are also three meanings:

first, although one has attained effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) within the signless (*animitta*) in the preceding stage, one has not yet been able to preach the Dharma according to the capacities of beings through the unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Now, this cultivation of progress is undertaken so as to realize that Dharma; for this reason, one comes.
The other two gates may be understood accordingly.
Third, regarding the obstacles to be abandoned: according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is the obstacle of being unable to skillfully benefit sentient beings.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The obstacle of being unwilling to act for the benefit of others refers to a portion of the innate aspect of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

It causes one to lack the desire to diligently engage in activities that bring happiness and benefit to sentient beings, instead delighting in cultivating one's own self-interest; this obstructs the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the ninth stage."

Upon entering the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*), one is able to sever them forever; for this reason, it is said that in the ninth stage one severs two delusions (*moha*) along with their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dauṣṭhulya*).

The first is the delusion regarding the mastery of *dhāraṇīs* and eloquence through wisdom concerning the immeasurable teachings, immeasurable phrases, names, and syllables, and those that follow them.

Mastery over the dhāraṇīs of the immeasurable teachings spoken refers to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*); that is, mastery over the retention of what is expressed, because within a single meaning one manifests all meanings.

Mastery over the *dhāraṇī* of immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables refers to the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*); it is mastery over the retention of that which expresses, because within a single name, phrase, or syllable, all names, phrases, and syllables are manifested.

Regarding "mastery over the dhāraṇī of wisdom and eloquence in successive stages," this refers to the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); it denotes mastery over the retention (*dhāraṇī*) that provides successive explanations of words and sounds, because within a single sound one manifests all sounds.
Second is the delusion regarding mastery over eloquence (*pratibhāna-vaśitā*).

Mastery over eloquence refers to the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), because it skillfully provides teaching by thoroughly understanding the appropriate capacities of others.
The delusions that can obstruct these four kinds of mastery are all subsumed within this ninth hindrance.
The commentary explains:

This takes as its essential nature the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that can obstruct the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), because from the eighth stage upward, the cognitive obstructions do not manifest within the six consciousnesses.

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "Though the Dharma taught is immeasurable, its names, phrases, and syllables are immeasurable, and the analytical wisdom [thereof] is immeasurable, one cannot thereby sustain ignorance."
"Second is the ignorance regarding the lack of mastery over the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of Liang states: "First is the ignorance regarding the *dhāraṇī* of mastery in eloquent speech that provides difficult answers, which consists of immeasurable correct teachings and immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables;
second is the ignorance regarding the resolution of doubts and the generation of understanding through the four unhindered analytical knowledges."
The commentary explains:

regarding the mention of the "four unhindered knowledges" (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) in the latter [section], this refers to the fourth [unhindered knowledge], which is consistent with the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other texts.
The remainder may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the fourth, that which is realized: in this stage, one realizes the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as the basis for mastery over knowledge (*jñāna-vaśitā*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains: "This means that once this suchness (*tathatā*) has been realized, one attains mastery over the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)."

As Asvabhāva explains: "Because in this stage one attains the basis for unimpeded eloquence (*anāvaraṇa-pratibhāna*), one partially realizes the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*). One does not follow the mere words regarding all phenomena, but is skillfully able to understand their underlying intentions and meanings, thereby truly accomplishing the attainment of supreme Dharma-joy for all sentient beings."
The commentary explains:
"Unimpeded eloquence" and so forth explain the meaning of the basis (*āśraya*);
"partial realization" and so forth explain the meaning of wisdom (*jñāna*).
"Not following words, etc. explains the meaning of mastery (*vaśitā*).
The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states: "There are four masteries:
first, mastery over non-conceptuality, which is mastery over marks (*nimitta-vaśitā*);"
Second, mastery over the pure lands;
third, mastery over wisdom;
fourth, mastery over karma.
The dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) serves as the basis for these four kinds [of mastery], which is termed the "meaning of the basis for the four masteries.
In the eighth stage, one is able to penetrate only the meaning of the basis for the first two masteries; the latter two correspond respectively to the final two stages.
Regarding the five practices, there are also three:
first, the practice of the power of resolve among the ten perfections;
second, the practice of skillfully attaining mastery over the vessels of the Dharma and teaching the Dharma with sovereign ease.
The *Vyūha-śāstra* states: "One accomplishes the maturation of sentient beings through mastery of the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
The three boundless dhāraṇīs for extensively receiving the practice of the Dharma are to be understood as explained in the subsequent text.

Regarding the six fruits obtained: according to the Liang commentary, through the dharma-realm that serves as the basis for mastery over penetrating wisdom, one obtains the fruit of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states that upon the ninth stage, one gives rise to the mind and attains the *jñānagarbha-samādhi*.
The stages and fruits of the grounds should be understood as explained below.
Seventh, regarding the explanation of the text, it consists of three parts as before.
Within the first part, the section on praise and request, there are nineteen verses, divided into four sections:
The first two [verses] describe the benefits of the preceding stage.
The second section contains two verses clarifying the offerings presented by the Bodhisattvas and celestial kings.
The third section contains fourteen verses of praise and entreaty by the goddesses; among these, the first one and a half verses issue forth sounds to extol the Buddha.
Next, three and a half verses praise the offering of the bodhisattva’s practice;
next, eight and a half verses praise the Buddha and bodhisattvas’ gathering and transforming of beings through the three wheels. First is the virtue of the body-action (*kāyakarman*);

next are the virtues of the speech-action (*vākkarman*) for five verses, which refers to manifesting sound where there is no sound and preaching the distinct teachings of the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle. This is because this stage is the rank of the Dharma-preacher (*dharmabhāṇaka*), and thus the characteristics of preaching the Dharma increase.
Next, the two [verses] concerning the virtue of mental action should be understood by analogy with the manifestation of illusions.
The one following is the celestial maiden’s conclusion in silence.
The final one of the four is the request for instruction by the leader.
In the second part, the Section on the Correct Exposition, there are four divisions:

first, regarding the accomplishment of the skillful means of the Dharma-preacher, this stage is able to give rise to eloquence for preaching the Dharma, and is thus called the Stage of the Dharma-preacher (*dharmabhāṇaka-bhūmi*).
Advancing toward the stages and practicing therein is called the accomplishment of skillful means (*upāya*).
Second, the accomplishment of the two knowledges (*jñāna*) is due to the accomplishment of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
Third, the accomplishment of entering into practice is due to knowing the vessels of those to be converted (*vineya*).
The fourth is called "accomplishment" because it is taught in accordance with the faculties [of the listeners].
The eighth, the Pure Land, and the ninth, Eloquence, distinguish the different aspects of practice.
"Accomplishing all characteristics" reveals the superiority over inferiority; that is to say, possessing the aforementioned four divisions is termed "all characteristics."

Regarding the first section on the skillful means of the Dharma Master: the initial part restates what precedes and introduces what follows; that is, "immeasurable wisdom" refers to the profound and vast wisdom of the preceding eight stages.
The section beginning with "desiring to seek" correctly elucidates the skillful means.

Regarding the statement that "benefiting others and benefiting oneself are each demonstrated by five and three phrases respectively": the first phrase concerns benefiting others and the second phrase concerns benefiting oneself; thus, it says "each.
Furthermore, the next five phrases also concern benefiting others, and the final three phrases also concern benefiting oneself; thus, it says "demonstrated by five and three phrases."

The initial statement regarding "seeking a further superior, tranquil liberation" refers to performing benefit for those sentient beings who can be transformed by means of the characteristics of liberation attained through the formless realm; that is, transforming them so that they may attain true nirvana.
"Second, the desire to transform, etc. refers to the basis for one's own benefit prior to attaining the ultimate Buddha-wisdom.
The following five phrases also clarify the benefit of others.
"Third, the desire to enter, etc. refers to transforming bodhisattvas whose faculties are matured, causing them to enter the profound and secret [teachings].
Regarding the fourth, "contemplating the [four] desires" and so forth: this transforms sentient beings who practice with wrong mindfulness, causing them to attain the practice of right mindfulness.

Regarding the fifth, "contemplating the various *dhāraṇīs*": this transforms sentient beings who do not yet know the Dharma, turning the wheel of Dharma so that they may come to know it; for it is because both the concentration and wisdom of *dhāraṇī* (total retention) are the basis for preaching the Dharma.
Regarding "the six desires for equality": by means of great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they transform those who follow false refuges, causing sentient beings to enter the True Dharma.

Regarding "the seven desires for discernment": because they have attained mastery over the distinctions of worlds, they manifest pure lands and convert those sentient beings who believe only in rebirth in the heavens, causing them to enter the Buddha-dharma.
The last three phrases clarify the practice for one's own benefit.
"Desiring to cultivate" and so forth refers to the desire to attain the Buddha’s great wisdom of internal realization and perfect enlightenment.
"Desiring to accord with" and so forth refers to the desire to attain the Buddha’s great wisdom of the wheel of Dharma for external transformation and the gathering of sentient beings.
Regarding "the ten desires not abandoning," etc.: it means desiring to attain the Buddha’s non-abiding nirvāṇa while not abandoning compassionate vows.
The conclusion below is clear.
Second, from "The Bodhisattva dwelling in this stage" onwards, the accomplishment of wisdom is explained.
Initially, one comprehends in general that the three natures are non-dual in terms of purity and defilement.
Subsequently, one distinguishes them within the wholesome category, opening them into three levels:

first, within the wholesome, one distinguishes between the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*). That which is wholesome prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) is called outflowing; that which is wholesome from the path of vision onward is called non-outflowing.

Furthermore, within the untainted (*anāsrava*) state, one distinguishes between the mundane and the supramundane: that which takes the cultivation of the *āgama* as its object is called mundane, while the correct realization of true practice is called supramundane.

Second, regarding those [beings], they are further distinguished as being capable of deliberation (*cintya*) or incapable of deliberation (*acintya*); that is, those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are capable of deliberation, while those on the stages are incapable of deliberation.

Within the category of those capable of deliberation, they are further distinguished as being determinate (*niyata*) or indeterminate (*aniyata*). Specifically, from the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) of the Śrāvakas onward, from the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) of the Pratyekabuddhas onward, and from the tenth Stage of Dedication (*daśama-pariṇāmanā*) of the Bodhisattvas onward, are all termed determinate; those below these levels are termed indeterminate.
This is according to the Initial Teaching (Ādikarmika-yāna).

If according to the Final Teaching (Niṣṭhā-yāna), from the entry into the Ten Abodes (daśa-vihāra) onward it is called "fixed" (*niyata*), whereas the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) are called "unfixed" (*aniyata*) because they are like light feathers.

Furthermore, this [Final Teaching] further differentiates the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) from within the wholesome; that is, based on the Three Vehicles, it distinguishes between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Specifically, the arising of the cultivation that realizes [the truth] is called "conditioned," while the true principle realized is called "unconditioned. Since all Three Vehicles rely upon the principle to establish their names, they are termed "conformable practices" (*anuloma-caryā*).
The Sūtra states, "All worthy and holy ones derive their names from the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)," which refers to this very meaning.
Third, the section beginning with "conforming to such" clarifies the accomplishment of entering into practice.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, a brief presentation of eleven topical headings; second, a sequential detailed explanation; and third, a concluding summary on abiding.
Regarding the first, the treatise and the sūtra simply refer to "mind."
Regarding the "bodhicitta" herein, this refers to those who possess the capacity as vessels for renunciation.
There are three parts to the commentary explaining this heading:
first, a brief explanation.

First, regarding that which is common: this refers to the mind, for it is difficult [to master] because it serves as the basis for both the wholesome and the unwholesome, as well as for defilement and purification; therefore, it is called "common.
Afflictions and karma constitute the next two.
Birth is the ninth [stage], which is categorized in the same location as the preceding stage because their characteristics of arising are closely related.
Furthermore, regarding the term "common" (*sādhāraṇa*): these four possess identical faculties, desires, dispositions, and upright minds.
Because they are similar in these four respects and are all fit vessels for the Dharma, they are called "common."
The "one who is defiled" refers to the mind that is subject to the proclivities (*anuśaya*).

Regarding the phrase "defilement and purity of afflictions," this refers to habitual practice; since habituation has no separate essence, it is mentioned by way of the residual traces (*vāsanā*) of defilement and purity.
Based on the categories of determinate and indeterminate, he raises the difficulty regarding the three groups [of persons].
Second, he provides a detailed explanation of the meaning of "similarity.
Regarding the phrase "the sequence of the faculties and so forth," it clarifies that faith and the other [faculties] arise based upon the faculties; hence, it is called "sequence."
Why does it arise based on that?
Because they are similar.
In what way are they similar?
This means that past habituation serves as the root; based on this root, desire arises, and desire necessarily resembles its root.
In the sutras, this is termed "faith" (*śraddhā*), which refers to profound acceptance and the inclination toward desire; the meaning is the same as here.
Habitual desire forms one's nature, and the nature resembles that desire.

Based on this nature, the manifest activity of the direct mind arises, and the mind, in turn, resembles the nature; it is only by depending on whether the preceding and succeeding moments are fixed or unfixed that such sequential distinctions arise.
The three fetters explain the meaning of the names:
"numerous" explains *vana* (forest),
and "difficult to know" explains *gahana* (thicket).
Since these two are both [subject to] conceptual formulations, they are said to be difficult.
Regarding "practice" (*yōgyō*), it refers to the correct and faithful understanding; Master Yuan's commentary explains: "Faith that realizes the principle can extinguish mental conceptions."
"Because mental conceptions cease, nothing proceeds.
Since there is no arising through the accumulation of faith, realization, and so forth, it is called "proceeding.
The second section, "Knowing the various minds of sentient beings," provides a detailed explanation in eleven gates, which constitute eleven segments.
The three difficulties regarding the initial resolve (*ādikarmika*) are as follows:
first, one sentence provides a general summary;
second, nine sentences provide a detailed exposition, which the treatise condenses into eight, namely: the first seven each constitute one, while the final two together constitute one.
Yuan says: "Of the eight [categories], the first four are the deluded mind and the latter four are the true mind.
Within the deluded [mind], the first concerns phenomena, the second characteristics, the third essence, and the fourth function.
Regarding the initial statement on "adorned worldly mind": the mind, by means of the eight consciousnesses, is able to adorn the world.

As for the treatise’s discussion of the sixfold distinctions of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*): "mind" refers to the *ālaya*, "thought" is the *manas*, and "consciousness" refers to the six consciousnesses; this is because while "mind" and "thought" each constitute a single category, "consciousness" comprises all six.

The six types [of consciousness] and the eight consciousnesses differ from one another; therefore, they are called "distinctions" (*viśeṣa*). When these distinctions exist in the same location, they are also called "mixed characteristics" (*saṃkīrṇa-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "the two quickly transform," this refers to the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of the mind, namely the transition and flow of the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).
This means that rapid transformation is "abiding-difference" (*sthity-anyathātva*), because it does not remain static.
Destruction and non-destruction are "arising and ceasing.

The three formless [aspects] are the essential nature of the mind; that is to say, when one contemplates that mind, the characteristics of the mind vanish, and thus it is called "transcending the mind."
The following commentary explains that because neither mind nor body can be apprehended, it is called "detachment.
Question:
Since the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is not the mind, why is this said?
Answer:

Because this mind arises from true nature (dharmatā) in accordance with conditions, as it is said: "The intrinsically pure mind (prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta), though unstained, becomes stained, thereby accomplishing the defiled mind."
Regarding the "four boundless states" (*apramāṇa*) and so forth: they are so called because they take as their objects immeasurable realms in accordance with their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
That is to say, the function of apprehending an object is the self-characteristic of the mind; because these objects are not singular, they are said to be "boundless."
The following clarifies the true mind.
Regarding the "fivefold purity": because its self-nature is unstained, this refers to the purity of the fundamental nature.

Regarding the "sixth, being stained yet stainless": this indicates that while it is identical to afflictions, it is not identical to them, clarifying that it remains unstained even when enmeshed within them.

Regarding the "liberation from the seven fetters": they are collectively termed "fetters" because they are bound by the conditions of the proclivities (*anuśaya*); their nature being detached from these is called "liberation.
The latter two are termed "causal characteristics," meaning that the power of aspiration and the power of karma draw forth the mind that undergoes retribution.

Eighth, because bodhisattvas take birth through the power of their vows, they manifest illusory and unreal forms that may appear similar to deceit; yet, as these actually accomplish benefit, they are said to be "upright and honest.
Ninth, because other sentient beings take birth according to their karma, it is said that [the bodhisattvas] "follow the path."

In the "Discourse on the Detailed Analysis of the Importance," the statement "by means of the intrinsically pure mind, the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses]" explains the basis for the defilement and purification of the two consciousnesses—the sixth and the seventh.
This means that if there were no fifth nature of pure mind, then the sixth and seventh lines would consist solely of defilement and bondage, with nothing that is neither defiled nor bound.
Furthermore, because these two lines involve the afflictions of defilement and bondage, they indicate that one takes birth in accordance with the Path in the subsequent line.
The second section, beginning with "This bodhisattva knows afflictions," clarifies the dense forest of afflictive conduct (*kleśa-caryā-gahana*).
Within this, there is first a detailed exposition followed by a summary.
Regarding the ten phrases in the detailed exposition, the treatise subsumes them into three groups: the first two each constitute one group, and the final eight constitute the other.
Regarding the first characteristic of depth: it penetrates far, reaching even to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
In the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), the Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is considered the peak;
in the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*), it extends to the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*).
Regarding the second, the superficial characteristic, the treatise refers to it in the sūtra as the "characteristic of boundless practice.
This means that when immeasurable roots of goodness are being cultivated and accumulated, the accompanying afflictions are difficult to discern.
Within the three types of defilement, there are eight phrases, which are divided into three groups:
first, three clarify the defilement of afflictions; second, two clarify afflictions by way of birth; and third, three clarify afflictions by way of karma.

Regarding the initial section, the statement that “the mind and its companions are characterized by non-separation” means that they follow what is bound; this is the sense of being bound by conditions.
“Mutually performing a common function” explains the meaning of co-arising; this refers to the mind and its companions, meaning that the mind-king and the afflictions support one another to arise.
"Mutually depending on one another" explains the meaning of non-separation; that is, once arisen, they depend upon each other and do not separate.
"Arising together and not separating" summarizes both points as stated in the sutra.
Regarding the second point, "the distinction between latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*"):

as for what constitutes a "bond," it refers to the latent dispositions. Because these latent dispositions exist and because one cannot attain liberation due to their presence, the latent dispositions are said to be the essence of that which binds. These consist of the ten latent dispositions and the ten entanglements; hence, they are called "distinctions."
Regarding the statement that "afflictions" (*kleśa*) and "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*) have the same meaning, this is presented as an exegesis based on the sutra.
That is to say, when explaining these afflictions, why are they called "latent tendencies"?
It is because they share this same single meaning.
If they constitute a single meaning, why does the subsequent text explain the latent tendencies (anuśaya) separately?
It is simply because these ten latent tendencies possess the sense of "binding," which is subsumed under this present section;
they also possess the sense of "pursuing," which is categorized under the following section.
In this version of the sutra, the *anuśayas* (proclivities) and *paryavasthānas* (envelopments) are distinguished; both are capable of binding.
The three terms "associated with the mind" (*citta-samprayukta*) and so forth refer to the objects that are bound.
By the word "mind," the essence of that which is bound is set forth.

The phrase "associated with the mind" (*cittasamprayukta*) and so forth is cited from the sūtra to provide a contrastive clarification, thereby re-explaining what it means to be "dissociated" (*viprayukta*).
To show that liberation can be attained: because the nature of the mind within its entanglements is eternally and fundamentally pure, this bondage can now be liberated.
The next two phrases, "arising in accordance with the paths" and so forth, clarify afflictions in terms of their arising.

When the treatise states that "the body's affairs arise from the causes of the paths and realms," it clarifies that these afflictions serve as the causal basis for the bodily affairs that arise within the six destinies and the three realms.
Regarding the indication of "arising from the defilement of afflictions" (*kleśasaṃkleśa*): this summary is established based on arising, as it clarifies the afflictions.
The three subsequent lines beginning with "craving and delusion" clarify the afflictions by way of defiled karma.

Regarding the three factors that obstruct liberation through the cause of karma: craving (*tṛṣṇā*), delusion (*moha*), and views (*dṛṣṭi*) constitute these three factors. Craving is the pursuit of sensual desire; delusion is the pursuit of existence; and views are the pursuit of false asceticism and celibacy (*brahmacarya*). All of these obstruct liberation, which is explained as a great fault.

Regarding the statement that the causes for the uninterrupted arising of bodily, verbal, and mental karma that conform to the world consist in committing grave karmic offenses through pride and delusion: this clarifies that the afflictions are the cause of these three types of karmic offenses because they are not severed.
The phrase "down to" serves as a concluding summary.

Regarding the "eighty-four thousand," according to the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*, there are three hundred and fifty *pāramitā* dharma-gates throughout the Buddha’s single lifetime; that is, beginning from the *Pāramitā of Infinite Radiance* and ending with the *Pāramitā of Distributing Relics*, each takes the six *pāramitās* as its cause, resulting in two thousand one hundred.
By using these as antidotes to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the six decays (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and the ten kinds of afflictions, there are thus twenty-one thousand [dharmas].
The four great elements are the internal retributive body.
The six decays refer to the six external sense objects; they are so named because they cause the decay and exhaustion of wholesome dharmas.

Each of these twenty-one thousand methods transforms four types of sentient beings—first, those with excessive greed; second, those with excessive anger; third, those with excessive delusion; and fourth, those with equal proportions of the three poisons—thereby forming the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of the various pāramitās.
The fetters that act as obstacles are precisely the eighty-four thousand afflictions; the same applies to karma and so forth.
The following sections are to be understood accordingly.
Third, from "This bodhisattva knows karma" onwards, the dense forest of karmic conduct is elucidated; here too, there is first a detailed exposition followed by a summary.
Within the separate [classification], there are ten phrases:
"good in the beginning" and so forth clarify that karma serves as the cause for the six realms of existence.

That is to say, among the good, the superior grade is the cause for the heavens, the middling is the cause for humans, and the inferior is for the asuras; among the evil, the three grades are the causes for the three evil realms.
The indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is not a cause; it is spoken of in relation to its counterpart.
Furthermore, it also possesses the meaning of "naming" (*nāman*) and "action" (*karma*).
Regarding the two types of discrimination (*vikalpa*), their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is volition (*cetanā*); however, because there are three kinds, they are termed "distinctions" (*viśeṣa*).

That is to say, the volition of deliberation (*santīraṇa-cetanā*) and the volition of determination (*niścaya-cetanā*)—these two reside in the mental ground (*manobhūmi*). As long as they have not yet manifested in body or speech, they are termed the "time of deliberation" (*tarka-kāla*); because [the action] has not yet been performed, it cannot be distinguished [as wholesome or unwholesome].

The volition of instigation (*abhisamskāra-cetanā*), which is precisely when [the action] is manifesting in body or speech, is termed the "time of performing the action" (*kriyā-kāla*); at this point, the wholesome or unwholesome nature of the karma is established and can be distinguished.
Regarding "the three minds and their associates," this refers to the differentiation of skillful means (*upāya*).

That is to say, this volition (*cetanā*) of karma arises together with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), each acting as an associate to the mind; once they have arisen according to their respective goodness or evil, they immediately infuse the foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) to form seeds.
Because the seeds resemble their perfumers, it is said that they do not produce fruits separately;
this explains "not being apart.
Regarding the four points such as "spontaneity" and so forth, they exhaustively encompass the distinctions among the fruits.
This means that while karma from beginningless time naturally perishes moment by moment, the accumulated fruit is not lost.
The phrase "conditioned karma" explains this natural perishing, because that which is conditioned is necessarily impermanent.
Regarding "the causes having fully assembled," this reveals that their functional efficacy is not lost, thereby explaining the sequence of the assembly of results.

Each of these momentary cessations is capable of inducing the result in its entirety; even the cessation through the practice of the path induces the result partially, as for example when heavy karma is transformed into light.
Since there are not merely these, it is said that they are "various characteristics in succession.
Regarding the five types such as "with retribution" and so forth, this refers to the distinction between those who have already received the fruit and those who have not yet received the fruit.
This means that past karma of retribution received in this life, having already been experienced in the present, is called "having retribution.
Past karma of subsequent retribution, not yet experienced in the present, is called "without retribution"; it does not mean that it is entirely non-existent.
Regarding the "six black-and-black" and so forth: this refers to distinctions; that is, by correlating the four types of karma, their distinctions are revealed.
Specifically, the first two phrases correlate the wholesome and the unwholesome, while the latter two phrases correlate the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, the seventeenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "All unwholesome karmas are exclusively termed 'black' because their nature is defiled.
Their maturation is also black because it is disagreeable."
The wholesome [karma] of the form realm is exclusively termed "white" because it is not intermingled with evil.

The formless realm is not mentioned [in this context] because it does not possess the two types of retribution—intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and birth (*upapatti*), nor does it possess the three types of action, such as bodily action and so forth.
Wholesome karma of the desire realm is called "black-and-white" because it is interspersed with the unwholesome.
Its maturation is also black-and-white because it is interspersed with undesirable black [results].
All outflow-free (anāsrava) karma is called "neither-black-nor-white."
The details are as explained therein.
Regarding the statement "that which can exhaust the characteristics of karma," this refers to uncontaminated (anāsrava) karma.
As for "the arising of karma," it arises because it depends upon conditions.
Regarding the dharma of receiving karma (*upādāna-karma*), because it is able to take up the fruit, the treatise on the sūtras names it "right reception" (*samyag-upādāna*).
As for the seven immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and so forth, these are distinctions of causes and conditions.
This means that through various causes and conditions, one is able to initiate karma.
Regarding the "eight worldly dharmas" and so forth, there is a distinction between those not yet accumulated and those already accumulated;
that is, supramundane [dharmas] are not yet accumulated, while mundane karma has been accumulated.
Regarding the "nine types of manifest retribution" (*pratyakṣavipāka*) and so forth, this clarifies the determinacy or indeterminacy of the three time periods.

That which is performed in the present and experienced in the present is called "manifest retribution" (*pratyakṣavipāka*); that which is experienced in the immediately following birth is called "retribution upon rebirth" (*upapadyavipāka*); and that which is experienced from the second birth onward is called "subsequent retribution" (*aparaparyāyavipāka*). Within these three, there is both the determinate and the indeterminate.

Regarding the ten [aspects] such as "according to the various vehicles," among the three types of vehicles there are those that are determinate and those that are indeterminate; this refers to whether one may regress or not. It does not mean that being determinate or indeterminate is based on whether it is easy or difficult to cross over within the mundane world.
In the treatise on the sūtras, it can be understood that for both vehicles and non-vehicles, there are determinate and indeterminate karmas.
The conclusion below regarding the eighty thousand [dharmaskandhas] and so forth can likewise be understood.

Fourth, from the passage "This bodhisattva knows the various faculties" onwards, the specific section clarifying the dense forest of faculties and practices is presented; therein, the categories of weak, medium, and superior are explained as being "vessels," meaning they are the vessels to whom the Dharma is to be bestowed.

They are also termed dull-facultied (*mṛdv-indriya*), medium-facultied (*madhya-indriya*), and sharp-facultied (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*). That is to say, one who quickly receives [the teaching] is called sharp; one who receives it slowly is called dull; and one who is of intermediate capacity is called medium.
Furthermore, one who receives what is profound is called sharp; one who receives what is shallow is called dull; and the case of intermediate capacity can be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, the same applies to extensive, limited, and intermediate reception;
each is consistent with both teaching and principle, which can be understood by analogy.
Regarding the two [aspects of] the prior and posterior limits, these refer to the distinctions in the transformation of the faculties (*indriya*).
"Roots of the prior and posterior" refers to understanding the roots of the prior and posterior limits.
"Because the prior root is lowered as the [subsequent] increases and levels" explains the distinction and non-distinction between them.
That is to say, the prior is the producer and the posterior is the produced; if that which is produced increases, the prior root is thereby lowered.
If that which is produced is inferior, the preceding faculty increases;
if they are similar, it remains level.
The three—superior, middling, and inferior—are the distinctions among the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).
This refers to the distinction between the natures of the three vehicles: the superior is the Mahāyāna, the middling is the Madhyamāyāna, and the inferior is the Hīnayāna.
Regarding the "companions of the four afflictions," this refers to the various classifications of afflicted mental states.

This refers to the five faculties of feeling—joy, pleasure, and so forth—which are called "companions of affliction" because they are inseparable from the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that defile them through the habituation of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The *Abhidharmakośa*, chapter three, states: "Within the context of total defilement (*saṃkleśa*), the five feelings, such as pleasure and the rest, possess a predominant function."

Why is this so? Because the sūtras state that craving increases in relation to pleasant feelings, hatred increases in relation to painful feelings, and ignorance increases in relation to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
The commentary explains:
"The meaning of 'faculty' (*indriya*) is that of predominant influence.
The phrase 'five according to the various vehicles,' etc., refers to the distinction between the determinate and the indeterminate."
Regarding "among the three vehicles" and "in the world," this explains what constitutes a vehicle and what does not.
As for "the certain and the uncertain, the matured and the immature," this is a general explanation:
that is to say, within the Mahāyāna, those who are matured are certain [of their attainment], while those who are not matured are uncertain.
In the Hīnayāna, those who have matured are not fixed, because they may turn toward the Mahāyāna.
Within the three vehicles, those who are each fixed attain liberation within their respective vehicle; therefore, it is said that "each vehicle" and so forth.
Regarding those whose retribution is fixed and who are to be abandoned: within the world, they cannot be transformed to enter the Path through any means; therefore, they are temporarily set aside.
This statement is made according to the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna, which allows for the existence of five distinct natures.

Regarding the phrase "six [factors] that follow the faculties" (*ṣaḍ-anuvartakā indriyāṇi*), this refers to the distinctions in the manner of conformity (*anukūla-pravṛtti*). There are three types of conformity:

first, conformity based on the body (*kāyāśrita-anukūla-pravṛtti*). Here, the faculties and their associated dharmas mutually and reciprocally revolve in dependence upon the body of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana-kāya*); because the six sense bases are interdependent, this explains "following the faculties."
Second, "arising and ceasing in accordance with practice" refers to being easily destroyed; this explains its susceptibility to ruin.
Third, "observing the marks of practice" explains the deep grasping of marks.

Regarding "the seven superiorities" and so forth: these refer to the distinctions of the Śrāvaka’s purity; because they can accomplish the meaning of destroying the obstacles to superior practice, they are termed "superior practice" in contrast to that of ordinary beings.
This explains the first phrase.
Next, "the accomplishment of the practice that eliminates obstacles" explains "indestructibility.

Regarding the eight transformations and non-transformations: these are the distinctions within the purity of a bodhisattva; those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are called "transformations," while those on the stages are "non-transformations."
Furthermore, the first seven stages are called "transformation," while from the eighth stage upward they are called "non-transformation.
The phrase "the nine, the three times, and so forth" indicates the distinctions encompassed by all faculties.

The initial stage of practice is called "beginning"; the correct cultivation of skillful means is called "maturation. Based on these three stages, the distinctions among the faculties (*indriya*) are discerned.
That is to say, when the faculty and the practice arise together, they are termed "co-arising" (*sahaja*); since the practice has a beginning and an end, the faculty likewise follows suit.
The subsequent summary can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the fifth [category], desire; the sixth, nature; and the seventh, upright mind—each has soft, medium, and superior degrees.
The *Śāstra* states, "Thus entering by way of nature," which explains why it is not explained in detail.
Because the four dharmas, beginning with the faculties (*indriya*), accord with one another in their essential nature and characteristics, they are not explained in detail.
From the eighth section, "Knowing the Latent Tendencies" (*anuśaya*) onwards, the dense forest of the activity of the latent tendencies is elucidated.
The term "proclivity" (*anuśaya*) carries the meaning of pursuing and binding; it is named after a metaphorical analogy.
Just as a public messenger pursues a thief and, finding an opportunity, binds him, so too do the afflictions (*kleśa*) pursue sentient beings and, finding an opportunity, bind them.
Within these ten statements, the first four clarify *where* [the mind] follows along, while the latter six clarify *by what* it follows along.
Regarding the former, there is following along in four locations:
one statement clarifies the location in terms of the mind, namely, arising from both common and non-retributive minds, and arising from uncommon retributive minds.
Second, regarding the realms (*dhātu*), the spheres (*āyatana*) are clarified: the desire realm is "lower," the form realm is "middle," and the formless realm is "upper.
When a mind arises within its own realm, it is termed "associated" (*samprayukta*); when compared with a different realm, it is "non-associated" (*asamprayukta*).
If it were not so, all would be associated; therefore, it is said that they do not depart from their characteristics.

Regarding the statement in the treatise that "there is entry into the distant," this clarifies the locations according to the stages, extending even to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); this section is missing from the sutra.

Third, regarding the locus as defined by time: it is said that those who have tormented sentient beings since beginningless time exist throughout boundless worlds; they fear only wisdom as if it were a hostile thief. Because they lack the wisdom born of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, they are not extinguished and constantly torment sentient beings.

Fourth, regarding the clarification of the bases (*āyatana*) in terms of practice: those things contrary to dhyāna and so forth cannot extinguish the mental tendencies that follow worldly dhyāna and the like.
If there are no underlying propensities (*anuśaya*), then these various virtues such as dhyāna immediately become supramundane.
This is contrary to the correct cultivation that transcends the world and does not allow one to attain liberation.
The following clarifies what follows along with it.
There are six kinds of such accompaniment:
"First, there is non-interruption of existence" is the thesis (*uddiśya*).

"By means of the non-interruption of existence, etc. is the explanation (*nirdeśa*); that is to say, because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of existence exist, they are able to cause the three realms of existence to continue in a similar succession; therefore, it is called "being bound to the three realms."
This explains "following along" (anubandha) with reference to the preceding section.

Second is "following along over a long duration," because it has followed one since beginningless time; it prevents immeasurable wholesome states of mind from manifesting, which is why the text says "immeasurable minds" and so forth.
"Third, the seeds follow along with the arising of a single body"—this is the heading, meaning that it clarifies how the manifest seeds follow along within this present single body.
The subsequent explanation regarding "the gateways of the eye and so forth" refers to the six sense faculties.
The "sixfold arising of the accumulated consciousness" refers to the six consciousnesses produced in dependence upon the sense faculties.
"Arising together and following along" clarifies that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) arise simultaneously with and follow along with the faculties and the consciousnesses.

Regarding "this is what is manifested and that which perfumes the ālayavijñāna": this perfuming of the fundamental consciousness clarifies how seeds follow along with manifestations, and how seeds and manifestations mutually support one another, causing the afflictions (*kleśa*) to flourish; thus it is said, "opening the gate of afflictions."
The treatise states that the "opening of various gateways" in the sūtras refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as the points where delusions arise.
Regarding the phrase "the four unrealities follow along," it means that because one does not obtain the true antidote, one is said to be "ignorant of the antidote."

5. "Subtle Pursuance" and below explain the characteristic of subtlety. This means that within the nine stages of the three realms, the body of afflictions pursues the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); because it is so subtle as to be invisible, it is called "non-existent," just as oil within sesame seeds cannot be perceived by sight.
Regarding the statement that the Sūtra conforms [to this], it clarifies that these [realms] exist.
That it does not conform [to other teachings] clarifies that they are subtle, being likewise non-existent [in the conventional sense].

Because the six types of practice for transcending the world—which involve distancing oneself from suffering and following after [the path]—cannot be accomplished by other practices, it is said that there is no Noble Path and so forth.
The ninth section, beginning with "This bodhisattva," concerns the knowledge of the dense forest of birth and conduct.
Within this, there are eight phrases:
first, "the body is manifold" clarifies that physical forms and types differ; therefore, it is called the differentiation of birth.
Second, they arise through differences in karma; this phrase does not appear in other sutras.
Third, regarding the various abodes, it clarifies that the six realms of existence are distinct; therefore, it says "hell and so forth."
The four types of form, with their various upper and lower distinctions, clarify that the three realms are not the same; hence it says "the realm of form, the formless realm," and so forth.
Question:
Since they are formless, why speak of the upper and lower [distinctions] of form?
Answer:
According to the Mahāyāna, there is subtle form within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which is the most refined among all forms.
The same applies to the superior and inferior grades within perception (*saṃjñā*); although non-Buddhists regard it as "non-perception," in reality, there exists a subtle perception.

Fifth, the various causes of external matter are similar; since they arise in dependence on the earth and so forth, being of the same category as grass and trees, it is said that "karma is by means of [causes] such as these.

Sixth, the various specific characteristics: this refers to name-and-form arising together with the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); as this is the very substance of retribution, it is said that "name-and-form arises together with [the consciousness] and so forth."

The seven kinds of causes that accord with origination (*anuvartaka-hetu*) should properly be called "causes that accord with primary origination" (*mūla-janma-anuvartaka-hetu*); because they arise from ignorance and craving and subsequently conform to them, they are referred to as "ignorance, craving, and so forth."
Regarding the eightfold classification of the truth of suffering as accumulation (*samudaya-duḥkha-satya*): it refers to how present existence can accumulate future suffering.
The different ways in which sentient beings, driven by the three types of seeking (*tri-ṣaṇā*), accumulate suffering are termed "various distinctions."

Regarding the statement "desiring birth," there is further pleasure; there are sentient beings who love their own bodies and the bodies of others, whose minds are attached to signs, and who, because they grasp at and cling to the upper and lower realms through coming and going, [seek rebirth].
The commentary states:

These are sentient beings with seeking; they love their own realm as their own body and love other realms as the bodies of others. Because they are attached to signs (*nimitta*), they come and go between the higher and lower realms.

Regarding "those who desire to act and desire to receive," the treatise and the sūtra refer to them as "those who desire to receive" because they take pleasure in greed and grasping, seeking after things everywhere.
These are sentient beings characterized by the pursuit of sensual desires (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*), for they seek and pursue objects everywhere through greed and grasping.
Those who "do not delight" and so forth are sentient beings seeking a false brahmacarya.
The terms "small," "great," and "immeasurable" explain the three realms.
"Non-perception" (asaṃjñin) specifically refers to the Heaven of Non-Perception, because non-Buddhists take that state to be nirvana.
The wheel-turning explains the continuity; in reality, it is because one falsely conceives of the wheel-turning as an emergence.
Below the phrase "This bodhisattva" in the tenth [section], there are ten points concerning the dense forest of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and conduct:

the first is the causal habitual tendency, referring to the wholesome and unwholesome karma performed in the past. Since those habitual tendencies may either arise simultaneously with the present fruit or not arise at all, it is said that they "arise or do not arise."

The second is the habit-energy of the fruits. "Paths" refers to the six realms of existence; "perfuming" refers to the habitual tendencies of those realms. For example, as when one comes from the heavens and remains fresh and pure even now, the detailed explanation of the habit-energy of the paths should be understood as it appears within the *Mahātejaḥpradīpa-ṛṣi-paripṛcchā-sūtra*; therefore, it says, "according to where they are born," and so forth.

Third is the habitual tendency of conditions (*pratyaya-vāsanā*): it is perfumed by associating with sentient beings; just as one becomes good by associating with a virtuous person and so forth, it is therefore said to "follow sentient beings" and so on.

Fourth is the habitual tendency of activity (*abhisamskāra-vāsanā*): it follows the afflictions that arise; for instance, repeatedly giving rise to greed and so forth forms a habituation, and according to the karma one performs there is likewise a habitual tendency—just as the son of a potter is capable of practicing *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) and so forth—and thus it is said to "follow karma and afflictions."

Fifth is the habitual tendency of karma (*karmavāsanā*), which refers to the repeated cultivation of actions such as those that are wholesome; thus it is said to be "wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth.

Sixth is the habitual tendency of renunciation, detachment from desire, and so on, through which these qualities become familiar and are subsequently easy to sever; thus it is said to be "renunciation of desire, and so forth."

Regarding the seven [types of] intermediate states (*antarābhava*) in relation to the present, they are explained as being characterized by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). For example, if a person currently delights in practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*), they will likewise remain free from desire and defilement even within the intermediate state; therefore, it is said that "they follow the subsequent body," meaning that the habitual tendencies of the preceding fundamental existence (*pūrvabhava*) persist within the location of the subsequent intermediate state body.

Eighth is "successive perfuming by the fruit," which means that according to a single continuous habituation, one receives bodies in succession throughout the various realms of existence, all of which possess that habituation; hence it is called "successive" and so forth.

9. "The Worldly Dhyāna is Perfumed by Causes" and below explain and establish [the point]: because within that dhyāna one does not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), and due to being dragged by those afflictions, one is born in the higher realms while still possessing the residual impressions (*vāsanā*) of them; therefore, it is said, "for a long time," and so forth.
This sutra lacks the final two phrases: first, the contrast between the heterodox and the orthodox.

That is to say, the "same dharma" refers to the liberation of the Two Vehicles; because the various non-Buddhists do not accord with the Buddha-dharma, it is called "different. They take the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) as liberation; since both these heterodox and orthodox positions possess habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they are called "perfumed. Thus it is said, "there is the real and the unreal": the "real" is the Lesser Vehicle, and the "unreal" is the external [non-Buddhist] path.

Second, regarding the contrast between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna: this refers to the statement that because one possesses habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) toward the persons and dharmas of the three vehicles—whenever one sees, hears, or associates with them.
From the eleventh section, "This Bodhisattva," onwards, one understands the dense forest of the practices of the three clusters (*triskandha*).
In this treatise, there are five sections;

the first distinguishes the three groups based on spiritual lineage (*gotra*). That is to say, those who lack the nature for *nirvāṇa* are of wrong determination (*mithyātva-niyata*), while those who possess the nature for *nirvāṇa* are of right determination (*samyaktva-niyata*).

Within right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are each distinct and exclusively self-contained; apart from these two, there is the indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*), which this treatise omits to explain in detail—this should be understood as being explained according to the initial teaching (*ādikarmika-naya*).
Second, the three groups are distinguished based on delusion and awakening. That is to say, right view is the cause of wholesome conduct.
Among the three roots of goodness, the single factor of right view invariably gives rise to wholesome karma; this is termed "right determination" (samyaktva-niyāma).
Non-attachment and non-hatred are called "indeterminate" because they do not invariably give rise to wholesome states.

Among the afflictions, false view is the cause of unwholesome conduct; because it invariably gives rise to unwholesome karma, it alone is termed "fixedly evil," while the others are termed "indeterminate."

Third, the three groups are distinguished according to their karmic actions: among the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), each individual crime is certain to bring about rebirth in the evil realms and is thus termed "fixed in the wrong" (*mithyātva-niyata*); the five faculties such as faith are certain to bring about rebirth in the good realms and are thus termed "fixed in the right" (*samyaktva-niyata*); those that differ from these two are termed "undetermined" (*aniyata*).

Fourth, the three groups are distinguished according to the positions of the heterodox and the orthodox: namely, by reversing those eight right [paths], one establishes the "eight heterodox [paths]" for non-Buddhists, which constitutes the position of the heterodoxly fixed;
the "right nature" that departs from birth is called the orthodox position, and based on this, the orthodox position of the Śrāvakas is established as the rightly fixed.
The five points directly distinguish the three categories based on the gains and losses of Mahāyāna bodhisattvas.

Regarding the statement that those who have deeply entered the category of the wrong (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi) are difficult to transform, the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra* refer to this as the characteristic of the non-turning of wrong certainty (*mithyātva-niyata-lakṣaṇa*), which consists of envy, stinginess, and evil conduct. This means being jealous when others excel oneself; because one does not give the Dharma as a gift and thus fails to relinquish those who could be converted, it is called "envy" (*īrṣyā*).
Because one is stingy with wealth and does not practice giving, it is called the fault of parsimony (*mātsarya*).
Because it can produce suffering for others, it is called misconduct (*duścarita*), which refers to killing, stealing, and so forth.

Regarding their opposition to the *pāramitās*: herein, the six obscurations hinder the practice of the six perfections, and thus they are said to be "opposed. Specifically, envy (*īrṣyā*) hinders the latter three [perfections]—wisdom, meditative concentration, and diligence; parsimony hinders the perfection of giving (*dāna*); and misconduct hinders the two practices of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*).
Due to these hindrances, the correct practice of all bodhisattvas fails to reach fulfillment, resulting in false certainty (*mithyā-niyata*).
Correct certainty (*samyak-niyata*) and uncertainty (*aniyata*) may be understood by analogy with this explanation.
From the words "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) onwards, the general conclusion for the preceding three types of accomplishment can be understood.
The fourth section, "The Bodhisattva dwells in this stage," and below, clarifies the accomplishment of the teaching.
Within this, there is first a general exposition and later a specific one.
In the general exposition, the phrase "knowing the various practices of sentient beings" restates the entry into practice in order to identify those who are vessels for the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "according to their liberation" and so forth, this correctly clarifies that teaching the Dharma in accordance with the faculties [of beings] enables them to attain liberation.

From the passage "This bodhisattva transforms... onwards, there is a specific clarification of the accomplishment of the teaching; the text consists of four sections and the meaning comprises three layers:
first, this initial section concludes with the accomplishment of wisdom (*jñāna-saṃpad*).
2. From "acting as a great Dharma teacher" onwards, the section accomplishes both wisdom and verbal karma;
3. From "employing immeasurable wisdom" onwards, it accomplishes only verbal karma;
4. From "attaining dhāraṇīs" onwards, this is the accomplishment of the Dharma teacher.
In the first section, there are two parts: first, clarifying that which accords with what is known, which refers to the Dharma taught;
second, that which accords with the basis, which refers to the vessels to whom it is addressed.

Regarding the former, "the Dharma for transforming sentient beings" means teaching the methods of transformation so that the vessels of liberation may reach maturity—that is, teaching the transformative Dharma so that the vessels of liberation among all sentient beings ripen.
Regarding the method for delivering sentient beings: because it delivers them by means of the correct essence of liberation, it means to cause them correctly to attain the fruit of liberation.

However, as for the distinctions among the liberations thus attained, they do not transcend the Three Vehicles; therefore, it is said that "one knows them as they truly are and speaks [the Dharma] accordingly," and so forth.

Second, regarding the section beginning with "according to reality, following sentient beings," which clarifies following the basis [of the teaching], there are two parts: first, a general explanation of preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of the vessels; second, a detailed analysis beginning with "following the mind."
The teaching of the Dharma accords with the capacity of the vessel, and understanding follows the mind.

To say that it accords with those to be delivered means that one bestows the remedial dharma; this refers to the understanding of the sūtras and treatises according to the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), because it serves as the remedy for those underlying tendencies.
The first two lines refer to those who serve as vessels for transformation.

To say that "the vessel for the Dharma has been perfected" clarifies the perfection of the vessel for the *Prajñāpāramitā*; it means that because they understand [the teaching] according to the faculties [of beings], the vessel is perfected and thus capable of receiving the Dharma.

Regarding "following the sphere of conduct": this refers to the spheres of objects that the mind follows; by using those very metaphors to cause understanding to arise, they are called "vessels" for that.
Regarding "following the sphere of wisdom": based on the aforementioned arising of understanding, it serves to give rise to various distinct practices; thus, they are called "vessels" for that.

Regarding the two phrases "knowing all conditioned phenomena" (*sarvasaṃskāra*) and so forth: they indicate that up until the attainment of the vessel of accomplishment, one clarifies the vessel formed by virtue based upon practice.

Regarding the phrase "according to the destinies" (*yathāgati*) and so forth: this refers to the vessel of eloquence in speech; it means that since birth, karma, and afflictions have been habituated for a long time and are difficult to eliminate, it is only through superior eloquence in teaching and transforming that one can cause them to be abandoned. Therefore, birth and the other factors are called the vessels for eloquence in speech.

The perfuming of the latent tendencies (vāsanā) leads to the transformation of practice through understanding; herein, the three aggregates such as meditative concentration (samādhi) are omitted for brevity.

Regarding the phrase "according with the vehicle" (*yānānulomika*), the treatise and the sūtra state that faith is the cause of the three vehicles, for it is capable of carrying one out of the vessel [of existence].
The second section, beginning with "This bodhisattva dwells in this stage," clarifies that both wisdom and verbal karma are accomplished.
Therefore, in the treatise, the verbal karma is first interrogated, and the conclusion states that wisdom is accomplished.
From the perspective of wisdom, it is "knowledge" because one knows the proper manner of exposition;
from the perspective of subsequent verbal action (*vākkarman*), it is "the Dharma-preacher" because one possesses twenty kinds of qualities of a Dharma-preacher.
In the treatise, "expounding" refers to verbal action that clarifies entry into profound meaning, while "retaining" refers to wisdom that achieves manifest protection of the Dharma.
The twenty kinds of matters concerning the Dharma-preacher are to be understood as they are fully explained in the treatise.
Third, from "employing the immeasurable" onwards, the accomplishment of verbal karma is correctly elucidated.
This section has two parts:
first, a brief explanation of how the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) can give rise to oral expression; second, a detailed analysis through ten successive gates.
Within the first part, the phrase "employing wisdom and skillful means" serves as a transition from the preceding to the subsequent discussion.
The names mentioned refer to the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*); by employing those [names], one gives rise to this unimpeded wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*).

The following clarifies that based on the four types of unimpeded wisdom, one gives rise to speech and preaches the Dharma; because what is attained is unimpeded and free from even momentary fluctuation, it is called "indestructible" (*akopya*).
The meaning of the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge is explained at length in a separate chapter.

Briefly stated, the essence of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); when categorized according to their objects of focus, they are divided into four types.
First, regarding the "dharma-body" (*dharmatā*), this clarifies the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
Second, regarding the essence of the sphere of the two dharmas: it refers to the sense of differentiation within the essence of the dharmas.
Third, regarding correctly bestowing [the Dharma] upon sentient beings: this means speaking of bestowing [the Dharma] upon sentient beings based on what one has personally attained.

Fourth, regarding correctly seeking to provide through immeasurable gateways: this means providing immeasurable gateways according to the various differences in the correct aspirations of sentient beings.
In the subsequent detailed explanation, the first part—explaining the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*)—distances itself from the two extremes.

That which is "subsumed under the phenomena of arising" excludes other phenomena and is therefore said to be free from the two extremes; it is called "subsumed under the phenomena of arising" because it expresses its own intrinsic nature.
Just as the characteristic of resistance in form is cited as an illustration to demonstrate [the principle], so it applies equally to all others.
Regarding the second explanation of non-obstruction in meaning, the phrase "that which is free from... restates the aforementioned phenomena.
"Knowledge as it truly is" (yathābhūta-jñāna) below distinguishes the object in terms of phenomena (dharma).
"The Bodhisattva abides therein" distinguishes the object in terms of persons (pudgala).
"Just as form" and so forth also cite examples to reveal false discrimination (abhūtaparikalpa), thereby correctly clarifying the meaning of differentiation.

While the Hīnayāna explains that form possesses such meanings as suffering and impermanence, here, according to the Mahāyāna, it is explained that this dharma of form is merely a false conceptualization; in its true principle, it fundamentally lacks the nature of being form.

Regarding the third explanation of the term, "possessing clear comprehension in speech according to what others prefer" means understanding and knowing the words that others find pleasing; this explains "clear comprehension."
"Following others," and so forth, explains "giving.
Within the fourfold explanation of eloquent speech (*pratibhāna*), first the preceding terms are cited; from "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) onward, it analyzes eloquent speech.
"Immeasurable and various meanings and words" refers to the distinctions within the terminology, explaining the "immeasurable gateways."
The phrase "knowing accordingly" (*anujñā*) below explains the granting [of eloquence].
It is newly termed the "analytical knowledge of non-obstruction" (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), meaning clear discernment and skillful exposition that causes others to experience joy;
it is also called "joyful speech" (*prātihārya*).

In the detailed explanation that follows, although in reality these four are present in all teachings concerning all phenomena, we shall now list ten categories based on the number ten. Among these, the first five provide a general understanding of principle and teaching, while the latter five concern the pure virtues of the Three Vehicles.
Regarding the preceding section, the first four [verses] clarify unimpededness with respect to the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), while the final one concerns the knowing wisdom (*jñāna*).
Within the former, the first three know the meaning (*artha*) and the final one knows the teaching (*dharma*).

Regarding the former [the two aspects], first, concerning phenomena as objects of cognition (*jñeya-dharma*): because these phenomena have distinct conditions and each abides without intermixture, they are termed "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Second, concerning phenomena as principles (*tattva-dharma*): because these principles are universally pervasive, they are termed "common characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
These two should clarify the phenomena for one another.
Third, distinguishing phenomena according to time: because the three periods of time flow and shift, they are termed "characteristics of activity" (*saṃskāra-lakṣaṇa*).
Fourth, teaching the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings is termed "characteristics of exposition" (*deśanā-lakṣaṇa*).

The fifth [category] distinguishes four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) based on the aspect of the knowing wisdom; it is not that these know the wisdom itself, and thus they are termed the "characteristics of wisdom.
Within the latter five [categories], the first generally knows the pure realization of the three vehicles' departure from marks, which is called "freedom from conceit" (*nirmāna*).
Among the latter four specific categories, one generally knows both the Small and Great Vehicles, while the remaining three specifically know the stages of a Mahāyāna bodhisattva.
The first [chapter] knows the cause, and the latter two know the fruit; thus, one essence and two functions may be understood.
In the subsequent sequential explanation, the commentary on these ten chapters is divided into ten sections.
Regarding the first [category], the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), "dharma" and "meaning" (*artha*) constitute the pair of the general and the particular.
Within dependently arisen phenomena, one knows their intrinsic characteristics in a general sense and knows their specific distinctions in a particular sense.
"Phrasing" (*vyañjana*) and "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) constitute the pair of the extensive and the concise: a few names that manifest a phenomenon are called "phrasing."
The stabilization of numerous diverse names is what constitutes their meaning; causing others to find delight therein is called "eloquent speech" (*pratibhāna*).

Regarding the phrase "stabilizing ideation" (*saṃjñā*): ideation is the basis upon which speech arises. Therefore, in other treatises, it is sometimes called ideation, sometimes sound, sometimes name, sometimes syllable, or sometimes designation (*prajñapti*); these are all alternative designations for "name."
Because one manifests meaning through names and words and causes that meaning to become firm, it is called "the firmness of conceptualization" (*saṃjñā-dārḍhya*).
There are many types of this firmness of conceptualization, which constitute the distinctions among names and concepts.
In the re-explanation, the term "indestructible" (*abhedya*) restates the preceding phrase.
"According to what is realized" means that one clearly understands for oneself.
"According to this or that" indicates teaching in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
That which is called "unceasing" because it proceeds in succession without interruption refers to constant preaching.
Regarding "immeasurable and manifold," this means that for each and every dharma, one can extensively explain it through immeasurable different names.
To "strengthen that meaning" means that by explaining it many times through various names, one intends to establish the fundamental meaning, thereby making it firm and secure.
The second section, beginning with "Furthermore," clarifies the common characteristics (*sādharmya*).
Within this, the meaning of the phenomena is divided according to the two truths; the latter two [sections] are likewise divided according to the extensive and the concise.

First, all phenomena are identical in their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); second, conditioned phenomena are identical in their characteristic of impermanence (*anitya*); third, regarding the identity of conventional designations (*prajñapti*), phenomena are identical in being nameless, existing only as provisional designations for the sake of explanation.
Regarding the four conventional designations being identical to conventional designations, they are further elucidated through conventional designations once again.
The subsequent section provides a detailed analysis.
