As for "entering non-self by means of impermanence," this explains the meaning in accordance with the Dharma; that is, by contemplating impermanence, one immediately understands non-self. Therefore, the second gate enters the cognitive sphere of the first gate.
Next is the citation of the textual passage.
Upon the previously mentioned dharmas of provisional designation, further provisional designations are applied as appropriate to the faculties.
Next, regarding "the indestructible and boundless," this cites the passage concerning eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Without destroying the preceding provisional designation, one is able to express it by means of another, different provisional designation.
This means that although a different name is used, it does not contradict the previous statement; therefore, it is said to be "undestroyed."
Third, from "Furthermore" onwards, the characteristics [of the analytical knowledges] are clarified.

Within this, to understand that a single moment of a presently arising conditioned phenomenon is called the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*); to understand the meanings of the distinctions among the past, present, and future is the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*); and to apply provisional names and designations to these two types of phenomena is the unimpeded knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
To proclaim that matter to all sentient beings by means of these very names is called "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*).

Regarding the subsequent detailed explanation, the phrase "because each world is present" refers to the fact that, when discussed generally, both the past and the future each possess their own present; therefore, it is said that they are subsumed within their respective worlds.
Thus, within each and every world-age, there are various gateways and divergent explanations.
The statement "seeing the past and not yet knowing the present" explains the meaning in accordance with the Dharma.

The passage beginning "In this way, the bodhisattva... concludes the latter [section] to establish the former; that is, it establishes through subsequent principles the objective sphere of the bodhisattva’s unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
The following explains the characteristics of the phenomena regarding the discourse on eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Regarding "not transcending the three times," this explains the phenomena previously mentioned; in each instance within the sutra, these phenomena do not transcend the three times.

Regarding the phrase "boundless illumination of the Dharma" (*ananta-dharmāloka*): it refers to the illumination of the Dharma that is distinct [from other forms]. This distinct illumination of the Dharma is precisely the wisdom of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*), because it illuminates the Dharma.

In the fourth section, from "Furthermore" onwards, within the explanation of the characteristics of teaching, the meaning of the Dharma is analyzed by relying on the interpretation of the fundamental teachings.

Regarding the verbal expressions that follow the mind, they are called "discourses of eloquence" (prapañca). This means speaking according to the sounds of various objects; hence, it is termed "conformable speech.
It means speaking differently according to the variations of the mind, yet the meaning and substance do not differ; hence, it is termed the "characteristic of similar speech."
The remainder of the text may be understood.
Fifth, from "Furthermore" onwards, the characteristics of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) are elucidated.

Within this, the factors of *dharma* and *artha* are divided according to the manifest portion (*darśana-bhāga*), while *nirukti* and *pratibhāna* are divided according to their shallow and deep aspects.

Regarding the beginning and middle [of this section]: through the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows the objects known by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*); yet the knowledge of phenomena itself is not the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena.

For example, knowing the suffering of the desire realm through the knowledge of suffering is called the knowledge of phenomena, whereas knowing the suffering of the higher realms is called inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*). Here, it is the same:
through the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the objects of inferential knowledge.

The *Abhidharmasamaya-nirdeśa* names these two types of knowledge "Dharma-knowledge" (*dharmajñāna*) and "Subsequent-knowledge" (*anvayajñāna*). However, according to the Sarvāstivāda school (*Vibhāṣā*), these two knowledges differ in their scope regarding time and realm: both know all three periods of time, yet they are distinguished by their objects. That which specifically knows the desire realm is called Dharma-knowledge;
that which specifically knows the higher realms is called Subsequent-knowledge.

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, while the locus is common but the time is distinct, both types of knowledge cognize all three realms: knowing the present is termed *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena), and knowing the past and future is termed *anvayajñāna* (subsequent knowledge).

According to the Mahāyāna school, both time and locus are distinct: knowing the present desire realm is termed *dharmajñāna*, while knowing the higher realms as well as the past and future is entirely *anvayajñāna*.

Regarding the statement in the text that "one who desires to obtain skillful means," this refers to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), which serves as the skillful means for attaining the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Regarding the statement within the context of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) that "one obtains wisdom," this refers to the teaching of the ultimate truth, so that one may correctly realize it.

In the detailed explanation of the lower section, within the explanation of the first [category], *dharma-jñāna*, it is stated that knowing the distinctions among the truths refers to the difference between the two truths (*dvaya-satya*). "Not differing from the means" explains the "unbreakable means" (*akopya-upāya*); that is to say, seeing that which is not different from the Dharma is called "unbreakable."

Regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and so forth, the sūtra is cited for comparative clarification. In explaining inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the phrase "thus, as it truly is," etc., clarifies the meaning of inference: by means of what is known through direct perception, one infers other dharmas.
Within the section on "Explanatory Eloquence," the phrase "not a perverted or divergent explanation" refers to speaking in accordance with principle.

From the sixth "Furthermore" onwards, the absence of the mark of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") is clarified; therein, the two observations of the ultimate and the conventional are used to distinguish between phenomena (*dharma*) and their meaning (*artha*).

This means that one contemplates the true single characteristic of non-self without impairment, and contemplates the conventional distinctions of the aggregates and so forth as non-self; this is called the "excellent and supreme portion" (*madhyama-praṇīta-bhāga*) of eloquence (*pratibhāna*). "Excellent" (*praṇīta*) refers to that which is pleasing and praised, while "supreme" (*praṇīta*) refers to that which accords with principle; it is so named because it gathers and leads others toward [enlightenment].
Because the principle is exceptionally sublime and its beneficial accomplishment is increasingly vast, it is called "unsurpassed.
Regarding the detailed analysis and explanation of the first unimpeded [knowledge] below, there is first an expository explanation, meaning that non-self is indestructible;

hence, there follows a counter-explanatory section, meaning that grasping at one's own capacity for understanding is termed "my knowledge," and grasping at one's own capacity for attainment is termed "my realization."
Such destructions as these clarify non-appropriation, which is termed "non-destruction.

Regarding the phrase "the skillful means of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth," this explains the meaning in accordance with the Dharma; that is, by taking the observation of the aggregates and so forth as a skillful means, one attains entry into the true reality of the dharma of non-self.

The section beginning with "Therefore" concludes the latter part to establish the former; thus, it establishes that this is the cognitive domain of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom. The section beginning with "One accumulation" explains and reveals non-self (*anātman*):

that is to say, because of delusion regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), one conceives of a self as an accumulation; because of delusion regarding the elements (*dhātu*), one conceives of a self as a distinct cause; because of delusion regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*), one conceives of a self as attachment through desire; and because of delusion regarding the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, one conceives of a self as an agent of action and attachment.
The teaching of these aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth serves as an antidote to the four [types of] self, thereby revealing selflessness (*anātman*).
The first chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* extensively elucidates the self that is the object of negation by means of the aggregates and other categories, and so forth.

The seventh section, from "Furthermore" onwards, clarifies the characteristics of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Within this, the doctrinal meanings are distinguished according to the provisional and the ultimate: that is to say, according to the ultimate truth, all are observed as being identical to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), whereas according to the provisional truth, they are spoken of as having distinct natures and thus existing as the Three Vehicles.

Dharma (words) and *pratibhāna* (eloquence) are divided into general and specific categories. To generally teach the Three Vehicles so that beings may attain liberation is called *dharmanirukti-pratisaṃvid* (unimpeded knowledge of dharma). To provide immeasurable varieties of teaching for each individual vehicle according to the mental dispositions of sentient beings is called *pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid* (unimpeded knowledge of eloquence).
The subsequent detailed analysis is clear in its text and can be understood accordingly.

From the eighth section, "Furthermore," onwards, the characteristics of the Bodhisattva stages (*bodhisattvabhūmi*) are elucidated. Within this, the categories of *dharma* (phenomena) and *artha* (meaning) are distinguished according to the essential nature and characteristics of the stages; the categories of *nirukti* (etymological expression) and *pratibhāna* (eloquence) are distinguished according to their identity and meaning.
This refers to the term "ground" (bhūmi); the differentiation within that term is called "eloquence" (pratibhāna).

The characteristic of wisdom is the essence of the ground, while the characteristic of teaching is the mark of the ground, because ten [grounds] are taught according to their respective characteristics.
Skillfully bestowing the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is termed "expedient means" (*upāya*),
because according to the inclinations of sentient beings, one causes them to enter each stage through immeasurable gateways.

In the subsequent detailed analysis and explanation of the bodhisattva practices (*bodhisattvacaryā*), the "dharma-practice" (*dharmacaryā*) and "wisdom-practice" (*jñānacaryā*) are presented as these two practices combined constitute the bodhisattva practice.

That is to say, realizing the Dharma and accomplishing practice is called "Dharma-practice" (dharmacaryā); the accomplishment of practice through wisdom is called "wisdom-practice" (jñānacaryā); because one can enter the stages (bhūmi) by means of this wisdom-practice, it is called "practice in accordance with wisdom" (anujñācaryā).
Regarding the phrase "because it is taught as contemplative wisdom" (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), this explains the reason. That is to say, why is it that the activity of wisdom is the bodhisattva practice?
The answer is:
because it is taught that contemplative wisdom constitutes the bodhisattva practice.
Next, regarding the explanation of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) within the unimpededness of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*):
"mind" refers to the essential substance (*svabhāva*) of the stages.
That is to say, the differentiation of the stages arises from the mind; it is spoken of as verbal expression.

In the subsequent explanation of the unimpededness of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), "non-erroneous understanding" refers to the teaching that accords with the stages of the path, while "indestructible speech" refers to the explanation thereof.

From the ninth section, "Furthermore," onwards, the characteristics of the Tathāgata stage are clarified; therein, "Dharma and meaning" are distinguished according to the Buddha’s essence and function, while "expression and eloquence" are distinguished according to their extensiveness and brevity.
First, the realization attained at the initial moment of thought is called the characteristic of the Dharma-body;
second, the manifestation in response to time and place is called the characteristic of the Form-body;
third, the distinctions in wisdom and virtue within these two bodies are called the characteristic of Perfect Enlightenment.
The fourth, which extensively reveals the immeasurable distinctions of the Buddha’s virtues in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings, is called the "characteristic of teaching.

Within the subsequent detailed analysis and explanation of the meaning, the phrase "in whichever kalpa a certain Buddha is accomplished" indicates the timing of the manifestation; for example, Śākyamuni Buddha was accomplished during the Bhadrakalpa.
Regarding the explanation of the "matter" (vastu), it says that whichever land it may be, it is the place where enlightenment was attained;
whichever Buddha it may be, it is the manifestation of the Buddha-body.

Regarding the explanation of the "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa), it says that according to what is recorded by the name, one is able to see and hear; this means that, as recorded by the name, the body, the land, the sounds, and the forms can be seen and heard.

Regarding the unimpeded mastery of etymological interpretation (*nirukti*), the phrase "according to the Perfectly Awakened One" (*samyaksambuddha*) and so forth is stated because, among the ten types of Buddhas, the first is named the Buddha of Perfect Awakening; therefore, it is said to be explained based on that.
From the tenth section, "Furthermore," onwards, the characteristics of performing and maintaining [the teachings] are clarified.
Within this, the meaning of the Dharma is distinguished according to the general and specific categories of the Buddha’s teachings.
The terminology used to explain these preceding meanings of the Dharma constitutes the "differentiation within the words," which is termed *pratibhāna* (eloquence).
The characteristic of initial awakening refers to the Buddha’s merit of initiating and maintaining the teaching.
Second, the characteristic of differentiation refers to the Buddha manifesting differentiated virtues according to the capacities of sentient beings;
third, the characteristic of teaching refers to teaching based on those aforementioned differentiations for the sake of sentient beings;
fourth, the characteristic of their immeasurability refers to teaching in various ways according to the diverse inclinations of beings' minds.
Within the detailed analysis of the "lower" [section], the words of the Buddha are so called because they are capable of being spoken.
Power (*bala*) refers to spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), for it shatters the arrogance of sentient beings.

Fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) subdues the heterodox; it is not shared with others and is distinct from the Lesser Vehicle. Compassion (*karuṇā*) enables constant preaching, while wisdom (*jñāna*) serves as the basis for such preaching. Turning the Dharma is the preaching that accords with reality.
All of the above is subsumed within omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Within the unimpededness regarding the interpretation of meanings (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), that which conforms to the nature of the mind refers to the distinctions among spiritual lineages (*gotra*); through this, one may know their faculties (*indriya*) and inclinations (*chanda*).
Regarding the phrase "the wisdom and practices of all Buddhas," this explains that within the context of eloquent exposition (*pratibhāna*), the name "wisdom-practice" refers to the *dharmakāya*.
This practice benefits sentient beings without being impaired; thus, it is called "perfection."
This is because the term "faith-following" (śraddhānusārin) is explained in accordance with that faith and so forth.
The fourth major section, beginning with "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva," clarifies the accomplishment of the Dharma-preacher.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, the accomplishment of retention, wherein the dharmas of the aggregates are held within the mind;
second, the accomplishment of exposition, wherein exposition arises based upon that retention.
Third, accomplishment through question and answer: when others harbor doubts or questions, the bodhisattva skillfully provides answers;
fourth, accomplishment through upholding: being able to further receive superior teachings and proclaim them for others.
Regarding the first part, we first cite the preceding section to introduce the subsequent one.
Second, the "attainment of the meaning of the assembly" and so forth correctly reveal the ten periods; these are all differentiated according to the karmic functions arising therein.

That is to say, the first three give rise to mental karma: first, the ability to know the meaning; second, the ability to know the teaching; and third, the arising of wisdom to transform beings through supernormal powers.
The next three give rise to bodily karma:
fourth, the body emits light, using compassionate radiance to gather in sentient beings who are gentle and virtuous.
Fifth, subduing and gathering stubborn sentient beings through majestic power, while appearing to oppose those things that require subduing, is skillful wisdom;
sixth, making supreme offerings to all Buddhas and gathering in the poor and destitute below, is why it is called "the wealth of the multitude."

The last four give rise to verbal karma. Regarding "the seventh [benefit] for those of narrow and inferior capacity within the Mahāyāna": it means demonstrating the renown and majestic power of the Mahāyāna so that they may abandon their inferiority and enter [the path] without difficulty.
"Eighth, uninterrupted" means teaching constantly.
"Ninth, inexhaustible" means teaching profoundly.
The "ten kinds" refers to the detailed exposition.
The concluding summary below is easily understood.
From this point onward, the Master of the Treatise does not provide an explanation.
The second section, beginning with "This bodhisattva, regarding one Buddha," clarifies the accomplishment of teaching.
It consists of three parts:
first, it clarifies the capacity to receive many teachings;...
2. From "This bodhisattva attains such [qualities]" onwards, he is able to expound the Dharma extensively;
3. From "This bodhisattva, seated upon the Dharma-throne, or with a single voice" onwards, he is able to give rise to mastery in preaching.
The third section, beginning with "This bodhisattva [regarding] all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm," clarifies the accomplishment of the dialogue.
This section has two parts:
first, answering the objection within a single world-system; second, clarifying all world-systems.
The fourth section, beginning with "By the Buddha's supernatural power," clarifies the accomplishment of upholding [the teaching].
This section has two parts:
first, regarding a single atom; second, extending this to all atoms.
Recollection and so forth may be understood as before.
Below, the fruits of the stages are explained; the three fruits are the same as previously mentioned, and their textual locations can be seen there.
In the third major section, the summary verses consist of forty-two and a half stanzas, divided into six parts:
The first four verses concern the skillful means of the Dharma Master;
the second four verses concern the accomplishment of wisdom;
and the third twelve verses concern the accomplishment of entering into practice.
The fourth section consists of fourteen and a half verses that explain accomplishment (*siddhi*). Among these, the first one and a half verses describe the accomplishment of wisdom (*jñāna-siddhi*);
the next three and a half verses describe the accomplishment of verbal action (*vāk-karma-siddhi*);

and the subsequent nine and a half verses describe the accomplishment of the Dharma-preacher (*dharma-bhāṇaka-siddhi*). Within this latter section, the first two verses concern the accomplishment of upholding [the teaching], the next two concern the accomplishment of preaching, the following half verse concerns question and answer, and the final five verses concern the accomplishment of receiving and maintaining [the teaching].
In the fifth [ground], there are seven verses; the three fruits of the ground may be understood.
In the sixth, the final verse praises its profundity and concludes the exposition.
This completes the *Sādhumatī* Ground.
The tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), likewise has seven gates identical to those previously mentioned.
First, regarding the explanation of its name, there are three meanings:
the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states, "The great cloud of dharma-wisdom contains the waters of manifold virtues; it is like a great cloud."

Wu-xing’s commentary states: "By attaining the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its collective object, one collectively takes all sūtras, dharmas, and so forth as objects without departing from *tathatā*.
This wisdom, which has these common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) as its objects, is like a great cloud."
The gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi are like clear water; wisdom is like clouds containing water, for it possesses the superior capacity to produce them.
"The two obscurations are like space, and their coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) is like a great cloud.

Amṛtākara’s commentary states: "Furthermore, just as a great cloud covers and obscures the void, so too does the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its object cover and obscure the two obstacles—of affliction and of knowledge—which are as vast and boundless as space."
Regarding the term "concealing" (*chādana*), it carries the meanings of "obstructing" and "severing.
The three qualities that fill the *dharmakāya* are like a great cloud.

As Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Furthermore, just as a great cloud pours down clear, cool water that fills the void of space, so too does the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its object give rise to immeasurable and preeminent virtues, filling the *dharmakāya* which is both the realized and the supported."

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The Great Dharma-Wisdom Cloud contains the waters of manifold virtues; it covers the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) as vast as space and fills the Dharmakāya; therefore, it is called 'Dharma-Cloud'."
In this regard, three points are identical to those in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states: "The Dharma-body is like space, and wisdom is like a great cloud; because it universally covers all things, it is called the 'Dharma-cloud' (dharmamegha)."
The *Tattvārthā* commentary states: "That which is 'like space' is a metaphor for the three kinds of *tathatā*.
Space has three meanings:
first, the meaning of receptivity, which is a metaphor for the fact that the *svabhāva-dharmakāya* is not obstructed by *saṃsāra*."
The second meaning of "boundlessness" illustrates the *dharmakāya*.

Although it is manifested, it is not yet ultimate; it is like space that is pure and free from dust and mist, and like the middle way within the path where the *dharmakāya* penetrates both afflictions and liberation.
The threefold purity, free from dust and mist, is analogous to the Dharma-body of the fruition of sainthood (*āryaphala-dharmakāya*).
Regarding "wisdom like clouds," there are three types of such wisdom:
first, that obtained by nature prior to the Path; second, that obtained through cultivation within the Path; and third, that obtained upon reaching the conclusion of the Path.
Regarding the text, "pervasive" (biàn) refers to the wisdom of suchness attained through one's nature, which pervades the principle of suchness.
"Fulfilled" (mǎn) refers to the wisdom of suchness attained through cultivation, which fulfills the principle of suchness.
"Covering" refers to the attainment of the wisdom of suchness, which covers the principle of suchness.
When the object and the wisdom correspond to one another, the cloud is itself the rain. This rain has three meanings:
First, it can obscure dust; this refers to the wisdom of intrinsic nature prior to the Path, whose meaning is purity and freedom from defilement.
Second, it can wash away impurities; this refers to the cessation of delusions and the removal of evil karma within the Path.
Third, it can produce sprouts; this refers to its ability to generate [virtue] like a sprout after the Path.
Furthermore, emptiness is like the Dharma-body, and clouds are like the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states: "In the tenth stage, by means of the gateways of samādhi and dhāraṇī, one gathers all causes of the perfuming of hearing, which pervade and fill the ālayavijñāna."
It is like floating clouds that pervade the void.

By means of this cloud of wisdom perfumed by hearing, in each and every moment, in each and every mark, in each and every minor characteristic, and from every pore, one rains down immeasurable and boundless Dharma rain, sufficing all sentient beings who are to be transformed.
"Because one is able to rain down the Dharma-rain like clouds, it is called the 'Dharma-Cloud' [Stage].
The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* refers to this as "Consecration.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that being able to rain down the Dharma-rain in Buddha-less worlds is called the "Dharma-Cloud Stage."

The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "The body of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) is as vast as space, while the Dharma-body is perfectly complete like a great cloud that can universally cover all; therefore, it is called the 'Cloud of Dharma' (*Dharmameghā*)."
The commentary explains:

Because the seeds perfumed by the grasping at a self and phenomena lack functional capacity, they are termed "coarse heaviness" (*dausthulya*). Since they universally obstruct the principle of the two kinds of emptiness and selflessness, the Sūtra says they are as vast as space.
Regarding this tenth stage, the tenfold dharma-realm is perfected within the dharma-body, which is likened to a great cloud.

When the dharma-realm is realized, because the dharma-body of perfection and the dharma-body born of cultivation obscure the vast and coarse latencies (*dauṣṭhulya*) as if covering the sky, it is called the "Dharma-Cloud" (*dharmameghā*).
The remaining meanings are as explained below in the section on "Explaining the Names.
Second, regarding the purpose for its inclusion, there are also three points:

first, although they previously attained that eloquence for preaching the Dharma, they were not yet able to bring the Dharmakāya fully before them; therefore, it is now introduced to cause them to further cultivate and realize it to perfection—this is the reason for its inclusion.
The other two gates may be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Within the nine stages, one has already purified the Buddha-fields and transformed sentient beings; in the tenth stage, one practices so as to bring the awakening of wisdom to fulfillment, for this is supreme."
Regarding the third, the obstacles to be abandoned: according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is the obstacle to attaining mastery over all phenomena.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "The obstacle to attaining mastery over all phenomena refers to a portion of the innate aspect of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which prevents one from attaining mastery over all phenomena."

Those obstacles to the great cloud of dharma-knowledge of the tenth stage, as well as the activities arising from what it contains and preserves, can be permanently severed upon entering the tenth stage.
For this reason, the tenth stage is said to sever two types of ignorance along with their coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*):

first, the ignorance regarding the great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which is precisely the activity arising from the obstacle within this context; [the second being the ignorance regarding the non-differentiation of the dharmas].
"The second is the awakening to the subtle secret ignorance; this is precisely the obstruction within this [stage] regarding the great cloud of wisdom and that which it contains.
The commentary explains:
"Its essence consists of a portion of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that can obstruct supernormal powers and so forth."

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "There is the ignorance of not yet attaining mastery over the greatest supernormal powers; there is the ignorance of insufficient cultivation regarding the subtle and secret treasury."
The *Liang* commentary agrees with this.
Furthermore, at the final moment of this stage, one also becomes free from the two obstacles and thereby attains the fruit of Buddhahood.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Although one has attained mastery over all phenomena (*dharma*) on this stage, there remain residual obstacles that prevent it from being called 'ultimate.'"
This refers to the co-emergent subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the seeds of spontaneously arising afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) manifests, these are all severed instantaneously, and one enters the stage of a Tathāgata.
For this reason, it is said that on the stage of Buddhahood two types of delusion and their corresponding coarse residues (*dausthulya*) are abandoned:
first, the delusion of extremely subtle attachment toward all objects of knowledge, which is precisely the subtle cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) herein;
second, the delusion of extremely subtle hindrance, which is precisely the seeds of all spontaneous afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) herein.

Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "At the time of attaining enlightenment, one simultaneously abandons the afflictive obstructions and the cognitive obstructions, thereby becoming an Arhat and a Tathāgata, realizing great nirvāṇa and great bodhi."
The commentary explains:
These two subtle faults are called "remaining obstacles" because they previously obstructed the external.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "There is ignorance that obstructs the subtle wisdom regarding all objective spheres."

The second refers to the future state where there is obstruction such that [the path] does not arise again; it is the ignorance regarding the non-attainment of the knowledge that [defilements] will not arise again.
This can be seen to correspond to what the *Liang* commentary calls "subtle obstruction" (*sūkṣmāvaraṇa*) and "subtle attachment" (*sūkṣmābhiniveśa*).
Regarding the fourth, that which is realized: it is the realization of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as the basis for mastery over karma and so forth.

Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "That is to say, this dharma-realm is the basis for mastery over the karmas of the body and so forth, as well as mastery over the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi."

As for the explanation by Asvabhāva: "The meaning of being the basis for mastery over karma and so forth refers to the mastery in the application of the actions of body, speech, and mind according to one's desire; by relying on the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā), all activities performed by oneself are successfully accomplished."
Because they have attained the sovereign power of the dhāraṇīs that retain both words and meanings, they are able to retain all the words and meanings proclaimed by the Buddhas without forgetting.

Because they have attained the sovereign power of samādhi, they are able to master all meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and concentrations (*samādhi*), manifesting at will various samādhis and samāpattis such as the Ākāśagarbha.
The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states: "Because one acts according to one's will to perform various deeds that bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
This is a general statement and does not provide specific distinctions.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* commentary states: "It means that once this suchness has been realized, one attains mastery over all supernormal powers, activities, dhāraṇīs, and meditative concentrations."
Explanation:
According to the various treatises mentioned above, one attains four kinds of mastery within this stage:

first, the five supernormal powers; second, the three types of karma; third, dhāraṇī; and fourth, the various meditative concentrations. One should consult the subsequent text of this section for further details.
The "Great Perfection Portion" (Mahāparinirvāṇa) and other texts shall be further explained together later.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Although the nature of true suchness (tathatā) is in reality without differentiation, ten types are provisionally established based on its preeminent qualities."

"Although everything has already been reached within the first stage (*bhūmi*), the practice of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-caryā*) is not yet perfected; in order to bring it to perfection, the subsequent stages are established.

Regarding the five types of practices to be accomplished (*niṣpādya-caryā*), there are also three kinds: first, the practice of accomplishing the reception of the rank (*pada-pratilambha*) and so forth; [the others follow].
Second is the practice of the perfection of wisdom;
third, according to the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, it is because the samādhi-gates and dhāraṇī-gates of the tenth stage are utterly pure.
Regarding the six fruits obtained: according to the Liang commentary, by attaining mastery over karma through reliance on the *dharmadhātu*, one obtains the fruit of the *nirmāṇakāya*.

The third fascicle of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "Upon the arousal of the mind in the tenth stage, one attains the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*; this constitutes the fruit of the stage of practice and the fruit of the position."

Furthermore, according to the *Liang* commentary on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, all ten fruits correspond to the great fruit of the Buddha-ground one is to attain; the others are all obtained in the present.
Moreover, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states that by practicing the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one obtains the fruit of the Great Dharani, as explained in that sutra.
In the seventh section, the commentary on the text, the first part—consisting of twenty-five verses—praises and requests [the teaching]. This is divided into five sections:
first, two verses clarify how the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven prepare exquisite offerings;
second, one verse clarifies the bodhisattvas’ offering of incense.

Three: two verses clarify the offering of precious robes by the retinue of the Heavenly King; four: eighteen verses clarify the offering of musical praise by the heavenly maidens. Within these, the first two generally clarify the performance of music;

the next two praise the Buddha’s qualities of universal physical marks and characteristics; the next three praise the Buddha’s qualities of accomplishing benefit through his activities; the next four praise the Buddha’s qualities of responding to capacities through the eightfold [marks]; the next two praise the Buddha’s qualities of vastness using the analogy of illusion; the next three praise the Buddha’s qualities of equality in the Dharma-body; the next two conclude with an exhortation to practice and study; and the final one concludes with the silence of the heavenly maiden. Five:
the final two verses, which constitute the formal request by the leaders of the assembly, are as can be understood.
The second part, the Section on the Correct Exposition, consists of eight divisions.
First, the Division on the Stage of Fulfillment through Expedient Means: this subsumes all practices cultivated in the preceding nine stages as expedient means to fulfill this present stage.

Regarding the second point, "attaining the factors of samādhi": the practices and virtues of one dwelling in the initial stage are immeasurable; since the reception of office in this stage necessarily relies upon samādhi, it is singled out for mention.

Third, the stage of attaining the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) refers to the practice of the true ground (*bhūmi*), so called because by relying on superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is able to encompass the Buddha-wisdom.

Fourth, the stage of entering great perfection refers to the practice of the fulfillment of the grounds; since this represents the ultimate exhaustion relative to what preceded it, being the pinnacle among all forms of exhaustion, it is termed "great perfection."
The fifth section, "Explaining the Name," means that in this stage, learning is perfected, virtues are distinguished, and the title is made manifest.

Regarding the sixth section, "The Power of the Six Supernormal Knowledges (ṣaḍabhijñā), Being Unsurpassed or Surpassable": because one possesses mastery over wondrous functions once the stage is fulfilled, it is called "supernormal knowledge" (abhijñā).
That which transcends the preceding is called "unsurpassed" (anuttara);
that which looks up to those inferior to the Tathāgata is called "surpassed" (sottara).
The latter two categories apply to all ten stages (daśabhūmi), but because the former subsumes the latter, they are included within this specific stage.
The sevenfold images illustrate the Dharma through metaphors, just as one knows the actual object by means of its reflection.
The eighth section on benefits demonstrates the superior advantages of the teaching, exhorting faith and entry.

Within the section on the fulfillment of skillful means (*upāya*), there is first a general enumeration: "immeasurable" refers to extensive wisdom (*vipula-jñāna*), and "well-cultivated" refers to profound wisdom (*gambhīra-jñāna*).

In the preceding stages, these two are fully aroused and collectively termed "skillful discernment" (*suvicaya*), because they constitute the decisive resolution (*viniścaya*) of sublime wisdom (*prajñā*).
In the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, bodhisattvas on the stages engage in two types of practice:
first, practice according to fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna), termed "practice as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-pratipatti*), which corresponds here to "skillful cultivation";
second, practice according to subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna), termed "universal practice," which corresponds here to "immeasurable wisdom."
The nine phrases within the intermediate section are individually analyzed below; the treatise subsumes them into seven:

the first three constitute one group, termed "those who practice well. This refers to those who, regarding all the stages (*bhūmi*), equally cultivate them well, realizing the aids [to enlightenment] while not abiding [in them], because they resemble the common characteristics found within the preceding eight stages.
This means that the white dharmas (pure qualities) are the realization, which can be known as the aids to the Path.
"Great merit" and so forth refer to non-abiding; because there is no abiding, one does not abandon merit.
"Protection" refers to non-abandonment; because there is no abiding in existence, one does not abandon wisdom.
These three phrases explain one another in sequence: by what cause is realization attained?
It is because of the arising of assistance.
By what cause is assistance accomplished?

Because of non-abiding, the following six phrases specifically clarify the middle [section]. The first phrase subsumes the characteristics of the two types of benefit (self and others) practiced in the preceding seven stages; since the eighth stage initially distinguishes the differences between the seven stages, this single phrase is used here to manifest their comprehensive inclusion.
The phrase "extensively practicing great compassion" is explained as being universal.
The seven [factors] that accord with one's own benefit explain "practice," while that which accords with and facilitates the benefit of others explains "great compassion."
Regarding the phrase "profoundly knowing discrimination and so forth," this specifically refers to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), which brings about the purification of the Buddha-fields.
The following four lines specifically refer to the practice within the ninth stage.

Among these, the first phrase refers to the practice of one's own stage within the nine stages; it is called "profound entry" because of the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings, which is precisely what is meant by "entering the dense forest of practices," and so forth.
The final three phrases clarify superior progress; therein, the first is understanding, the next is practice, and the last is realization.
The phrase "entering into all [dharmas]" refers to understanding the dharma of the *tathatā* realm as practiced by the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "tending toward" (*ābhimukhya*) and so forth, it refers to the practice of seeking the fruit of Buddhahood without weariness or satiety.

Regarding the phrase "attaining" (*prāpti*) and so forth, it refers to reaching the ultimate limit and entering [the realization]; that is to say, the exhaustion of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) is termed "reaching the limit," while the attainment of realization based on practice is termed "entering."
Because one receives the office of Buddha-wisdom within this stage, it is called the "Stage of Omniscience.
The second section, beginning with "The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices in this manner," clarifies the division on samādhi.
Within this, the first part restates the preceding section to introduce the subsequent one;
from "then he attains" onwards, it correctly reveals what is attained, which consists of four parts:

first, the individual exposition of the ten gates; second, the general conclusion regarding the hundred thousand [gates]; third, from "this bodhisattva" onwards, the clarification of the ability to enter and know; and fourth, the revelation of the final name.
Regarding the first internal [category], the treatise cites the beginning and so forth of the subsequent [categories], hence it says "stainless" (*vimalā*) and so on.
It cites the latter [category] of one million, hence it says "retinue.
The phrase "free from the stains of affliction" explains and reveals its characteristic, because this stage is the point where all obstructions are exhausted.
"Without applying effort" means that accomplishment is attained through correspondence.
The remaining nine are distinct because the sixth and seventh concentrations together abandon one type of defilement; thus, eight types of defilements are abandoned.
First, "entering the distinctions of the dharma-realm" refers to entering the secret and stainless state; that is, the profound depth of the dharma-realm is called the "secret place."
Second, practicing the two paths in proximity to the fruit of Buddhahood is called adorning the site of enlightenment;
third, the activity of the light of the three bodies;
fourth, eloquence and dhāraṇī.
Fifth, the manifestation of supernormal powers through mental karma;
sixth, extensiveness;
seventh, depth—these together reveal the Pure Land. "Immeasurable" explains extensiveness, and "right contemplation" explains contemplation; these are the virtues of the one who has come from above.
Regarding "the eight [perfections] that follow all [beings] equally," etc.: this refers to the stainless virtue of benefiting others through the transformation of sentient beings;

the aforementioned two [perfections] are the practice of benefiting oneself. Regarding "knowing things as they truly are," etc.: this refers to the superior progress. The supreme awakening is called "stainless right awakening" (*samyak-saṃbodhi-vimala*); it means that when one is about to achieve perfect awakening, all Buddhas appear before one and mutually certify this realization, as explained below in the section on receiving the office (*abhiṣeka*).
The statement that "the knowledge of all-knowledge is non-conceptual" explains the nature of all-knowledge.
"The knowledge of all-knowledge equally receives the position" restates the knowledge and explains the receiving of the position.
The fulfillment of the matters of samādhi is explained by Śākyamuni as entering [them] completely.
Its essence is known, and its functional activity can be understood.
Third, from "this samādhi manifests before one" onwards, the section on receiving the position is clarified.
Within this, there are six points.
First, as for what kind of seat [is used]: for example, when a prince of the world receives his office, he sits upon a precious throne of Jambūnada gold on a white elephant.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: when receiving the office of a Buddha, he dwells upon the throne of the Great Jewel Lotus King.

Second, as for what kind of body it is: it is like the son of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), born with the precious jade woman and fully endowed with the marks of a king; this is the "body for attaining the position."
The Bodhisattva is likewise; his sublime form constitutes the body that receives the office.

Regarding the third point, "what kind of retinue [he has]," it is like when a prince of the wheel-turning king (cakravartin) ascends the throne: the civil and military officials, numbering in the hundreds, all assist and support him.
When a bodhisattva likewise receives the office of a Buddha, they are surrounded by all the great bodhisattvas.

Regarding the four kinds of signs: it is like when a prince of the world receives his position; the streets and alleys are swept and cleaned, silk banners and canopies are hung, and bells and drums resound.

When a bodhisattva thus receives the office of a Buddha, the great earth trembles, the evil realms are stilled, and light is emitted that universally illumines and purifies the world; these serve as its signs.

Fifth, regarding the source from which it emerges: it is like when a prince of the world receives his office; from his mouth issues a proclamation of amnesty, whose grace extends throughout the realm, whereby prisoners are released and the treasury opens to bestow gifts upon his ministers.
In this way, the Bodhisattva emits light from ten locations, causing those in the evil realms to escape and increasing the practice of the Bodhisattvas.

Regarding the six types of attainment according to their respective stages: it is like when a prince of the world receives his position; at that time, the father king takes a golden vessel filled with the waters of the four oceans and pours them over the crown of the crown prince’s head, whereupon he is named a consecrated Wheel-Turning King.

In this way, when the light of omniscience emitted from the white tuft between the eyebrows of the Buddhas of the ten directions enters the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head, it is called "receiving the rank of a Buddha.
Regarding these six sections of the sūtra, the commentator explains the first three passages together in one place,
and the following two together in another.
The latter part provides a separate explanation.
Within the first section, there are ten characteristics:
first, the Flower King is the characteristic of the sovereign, because of its mastery.
1. The two aspects of being "perfectly circular" and so forth are the characteristics of its dimensions, because they are vast. 2.
The third aspect, consisting of "various jewels" and so forth, is the characteristic of excellence, because it possesses sublime qualities.
3. The fourth aspect, "surpassing [all others]" and so forth, is the characteristic of the ground, because it is the place of birth.
The five qualities, such as transcending the world, are the characteristics of the cause, because they arise from that [emptiness].

The sixth quality, the knowledge of all things, is the characteristic of the result, because it is accomplished by the wisdom of emptiness, just as a worldly lotus is accomplished through cultivation.

The seven kinds of radiance and so forth constitute the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Just as a worldly lotus causes the mind to become attached, the lotus seat of the Bodhisattva excellently illuminates the *dharmadhātu*.
One may understand that the treatise focuses on the illumination of principle (*li*), while the sūtra focuses on the illumination of phenomena (*shi*).
The eight marks of merit are not mentioned in the sutra; because they resemble the characteristics of the earth, they are not distinguished here.
Furthermore, this clarifies that the characteristics of the fruit produced differ from those previously described.
The nine [lotuses], such as those made of lapis lazuli, constitute the characteristic of substance, because their stalks and so forth are the physical forms of that substance.
The ten [lotuses], such as those of immeasurable light, constitute the characteristic of adornment, because they are fully endowed with virtuous functions.
2. From "At that time" onwards, it clarifies what kind of body [is present]: the body is exquisitely beautiful and widely praised as a flower seat. 3.

From "Immediately" onwards, it clarifies what kind of retinue [is present]: namely, those seated there who have attained meditative concentration, whose minds are reverent and whose eyes gaze upon [the Buddha].
4. "This Bodhisattva ascends... and below clarifies by what marks [he does so]; there are five marks: first, shaking the earth;
second, ceasing suffering; third, illumination; fourth, adorning the realm; and fifth, seeing the Buddhas, etc.
5. From the words "For what reason" (*kiṃ kāraṇam*) onwards, the various sources from which [the light] emerges are clarified.
The phrase "for what reason" serves as an inquiry that introduces the subsequent explanation.
The *Śāstra* states, "Because it emits radiance," which provides a general explanation of the sources.
The passage contains three parts:
first, the emission of light from ten locations;
second, from the words "At that time" onwards, how all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas become fully aware through the universal illumination of the light; [and third, the response of those beings].
Third, from the phrase "immediately" (*sadyas*) onwards, because of their awakening and awareness, bodhisattvas of the lower stages all come to offer worship.
Regarding the first part [of this section], these ten lights are categorized into three types in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*:
the first nine constitute acts of benefit, specifically the first five of which benefit ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The next two benefit those of the One Vehicle;
the final two benefit bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, the eighth, ninth, and tenth are termed the "activities that awaken realization" (*bodhana-karman*): the eighth awakens realization from the initial generation of the mind up through the ninth stage; the ninth awakens realization for bodhisattvas of the tenth stage; and the tenth awakens realization for all Buddhas.

Furthermore, the eighth and ninth rays are named "Subduing Activities. This means that the eighth ray is able to gather, causing all Bodhisattvas from the first up to the ninth stage to come and offer worship;
the ninth ray is able to subdue, causing the palaces of Māra to be obscured.
Regarding the tenth, the light from the crown, there are four parts:
first, it illuminates the ten directions; second, it forms a platform of light; third, it presents offerings; and fourth, it enters beneath the feet.
The first two are easily understood.
Regarding the offerings, there are three parts:
first, manifesting the excellence of the offering; second, the actual offering to the Buddha; and third, clarifying the benefit of the offering.
Concerning the phrase "certainly for the unsurpassed path," the treatise provides two interpretations:
The statement "in the earth" refers to the meaning of certainty; this concerns the realization of certainty on the stages (*bhūmi*).

The phrase "furthermore, there are other meanings," etc., concerns the benefit of causing those in lower stages to enter right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*); that is to say, for one who is certainly diligent, it is the certainty of being free from evil.
Regarding "the mind determined by the deeds performed," this refers to the accumulation of wholesome concentration (*samādhi*).
As for the phrase "entering beneath the Buddha's feet," Master Huiyuan offers three interpretations:
first, from the perspective of the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*), the light from the crown of the head entering the feet manifests profound reverence.

Second, regarding the manifestation of reality through its characteristics: the light of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom realizes and enters the Buddha-realm; because it enters from below, it is called "entering the soles of the feet," and thus the treatise names this the "encompassment of the Wisdom of Equality."

Third, discussing this in terms of actual reality: when a bodhisattva proceeds from their own causal practices toward the attainment of fruition, their entry from below is called "entering the Buddha’s foot.
Second, from the passage beginning with "At that time," the light shines universally so that all Buddhas and bodhisattvas may take full knowledge [of it].

Third, the section beginning with "Immediately" clarifies how, through the power of awakening and awareness, one brings about what is to be done. This section has two parts: first, bodhisattvas from lower stages come here to offer worship, which means they first make offerings and subsequently gain benefit; second, [the Buddha] bestows predictions upon them. Regarding the first part: "Immediately," that is, at that very moment, bodhisattvas from the ten directions—having heard the Buddha’s voice and perceived the light—came to this place to present offerings. They did so because they had previously received a prediction from the Buddha, and now, having heard the Dharma and seen the light, they came to pay homage to the Buddha and to hear the Dharma. As for "first making offerings": these bodhisattvas, having arrived, first presented various offerings to the Buddha and his assembly. What were these offerings? There were five kinds: first, offerings of flowers; second, offerings of incense; third, offerings of necklaces; fourth, offerings of garments; and fifth, offerings of parasols. Among these, "flowers" refers to celestial flowers such as the *māndārava*, *mahāmāndārava*, *manojña*, *sumanojña*, *roca*, *rocana*, *prabhākara*, *vairocana*, *sarva-gandha*, *sarva-rasāgratā*, *sarva-varṇa*, *sarva-śobhana*, *sarva-prītikara*, *sarva-manoratha*, *sarva-kāma*, *sarva-sukha*, *sarva-priya*, *sarva-viśiṣṭa*, *sarva-loka-abhyudgata*, *sarva-loka-anabhibhūta*, *sarva-loka-viśiṣṭa*, *sarva-loka-adhipati*, *sarva-loka-anatikrānta*, *sarva-loka-asamanta*, *sarva-loka-aparājita*, *sarva-loka-anupalipta*, *sarva-loka-anavadya*, *sarva-loka-anuttara*,
