Second, the Bodhisattvas of equal rank assist with their light of virtue; likewise, the light enters first and the clarity benefits afterward.
This is because the Bodhisattva possesses ten thousand virtues within, and thus the mark of the ten-thousand-character (萬字) appears upon his chest.
The commentary may be understood accordingly.
The sixth section, beginning with "At that time, the Buddhas," clarifies the attainment of the respective stages.
This contains four parts:

This consists of the application of the principle (*dharma*), the illustration (*udāharaṇa*), the synthesis (*anvaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). Within the first section, the application of the principle, there are also four parts:
first, the emission of light; second, the entry into the crown; third, the attainment of benefits; and fourth, the conclusion of the stage.
At the beginning and middle, light possesses ten functions:
first, "increasing wisdom," which is the function of benefiting;
second, the "causal function"; [and so forth].
Third, illuminating and manifesting the Buddha’s power to cause others to feel reverence is called the activity of reverence;
fourth, exhorting and encouraging others and so forth is called the activity of exhortation;
fifth, [reaching] the ten directions and so forth is called the activity of vibration.
Sixth, the activity of eradication and so forth is called the activity of cessation;
seventh, the activity of subjugation;
eighth, the activity of manifestation.
Ninth is the activity of expanding and contracting;
tenth is the manifestation of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth, which is the activity of transformation (*nirmāṇa*).

Regarding "the two enter the crown": this refers to the light of the [physical] object entering the crown, which is equivalent to the light of the Dharma entering the mind, thereby increasing one's stage.
The title of the treatise is *Tathāgata-prabhā*.

Regarding the phrase "those bodhisattvas mutually embrace through the equality of wisdom," this refers to the light from the crown of the bodhisattva’s head entering the Buddha’s feet; this is because it represents upward advancement.
The Buddha’s light enters the crown of the Bodhisattva because it descends to gather [the beings] below.
Because cause and effect are mutually integrated, it is called "equality.
Since the radiance of the body is itself wisdom, it is called "wisdom."
The three benefits gained can be understood [from the preceding].
Fourth, regarding the summary of the stages: entering the realm of the Buddha, that which is realized is the same;
possessing the ten powers, the qualities of practice are the same.
One falls into the category of Buddhas and becomes equal to humans.

By accomplishing the virtues of a Buddha, one falls into the category of Buddhas; this is like how one who has newly left the household life falls into the category of the Sangha even before receiving the precepts.
The sections on the analogy, the application, and the conclusion can be understood accordingly.
Fourth, from "Abiding in the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma, knowing it as it truly is" onwards, the section on the Great Perfection is elucidated.
This contains five parts:
First is the greatness of wisdom, based on the meaning of the true wisdom of perfect enlightenment;
second is the greatness of liberation, based on the meaning of mastery over the mind;
third is the greatness of samādhi, based on the meaning of accomplishing all tasks immediately upon generating the resolve for enlightenment.
Fourth is the greatness of the four dhāraṇīs, based on the sense of benefiting sentient beings in accordance with all worlds;
fifth is the greatness of the five supernormal powers, based on the sense of being capable of delivering sentient beings.
The first two pertain to self-benefit: first, internal wisdom; second, external application.
The latter three pertain to benefiting others: first, the arising of activity through mental karma; second, relying on the production of verbal karma; and third, the transformations of bodily karma.
Regarding the first, within the greatness of wisdom there are seven kinds of greatness:

First, the greatness of the knowledge of the accumulation [of conditions] (*samudaya-jñāna-mahattva*), which is the power of knowing the causal accumulation of phenomena through which doubt is severed.
Second, the greatness of the knowledge of transformation (*nirmāṇa-jñāna-mahattva*), which refers to the activity of transformative knowledge arising in dependence upon the body.

Regarding the "greatness of the wisdom of the three empowerments": this refers to the manifold transformations, activities, abidings, and manifestations of the transformative function; it is stated thus with emphasis.
Because these constant transformations are uninterrupted, they are called the power of transformative activity.
Regarding the fourth, "entering into subtle wisdom": this is the gate of subtle mutual containment and establishment, wherein [the Buddha] constantly manifests the eight phases of enlightenment.
Because within a single manifestation of one phase, all are revealed, it is called "subtle."

Based on those [three types of wisdom], such as the transformative and so forth, one restates the previous three wisdoms and names them "non-dual" (*advaya*), based on the manifestation of the subtle and minute.

First, transformation; second, empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); third, gathering. By combining these three wisdoms and relying upon them to achieve Buddhahood, they are termed "action" (*kriyā*); this is precisely the subtle and minute.
Regarding the "wise one of the five secret places," this is the gateway of the secret method in which both the hidden and the manifest are accomplished together.

That is to say, in order to protect those beginners whose faculties are not yet mature, one manifests the coarse while concealing the subtle, so as not to cause them fear; based on that [concealment], one speaks of the submergence of this subtle wisdom.
Regarding the wisdom of entering the kalpas (*kalpa-praveśa-jñāna*): skillfully understanding how all kalpas mutually interpenetrate is called the wisdom of entering the kalpas.
The continuous succession of time and kalpas is designated as "life" (*jīvita*).
Their constant flux is termed "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
To encompass all within one is called empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
To enter all within one is termed relinquishment (*tyāga*),
for it is defined as relinquishing oneself to follow others.
The kalpas follow the movement of the mind; this is called mastery of the will (*vaśavarti-citta*).
Regarding the "seven knowledges for entering the path": because one knows that all worldly dharmas can serve as remedies for transcending the world, it is called "entering the path."
Regarding "first, the great collection of wisdom," various commentators state that it should be understood as the wisdom of the collection of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, the phrase "according to whatever portions are defiled, purified, or extinguished" is the general explanation.
Within this, there are six layers:
first, those that are exclusively defiled, namely the first five phrases and the collection of afflictions such as wrong views;
second, those that are exclusively pure, namely the collection of nirvāṇa and the collections of śrāvakas and so forth.
Third, cessation alone, namely space;
fourth, the union of defilement and purity, namely consciousness and the formation and destruction of the conditioned world;
fifth, the union of purity and cessation, namely the unconditioned and nirvāṇa.
The six [categories] pertain to defilement, purity, and cessation; that is to say, they are the collection of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

In the treatise, these are called the "dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*): specifically, the unwholesome dharma-realm is termed "defilement," the wholesome dharma-realm is termed "purity," and the unconditioned dharma-realm is termed "cessation."
In the detailed explanation of the treatise, the phrase "in all places within the three realms" explains the first three lines, which can be understood accordingly.
The phrase "all sentient beings" explains the following two lines, which can likewise be understood.
"Following all minds, whether defiled or pure," explains that the collection of consciousness can be understood.

"Following all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, because of the knowing of what is unknowable," explains the collection of the conditioned and the unconditioned; that is, because the conditioned possesses mind, it is called "knowing," while the unconditioned lacks mind and is thus termed "unknowable."
"Wherever there is space, etc. explains the collection of space (*ākāśa*), because it is the locus upon which worlds and so forth depend.

"Whatever dharmas are taught, whether correct or incorrect" explains the collection of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); herein, pure dharmas are termed "correct" and defiled ones are termed "incorrect," while "etc. includes cessation (*nirodha*).
"Non-attainment according to what is realized" refers to *nirvāṇa*; this explains the accumulation of *nirvāṇa* because it is that which is realized by the Noble Ones (*ārya*).
What follows clarifies "non-attainment," which is an explanation of wrong views and so forth.
For what reason is it not realized?
Because of wrong view.
Whose is this wrong view?
This means that other non-Buddhists and the like cannot realize it.
One should understand the explanation according to whatever world-receptacles (*bhājana-loka*) there may be, regarding their formation and destruction.
Regarding the distinctions in the accumulation of those belonging to the three vehicles, one should know that the explanation concerns the *śrāvakas* and so forth.
The concluding text is clear.
Second, from "This bodhisattva, by means of such... onwards, the wisdom of responsive transformation (*nirmāṇajñāna*) is explained.
Within this, there is first a detailed exposition and subsequently a summary.
Within the [section on] differentiation, there are ten phrases.
The first four clarify the sovereign transformation of the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).

This refers to manifesting sentient beings and the karma they perform, as well as manifesting poverty and so forth, and demonstrating false views; therefore, the treatise states: "The response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifests afflictions, because it produces defiled views."
The first line refers to the sovereign transformation of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
The following five lines refer to the sovereign transformation of the world of the Perfectly Awakened One through wisdom (*jñāna-saṃbuddha-loka*).

Regarding the term "Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*): because it is the practice of the Dharma that is taught, it manifests the teachings of the Three Vehicles, all of which possess the sense of awakening.
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), that which manifests through volitional effort is called "discrimination," while that which manifests as insentient matter is called "non-discrimination.
Another explanation states:
that which manifests through mental attention (*manasikāra*) is called "discrimination," while that which manifests spontaneously is called "non-discrimination."
This passage is explained according to the first meaning, as it pertains to the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), which is characterized by effortlessness (*anābhoga*).
From the third section, "This bodhisattva... onwards, the wisdom of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*) is elucidated.
Within this, there are ten [points]:

first, the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha constitute the "sustenance of the objective" (*ālambana-dhāraṇī*), meaning that constant and uninterrupted transformation is called the sustenance of the Buddha's power; the same applies to the Dharma and the Sangha, though the *Sūtra* omits the mention of the Sangha's sustenance.
The remaining eight phrases constitute the "sustenance of practice" (*caryā-dhāraṇī*).

The first two are the maintenance through retrogression; as described in the expedient means below, he commands the Brahmins to maintain the myriad practices by means of the five heats and the mountain of knives—this is the maintenance through karma.
Just as one retains afflictions to bring the correct practice to fulfillment, this is called "retention by affliction" (*kleśa-dhāraṇī*).

The subsequent five phrases constitute "retention through conforming practice": accumulating practice over a long period is called "temporal retention" (*kāla-dhāraṇī*); initiating practice through aspiration is called "vow-retention" (*praṇidhāna-dhāraṇī*); enabling practice to arise through past roots of goodness is called "prior-life retention" (*pūrvajanma-dhāraṇī*); initiating practice based upon [previous] practice is called "practice-retention" (*caryā-dhāraṇī*); practicing throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is called "kalpa-retention" (*kalpa-dhāraṇī*); and being able to initiate practice by relying upon the retribution of life is called "life-span retention" (*āyuḥ-dhāraṇī*).

Regarding the next phrase, "maintaining the fruit," the *Śāstra* states: "In this context, 'maintaining through wisdom' refers to the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), for this wisdom is capable of accomplishing all tasks."
The first phrase explains "wisdom" (jñāna), and the second phrase explains "retention" (dhāraṇī); this may be understood accordingly.
The fourth section, beginning with "This bodhisattva dwells in this," clarifies the entry into subtle wisdom; that is to say, knowing the Buddha’s transformative activity as subtly sovereign.
Among these, the practitioner constitutes the lower [level], while the activities performed above are those of the middle Tuṣita Heaven.
The sūtra lacks the section on "exertion" (vega), but the remaining text may be understood by applying the same principles of interpretation.
The fifth section, beginning with "Furthermore, the Buddhas," clarifies the wisdom of the secret sphere (*guhyasthāna-jñāna*), which refers to knowing the secret meanings manifested by the Buddhas.
Within this, the first three [points] concern the three types of action (*karman*);
the subsequent point concerns deliberating upon whether sentient beings are at the appropriate time or not for receiving transformation (*pariṇāmana*).

Next, there are those who have already attained Buddhahood long ago yet manifest the receiving of a prediction (vyākaraṇa), or those who see a white dove as a sign that they shall attain Buddhahood; such categories as these are termed the "secrecy of prediction."
For instance, speaking with loving words to Rāhu while rebuking Devadatta is the secret of subduing sentient beings.
In reality, there is but the One Vehicle, yet the expedient teaching of three or five vehicles is called the secret of the differentiation of vehicles.

Next, regarding the objects of knowledge: this refers to knowing the ripening of the faculties, knowing the sequence of karma before and after, and knowing the practices of the direct and the indirect paths, whereby one attains enlightenment together with others.

The sixth section, beginning with "This bodhisattva," clarifies the wisdom of entering the kalpas; the *Śāstra* states: "In this context, 'entering' means the equal liberation wherein all kalpas mutually enter one another."
This refers to the inconceivable dharma of liberation, which is equal and uniform throughout the ocean of all kalpas, thereby causing all kalpas to enter into one another in succession.
The remaining text is as explained above in the "Chapter on Generating the Resolve" and other sections.

The seventh section, beginning with "This bodhisattva," clarifies the wisdom of entering the path; within this portion of the sutra, the initial wisdom of entering the path of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is missing. The *Śāstra* states, "relying on the stage of ordinary beings," which is an explanation of this phrase.
Regarding those who practice based on the conceit of self (*asmimāna*), this explains the wisdom of atoms (*paramāṇu-jñāna*).
This means that by analyzing form (*rūpa*) into atoms, one causes them to abandon the conceit of self.

Regarding those who give rise to birth in heaven based on faith, this explains the wisdom of the land (*kṣetra-jñāna*); it means that wisdom manifests the pure land, surpassing what they previously believed.

Regarding the statement "relying on vitarka and vicāra," this explains the wisdom concerning the body and mind of sentient beings; that is to say, the afflictions that disturb the mind are collectively termed *vitarka* (initial application) and *vicāra* (sustained application).

The six subsequent phrases concern their transformation through union and separation: that is, knowing the destination of those to be transformed while practicing the Buddha-way, demonstrating inconceivable conduct both contrary and compliant, and being able to understand the three vehicles simultaneously.
The concluding passage is clear.
Second, from "This bodhisattva-mahāsattva" onwards, the greatness of liberation is elucidated; herein, there is first a detailed analysis followed by a summary.
There are ten further categories:
first, those whose liberation is not through thought rely on the sphere of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), meaning they possess mastery over transformations that are difficult to fathom.
Second, those who are unimpeded are able to reach immeasurable worlds because their wisdom of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*) is unobstructed; this constitutes swift mastery.
Regarding the three types of pure conduct (*śuddhacaryā*), the treatise refers to them as "pure wisdom" (*jñāna-śuddhi*). There are briefly three gateways for understanding these pure conducts:
first, knowing the mundane and supramundane, distinguished by way of stages;
second, knowing the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), distinguished by way of cause and fruit.
Third, the knowledge of śrāvakas and others is distinguished according to individuals;
this constitutes mastery over the knowable (*jñeya-vaśitā*). Of these, the former two are supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and this one is wisdom (*jñāna*).

Fourth, the illumination of the universal gate (*samanta-mukha-prabhāsa*) refers to the activity of transforming according to one's will; that is, in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings, manifesting one’s own body within all gates of forms and images, such as Avalokiteśvara and others, and is thus called mastery of the universal gate (*samanta-mukha-vaśitā*).

The fivefold Tathāgatagarbha is the Dharma-dhāraṇī; that is to say, the accumulation within the *tathatā* (suchness) of all that is knowable of the merits of the Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is called the dhāraṇī of the Dharma known as the Tathāgatagarbha.
Sixth, regarding the wheel of unimpeded accordance: it is so called because one can shatter the intentions of others without retreating.
Seventh, regarding entry into the three periods of time: it is the wisdom of entering eons, whereby one dwells and maintains oneself within the kalpas of the three periods according to one's will.

The eighth is the treasury of the nature of the eightfold dharma: it is the wisdom that gathers all causes and conditions for all phenomena in all their aspects; this is the same as the aforementioned "wisdom of gathering.
The ninth is the clear liberation: its light does not leave the body, yet it is able to shine everywhere.
Regarding the ten superior advancements: based on knowing the minds of all sentient beings in immeasurable worlds simultaneously, the summary may be understood.
Next, the greatness of samādhi; next, the greatness of dhāraṇī; and finally, the greatness of supernatural powers—all of these may likewise be understood.
The section on the "Great Perfection" is concluded.
The fifth major section, beginning with "This bodhisattva accomplishes," clarifies the section on the explanation of names.
Within this, there are three parts:

First, the ability to receive the clouds and rain of the Buddhas’ preaching of the Dharma is called the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*); second, from the passage beginning with "By the power of his vows" onwards, the ability to pour down the rain of Dharma to extinguish the dust and flames of affliction in all sentient beings is called the Dharma-Cloud Stage; third, from the passage beginning with "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha," the clarification of the ability to pour down the rain of Dharma to produce the roots of goodness in beings is called the Dharma-Cloud Stage.

Regarding the beginning and middle [of this stage]: if it were named according to what is received, it should be called the "Stage of the Rain of Dharma" (*dharmavarṣā-bhūmi*); if it were named according to that which receives, it should be called the "Stage of the Ocean of Dharma" (*dharmanidhi-bhūmi*).

However, here it is designated as the "Stage of the Cloud of Dharma" (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) based on the locus where the Dharma is received. Therefore, the commentary explains that it is similar to a single cloud of Dharma because it completely covers [all things].
Regarding the phrase "in this stage, hearing the Dharma is similar [to a cloud]": the Dharma heard here is vast and all-pervasive; therefore it is called a "cloud," as it resembles the Dharma.

As for the statement "because the body [of the hearer] pervades like space," this clarifies the body that hears the Dharma; that is to say, since it is only space that can receive the rain from the clouds.

It is said that the Dharma-body which receives [the teaching] is like space; according to the circumstances of those it encounters, the Buddha’s body is like a cloud and his preaching of the Dharma is like rain.
Thus, that which is received is like the rain, and that which receives it is like the ocean.
If one regards the Dharma being taught as being like clouds that cover everything, then that which is received is like the clouds, and that which receives it is like space.
The two points regarding the extinction of dust and the third regarding the deliverance of beings can be understood from the treatise.

Regarding the first part, the initial section first provides a general explanation of one who has achieved the power of mindfulness; this is because it refers proximately to the meaning of "receiving and upholding," that is, hearing from the Buddha and explaining the meaning of receiving and upholding.
Second, the passage beginning with "Able, in a single thought-moment" separately explains the method of receiving [the teaching].
This section has three parts:

first, hearing and receiving many teachings from a single Buddha; second, "like a great ocean" and so forth, hearing and receiving the true Dharma from many Buddhas; third, a question-and-answer session clarifying the scope of the preceding two types.

Within the preceding section, there are the elements of the thesis (*dharma*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*). In the commentary, because it first provides a general explanation stating that [the dharmas] are numerous, the explanation of the *dharma* refers to the "immeasurable illumination of dharmas."
Second, "entering the subtle and secret realm of the Tathāgata" explains the subtle and secret rain of Dharma within the midst of integration.
Third, "swiftness" explains the ability to receive [the teaching] in a single thought-moment;
because hearing is superior in this stage, one is able to receive many teachings.

Although one may receive many teachings, if they are coarse, superficial, and easy to understand, receiving them is not remarkable; furthermore, it is said that although the secret teachings (*guhyadharma*) are numerous, if one receives them after a long period of accumulation, the task is not difficult.
Here, it is clarified that being able to uphold them with the swiftness of a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) is what makes this superior.
The treatise states: “Among these, ‘immeasurable’ and below provides a detailed explanation of the preceding three:
the first two are the dharmas heard, and the last one is the virtue of the hearer. First, the dharmas heard are explained:

because they are both intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and produced (*kṛtaka*), they are opened into two aspects. These refer to the dharma-nature known by the three types of wisdom; because it is taught and bestowed upon sentient beings, it is called "produced."

In the detailed explanation of their nature, the "great illumination of the Dharma" is subsumed under the wisdom of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*), while the "great radiance of the Dharma" is subsumed under the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
This phrase is missing from the sutra.
How does one bring down the great rain of the Dharma?
It is by bestowing the rain of the Dharma upon others like a great cloud.
The following explains the capacity for hearing: "arousing faith" is termed "receiving," and "accepting the teaching" is termed "being capable"; this refers to the retention of the text.
"Grasping the meaning" refers to reflection (*cintā*); this is the "retention of meaning.
"Not losing" refers to retention (*dhāraṇī*); this applies to both preceding positions.
In the sutra, the two phrases concerning "being capable" and "reflection" are omitted for brevity.
In the second section, which explains the Dharma received by many Buddhas, the great ocean also possesses four meanings, which can be understood from their manifest characteristics.
In the third section, which distinguishes the boundaries through question and answer, there is first the question and subsequently the answer.
The response also consists of two parts:
first, by means of a comparative calculation, it demonstrates the vastness and abundance of what has been heard, thereby clarifying the first section;
second, from the phrase "as at the place of one Buddha" onwards, it analogically demonstrates the presence of many Buddhas, thereby clarifying the second section.

Regarding the phrase "the treasury of dharmas of the three periods" mentioned previously: the treatise explains that within the *dharmadhātu* there are three kinds of treasuries of phenomena—namely, illumination, radiance, and rain—which are stored within the *dharmadhātu* and thus termed a "treasury."
In the second section, the explanation of the names: first, by means of metaphors such as clouds and thunder, it reveals the Bodhisattva’s virtue of being able to transform others;
second, by means of "a single thought-moment" and so forth, it clarifies the brevity of the time of transformation.
In the aforementioned [categories], the first clarifies the breadth of the sphere of transformation;
the remainder clarify the excellence of the benefit of transformation.
Furthermore, regarding wind, clouds, rain, and so forth, they should be understood as explained in the treatise.
In the third section, "Explaining the Names," the manifestation and accomplishment of the eight aspects and the gradual growth of the virtues of things can be seen in the textual passages.
The sixth section, beginning with "This bodhisattva dwells in this stage," clarifies the division concerning the unsurpassed and surpassed powers of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*).

The treatise opens with six categories: first, that which relies on the internal. This refers generally to internal virtues, of which there are four kinds. These correspond to the five kinds of "greatness" (*mahattva*) within the previously mentioned section on the Great Perfection; however, because the greatness of wisdom (*jñāna-mahattva*) and the greatness of dhāraṇī are explained together as one, there are four. Since these are all the functional virtues of this stage, they are discussed here collectively.
Second, regarding that which relies on the external: the functional activity of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) arises in dependence upon external objects.
Third, regarding specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*): the power of transformation is the characteristic of supernormal powers.
These two preceding sections share the same scriptural text; they are divided into two sections for the purpose of explaining their distinct meanings.
Fourth, as for acting as a sustainer, one’s activity is constant and uninterrupted.
Fifth, as for causing joy, one cuts off the doubts and afflictions of the multitude.
Sixth, as for great superiority, one transcends the preceding stages.
Regarding the second point, "depending on the external," external phenomena such as the earth refer to the world that is moved, as it constitutes the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive support).

Furthermore, there are external phenomena such as one's own and others' bodies; these refer to the subsequently manifested bodies and so forth, which constitute the *sākṣāt-vipāka* (direct retribution).
Why are the body and so forth described as "external"?
Explanation:
Because they are contrasted with the aforementioned internal qualities such as liberation and greatness, these—the body and so forth—are designated as external phenomena.
The threefold self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is also of two kinds:
first, transformed external objects and so forth; "external" refers collectively to the [pure] land and the bodies of others.
Second, the manifested self-body and so forth. These two also encompass this section of the text.
Regarding the first turning of external phenomena, there are three aspects:

first, the abbreviated and expanded turning of similar types; second, the turning of distinct phenomena such as defilement and purity; and third, the sovereign turning of objects, the receptacle world, and so forth.
Second, "manifesting all Buddhas within a single atom" refers to the mastery in performing deeds such as manifesting transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Fourth, from "or in a single thought-moment" onwards, it clarifies the performance of sustaining power (*dhāraṇa*).
Within this, there are ten [sections]:
first, offerings and praise through body and speech;
second, the eightfold correspondence with the capacities of beings.
The three bodies manifest throughout the three periods of time;
the four bodies contain all lands within themselves—herein, the Vajragarbha Bodhisattva relies on this gate to sever the doubts of the assembly;
and from his pores, winds issue forth.
Sixth, the Buddha Flower-Displaying Ocean;
seventh, Body-Radiance-Pervading-Illumination;
eighth, Mouth-Breath-Moving-the-Earth.
Ninth, the three calamities are extensively demonstrated;
tenth, the bodies, lands, and characteristics of the Buddhas are manifested.
From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the conclusion is as can be understood.
Fifth, from "At that time" onwards, it clarifies causing joy; causing joy means severing doubt.
This has two aspects:

first, manifesting one's own supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to sever the doubts of the assembly; second, from "In accordance with the Tathāgata’s body, speech, and mind" onwards, it clarifies the teaching of all dharmas to sever the doubts of the assembly.
Within the preceding section there are also two parts:
the first question-and-answer reveals that his supernormal powers are unsurpassed, causing the assembly to rejoice;
the second question-and-answer clarifies that his supernormal powers have superiors, causing the assembly to rejoice.
The preceding section also has two parts:
first the question, and second the answer.
Within the first part, there are likewise two sections:
First, the great assembly harbors doubts; specifically, they raise doubts regarding the Bodhisattvas rather than the Buddha.
Subsequently, Vimukticandra takes up these doubts as a formal request.
In Gaṅgottara’s response, there are four parts:
First, entering meditative absorption to sever doubts; second, revealing the name of the concentration; third, the scope of its functional activity; fourth, categorizing its vast multiplicity.

Within the first section, there are also four parts: first, the Dharma Lord enters meditative absorption; second, the assembly perceives his entry into the body; third, they perceive the Buddhas within the body; fourth, he withdraws his function and returns to his original state.
Regarding the manifestation of the name, there is first a question and subsequently an answer.
Since its name was already manifested at the time of entering meditative absorption, why is it asked again? The explanation is as follows:
At that time, the Master of the Dharma entered meditative absorption in silence; later, the compilers of the canon selected this passage and placed it therein.
Because it was not made manifest at the time [of the Buddha’s passing], this question was raised.

In the response, the mention of the "essential nature of the Buddha-land" means that by entering this samādhi, one is able to manifest the Buddha-land; therefore, this concentration is named as its essential nature.
Third, the section beginning with "The question says" clarifies the scope of its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*).
This section has two parts:
first, the question; second, the answer.
In the response, it is shown that not only does he manifest a single Buddha-field as previously described, but his power is such that he can manifest more than the number of atoms [in all worlds].
Fourth, from "The Bodhisattva in the Cloud of Dharma" onwards, it clarifies the vastness and multiplicity of these manifestations.

Within this section, there are three parts. First, the vastness and multiplicity of what is attained: this refers to the fact that what is attained on this stage is not merely one or two things; hence it says, "attaining such immeasurable [qualities]," and so forth.

Second, from the words "Therefore" onwards, it clarifies that the functional activity is difficult to fathom. Within this, the first three items clarify the difficulty of fathoming the activities: spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) is the greatness of the aforementioned supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); next, observing the three periods of time is the great wisdom of the three types of penetration (*trividyā*); next, samādhi is the greatness of the aforementioned samādhis; next, the power of wisdom is the greatness of the aforementioned wisdom; next, roaming in liberation is the greatness of liberation; and transformations, etc., refer to the transformation of external objects, which can be understood accordingly.
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the extensive details may be understood through the summary.
Second, from "Vimukticandra said" onwards, it clarifies that this [assembly] surpasses others in its excellence before the Buddha; herein, there is first a question and subsequently an answer.
In the question, the Bodhisattva raises the doubt that the Buddha is not superior, with the phrasing of the inquiry being the same as above.
However, the underlying intent of the doubt differs; this should be understood by referring to the response that follows.
In the formal answer below, there are three parts:
First, there is a general rebuke of the question:

if one compares a single four-continent world-system to the worlds of the ten directions, the former is already small; yet, within that four-continent world-system, taking even a single grain of soil from it is the smallest of the small.

These four continents, when compared to a patch of earth the size of a bean, are already considered much; yet those ten directions of worlds, when compared to these four continents, are even more so—they are the most numerous among the many.

If even a small amount of doubt is already considered unacceptable, how much more so when a small portion of that small amount seeks to be categorized with the great majority of it? This is utterly impermissible; therefore, I say that what you have asked is exactly as I have stated.
The Tathāgata is immeasurable and so forth; this concludes the inquiry.
Second, from the words "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, it is explained by way of concrete examples.

That is to say, among the virtues of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), that which has already been described is like a handful of soil, while that which remains undescribed is like the soil of the four continents.

The merits of the Tathāgata may be compared to the lands throughout the realms of the ten directions; yet even the qualities of the earth as described cannot be compared to those not yet described, so how could they be compared to the merits of the fruit of Buddhahood?
3. From "I shall now speak" onwards, the Buddha is cited as testimony to establish that the virtues of the stages (*bhūmi*) are immeasurable.
Although the virtues of the stages are immeasurable, they do not equal those of the Buddha.
Because the meaning is difficult to believe, the Buddha is cited as testimony.
From "As in the ten directions" below, it can be understood that this correctly reveals how the Bodhisattva’s virtues are inferior to those of the Buddha.

Second, from "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva follows such wisdom and accords with the Tathāgata" below, this is precisely the fruit of being harmonious and supple, as well as the vows, knowledge, and so forth that encompass the retribution.
Within the fruit of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), there are four parts:

first, the explanation of the practice of pliancy; second, from "The Bodhisattva dwells in this stage" onwards, the explanation of the purity of the wisdom of the teaching; third, from "The Buddhas of the ten directions speak of the three periods of time" onwards, the explanation of attaining mastery over the Dharma; fourth, from "This is called" onwards, the summary of the characteristics of this stage.

Among these four, the first two sections of the treatise are called "Teaching the Dharma to Bring Joy," while the remaining [sections] and the final two results are both termed "Greatly Superior Parts.
Within the former [two], there are three elements—thesis, example, and application—to be understood within the initial "Conduct of Flexibility."
Within the second [section], the purity of teaching and wisdom, the dharma, the metaphor, and the application may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the sixth, the Great Excellence: first, the names such as "the three times" and so forth refer to the excellence of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Second, within the excellence of maturation (*vipāka*), attaining samādhis numbering as many as the atoms in ten unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of worlds is called the excellence of calculation (*gaṇanā*).
These two matters surpass all preceding stages; therefore, they are called "Greatly Surpassing.
Within the former [section], the first five phrases provide specific clarifications, while the final one summarizes the five.
In this treatise, these are subsumed into three:
the first two each constitute one, and the latter three constitute one; thus, there are three.

First, the knowledge of the three times is the practice for severing doubt; because it penetrates the three times as a supramundane path, its meaning as a "path" (mārga) should be understood accordingly.
The second is the wisdom of the dharma-realm, which is the practice of swift supernatural power because it involves hearing the teaching of the Tathāgata’s secret Dharma;
the third consists of the three subsequent phrases, termed "auxiliary practices of equal action," meaning the impartial transformation and benefit of sentient beings.
The "wise ones of all worlds" establish the equality of purifying Buddha-lands for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Second, regarding "universal illumination and so forth," this refers to the equality of the light of the Dharma; it is the transformation through the wisdom of teaching.
Regarding "the three great compassions" and so forth: it refers to the manifestation through wisdom that realizes the equality of perfect enlightenment.
The section beginning with "summarizing the essentials" concludes [the discussion].
The remaining text is self-evident.
The seventh major section, following "The Sequential Order of the Ten Stages of this Bodhisattva," clarifies the "Section on the Images of the Stages.
This contains four parts, namely: the pond, the mountain, the ocean, and the jewel.
These illustrate four kinds of merit: the first three are the merits of scripture (*āgama*), and the last one is the merit of realization (*adhigama*).
Within the former, the pond illustrates the merit of practice—that is, the cultivation undertaken throughout the various stages (*bhūmi*);
the mountain illustrates the merit of superior excellence—that is, the qualities perfected through cultivation, which stand high above all other ranks.

The third simile, that of the ocean, represents the merit of being able to cross what is difficult to cross and attaining the great fruit; this refers to the virtue produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya-guṇa*), which is able to reach the great fruit, and "crossing" (*tīrṇa*) means having arrived [at the other shore].

The fourth simile, that of the jewel, represents the merit of transformation, exhaustion, and firmness: it is called "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) because one progresses from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) up to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*); it is called "exhaustion through transformation" (*parāvṛtti-kṣaya*) because the stages have reached their limit and obscurations are exhausted; and it is called "firmness" (*dṛḍha*) because the realization of principle has reached its ultimate consummation.
Regarding the first stage, the cultivation of merit, there are the Dharma, the analogy, and the application.
In the explanation of the Dharma, beginning from the Stage of Joy and ending with the Cloud of Dharma, these are termed the "successive practices."
Because small causes produce great fruits, it is called "tending toward omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*).
In the analogy, Anavatapta is here named the "Pool Without Heat," because this dragon king is free from the three kinds of suffering, such as hot sand.

Regarding the emergence of the four rivers: the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* mentions eight rivers, while the *Āgama-sūtras* mention twenty; each has its own basis. The account of the four rivers is based on the fundamental description:

it states that this lake is situated atop Mount Gandhamādana, from which the Gaṅgā River flows from a golden elephant’s mouth on the eastern side, the Sindhu River flows from a silver ox’s mouth on the southern side, the Sītā River flows from a lapis lazuli horse’s mouth on the western side, and the Vakṣu River flows from a crystal lion’s mouth on the northern side.

Each of these four rivers issues from its respective pond; at a distance of forty *li*, each divides into four branches that encircle the pond once before flowing back into the great ocean from their original directions.
Therefore, together with the four fundamental rivers, they constitute twenty rivers, the names of which are listed in full in the *Vibhāṣā*.
Since the Tathāgata appeared in the world to the east of those mountains, all people clearly see the five rivers on the eastern side; thus, these are taken collectively as a metaphor.
The other three rivers possess great renown; although people may not see them, there is no one who does not hear of them, and thus they are also taken as metaphors.
Together with the previous ones, these constitute eight.
The remaining rivers are minor in name and some people may not even hear of them, and therefore they are not discussed.
Regarding the phrase "filling the four worlds" (cāturdvīpaka): it does not mean that four rivers each flow through a separate world; rather, this refers collectively to a single Jambudvīpa.
For what reason, then, is it called "the four worlds"?
Commentary:
This is a case where the words are general while the meaning is specific.
Since this Jambudvīpa is comprised within one of the four continents, the general mention of "the four continents" actually intends Jambudvīpa.

In the aforementioned passages where the assemblies are unified and extended, statements such as "just as it is for these four continents, so it is for the ten directions" are all of this same category.
Within the synthesis, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) benefit others, while the synthesis of the four rivers brings fulfillment.
Being inexhaustible, it reaches all-knowledge; by increasing and perfecting self-benefit, one attains great enlightenment and merges into the great ocean.
In this treatise, regarding those who practice through the power of their original vows, it explains how the water of great vows—the roots of goodness—flows forth from the bodhicitta.
In this context, the term "bodhisattva" alone necessarily implies the possession of the bodhicitta, as there is no need for it to be stated explicitly.
Regarding the practice of benefiting others through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), these are explained as fulfilling the needs of sentient beings.
Regarding "one's own virtue" and so forth, the benefit for oneself can be understood through this explanation.
Within the second section, the analogy of the mountain regarding superior qualities, there are four parts:

first, a general presentation of the phenomena; second, the enumeration of the mountain names; third, the manifestation of the objects within the mountains; and fourth, the application of these to the Dharma.

Regarding the initial statement that the ten stages (daśabhūmi) have distinctions because they exist due to the Buddha’s wisdom: this means that taking the Buddha’s wisdom as the supporting cause, the distinct characteristics of the ten stages arise, just as the ten mountain kings exist by virtue of being supported by the preeminent foundation of the great earth.
The treatise states: "Because one relies upon the ten stages of superior practice for the sake of all-knowledge.
Regarding the listing of the names, as for Mount Khadiraka, it is so named because *khadira* wood grows on this mountain.
Khadira is here translated as "bitter whipwood.
Gandhamādana is named "Holding the Pair" Mountain.
Nimindhara is named "Holding the Edge" Mountain.
*Kakara* is translated here as "Cakravāḍa Mountains" (Wheel-Encircling Mountains).
Other names may be understood accordingly.
Third, from the passage beginning "Like the Snowy Mountains," the objects within the mountains are revealed to serve as metaphors for the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Among these, the first metaphor illustrates the wondrous medicine of the noble wisdom of the first stage;
the second illustrates the fragrance of the precepts of the second stage;
and the third illustrates the wondrous jewel of meditative concentration of the third stage.
The fourth stage is like a world-transcending immortal (*ṛṣi*);
the fifth uses the metaphor of a yakṣa to illustrate the mastery of skillful means in the fifth stage;

the sixth uses the metaphor of fruit to illustrate the contemplation of the accumulation of causes and conditions in the sixth stage. As for the statement that the fruits of the śrāvakas are inexhaustible, it is because the sixth stage transcends the realm of the śrāvakas, and thus those [fruits] are said to be without end.
The seven dragons symbolize the seven stages (*bhūmi*), as they have transcended the *pratyekabuddhas* and are able to expound their path;
the eight "mastery of mind" beings are the Guhyapatis (Secret-Trace Deities), known as the "Mastery Assembly," symbolizing the ten masteries and so forth within the eighth stage;
the nine *asuras* symbolize the characteristics of great power in the ninth stage, which skillfully gathers and sustains sentient beings.
The ten celestial deities symbolize the fulfillment of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, the treatise explains:
herein, the mountains of pure jewels symbolize the eight kinds of stages that involve detachment from the stages.
Regarding "because of being well-purified": this means that among the ten mountains, excluding the first two—the Snowy Mountain and the Fragrant Mountain—these are mountains of earth and stone;
the remaining eight are all mountains of gold and jewels, and are therefore called "pure precious mountains."

The analogy for those who weary of the stages from the eighth stage onward refers to the third stage; therein, by means of pure dhyāna, they weary of and leave behind afflictions, just as a jewel is utterly pure.
Those who are "well-purified" refer to the fourth stage and above; therein, by means of the untainted (*anāsrava*), they sever all afflictions, just as a jewel is utterly pure.

The passage beginning with "Furthermore, regarding the various mountains" explains all the things contained within those mountains; that is to say, beings such as seers and immortals belong to the category of sentient beings, whereas medicinal herbs, jewels, and the like belong to the category of non-sentient things.
Among these, things such as medicine that can support the internal retribution are called "objects of enjoyment" (*paribhoga-vastu*).
That is to say, medicine being able to eliminate illness is termed "remedy for increase and decrease" (*vṛddhi-hāni-pratipakṣa*);
fragrant fruits supporting the body are termed "objects of nourishment" (*puṣṭi-vastu*).
The two jewels do not sustain the body; they can only be stored up to eliminate poverty, and are therefore called "guarding" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "relying on the Snowy Mountains and so forth," this specifies their location, namely the first three and the sixth; these four are the bases for that which is not of the category of sentient beings (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*).
In the following explanation of the category of sentient beings (*sattva-gaṇa*), six kinds of difficulties are addressed:
First, the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) possessing the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) provides sustenance that generates wealth; thus, it addresses the difficulty of poverty.
Second, the yakṣas exercise authority over their retinues, preventing them from harming others; thus, it addresses the difficulty of death.
First, the three dragons descend with timely rain to remedy the difficulty of calamities.
Second, the Vajrapāṇi spirits subdue and conquer evil persons to remedy the difficulty of unruliness.
Third, the asuras recite the power of mantras to harmonize their retinues so they no longer commit acts of slaughter, which is called remedying evil karma.
On the summit of Mount Sumeru, Śakra and others are called "Masters.
On the slopes of Mount Sumeru dwell the Four Kings, who are known as the Four Heavenly Kings; they are able to counteract the enemies, the asuras.

The following explains the meaning of "not being exhausted within the collection. This means that because the phenomena mentioned above are capable of producing all things, it is said that they are contained within that collection.

"Proceeding in accordance without interruption or cessation" explains the meaning of inexhaustibility: that which proceeds in successive succession is called "proceeding in accordance"; because it is not permanently severed, it is called "uninterrupted"; and because it is not merely temporarily absent, it is called "unceasing."

The following explains how the mountains derive their names from the ocean: it means that the mountains attain their loftiness and excellence because of the ocean, while the ocean attains its depth and vastness because of the mountains.
As for the previous mention of "relying on the earth" and the current mention of "relying on the ocean," these are cited alternately because those ten mountains depend upon both of these locations.

The following explains the analogy of the Dharma: the Buddha’s wisdom is like the ocean; because the high and deep characteristics of the ten stages arise based upon it, it is said that "cause and effect manifest each other.
This means that beneath each mountain there is a great ocean, and within each stage there is the Buddha-stage; this is the meaning within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
If, in other teachings, one must reach the stage of Buddhahood only after the tenth bhūmi, this may be inferred accordingly.
The third "great ocean" clarifies the ten characteristics of the great fruit of merit, which is difficult to attain yet capable of being attained.
Within this, there is first the analogy and subsequently the application, each having both general and specific aspects.

Regarding the general aspect, the term "indestructible" means that these ten characteristics are like a single great ocean that cannot be altered or taken away; therefore, they are called indestructible.
The dharmas of the stages are likewise so.
Although they share the same Buddha-wisdom, they are divided into ten stages according to their meaning, for they cannot be altered or taken away.
The Treatise says: "Because cause and effect correspond to one another, the ten stages are like a great ocean."
"Difficult to cross, yet able to cross, because one attains the fruit of great Bodhi.
In the subsequent explanation of the individual [categories], ten are subsumed into eight:
the sixth and seventh are combined into one, and the ninth and tenth are likewise; thus there are eight.
The first three can be understood as before.
Regarding the fourth, the merit of protection (*paritrāṇa*): "protection" is defined as relinquishment (*tyāga*), because it relinquishes all other differentiated characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, it is explained:
It protects with a single flavor because it never loses its constancy.
It is said to be inexhaustible because its waters—consisting of the six depths and seven expanses—never run dry.
It is said to protect the world through its merit because its tides do not exceed their bounds and it does not harm or injure living beings.

This metaphor illustrates how, on the ninth stage, one preaches the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings; like the ocean that receives water without weariness and can contain the hundred rivers, it does not allow other waters to damage the world.

On the subsequent Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), one receives the rain of the Buddha-Dharma to benefit the world. Other points regarding the convergence of dharmas and so forth may be understood from the text as it stands.
The fourth jewel, consisting of ten matters, serves as a metaphor for the merit of the transformation and exhaustion of the firm [nature].
Within this, there is first the metaphor and subsequently the application (the *yōga*), each having both general and specific aspects.
In the treatise, the general aspect is explained first; the ten jewels therein may be understood as the "transgressions" (*atīta*).
"Because they have emerged, they are taken"—this is the first phrase in the sutra, meaning that because they have emerged from the ocean, they are taken for practical use.
"Ratnaprabhāsa" (Emitting Light) is the ninth, and "Saṃdarśana" (Manifestation) is the tenth; by skipping the middle ones and citing the last, it says "up to and including."
Regarding the condensation of ten into eight, this is because the [sections on] six, seven, and eight are combined.
Within these eight, the first and last phrases clarify the Dharma by means of metaphors, while the remaining ones merely explain those metaphors.
Emerging from the ocean at the outset to benefit sentient beings is therefore called "merit" (*guṇa*).
"Observing well" (*sudarśana*) reveals the Dharma; that is to say, the noble wisdom of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) emerges from the ocean of afflictions and observes skillfully.
The two bodies (*dvaya-kāya*) have their forms clearly distinguished.
Third, it is perfectly round and pleasing;

fourth, all impurities are exhausted; fifth, its color and luster are fresh and radiant; sixth, it is adorned with various marks—these are called the "arising of conduct," the explanation of which can be understood by combining the three phrases;
seventh, the emission of light is called "spiritual power."
Eighth, because the rain of jewels follows the king, there is no sense of guarding or cherishing them.

This next section reveals the Dharma: by taking one's own roots of goodness and making them a single treasury of goodness shared with all sentient beings, one unites these with the treasures of all beings.
The passages concerning "surpassing the ten holy ones" and so forth can be understood from the text as they stand.
This concludes the section on "Images.
Below the eighth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva," the section clarifying the benefits of the stages (*bhūmi*) is presented.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the manifestation of the benefits of the Dharma; second, the universal application throughout the ten directions; and third, the testimony of those coming from other regions.
According to the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra*, there is further a fourth part, the Tathāgata’s rejoicing, and a fifth, the conclusion of the teaching by the Buddha while descending.
Now, based on this sutra, there are two parts to the beginning:
first, the merit of generating faith; second, the merit of making offerings, such as raining down flowers.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, the benefit of hearing; second, the shaking of the earth.
Within the first part, there are also two sections:
First, a general statement regarding the difficulty of hearing [this teaching]; second, questions and answers that reveal its benefits.
Within the answers, there are also two parts:
first, the actual exposition, which consists of citing the Buddha as the source of the Dharma and emphasizing the difficulty of hearing this Dharma.
Second, from "For what reason" onwards is the explanation and establishment.

Because those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta and practice the bodhisattva path are the vessels for this Dharma, it is only for them that hearing is taught; therefore, this hearing must accord with that Dharma, so that the benefit accomplished may be vast and great.
The shaking of the earth is the merit that gives rise to faith; it serves as the condition for the meaning of "arising.
The explanations regarding the eighteen marks and so forth, as well as the four types of sentient beings and so forth, are all as previously stated in the first assembly.
The remaining sections, such as the general proofs and so forth, are all to be understood as identical to those in the previous assemblies.
Within the second part of the third major section, the Verse Summary, there are two parts:
first, the observation and explanation of the intent behind the verses.
The ten purposes for which this is taught are the same as those explained in the preceding assembly and may be understood accordingly.

The ninety verses of the main body of the stanzas are divided into nine sections: first, twenty-nine verses praise the section on the fulfillment of the stage through skillful means (*upāya*). Within this, the initial seven verses provide a general summary of the "discriminative wisdom" (*pratisaṃkhyāna-jñāna*) across the nine preceding stages; the next two verses specifically summarize the first stage; the next two summarize the second stage; the next two summarize the third stage; the next two summarize the fourth stage; the next two summarize the fifth stage; the next two summarize the sixth stage; the next two summarize the seventh stage; the next three summarize the eighth stage; and the final five summarize the ninth stage.
2. The section on Samādhi, consisting of two verses beginning with "Desiring to attain";
3. The section on Receiving the Position, consisting of ten verses beginning with "If one is able";
4. The section on Great Perfection, consisting of seven verses beginning with "Abiding in this stage."
5. The six verses beginning with "This stage" explain the section on the definition of the names;
6. The seven verses beginning with "The Great Being" explain the section on the powers of supernormal knowledge—whether unsurpassed or surpassed;
7. The eight verses beginning with "When a bodhisattva dwells here" explain the section on the fruits of the stages, such as being pliant and so forth.
8. The section on "Images" (*pratibimba*) consists of nineteen verses beginning with "For the sake of attainment.

Within this, the first eleven verses provide the analogy of mountains; the next four verses provide the analogy of the ocean; and the next four verses provide the analogy of jewels. The analogies of the pond, the benefits of the nine stages, and so forth are omitted from the verse recitation. At the end of the ninth stage, the final two verses conclude by explaining its inexhaustibility.
The "Chapter on the Ten Grounds" concludes.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Fazang of Xisi Monastery in the State of Wei.
Chapter Twenty-Three: The Ten Clarities (Daśavidyā). Regarding the initial explanation of the title:
it refers to the sovereign mastery of wondrous function; because it illuminates exhaustively, it is termed "clarity" (vidyā).

The "unlimited application of clarity" (*amitā-prayoga*) is explained by means of the "tenfold perfect discernment" (*daśavidha-pariccheda*), which is an interpretation based on numerical enumeration.
Second, regarding the purpose of this section: it serves as a general introduction to the purpose of the following five chapters.
This means that while the preceding section revealed the fulfillment of the stage of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), the following clarifies its superior practice and function (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, the preceding section concerned the essence of the stage (*avasthā-svabhāva*), whereas this section distinguishes its practice and function.
Moreover, the former refers to the practice within the stage, while this refers to the practice subsequent to the stage.
Furthermore, while the preceding section established the fulfillment of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), this section now elucidates the great function of subsequent wisdom (*prṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*).
It is for these four reasons that [this chapter] follows.

Although ancient masters have also correlated this with the stages of Equal Enlightenment (*samaya-buddhatva*) and Sublime Enlightenment (*sugata-buddhatva*), this meaning is not distinguished within this sutra; moreover, the meaning of Equal Enlightenment has already been revealed at the final moment of the preceding Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmamegha-bhūmi*).
Second, the specific explanation of this chapter:

it answers the ten previous questions regarding mastery (*vaśitā*), for in the alternative translation of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-karmavibhāga-sūtra*, those questions are termed the "Ten Clarifications" (*daśa-vyākaraṇa*).

Regarding the three essential principles (*piṇḍārtha*): these ten clarifications (*daśa-vaiśāradya*) consist of the two types of knowledge—logical reasoning (*yukti*) and valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Their essential principle is the unimpeded mastery of their manifest functions.

The meaning of the ten clarifications is briefly presented through three gates: First, the manifestation of their names: (1) the knowledge of others' minds; (2) the divine eye; (3) recollection of past lives; (4) the limit of the future; (5) the divine ear; (6) fearless supernormal power; (7) vocal sound; (8) the physical body; (9) reality; and (10) the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Among these, the feelings associated with the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) are designated as "divine eye" and "divine ear" based on their destination and faculties; the others are named after their objects. Since all ten are the functional activities of wisdom, they are collectively termed "functions of wisdom."
The two [wisdoms] are identical in essence, taking great wisdom as their nature; yet they encompass the wisdom of Samantabhadra’s nature-arising.

If distinguished according to their phenomenal aspects, the former eight are wisdom of cognition (*jñāna*), while the latter two are wisdom of principle (*tattva*). In reality, however, there is only one unimpeded wisdom, because the latter two clarify that the manifestation of function is not obstructed, and the former eight do not abandon the state of being quiescent within that very manifestation.
Third, within the analysis by way of various gates, there are ten points:

first, regarding the mutual inclusion of these with the ten illuminations (*daśa-vidyā*) in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokātīta-parivarta*), that text refers to clarity regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), not to mastery over functional activity (*karma-vibhutva*).

Only that fourth [wheel] produces inconceivable, pure, and wondrous sounds; its light of expedient wisdom is heard everywhere throughout immeasurable worlds. This one is identical to the present [wheel] in terms of its function, while the others are all distinct matters.

Second, regarding the mutual inclusion between these two [categories] and the ten [knowledges]: herein, the knowledge of others' minds, the divine eye, the recollection of past lives, and the divine ear correspond to four of the ten knowledges as designated by their names.

Among these, the power of fearlessness encompasses the fifth superknowledge of manifesting inconceivable mastery in birth for the sake of sentient beings, as well as the seventh superknowledge of traveling in a single thought-moment to unspeakably unspeakable worlds.

Among these, the adornment of the form body subsumes the sixth supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) of manifesting a single body in inconceivable worlds, as well as the ninth supernormal knowledge of manifesting unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings. Furthermore, the eighth supernormal knowledge of manifesting all worlds adorned with inconceivable ornaments is also included herein; the former pertains to the adornment of the *sāmbhogika-kāya* (enjoyment body), while this pertains to the adornment of the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body).
Among these, the illumination of knowledge regarding the future limit also includes the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), because that which is seen by it is included therein.
Among these, the illumination of knowledge regarding sounds also includes the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*).

Among these, the final two illuminations include the tenth [illumination]: the inconceivable manifestation of the wisdom-attainment (*jñānābhijñā*) for sentient beings, which consists of attaining unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*) throughout unspeakable worlds.
The remaining points may be understood by analogy.
Regarding the third point, the inclusion of these [three knowledges] within the "Threefold Knowledge" (*traividya*) as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are two senses:
first, they are not subsumed under the Threefold Knowledge, because that [Threefold Knowledge] is also attained by the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*), whereas this is not the case here.

Second, even if one considers the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*) attained by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, among these ten [knowledges], only three subsume five, and thus they do not exhaust them all. That is to say, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) subsumes two: the divine eye and the knowledge of the future limit (*anāgata-koṭi-vidyā*);
the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) subsumes only one;
and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vidyā*) subsumes two: namely, the last two [of the ten].
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are likewise three kinds of clarity (*vidyā*):
first, the clarity of all Buddhas, which refers to omniscience;
second, the clarity of Bodhisattvas, which refers to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Third, regarding the three types of ignorance (avidyā), it refers to ultimate emptiness (atyanta-śūnyatā);
this is different from the former.
Fourth, concerning the mutual inclusion of the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍ-abhijñā), there are also two meanings:
First, one [power] is not included within the six, because it is also attained by those of the two vehicles;

second, if it is that which is attained by a Buddha, its inclusion is exhaustive, meaning that among the six, the divine eye, divine ear, supernormal power, and the exhaustion of outflows—these four are each divided into two, thus making ten.

Regarding the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), it is divided into two based on the distinction between seeing the present and the future; this is because the clear knowledge of future births and deaths is also that which is seen by the divine eye.
Regarding the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), it is divided into two based on the distinction between hearing the sacred teachings and discriminating sounds.
The supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) are categorized into two based on their functional activity and physical form.

The exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is categorized into two based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). The ninth [power] is wisdom; since the remaining two are not further divided, the six categories subsume the ten.
Regarding the distinction between the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the clear knowledges (*vidyā*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle three, states: "Question:
What is the difference between supernormal powers and clear knowledges? Answer:"
To directly know past lives is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*); to know the causes, conditions, and karmic actions of the past is called clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, to directly know dying here and being born there is called supernormal power; to know that the convergence of karmic actions and conditions is never lost is called clear knowledge.

Furthermore, to directly know that the fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted, yet not knowing whether they will arise again or not, is called the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-abhijñā); if one knows that the outflows are exhausted and will never arise again, this is called clear knowledge (vidyā).

Sixth, regarding the distinctions revealed through the classification of teachings: if one considers the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Triyāna, they all possess the three knowledges (*vidyā*) and six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), though they differ in their respective scope and limits.
In the case of the Ekayāna, the ten knowledges (*vidyā*) and ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) differ from the former in terms of their breadth and narrowness.

Seventh, regarding the delimitation of what is known, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle three, states: "These three types of supernormal knowledge are also attained by those of the Two Vehicles, yet they are incomplete."
This means that regarding the past, they may know up to one lifetime, at most eighty thousand lifetimes, but beyond that they cannot know;
the same applies to the future.

Furthermore, they cannot instantaneously know in a single thought-moment the characteristics of the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the four truths, the fifteen moments of mind, and the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). Therefore, they are not equal to the Buddha, because the Buddha knows the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
The commentary explains:
Those of the Hīnayāna know only the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*), yet their knowledge is not all-pervasive.
The three types of supernormal knowledge of those of the Three Vehicles, however, mutually encompass all-pervasive and complete knowledge.
The single vehicle and ten clarities form a multilayered, all-pervasive Indra’s net, meaning that a single thought-moment encompasses the nine periods of time and so forth.
Within a single atom are ten lands; the same applies to all other thoughts and atoms, and everything contained therein is known as it truly is.

Regarding the classification according to the three types of action (*trikarma*): among the ten [powers], the divine ear and its object, sound, constitute the purity of vocal action; supernormal power and the physical body constitute the purity of bodily action; and the remaining six belong to the purity of mental action.
If judged by their intrinsic nature, these are exclusively mental actions (*manas-karman*), because they are entirely characterized by the clarity of wisdom (*jñāna-prabhāsvara*).

Regarding the classification based on vision (*darśana*) and so forth: among the ten [powers], two are vision, namely the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) and the knowledge of future lives (*anāgata-jñāna*).
The second is hearing, which refers to the divine ear and sounds;
the remainder are all forms of knowledge (*jñāna*).

Regarding their establishment, within the three vehicles and so forth, the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*) are established solely in relation to the three periods of time as objects of cognition.

Now, as for this One Vehicle, its principle is in truth luminous and its function is limitless; it relies on [the stages] to manifest perfection and employs the number ten to reveal it. Therefore, only ten are taught, neither more nor less.
The commentary on the text has two parts:
first, the actual exposition of the ten clarities; second, from "abiding securely" onwards, the concluding praise that reveals their excellence.
Within the first part, there are three sections: first, stating the number; second, the detailed explanation; third, the summary of the number.
In the commentary, the ten clarifications constitute ten sections; each consists of two parts: first, the explanation, and second, the conclusion.
Regarding the first, the clarification of skillfully knowing the minds of others, there are two parts within the explanation:

first, knowing the minds of sentient beings within this one great trichiliocosm; second, from the passage "such hundreds of worlds" onwards, knowing the minds of sentient beings in the infinite worlds of the ten directions.
Regarding the preceding section: first, a general summary; second, the specific details beginning with "That is to say" (yad uta); third, the conclusion beginning with "In this way.
Within the specific details, there are two parts to the knowledge of the thirty kinds of mind:
first, clarifying the mind in terms of its activity; second, clarifying the mind in terms of its retribution, beginning with "The śrāvakas."
Regarding the preceding section: first, the initial three natures of mind are presented collectively.
Second, regarding breadth and narrowness, distinctions are made within the category of wholesome minds.
Third, regarding the superior nature of evil: that which accords with the higher [unwholesome states] is termed an "evil mind," while the opposite is termed "superior."
The indeterminate is "flowing with the current," while the opposite is "against the current.

Second, regarding retribution: the Bodhisattva possesses a broad and superior mind, whereas the followers of the Two Vehicles possess a narrow mind; thus, both [the Two and Three Vehicles] are "against the current," while the Eight Classes of Beings flow with the current, and the Three Evil Realms constitute the "evil" state.
The rest is all visible.
Second, the clarity of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is explained in three parts:
first, a general enumeration; [the remaining two follow].
Second, from "good and evil" downward, the objects perceived are presented; therein, "good and evil" and so forth are general [objects], while "gods, nāgas," and so forth are specific ones.

Third, from "bodhisattva" downward, it reveals that among those capable of seeing with the divine eye, one who possesses an unimpeded, clear, and pure divine eye does so because the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) have been exhausted, resulting in the sovereign clarity obtained as a karmic reward.
Regarding "seeing below," this refers to seeing the birth, death, and so forth of sentient beings in the present.

The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in the "Chapter on the Six Perfections," states: "A bodhisattva’s divine eye is of two kinds: that obtained through cultivation and that obtained as a karmic retribution."
Because he has attained the divine eye, he sees the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Attaining the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) is the practice of the Bodhisattva path through the five supernormal powers obtained as a karmic reward. He asked:

If the divine eye-faculty (*divyacakṣurindriya*) were to see, the faculty itself would be an obstruction; thus, it should see forms within the obstruction but could not see forms beyond the obstruction. Answer:

When the divine eye is attained through cultivation, the faculty is termed the "supernormal power of the divine eye" (*divyacakṣurabhijñā*). Since this supernormal power has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence, it sees forms beyond obstructions.
If one perceives forms beyond obstructions, why is it that Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas perceive them at varying distances?
Answer: Because their supernormal wisdom (abhijñā) possesses degrees of intensity and subtlety.
There is a distinction between what is near and what is distant, just as a magnet does not attract everything that is not within its reach.
Among these, that which is subject to reversal refers to indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karma*) that can be changed or altered.
The rest may all be understood by reference to the text. Regarding the third [clairvoyance], the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), there are two parts:

first, recollecting and knowing the past events of oneself and others; second, from "Furthermore, he recollects" onwards, recollecting the causes, effects, and other matters concerning the Buddhas of the past.
Because he is a Buddha who appears in the world for the sake of sentient beings, he is primarily distinguished by means of the eight phases [of a Buddha's life].
Since this Bodhisattva has attained the eye of the nine periods of time and thus perceives the phenomena of the past and present, that which he knows is without limit.
If it were not so, then those past phenomena would not be past if they had not yet fallen away;
if they had already ceased and perished, they would be non-existent;
and to perceive what is non-existent is not reality.

If it is argued that one merely recollects and knows because a mental image of what was previously experienced appears before the mind, then this person sees only the reflection of their own mind and does not see those external phenomena.
Furthermore, since this [object] has never been experienced, it should not be recollected or known.
Moreover, if one perceives only the present and not the past, how can it be called the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*)?
The remaining text is self-evident.
Within the fourth section, the "Clarity of Wisdom Regarding the Future Limit," there are also two parts:

first, knowing the characteristics of the karmic retributions of future sentient beings; second, from the phrase "knowing the future" onwards, knowing the characteristics of the causes and effects of future Buddhas.
Regarding the preceding section, there is first a general understanding, and second, from "knowing the karma of sentient beings" onwards, there is specific knowledge.
Briefly stated, ten pairs are presented:
first, the pair of karma and its retribution.
Second, knowing what is wholesome and unwholesome;
