This refers to what was stated above: "Abiding in one stage universally encompasses the merits of all stages.

Second, regarding the inclusion of gates by gates: because each and every one of the two hundred gates individually subsumes all other gates, this results in two hundred sets of two hundred, which constitute the eighty thousand practices.
Third, by subsuming practices within practices—meaning that within each of the two thousand practices, every single practice is subsumed—one arrives at two thousand sets of two thousand.
This exceeds billions and trillions; this is what is meant by "equality."

Fourth, the concise summarizes the extensive; as for the two thousand practices and so forth mentioned above, the concluding verse below states: "As in the teaching of a single mote of dust upon the great earth."
By means of this brief exposition on a single atom, one does not depart from the vast ground of the ten directions; therefore, even when the vast is subsumed, nothing remains unexhausted.
This is the infinitely equal Dharma-realm and the boundlessly transcendent void. As it says below: "The void may be measured, but the virtues of the Bodhisattva are inexhaustible."
This is what is meant by that.
Regarding the five aspects of the characteristics of practice, one should understand them according to the textual exegesis.
Within these two thousand practices, they are divided into six based on the preceding six stages, as should be understood from before.
The first two hundred phrases answer the preceding twenty questions regarding faith.
Within this, they clarify the practices of the stage of clear faith, which is divided into three parts:
the first ninety phrases clarify the fulfillment of one's own portion of practice;
2. From "The ten kinds of entry" below, eighty phrases clarify the perfection of superior progress;
3. From "The ten kinds of indestructible wisdom" below, thirty phrases clarify the culmination of the two practices.
Regarding the first part, why is the fruit of reliance explained at the very beginning?
It is because this is the primary basis for the arising of practice and the foremost state of tranquil abiding.
There are four sections within the text:
First, a general enumeration; second, listing the names and explaining their meanings; third, concluding by defining the scope; and fourth, praising the excellence and exhorting study.
Most of the subsequent texts contain all four of these elements, though some do not; this shall be understood as one encounters them in the text.
Regarding the term "supporting fruit" (*niśraya-phala*): it is distinguished from fruits produced from causes, nor is it the fruit of the world as a supporting retribution (*āśraya-vipāka*).

Rather, it refers to the fact that various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—whether arising sequentially from prior to subsequent or depending upon one another—each attain growth; thus, it is so named.
The fruit that arises based on mutual dependence is called the "fruit of dependence" (*niśraya-phala*).
Another explanation states:
it is like the world as a fruit of dependence, which serves as the support for sentient beings.
If the fruit of reliance were to increase, one would lose that which is relied upon, and the primary retribution could not be established.
Now, it is the same for the Bodhisattva: these ten dharmas serve as the fruits of reliance upon which he dwells.

If this were to be severed, one would lose their basis and would no longer be a bodhisattva; just as one who forgets the bodhicitta is no longer a bodhisattva, the text therefore takes "not forgetting" as the means to establish this point.
Within these ten [categories], each first presents the name and subsequently explains the meaning.

The first sentence is the general heading; because the bodhicitta is the root of all practices, it alone is established at the beginning of the two thousand [items]. This means that only by relying on this unforgetting bodhicitta can all other practices be made to grow and flourish.
Second, although one may possess a superior mind within, if there is no virtuous friend without, one's practice will not reach fulfillment.
If one does not accord with them, the virtuous friend has rendered no service; thus, it would not constitute a fruit of reliance.
Therefore, it must be explained through the principle of conformity and harmony that this constitutes the fruit of reliance.

Third, although one may encounter virtuous friends, if one lacks roots of goodness from the past, one will be unable to practice in accordance with them; furthermore, because of other obstacles such as illness, one must rely on past goodness to further increase new practices.
Fourth, although one may possess past roots of goodness, if one does not obtain the dharmas of the various practices of the perfections (pāramitās), there will be nothing to cultivate.

Fifth, although one may obtain the practice of the dharmas, if one does not penetrate the principle that all dharmas are empty and pervasive, then one will encounter obstacles at every turn; therefore, by relying on [the realization that] all dharmas are [empty], one attains liberation.
Sixth, although one may attain the principles of the Dharma, if there is no great vow, one will stagnate in quiescence and fail to increase one's bodhi.
Seventh, although one possesses the practices of one's own level, if there is no superior progress and extensive cultivation, there is no way to reach the ultimate goal.

Eighth, although one may internally possess both practices, one must externally rely upon a superior companion; for a Bodhisattva in their final birth serves as an elder brother or senior to other Bodhisattvas, and only then is he fit to be relied upon—this is stated according to the ultimate case.
Ninth, although one relies upon a bodhisattva, it is logically appropriate to offer worship to the Buddha in order to establish firm faith.

Tenth, the Tathāgata alone is the ultimate object of reliance, because he can provide correct instruction that causes one to abandon errors, because he can provide authentic instruction, and because his instruction is free from error.

In the fourth section, which praises excellence and encourages study, it is stated that because Bodhisattvas dwelling in these ten dharmas shall likewise attain that [result], the Buddha takes the wisdom of the unsurpassed fruit as the "fruit of reliance. This is what is meant.
Another explanation:
A bodhisattva never fails to rely on the bodhicitta, because they never forget it.
Second, a bodhisattva never fails to rely on virtuous friends, because they always follow them and remain in harmony with them.
Third, the bodhisattva never fails to rely upon roots of goodness, because they constantly nurture them.
The others should be understood by analogy in this same way.

Second, regarding the ten extraordinary conceptions (*daśa-vicitra-saṃjñā*): previously, one established all practices by relying on causes and conditions; now, one gathers roots of goodness by relying on these superior conceptions.
Among these ten, the first is called "extraordinary" because one takes the roots of goodness from others as one's own roots of goodness through sympathetic joy.
The second is called "seed" because the virtues of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are all capable of attaining Buddhahood.
Third, even those who have descended to the level of icchantikas are all vessels for bodhi, because they all possess buddha-nature.
Fourth, it is because the vows of all bodhisattvas are identical to one's own vow.
Fifth, it is because the nature of all dharmas is pure and is not subject to birth-and-death.
Sixth, because others are of the same substance as oneself, the actions of others are immediately one's own actions.
Furthermore, because what others practice is the dharma that one practices oneself, the notion of "self" arises.
Seventh, because all dharmas are precisely suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, because all dharmas are capable of realizing enlightenment, they are called "Buddha-dharma.
Because all speech is capable of functioning as the Wheel of Dharma, it is called the "Path."
Ninth, one knows that the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas are the very essence and constituent parts of the compassion of all Buddhas; therefore, they are called "loving fathers.
Tenth, one knows that all Tathāgatas are of one and the same body; therefore, they are said to be "non-dual."
These ten all transcend conceptualizations beyond the ordinary; therefore, they are called "extraordinary.

If one attains these conceptualizations, one immediately attains the ability to transform all phenomena, for all phenomena follow conceptualization in their transformation—this is the virtue of the Buddha.
Third, regarding the ten types of practitioners: because they initiate these great practices based on the understanding of superior conceptions (*adhimukti*), they are explained next.

Among the ten, the first four are the practices of ethical discipline (*śīla*): therein, the first two are the precepts for gathering sentient beings (*sattvasaṃgrahaśīla*), the next one is the precept of restraint (*saṃvaraśīla*), and the last one is the precept for gathering wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharmasaṃgrahaśīla*).
The next one is the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Next are two practices of wisdom: first, the practice of application; second, the practice of correct realization.
Next is one practice of adorning the Buddha-fields;
finally are two practices of repaying kindness.
Fourth, regarding the ten spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*): because the practice must necessarily rely upon virtuous friends for its arising, they are explained next.

The first causes one to generate a firm resolve; the second causes one to practice and cultivate goodness; the third causes one to fulfill the practices of the perfections (*pāramitā*); the fourth causes one to attain the practice of wisdom; the fifth causes one to perfect the practice of compassion; the sixth causes one to possess the conduct of eloquence; the seventh is the practice free from attachment; the eighth is the practice free from weariness; the ninth is the practice that becomes universal; and the tenth is the entry into the Buddha-wisdom.

Fifth, regarding the ten types of diligence: although one may encounter virtuous friends, if one does not exert oneself with earnest application, there is no way to progress; therefore, this is explained next.
The intent here is: for what purpose is this diligence cultivated?
Desiring to perform these ten kinds of activities,
"entering into all phenomena therein" refers to entry through the realization of wisdom.
"Causing sentient beings to extinguish evil" refers to extinguishing the causes of their suffering.
The remainder is clear from the text.
Sixth, regarding the ten types of right aspiration: because of the preceding diligence, one aspires for oneself and others to bring their practice to completion; therefore, this is explained next.
Among these, the first one pertains to the basis of practice;
the next two pertain to the abandonment of faults;
and the final two pertain to the accomplishment of practice—the first being the cause of practice and the second being the fruit of practice.

The next three [categories] concern realization and entry: first, the stage of realization; second, the dharma realized; and third, the path of realization—meaning that one is free from slander by virtue of realizing the dharma.
The final two concern the superior progress toward the fruit of Buddhahood: first, the fulfillment of the Buddha’s vows; and second, the perfection of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "aspiring for the unsurpassed, equal great wisdom": it is called "equal" because the stage of Buddhahood is effortless (*anābhoga*);
it is also called "aspiration" because it embraces sentient beings without end.
Seventh, regarding the ten dharmas that bring sentient beings to maturity, there are two meanings:
first, these ten dharmas are applied universally to mature all sentient beings; second, each is applied individually to mature a specific class of sentient beings.

Among these, there are ten types: first, sentient beings who are stingy and greedy and thus impoverished; second, arrogant sentient beings; third, deluded sentient beings; fourth, stubborn and recalcitrant sentient beings; fifth, sentient beings who crave and cling; sixth, sentient beings who delight in the Two Vehicles; seventh, sentient beings who do not weary of the mundane world; eighth, sentient beings who do not aspire to the fruit of Buddhahood; ninth, sentient beings who take refuge in false objects; and tenth, sentient beings with false wisdom who are crafty and sly.
By means of these ten dharmas, one teaches and transforms beings in their respective order, causing them to enter the Way; therefore, they are said to be "accomplished.

Eighth, regarding those who possess the ten precepts: because they rely on the aforementioned ten dharmas to bring sentient beings to accomplishment, there is no evil they do not abandon and no goodness they do not accumulate; thus, they are explained next.

Among these ten, the first is that if one loses or destroys the bodhicitta, it constitutes a breach of the bodhisattva precepts; even the tenth, if one grasps at or becomes attached to the body of the Tathāgata, constitutes a violation of the precepts. The others should be understood accordingly.
These ten [virtues], as appropriate, are subsumed within the three aggregates (*tri-rāśi*).

Regarding the ninth, the ten kinds of self-knowledge of receiving the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*): based on the previously established virtues of being free from faults, one personally verifies that one's own practice will certainly result in the attainment of the fruit. Thus, it is called "self-knowledge of receiving the prophecy."
First, one verifies for oneself that the bodhicitta never turns back;
second, one verifies for oneself that there is no weariness in the bodhisattva’s practice of asceticism;
third, one considers even many eons of cultivation as if they were but a brief moment.
Fourth, because one personally verifies that one does not contradict the Buddha’s teachings;
fifth, because one personally knows that one has attained decisive faith in the profound Dharma spoken by the Buddha;
sixth, because one personally knows that the roots of goodness one has cultivated are entirely complete.
Seventh, one knows for oneself that one can cause sentient beings to abide in the bodhicitta;
eighth, one knows for oneself that one does not contravene the instructions of virtuous friends, sharing the same roots of goodness as they do, such as Sudhana and others;
ninth, one knows for oneself that one has perfected the perception of virtuous friends as Buddhas.
Tenth, because they maintain the great vow for bodhi and never forget it;
when one observes oneself as possessing even one of these ten practices, one knows that one will certainly receive the prophecy of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is stated that a bodhisattva receives the prophecy of Buddhahood by way of six characteristics:
First, the stage of abiding in the lineage before generating the resolve;
second, the stage after having generated the resolve;
third, the stage of manifest abiding.
Fourth, abiding without manifest presence;
fifth, having a fixed temporal limit, meaning that enlightenment is realized within a specific duration;
sixth, lacking a fixed temporal limit, meaning that no time limit is specified for the bestowal of the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Furthermore, the *Śīla-sūtra* states: "It is not only those of noble lineage (*gotra*) who receive the prediction [of enlightenment]; even those without noble lineage may receive it.
The commentary explains:

Just as the Bodhisattva Asaṃkīrṇa (Not-Light) paid respect to the fourfold assembly and bestowed predictions upon them, this was because he considered that even those without noble lineage would eventually attain it; therefore, they too received the prediction.
As recorded in the Ten Faiths, these are persons of the lineage (*gotra*), because they are determined by virtue of their lineage.
Just as those who have already resolved their minds (*cittotpāda*) are certain not to regress, so too are these [stages] the three levels of the virtuous aids (*tri-śuklāṅga*).
This is as stated in the sixth fascicle of the *Liang* [translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*]: "The Bodhisattvas of the ten practices are those who receive the prediction.
Because they have realized the principle and achieved perfection from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, they receive the prediction, as explained in the *Dilun*.
Just as in the eighth stage one receives a prediction because the practice of effortlessness has been perfected— as in the case of receiving a prediction from Dīpaṃkara Buddha—
these ten types, according to the Perfect Teaching, apply throughout all stages;
yet from the perspective of the beginning, they reside within the ten levels of faith.
The remaining meanings are as explained elsewhere.
The above ninety phrases conclude the explanation of the practice of self-benefit.
Below, from the second section beginning with "ten kinds of entry," eighty phrases distinguish the practice of superior progress.
Regarding the first ten entries therein: once one's own stage of practice has been accomplished, the next clarifies superior progress, entering into all the places that are to be entered.
"Entering" (入) means to realize or to attain.

1. Entering the great vows and practices; 2. Entering the eighty-four thousand clusters of Dharma and so forth; 3. Entering the ten perfections and so forth; 4. Entering the perfection of the stages of practice, hence "endowed with"; 5. Entering the distinct great vows; 6. Realizing and entering true nature; 7. Entering the adornment of buddha-fields; 8. Manifesting spiritual powers according to the minds [of beings]; 9. Entering all worlds to manifest birth.

Second, regarding the ten types of profound entry into the Tathāgata: the preceding section clarified the objective realm of the cause for entry; the present section clarifies the progressively superior objective realm of the fruit of entry.
The first [type] demonstrates the attainment of *bodhi*; the next eight demonstrate the transformation and guidance through the three wheels; and the final one demonstrates the entry into *nirvāṇa*.

Among the first eight, the initial four concern verbal action: first, the general presentation of the Wheel of Dharma; second, the skillful means of the Dharma being turned; third, the sublime voice of the one who turns it; and fourth, the correct training of sentient beings. The next two concern bodily action:
first, manifesting supernatural powers based on the body; and second, manifesting many diverse bodies. The final two concern mental action:
first, meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and second, wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, because all Buddhas of the three periods of time likewise perform such activities, it is said that they "also enter together.
Within this faith, one also attains this Dharma because it is the aspect of Samantabhadra’s practice within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Third, there are ten kinds of entering into the mental activities of sentient beings. Whereas the preceding section concerned entering the realm of the Buddhas, this section distinguishes the downward entry into sentient beings.
The first three [points] generally clarify the entry into the mental activities of sentient beings across the three periods of time;
the subsequent two specifically address the entry into sentient beings who are virtuous or non-virtuous.
Sixth, penetrating the mental activities of those who delight in sensual pleasures;
seventh, penetrating the sharpness or dullness of their faculties;
eighth, penetrating the distinctions among their spiritual lineages.
Ninth, the lightness or heaviness of the afflictions;

tenth, the difference in the arousal of remedies, meaning that for those whose faculties are not yet matured, one must wait for the time [of maturity], whereas for those whose faculties are already matured, one does not wait for the time.
Another explanation states:
"Appropriate time" refers to taming [beings] by waiting for the time when they are ripe; "inappropriate time" refers to awakening them through skillful means without waiting for such a time.
Furthermore, by means of these ten entrances, one universally enters into all that is identical to the fruit of Buddhahood.
Fourth, there are ten ways of entering the world: whereas previously one knew the primary retribution (*vipāka*) of sentient beings, now one knows their secondary retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
Among these, the first two concern defilement and purity;
the next four concern the coarse and the subtle.
The next two [postures] concern their shape: "prostrate" means facing downward, while "upturned" means facing upward;
the final two concern the presence or absence of a Buddha.
Furthermore, the phrase "universally entering all" is because one does not depart from these ten.
Fifth, there are ten kinds of entering the *kalpa*. While the previous section clarified the locus of entry, the present section distinguishes the timing of entry.
Within this, the first five concern entering individual *kalpas*, while the latter five concern entering encompassing *kalpas*.
Regarding the preceding section: the first three [phrases] separately enter the three time-periods (trikalpa); the next two separately enter many or few kalpas.
Within the latter five [phrases] concerning mutual inclusion: the first uses the few to include the many, hence it says "countable" and "uncountable";
the second uses the many to include the few.
Third, by subsuming phenomena into principle, kalpas enter non-kalpas;
fourth, by arising phenomena from principle, non-kalpas enter kalpas;

fifth, the two phenomena are mutually identical—meaning that "countable" and so forth refer to the gate of mutual dependence in dependent origination, while "non-kalpa" and so forth refer to the gate of the interpenetration of the nature of dharmas.
That all these kalpas are but a single thought-moment is because they are universally encompassed by the two gates [of time and space] in unimpeded mastery.
Furthermore, because they are all manifestations of the consciousness of enumeration, one attains such mastery.

Sixth, regarding the ten ways of explaining the three periods of time (*tryadhvan*): the former [section] was based on *kalpas*, whereas this section is based on the periods themselves; therefore, it is explained here.
Within this, the first nine are specific explanations, while the last one is a general manifestation.
Regarding the distinction within this, it is said that the future is inexhaustible because it continues to arise; why then is it not the same for the past?
Explanation:
It is called "inexhaustible" because the future arises in succession.
Because the past does not arise, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, when the present speaks of the present, it is no different from the present itself; thus it is called "equality.
When the past and future speak of the past and future, why should they not likewise be the same?
Commentary:
Because the past and future are non-existent as such, while the present exists, they are not the same.
Other meanings are explained as analyzed in the "Chapter on the Ten Times."

Seventh, there are ten kinds of entry into the three periods of time. Since it was previously established that one has attained unimpeded mastery over time and kalpas, this section now clarifies the entry into the phenomena within those times; therefore, it is explained next.
Among these, the first one generally clarifies that which is entered, while the remaining nine specifically clarify that which is entered.
Herein, the first takes language as the path, because it reveals the meaning to be expressed.
The second is "nature" (*svabhāva*), which refers to the nature of syllables; "class" (*jāti*) refers to the phonemic bases (*dhātu*) and so forth.
The third is "designation" (*prajñapti*), because it is a conventional designation through verbal instruction.

The fourth is "perception" (*saṃjñā*), which refers to establishing names and so forth based on perception; this is synonymous with "name" (*nāman*) and the like, as the treatise states: "Abhidharma has perception as its defining characteristic," and so forth.
The fifth, "names" (*nāman*), correctly reveals the bodies of phrases, sentences, and syllables.
The sixth, "speech" (*vāk*), clarifies vocal sound as vocal karma.
If one asks how this differs from the former [category], the former establishes that which expresses, whereas this includes all instances generally, such as sounds like *a*, *e*, and so forth.
The seventh, "inexhaustibility," clarifies that all the aforementioned gates are merely provisional designations, for they have no end.
The eighth, "freedom from desire," is because their essence cannot be apprehended.
The ninth is "quiescence," because its nature is pure.
It is said that these ten dharmas all pass through the three periods of time—past, present, and future—and therefore they are called "entering the three worlds."
Another explanation:
the preceding "path of linguistic expression" refers to the phenomena that are expressed, for it is the path traversed by language;
the second nature, which is the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), is also what is expressed, as this is the realm of principles (*yukti*).
The next four are the world of verbal expression;
the final three are the world of ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).
Another interpretation states:

Among the ten [categories], the first is the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*); the next six are the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*); and the final three are the world of the perfectly awakened ones of wisdom (*jñāna-samyaksambuddha-loka*).
Although there are three interpretations, the first interpretation accords with the text.

Eighth, regarding the ten kinds of abandoning sorrow and affliction: since one has already attained understanding of the nature of time and phenomena and has initiated practice to gather the mind, one is thus free from sorrow and the like.
This means that as one’s practice succeeds and one’s aspirations are fulfilled, one abandons sorrow and affliction; time is not spent in vain, and the mind is free from weariness or regret.
Among these, the first four—making offerings to the Buddha, associating with spiritual friends, seeking the Dharma, and hearing the Dharma—are practices for one’s own benefit.

The subsequent three concern the gathering of sentient beings: first, preaching the Dharma; second, disciplining them so they may leave behind transgressions; and third, causing them to abide in the path of the Buddha.
Next, one section clarifies the extensiveness of self-cultivation;
next, one section distinguishes the extensiveness of transforming others;
finally, one section clarifies how the fulfillment of these two practices gives rise to the fruit of Buddhahood.
The preceding eighty phrases conclude the explanation of the superior progress within the section on clear understanding.
From here on, the third section—consisting of thirty phrases beginning with "ten kinds of indestructible wisdom"—clarifies the culmination of the previous two practices.
Regarding the first ten kinds of indestructible knowledge among them: it is called "indestructible" because one knows in accordance with reality (*yathābhūta*) without further alteration.

Among these, knowing sentient beings and so forth refers to defiled phenomena (*saṃkliṣṭadharma*); knowing the Three Jewels and so forth refers to purified phenomena (*vyavadānadharma*); knowing worlds and so forth refers to that which is both defiled and purified; and knowing the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) refers to that which is neither defiled nor purified—all of this may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the second [category], the ten kinds of *dhāraṇī*: since it was previously stated that one knows the dharmas without impairment, this clarifies that one maintains the dharmas without loss.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* takes concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence; the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* take superior mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom as its nature. This is because wisdom illuminates the dharmas, while mindfulness recollects and maintains them.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, "samādhi" is correctly translated as "holding" (*dharana*), because it can hold various wholesome dharmas so that they are not lost, like water held in an intact vessel.
Alternatively, it is called "obstructing" (*vāraṇa*), because it can obstruct various unwholesome states of mind and prevent them from arising.
In works such as the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there are four types—namely, dharma, meaning, mantra, and patience—which cannot be subsumed within these ten categories because their classifications differ.
Among these, the first two uphold the Dharma of teaching: the first upholds the Sūtra-dharma and the second upholds the Abhidharma-dharma;
the third upholds the Dharma of principle;
and the fourth upholds the Dharma of wisdom.
5. Retaining the dharmas of meditative concentration;
6. Retaining the languages of different regions;
7. Retaining the diverse meanings of the three periods of time.
Eighth, the dharma of maintaining eloquence;
ninth, the dharma of maintaining the unimpeded faculty of hearing;
tenth, the dharma of maintaining the fruit.
"Abiding securely" means being in accord with [the Dharma].
Regarding the third section, which distinguishes and explains the ten Buddhas: previously, the upholding of the Dharma was clarified; now, the understanding of the Buddhas is being analyzed.
Furthermore, because one attains the fruit of Buddhahood upon the fulfillment of this faith, it is called "clarity" (*vidyā*).
If that is so, since one also attains the fruit of Buddhahood when the subsequent stage of liberation is fulfilled, why is it not called "clarity"?
Commentary:
Because faith is primary, the understanding follows from this.
These ten meanings of the Buddha are fully detailed in a separate chapter; here, I shall briefly explain their names.
First, spontaneous awakening is called Right Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), and Right Enlightenment is the Buddha;
second, the fulfillment of the unimpeded great vows inherent in one's own essence—vows are themselves the Buddha;
third, because it is induced by the causes of myriad practices, it is termed karmic retribution.
Fourth, it is formed by the accumulation of forty thousand virtues and maintains them without loss;
fifth, it manifests transformations in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings;
sixth, it is universally pervasive in accord with principle.
Seventh, it is manifested solely by the mind;
eighth, it is eternally and constantly in meditative concentration;
ninth, its true nature is unchanging.
The ten great functions of non-exertion are called the Wish-Fulfilling Buddha, like the maṇi jewel and so forth.
Furthermore, it is explained:
this should be understood by applying the same interpretation as that used for the ten ways of seeing the Buddha mentioned below.
The preceding two hundred phrases answer the previous twenty questions, clarifying that the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) and the ten practices (*caryā*) have reached full maturity.

From here on, the second major section—beginning from "The Tenfold Arousing of the Mind of Samantabhadra"—contains two hundred phrases that answer the previous twenty questions regarding the methods of practice within the ten abidings (*vihāra*).
Within this, there is a rough division into four parts:
first, sixty phrases that specifically clarify the meaning of the first stage, the Stage of Resolving the Mind (*prathamacittotpāda*), among the ten stages of understanding (*daśavihāra*);
second, from "The Ten Perfections" (*daśapāramitā*) downward, sixty phrases that clarify the internal virtuous practices accomplished within the remaining nine stages.

3. From the "Ten Kinds of Teaching the Dharma" downward, thirty phrases clarify the practices for gathering and transforming sentient beings through external transformation during the various stages (*vihāra*).
4. From the "Ten Kinds of Supreme Dharmas" downward, fifty phrases clarify the unimpeded and extraordinary practices.

Regarding the first section: having newly attained the stage of abiding, one takes the great mind as the foundation; therefore, at the very outset, one clarifies the arousal of the Universal Worthy (Samantabhadra) mind.

Within this, the first three [verses] concern the mind that rescues and protects sentient beings below; the next three concern the mind that seeks the fruit of Buddhahood above; and the final four concern the mind of weary detachment from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Possessing these three minds is what is termed the Great Bodhicitta.
Another explanation is as follows:
the first six [aspects] protect the mind of the Hīnayāna; therein, the first three protect the narrow mind and the latter three protect the small mind.
The remaining four protect the mind of afflictions. For these reasons, it differs from that of ordinary beings and the Hīnayāna, and is thus called the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, these ten minds each constitute a distinct practice and do not subsume one another, thereby manifesting their inexhaustibility.
Each is first indicated and subsequently explained, as can be understood.

Regarding the second point, the ten kinds of Samantabhadra’s methods of vow and practice: this refers to the arising of extensive vows and practices based on the aforementioned great mind; therefore, they are explained next.
Within this, the first nine [sections] have broad cultivation of causes, while the final one has broad realization of the fruit; this is because Samantabhadra encompasses both cause and fruit.

Among the former, the first two concern the broadness of self-cultivation, the next one concerns the broadness of benefiting others, and the remainder concern the broadness of both practices. Because all of these extensively establish great and limitless vows, they are collectively termed the "Vows of Samantabhadra. Since practice is accomplished in reliance upon these vows, they are called the "Dharma of Vow and Practice" (*praṇidhāna-caryā-dharma*).

Regarding the "three kinds of tenfold great compassion," this is distinguished separately from within the previously mentioned *Samantabhadra-caryā* practices; it is explained next because of its profound importance.
Therefore, the treatise states: "Because the Bodhisattva takes great compassion as his foundation," it is specifically elucidated.
Employing this compassionate mind, one contemplates sentient beings without ever ceasing for even a moment; hence it is called "constant observation.
Within this, there are two aspects: first, they are oppressed by suffering and have no refuge;
second, even if they seek a reliance, they mistakenly turn to heterodox paths.
Third, even if they wish to turn toward the Right, they are impoverished by a lack of past roots of goodness;
fourth, even if they possess minor virtues, they are attached to birth and death and cannot awaken;
fifth, even if they wish to seek awakening, they act only perversely and unwholesomely.
Sixth, even if one cultivates goodness, one cannot transcend desire;
seventh, even if one seeks to transcend desire, one returns once more to saṃsāra;
eighth, one is afflicted by beginningless ignorance from long ago.
Ninth, not desiring the causes of Buddhahood;
tenth, losing the dharmas of the fruit of Buddhahood.
Another explanation states:
Among these ten, the first two concern sentient beings who are inverted: first, those who lack the true; second, those who pursue the false.

The next four concern sentient beings who seek [desire-realm existence]: first, those lacking the cause for transcendence; second, those lacking the fruit of transcendence; third, those possessing the causes of bondage; fourth, those abiding in the fruits of bondage.
The final two concern sentient beings who seek [existence-realm existence]: first, those who are deep [in ignorance]; second, those who are far [from liberation].
Regarding the latter two types of seekers of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), there are those who seek by way of heterodox paths and those who seek a heterodox liberation.
It is with these beings as objects that the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), vowing to rescue and deliver them.

Regarding the four types of ten causes and conditions for generating the mind [of enlightenment]: since the arousal of compassion, vows, and practice must necessarily rely upon their respective causes, they are explained next.
Furthermore, while the preceding section clarified the essence of the generated mind, this section distinguishes the causes for generating that mind.
Alternatively, there are four conditions for the arousal of the bodhicitta, as described in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, and other texts;
or there are seven conditions, as described in the *Jñānamudrā-sūtra*, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, and other texts.
This is as previously explained.
Now, ten conditions are revealed to clarify inexhaustibility.
Among them, the first five below take sentient beings as their condition, while the latter five above take the fruit of Buddhahood as their condition.
The Treatise states: "The Bodhisattva takes the bodhisattva as the object of focus (*ālambana*). This is precisely what is meant.
Among the first five [categories], the first is general and the latter four are specific.
Within the distinct [categories], the first two exclude suffering and pleasure; the latter two exclude ignorance and wisdom.
Within the latter five, the first is general while the latter four are specific.
Among these specifics, the first two accord with the teachings and their characteristics, while the latter two accord with the meaning and manifest its virtues.
The remaining meanings may be understood.

Regarding the fifth point, the ten kinds of drawing near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*): once the resolve has been generated, it is logically appropriate to draw near to spiritual friends and possess the bodhicitta so that it may increase; therefore, this is explained next.
Another explanation:

These fifty preceding categories of practice are all simultaneous; yet they are described as having a sequence because it is only by relying on a spiritual friend that one is able to generate the aspiration for enlightenment and so forth.
Within this, there are five parts:
first, the statement of the intent; second, the inquiry; third, the general explanation; fourth, the detailed analysis; and fifth, the summary of the number.
Within the ten items of the detailed analysis, the first is bodily action as service.
Second, their speech accords with the instructions;
third, their minds are not discordant;
fourth, both body and mind are joyful, as they also rejoice at seeing virtuous friends.
Fifth, their five sensory desires are free from seeking;
sixth, they aspire solely to the path leading out of suffering;
seventh, they share the same superior conduct.
Eighth, they share the same formal commitment;
ninth, they revere their teacher as a Buddha;
tenth, they equally achieve the perfection of the fruit.
Furthermore, of the ten types of friends, the first six are those with whom one practices together, while the latter four are those who practice in concert.
Regarding the ten kinds of purity possessed by these six, it is because, based on the previously mentioned resolve for enlightenment, they attain this pure retribution.
This is the proximate fruit of the family that generates the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
Within this, the first six [verses] clarify the purity of the three types of action (*karman*): namely, the purity of essence in the first three and the purity of function in the latter three.
Following that, from "Retinue" (*parivāra*) onwards, the next two clarify the purity of the companion and the master.
The final two [verses] clarify the purity of aspiration and practice;
both may be understood accordingly.
Thus concludes the detailed explanation of the first stage (*bhūmi*).

The second section below, consisting of sixty phrases starting from "the ten perfections" (*daśa-pāramitā*), generally clarifies the internal virtues accomplished during the remaining stages (*vihāra*).

Within this, the first ten lines specifically clarify the practices performed during each stage; therein, the ten perfections are all explained in terms of their profound and superior nature. Consequently, under the perfection of giving (*dāna*), it does not mention the relinquishing of wealth and so forth, but rather speaks of "relinquishing all existence" (*sarva-bhava-tyāga*).
It should be understood that [the remaining perfections] include purifying the Buddha’s precepts, possessing the Buddha’s patience, and so forth.
The sixth, *prajñā* (wisdom), pertains to the wisdom of the fundamental essence (*mūla-jñāna*), and therefore takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.
The final four are for the most part all subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
The seventh should be named "Skillful Means" (*upāya*), because it is able to enter deeply into the power of the Buddha; thus, the name "Wisdom" (*jñāna*) is established for it.
The tenth should be named "Wisdom," because it is able to encompass all the Buddha-dharmas; its name is derived from its object.
The rest is as previously explained in the section on the ten bases of practice.

Regarding the second point, the "ten factors conducive to realization": because they are accomplished through the preceding practices, one is able to realize the objects of knowledge without error; therefore, they are called "factors conducive to realization."
Within this, first, one knows the many gates of distinction between the defiled and pure aspects of the dependent retribution;
second, one knows the inconceivable diversity of the primary retribution of sentient beings;
third, one knows that the phenomena of dependent origination are neither identical nor different and abide nowhere.
Fourth, knowing that the *dharmadhātu* of *tathatā* is equal and free from characteristics;
fifth, knowing that space is unconditioned and boundless;
sixth, seventh, and eighth, knowing the worlds of the three periods of time, and further knowing that all are equally of the past, present, and future.
Ninth, knowing that all Buddhas possess the ten thousand practices within a single thought-moment;
tenth, knowing that all Buddhas share the same practice throughout the three periods of time.
Regarding these "ten determinate knowledges," they are achieved because one attains this determinate wisdom through the aforementioned compliant and non-erroneous realization.
Among these, the first two know phenomena with clarity.
First, "knowing within a single thought-moment" reveals the swiftness of their cognition.
Second, "knowing through unimpeded wisdom" reveals the mastery of their cognition.
Because there is no cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is said to be "unimpeded.
Next, the five [knowledges] know sentient beings:
first, knowing their mental inclinations and desires.
Second, knowing that the faculty of knowledge is identical to true nature, it is likewise identical to the root of bodhi.
Third, knowing the subtle habitual tendencies of afflictions.
Fourth, knowing the activity of the primary motivating forces.
The fifth [knowledge] is knowing whether those to be converted are virtuous or non-virtuous.
Regarding the latter three [knowledges], they concern the Bodhisattvas and Buddhas; it appears one section is missing, so consult other editions.
As for the fourth [section], the Ten Powers (*daśabala*): because wisdom is already definitive, there is great capability, and thus these are explained as "powers."
Among these, the first is general while the remaining nine are specific.
Within the specific ones, the first two explain the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as being like an illusion or a magical transformation;
the third explains the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Fourth, because one understands that the nature of what is grasped is emptiness, there is no defilement;
fifth, seeking the practice of the Dharma;
sixth, the power of revering and supporting virtuous friends, for it is from them that one obtains the Dharma, and thus the power of seeking remains unimpaired.
Seventh, by the power of dedication, one is able to cause roots of virtue to reach the fruit of Buddhahood;
eighth, by the power of resolute belief, one is able to avoid slandering the profound Buddha-dharma;
ninth, the mind seeking the great fruit is firm and does not retreat.
Another explanation is as follows:
the first five are the powers of understanding (*jñāna-bala*), and the latter five are the powers of practice (*caryā-bala*).

Regarding the ten kinds of equality within these five: since one possesses the capability of intellectual power, one is able to perform the true contemplation of equality regarding all phenomena; therefore, they are explained next.

Within this, there are ten points: first, the severance of feelings regarding enemies and kin; second, the single flavor of the ultimate and the conventional; third, the equalization of the principles of defilement and purity; fourth, the non-duality of the single path; fifth, the common convergence upon one nature; sixth, how the dharmas of the fruit could possibly differ; seventh, the absence of divergent vows as causes; eighth, the simultaneous perfection of the ten perfections; ninth, conduct that accords with the fundamental source of principle; and tenth, the equality and non-duality of the dharma-body.
Another explanation:

regarding the first five "equalities," first is equality of compassion, second is equality of wisdom, third is equality of purity, fourth is equality of practice, and fifth is equality of cultivation;

regarding the latter five "virtues" and so forth, first is the equality of the fruit-virtue, second is the equality of vows and practices, third is the equality of the six perfections, fourth is the equality of causal practices, and fifth is the equality of the Dharma-body.

Regarding the ten kinds of skillful means as phrases of the Buddha-dharma: since one has already realized the principle through the equality of direct realization, it is appropriate to subsequently give rise to skillful means and establish the teachings; therefore, they are explained next.
Within this, first, knowing that all phenomena are merely verbal designations refers to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).

Second, appearing as if real like an illusion; third, quickly perishing like lightning; fourth, lacking intrinsic nature while arising from conditions; fifth, being originally pure by virtue of conditions; sixth, verbal existence being merely a name—these above points refer to the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).

Seventh, the truth of non-arising; eighth, the truth of signlessness; ninth, the truth of the nature of lack of intrinsic nature—these above points refer to the *śūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha* (the emptiness of the tathāgatagarbha).
The ten dharmadhātus endowed with excellence constitute the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Because these ten meanings are revealed through the phrases of the Buddha-dharma, they are collectively given this name.
The preceding section on the accomplishment of internal virtues is concluded.
The third section below, "Ten Kinds of Teaching the Dharma," contains thirty phrases that clarify the practices for externally transforming and gathering sentient beings.
Within this, the first ten concern the ability to expound the teachings; the next ten concern the ability to uphold the Dharma; and the final ten concern the ability to discern the words.
Within the first ten [verses], the first two explain the Dharma of Principle—one profound and one subtle;

the next four explain the Dharma of Practice—namely, the dharma of possessing virtues, the dharma of Buddha-wisdom, the dharma of conforming to the [six] perfections, and the dharma of producing the fruit;

the final four explain the Dharma of Cause and Effect, where the first explains the cause and effect of defiled dharmas across the three periods of time, and the latter three explain the cause and effect of pure dharmas, as should be understood.
Regarding the "ten kinds of upholding" mentioned secondly: since the former were proclaimed verbally, these are now stored within the mind; therefore, they are explained next.
Within this, the first seven concern the dharmas that record causes, while the latter three concern the dharmas that record results.
Regarding the preceding section, there are three types: first, the retention of the practice of the Dharma;
second, the retention of the teaching of the Dharma;
and third, the retention of the analogies that accord with the Dharma.
Fourth, the method for skillfully producing understanding;
fifth, the method for producing dhāraṇīs, which refers to such things as condensing many meanings into few words;
sixth, the method for answering difficult questions and severing doubts.
The seventh is the dharma of the stages of the bodhisattva’s practice.

Among the latter three, the first is the dharma of the Buddha’s concentration, the second is the dharma of the Buddha’s wisdom, and the third is the dharma of the Buddha’s supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Regarding the ten kinds of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), while the former clarified that they are maintained in the mind through mindfulness, the present passage clarifies their skillful proclamation through speech.

Among these, first, it is called "eloquence" (vāda) because it does not grasp at emotional attachments; this means that if one remains attached to inherent nature, then even if one employs a hundred forms of clever speech, it is not yet sufficient to be considered eloquence.
Second, it accords with the Dharma and is without activity.
Third, it manifests the Dharma of non-attachment.
Fourth, this eloquence is itself empty, only then constituting true eloquence;
fifth, its essence is free from ignorance;
sixth, its eloquence is identical to that maintained by the Buddha.
Seventh, the eloquence that enables others to awaken through the teaching of the Dharma;
eighth, skillfully employing names and phrases to explain phenomena that are ultimately nameless and signless, so that others do not mistake the words for the reality they denote;
ninth, the eloquence that explains the various categories of meaning concerning sentient beings.
The former corresponds to the eloquence that delights beings according to their capacities.

Furthermore, the first five constitute the eloquence of purification through non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-viśuddhi-pratibhāna*), while the latter five constitute the eloquence of purification through action (*sabhisaṃskāra-viśuddhi-pratibhāna*).
Thus concludes the section on the practices for externally transforming and gathering in sentient beings.

Below the fourth section, "Explaining the Ten Kinds of Supreme Dharmas," there are fifty phrases that clarify unimpeded and extraordinary practice; these are also the practices for achieving fulfillment in this stage.

Among these, regarding the first ten "superior dharmas" (*viśeṣa-dharma*): because his eloquence was previously unimpeded, he thereby manifested a virtuous character that rose far above that of ordinary and small-vehicle practitioners; hence they are called "superior dharmas."

Among these, there are ten: first, excellence in compassion; second, excellence in wisdom; third, excellence in cultivation; fourth, excellence in conduct; fifth, excellence in precepts; sixth, excellence in dedication; seventh, excellence in diligent exertion; eighth, excellence in subduing Māra; ninth, excellence in causal practice; and tenth, excellence in the fruition.

Regarding the second [stage], which has ten [aspects] and is called "non-attachment" (*asaṅga*): because the virtues of the preceding practice have transcended and ascended, one now lacks grasping toward objects; hence it is termed "non-attachment.
Furthermore, the former refers to the excellence of the practice being lofty and sublime, while the latter refers to being free from defiled attachment below.
These ten are all manifestations of one's own mind and are produced by mental verbalization; therefore, wisdom does not cling to them.
First, it does not cling to the place of transformation;
second, it does not cling to those who are transformed.
Third, non-attachment to the phenomena of transformation;
fourth, non-attachment while correctly performing the work of transformation;
fifth, non-attachment to the virtues accomplished through transformation.
Sixth, non-attachment to taking birth in accordance with the needs of sentient beings;
seventh, non-attachment to one's own original vows;
eighth, non-attachment to the practices one performs.
Ninth, non-attachment to causes;
tenth, non-attachment to results.
By personally abiding in this wisdom of non-attachment, one is able to swiftly transform divergent thoughts and manifold perceptions, attaining the Buddha’s unsurpassed, non-attached wisdom.

Regarding the third [set], the ten minds of equanimity: because they accomplish non-attached wisdom, the mind is free from discrimination amidst all phenomena; hence they are called "minds of equanimity."
If one asks how this differs from the ten types of equality mentioned previously:
the former distinguishes equality in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), while this distinguishes it in terms of mind; hence it is called "the mind of equality.
Within this, the first eight concern equality in terms of causes, and the latter two concern equality in terms of results.

Regarding the preceding [section], there are eight: first, with respect to that which is nurtured; second, with respect to the speech uttered; third, with respect to the beings to be converted; fourth, with respect to the causes and effects for those to be converted; fifth, with respect to the dharmas to be known; sixth, with respect to the defiled and pure lands; seventh, with respect to people of good and bad character; and eighth, with respect to the practices performed.
Regarding the latter two, the first is the wisdom of merit and the second is the wisdom of correct realization.
Because one does not give rise to divergent thoughts regarding these ten, it is called the "mind of equanimity."
Regarding the four kinds of wisdom that arise in ten ways: it is said that from the prior state of the quiescent, equal essence, there arises the subsequent superior wisdom.
Among these, "first entering the nature of sentient beings" refers to realizing and entering the true nature of sentient beings.
"Arising of the wisdom of the knower" refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that arises after [the wisdom of] entry.
The remaining passages regarding entry and emergence should be understood accordingly.
"The two lands are neither one nor different" is because, in terms of their essence, both are equally transcendent.

Furthermore, because the characteristics are subsumed within the substance, they are shown to be non-different; because the substance is derived from the characteristics, it is shown to be non-identical.
Moreover, since the many are one, there is no difference; since the one is the many, there is no identity.

Third, knowing that worlds are like Indra’s net; fourth, knowing the forms and characteristics of lands; fifth, skillfully entering the essence of phenomena as being neither one nor different—the three explanations regarding "identical lands" should be understood here;

sixth, knowing the retributive bodies of various classes; seventh, knowing the causes of bodies characterized by inverted delusions; eighth, knowing the ultimate penetration of the One Vehicle through both the general and the specific; ninth, knowing the virtue of mastery over the dharma-realm; tenth, knowing the virtue of the uninterrupted lineage of the Buddhas.

Regarding the ten kinds of transformations of the five [wisdoms]: the former arise based on the fundamental realization (*mūla-adhigama*), whereas the present arises based on the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) to initiate sovereign functions; therefore, they are explained next.
This means that what originally did not exist is transformed and manifested into existence; hence it is called "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*).
Within this, the first is the transformation of the bodies of other sentient beings, such as when Mañjuśrī transformed Śāriputra and others;
the second is the transformation of one's own body into various other forms.
Third, transforming defiled lands into pure ones and so forth;
fourth, manifesting fragrant flowers and so forth;
fifth, manifesting speech and sounds and so forth.
Sixth, manifesting through vows and practices;
seventh, manifesting as one who disciplines sentient beings, such as King Tuṣita and others;
eighth, manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood.
Ninth, manifesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
tenth, manifesting śarīra relics and so forth. Furthermore, another explanation states:
These ten [stages] also manifest their equality through practical application.
The preceding four sections, comprising two hundred phrases of text, complete the explanation of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*).

From this point downward, in the third major section, there are three hundred phrases following the "Ten Kinds of Sustenance" (*daśavidhadhāraṇī*), which answer thirty questions regarding the methods of practice within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
This section is divided into three parts:
first, sixty lines clarify the practice of vast and far-reaching great resolve;
second, from "Ten kinds of inconceivability" downward, ninety lines clarify the practice of the functional application of meditative concentration and wisdom.
Third, from the section on the "Ten Kinds of Groves" below, there are one hundred and fifty phrases that clarify the perfection of the practice of complete virtue.
Within this initial section, there are two parts:
first, twenty phrases clarify the practice of generating great aspiration based [on these groves]; second, forty phrases clarify the practice of generating superior mindfulness based [on them].

Regarding the ten types of upholding (*dhāraṇī*) mentioned previously: the first ten constitute the basis for the practice of upholding. This means that by relying on the power of these upholdings, one is able to give rise to great resolve.

Within this, the three types of upholding from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* and the ten types of upholding from the "Chapter on the Grounds" (*Bhūmivarga*) are comprehensively subsumed; they should be understood through comparative analysis.
Among these, the first three are sustained by the power of the Three Jewels, for sentient beings constitute the Sangha Jewel;
the fourth is called the sustenance of karma, produced by the four great compassions;

and the fifth is the power of the fifty great vows that causes practice to continue uninterrupted, which also occurs because it is sustained by the power of the Buddha, such that the transformative function of the Buddha-fruit extends to the end of the future.
Sixth is the power of practicing the sixty perfections, which sustains all that remains;
seventh is the sustaining of sentient beings and bodhi as the objects of focus, giving rise to the mind of the Bodhisattva’s practices of compassion and wisdom;
eighth is taking the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) as the sublime.
The nine blessings and the ten knowledges each possess superior power; therefore, they are called "retentions" (*dhāraṇī*).
Question:
How do these retentions differ from the ten *dhāraṇīs* and the ten kinds of "receiving and maintaining" (*parigraha*) mentioned previously?

Answer: A *dhāraṇī* is the retention of both the words and their meanings; "receiving and maintaining" (*śrutadhāraṇa*) refers to the acts of receiving, internalizing, and remembering; whereas here, it refers to empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth—thus, they are not the same.

Regarding the second point, the ten kinds of great and correct aspiration: based on the power of the aforementioned practice, one gives rise to this vast and boundless yearning; this is called "great and correct aspiration."
What is the difference between this and the previous "correct aspiration"?
The former refers to one's own level (*svabhāga*), and thus does not speak of "greatness"; the present case is based on superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*), and therefore they are not the same.
For what reason does one give rise to this great desire and vow?
This is because practice is accomplished by means of this.
As the preceding text states: "The King of Wisdom has taught that desire is the root of all dharmas.
One should give rise to pure desire and aspire to seek the unsurpassed path."

This is what is meant. Among these, the first concentration aims at following the Buddha’s will to please him; the second concentration aims at making offerings to the Buddha until they are exhausted; the third concentration aims at practicing in accordance with the Dharma together with others; the fourth concentration aims at long-term cultivation; the fifth concentration aims at being free from fear; the sixth concentration aims at causing sentient beings who have already attained Buddhahood to flourish; the seventh concentration aims at exhausting the adornment of the ocean of lands; the eighth concentration aims at causing sentient beings to extinguish the causes and effects of evil and establish the causes and effects of goodness; the ninth concentration aims at seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma with a straightforward mind; and the tenth concentration aims at turning the Great Wheel of Dharma throughout the limits of the future.

The third section contains ten types of those who deeply enter the Buddha-dharma; this clarifies that through unceasing aspiration, one is able to enter deeply. Therefore, it is said that by relying on the aforementioned great desire, one is able to exhaustively reach the profound and distant limits of the Buddha-dharma.
Within the forty phrases below, the first twenty constitute the basis (*āśraya*) and the latter twenty constitute that which arises (*utpanna*).
Within the former, these initial ten represent profound internal realization.

Among these, the first four [entrances] pertain to the Buddha-dharma of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*); because each and every individual world enters all worlds, it is said that "all worlds enter all worlds individually.
The next two pertain to the Buddha-dharma of the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*);
the final three pertain to the Buddha-dharma of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

The latter [section] generally concerns entering the Buddha-dharma from the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Because it distinguishes practice according to principle, it is said that "within non-identity and non-difference, one speaks of identity and difference. This means that while the stages of the five vehicles are distinct, attaining Buddhahood is one; since their practices are identical in their convergence toward principle, it is called "entering that which is nowhere to enter."
Regarding the "ten kinds of bases for the two [types of practice]": the former [section] revealed the profound entry into practice; here, we distinguish the conditions upon which one relies.

Among these: (1) relying on the instructions of virtuous friends; (2) relying on the power of the熏 (*vāsanā*) from extensive learning; (3) relying on a favorable dwelling where material requisites are not lacking; (4) relying on the power of compassion; (5) deeply realizing the Great Practice; (6) relying on the power of fulfilling one's original vows; (7) relying on the original bodhicitta; and (8) relying on the fruit of Buddhahood, as this is that which is sought. Thus, the ninth and tenth are excluded; one must consult other versions [of the text].

Regarding the third point, the ten kinds of generating the mind of fearlessness: since there is already the path upon which one relies, it causes the practicing mind to become profoundly superior; thus, one is able to be fearless toward things that would normally inspire fear, because there is nothing difficult to perform that one cannot perform.
Among these, the first, by virtue of exerting great heroic vigor, is able to accomplish all ten kinds of difficult tasks:

first, the difficulty of extinguishing evil karma; second, the difficulty of protecting the bequeathed Dharma; third, the difficulty of subduing Māra; fourth, the difficulty of relinquishing body and life; fifth, the difficulty of overcoming non-Buddhists; sixth, the difficulty of satisfying beings' minds with material gifts; seventh, the difficulty of pleasing the great assembly; eighth, the difficulty of disciplining the eight classes of supernatural beings; ninth, the difficulty of departing from the Lesser Vehicle; and tenth, the difficulty of cultivating superior practices. Regarding these ten difficulties, he is entirely without fear.
Furthermore, the sixth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Bodhisattva possesses four kinds of fearlessness:

first, possessing the power of hearing and retaining the teachings, he preaches them well; second, knowing the faculties and inclinations of others, he preaches so as to bring them to liberation; third, throughout all directions, he sees no one who can challenge him with a question that he cannot answer; and fourth, he sees no one who can raise a doubt that he cannot resolve."

Regarding the four types of persons who give rise to a mind free from doubt, there are ten kinds. As previously stated, because they have no fear regarding what is difficult, they know for themselves that all their undertakings are easy; therefore, they are without doubt.

Among these, first is gathering in and nurturing sentient beings through the ten perfections; second, making offerings to the Buddhas and adorning the lands; third, having no weariness in the great mind; fourth, fulfilling one's original great vows; fifth, being determined to become a lamp for the world; sixth, skillfully expounding all dharmas as being capable of gathering in and nurturing sentient beings—all of which are the Buddha-dharma; seventh, being certain to achieve perfect enlightenment; eighth, realizing that phenomena are identical to principle; and ninth, extinguishing inversions to manifest wisdom.
The preceding sixty lines clarify the completion of the practice of vast and far-reaching great resolve.

Following this, the second section, consisting of ninety lines beginning from "Ten kinds of inconceivability," clarifies the practice of the functional application of meditative concentration and wisdom.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, thirty phrases clarify the practice of transcending emotions through integrated wisdom;
second, twenty phrases beginning with "the thirteen samādhis" clarify the practice of universal pervasion through profound meditative concentration.
The forty phrases following the "Ten Dharma Gates" below clarify the practice of mastery over karmic functions.
Regarding the first section: the initial ten concern conduct, the next ten concern speech, and the final ten concern wisdom.
Regarding the ten kinds of inconceivability within the context of practice: because the preceding mind is resolute and free from doubt, that which is cultivated becomes unfathomable.

Among these, first, even a single thought-moment of roots of goodness reaches the fruit of Buddhahood; thus it is called "inconceivable," like the *nyagrodha* tree, whose seed is small while the tree is vast.

Second, by the power of original vows, its fruit and function operate spontaneously and effortlessly without thought, as in the case of the power of vows prior to the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Third, it is like illusory phenomena, being non-existent yet appearing to exist. Fourth, it relies on non-abiding while never losing its goodness. Fifth, it attains the principle without abandoning phenomena. Sixth, it can manifest the fruit while still within the cause. Seventh, it attains the fruit without abandoning the cause—all of these are inconceivable.
The eighth is the unimpeded liberation regarding phenomena (*dharmāpratighāta-vimokṣa*). Within this, there are five pairs of ten phrases.
The first concerns the objects of delusion and awakening.

That is to say, ordinary beings falsely perceive the signless (*animitta*) as having signs (*sanimitta*), whereas the noble ones, through their awakening, perceive the signless within what ordinary beings perceive as having signs.

Furthermore, that which is a characteristic is itself the absence of characteristics, and the absence of characteristics is itself a characteristic; because these two aspects are simultaneously transcended, it is inconceivable.
Other points should be understood by analogy.
The ninth explanation concerns the arousal of the mind and so forth as being identical to Bodhi, wherein the beginning is made equal to the end.
The second phrase brings the end back to the beginning;
because the final mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are these three without distinction, and because the understanding of the mind is unerring, there are no three inversions.
The three inversions are explained as before in the "Chapter on Generating the Mind."
Among the ten points, there are four propositions:

first, the exhaustion of fluxes and the non-exhaustion of fluxes are non-dual; second, the Buddha-dharma and worldly dharmas are one yet not intermingled; third, the encompassing of phenomena and the sameness of principle involve entry yet no entry; fourth, the explanation that establishes non-duality and immutability—because they are of a single flavor, they are non-dual, and for this reason, both are inconceivable.

Regarding the second point, the ten kinds of skillful means and esoteric speech (*sandhyābhāṣa*): it is precisely because internal practice is difficult to fathom that one’s speech becomes skillfully subtle and secret.
Generally speaking, there are five types of esoteric speech:
first, it is called esoteric speech because it explains profound and secret teachings, such as the "Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata" mentioned in the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava* chapter above.
Second, explaining all dharmas with a single word is called "esoteric language.
Third, being near yet not hearing, as in the case of Śāriputra who was like one who is deaf;
or being distant yet without limit, as in the case of Maudgalyāyana following the sound—these are called "esoteric language."
Fourth, when the words are near [in meaning] but the intent is far-reaching, such as teaching the three vehicles as the ultimate, this is also called "esoteric speech.
Fifth, when different words are used to express different dharmas, such as teaching that what is not firm is firm.
In this present text, the explanation is given solely according to the first meaning.
Within that, the first part concerns the teaching of the Dharma, because it captures the profound intent and reconciles similarities and differences.
The second part demonstrates identity with *nirvāṇa* while secretly manifesting the taking of birth.
Third, as when one enters meditative absorption in the east and emerges mysteriously in the west, and so forth.
Fourth, skillfully explaining that within the good of sentient beings there is evil, and within suffering there is pleasure, and so forth.
Fifth, skillfully explaining that sentient beings are defiled when they are undefiled yet become stained, and pure when they are stained yet remain undefiled.
Sixth, skillfully explaining that within one there is all, and so forth.

Seventh, explaining that within destruction there is formation, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*: "While devas and humans see the end of the kalpa, this land remains eternally peaceful and secure," and so on.
Eighth, because he speaks upon seeing this secret place—the Buddha’s manifest birth and entry into nirvana everywhere.

Ninth, because he understands that sentient beings are themselves nirvana and do not undergo further extinction, yet does not abandon his great vows to gather in and sustain all beings; this constitutes his skillful secrecy.
"Ten: though one has attained self-awakening without depending on others, one seeks virtuous friends without ceasing, regarding this as skillful and subtle.

Regarding the 'ten kinds of skillful means for the wisdom of discernment' in the three realms of existence: since the previous section already explained the skillful teaching of the subtle points, it is said here that one now possesses the wisdom that reaches clear understanding."

The first two know that the world is partly pure and partly defiled; the next three know the capacities of sentient beings; the next three know the characteristics of the practices of the Three Vehicles; and the final two know mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Another interpretation:
the first two refer to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), the next seven to the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), and the last to perfect wisdom-awakening (*samyaksambodhi*).
Another interpretation:

Regarding the first two [verses], where is the transformation performed? Regarding the next three, what is it that is transformed? Regarding the subsequent three, in what location is the transformation established? Regarding the final two, by what dharma is the transformation effected?
The preceding thirty phrases clarify the completion of the practice of transcending the mundane through the wisdom of integration.
The second section, "There are ten kinds of samādhis," consisting of twenty phrases below, clarifies how profound concentration universally pervades all.
Within this, the first ten clarify the essence of concentration, while the latter ten clarify its functional activity.
Furthermore, the former clarifies profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while the latter reveals its universal pervasiveness.
Within the former, first is the clarification of the locus of entry into concentration, meaning it pervades all various realms;

second is the clarification of the body through which one enters concentration, meaning one enters concentration by means of the bodies of all sentient beings, such as entering meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in the form of a youth, and so forth.
1. The third concentration definitively illuminates the reality of phenomena;
2. within the fourth concentration, one sees the Buddha; 3.
the fifth concentration sustains [the practitioner] through many kalpas, as explained in the tenth chapter, "The Ten Illuminations," regarding the light of wisdom.
Sixth, manifesting from the body clouds of concentration, as in the case of the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja and others;
seventh, manifesting entry into concentration by means of a buddha-body;
eighth, entering concentration for the purpose of awakening sentient beings.

Regarding the latter two, in each single moment of thought, one attains all the samādhis and wisdom of all bodhisattvas, becoming fully endowed with these two practices and entering meditative absorption.

Furthermore, the first refers to the locus of entry into absorption; the next, to the body that enters absorption; the next six, to the functions of entering absorption; and the final two, to the time of entering absorption.

Regarding the ten kinds of "all-pervading bases" (*sarvatraga*), the former [section] clarified entering meditative absorption, whereas the present [section] distinguishes the arising of function from that absorption so as to pervade all places.
First, the basis of entrusting compassion;
second, the basis upon which the body relies.

Next, there are three locations for the arising of understanding: first, understanding the root-nature of the primary retribution; the latter two, understanding the kalpa-destruction of the secondary retribution—among the three calamities, the wind calamity is briefly omitted;
next, one is the location of that which is offered;
next, two are the locations of that which is accomplished: one is the secondary retribution and one is the primary retribution.
The latter two are the spheres of activity, consisting of one wisdom and one merit.
The preceding section concludes the universal practice of profound meditative concentration.
From the third section, "There are ten kinds of dharma-gates," onwards, the forty phrases clarify the practice of mastery over karmic functions.

Within this, the first ten clarify the Dharma-gate of Manifesting Sovereignty: first, the single body manifesting universally; second, manifesting diversely in many places; third, causing many to enter into one; fourth, not losing the maintenance [of the state]; fifth, manifesting in accordance with the fruit above; sixth, being omnipresent in no place; seventh, being omnipresent at no time; eighth, manifesting many bodies in a single land; ninth, manifesting a single body in many places; tenth, universally manifesting in a single thought-moment.
These are all gates of the interpenetration of the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and are therefore called "dharma-gates" (dharmamukha).

Regarding the second point, the ten kinds of supernormal powers (abhijñā): this refers precisely to the manifestation of the body as a dharma-gate, so it is said because its karmic functions are limitless.
First, the knowledge of past lives;
second, the divine ear;
third, the knowledge of others' minds.
Fourth is the divine eye;

next are the five bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*): first, manifesting supernormal powers; second, manifesting multiple bodies; third, traveling swiftly; fourth, adorning buddha-fields; fifth, manifesting transformation bodies;
and finally, demonstrating the attainment of enlightenment through the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
These ten all take supernormal wisdom (*abhijñā*) as their essence; therefore, they are called "wisdom-powers" (*jñāna-abhijñā*).
Since they all arise from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are collectively termed "births.

Regarding the three types of tenfold clarity (*vidyā*): previously, they were called "powers" (*abhijñā*) because they are unobstructed; now, they are specifically designated as "clarities" (*vidyā*) because they are fully manifest.

Among these, the first is knowing the distinctions between the karmic fruits of sentient beings; the second is knowing that sentient beings give rise to pure faith toward the realm of cessation; and the third is knowing that sentient beings realize and enter the wisdom of principle—these three knowledges concern those to be converted.
Fourth is verbal action, fifth is mental action, and sixth is physical action; these three manifest the capacity for emanation.
Seventh is that which, regarding objects, transforms discriminative conceptualization into the cause of right knowledge.
