The latter four are the functional manifestations of the Buddha’s three karmas, having pure consciousness as their essence.

Regarding the "two factors of the path": it is said that because the prior defilement and purity are without limit, the conditions for the Bodhisattva’s arising of the path are likewise without limit.
Based on the ten kinds of vastness previously known, this reveals that the arising of the collection of the knower is likewise without limit, and there is no separate dharma whatsoever.

Regarding the third, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*): it is called the path of cultivation because one performs practices in response to conditions; it is not the same as the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) or the preparatory path (*prayogamārga*).
Furthermore, the "comprehensive collection of cultivation" mentioned in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* is also situated on the [supramundane] stages, which is consistent with this view.

On the first three days, one specifically cultivates the three types of non-substantiality: within the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*), one does not perceive any defiled phenomena of grasping to which one might become attached, nor does one perceive any pure phenomena upon which one might rely for liberation; by means of this, one is able to ensure that the three karmas are free from error.

Second, within the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*), one perceives neither a defiled portion that can be diminished nor a pure portion that can be increased, because the principle of non-arising is real.

Third, within the contemplation of the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā-svabhāva*), one does not perceive the former two natures as existent, nor does one perceive the three absences of intrinsic nature as non-existent; furthermore, the characteristic of true suchness (*tathatā*) is neither an existent entity nor a non-existent one.
The first [verse] refers to the wisdom of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra-jñāna*).

The latter four refer to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); therein, one specifically practices based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), contemplating that consciousness-only is like an illusion and so forth, thereby accomplishing non-erroneous practice.
Fifth, although one practices the three gates of liberation, one does not depart from the triple world, for the purpose of cultivating roots of goodness therein.
Sixth, one does not cling to the teachings.
Seventh, within the ultimate principle, the dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges remain unimpaired.
Eighth, equality regarding the true essence;
ninth, vigor in initiating practice;
tenth, equality and lack of doubt regarding the Buddha’s virtues.
The "four paths of adornment" refers to the fact that the practices of the path of cultivation mutually embellish one another; thus is their name derived.
Furthermore, it is explained:
all are used as counteractive practices to adorn the path.
Among these, the first five are undefiled in their own practice: one remains constantly in meditative concentration despite being amidst distraction;
the next two dwell in the small while constantly abiding in the great;
the final two abide in the realm of desire while practicing dhyāna.

Next are the three practices of conversion and guidance according to circumstances: first, converting those in the world of desire; second, converting those on heterodox paths; third, converting those who violate precepts to rescue them from suffering.
Ninth is the fulfillment of one's own practice, which consists of three parts: first, the attainment of the perfection of the Dharma;

second, the skillful manifestation [of the Buddha-body] as indicated by the passage beginning with "For the sake of all sentient beings"; and third, the explanation and establishment of this skillfulness as indicated by the passage beginning with "Why is this?"
The ten causes are perfected and the fruit is fulfilled; herein there are three parts:

first, attaining the fruit through the perfection of the causes; second, from "and yet it is not severed" onwards, clarifying that upon attaining the fruit one does not abandon the causes; third, from "Why is this? onwards, explaining the characteristics of the practice—these may be understood accordingly.
The fourth section below, consisting of two hundred gates starting from "Tenfold," elucidates the practice of the matured retributive virtues from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward.
This is divided into five parts;
first, twenty phrases elucidate the practice of external activities of the hands and feet.
Second, from "ten bellies" downward, thirty phrases clarify the practice of internal virtues being full and complete;
third, from "ten adornments" downward, twenty phrases clarify the practice of external marks being fully prepared;
fourth, from "ten heads" downward, seventy phrases clarify the practice of the functional activities of the six sense organs.
Fifth, from the "Ten Practices" (*daśa-caryā*) downward for sixty [sections], it clarifies the conduct of the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*).

Regarding the first of these, there are ten [sections]; "walking" (*caryā*) involves advancing and traversing, which symbolizes the feet. Since one begins from the bottom, this is therefore explained first.
Among these, the first two concern practice— one of ethical discipline and one of diligence;
the next two concern penetration—
one general and one specific.
The next two concern the mind: one is faith and the other is aspiration;
the next two concern the Dharma: one is protection and the other is listening;
the final two concern merit: one is merit and the other is abandonment.
Regarding the second [set], the ten hands signify the physical body through their functions of taking and giving.

Among them, the first four pertain to one's own practice: first, taking; second, giving; third, showing respect to those below; and fourth, honoring those above. The subsequent four pertain to benefiting others:
first, removing the net of doubt; second, pulling one out of the mud of desire; third, rescuing from the four currents; and fourth, bestowing the True Dharma.
The final two [verses] clarify the fulfillment of the two practices: first, the removal of the disease of afflictions; second, the destruction of ignorance.

Within the thirty phrases beginning with "having ten bellies," which clarify the fullness of internal virtues, the first "belly" is as follows: just as the belly of a worldly person contains impurities, here it is explained that the belly of the Bodhisattva’s practice is the opposite of that, being pure.

Among these, the first three concern purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*): first, the mind that maintains the precepts; second, the correct guarding of the precepts; and third, not concealing one's transgressions.
The next one concerns purity of meditative concentration (*samādhi-viśuddhi*), namely, a concentrated mind free from attachment.
The latter six are categorized according to the purity of wisdom: first, the severing of the obstacle of afflictions;
second, the extinguishing of the obstacle of karma;
third, the internalizing of the true Dharma, which is like the thought of having eaten one's fill until the stomach is full.
Fourth, awakening to dependent origination;
fifth, realizing the Eightfold Noble Path;
sixth, destroying false views.

Regarding the second point, "there being ten treasuries": previously, the abdomen was mentioned in general; now, it is clarified that within that aforementioned abdomen there are five internal organs which possess a similar sense of containment and storage, and thus they are explained next.
Within this, the first six [verses] encompass the gathering of sentient beings below, while the latter four encompass the Buddha-fruit above.

Regarding the former, the first three provide a general summary: first, bestowing understanding; second, causing practice; and third, accomplishing virtue—which refers to the accomplishment of the Sangha Jewel.
The latter three specifically encompass the three categories of sentient beings.
The statement that "the Tathāgata certainly causes sentient beings to give rise to roots of goodness" refers to the Bodhisattva acting as an external condition.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "Although an icchantika has severed their roots of goodness, by the power of the Buddha-nature, their roots of goodness will yet grow again in the future"; this refers to the internal causal power.

Regarding the inclusion of the latter four within the superior category: first, the inclusion of the ten powers of a Buddha; second, the inclusion of the four fearlessnesses; third, the inclusion of the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*); and fourth, the inclusion of the Buddha’s realized wisdom (*pratyātma-jñāna*).

Regarding the "three [sections] with ten minds": whereas the preceding section generally clarified the various internal organs within the abdomen, this section specifically clarifies the heart-organ (*hṛdaya*). This is because it is the most preeminent, the sovereign of the five organs, the core of reality, and the source of mental aggregation and arising.
Among these, the first two encompass the mind that gathers virtue: first, courage; second, diligence.
The next two destroy the mind that produces evil: first, destroying evil conditions; second, destroying evil causes.
The final two constitute the mind that accomplishes practice: first, firmness; second, purity.
The topmost sixth [stage] is self-cultivation.
The following two involve the mind that gathers and nurtures sentient beings: the first causes them to awaken;
the second is compassionate rescue, which refers to the Brahma-abodes, namely, loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
The latter two constitute the mind of perfected virtue, which is first profound and second firm.
The third section, from "The Ten Adornments" downward, clarifies the twenty aspects of practice regarding the perfection of external marks.

The first ten [perfections] are still similar to the worldly adornment of the body: the first two are the adornment of compassion; the next two are the adornment of aspiration and seeking; the next three are the adornment of gathering sentient beings; and the final three are the adornment of gathering virtues.

Regarding the second point, "possessing ten types of weapons": since he has already girded his waist and adorned his body, he now firmly grasps and wields these weapons to manifest the capacity to eliminate obstacles.
Of these, the first five are weapons of compliance used to break through obstacles;
the subsequent three are weapons of opposition used to break through obstacles, just as one might seize a thief’s weapon and use it to harm that very thief.
The latter two constitute the staff for accomplishing virtue and establishing merit.
From the fourth section, "Having ten heads," onwards, seventy phrases clarify the activities and functions of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*).
First, the heads are clarified because they are situated above the body.

Among these, the first represents the depth of the virtue of abandonment; the next three, the loftiness of the virtue of merit; the next one, the firmness of the virtue of compassion; the next two, the extensiveness of the virtue of wisdom; the next two, the virtue of gathering and sustaining sentient beings; and the final one, the virtue of protecting the Dharma.
Regarding the second point, "possessing ten eyes": because their practice, virtue, purity, and excellence illuminate and comprehend all conditions (*ālambana*), they are identical to the eye.
The meaning of the ten eyes is briefly presented through four sections:
first, the explanation of names; second, the essential nature (*svabhāva*); third, various categories. The first three have been explained elsewhere.
Regarding the fourfold explanation of the text: In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is stated that "the impermanent fleshly eye does not see other directions because it fears the great winds.
This sutra, however, refers to the true and eternal fleshly eye, which sees the forms of the ten directions.
In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, the wisdom-eye perceives the truth, while the dharma-eye observes the ultimate nature of all paths;
the differences between these two may be understood according to their respective commentaries.
In this context, it should be understood that the names are all established based on their respective faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*).
Among the latter five, "the eye of wisdom" refers to the discernment of phenomena; "the unobstructed eye" refers to seeing phenomena without being hindered by principle (*li*).
The Universal Eye perceives the equality of five things;
the rest may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the third [category], there are ten ears, because one listens to the teachings according to principle and initiates practice based upon what has been heard.

The first two [stages] involve distancing oneself from the adverse and the favorable; the next two involve abandoning the minor and rejoicing in the great; the next two involve pitying suffering and detaching from pleasure; the next two involve seeking Buddhahood and investigating the Dharma; and the final two involve understanding the conventional and reaching the ultimate truth.
Regarding the four types of nose, there are ten kinds: smelling, inhaling, exhaling, and the fragrance of conduct; these are so called because the path is developed in dependence upon the nose.

Among these, the first four refer to the substance of smelling fragrances. While the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* mentions only three types, this text lists four; the reconciliation of these differences can be understood accordingly.

Next, the three instances of smelling fragrances illustrate their functional application; according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts, since the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue do not exist in the upper two realms, the two objects of fragrance and taste likewise do not exist there.

Regarding the statement here that one smells odors such as "neither-perception-nor-non-perception," this clarifies that subtle odors and the like are not non-existent; for because the bodhisattva’s nose-consciousness transcends those of humans and devas, he is able to discern them.
The latter three [perfections] are like the fragrance of the Dharma of those who have left the mundane world.
Regarding the fifth [perfection], the ten kinds of tongues, this clarifies mastery over verbal karma, for it is by relying upon them that one increases in goodness.
Within this, the first five manifest its virtues by way of eloquent exposition, while the latter five manifest its stages by way of compliant application.

Regarding the six [kinds of mastery] that possess ten bodies: this clarifies mastery over bodily action (*kāyakarman*), because one manifests forms in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
Among these, the first three manifest the bodies of ordinary beings;
the next five manifest the bodies of the Three Vehicles.
The latter two manifest the bodies of essence and function; one is function and the other is essence.
Regarding the seven [categories] having ten meanings, this clarifies mastery over mental karma (*manas-karman*).

Within these, they are: first, faith; second, hearing; third, reflection; fourth, cultivation; fifth, tranquility (*śamatha*); sixth, insight (*vipaśyanā*); seventh, general regulation; eighth, regulating internal thought; ninth, regulating external objects; and tenth, clarifying the Buddha’s meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Fifth, regarding the sixty sections beginning with "There are ten kinds of conduct," which clarify the conduct of the four postures and movements: the first ten conducts refer to the act of setting out and wandering.

The first two are able to listen and speak; the next three are for self-discipline and transforming sentient beings; the next one is for purifying one's own wisdom; the next two are for transforming those below and receiving respect from those above; and the final two concern attaining the fruit while maintaining the cause.
Regarding the "ten kinds of abidings": because there is a cessation of activity, their abidings are clarified.
While the Lesser Vehicle causes one to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth, here it clarifies that the Bodhisattva abides in these ten practices.

First, abiding in the fundamental practice; second, abiding in the characteristics of practice; third, abiding in right wisdom; fourth, abiding in the locus of concentration; fifth, abiding in the locus of precepts; next, two [stages] for conforming to persons and dharmas; next, two [stages] for the perfection of knowledge and patience; finally, one [stage] for abiding in the fulfillment of the fruit.

Regarding the ten kinds of sitting within the three realms of existence: because abiding in the precepts involves weariness, "sitting in peace" is clarified; it is because the Bodhisattva dwells in these states to accomplish practice and gather in sentient beings.
The first four are identical to worldly sitting for the purpose of gathering beings;
the latter six are sitting through the Dharma to perfect virtue: first, discernment; second, upholding; third, concentration; fourth, loving-kindness; fifth, compassion; and sixth, power.
Regarding the four types of lying down, which consist of ten kinds: one must also lie down while sitting, as this is said to manifest the resting and returning to stillness.
The preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for the first two dhyānas are: first, ceasing clamor; second, entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*);
and next, attaining meditative absorption.

The seven fruits of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) that follow are: first, the arousal of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); second, the departure from regret; the next two are the awakening through wisdom; the next is the fulfillment of wishes; and the final two constitute the completion of the practice.

Furthermore, as stated in the sūtras, one should not sleep lying face up or face down, nor on the left side, but rather on the right side while contemplating the signs of light (*ālokasaṃjñā*). Now, this bodhisattva, in accordance with the Dharma, employs the light to subsume function within the essence; thus, he sleeps.
Regarding the "five kinds with ten types of abiding": because clear wisdom has a place of rest, it is called "abiding.
The preceding section clarified that which is able to abide; this section distinguishes that in which one abides.
Furthermore, the preceding section clarified abiding of the body; this clarifies abiding of the mind.
Therefore, while the preceding [sections] pertain to the four modes of deportment, this section concerns the mental activities.

Within this, the first four stages dwell in the four immeasurables; the next one stage dwells in the six perfections; the next three stages dwell in the three doors of liberation; and the final two stages fulfill the position of practice.
Regarding the six types of practice that comprise ten kinds, Master Yuan explains:
the preceding section clarifies the practice of benefiting others, while this section clarifies the practice of self-benefit.

Furthermore, it is correctly stated that the preceding section clarifies the skillful means from beginning to end; therefore, "delighting in hearing [the Dharma]" and so forth are taken as the practices.
Now, because this refers to the cultivation of mature clarity, right mindfulness and so forth are taken as the practice.
Furthermore, it is said: "The former refers to the practices of walking and standing among the four postures; this explains the practice of initiating the path from beginning to end."
Now, it is said that the former [passage] refers to physical conduct, while this refers to mental activity.
If that is so, why is it that mental activity also arises in the ten preceding [stages]?
Explanation:
In this sutra, the external matters concerning the bodhisattva’s person are all revealed through his internal practice.
This pattern holds true throughout; therefore, there is no cause for doubt.

Within this section, the first four points concern his own practice: (1) preparatory application, (2) awakening to the principles of the Dharma, (3) subsequent wisdom in accordance with the Buddha, and (4) the undertaking of the practices of the six perfections.
Next are the four practices for gathering and benefiting beings: first, a general enumeration;
second, acting in concert with others (samānārthatā); third, kind speech (priyavāditā).
The four benefits refer to manifesting as if one were subject to greed and so forth in order to awaken others.
The latter two [benefits] refer to the fulfillment of the two practices.
The preceding five hundred and twenty phrases complete the explanation of the characteristics within the fifth major section, the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

From this point downward, the sixth major section, beginning from the "Ten Kinds of Contemplation" and comprising five hundred and ten phrases, answers the aforementioned sixth [section] concerning the practice of the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of results.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, three hundred and twenty phrases clarify the ultimate practice of perfected causes, which corresponds to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*);

second, from "The ten kinds of dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven" onwards, one hundred and ninety phrases clarify the practice of manifesting perfected fruits, which corresponds to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*vimalā-buddhatva*).
Within the preceding section, there are three divisions:
first, one hundred and forty gates that clarify the essential nature of causal practice;
second, from "The Ten Meanings" downward, eighty gates that clarify the cultivation of expedient means.
Third, from the section on the "Ten Kinds of Māras" downward, there are one hundred gates that clarify the removal of obstacles through practice.
This section consists of two parts:

first, the initial forty gates clarify the skillful means for initiating practice; second, from the section on the "Ten Kinds of Giving" downward, they clarify the essential nature of the ten pāramitās.

Regarding the preceding section: first, twenty [points] clarify the observation of mental action (*manas-karman*); next, ten clarify the vigor of physical action (*kāya-karman*); and finally, ten clarify the roar of vocal action (*vāk-karman*).

Within the first of these, the ten kinds of observation are for the purpose of cultivating the skillful means of contemplative understanding and for thoroughly mastering the characteristics of the obstructions and openings within the sphere of practice.
Among these, the first three contemplate those to be converted: first, knowing their karma;
second, knowing their retribution;

and third, knowing their faculties—meaning that one is not deluded regarding the fundamental nature which lacks fixed faculties, yet is able to contemplate the distinctions among faculties according to specific circumstances.
Next are the six dharmas of the Jewel of Awakening: first, the dharma of principle;
second, the dharma of fruition;
third, the dharma of teaching; [and so forth].
The four dharmas of practice;
the five dharmas of the stage of contemplation: first, the elimination of hindrances, and second, the attainment of the prediction.
Finally, the dharma of fixed concentration, which is also the functional result of what has been accomplished.
Regarding the "ten kinds of pervasive observation," this refers to thorough investigation and exhaustive examination, as well as the understanding that enables the initiation of practice.
Another explanation states:
the former [type of observation] involves deliberation and calculation, whereas this clarifies the act of looking around with one's eyes to observe everything comprehensively.
The first six [perfections] cause sentient beings to attain the practice of the six pāramitās;
the latter four cause others to attain the four dharmas of a great man: first, associating with spiritual friends;
second, hearing the Dharma.
Third is contemplation, which means not abandoning compassion;
fourth is practice, for the purpose of attaining bodhi.
Another explanation states:
The latter four constitute self-benefit: first, honoring persons; second, conforming to the Dharma; third, compassion; and fourth, wisdom.
Regarding the "ten kinds of prowess" (*vikrīḍita*) possessed by these three [qualities]: it means that while true practice fills the interior, majestic virtue overflows outwardly.
Furthermore, because he establishes merit at the ultimate limit, and is majestic, solemn, courageous, and robust, he is named "Vigorous Advancement" (Fenxun).

First, excellence of body; second, greatness of mind; third, majesty of teaching; fourth, application of practice; fifth, destruction of heterodoxy; sixth, extinction of delusion; seventh, realization of the Dharma; eighth, extensive upholding; ninth, possession of eloquence; tenth, the perfect fruit.
Regarding the four kinds of lion’s roar, there are ten types; because one who is courageous, robust, and fearless is able to proclaim with certainty, it is so named.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are eleven matters concerning the lion’s roar, as fully explained therein.

Among these, first is the roar of the awakened mind; second, the roar of great compassion; third, the roar of repaying kindness; fourth, the roar of great vows; fifth, the roar of pure precepts; sixth, tirelessness in accumulating merit; seventh, insatiability in accumulating wisdom; eighth, the certainty of realizing the principle; and the final two concern the certainty of accomplishing the fruit.
It should be understood that in all these cases, the result to be accomplished is first revealed, followed by the concluding summary of the practices that accomplish it.
From the second section, "There are ten kinds of pure giving," through the one hundred gates, the practice of the ten perfections (daśapāramitā) is elucidated.
Regarding the first ten types of giving: because one relinquishes oneself to bestow upon others, they are: (1) giving with a mind of renunciation;

(2) fulfilling vows; (3) single-mindedness; (4) discerning the field; (5) non-discrimination; (6) non-attachment; (7) relinquishing both body and wealth; (8) seeking the great fruit; (9) benefiting sentient beings; and (10) purifying the three spheres.
Regarding the ten kinds of precepts: they prevent non-virtue in the three types of action and encompass both the prohibitions (*saṃvara*) and the practices (*caryā*).
Among these, the first seven belong to the category of "one's own level" (*svabhūmi*): the first three are the precepts of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*);

the next three are the precepts for gathering virtue (*kuśalasaṃgrāhaka-śīla*), which respectively: (1) transcend the state of ordinary worldlings, (2) turn away from the Lesser Vehicle, and (3) accord with the Great Vehicle.
Next is the precept of gathering sentient beings, which is called "subtle and secret" because it skillfully extracts those who have violated the prohibitions;
the final three pertain to superior progress, and their three clusters may likewise be understood.
Regarding the ten kinds of patience within the three realms, they consist in the mind finding peace in the Dharma.
The first three are the patience of enduring enmity and harm, because one endures the afflictions caused by the three types of karma of others;

the next five are the patience of accepting suffering, which are: first, not harming others; second, not sparing one's own life; third, not disparaging the lowly; fourth, enduring being cut and mangled; and fifth, enduring harsh and evil treatment.
The latter two dharmas involve the patience of reflection (*cintā-kṣānti*), which consists of two aspects: first, the separation from delusions; second, the attainment of the Dharma.
Regarding the "four types of tenfold vigor" (*daśavidha-vīrya*), it is because one diligently exerts oneself in accordance with principle.

The first five clarify the vigor of the three karmas: the first two pertain to body and speech, while the third pertains to the mental karma of the three minds; these are also the vigor of diligent courage.
Sixth is tireless diligence; seventh is indestructible diligence; eighth is diligence in accomplishing tasks; ninth is diligence in entering into principle; tenth is applied diligence.
Regarding the five who possess ten meditations: it is because they gather the mind so that it does not scatter.

The first four are the preliminary practices: first, renouncing the worldly life; second, associating with virtuous friends; third, dwelling in seclusion; and fourth, avoiding clamor. The next two are the primary concentrations:
first, initial attainment; and second, firm accomplishment. The following two are the arousal of wisdom:
first, the arising of knowledge; and second, the severance of delusions. These eight constitute the dhyānas for dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Ninth is the dhyāna for benefiting sentient beings; tenth is the dhyāna that gives rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth.
Regarding the six [dhyānas] possessing ten wisdoms (*prajñā*), because they correctly understand and illuminate the principles:

the first three are the wisdom of understanding phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-prajñā*): first, understanding that the cause is not identical to the fruit; second, understanding that conditions are not separate from the fruit; third, understanding that the fruit is neither interrupted nor eternal.
Next are the four wisdoms that nurture beings: first, uprooting error; second, knowing the vessel; third, bestowing the Dharma; and fourth, subduing Māra.
Following these are the three wisdoms that realize principle: first, seeing the Dharmakāya; second, encompassing supreme virtues; and third, awakening to equality.
Another explanation is as follows:

it should be understood that the first three [perfections] constitute the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the next four the subsequently attained state (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*), and the final three the actual essence (*maula*).
Regarding the statement that "the seven possess ten types of loving-kindness," this is because they have the intention to bestow happiness.
First, one distances oneself from enemies and kin;
second, one enables others to obtain actual benefit rather than mere words, meaning one causes them to leave behind the causes of suffering;
third, one rescues them from the fruits of suffering.
Fourth, it bestows the causes for happiness;
fifth, it enables the attainment of the fruit of cessation;
sixth, it inspires the pursuit of the fruit of wisdom.
Seventh, the seven bodies emit the light of loving-kindness;
eighth, the mind is as vast as space—these first eight take sentient beings as their object of compassion; ninth, taking phenomena as the object;
[tenth, taking no object].
The ten types of objectless [compassion] can all be understood accordingly.
In the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, compassion with phenomena as its object takes the five aggregates as conventional dharmas; this differs from the present case.
Regarding the eight [types of compassion] that possess ten aspects, they are so called because their intent is to extract beings from suffering.
Among these, the first one manifests compassion in general, while the remaining nine distinguish it specifically.
Within the specific categories, the first six give rise to compassion toward objects.

The latter three bestow their benefits as follows: first, out of pity for those whose countenances are deluded, they act to extinguish [delusion]; second, grieved that the truth is concealed, they act to reveal it; third, mindful that others do not know, they cause them to awaken.
Regarding the nine types of existence and ten kinds of joy, these celebrate the benefits obtained by sentient beings.

Among them: first, rejoicing in one’s own generation of the resolve for enlightenment; second, rejoicing in the relinquishing of all possessions; third, rejoicing in the rescue of those who have violated the precepts; fourth, rejoicing in the reconciliation of disputes; fifth, rejoicing in the protection of the True Dharma; sixth, rejoicing in delighting in the True Dharma; seventh, rejoicing in others practicing together with oneself; eighth, rejoicing in one’s own making offerings to the Buddha; ninth, rejoicing in others attaining meditative concentration; and tenth, rejoicing in the perfection of others’ wisdom.
Regarding the "ten things to be relinquished," this is because the mind is free from attachment and grasping:
first, relinquish greed and anger;

second, relinquish worldly dharmas—namely, within the eight worldly concerns, gain and loss depend on the body, praise and blame, and defamation and fame depend on speech, while pleasure and pain depend on the mind.

Furthermore, gain and praise are causes for the arising of pleasure, while loss and defamation are causes for the arising of suffering; because these are explained by combining cause and effect, there are eight [factors].

Third, abandoning those who are not suitable vessels: this means that regarding sentient beings who are vessels for the Dharma, one teaches the Dharma at the appropriate time, whereas regarding those who are not vessels for the Dharma, one abandons them without resentment.
Fourth, abandoning the two vehicles;
fifth, abandoning afflictive defilements;
sixth, abandoning the turning away from existence.
Seventh, relinquishing divergent speech.
Eighth, relinquishing at the improper time; that is, when the faculties [of others] are not yet mature, one waits for the right time and temporarily relinquishes [the teaching].

Ninth, relinquishing due to non-conditions; that is, there are sentient beings who should receive transformation by the Buddha but are not those to be transformed by a Bodhisattva, nor does [the Bodhisattva] forcefully transform them; therefore, he relinquishes [the effort].
Tenth, abandoning divergent views.
The preceding section concludes the clarification of the essential nature of causal practice.
Second, from the passage beginning "There are ten kinds of meanings" below, the eighty gates clarify the skillful means of cultivation.

Within this, the first forty [verses] clarify the practice of self-benefit, while the subsequent forty, beginning from "the ten kinds of clear-footedness" (daśa vidyā-sthānāni), manifest the practice of supreme progress.
Regarding the former, the first ten items represent the essential meanings to be expounded; since practice is established in reliance upon these meanings, they are termed "clarifications" (vidyā).
First, the teaching of the fundamental principle;
second, the understanding of conventional truth;
the remaining eight understand ultimate truth, the first of which is the detachment from signs.
Second, freedom from defilement;
third, transcendence of speech;
fourth, equality.
5. One taste; 6.
Realization, meaning that through right knowledge one realizes the principle and comes in accordance with suchness (tathatā), and is thus called a Tathāgata;
7. Reality;
The eight cessations can all be understood accordingly.
As for the ten dharmas in the second [category], because they maintain their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one accomplishes practice through these dharmas.
The first one is the practice of the actual method; the next four are the methods for removing obstacles; the next three are the methods for removing signs;
and the final two are the methods for the fruit. Regarding the phrase "possessing the ten merits": these are the conditions for accomplishing merit, which is why they are said to be "possessed."
First, it means not severing the Three Jewels.
By what means is this dharma of merit accomplished?
It is accomplished by exhorting sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta; therefore, this exhortation is called the complete condition for merit.
The remaining phrases follow this pattern.
Second is skillful dedication;
third is correctly instructing others through wisdom.
Fourth, compassion without weariness;
fifth, the ability to relinquish body and wealth;
sixth, diligent cultivation of the primary and secondary marks.
Seventh, not disparaging even small acts of goodness;
eighth, not looking down upon ordinary people;
ninth, revering and supporting great persons.
The tenth is the vastness of the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*).
Regarding the phrase "possessing ten kinds of wisdom," it is called "possessing" because one becomes endowed with the causes and conditions for wisdom.
Among these, the first is called "possessing" because one can attain wisdom by associating with superior persons; the following cases should be understood accordingly.
Second, inwardly harmonizing the mind;
third, abiding in mindfulness and wisdom, wherein the ten knowledges manifest inexhaustibly as previously described;
fourth, delighting in the true Dharma-delight.
5–6. The four immeasurables (brahmavihāras) are practiced six times because they involve self-subjugation;
6. The sixth concerns the renunciant guarding the mind, where desire, anger, and delusion constitute the three perceptions;

7. Contemplating the emptiness and purity of phenomena is like the "Indra-array" (indralaya), which refers to when Śakra, in battle with the asuras, deployed his troops in the sky so that their reflections appeared upon the great ocean.
Eighth, profound understanding of the two kinds of emptiness;
ninth, reaching the other shore of signlessness;
tenth, attaining wisdom through gradual progression, which refers to the mutual support obtained through the five stages of gradual succession.
The section on one's own practice is concluded.

Regarding the second part, the forty modes of superior progress beginning with "ten kinds of clear-knowledge" (*vidyā-sthāna*): as for the first ten clear-knowledges, they are called "clear" (*vidyā*) because they involve detailed understanding, and "sufficient" (*sthāna*) because they are complete and comprehensive.
Furthermore, because the darkness of delusion has been exhausted and the function of wisdom is fulfilled:

the first seven [stages] constitute the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*), while the latter three specifically manifest the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*), as should be understood.
Regarding the second [section], there are ten kinds of seekers of the Dharma; by relying on the seeking of the true Dharma, they accomplish superior practices.

Regarding the first five types of profound resolve for seeking the Dharma: some possess a sincere heart but cannot seek diligently; some possess diligence but cannot sacrifice their lives; and some can sacrifice their lives but cannot do so for the sake of others.
The Bodhisattva is not like this, and therefore is capable of all these.

Regarding the latter five [perfections], one seeks the Dharma with a broad mind: the first two serve as wisdom for dwelling deeply in the Dharma; the next two serve as the bestowal of the Dharma to sever doubts; and the last one serves to bring the True Dharma to fulfillment.
Regarding the "three [stages] with ten kinds of clear and lucid dharmas": this refers to having already sought and attained the Dharma, and thus understanding it thoroughly and penetratingly.

Within these, one uses the *Samantabhadra* Dharma to clearly know the distinctions between the three vehicles and the ordinary and holy beings: the first concerns the stage of external ordinary beings; the second is the beginning of internal ordinary beings, called the Stage of Practice through Faith (*śraddhācaryā*); the third is the end of internal ordinary beings, called the Stage of Practice through Dharma (*dharmacaryā*); and the fourth is the beginning of abiding in the holy state, called the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka*).
Some explain: the eight persons are defined in relation to the eight patiences (*kṣānti*). Our explanation, however, is as follows:

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, this is called the "eighth person," meaning that counting backward from the Arhat to the candidate for the first fruit (*srotāpanna-pratipannaka*), one arrives at the eighth.

Regarding the five who have correctly attained the first fruit and extinguished the multitude of fetters: they have extinguished the eighty-eight fetters—the afflictions to be abandoned through insight—and have severed the flow of birth and death within the evil realms.

The sixth [type of person] attains the second fruit; having observed that the flavor of desire is a source of suffering and has exhausted it, yet because the remaining three grades of afflictions are not yet exhausted, they moisten one further rebirth, and thus it is said they "return to receive birth."
Seventh, those who attain the third fruit; these three fruits involve only the abandonment of the desire realm.
This refers to actual dharmas, which generally involve detachment from all three realms.
Eighth, the arhat.
Ninth, the pratyekabuddhas;
tenth, the bodhisattvas.
Regarding the four types of beings who possess the tenfold dharmas of orientation: they are so called because they accord with and orient themselves toward the dharma-realm of Samantabhadra.

First, if one violates a virtuous friend, one turns away from the Dharma-gate; therefore, the opposite of this is called "turning toward the Dharma," and all other cases should be understood accordingly.
Second, awakening the various devas so that they do not become attached to pleasure is called "turning toward the Dharma.
Third, constantly harboring a sense of shame and remorse is always turning toward the Dharma-gate.
Fourth, turning one's back on the two vehicles is called "orientation toward the Dharma";
fifth, accomplishing tasks with a sincere mind;
sixth, relinquishing the Lesser Vehicle.
Seventh, the abandonment of what is blameworthy;
eighth, turning away from the causes and conditions of defilement;
ninth, preaching the Dharma in accordance with the faculties [of the listeners].
Tenth, abiding within the *dharmadhātu*.
The preceding section concludes the exposition on the practice of cultivation.
Third, from the passage "There are ten kinds of *māras*" onwards, one hundred sections clarify the practice of abandoning hindrances, which is divided into two parts:
The first fifty [verses] clarify the accomplishment of practice through the removal of hindrances, while the latter fifty clarify the empowerment through the removal of hindrances.

Within the former, the initial twenty clarify the nature of the hindrances to be removed; the next ten clarify the skillful means for removing those hindrances; and the final twenty manifest the accomplishment of practice through the vision of the Buddha.
Regarding the first ten among the preceding [twenty] māras, they constitute obstacles on the Path.
The first excludes the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) which are without grasping, hence it says "clinging," because those are not *māra*;
the second excludes non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) and so forth, hence it says "defilement" (*saṃkleśa*), because cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the like are not *māra*.
Third, because wholesome karma is excluded, it is called an "obstruction";
fourth, this refers to the pride of the sixth consciousness-mind and not that of the other consciousnesses;
fifth, the disintegration of the five aggregates is called death, hence it is said that one "abandons [the present life] and takes birth [in the next]."
Sixth, because the devas of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (paranirmita-vaśavartin) cause agitation and envy;

seventh, because one commits transgressions without repentance, causing all virtues to be lost, and further, because one falls away from the roots of goodness without the mind giving rise to regret, they are called Māras;
eighth, because attachment to the flavor of meditative concentration (samādhi-rasa) neglects the Path.
The ninth is attachment to emotional intimacy, such as relying on a person rather than relying on the Dharma;
the tenth is being deluded regarding one's goals and failing to give rise to the Great Vow.

These ten types of *māra* are all explained by the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound, meaning that the aggregates (*skandha*) are themselves the *māra*; yet, one fails to realize that they are indeed the *māra*.
Question:
Do these ten māras subsume the four māras? Answer:
Some are subsumed: namely, one each for the aggregates (*skandha*), heavens, and deaths; the remainder are all included within the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Others are not subsumed: because those four and these six are each distinct categories (*dvāra*) and are intended to manifest inexhaustibility; the former are based on specific categories, while the latter concern the universal.
Regarding the "ten kinds of demonic activities (*mārakarman*)," the former [section] was based on the essence of the demon, whereas this [section] explains their causes; thus it is so stated.
Furthermore, these ten activities summon and induce celestial demons (*devaputra-māra*).
First, if one forgets the awakened mind while cultivating roots of goodness, one will only bring about rebirth among humans or devas; is this not the work of Māra?
This is because it is a "perverse root of goodness.

Second, seeking worldly fame is called an "evil gift"; as the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* states: "If there is one who practices giving but is quick-tempered and full of anger, upon death they become a powerful dragon."
3. Rejecting and abandoning evil persons, because they have discarded great compassion;

4. Internally possessing four gates: first, stinginess regarding the Dharma; second, disparaging those who are vessels for the Dharma to cause them to retreat from study; third, preaching for the sake of seeking profit; fourth, preaching the profound to those who are not vessels;
5. Not practicing in accordance with what has been heard.
Sixth, taking pleasure in the Lesser Vehicle;
seventh, harboring anger in the mind while speaking ill with the mouth and looking upon others with malevolent eyes;
eighth, slandering the Dharma and disparaging others.
Ninth is the worldly discourse on literary composition;
tenth is abandoning danger to seek safety;
eleventh is arrogance toward the Dharma and mental distraction—adding one more item increases the count to ten.

Regarding the ten kinds of abandoning the deeds of Māra within the three realms of existence: because one counteracts and cultivates the obstacles, they are termed "abandoning. These are: first, abandonment through the power of others;

second, abandonment through one's own power; third, the power of sincere faith; fourth, the power of recollecting the origin; fifth, freedom from negligence; sixth, seeking the fundamental Dharma; seventh, delighting in the profound Dharma; eighth, taking refuge in the Buddha; and ninth, mindfulness of the Buddha.
As for the Bodhi tree, it is so named because one dedicates one's roots of goodness with the intent that awakening (bodhi) shall be attained beneath this very tree.
The ten roots of goodness share the same nature and likewise yield the same fruit.
Regarding the fourth section, "The Ten Ways of Seeing the Buddha": since the obstacles to practice have been removed, the realm of the Buddha manifests; hence it is called "seeing the Buddha.
Within these ten, each is designated by name and its meaning is explained.
The first, "Abiding in the World," demonstrates non-attachment to *nirvāṇa*.
Becoming a Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) demonstrates non-attachment to the world; therefore, he is named the Buddha "Non-Attached" (*Asaṅga*).
Another explanation:

"Non-attachment" (asaṅga) has the meaning of being unimpeded. That is to say, while remaining unimpeded within the quiescence of the essence, one manifests in the world to demonstrate the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
This is the general statement.
The following nine points specifically clarify this:
first, because they appear through the power of vows, the preceding text states, "By the power of the Buddha's vows, all are seen.
Second, it demonstrates that one attains these sublime fruits through past virtuous karma, thereby causing others to believe and know that karma is never in vain.
Another explanation is as follows:
because this body of marks and signs is produced by superior meritorious karma, it causes sentient beings to give rise to faith.
Furthermore, the substance of the three purified consciousnesses maintains the roots of goodness, accords with and brings about perfect enlightenment, and also sustains the pure land and so forth.
Fourth, although it manifests in the world, it eternally abides in nirvāṇa;
thus, while the former involves maintaining [beings] so that they arise in accordance [with the path], this involves the desire to deliver them through eternal cessation, as there is no obstruction.
Question:
How can this constitute a general explanatory statement?
If it were not so, how could it be established as perfect enlightenment?
The fifth is the principle-dharmadhātu; therefore, it pervades all conditioned activities.
Furthermore, this body of manifest awakening pervades all locations; thus, it is called the Dharmadhātu Buddha, like the Buddha who manifests throughout all realms.
As stated above, this is precisely the Buddha-body pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

Although the six Buddhas universally manifest within the mind that responds to conditions, it is only when one abides in the realization that the mind itself is the Buddha that [true awakening occurs].
The preceding passage says, "The vessels to be transformed are all filled.
Furthermore, because this is an accumulation formed by the arising of a pure mind, it is said to be "abiding.

Seventh, although [the Buddha] manifests within the minds [of beings], he constantly remains in profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*), for he is entirely without attachment in manifold places.

Because the eightfold nature is unchanging, it is called "definitive"; this applies universally to those both within the bonds of affliction and others, for it is through these that one attains perfect enlightenment;
were it otherwise, it would not be so.
Ninth, it is because the transformative mind can universally cover all capacities;
furthermore, it is because the minds of those being transformed are all universally covered;
and furthermore, it is like a maṇi jewel, which universally covers according to needs without any deliberate thought.
Another explanation is that "as one wishes" (yathā-icchā) refers to the sovereign great function [of the Buddha].
Within this context, the ten Buddhas are to be understood according to the six aspects of totality and differentiation, and so forth.
Furthermore, these ten Buddhas are subsumed into five pairs:
the first two constitute the pair of the "produced" and the "producer," meaning the former is that which is produced and the latter is that which produces it.
The next two constitute the pair of the "primary retribution" and the "supporting environment," meaning the former is the primary retribution and the latter sustains the supporting environment.
The next two constitute a pair of permanence and pervasiveness, meaning that nirvāṇa is eternal and the dharma-realm is omnipresent.
The following two constitute a pair of manifestation and abiding, meaning that [the Buddha] manifests within the minds of sentient beings and abides in meditative concentration without attachment.
The latter two constitute a pair of essence and function:
the first is the immovability of the essential nature, and the latter is the pervasiveness of function throughout the Dharma-realm.
The remaining categories are as explained elsewhere.
Furthermore, the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* states: "When a bodhisattva enters ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to know all Buddhas.
What are these ten? They are:

the Buddha of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-buddha*), the Buddha of karmic retribution (*vipāka-buddha*), the Buddha of samādhi (*samādhi-buddha*), the Buddha of vows (*praṇidhāna-buddha*), the Buddha of mind (*citta-buddha*), the Buddha of reality (*tattva-buddha*), the Buddha of equality (*samatā-buddha*), the Buddha of transformation (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), the Buddha of offerings (*pūjā-buddha*), and the Buddha of images (*pratibimba-buddha*)."
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding the "five kinds of tenfold buddha-activities": previously, the Buddha-body as it is perceived was elucidated; now, the causes for attaining Buddhahood are being distinguished.
Furthermore, because these practices accord with the Buddha, they are termed "buddha-activities."
Each has its own heading and commentary.
The first one summarizes the general aspect of birth by transformation;
the following two clarify the practices for self-benefit.
The next two concern specific types of *upapāduka* (miraculous birth): first, those who transform beings bound by the fetter of regret; second, those who transform ordinary beings of small capacity.

The next two concern the practice of protecting the Dharma during evil times: first, during times when the True Dharma is difficult to maintain; second, when demonic activities arise. The eighth is not to grasp at inferior fruits.

Ninth, not abandoning the original vow; tenth, accomplishing unimpeded practice. Within these, there are seven points: first, seeking the Way without being hindered by renunciation; second, from "In the presence of the Tathāgata" onwards, being unstained while seeking; third, from "Causing all" onwards, adorning the lands without being hindered by emptiness; fourth, from "Transforming and teaching" onwards, transforming sentient beings without being hindered by non-existence; fifth, from "The various supernormal powers" onwards, possessing the fruit without abandoning the cause; sixth, from "Manifesting" onwards, displaying perfection without abandoning the partial; seventh, from "Manifesting the Great" onwards, manifesting quiescence without hindering birth.
The preceding fifty lines clarify the completion of the practice of being free from hindrances.
The second section, beginning with "There are ten kinds of prideful actions," consists of the following fifty lines, which clarify the practice of empowerment through freedom from hindrances.
Within this, the first twenty [verses] establish the practice of being free from obstacles, while the latter thirty distinguish the practice of external empowerment.
In the former of these two sections, the first ten enumerate the obstacles and the latter ten manifest their remedies.
The karma of pride (*māna*) consists of grasping at a self and exalting oneself while disparaging others.

First is slighting others; second and third are the two types of pride regarding the Dharma; fourth is self-exaltation; fifth is envying others; sixth is slandering the Dharma; seventh is self-reliance; eighth is seeking out the faults of one's teacher; ninth is being unable to inquire; and tenth is clarifying how pride obstructs the Path.
The second, the ten kinds of intellectual activity (*jñānakarman*), reveals the practice of counteractive cultivation (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*).

That is to say, having recognized the hindrances and delusions so as not to allow them to increase, one brings the emotional mind into accord with principle and reveres the practice of the Dharma; therefore, it is called intellectual activity.

The first two [stages] involve faith in the Dharma and mindfulness of the Buddha; the next two involve drawing near to others and delighting in the Dharma; the following two involve honoring others and purifying oneself; the subsequent two involve conforming to principle and emphasizing practice; and the final two involve perfecting virtues and extinguishing delusions. These names are derived from the functions of this wisdom.
Second, from "There are ten types of those sustained by Māras" onwards, thirty [verses] distinguish the practices of external empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
The first ten clarify the empowerment of hostile obstacles, which are the obstacles to be abandoned;
the latter twenty clarify the empowerment of the Buddha-dharma, which are the remedial practices.

Regarding the preceding section: because internal practice deviates from principle, external Māras find an opportunity; thus, it is called "appropriating. Furthermore, practice that deviates from principle is itself the appropriation by Māra.

The first two [cases] involve abandoning the Dharma through a mind of indolence; the next two involve seeking self-deliverance through the arousal of greed; the next two involve abandoning the vow and giving rise to nihilism; the next two involve achieving the small and abandoning the great; and the final two involve abandoning compassion and slandering the Dharma.

Regarding the second point, "being sustained by ten Buddhas": having already escaped the influence of Māra, one is then sustained by the Buddhas' empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); it is therefore logical that one distances oneself from heterodoxy and enters into the correct path.
The first two [pairs] concern sustaining through the mind;
the next two concern sustaining through the arousal of practice.
The next two are categorized according to compassion and wisdom:
first, compassion; second, wisdom.
The following two are categorized according to skillful means and insight: first, skillful means; second, insight.
The latter two concern wisdom and abandonment—one being abandonment and the other wisdom—and both are sustained by the power of the Buddha, causing such practices to be accomplished.
Regarding the third point, that there are ten kinds of dharmas which sustain: they are called "sustaining" because one abandons faults and follows the Dharma.
The first four are the dharmas of the Four Seals;
the next twenty-two are the dharmas of Dependent Origination;
the final two are the dharmas of the Three Vehicles.
Regarding the latter two types of this pure dharma, there is first, natural purity, and second, purity through abandonment.
These various practices are accomplished through the power of the Dharma; therefore, they are called "upholding.
The preceding three hundred and twenty sections have completed the explanation of the ultimate perfection of causes.
The second section, "Dwelling in Tuṣita has ten matters," consists of one hundred and ninety gates, clarifying the practice of the perfection of the fruition's function.

Although these mostly clarify the Buddha’s function through the manifestation of the eight phases of birth, this also encompasses the functions of Samantabhadra and others; it is not explained in terms of the Pure Land or the place of true retribution.
Another explanation:
This is solely the activity of a Bodhisattva; therefore, it only demonstrates the attainment of Buddhahood through the eight phases, rather than actual attainment by others.
Another explanation:
He has indeed attained Buddhahood, yet there is neither attainment nor non-attainment; since it cannot be expressed in words, it is explained by means of the eight phases.
This is divided into six parts:
the first twenty [verses] concern his conduct while in the heavens.
Second, from "The Ten Kinds of Descent" downward for twenty [items], it clarifies the practice of entering and abiding in the womb;
third, from "The Ten Kinds of Birth" downward for ten [items], it clarifies the practice of emerging from the womb;
fourth, from "The Ten Kinds of Great Adornments" downward for forty [items], it clarifies the practice of living as a householder in conformity with worldly customs.
5. From "There are ten kinds of renunciation" below, spanning sixty [sections], the period of renunciation and the practice of the path are distinguished;
6. From "There are ten kinds of awakening to the Tathāgata’s powers" below, spanning forty [sections], the virtuous qualities of the fruition of Buddhahood are elucidated.
Regarding the beginning and middle [of the text]: the first ten [chapters] concern the conduct while dwelling in heaven, and the latter ten concern the conduct at the time of passing away.
Within the former, it describes what kind of activities a bodhisattva in their final birth performs while residing in that heaven—namely, these ten kinds of deeds.

First, manifesting as gods of the desire realm; second, manifesting as gods of the form realm; third, manifesting birth within the three-thousandfold world system; fourth, preaching the Dharma of descending to birth for those of similar kind throughout the ten directions; fifth, bestowing the transformative teachings of the Dharma upon those in the same locations throughout the ten directions; sixth, preaching the Dharma to subdue Māra; seventh, manifesting delightful sounds for the retinues and the various gods of the desire realm; eighth, approaching the Buddhas to hear the Dharma; ninth, making offerings to many Buddhas; tenth, manifesting many bodies to benefit sentient beings.
Regarding the second point, the manifestation of ten matters at the end of life: having completed what was to be done and being about to descend for rebirth, he manifests these ten clarities.

As stated in the lower fascicle of the *Mahāyāna-upāya-sūtra*: "The Bodhisattva, in accordance with his original vow, dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven palace; he is capable of attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and turning the wheel of the Dharma—it is not that he is incapable."
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"The people of Jambudvīpa cannot come here to the Tuṣita Heaven to hear and receive the teachings of the Dharma; however, the devas of Tuṣita can descend to Jambudvīpa to hear the Dharma."
"For this reason, the Bodhisattva descended from Tuṣita Heaven and attained Buddhahood in Jambudvīpa.
First, the light from one wheel of hair extinguishes suffering, awakening those so that they may know;
second, the light from the ūrṇā-hair awakens them with wonder, [revealing] those with whom he shared karmic affinities in past lives.
Third, the realm of Hand-Radiance Adornment (Kara-prabhā-alaṃkāra) was cleared of those who were not worthy vessels;
fourth, the devas of Knee-Radiance Awakening (Jānu-prabhā-bodhi) were commanded to distinguish between offerings and attendants;
fifth, the Malla warriors of Heart-Radiance Awakening (Hṛdaya-prabhā-bodhi).
Sixth, the light from the body hairs assists in transformation;
seventh, the light from the hall illuminates the dwelling place, and the retinue is born together with him;
eighth, the light from the tower illuminates the mother, and a pavilion appears within her womb.
The ninth is the Light of Extended Life;
the tenth is that among the minor marks, the light manifests the eight signs.
The remaining ones, such as the "one million" and so forth, may be understood accordingly.
The second section, "Ten Matters of Descending the Spirit," consists of twenty items: the first ten clarify the entry into the womb, and the latter ten clarify the dwelling in the womb.
Within the former, for what reason does he enter the womb?
It is for ten reasons:
first, to transform those of inferior faculties;
second, to gather and sustain one's retinue.
Third, his mindfulness remains undisturbed;
fourth, he manifests wondrous and vast benefits;
fifth, he accords with the original vows of sentient beings, meaning that he should undergo transformation while still in the womb.
Sixth, because they belong to the same class of human beings;
seventh, because their faculties and inclinations are seen to be similar;
eighth, because those of the same class gather together.
Ninth, manifesting wonders through the power of meditative concentration;
tenth, making offerings to the Buddhas and hearing the Dharma.
Question:

Based on the preceding passage stating that one passes away from Tuṣita and immediately enters the womb, why does the Liang dynasty’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* clarify that the nirmāṇakāya remains in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for twenty years?
Answer: In the *Commentary on the Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* (Jinguangming shu), the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha explains: "A teacher of a particular school within the Hīnayāna says:
'Because one must wait for the parents to have completed the act of procreation before being born, one remains in the intermediate state (antarābhava) for twenty years.'"
Now, the explanation is as follows:
these are all manifestations appearing in response to karmic conditions, and thus what is perceived by each is distinct.

Regarding the second category, the "ten subtle realms," this clarifies that within the womb there is a vast inclusion of profound and secret states that are difficult to know; therefore, they are called "subtle."

The first [moment] manifests the practice of the original cause; the next eight manifest the eight phases; and the final one manifests the supernormal powers—all appearing simultaneously while still within the womb.
Regarding the third [category], the "ten births," these ten types occur at the moment of emerging from the right side of the mother's flank.
First, internally, he is free from the darkness of delusion;
second, externally, he emits great light;
third, there shall be no more in the future, for this is his final limit.
Fourth, it arises in accordance with principle;
fifth, it appears like an illusion;
sixth, it manifests instantaneously throughout the ten directions.
Seventh, the internal wisdom is complete;
eighth, the external radiance is functional;
ninth, meditative concentration and wisdom are fulfilled.
The tenth is the benefit of the earth-shakings.
The fourth section, beginning with "There are ten great adornments," clarifies the forty points concerning the practices of householders.
The first ten clarify that prior to his initial birth and before he had yet begun his practice, he adorned himself through his great vows.

First, they pull themselves from the mire of desire; second, they open the eye of wisdom; third, they attain a superior body; fourth, they subdue arrogance; fifth, they receive those who are despondent; sixth, they cause great benefit to arise; seventh, they behold the power of the Buddha; eighth, they awaken to their shared practice; ninth, they rescue those who are weary and exhausted; tenth, they receive the touch of the light. In all these ways, they rouse their great resolve to adorn themselves.
The second consists of ten matters of practice.
Regarding the "seven steps": this refers to the initial commencement of the journey, manifesting the appearance of sovereign mastery.
The first step demonstrates the possession of innate power (*sahaja-bala*).
Second, if one remains at home, there are the seven treasures of a wheel-turning monarch; if one leaves the home life, there are the seven treasures of the noble ones.
Third, fulfilling the original vows of others.
Fourth, manifesting for oneself that one has transcended [the world].
Fifth, manifesting the modes of conduct of great beings;
sixth, manifesting the appearance of treading upon the earth;
seventh, bestowing power upon others.
Eighth, they manifest through identical numerical characteristics;
ninth, they demonstrate their own self-awakening;
tenth, they proclaim themselves to be most supreme.
The Bodhisattva in his final birth, in order to transform sentient beings, conforms to the thirty-seven [auxiliaries to enlightenment]; therefore, there is neither addition nor subtraction.
Regarding the ten matters that manifest in the stage of the youth: it is because he is innocent and untainted, yet manifests the study of gathering and transforming sentient beings.

The first three [stages] accord with worldly affairs; the next two are constantly free from transgression; the next three provide the power to save sentient beings; and the final two consist of making offerings to the Buddhas and receiving the Dharma.
Regarding the four [stages] where ten matters manifest while dwelling in the central palace: surrounded by court ladies, one manifests conduct that is untainted.
First, because he acts in concert with them among the court ladies, as seen in the following passages concerning the lady Jñānāvatī and others;

second, because his practice differs from the wholesome conduct of the two vehicles who renounce desire, it is said that this clarifies the wholesome conduct of a bodhisattva, such as when Mañjuśrī sat out the summer retreat in the palace of the dragon girl;
third, by being situated there, he is able to renounce [desire] himself in order to transform those attached to pleasure.
Fourth, they accord with and follow along with the turbid world;
fifth, they practice dhyāna and other meditations while remaining within the realm of desire;
sixth and seventh, they correspond to their original vows, meaning that they have received transformation and instruction here [in this world].
Eighth, making offerings to the Buddha with worldly pleasures;
ninth, manifesting mastery over meditative concentration;
tenth, protecting and upholding the Dharma.
The preceding section concludes the practice for laypeople.
The fifth section, "Ten Matters Concerning Renunciation," comprises sixty gates that clarify the practice of leaving home to aspire toward the Way.

Within this, the first part clarifies the internal aspects of renunciation: the first two [gates] cause one to cultivate revulsion and abandon defilement; the next two manifest excellence to inspire aspiration; the next two cause one to abandon delusions; the next two manifest the virtues of outstanding transcendence and mastery; and the final two accord with the fruit by following the cause.

Regarding the second section on the ten matters concerning the manifestation of ascetic practices, this clearly demonstrates the similarities and differences between the various paths and subdues all false views.

The first point concerns those sentient beings with the predispositions of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), who ask: "If a Bodhisattva is born in a royal palace and has not yet undergone ascetic practices to discipline the spirit, how can he possibly attain the Way?"
Thus, he manifested this transformation to instruct them.
Second, regarding the heterodox views of the non-Buddhists who take self-starvation as the path:

the Bodhisattva demonstrated that by starving for six years one does not attain the Way, but only after consuming the milk gruel did he realize Bodhi; it was for this reason that he refuted their false views.

Regarding the third point, the false view that there is no karmic retribution for transformative manifestations: as stated in the second fascicle of the *Mahāyānopāya-kauśalya-sūtra*, "In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, in order to transform five non-Buddhist practitioners and cause them to attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the Buddha had to revile Kāśyapa Buddha on their behalf, saying:
'Shaven-headed mendicant!'"
"How could one who is bald attain Bodhi?
He spoke these words while truly observing emptiness through Prajñā; he manifested this karma, and thus the retribution was not lost.

By practicing austerities for six years, he caused other sentient beings to believe and know: "If even a Bodhisattva in his final birth still receives such retribution as a result of his skillful means, how much more so must it be for us?"
...and so on, as extensively explained.

Regarding the four conditions conducive to the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*): it means that sentient beings amidst the five corruptions all possess grave offenses; their minds are shrouded by anxiety and distress, and they cannot attain liberation.
To remove their sorrow, he showed them this karmic retribution so that they would think:
"If even a Bodhisattva who slandered the Buddha attained liberation, how much more so for us? Thereupon, they should immediately repent and eliminate [their transgressions].
As it is also said in that sutra:
fifth, to spur on laziness;
sixth, to cause one to seek the Dharma.
Seventh, causing [beings] to depart from self-centered pleasure;
eighth, manifesting excellence, which demonstrates that these ascetic practices are not the correct path, thereby contrasting them with the superior conduct of the Bodhisattva.
The ninth is to plan for the future;
the tenth is to wait for the roots to ripen.

Regarding the three types of practitioners who possess ten matters for approaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*): this clarifies the abandonment of the heterodox and the pursuit of the orthodox, which is also the perfection of causes leading toward the fruit.

Among these, the first two concern the place where he appears; the next two, his physical body; the next two, the adornment of that place; the next two, seeing the Buddha entering meditative absorption; and the final two, delighting in making offerings while contemplating the Buddha. These ten matters all occur at the time when he is proceeding along the path toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Regarding the four [aspects] with ten matters concerning those who sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*): it is because they abide here to receive the Way.
The first four concern the manifestation of signs in terms of location;
the subsequent three concern the manifestation of signs in terms of the three types of action (*trikarma*).
The final three are marks of perfected virtue: first, the fulfillment of the diamond-like samādhi;
second, receiving the seat upon which former Buddhas sat—though other sutras state it was a seat of auspicious grass;
and third, receiving those beings who are to be transformed.
Regarding the five types of tenfold wonders: they are so named because extraordinary signs appear beforehand when great fruits are about to arrive.
The first two concern the Buddhas' bestowal of praise;
the next two concern the convergence of people and things.
The next two [stages] attain meditative concentration and dhāraṇī;
the following two are endowed with supernormal powers and wisdom, which likewise constitute the higher offering to the Buddhas and the lower recognition of those to be transformed;
the final two clarify the essence and function of the physical body—first the essence, second the function.
Regarding the six types of subduing Māra, there are ten kinds; this refers to how he manifests as a supreme banner of victory, standing alone and peerless, in the face of the enemy Māra.
According to the lower fascicle of the *Upāya-kauśalya Sūtra*: "If it were not for the Buddha’s power summoning them, those evil Māras would not be able to approach the Buddha."
Within the realm of desire, this [tree] is the most honored and supreme; if the honored and supreme is subdued, all others will follow in submission.
Māra Pāpīyas led a fourfold army filling thirty-six *yojanas* to surround the Bodhi tree, intending to create obstacles.

The Bodhisattva, abiding in compassion, loving-kindness, and wisdom, pointed to the earth with his finger; everything was shattered and destroyed, and eighty-four thousand members of the eight classes of beings resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The details are as explained therein.
This refers to the transformation of Māra’s retinue.
Originally, the devas saw that the Māra King possessed sovereign power and presumed him to be superior to the Buddha; in order to resolve their doubts, it is said that [the Buddha] "subdued" him.
Fourth, demonstrating the signs for entering the Path;
fifth, manifesting one's own power of virtue;
sixth, giving rise to the power of faith in others.
The seventh and eighth [stages] constitute the rules for the future; that is to say, during the time of practice, one cannot yet avoid demonic obstacles and must not be negligent.
The ninth [stage] reveals that the afflictions are inferior while the virtues are superior.
Tenth, because they accord with the dharmas of the degenerate age.
The forty sections beginning with the sixth, “There are ten kinds of awakening to the Tathāgata’s powers,” clarify the attainment of Buddhahood and the gathering of beings for transformation.
Within these, the first ten concern the attainment of Buddhahood, the next twenty concern the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the final ten concern entry into *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s power of initial and intermediate awakening: the former refers to the subduing of Māra during the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) where obstacles are severed; this [latter] refers to the realization of the fruit during the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
In the initial stage, Māra represents adverse conditions and afflictions represent adverse causes; these two are the obstacles to be abandoned.
Ultimate practice is the perfection of the path of cultivation.
The next two [stages] involve attaining mastery over meditative concentration.
The final two involve the fulfillment of two virtues: first, the perfection of one's own qualities, and second, the completeness of the qualities for transforming others.
Next, the three [stages] possess the three karmas;

the final two are identical to those of the Buddhas: first, their three karmas are identical, and second, their ten powers are identical. For this reason, they are designated by the name "Tathāgata" and not "Bodhisattva."

Regarding the second point, the tenfold turning of the Wheel of Dharma: once Great Enlightenment was perfected and the time for those with receptive capacity had arrived, it was appropriate to open the gate of ambrosia and bestow the True Dharma.
In other sūtras, there is an invitation by Brahmā; here, however, [it is otherwise].
Within this, the first ten clarify the Wheel of Dharma that is turned, while the latter ten reveal the causes for its turning.

Regarding the former, in the case of the Wheels of Dharma such as those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, there are four aspects—view (*darśana*), knowledge (*jñāna*), clarity (*vidyā*), and awakening (*buddhi*)—for each of the Four Truths;
here, these ten aspects are presented to manifest their inexhaustibility.
Furthermore, since those four modes of practice already exist within the [Four] Truths, these now likewise exist beneath the ten truths;
each has ten modes of practice, forming one hundred modes of practice for turning the wheel of Dharma, all as explained previously in the "Chapter on the Wheel of Dharma."
Among these, the first three may be understood; these are all the dharmas that are transformed, not the one who transforms who possesses them.
The fourth is the dharma of unhindered entry into the fruit of Buddhahood;
the fifth is the dharma of compassion universally covering all.
Sixth, the teaching that the Dharma is not in vain;
seventh, the manifestation of past causes;
eighth, the manifestation that the sound of the teaching reaches all places.
The ninth [turning] exhausts all time;
the tenth encompasses all phenomena.

Regarding the "three causes and ten pure dharmas" and so forth: this reveals that the cause capable of effecting the transformation is the Buddha’s untainted (*anāsrava*) pure *dharmadhātu*, and is thus termed "pure white. Through this, it enters the minds of sentient beings and becomes the seeds of hearing-perfuming (*śrutavāsanā*).
"Arising from the signless" means that the noble wisdom of signlessness arises based on this seed.
