"Decisively non-illusory" means that there is no other cause.

The passage in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* stating that "the permeation of extensive learning arises as an outflow from the most pure dharmadhātu and is undefiled and manifest" refers to this very meaning.
First, by the power of the Buddha’s past great vows, this Dharma enters the minds of sentient beings, giving rise to the signless; it is certain and not in vain, and the same applies to the others.
Second, because it is sustained by the Great Compassion of his former lives.
Third, because he does not abandon sentient beings in the present.
Fourth, teaching the Dharma in accordance with the faculties;
fifth, not missing the proper time;
sixth, not causing weariness, nor being deficient.
The seventh is the knowledge of the three periods of time;
the latter three are the three types of sublime karma.

Regarding the fourfold manifestation of great *nirvāṇa* through ten meanings: once the conditions for transformation are exhausted, one ceases activity and returns to the truth; therefore, it is called the manifestation of great *parinirvāṇa*.
The first two [verses] reveal the faults of the conditioned;
the next two reveal the virtues of nirvāṇa;
and the fifth causes one to seek the dharmakāya.
Sixth, the certainty of impermanence;
seventh, clarifying that there must be separation from what is loved to demonstrate a lack of autonomy;
eighth, summarizing that all three realms are fundamentally unstable.
The latter two [verses] reveal the essence and characteristics of *nirvāṇa*: first, its essence; second, its characteristics.
From the passage "O Son of the Buddha, all Tathāgatas... onwards, it summarizes that the transformative rituals of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are equal.
The preceding one hundred and ninety phrases complete the explanation of the practices within the sixth stage, the Ultimate Stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*).
Thus far, the distinctions between the six stages across two thousand modes of practice have been fully analyzed, concluding the fifth major section: the Section Spoken by Samantabhadra.
The sixth major section, beginning from "O Sons of the Buddha, this is the purity of the bodhisattvas," clarifies the division on the conclusion and exhortation to practice and study.
It contains two parts:

first, the conclusion of the meaning and the exhortation to practice; second, from "O Sons of the Buddha, this sutra gives birth to... onwards, the conclusion regarding the title and the exhortation to study.
The preceding section also has two parts: first, the summary of the meaning; second, from "If there are sentient beings... onwards, the exhortation to believe and practice.
Within the first part, there is first a general summary and second, the citation of scriptural evidence.

Among these four—purity (*śuddhi*), excellence (*viśeṣa*), greatness (*mahattva*), and subtlety (*praṇīta*)—the exhaustion of hindrances within the fetters is called purity; the loftiness of virtue is termed excellence; the breadth of function is designated as greatness; and the profundity of principle is considered subtlety. Of these four, purity and excellence constitute practice (*caryā*), while greatness and subtlety constitute the Dharma (*dharma*).

Second, the section beginning with "What has been taught by all Buddhas" cites scriptural authority; that is to say, what has been stated above was all spoken by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, intended to enable those with wisdom and others to clearly understand its benefits.
Second, regarding the section "If there are, O Son of the Buddha," which encourages faith and practice, there are three parts:

first, the indication of the benefits; second, the explanation and establishment [of those benefits] starting from "Why is this?"; and third, the concluding exhortation starting from "O Son of the Buddha."
The second section, "O Son of the Buddha, this sutra gives birth to... and below, consists of two parts:
first, the conclusion of the title; second, the exhortation to uphold it, beginning with "Therefore... and below.

The names therein are tenfold: first, generating all conditioned phenomena; second, manifesting sublime virtues; third, entering profound wisdom; fourth, gathering the gates of Dharma; fifth, transcending the mundane world; sixth, distancing oneself from the two vehicles; seventh, revealing the unshared [qualities]; eighth, universally illuminating the Dharma; ninth, increasing the roots of goodness; and tenth, delivering sentient beings.

Regarding the "Flowers of the Meaning of Merits in the Preliminary and Intermediate Stages": these are the flowers of meritorious and sublime practices interspersed like blossoms, forming a magnificent adornment.
Just as this aforementioned cluster of merit-flowers resembles the ten practices, the name "Adornment of Flowers" is established based upon this.
These ten are all the meanings that are explained; they are named according to those meanings.

Within the section on "Exhortation to Uphold," there is first a general exhortation, followed by an exhortation to uphold based on the benefits enumerated from the words "If a bodhisattva" onwards, which may be understood accordingly.
The preceding section on the conclusion and exhortation of the distribution is finished.
The seventh major section, beginning from "When this was spoken," clarifies the section on the manifestation of auspicious signs as proof.
This section contains two parts:
First, the manifestation of auspicious omens accompanying the preaching of the sutra, namely the shaking of the earth and the emission of light;
second, the certification by all Buddhas from the passage beginning with "At that time," which contains four parts:
First is a general praise for his excellent teaching; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, you have already... onwards, is a specific eulogy of his virtue of teaching.
Within this, he has long since studied well, attained definitive realization in the interim, and now speaks with eloquence when the occasion arises.
3. From "We [all]" onwards, it is shown that they have spoken in unison, clarifying that their current teaching is no different.
4. From "Therefore" onwards, it describes how they have already provided protection and preservation, ensuring that [the teaching] will not be interrupted in the future.
The preceding section on the "Manifestation of Auspicious Signs" is concluded.
The eighth major section, beginning from "At that time, Samantabhadra," clarifies the "Versified Section.
This contains two hundred and thirty-one verses, divided into four parts:
First, there are sixteen verses that reveal the vastness of his virtues, making them difficult to describe;

second, from "Upholding the roots of goodness of sentient beings" onwards, there are one hundred and thirty-three and a half verses that clarify the characteristics of the distinctions between his practices and virtues;
third, from "Constantly relying on the Tathāgata" onwards, there are forty-three verses that correctly provide a concise summary of the two thousand aforementioned aspects of practice.
From the thirty-eight and a half verses beginning with "The Bodhisattva cultivates all... below, the text summarizes and exhorts the practice of the preceding [sections].
Within the first sixteen verses, each pair of verses forms a single summary, resulting in eight topics:

(1) praising the practice of making offerings to the Buddhas and gathering in sentient beings; (2) the practice of being untainted by either of the two aforementioned matters; (3) the practice of subduing Māras and extinguishing delusions; (4) the practice of manifesting transformations for the sake of beings; (5) the practice of saving sentient beings while seeking the fruit [of enlightenment]; (6) the practice of the six perfections and the four immeasurables; (7) the practice of relinquishing oneself to preserve others; and (8) the general summary that, although the teachings are vast and manifold, only a small portion has been explained.

The second section, "Sustaining Sentient Beings," consisting of one hundred thirty-three and a half verses, provides a brief indication of the characteristics of the distinctions between practices and virtues. This is divided into two parts:
first, sixty-seven verses clarify the representation of phenomena through specific events, manifesting the excellence of the aspects of practice;
second, from "A single body has no boundaries" onwards, sixty-six and a half verses clarify the vastness of the application of practice.
Regarding the preceding [section], there are fifteen types of modes of practice (*ākāra*). First, the eight verses clarify the practices of the Dharma-tree, birds, and beasts;
second, the four verses beginning with "Birth and Death" clarify the practices for guiding the deluded and treating afflictions;
third, the four verses beginning with "The Bodhisattva as Dharma-King" clarify the practices of the Wheel-Turning King of Dharma.
4. The four verses beginning with "The Profound Ocean of Wisdom" clarify the practice of the Great Ocean and Mount Sumeru;
5. The four verses beginning with "Deep Resolve" clarify the practice of the Vajra Rain of Dharma;
6. The four and a half verses beginning with "Pure and White" clarify the practice of the Golden-Winged Bird of the City of Dharma.
7. The four verses beginning with "Pure Precepts" explain the practice of the sun and moon shining upon all;
8. The four verses beginning with "Sovereignty" distinguish the practices of the Dharma King and Brahmā;
9. The four verses beginning with "Detachment" describe the abandonment of faults and the accomplishment of virtuous conduct.
10. The four verses beginning with "Immeasurable Expedient Means" clarify the practice of the four great precious jewels;
11. The four verses beginning with "Bodhisattva Merit" clarify the practice of flowers, incense, banners, and canopies;
12. The four verses beginning with "Supreme Bodhisattva" clarify the practice of the dragon-elephant’s rare lamp.
13. The four verses following "The River of Bodhisattva Merits" clarify the practices of the river, boat, grove, and medicine;
14. The six verses following "Bodhisattvas are Equal to Tathāgatas" clarify the practice of being identical to the fruit of Buddhahood;

15. The four and a half verses following "Bodhisattvas Fully Accomplish" clarify the supreme practice of the exhaustion of obstacles and the perfection of virtues, providing a brief conclusion and exhortation that brings to an end the demonstration of the extraordinary characteristics of these practices.
The second section, consisting of sixty-six and a half verses beginning with "A single body is boundless," clarifies the vastness of the application of practice and is divided into ten parts:
first, six verses clarify the profound and extensive practice of the three karmas;
second, five and a half verses beginning with "The Bodhisattva manifests thus" clarify the practice of making offerings to the Buddhas and receiving the Dharma of concentration and wisdom.
3. From "Manifesting various [forms]" onwards, four verses clarify the perfection of merit through the practice of both regressive and progressive conduct;
4. From "Or manifesting as a śrāvaka" onwards, five and a half verses clarify the inconceivable practice of manifesting bodies according to the various classes of beings;
5. From "Or in celestial palaces" onwards, eight and a half verses clarify the practice of the Dharma-seal of mindfulness regarding the eons through the eight manifestations.
6. The seven verses beginning with "Thus knowing sentient beings" clarify the profound practice of discerning the faculties, desires, and conduct of sentient beings;
7. The seven and a half verses beginning with "In a single thought-moment, the Bodhisattva" clarify the profound practice of the swift functioning of body and mind;
8. The six and a half verses beginning with "Just as a person in a dream" clarify the vast, profound, and transcendent practice of wisdom and compassion.
9. From "Contemplating form as like a mass of foam" onwards, eleven verses clarify the practice of the perfectly luminous illumination of the Dharma through the perfection of wisdom and virtue;
10. From "Extensively entering the profound" onwards, five verses clarify the inexhaustible function of the virtues that culminate in the excellence of the perfected qualities.

This brief summary of what has been explained serves merely as a foundation; for when merit is perfected, virtue is established, and practice encompasses the entire Dharma-realm, its purport becomes so profound that how could it ever be fully described? I have thus tentatively cited the teaching of a single mote of dust to approximate its mysterious essence.
Third: The forty-three verses beginning with "Always relying on the Tathāgata" correctly versify the two thousand practices of the preceding [section].
Within this, the verses for the preceding six stages are divided into six sections:
the first four verses [versify] the two hundred gates of practice within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
2. The four verses beginning with "All Sublime Merits" [expound] the two hundred practices within the ten stages (*bhūmi*);
3. The six verses beginning with "Abiding Throughout All Kalpas" [expound] the three hundred practices within the ten practices (*caryā*);
4. The six verses beginning with "The Abode of the Wondrous Vajra Jewel" [expound] the three hundred practices within the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).
5. “Purification of the Body and Bodily Action,” with ten verses below, [describes] the five hundred modes of practice within the ten stages (*bhūmi*);

6. “Contemplating the Wisdom of the Sugata,” with thirteen verses below, [describes] the five hundred modes of practice within the ultimate stage where the causes are perfected and the fruit is fulfilled.

The fourth section, "Bodhisattvas Cultivate All Practices," consists of thirty-eight verses. This section follows the preceding summary and exhortation to practice and study, and is divided into three parts:
first, one verse that summarizes what has been taught—namely, concluding the previous two thousand names by citing a small portion;
second, thirty-three and a half verses beginning with "For immeasurable eons" (*anekakalpa*), which specifically conclude the qualities and functions; [and third, the remaining verses].
The final four verses of the third section summarize and extensively exhort practice.
Within the preceding section on specific [qualities], there are two parts:

first, twenty-one and a half verses that specifically conclude upon the vastness of the qualities and functions; second, twelve verses beginning with "Purifying the Body" that conclude upon the excellence of the qualities of specific practices.
The preceding section is divided into five parts:
first, five and a half verses clarify mastery over the buddha-fields;
second, six verses beginning with "Immeasurable Diamond Mountains" clarify mastery over the three karmas.
3. The three verses beginning with "All past kalpas" clarify mastery over the three worlds;
4. The five verses beginning with "Deeply knowing" clarify mastery over body and wisdom;
5. The two verses beginning with "Manifesting in this way" conclude by showing that such mastery is inexhaustible.
Second, regarding the twelve verses beginning with "Purifying the Body" (*śuddhakāya*), which separately conclude the section on the excellence of the qualities of practice, there are three parts:
first, six and a half verses clarify the seven treasures, palaces, vessels, and weapons of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*);
second, from "Dhāraṇī" onwards, three and a half verses clarify the enjoyment of groves, springs, excursions, food, drink, and vehicles.
Third: The two verses beginning with "These" conclude that the aforementioned practices were attained through cultivation over many eons.
Within the final four verses, the first two summarize the inexhaustibility of his virtues, while the latter two cite the benefits to encourage practice.
The "Chapter on Transcending the World" concludes.

Entering the Dharma Realm. Chapter Thirty-Four: Entering the Dharma Realm.
Regarding the explanation of this chapter, the four gates are the same as before.
First, regarding the explanation of the title, there are three parts.

First, as for the designation of the section: it is called the "Section on Entering Realization and Accomplishing Virtue by Relying on the Person" because it extensively relies upon the Victorious Friend (Guṇamitra) and deeply realizes the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).

Regarding the names of the two assemblies: based on their location, the first is called the "Assembly at the Gabled Hall of Jetavana. This signifies that this Dharma rescues sentient beings and gathers in all life, which is why it was held in the Jeta Grove;
furthermore, it reveals the aspect of great compassion arising from fundamental wisdom, which is why it was held in the gabled hall.
Regarding the names of the three categories: "entry" (*praveśa*) refers to that which enters, meaning the act of awakening to, understanding, and realizing [the truth].
"Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*) is that which is entered. There are three meanings of "dharma": [1] phenomena; [2] the teachings; and [3] the ultimate reality.
First is the meaning of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), second is the meaning of rule (*vidhi*), and third is the meaning of object (*artha*).
The realm (*dhātu*) also has three meanings: first is the meaning of cause (*hetu*), because it serves as the basis for the arising of the noble path (*āryamārga*).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) refers to being the cause of all pure dharmas.
Furthermore, the *Madhyāntavibhāga* states: "Because it has the meaning of being the cause of the noble dharmas, it is therefore called the dharma-realm."
The noble dharmas arise based on this object; herein, the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*) is the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*).
Second is the meaning of "nature" (*prakṛti*), meaning that it is the nature upon which all dharmas depend.
This is because the preceding text of this sutra states: "The Dharma-realm, the Dharma-nature, and the exposition are likewise.
Third is the meaning of "delimitation" (*prabheda*), which refers to the fact that the characteristics of various dependent originations (*pratītyasamutpāda*) do not intermingle.
The first [term] is explained solely as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound), the last solely as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), and the middle one admits both interpretations.
Because the mind and its objects are conjoined, it is called "entering the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-praveśa*).

Second, regarding the intent of this section: first, it clarifies the sequence of the progression; that is to say, the preceding section revealed the progressive cultivation based upon the Dharma, whereas the present section distinguishes the entry into realization by relying on persons. It is for the sake of this sequential logic that this section follows.
The "Assembly" and "Coming" chapters are also explained in the same manner.
Regarding the essential purport of the Three Insights, they likewise share the same assemblies and chapters; since they clarify the entry into the Dharma-realm, this is taken as their central theme.
Within this, there is a detailed analysis presented through three gates:
first, by way of meaning; second, by way of category; and third, by way of stage.
Regarding the first, we first clarify the *dharmadhātu* that is entered, which has five gates of meaning:

1. The conditioned dharma-realm; 2. The unconditioned dharma-realm; 3. The dharma-realm that is both conditioned and unconditioned; 4. The dharma-realm that is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; 5. The unobstructed dharma-realm.
First, regarding the conditioned dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there are two gates:

first, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) which is able to sustain the seeds of all dharmas is called the dharma-realm; as the treatise says, "The realm from beginningless time," etc., which refers to its meaning as a cause.

The ultimate limit of the distinctions among all phenomena across the three periods of time is called the *dharmadhātu*. As the "Inconceivable Chapter" states: "All Buddhas know all past *dharmadhātus* without exception; they know all future *dharmadhātus* without exception; they know all present *dharmadhātus* without exception," and so forth.
The second, the unconditioned dharma-realm (*asaṃskṛta-dharmadhātu*), also has two gates:
first, the gate of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), which refers to the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), because its nature is eternally pure;
it is the single flavor of true emptiness (*tathatā-ekarasa*), devoid of differentiation.

Second is the gate of freedom from defilement (*vimala-mukha*); this refers to how purity is manifested through its respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), and because it is divided into ten types according to the depth of one's practice.
Third, regarding that which is both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there are likewise two gates:

first, the gate of following characteristics (*lakṣaṇānuvartin-mukha*). This refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-skandha*), the five kinds of form (*rūpa*), and the eight unconditioned phenomena; these sixteen dharmas are known solely by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and are termed the "dharma-element" (*dharmadhātu*) among the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*).
The second is the gate of non-obstruction, which means that within the single dharma-realm of the mind there are two gates:
first, the gate of the true suchness of the mind; second, the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind.

Although these two gates each comprehensively encompass all phenomena, their two positions are never intermingled—just as the waves that comprise water are not still, and the water that comprises waves is not moving.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Dedication" states: "One emerges from the realm of the unconditioned into the realm of the conditioned, yet does not destroy the nature of the unconditioned;
one emerges from the realm of the conditioned into the realm of the unconditioned, yet does not destroy the nature of the conditioned."
Regarding the fourth [category], that which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned, there are likewise two gates.
First is the gate of mutual negation (*xingduo*): because there is no condition that does not accord with principle, it is not conditioned;
because there is no principle that is not the object of conditions, it is not unconditioned.
The essence of the Dharma is equal, wherein form and negation both vanish.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle thirty-nine, states: "Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
'This equality of the Dharma—is it a conditioned phenomenon?'"
"Is it a conditioned dharma or an unconditioned dharma?
The Buddha said:
"It is neither a conditioned dharma nor an unconditioned dharma."
Why is this? Apart from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) cannot be found;
apart from unconditioned phenomena, conditioned phenomena cannot be found.
"Subhūti! These two dharmas—the nature of the conditioned and the nature of the unconditioned—neither conjoin nor disperse.
This is what that means.

Second is the gate of non-reliance: this dharma-dhātu is devoid of characteristics and devoid of intrinsic nature; therefore, it is neither of these two. Because it is devoid of characteristics, it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); because it is devoid of intrinsic nature, it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, because it is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); because it is the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*), it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Moreover, because it cannot be reached by either of the two types of conventional expression (*vyavahāra*), it is thus neither of the two.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, chapter one, states: "All phenomena are, in brief, of two kinds: namely, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Among these, the conditioned is neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
the unconditioned is neither unconditioned nor conditioned."
...and so forth, as extensively explained.
Regarding the five unobstructed dharmadhātus, there are also two gates:

first, the gate of universal inclusion (*saṃgraha*), which means that within any one of the aforementioned four gates, all others are subsumed. Therefore, when Sudhana either beholds mountains and seas or sees halls and pavilions, these are all termed "entering the dharmadhātu."

Second is the gate of perfect interfusion (*yuanrongmen*), which means that because principle (*li*) harmonizes with phenomena (*shi*), the entirety of phenomena is without boundaries: thus, even a minute atom (*paramāṇu*) is not small, for it can contain ten lands;
and the ocean of lands is not large, for it can secretly enter into a single atom.
Because phenomena are integrated with principle, the entirety of that principle is not without parts; this means that the one and the many are without obstruction.

It is called either "the single dharma-realm" or "the various dharma-realms. The "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" states: "For example, regarding all dharma-realms, no boundaries can be apprehended; they are neither 'all' nor 'not-all,' and being invisible, they cannot be grasped."
This clarifies that all things are neither "all" nor "not-all.
The "Śānta Chapter" states: "Within this Lotus Treasury World-Ocean, within each and every atom, one perceives the entirety of the Dharma-realm."
This clarifies that "one" is not "one.
Therefore, Sudhana’s grasping of a hand for a mere moment yet passing through many kalpas, or his entering a tower and pavilion to see the entire trichiliocosm, are all of this same category.

The five gates and ten meanings presented above collectively clarify the *dharmadhātu* that is entered; this should be understood through the six aspects of totality, particularity, and perfect fusion.
Second, the analysis of that which enters [the dharmadhātu] also comprises five gates:
first, pure faith; second, correct understanding; third, cultivation; fourth, realization; and fifth, perfection.
Regarding these five, within the five gates of the dharmadhātu previously entered, there are two aspects:
first, each of the five capacities for entry (praveśa) pervades all five objects of entry (praveśya), and each of the five objects of entry pervades all five capacities for entry;
second, these five capacities for entry enter, respectively, one from among the five objects of entry according to their sequence.
Furthermore, these ten gates regarding the two meanings of the superior mind and phenomena are unimpeded and perfectly interfused, forming a single whole.
One should contemplate how the non-obstructed dharma-realm is likewise subsumed through the six characteristics.
The second category, the classification of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), also consists of five gates: that which is entered, that which enters, existence, non-existence, and non-obstruction.
Within the first gate, that which is entered, there are likewise five stages:

first, the Dharma-realm of phenomena; second, the Dharma-realm of persons; third, the Dharma-realm of the mutual fusion of person and phenomenon; fourth, the Dharma-realm of the simultaneous sublation of person and phenomenon; and fifth, the unobstructed Dharma-realm.
The first part consists of ten [points]:
first, the phenomenal dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), referring to the ten layers of residences and so forth;
second, the principle dharma-realm, referring to the single flavor of profound stillness and so forth.
Third is the dharma-realm of objects, which refers to the limits of what is known and so forth;
fourth is the dharma-realm of practice, which refers to the vastness and depth of compassion and wisdom and so forth;
fifth is the dharma-realm of essence, which refers to quiescence, non-arising, and so forth.
Sixth is the utilization of the dharma-realm, which refers to supreme mastery, universal penetration, sovereignty, and so forth;
seventh is that which accords with the dharma-realm, which refers to the correct practice of the six perfections and so forth;
eighth is that which opposes the dharma-realm, which refers to the five heats, the *caṇḍāla* [austerities], and so forth.
Ninth is the dharma-realm of teachings (*dharmadhātu*), which refers to the spoken words and discourses that are heard;
tenth is the dharma-realm of meaning (*arthadhātu*), which refers to the intended significance and purport that are elucidated.
These ten dharma-realms share a single dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), being unimpeded and seamlessly fused such that each contains all others—this can be seen through reflection.

Regarding the "Dharma-realm of the two persons," according to the following text, there are likewise ten categories: namely, humans and devas; male and female; lay and ordained; non-Buddhist practitioners and various deities; and bodhisattvas and buddhas.

These are all the manifested parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) of dependent origination; they are interpenetrating yet distinct. Because Sudhana, upon seeing them, immediately enters the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is called the "human Dharma-realm.

Regarding the "Dharma-realm where the three—persons and dharmas—are mutually fused," this means that the ten preceding persons and the ten dharmas share a single dependent origination. While they are differentiated according to their respective meanings, they are harmoniously integrated without duality; this can be seen through reflection.

Regarding "the Dharma-realm in which the four dharmas are simultaneously extinguished": this refers to the ocean of the fruit of equality, which transcends words and numbers; its dependent origination, both in nature and appearance, is utterly ineffable.

Regarding "the fivefold unobstructed Dharma-realm": this refers to the synthesis of the preceding four propositions. Within that [realm], there is no obstruction regarding the person and phenomena, nor between identity and difference; existence and non-existence do not hinder one another, being sovereign and perfectly interfused. Contemplate this according to the principle.

Second, the clarification of the capacity for entry also comprises five stages: first, the body; second, wisdom; third, their coexistence; fourth, their dissolution; and fifth, their perfection. These refer to: entering the towered pavilion and returning to merge with the body, which is the realization of the body; reflecting upon the principles and phenomena of the boundless, which is the realization of wisdom; being identical to Samantabhadra and pervading everywhere, which is the realization of their coexistence; the mutual identity of body and wisdom such that both vanish, which is the realization of their dissolution; and the unimpeded, sovereign, and perfect fusion of oneness and difference, existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on Arousing the Mind" states: "The profound and true nature of phenomena is entered into by sublime wisdom; throughout boundless Buddha-lands, one pervades them all in a single thought-moment."
The commentary states:

Of the four phrases, the first two refer to the entry of wisdom into the Dharma-realm, while the latter two refer to the entry of the body into the Dharma-realm. Because body and wisdom are non-obstructive, wisdom enters into principle while the body pervades all lands.
The rest may be understood by analogy.

Third, the subject that enters and the object entered are fused and non-dual, with no boundary between them; yet while they are distinguished as different according to their functional meaning, in principle they remain unmixed.
These five aspects of subject and object are respectively interpenetrated as explained above; they should be understood through correct reflection.
In the fourth, subject and object are perfectly fused such that their distinct forms are sublated and both vanish.
In the fifth, identity and difference, existence and non-existence, are unimpeded and fully present.
The preceding section has concluded the analysis by way of categories.

Third, regarding the clarification of entering the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) by way of stages: according to the subsequent text, there are two major divisions within the Dharma-realm that is entered, namely, cause and fruit.

Regarding the preceding persons and dharmas, there are none that are not subsumed within the fruit of Buddhahood; this is precisely the mastery over the dharma-realm manifested through the Tathāgata’s Lion’s Vigorous Stride Samādhi.

Furthermore, regarding the former [classification], there are no dharmas that are not subsumed within the stage of cause; this refers precisely to the Dharma-realm Dharma-gates manifested by Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
Within this stage of cause, there are five distinct divisions, which are the Dharma-realms of the five stages beginning with faith; this may be understood by analogy with their inclusion.
Second, the clarification of the "ability to enter" also consists of two parts according to the text:

first, clarifying how the various bodhisattvas enter the dharma-realm instantaneously from the perspective of the preceding stage of fruition; second, illustrating how Sudhana enters the dharma-realm gradually from the perspective of the preceding stage of causes.

Since cause and effect are mutually unimpeded, the gradual and the sudden are likewise perfectly integrated; they differ only in that the teaching is established through exposition, which relies upon these distinct stages.
Fourth, regarding the commentary on the text: within this chapter, there are two major divisions;
the first clarifies the primary assembly.
2. From "At that time, Mañjuśrī emerged from the Pavilion of Excellent Abiding" onwards clarifies the final assembly.
This also consists of first clarifying the resultant dharma-realm (phala-dharmadhātu) and subsequently clarifying the causal dharma-realm (hetu-dharmadhātu).
Furthermore, the former clarifies the sudden entry into the Dharma-realm, while the latter clarifies the gradual entry into the Dharma-realm.
Moreover, the former is general and the latter is specific.
Thus, the beginning and the end are perfectly interfused and unimpeded; reflect upon this.
Regarding the ten divisions of the original text of this assembly: first, the introductory division;

second, the division on the invitation; third, the division on samādhi; fourth, the division on manifesting the pure land; fifth, the division on gathering the new assembly; sixth, the division on elevating the inferior to reveal the superior; seventh, the division on verses praising virtues; eighth, the division on Samantabhadra’s manifestation; ninth, the division on the light from the brow-hair showing benefits; and tenth, the division on Mañjuśrī describing virtues.
Regarding the first part, the introduction, there are three sections:
first, "At that time the Buddha was dwelling," which represents the perfection of the world through the enlightened one who is wise and perfectly awakened;
second, "the city of Śrāvastī," which represents the perfection of the receptacle world.
Together with five hundred other sentient beings, they were complete within the world.
The first part [of the text] is understandable.
Within the vessel there are three things: namely, first, a city; second, a garden; and third, a pavilion.

The city’s full name is Śrāvastī; it is vulgarly abbreviated as Śā-vèi (Śrāvasti), which translates as "City of the Hearer. This is because in the past, there lived an ancient seer in this place, and there was also a junior seer named Śravaṇa who received the essential teachings from the elder seer.
After the old king passed away, a city was established at this location, and it was named after him.
The garden is located about three or four *li* south of the city.
"Jeta" is the name of the Prince; its full expression is Śvetaketu, which here means "Victorious in Battle."

Furthermore, one without a father is called "orphan" (gu), and one without a son is called "solitary" (du); because the Elder Sudatta provided him with the means of sustenance, he was named Anāthapiṇḍada (Givigudu).

However, as the Elder purchased the land by laying out gold and the Prince offered the trees, both contributing equally to its completion, they jointly established the monastery; thus, it is named after both of them.
Within the garden is a separate pavilion, a place for proclaiming the Dharma, named the Lecture Hall.

It is called "Great" (Dai) because its substance is all-pervasive; it is called "Austere" (Gen) because its virtues are fully complete; and it is called a "Multi-storied Pavilion" (Jū-kaku) because its function arises based upon that substance.
Within the third assembly there are also three types: first, bodhisattvas; second, śrāvakas; and third, various celestial kings.
Within the initial group of bodhisattvas there are likewise three parts: first, stating the number; second, enumerating their names; and third, praising their virtues.
Regarding the names, the two primary leaders are first designated because they are the principal figures who assist in the transformation of beings.
There are three meanings for this explanation:
first, Samantabhadra represents the gate of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is that which is entered.
Mañjuśrī presides over the gate of Prajñā; he is "able to enter," signifying his entry into the Dharma-realm.
Second is Samantabhadra’s mastery of samādhi, while Mañjuśrī possesses mastery of prajñā.
Samantabhadra clarifies the meaning of vastness, while Mañjuśrī clarifies the meaning of profundity.
As these two form a pair of the profound and the vast, they are designated as the foremost.
Following this, among the listed names, there are one hundred and forty-one major positions, arranged in fourteen groups of ten.
The first ten are all named "Banner" (*dhvaja*), signifying that their virtuous conduct is loftily eminent.
The next twenty are all named "Majestic" (*vyūha*), representing the two adornments of merit and wisdom.
That one is missing from among these ten constitutes a reduction in number.
The thirty are called "Treasuries" (*kośa*) because they manifest virtue and fully encompass all things.
The forty are called "Eyes" (*cakṣus*) because they illuminate the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Among these ten [categories], two are added because they represent an increase in number.
Fifty are named "Heavenly Crown" (*devamakuṭa*), signifying that pure virtue crowns the summit of the mind.
Sixty are named "Cūḍā," here translated as "topknot," signifying that his virtues are weighty, honored, and sublime.

Seventy [Buddhas] share the same name, "Light. Within the fourteen positions, each explains "Wondrous Light" (*Prabhāsa*) through two meanings: because it possesses the illumination of both body and wisdom, it shines upon both the internal and external.

Eighty [Buddhas] share the same name, "Banner" (*Dhvaja*). A banner has two meanings: the former clarifies the meaning of standing out alone, while the present distinguishes the meaning of subjugation.
The ninety [deities] share the same name "Sound" (*svara*), because they clarify beautiful sounds and gladden the faculties.
The ten [deities] of each group share the same name "Supreme Virtue" (*uttama-guṇa*), because they transcend all manifest signs.
The eleven [deities] of each group share the same name "Sublime Virtue" (*praṇīta-guṇa*), because their auspiciousness manifests excellence.
The ten and twenty are both called "Kings" (*rāja*) because they possess mastery over the Dharma.
Adding one to the ten is likewise an instance of increasing the numerical count.

As for the thirteen and thirty being again called "Voices" (*svara*), there are two meanings to "voice": the former clarified the excellence of the essence of the voice, while the present reveals its skillful articulation of the sublime Dharma.
If one is added to ten, the increased number may likewise be known.
"Four" and "ten" share the same name, "Awakening" (*jue*), because they both discern principle and examine capacity.
If two are subtracted from ten, the decreased number may likewise be known.
Such as these are the concluding [verses].
Within the ten phrases of the praise of virtues (*guṇa-varṇana*), there are two meanings:
first, that these ten phrases of virtue universally apply to all the aforementioned bodhisattvas, each of whom possesses them in full.

Second, there is a specific praise of the virtues of the preceding fifteen stages. Specifically, the first sentence praises the virtues of the two preceding leaders; because their universal practice and universal objects both penetrate all things, these two together accomplish this virtue.

The second section, "Holding the Immeasurable and so forth," praises the two classes of bodhisattvas—the Ten Banners and the Ten Adornments—stating that the Banner of the Body stands out alone, being endowed with virtue, dignified and majestic, and capable of reaching everywhere.

The third section, "Endowment with the Three Unimpeded [Qualities]," praises the two stages of the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Treasuries and the Ten Eyes; that is to say, they are endowed with the treasury of non-obstruction because they see the Buddha with pure eyes.

The four [bodhisattvas] reaching the Immeasurable and so forth praise the Ten Heavenly Crowns; these are the ten Cūḍāmaṇi Bodhisattvas, who adorn their bodies with heavenly crowns and topknots, appearing in forms identical to those of Brahmā kings. They go to the places where the Buddhas attain enlightenment and contemplate the Buddha without ceasing, requesting him to preach the Dharma.

The five bodhisattvas, including Wisdom Light (Jñānaprabha), and others, praised the ten bodhisattvas, Jyotirasa and Daśadhvaja, saying: "Because Wisdom Light universally illumines the profound Dharma and because it subdues the darkness of delusion."
Sixth, regarding the "Immeasurable" and so forth, he praises the ten Bodhisattvas of Sound, namely, Beautiful Sound and Clear Eloquence, because they preach inexhaustibly.

Seventh, regarding the "Ultimate" and so forth, he praises the ten Bodhisattvas of Superiority and the ten Bodhisattvas of Sublime Virtue; that is to say, their superior wisdom is identical to empty space, and their sublime virtues pertain to the ultimate purity of the objective realm.

The eighth [verse], beginning with "without dependence," praises the ten Bodhisattva Kings; it means that they are kings because they manifest forms with mastery while remaining without dependence, and because they also manifest their own royal bodies.

The ninth [verse], beginning with "elimination," praises the ten Bodhisattvas of Sound; it means that they have internally abandoned the cognitive obscurations and skillfully explain the realms of sentient beings through discernment.
The ten [qualities], such as the Wisdom of Space (*ākāśajñāna*), praise the ten Bodhisattvas of Awakening; that is to say, they emit the light of *āgama* so that the Good Awakening may illuminate.
Furthermore, another interpretation states: these ten phrases are subsumed into five pairs.
The first pair consists of two stages: first, the virtues of practice are fully internal; second, they pervade extensively throughout many bodies.
The next pair consists of two stages: first, observing the Buddha with pure eyes; second, observing him without satiety.
The next pair consists of two aspects: first, internal wisdom illuminating the Dharma; second, inexhaustible eloquence in exposition.
The subsequent pair likewise consists of two aspects: first, internal wisdom being identical to emptiness; second, manifesting bodies to respond universally to all beings.
The next two pairs consist of the first, which internally abandons the cognitive obscurations, and the latter, which externally radiates the light of wisdom.

Furthermore, it is explained that among these ten phrases, the first is the general [heading] while the remaining nine are the particulars; this is because they all without exception manifest the conduct of Samantabhadra.

1. The universality of approaching the Buddha with a single body; 2. The universality of seeing the Buddha everywhere; 3. The universality of seeing him without ceasing; 4. The universality of wisdom illuminating principle; 5. The universality of discerning many eons; 6. The universality of the purity of wisdom and principle; 7. The universality of manifesting bodies through immeasurable wisdom; 8. The universality of severing hindrances; 9. The universality of the radiance of light. These may be understood according to the previous explanations.
Second, within the assembly of *śrāvakas*, there are also two parts: the enumeration of their number and the praise of their virtues.
Regarding the term *śrāvaka*, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because they enter the noble path by hearing the Buddha’s spoken voice, they are called *śrāvakas* (Hearers)."

Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 82, states: "Because one hears the sounds and words of the sublime Dharma from others, and is also able to cause others to hear the sounds of the sublime Dharma, one is called a Śrāvaka (Sound-Hearer)."
"Great" refers to being the fruit of the fourth [dhyāna], and also because it is of the immovable lineage (*akopya-gotra*).
It is the most honored and great among all śrāvakas, such as Śāriputra and others.
Furthermore, these are all Śrāvakas who have turned toward the Mahāyāna; therefore, they are called "Great. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"According to the true meaning, these are all Śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage who, having attained the minor fruits, proceed toward great enlightenment; thus, they are named 'Great'."
The commentary explains:

Because they have not yet entered the *ekayāna* (One Vehicle) of Samantabhadra’s Dharma within the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), the subsequent passage describes them as being like the deaf and blind.
As stated in the aforementioned “Chapter on the Arising of Nature” (*Xingqi pin*): “Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not hear this sutra.”

It further states: "If a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās and plants roots of goodness conducive to the path for billions of nayutas of kalpas, yet does not hear this sutra, or hears it but does not believe it, such individuals are still merely 'bodhisattvas by name.'"
This is what is meant by that.

Furthermore, it is explained that these are all great bodhisattvas manifesting as śrāvakas, as stated in the "Inconceivable Realm" chapter (*Acintyaviṣaya-parivarta*) of the newly translated *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. They manifest as if deaf and blind in order to reveal the profound and supreme nature of this Dharma.
In the second section, the "Praise of Virtues," there are ten phrases divided into four parts.
The first four phrases concern the realization of *nirvāṇa* and the relinquishing of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
This refers to the "awakening to the ultimate truth" (*tattva*), which is the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Realizing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Penetrating deeply into the nature of phenomena refers to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Because one realizes the principle through these paths to fulfillment and abandons the state of fragmented existence (*pariccheda*), it is said that one leaves the ocean of birth and death.
Furthermore, it is called "detachment" because of the fear of birth and death.
Moreover, due to the absence of wisdom accompanied by skillful means, one realizes the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
and due to the absence of great compassion, one abandons and detaches from birth and death.
The second pair of phrases concerns abiding in emptiness and severing the fetters.

Regarding "abiding in emptiness" in the first instance: this refers to the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), which is also one of the two types of emptiness of the Tathāgata; therefore, it is called the "domain of the Tathāgata."
Because one accords with this portion alone, it is called "abiding securely.

The subsequent phrase refers to severing and abandoning the delusions of the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*) by means of dwelling in the emptiness of persons; these are the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) associated with the nine fetters (*nava-saṃyojana*) and the ten proclivities (*daśānuśaya*).
The second line of the third verse concerns mastery through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
It means that because one is unstained by the world, it says "not clinging to anything.
Because one travels everywhere through supernormal powers, it says "wandering through space."
The four instances of two phrases indicate the exhaustion of doubt and the firmness of faith, meaning that one has achieved indestructible faith (*avetyaprasāda*).
Another interpretation states:
these all refer to faith in the Buddha’s profound and sovereign dharmas of fruition; thus, it is clearly known that [the subject] is a great bodhisattva.
Third, among the various devas there are also two [sections]: enumerating the number and praising their virtues.
Within the praise of virtues, there are ten phrases, which are subsumed into five pairs.
The first pair praises the virtue of past causes, meaning they have already made offerings to past Buddhas and have long since benefited sentient beings.
From here downward, all passages praise the virtue of manifest activity (*samudācāra*).

The next two pairs praise the virtue of practicing compassion and entering into wisdom; that is to say, through uninterrupted compassionate mindfulness, one enters into wisdom for the sake of saving sentient beings.

The next two pairs of verses praise the virtue of manifesting purity while remaining within defilement; that is, not abandoning sentient beings in their state of defilement, yet bringing forth the Buddha’s truly pure Dharma.

The subsequent two pairs of verses praise the virtue of protection and maintenance; that is, protecting the resultant Dharma so that the correct teaching circulates, and maintaining the causal Dharma so that the realization of its nature is certain.
Furthermore, externally they are able to protect those who uphold the Dharma, while internally they themselves receive and maintain the Buddha’s true nature-dharma (*dharmatā*).
The latter two [verses] form a pair praising the virtues of their family heritage: namely, being born into the Buddha-family and performing the deeds that seek Buddhahood.
The cause of all-knowledge is called the "gate of wisdom" (*jñānamukha*); because it enables one to reach the wisdom of a Buddha, it is termed a "gate.
The preceding section on the Introduction is concluded.
In the second section, the Request, there are three parts:
First, the assembly’s thought of requesting; second, the thought of what is requested; third, the thought of the manifestation of the request.
Question:
According to the following passage, the śrāvakas are all like those who are deaf and blind; why, then, do they harbor identical doubts here?
Answer: Master Fayi explains: "Because the principle and the locus are not separated, they may share the same doubt.
However, because the great mind has not yet been accumulated, it should not occupy that position."
Another explanation states:
Because they were both present at the Jeta Grove, they made their request with a shared intention.
Because the universal eye had not yet opened, they were like those who are blind.
Another interpretation states:
He is in fact a bodhisattva, and thus his mindfulness is identical [to that of a buddha];
he manifests the traces of a śrāvaka, and is therefore like one who is blind, and so forth.
Within the requested text, there are sixty sentences in total.
An ancient master’s commentary states:
"The first thirty clarify the Buddha’s own entry into the Dharma-realm; the latter thirty clarify the Buddha’s causing others to enter the Dharma-realm."
Now, the explanation:
among the sixty [verses], the first ten invoke the dharmas that are fruits.
How is it known that what is invoked is the fruit?
This means that because those in the lower stages cannot fathom the subsequent ten luminosities,
and since they cannot know them, how can you now request them?
It is said that by the power of causes and conditions, those in the subsequent ten luminosities may also come to know them.
Although one possesses the power to know, it remains uncertain whether this assembly possesses the power of knowledge;
thus, the subsequent ten [verses] reveal that this assembly is endowed with the power of the spiritual faculties (*indriya*).
Even if the assembly possesses the necessary vessels, if there is no power of the Buddha, they would still be unable to know.
This refers to the next ten [perfections] which constitute the causes for the Buddha’s altruistic activity.

Although these causes for benefiting others are complete, if the functional result of manifesting altruistic activity were absent, there would likewise be no means by which [beings] could be made to know [the Buddha].
Next, the ten [verses] distinguish the function of the fruit in encompassing the production [of beings].
Since these conditions are complete, the conclusion of the request says: "I only pray that you will manifest [the Buddha-body]," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is explained:
Within this, the first thirty phrases constitute the invocation by mindfulness of the Dharma, while the latter thirty phrases constitute the invocation by mindfulness of his virtues.

Regarding the former, the first ten clarify the resultant dharmas that are invoked; the next ten clarify that [the Dharma] is profound, mysterious, and difficult to fathom; and the final ten clarify that it can be traversed through the convergence of conditions.

Regarding the beginning and middle [of this section], there are three inquiries: first, the unimpeded, effortless practice of compassion and wisdom, as explained in the "Nature-Arising" (Xingqi) Chapter;
second, the non-obstruction between the ultimate and conventional truths known by the Buddha’s wisdom, also as explained within the "Nature-Arising" realm;

and third, the boundless mindfulness and wisdom of the dhāraṇīs of the Buddha-ground, as distinguished by the Buddha Sustaining (Chi) among the ten Buddhas, and as explained in the "Inconceivable" (Bùsīyi) Chapter regarding the ten dhāraṇīs and so forth.

Fourth, the ten powers such as the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*), as well as the ten kinds of great strength such as Nārāyaṇa-dhvaja, also as described in that chapter;
fifth, the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) and the ten fearlessnesses;
sixth, the immeasurable oceans of samādhis, such as the lion’s sport (*siṃhavikrīḍita*).
The seven principles and merits, along with all the buddha-fields, are all that in which the body and wisdom of the Tathāgata abide, as explained in the "Inconceivable Chapter";

eighth, the eight supreme merits—the first two of which were termed the "Supreme Dharmas of the Buddha" in the Questions of the First Assembly—were discussed there in general terms, whereas here they are distinguished specifically by way of their merit to manifest their excellence;
ninth, the characteristics of the perfection of the three bodies and the ten bodies.
The fourteen knowledges and the ten knowledges are harmoniously integrated and mutually illuminating through principle and measure.
Furthermore, there is a version of the sūtra that contains an additional phrase here, which reads "the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
This may be an interpolation, or it may serve as a concluding summary of the preceding phrases.
Furthermore, these ten questions are for the most part identical to those asked in the first assembly; therefore, the framework used therein is appropriate for application here.
Moreover, among the ten, the first is general while the remaining nine are specific.

Within this classification, it should be understood that the first [of the ten powers] is the virtue of wisdom; the next three are the virtues of the application of wisdom; the next one is the virtue of great meditative concentration; the next one is the virtue of the basis; the next one is the virtue of supreme merit; and the final two are the virtues of body and wisdom.

Second, regarding that which cannot be measured by inferior levels: among the ten aforementioned qualities of the Tathāgata, because they are lofty, one cannot know them; because they are vast, one cannot fathom them; because they are profound, one cannot reach their bottom; and because they are manifold, one cannot contain them—these four are not the domain of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Because they are mysterious, one cannot contemplate them; and because they are subtle, one cannot observe them—these two are beyond the spheres of reflection (*cintā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Because it accords with the dharma-realm, it cannot be differentiated.
Because one is all, one cannot hear the wisdom that initiates [enlightenment].
Because it is not realized, it cannot be proclaimed or clarified.
Because it transcends all verbal discourse, it cannot be explained.

Furthermore, the first six [aspects] transcend the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*), and the latter four transcend the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*): that is, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) cannot differentiate them; the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) cannot elucidate them; the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) cannot proclaim them; and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) cannot expound them.
Another explanation:
these ten correspond to the preceding ten types, sequentially revealing the meaning of profundity; this may be understood by analogy.
Another explanation:
Regarding the first meaning, there are these ten; regarding this one gate, there are likewise the preceding ten. By analogy, it should be understood that there are one hundred gates and so forth.

Within the third section, "knowing through the convergence of conditions," the first four have the power of the Buddha as the condition (*pratyaya*), while the latter six have the power of the faculties (*indriya*) as the cause (*hetu*); only then can [the truth] be known.

Regarding the beginning and middle [of the sūtra], "the power maintained by the Buddha" refers to the Buddha’s power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). For example, he empowered the Bodhisattva Blue Lotus so that he might know the Buddha’s merits and preach the "Inconceivable Chapter" (*Acintyaparivarta*) and other sections.
Second, the power of mastery (*vaśitā-bala*) is the unimpeded power of transformation, such as when Mañjuśrī transformed Śāriputra so that he would come to know and expound the profound principle.
Third, the power of majestic spiritual authority (*prabhāva-bala*) is to secretly bestow majesty so that one may recognize virtue, such as causing Kāśyapa to know the mind of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the four powers of the original vows: these are the powers of the Buddha’s own original vows from the past; therefore, they cause others to know the Buddha’s profound virtues. Within the subsequent six [powers], they are as follows:

first, the power of having planted roots of goodness over many lifetimes in former existences; second, the power of having drawn near to spiritual friends of the One Vehicle over many lifetimes; third, the power of deep and penetrating pure faith in the present life; fourth, the power of aspiration and seeking for the aforementioned supreme Dharma; fifth, the power of the great bodhicitta produced by the true Dharma, unmixed with ignorance; and sixth, the power of a profound mind that single-mindedly seeks all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) without being mixed with the two vehicles.
Among these ten, one may discern each according to a single power, or two, three, or even up to ten kinds, in order to manifest their inexhaustibility.

In the second section, the "Request for the Virtue of Mindfulness" consisting of thirty phrases, the first ten verses praise the virtue of the audience’s capacity to receive [the teaching], while the latter twenty verses praise the Buddha’s virtue of being able to preach it.
In the beginning and middle [stages], because this mental faculty (*manas*) involves much deliberation, it is manifold.
From deliberation arises desire; when desire increases, it is termed "resolution" (*adhimokṣa*), which refers to the firm grasping of conviction.
Because speech is uttered according to understanding, regional dialects also differ; because the stages and positions of practice vary in quality, they are called "grounds" (*bhūmi*).
Because the faculties for receiving the Dharma differ in sharpness or dullness and maturity or immaturity, there are three grades, and thus they are called "faculties" (*indriya*).
Because the activities performed according to the faculties differ in their cultivation, they are called "the activity of skillful means" (*upāya-karman*).
Because the characteristics of the objects of focus are not uniform, they are called "objects" (*viṣaya*).

All of these take the fruit of Buddhahood as their condition, entering the Dharma through various distinctions—whether by relying on the Buddha’s light, or due to his preaching of the Dharma, and so forth.
Because they delight in hearing the teachings—whether shallow or profound, extensive or concise, each differing in degree—they are said to "delight in hearing the Dharma.

Second, regarding the praise of the Buddha’s ability to teach: the first ten [verses] contemplate the perfection of the causes of the Buddha’s teaching, while the latter ten contemplate the completeness of the resultant virtues of his teaching.
Among the first ten [sections], the first clarifies the initial aspiration for bodhicitta made in the past;
the second concerns the initiation of practice based on that aspiration, hence it is called "purifying the pāramitās";
and the third concerns the entry into the stages upon the completion of practice, hence it is called "the various bhūmis."
Fourth, because practice is perfected through the stages, it is called "fulfilling practice";
fifth, because all practices are said in general to possess both types of adornment, it is called "the bodhisattva's adornment";
sixth, because one specific practice is skillfully shown to encompass all others, adorning one another, it is called "adornment through skillful means."

Seventh, the specific manifestation of self-benefiting conduct is subsumed under the same name as before, "Adornment of the Path," because the path has the meaning of cause and extends through to the fruit;

eighth, the specific clarification of altruistic conduct is skillful and manifold, hence it is called "Emerging from the Ocean of Expedient Means," while the meaning of adornment is the same as before;
ninth, the two benefits are unimpeded and mutually fused to their ultimate extent, with each encompassing all to constitute the conduct of Samantabhadra, hence it is called "Sovereign Adornment."

Having received bodies for over ten *kalpas* and constantly cultivated supreme practices, it is called the "Ocean of Jātaka Tales. This indicates that because the bodies of these previous births are as numerous as the ocean, and because he practiced through many bodies, his practices were likewise vast and manifold.
The latter ten [verses] clarify that the Buddha’s teaching on the perfection of the fruit is complete. First, since the causes have already been perfected, what is there to be attained?
It is said to be the mastery of bodhi.
Second, having already attained bodhi...
What is its purpose?
It is to turn the wheel of Dharma with mastery.
Third, where is it turned?
These are all pure lands.
What is the benefit of the fourth transformation?
It is said to be the adornment of the realm of sentient beings.
What is the fifth transformation?
It is the Dharma of the Dharma-King.
What wisdom is used for the sixth transformation?
This refers to the wisdom of the illumination of the Path.
As for the seven Buddhas’ wisdom illuminating the Dharma, by what means do sentient beings awaken?
It is because they possess the sovereign power to enter the realms where sentient beings dwell.
What benefit is gained by the eight entrances reaching the locus of the recipient?
It is said: because they constitute a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Ninth, by what means is merit accomplished?
This refers to what is called the "attainment of merit" (*dāna*).
Regarding "attainment" (*da*), the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* uses the term *dāna*, which here means "material giving.
The Vinaya states that the name for the method of giving is *dakṣiṇā*; it also means "guiding," as it leads others toward benefit, and is thus termed "attainment" (*da*).
The *Xiyuji* states: "The correct term is *dakṣiṇā*, or *dākṣiṇī*; this means 'right.
It is so named because one receives the offerings of others with the right hand, thereby generating merit for them."
Now, it is clarified that the Buddha bestows merit upon sentient beings; therefore, it is said that "merit reaches the coffin.
By what means does he transform and gather sentient beings?
It is by the three wheels:
The wheel of supernormal power of the body-karma destroys doubt and establishes faith;
the wheel of correct teaching of the speech-karma destroys delusion and establishes understanding;
the wheel of mindfulness of the mind-karma destroys the fetters and establishes practice.
The concluding invitation may be understood.
The section on the invitation is finished.

Regarding the third section, the Section on Samādhi: as for why he enters [samādhi], it was previously asked that his vows be fully manifested; therefore, he now enters meditative concentration to manifest them for him.
Why is it that in previous assemblies the multitude entered meditative absorption after [the teaching], whereas here it is placed first?
Explanation:
Previously, it was clarified how one enters reality from its signs; now, it is distinguished how function arises based on the essence.
Furthermore, whereas previously it was due to the person entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), now, at the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), there is mastery; thus, they are not the same.
Why does the Buddha himself enter meditative concentration in this assembly?
It is to signify that the liberation and mastery within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are fully realized only by the Buddha, who has exhausted the source.

The text contains four sections: first, the conditions for entering meditative concentration; second, the causes for entering meditative concentration; third, the actual entry into meditative concentration; and fourth, the purpose of entering meditative concentration.

Regarding the first section, "knowing the thoughts of others" refers to employing the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) to comprehend the preceding doubts; this constitutes the condition for entering meditative concentration.
Second, by means of the four kinds of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the cause for entering meditative absorption is clarified.
That is to say, entering absorption to benefit sentient beings must take great compassion as its foundation; therefore, it is established as the cause.
The "one body" refers to the body that benefits sentient beings; it is established through the accumulation of compassion and is the very body upon which samādhi relies.

Regarding the "two gates," although the Buddha possesses gates such as great wisdom, great concentration, and great compassion, because he now wishes to increase the benefit for others, he relies solely on the gate of great compassion.
Furthermore, this door of compassion is opened in order to gather all classes of beings.
As for the "three heads," this clarifies the benefit of sentient beings; since all that is undertaken is preceded by great compassion, it is designated as the "head."

Regarding the four methods that accord with skillful means: although compassion is primary, if one lacks skillful means, then even if the compassionate dharma accords with the faculties and conditions of sentient beings, there is no way to cause them to enter the Dharma-realm together.
These four also represent the gradual progression from the Buddha toward the sentient beings.
Third, "Entering Samādhi Proper" clarifies the functional application of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and is named after a metaphor.

This means that when a lion displays his prowess, his sensory faculties expand, the hair on his body stands erect, and he manifests his majestic power; through the manner of his roar, he causes other beasts to lose their courage and flee cowering, while causing the lion cubs to increase their own ferocity and attain full growth.
Now the Buddha is likewise:

first, he stirs his body of the Great Compassion of the Dharma-realm; second, he opens the root-gates of Great Compassion; third, he raises the vanguard of the bristling hairs of compassion; fourth, he manifests the majestic power that accords with the capacities of beings, roaring the Dharma-gate of the Dharma-realm, causing the beasts of the two vehicles to hide away in deafness and blindness, while increasing for the Bodhisattvas, the children of the Buddha, hundreds of thousands of oceans of samādhis and oceans of dhāraṇīs.
Because they are similar in this way, they are used as metaphors.
Furthermore, the ten kinds of "lion’s playful strides" (*siṃhavikrīḍita*) from the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*) are discussed in detail herein.

Fourth, the section beginning with "causing all" clarifies the intent of entering meditative concentration; that is, by manifesting these pure dharmas of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one causes the multitude to behold and enter it, which is called "delighting in the Dharma."
The section on the divisions of samādhi is concluded.
The fourth section, on the manifestation of the pure land, has three parts:
first, the perfection of the receptacle world; second, the perfection of the world of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment; and third, the perfection of the world of sentient beings.
The first part has two sections:
first, clarifying how this Jeta Grove manifests as a pure land; second, by analogy, concluding that the ten directions likewise manifest pure lands.
Within the former section, there are also two parts:
The first part correctly reveals the adornments, and the latter part sets forth their causes.
Within the former, there are three sections:
first, the adornment of the multi-storied pavilions; second, the adornment of the gardens and groves; and third, the adornment of the sky.

Guangtong said: "The 'Austere Emptiness' represents unconditioned dependent origination; the 'Austere Garden' represents conditioned dependent origination; and the 'Austere Pavilion' reveals dependent origination as the self-substance."
The first two sections of the beginning are as follows:
first, the vastness of the locus is boundless.
That which is suddenly expansive refers to employing provisional means to reveal the ultimate reality, thereby shattering deluded attachments to manifest the Dharma.
Second, the actual manifestation of the adornments. Within this, there are ten types: first, the golden ground;

second, from "all mani-jewels" downward, clarifying the arrangement of treasures upon the ground; third, from "lapis lazuli" downward, clarifying the pillars of the pavilions; fourth, from "Jambū-river gold" downward, clearly explaining the completion of the pavilions; fifth, from "mani-jewels" downward, explaining the installation of nets atop the pavilions; sixth, the erection of precious banners; seventh, the hanging of pennants and canopies; eighth, the emission of light that illuminates the dharma-realm; ninth, the external adornment with various jewels; and tenth, the stairways on the four sides made accessible for ascent and descent.
Within the two types of adorned gardens, the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is the cause.
That they suddenly become vast and equal reveals the extent of their breadth.
From the phrase "various jewels" (*nānā-ratna*) downward, there are likewise ten kinds of adornments:
1. A general summary;
2. the ground strewn with jewels; 3.
the jeweled walls;
Fourth, trees made of the four jewels;
fifth, rivers of fragrant incense;
sixth, many multi-storied pavilions.
Seventh, it is illuminated by seven rays of light;
eighth, its ground is adorned with jewels;
ninth, it emits wondrous fragrances.
There are seventeen kinds of precious banners erected.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of adornments of space:

first, celestial jewel palaces; second, fragrant trees; third, Mount Sumeru; fourth, precious music; fifth, jewel trees; sixth, jewel thrones; seventh, jewel images; eighth, pearl nets; ninth, multi-storied pavilions; and tenth, the music of liberation.
The second section, "Manifesting the Adornments," contains two parts:
first, the interrogation, which asks why these inconceivable adornments exist;
second, the explanation, which consists of ten phrases.
First, because it is produced from the inconceivable roots of goodness of the Tathāgata; this refers to the cause.
Second, because it is the untainted dharma of the fruit of Buddhahood; this refers to the essence of the fruit.
The following clarifies the function of the fruit:
(3) a general presentation of supernormal powers;
(4) a specific presentation of the power of physical transformation.
Verses 56 and 57 clarify the subtle characteristic of the mutual interpenetration of body and land without obstruction.
Verses 78 and 79 manifest past Buddhas illuminating present lands.
Verses 90 and 91 show Buddhas emerging from and manifesting within lands.

These aforementioned adornments are all such as the essence and function of the Buddha-fruit; they cannot be known by those in other stages, and for this reason, they are all described as "inconceivable.
The foregoing concludes the section on the Jeta Grove in one direction.
Among the two types of fetters (*saṃyojana*), this refers to [the category] exemplified by the Jeta Grove and so forth.
All dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) are universally pervasive throughout the dharma-realm, appearing as lands in the same manner as this one.

In terms of its gross manifestation, this site was constructed by Sudatta; yet in terms of its subtle reality, it is said to pervade the entire Dharma-realm, encompassing the ten directions and exhausting the three periods of time.
Because the universal does not obstruct the particular, Sudatta was able to newly construct it;
because the coarse is not different from the subtle, that which was constructed was micro-fine and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
Such is the case with his constant presence on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and his manifestation at the place where he rested his foot; all are of this same category.
The two Tathāgatas, being equal in fulfillment, possess clear wisdom and perfect enlightenment regarding the world;
each of them has appeared within this manifested realm, and both have come together to this full Jeta Grove.
Within the third section on the world of sentient beings, there are two parts:
first, the bodhisattvas fill [the realm], and second, ten kinds of clouds of offerings rain down.
This concludes the preceding section on the manifestation of the pure land.
In the fifth assembly, the section on the gathering of the new multitude, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the multitude gathered;
second, the phrase "all because of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power," which explains the reason for the gathering.
The preceding section also has two parts:
first, the individual collection of the ten directions; second, the general praise of their virtues.
Within the former, the ten directions constitute ten sections.
Among these, the first two and the sixth each have nine gates, while the others have ten.
First, regarding the nine meanings of the eastern direction:
(1) the distance of the place of assembly, meaning that it is beyond unspeakable numbers of lands as numerous as atoms, which signifies the profound depth of the Dharma.
The second is the world-ocean named Vajra-ādi (Vajra, etc.), which symbolizes the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) that serves as the basis.
The term "vajra" has two meanings: first, firmness; second, sharpness.
Clouds also have two meanings:
first, pervasion; second, moistening.
Clarity and purity also have two meanings:
First, Universal Illumination; second, Freedom from Defilement.
Now, consulting the Sanskrit original, these names are merely terms for clarity and purity; both are the Sanskrit name Vairocana.
A lamp also has two meanings: first, dispelling darkness; second, illuminating what is present.
Adornment also has two meanings:
first, embellishing phenomena; second, adorning principle.
The three Buddha-names and so forth represent the perfect fruition that depends [upon the cause]; that is to say, their clarity and purity are the same as before.
"Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode) is the Sanskrit name Śrī, which refers to the supreme virtue of auspiciousness.
The King is manifest in his sovereignty.
The four headings above list the names of the Bodhisattvas, manifesting the causal factors of the dependent aspect.
Their clarity and purity are the same as before.
The vow is the great vow of the self-nature.
Its radiance shatters ignorance and illuminates the dharma-realm.
It arrives together with its five retinues.
Sixth is the cloud of making offerings, which refers to filling the void with material offerings such as celestial flowers.
Seventh is the offering of approaching the Buddha to pay homage.
Eighth is manifesting pavilions and flower-seats in their respective directions and sitting cross-legged upon them.
The body is covered by a net of nine jewels, manifesting supreme virtues as natural adornments.
If one follows the other directions mentioned below, a tenth item is added—either a crest-jewel or a celestial crown—to signify his supreme characteristics as a distinguishing mark.
The names of the Buddhas in other world-systems and so forth may be understood by analogy with this explanation.

Regarding the offerings in the south, such as "wondrous incense" and other miscellaneous items that fill all Buddha-worlds: these are all dharmadhātu-dharmamukhas (Dharma-gates of the Dharma-realm), for it is through their accomplishment that these offerings are made. Therefore, they may be described as filling empty space, pervading the Dharma-realm, encompassing all lands, or suffusing the realm of sentient beings; in all cases, there is no obstruction, and while they interpenetrate, they do not become confused.
Among the offerings in the western direction, those named "Clouds of Mount Sumeru" manifest the characteristics of the Wondrous High Mountain possessing all virtues.
