Gradually reaching the center, the sun sets as he enters the city; this signifies that the stage of practice has reached its ultimate consummation.
The third section, beginning with "Pervadingly," clarifies the acts of seeing, paying homage, and making a formal request.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, the investigation;

second, from "In the middle of the night" onwards, seeing his environment (*niśraya-vipāka*), which refers to the light of the Dharma upon which he relies, for it destroys the darkness of the two extremes.
Third, from "At that time, Sudhana" onwards, one sees his primary retribution (*vipāka*).
"The dawn breaks" means that as obstructions are exhausted, the stage [of realization] becomes manifest.
"Ascending the mountain" means that he has attained a state corresponding to that stage.
"Seeing the non-Buddhists" refers to the realization of the realm of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-dhātu*).
"The ten thousand Brahmās and others" refers to the perfection of the principal and the retinue.
The fourfold expression of reverence and formal request may be understood accordingly.
The fourth section, "Answering and Speaking," bestows the Dharma-realm upon oneself.
Within this, there are four parts;
first is the praise of the arousal of the bodhicitta.
1. "I have already established myself" and below indicate the essential qualities of one's own dharma-gate; 2.
"By means of equality" and below manifest the functional activity of the dharma; 3.
"I alone" and below conclude with one's own self-nature.

Regarding "reaching all places" at the beginning and middle [of the stages], this clarifies that the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) have been fulfilled; it refers to the fact that the tenth stage, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), possesses universal knowledge.
There are two meanings:

first, relying on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to give rise to wisdom that universally illumines the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); second, relying on meditative concentration to give rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) that reach everywhere.
The final two lines explain these two meanings, which should be understood respectively.
Within the functions of the three types of karma, there are also two:
first, the function of the wisdom of universal observation; second, the function of unconditioned universality.

Regarding the three sections within the first part: first, the raising of the light of impartial wisdom; second, from "observing" downward, the illumination of the differences among sentient beings' capacities; and third, from "with wondrous wisdom" downward, the preaching of the Dharma to bring benefit.
"Furthermore," the second section on the universal nature of non-action has two parts:
first, the inscrutability of its function; second, the manifestation of its types throughout the ten directions.
Various forms of wisdom constitute mental karma, while physical forms and sounds constitute bodily and vocal karma.
The phrase "it is also like this" has two meanings:

first, it clarifies that the forms and images manifested by the non-active *ṛddhipāda* (supernormal power) are likewise like the skillful wisdom that pervades the ten directions; thus it says, "it is also like this.

Second, it uses the city of Saṃkhyāvatī as a model for Jambudvīpa, Jambudvīpa as a model for the trichiliocosm, and the trichiliocosm as a model for the worlds of the ten directions; thus it says, "it is also like this."
This concludes the double summary of the three karmas endowed with the supernormal power of knowledge (*jñāna-abhijñā*).
Regarding the fifth section, "The Great Bodhisattvas" and below, there are ten phrases that look upward to recommend further advancement:
first, "the body equaling the number of sentient beings" reveals that his supernormal power of going everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-ṛddhi*) surpasses that of himself.
The next single phrase refers to the fault of the meditative concentration that serves as the basis;
the following two phrases refer to the fault of the [wisdom] produced therefrom;
and the remaining phrases refer to the fault of the wisdom produced therefrom.
“‘I shall... and so forth concludes that which does not belong to oneself.
This ends the tenth line.
From here begins the fourth major section, consisting of ten points of knowledge, which elucidates the virtues of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

The initial section on the "Land of the Flavor of Ambrosia" and so forth clarifies the first dedication: "Rescuing and Protecting Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings.
Within this, the five meanings are the same as those previously explained.
Regarding the initial exhortation to practice by citing the Dharma, "the flavor of ambrosia" refers to the supreme flavor of skillful means for saving living beings.
The Elder was as described previously.

Because his virtuous marks were pure and superior, he was named Blue Lotus; because he was skillfully knowledgeable of all fragrances, he was further named Fragrance; thus, from both his marks and his wisdom, he was called Blue Lotus Flower Fragrance.
The second section, "Then Sudhana," and so forth, concerning the pursuit according to the instructions, has four parts:
first, paying respects and withdrawing;

second, "At that time," and so forth, generating superior aspiration, which contains four sub-sections: first, non-attachment to the world; second, "Always delighting in," and so forth, single-mindedly longing for the Great Practice; third, "Single-mindedly seeking these," and so forth, concluding his intention; fourth, "Gradually traveling," and so forth, clarifying the arrival at subsequent stages.
The third section, "Seeing and Paying Homage and Submitting a Petition," has three parts:
first, the expression of homage;

second, from "He said" (*āha*) onwards, the presentation of the intent in ten phrases—the first five seeking the fruit of supreme virtue, and the latter five aspiring to the causal practices; third, the actual submission of the petition.
Third, from "but [he] did not yet know" onwards, he asks about what is required.
Fourth, from "he replied" onwards, he reveals his own *dharmadhātu*.
This section contains two parts:
First, the praise for the arousal of the mind;
second, the actual bestowal of the Dharma-realm, which first presents the dharma-gates that are to be known and subsequently concludes with their names.
Within the former [section], there are three parts:

First, the substances of fragrance to be known are listed; there are thirty kinds. Among these, one first understands the perfuming of the mundane environment and its inhabitants (*sāśraya-dharmadhātu*); second, from "the eradication of afflictions" onwards, one understands the perfuming of supramundane correct practice, by which the Bodhisattva benefits sentient beings.
Second, from the passage "The arising of that fragrance" onwards, it is explained that there are ten aspects to the meaning of the dharma of fragrance:

first, knowing the cause from which it arises; second, knowing the place to which the fragrance reaches; third, knowing the benefit once it has reached its destination; fourth, the perfection of what is accomplished; fifth, the ability to bring about joy and purity; sixth, causing one to be free from affliction and to dwell in peace; seventh, skillful means for entering the Dharma; eighth, the limits of what is known; ninth, the karmic activities performed; and tenth, the ultimate foundation.
3. From "Good son" onwards, the functional application of fragrance is known; briefly, ten types are enumerated.
First, it is known through ten internal meanings.
Regarding "that which arises from the battle of dragons," this refers to the knowledge of its origination.
That clouds of light cover the Land of Sweet Flavor signifies knowledge of what is practiced.
That fragrant water descends signifies knowledge of accomplishment.
That the body is clothed in golden color signifies knowledge of being fully endowed.
"Delighting in the fragrance upon hearing it" refers to knowing purity.
"Extinguishing all illnesses and so forth" refers to knowing security.
"Being single-mindedly directed toward it" refers to skillful means.
"Knowing them" refers to the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).
"Expounding the Dharma for them" refers to the practice (*karmapatha*).
"Causing their resolve to be non-retrogressive" refers to the root (*mūla*).

The nine types of substances, such as ox-head incense (*gandha-mūla*), each possess ten meanings; because they are abbreviated in the text, one should apply these [ten meanings] by analogy to those instances where only two or three are mentioned.
*Sindhava* is the name for rock salt; here it is translated as "stone salt."

In the fifth section, "Looking Upward with Reliance," first the object of reliance is presented. Within this, there are two parts: first, the removal of obstacles; second, from the word "wisdom" onwards, the accomplishment of the fragrance of the three stages of training for transcending the world.
Finally, from the words "I shall," the conclusion is made that these are not within one's own domain.
The first dedication is concluded.

Regarding the second, the "Indestructible Dedication," within the section on spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), the initial presentation of the Dharma to encourage practice is as follows: the city named "Pavilion" represents the manifestation of Great Compassion arising from the excellence of reliance upon wisdom.
The Master of the Sea, Sovereign One (Sāgarasena), is so named because he is able to skillfully penetrate and ferry others across both the ocean of the Buddha-dharma and the ocean of birth and death;
this can be understood from his teaching and inquiries.
The second section, "Entering According to the Teaching," has three parts:
first, withdrawing after offering words of respect;
second, giving rise to sublime mindfulness while on the road, which includes first contemplating the correctness of the Dharma; [and third, contemplating the excellence of the teacher].

2. "Furthermore, he acts" and below: the recollection of the Dharma depends on the person; it gives rise to the mind of seeking, first through general recollection, and subsequently, from "Why... onwards, through detailed explanation; 3.
From "He forms this thought" onwards, up to the point where he investigates that [object].
The third section, "Seeing, Paying Respect, and Submitting a Petition," contains three parts:
first, seeing the location—referring to places such as seashores—which indicates the site where the Dharma is preached;
second, paying respect; and third, submitting the petition, both of which are easily understood.
The fourth section, beginning with "He replied," demonstrates his own *dharmadhātu*.
This consists of two parts:
first, praising the aspiration that enables him to ask the question; second, from "I have accomplished" onwards, presenting the Dharma to bestow it upon him.
The preceding section has three parts:

first, praising and inquiring about the essence of the practice; second, from "attaining" (*caidad*) onwards, clarifying the function of the practice; third, from "sarvajñā" (*薩婆若*) onwards, clarifying the fruit attained through the practice.
Within the second [section], the conferral of the Dharma, there are also three parts:
first, the presentation of the name and essence; second, the clarification of its function, beginning with "In this"; and third, the conclusion regarding one's own scope, beginning with "I only."

Regarding the beginning and middle [of the practice]: the practitioner of pure conduct who is the Banner of Great Compassion uses his preeminent great compassion to rescue sentient beings from the mountain of birth and death; this is called "pure conduct."
Within the second section on "karmic activity," there are two parts:
first, saving sentient beings through ascetic practices within this city;
second, from the passage "I know the ocean" onwards, skillfully understanding the characteristics of the sea and thereby saving sentient beings by entering the sea.
The preceding section has three parts:
first, the expedient means for bestowing the Dharma; second, from "extensively explains" downward, the actual exposition of bestowing the Dharma; third, from "I abide" downward, the conclusion.
Within the context of conferring the Dharma, the arousal of bodhicitta through the awakening of one's past roots of goodness is the general [category];
the three subsequent minds are the specific ones.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "One who arouses bodhicitta arouses three kinds of mind:"
First is the straightforward mind, because it correctly contemplates the true nature of reality;
second is the profound mind, because it delights in cultivating all virtuous practices;
third is the mind of great compassion, because it rescues and delivers all suffering sentient beings.

The section beginning with "Eliminating birth and death" below reveals the functional activity of the three types of mind: first, the straightforward mind (*ṛjukacitta*) which is free from suffering; second, the compassionate mind (*karuṇācitta*) which, starting from "gathering in," embraces sentient beings; and third, the profound mind (*gambhīracitta*) which, starting from "attaining all," realizes the Dharma.
The lower section concludes with the increase of benefit for sentient beings.

Regarding the second part, "knowing the ocean" within the increase of benefit for sentient beings, there are two sections: first, the wisdom that knows the ocean; second, from "I have already accomplished... onwards, the actual manifestation of the increase of benefit.
Regarding the preceding section: the first ten phrases concern the knowledge of jewels; next is the knowledge of the difficulties of the dragon palaces and so forth.
The "Great Body" (Mahākāya) should be an asura, because the four classes of asuras all reside beneath the sea.
Next, regarding the knowledge of the water’s color and the timing of the winds and so forth:
within the second section on "Correctly Producing Benefit," the phrase "one who has accomplished such wisdom" restates what was previously understood.

Consequently, acting as a guide for entering the ocean, one preaches the ocean of Dharma to deliver sentient beings; thus it says, "for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, one enters the ocean," and so forth.
The phrase "causing all to" (*xi lìng*) below specifically reveals the characteristics of the benefits, which consist of ten oceans of dharmas:
the first four are the ocean of self-benefit, and the latter six are the ocean of benefiting others.
Below, there are two concluding sections:
First, the vow for benefit is not in vain; second, the vow consists of a single dharma.
Regarding the fifth section, "The Great Elements" and below, there are two parts within the upward inference:

first, the presentation of what is inferred, which begins with the inference of the ocean of one's own practice; second, from "By means of skillful expedients" onwards, the inference of the ocean of benefiting others.
The subsequent section beginning with "I shall" concludes that [the merit] does not belong to oneself.
This ends the second dedication.

Regarding the third, the dedication equal to that of all Buddhas, within the context of the field of knowledge (*jñeya*), the initial passage cites the Dharma to exhort practice toward the internal: as for the name of the city, "Delightful," it refers to a realm already equal to a Buddha-field, which one should aspire to and delight in.
The Elder Anuttara-jina (The Unsurpassed Victor) was so named because he had attained supreme supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) beyond which nothing could surpass him.
Regarding the second section, "Entering According to the Teaching," there are three parts:
first, withdrawing after offering words of respect; second, reflecting on the Dharma while on the road; and third, seeking [the truth] upon arrival.

Within the section on "Contemplating the Dharma," there are two parts: first, the expansion of one's own portion; second, from "Cultivation" downward, the cultivation of the eight stages of superior progress.
Third, from "To the East of the City" downward, the clarification of the vision, reverence, and formal request, which contains three sub-sections:
the first clarifies the location of the physical environment (*upādāya-vastu*).
Regarding "the groves to the east of the city" and so forth: these provide the convenience for dwelling while gathering and transforming beings within the city.
Teaching the Dharma there specifically clarifies the manner of such gathering and transformation.
Second, from "At that time" onwards, [the text describes] seeing [the Buddha] and paying homage.
Third, regarding the section beginning with "He addressed [the Buddha] in white" (*śuklavāda*), within this petition: first, he prostrated himself for a long time, using his body to express his mind;
then, he repeatedly uttered his own name, using speech to express his mind, thereby manifesting the utmost depth of his earnest entreaty.
Furthermore, this reveals that [the listener] is already a fit vessel for practice, expressing the hope that he will preach the Dharma.
The fourth section demonstrates two aspects within his own dharma-realm:
first, praising his arousal of the bodhicitta as a skillful means for conferring the Dharma.
Second, from "I have accomplished" onwards is the actual conferral of the Dharma upon oneself, which consists of three parts:

first, the title that presents it as a whole; second, the explanation of the meaning and function of the Dharma starting with "What is..."; and third, the conclusion that attributes the Dharma to its source, beginning with "I only..."
At the beginning and middle, the supernormal power that reaches everywhere where sentient beings dwell is called "reaching all destinies.
Within this, preaching the Dharma to benefit and increase [the roots of goodness] of others is called "adornment of pure conduct."
This reaches all realms of existence spontaneously and effortlessly; therefore, it is said to be "without support and without effort.
Because it is not sustained by the power of another, it is said to be "without support."
Because it is not produced through one's own volitional effort, it is called "unconditioned" (anabhisaṃskṛta).
This refers to its pervasiveness in accordance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
In the commentary, there is first a formal inquiry, followed by the actual explanation.

In the formal explanation, first, having reached all realms of existence within these three thousandfold world systems, he teaches the Dharma to benefit sentient beings and establishes them in pure conduct and adornments.
"Various treatises" refers to the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and so forth.
2. From "In this way" down to "all realms in the ten directions," it constitutes the adornment of pure conduct.
From "I only" onwards, he concludes his own scope.

In the fifth section, from "The great [beings]" onwards, within the context of looking upward to recommend superior progress, there are three parts: first, clarifying the pervasiveness of the physical action (*kāyakarman*), meaning that the body and so forth are equal to the lands without depending on supernatural power; thus, it surpasses what preceded, and this is what is being recommended. Second, from "Having attained" onwards, it clarifies the verbal action (*vākkarman*). Third, from "Discerning" onwards, it clarifies the mental action (*manaskarman*).
“‘I shall’... and so forth concludes that it is not known by oneself.
This completes the dedication of all Buddhas.

Regarding the fourth [section], the dedication of reaching all places within the context of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), there are also three parts in the initial exhortation to practice by citing the Dharma:
First, he indicates the location; second, he identifies the person; third, he instructs on how to inquire.
That the country is named "Enduring the Difficult" (Kṣāntivādin) signifies the ability to realize that which is difficult to realize.
"Kaliṅga" is translated here as "the time of strife."
"Badhi" is correctly transcribed as "vana," which means "forest.
It refers to that bodhisattva preaching the Dharma within this forest to destroy obstacles; thus, it is called "strife" (or "battle").
To manifest the principle amidst contention is also called "difficult forbearance.
A *bhikṣuṇī* manifests compassion and pure wisdom.
She is named "The Lion’s Vigorous Dash" because her pure wisdom is fearless and she definitively expounds the Dharma.
The second section, "Entering According to the Teaching," has three parts:
first, departing after offering words of respect; second, arriving and conducting an investigation; third, indicating the location.
According to the Vinaya, the nuns all reside at Rājagṛha, for it is by relying on external protection that they are able to pursue the long path.
The third section, "Seeing, Paying Respect, and Making the Request," also has three parts:
first, seeing; second, paying respect; and third, making the request.
Within the initial section on "seeing," there are also three parts:
First, seeing the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment); second, seeing the *sambhoga-vipāka* (the inhabitants); third, a summary of their extraordinary nature.
Regarding the first, the pure land as the *niśraya-vipāka*, six points are briefly revealed;
the first is seeing the adornments of the great trees, of which eight types are briefly enumerated.
Second, he further beheld that garden’s streams and cascades flowing down into the jewel-encrusted ponds.

As for the water of eight virtues (*aṣṭāṅgopeta-vāri*), they are: first, light; second, cool; third, soft; fourth, delicious; fifth, pure; sixth, odorless; seventh, refreshing when drunk; and eighth, free from ailment after drinking.
Third, from "under each and every tree" downward, the arrangement and adornment of the seats is described.
Fourth, from "immeasurable adornments" downward, various kinds of adornments are clarified.
Fifth, from "Sudhana saw" downward, their causes are revealed; that is to say, they are all accomplished through supramundane roots of goodness and wisdom that is like an illusion.
Sixth, from "Three Thousand" onwards, it clarifies that the fruit-activity is sovereign, unobstructed, and unhindered.
Within the second section, "Seeing the Primary Retribution," there are two parts:
first, seeing [the Buddhas] seated universally upon all thrones, with their supreme virtues manifest and glorified.
Within this, first there is the universal seating, followed by the manifestation of virtues through ten similes.
As for Varuṇa, this means "water"; he should be the Buddha of the Water Deity, for it is said that merely seeing him brings about benefit.
Second, from "The Place of Vision" (*jñānasthāna*) onwards, it clarifies how he sits everywhere in the place of vision and extensively expounds the essentials of the Dharma;

herein there are five parts: first, preaching the Dharma for the eight classes of beings; second, from "Those who delight in the Śrāvaka vehicle" onwards, preaching the Dharma for those of the two vehicles; third, from "For those who delight in the Mahāyāna" onwards, preaching the Dharma for Bodhisattvas; fourth, from "The place of vision is thus" onwards, summarizing the benefits of the transformation; fifth, from "Why is this? onwards, explaining the reasons therefor.

Regarding the initial teaching on the inexhaustible for the Śuddhāvāsa deities: because the forms of those deities are the most pure among all forms, yet they are impermanent and subject to exhaustion, [the Buddha] taught them the supramundane nature of inexhaustibility.

Regarding the "Universal and Wondrous Sound" spoken for the Brahmā gods: among those in the world who consider their own voices to be excellent, he speaks for them of the universal and wondrous sound that is the supreme flow of the Dharma-realm.
Regarding the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, because they exercise mastery over the world, he speaks for them of the mastery of the Bodhisattvas.
For the gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, he taught the dharma of pure conduct, adorned with virtuous qualities.
For the Tuṣita Heaven, he taught the "Revolution of the Heart-Treasury," which refers to the great dedication that leads to non-retrogression.
For the Yāma Heaven, he overturned their "measured adornments" and taught them "immeasurable adornments.
For the Śakra Heaven, he preached so as to cause them to cultivate weary detachment from the five desires.

Regarding the teaching for the dragon kings on the skillful means to rescue and protect sentient beings: it refers to the skillful means of sending down rain to relieve sentient beings, as well as using the Dharma to save the dragons from the sufferings of the *garuḍas* and others.
For Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others—the term "and others" including the remaining three Heavenly Kings—he preached the Dharma of inexhaustible practice.
For the Mahoragas and others, he taught the skillful adornment of wisdom and principle.

For the Garuḍas and others, he preached the Dharma of relinquishing great power within the ocean of the world, so that within the ocean of birth and death, they might be rendered fearless through the power of compassion and wisdom.
For the *kiṃnara*s, he spoke of the Buddha’s wisdom-light of correct practice to cause them to shatter their attachment to pleasure.
For the *mahoraga*s, he spoke of the Buddha as one who brings joy; because the nature of snakes is prone to anger, they feel joy upon hearing of the Buddha.
For those human beings, he expounds the supreme path that transcends the world;
for the rākṣasas, he teaches compassion so as not to allow them to take life.

Regarding the section below for those of the two vehicles: first, for those who delight in the Śrāvaka vehicle, he speaks of the "light of supreme wisdom" in order to cause them to abandon the limited wisdom of the small vehicle and to delight in the light of the Mahāyāna wisdom.
This is taught for the sake of those who delight in the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, so that they may abandon inferior pleasures and [aspire to] the Buddha’s supreme merits.

Below, it clarifies the teaching for those of the Mahāyāna: first, for those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), it explains the light of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); next, for those on the stages, starting from the first stage, it explains the ten great vows; the remaining nine stages may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the statement "explaining the wisdom-vajra to the Vajrapāṇis," this refers to the explanation of the wisdom of the vajra-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) after the completion of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), which destroys subtle attachments and the like.

Since this bhikṣuṇī expounds the Dharma for bodhisattvas of the tenth stage and others, it is clear that she is not an ordinary person occupying a provisional rank; therefore, she must be at the stage of dedication (pariṇāmanā).
4. From "Seeing thus" onwards is the summary of the benefits of transformation.

5. From "Why is this? onwards is the explanation of the underlying cause; within the section on "By means of this, the nun accomplished one million [stages]," ten gateways of Prajñā are briefly cited, which are the very dharma-gates and so forth previously explained.
Third, from "Sudhana sees" onwards, the summary of the marvelous sights and sounds can be understood.

Second, from "With his five limbs" onwards, it clarifies the performance of reverence; because the faculties and conditions correspond to one another, he perceives his own body pervading all places where [the Buddhas] reside, circumambulating them all to the right, thereby equaling those [Buddhas] who have entered therein.
Furthermore, this is also the dedication that reaches all places, because it accords with the mastery of the mind.
Third, the section beginning with "He addressed [the Buddha]" (白言) can be understood as the formal request.
Fourth, the section beginning with "I have accomplished" (我成就) correctly demonstrates his own dharma-realm.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, the designation of the name; second, the manifestation of the essence; third, the discernment of the function;
and fourth, the conclusion regarding the stage. Regarding the first: "the bodhisattva’s foundation of all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā-tala) has three meanings:

First, this Bodhisattva attains the functional wisdom of the *prajñā* of a million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, reaching the very source and bottom of all the Buddha’s omniscience; as stated in the preceding text, he even preaches the Dharma for Bodhisattvas of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi-bhūmi*), a feat impossible for those on lower stages, and thus he attains this name.
Second, the light of his two wisdoms suddenly illuminates the three periods of time, exhausting the realm of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); therefore, it is used as his name.
Third, he extensively offers worship, reaching the very source and bottom of the wisdom of the eight phases of a Buddha’s life; hence he receives this name.
Second, from "The Great Sage" onwards, the essence [of the Prajñāpāramitā] is clarified.
Within this, there is first a question and subsequently an answer.
The phrase "Wisdom-light and so forth" clarifies that Prajñā is endowed with all virtues.
"In a single thought-moment" means instantaneous illumination.
"Universally illuminating the three periods of time" means expansive illumination.
Thus, its essential nature consists of expansive wisdom endowed with all virtues.
Third, within the section clarifying the functional activity (*karmaprayoga*) following "The Great Sage," there is likewise first a question and then an answer.

In the answer, there is first a discernment of the basis upon which the functional activity relies; that is to say, prior to the sphere and function of this dharma-gate, there exists the *dharmavana-samādhi*, and having now entered this meditative concentration, these functional activities are manifested.
Below, the actual manifestation of the functional activity is presented in three parts:

First, making offerings to the Buddhas of the Eight Manifestations; second, from "If there are sentient beings" onwards, clarifying the downward salvation of sentient beings; third, from "I do not give rise to" onwards, distancing oneself from the two marks to reveal the non-conceptual activity of karma.
4. From "I alone" (*mātra*) onwards, the stage of one's own realization (*sva-bhūmi*) is concluded.
Fifth, from "The great [elements]" (*mahābhūta*) onwards, there is the upward inference toward superior progress; herein, there are ten matters in five pairs:
first, the thorough mastery of phenomena without attachment (*anāsakti*).
Second, externally it is vast and pervasive, while internally it is all-encompassing;
third, externally it moves swiftly, while internally it contains power;
fourth, externally it lifts everything universally, while internally it has broad capacity.

The first [section], "a single thought-moment universally encompasses sentient beings," subsequently encompasses many eons; thus, one knows that within each and every thought-moment, the encompassing of sentient beings is inexhaustible.
From "I shall" onwards, he concludes that this is not his own portion.
The dedication reaching all places is concluded.

Regarding the fifth dedication, the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit," within the section on spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), there are first three internal points that raise the Dharma to exhort practice: namely, that the path contrary to craving is termed a "perilous difficulty," and that being fully equipped within true practice is termed "jewel adornment."
Vasumitra, which is translated here as Shiyou (World-Friend) and also named Tianyou (Heavenly-Friend), so called because he is skillfully able to attract and gather all worldly beings.
The second part, entering the middle stage according to the teaching, also has three sections: respectful departure, mindfulness of the Dharma, and arrival at the subsequent stage.
Regarding the contemplation of the Dharma: first, because the former nun previously enlightened her mind, it causes the Buddha-wisdom to be nurtured;
second, from the section on "single-mindedness" downward, by contemplating the aforementioned Dharma, compassion, wisdom, vows, and practices are further increased.
Proceeding to the subsequent section, there are four points to be investigated:

first, the inquiry into superiority; second, the expression of doubt and wonder by those of shallow wisdom; third, the praise of excellence by those of profound wisdom; and fourth, the indication of its location.
Question:
Why was it that previously, when anger and wrong views were displayed, Sudhana himself doubted;
yet now, when the signs of greed are manifested, he causes others to doubt?
Answer:

Because the two types of parents obstruct the bodhisattva path, and because craving—which accords with compassion—obstructs inferior practice; for this reason, the *Vinayaviniścaya-sūtra* states that a bodhisattva would rather give rise to hundreds of thousands of thoughts of greed than a single thought of anger.
Another explanation:
Sudhana has already been tamed regarding his previous anger and wrong views; therefore, he does not dare to harbor further doubts here.

Regarding the instruction that [the Bodhisattva] is within the deep palace: according to the *Tri-dharmaka-sūtra*, the country represents the sphere of wisdom (*prajñā*), the city represents the sphere of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the palace represents the sphere of teaching the Dharma (*dharma-deśanā*).
Now, this woman has directly realized the suchness of desire; therefore, she resides within the deep palace.
To approach the gatekeeper signifies the completion of the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) and the arrival at the gateway of the samādhi of direct realization.
The third section, beginning with "Sudhana hears," clarifies the acts of seeing, revering, and requesting; herein there are three parts:
namely, seeing, revering, and requesting.
Within the section on seeing, there are two parts: [End of segment]
First one sees the environment as the fruit of support, and subsequently one sees the primary retribution.
Regarding the environment, an ancient commentary states:
"The tenfold walls of precious jewels represent the ten stages (*bhūmi*)."
The ten rows of trees represent the practice of the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*).
The tenfold moats represent the conduct of ethical discipline (*śīla*) within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The water of eight virtues represents the overflowing waters of the eight meditative concentrations (*aṣṭasamādhi*).

"Adorned with flowers of enlightenment and featuring towers and pavilions" refers to the subsequent attainment of the essence of the primary and secondary environments (*āśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*), which are reconstituted.

Second, regarding the observation of the primary retribution (*sambhogakāya*), there are two parts: first, observing the superior characteristics of the three karmas; second, from "The Great Assembly" onwards, manifesting the excellence of the retinue.
The respectful petition may be understood [from the preceding].
Fourth, from the words "He replied" onwards, he reveals his own *dharmadhātu*, which contains four parts:

first, designating the name and manifesting the essence; second, from "If a deva sees" onwards, distinguishing its functional activity (*karmayoga*); third, from "He said" onwards, the causes and conditions for attaining the Dharma; fourth, from "I only" onwards, concluding with his own self-limitation.
Regarding the first part, the "Dharma-gate of the Purity of the Ultimate Reality (bhūtakoṭi) through Detachment from Desire" has two meanings:

First, concerning one's own practice, although one remains in the realm of desire by intentionally retaining afflictions out of compassion and vow, great wisdom illuminates that desire is empty of intrinsic nature; this is called the purity of ultimate reality.
As it says in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*: "Practicing dhyāna while remaining amidst desires," and so forth.
Furthermore, the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa* states: "Lust is itself the Path; so too are anger and delusion."

Second, regarding the benefit of sentient beings: although they retain afflictions to manifest as dwelling in desire, they cause those sentient beings who dwell in desire to necessarily leave desire behind, so that they may attain this actual reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of pure Dharma—just as in the case of Ambaṣṭhā and others.
The second section, clarifying the activity (*karman*), has two parts:
first, manifesting in bodies identical to the vessel-world; second, from "If there are sentient beings... onwards, benefiting others through the Dharma.

Within this [second part], there are ten kinds of samādhis; all of these are for the purpose of transforming sentient beings according to their inclinations, enabling them to attain such profound samādhis.
*Āliya* means "embracing and touching" (抱持摩觸); it is a sign of gathering [the mind], and thus one attains that samādhi.
*Añjavi* means "kissing" (嗚口); one thereby attains the concentration of the secret treasury of verbal teachings.

The passage beginning with "In this way" serves as a summary; it is that which is accomplished by Bodhisattvas at the ultimate stage and is not something known by those at lower stages, as explained in the section on the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*) within the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Regarding the two sections on the causes and conditions for attaining the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividya*),
there is first the question and then the answer.

Within the answer, it should be understood that the first part answers where the roots of goodness were planted, while the section beginning with "Good son" answers what kind of practices were cultivated.
4. From "I only" below, he concludes that he knows only this single skillful means. 5.

From "The great [bodhisattvas]" below, he looks upward to recommend further progress, [thinking]: "The great bodhisattvas possess immeasurable and vast skillful means; how could I possibly know them?"
The dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit is concluded.

Regarding the sixth dedication, "the dedication of roots of goodness that accord with equality," within the section on spiritual friends, first, the instruction to practice by citing the Dharma is presented: *śubhapāramitā*, which is translated here as "the excellent and wondrous arrival at the other shore."
"Abiding securely" means that one has attained the Buddha-dharmakāya and constantly dwells in making offerings.

Furthermore, according to the Indian manuscripts, it should be named "sustaining" (*saṃdhāraṇa*), or "grasping and sustaining and incorporating," because it gathers and incorporates all wholesome dharmas.
Regarding "constantly making offerings to the stūpa," this is because one constantly beholds the Dharma-body at the site of the stūpa.
In the second section, "entering by relying on the teaching," the practice of mindfulness is omitted.
In the third section, "beholding, honoring, and inviting," the acts of beholding and honoring are omitted; therefore, it says "up to and including" (乃至).
The fourth section, "The Response," below, demonstrates four aspects within one's own *dharmadhātu*:
first, the designation of the name; second, the clarification of the essence; third, the functional activity; and fourth, the summary of its virtues.
First, the eternal body of all Buddhas is called "non-extinction.
When the stage of causal practice illuminates and penetrates it, it is called the "Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva.
Second, from the passage beginning with "Abiding herein" onwards, within the section revealing the nature and characteristics, there are two parts:

Regarding the statement that when first seeing the Buddha’s merit-body (guṇakāya), it is eternal, except for those who transform sentient beings: this merely involves altering the minds of others to make them perceive his appearance and disappearance; in reality, his eternal body has neither arising nor ceasing.
Furthermore, the Buddha-moon is eternally abiding; it is only that the reflections in the water of sentient beings' minds appear and disappear.

Second, from the passage "opening the stupa door" onwards, one perceives that the Buddha's Dharma-body is eternal, because one sees that the essence and nature of the Buddha are limitless and inexhaustible.
"Opening the stupa" refers to opening its phenomenal characteristics (*samskāra*).
"Attaining meditative concentration" refers to perceiving the principle of nature (*dharmatā*).
"Attaining the wondrous Dharma" refers to attaining the ocean-like, *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*-sands of meritorious qualities within that principle.
Third, regarding the section "He spoke thus," which clarifies the functional application [of the practice], there is first a question and subsequently an answer.
Within the answer, there are two parts:
first, seeing the Buddhas of the three periods of time in this realm; second, extending this by way of analogy to the ten directions.
Regarding the preceding section: first, one perceives the causes, effects, and other matters of past Buddhas; second, one similarly classifies those of the future and present.
From "I alone" (*ahaṃ kevalam*) onwards, the stage of one's own realization (*svabhāva-avasthā*) is concluded.

Fifth, regarding the section "The Great Elements" and below, within the context of advancing through superior progress: although the elder knows that the Buddhas of the three periods of time do not perish, he is as yet unable to realize the non-duality and equality between the single thought-moment by which he knows and the three temporal limits that are known;
second, he is unable to immediately abide in the state of a Buddha, which is the object of the wisdom that knows;
third, while he knows all kalpas before and after, he cannot know the absence of the conceptualization of kalpas.
Fourth, although one sees that the Buddha does not perish, one cannot know the meaning of the equality between this Buddha and that Buddha;

fifth, from the passage "Tathāgata" onwards, one cannot [realize] that the defiled and the pure, the subject and the object, are equal and non-dual—namely, that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are these three without distinction;
sixth, from the passage "Pure Adornment" onwards, although one illuminates the three periods of time, one cannot [understand] how wisdom subsumes all virtues.
7. Although one knows the Buddha from "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) onwards, one has not yet attained the Buddha's majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*);
8. From "Discrimination" (*vibhāga*) onwards, one is unable to exercise mastery over the Dharma.
The section beginning with "I shall" concludes the inability [to fulfill the vow].
This ends the stage of dedicating firm roots of goodness.

Regarding the first part of the seventh dedication, "Knowledge for Accordant Contemplation of All Sentient Beings," which introduces the Dharma to encourage internal cultivation: as for "Mount Radiance," the trees and flowers on that mountain constantly emit light, symbolizing the universal manifestation of the radiance of great compassion.

This mountain is located on the southern border of South India; its original name in India is Potalaka Mountain, which has no direct translation, but is translated according to its meaning as "Mountain Adorned with Small Trees and Creepers."
Furthermore, the *Ekādaśamukha-sūtra* was preached on this mountain.
As for Avalokiteśvara, he is named Guanshiyin, and he is also named Guanzizai; his name in Sanskrit is Bhūṣukuṭi-śvaras.
*Puluke* (逋盧羯底) means "contemplation" (*guan*) in this language;
*Vilū* (毘盧) means "light" (*guang*).
Because the sounds and characters are similar, it is translated here as "light."
*Śvara* is translated here as "sovereignty" (*zìzài*).
*Śabda* is translated here as "sound" (*yīn*).
Upon examining various Sanskrit sūtras, some have *śabda* while others have *śvara*; it is for this reason that the translations differ.
In the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, it is said that "those who immediately contemplate his voice shall all attain liberation.
The commentary explains:
He impartially contemplates the world and rescues beings from suffering according to their cries; thus he is named Avalokiteśvara.
That sūtra contains three wheels in full:
first, the vocal action (*vākkarman*), which consists of reciting names to eliminate the seven calamities, such as those caused by water and fire;
second, the physical action (*kāyakarman*), which consists of performing prostrations to fulfill two types of wishes, such as seeking male or female offspring.
Regarding the three mental actions (*manas-karman*), he maintains mindfulness to eliminate the three poisons— namely, greed and so forth—
as explained therein. As for why he is specifically designated by the name Avalokiteśvara in relation to vocal action (*vāk-karman*), it is because the activity of that [vocal] karma is predominant.
If one considers him from the perspective of body and speech, he is named Avalokiteśvara, because his bodily light shines upon [beings].
If he possesses the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*) and gathers beings without obstruction, he is named Avalokiteśvara.
The second section, "Entering by Relying on the Teaching," also has three parts:
within the ten phrases concerning the recollection of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*), all are practices that increase through the power of the aforementioned teaching.
The remainder can be understood accordingly.
The third section, "Seeing, Paying Homage, and Making a Request," also has three parts.
Within the first part, "Seeing," there are two sections: first, Sudhana sees Avalokiteśvara; second, Avalokiteśvara praises Sudhana.
Within the former, there are four sub-sections:
"First, seeing the excellence of the environment and its inhabitants;
second, dwelling on the western slope of the mountain"—this means dwelling facing east upon the mountain slope, which is a sign of turning toward the light;
"third, preaching the Dharma for the assembly."
Third, the contemplation of the three truths without blinking;
fourth, "forming such a thought" and below, the superior mindfulness perfuming the mind.
Within this, the first eight lines are a specific exposition, while the final two lines are a summary.
2. From "At that time, Avalokiteśvara" onwards, there are ten phrases praising the virtues of Sudhana:
first, praising the excellence of his mind, meaning he possesses the three minds;
second, from "Toward Samantabhadra" onwards, praising the excellence of his conduct and vows.
3. From "desiring to hear" onwards, it praises the excellence of upholding the Dharma.
4. From "increasing" onwards, it describes the insatiable cultivation of goodness.
5. This accords with the teacher's instructions.

Sixth, from "From Mañjuśrī" onwards is the section on the supreme basis (*āśraya*). Because it relies upon that [Mañjuśrī] to give rise to the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), it is said to "arise from that ocean.
Furthermore, another interpretation states: because it flows from fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*), it is said to "arise from that wisdom."
7. From "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) onwards, he praises the perfection of the roots of goodness; thus, he attains the power of the Buddha’s empowerment and meditative concentration.
8. From "Free from Laziness" (*kausīdyavigata*) onwards, he praises the single-minded sincerity in seeking the Dharma.
The ninth [section] is the praise for seeing the Buddha’s accomplishment of practice.
The tenth, from “Wisdom” (*prajñā*) onwards, is the praise for the fulfillment and perfect realization of wisdom.
From “At that time” (*tadā*) onwards, the respectful invitation may be understood accordingly.
The fourth section, "Answering," below, demonstrates two aspects within his own dharma-realm:
first, praising the arousal of the bodhicitta to clarify the skillful means for bestowing the Dharma;
second, from "I have already... onwards, correctly demonstrating his own Dharma, which contains four parts:
First, the designation of the name; second, the elucidation of its virtues; third, the manifestation of its function;
fourth, the conclusion regarding its stage. Regarding the first: "Great Compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) refers to compassion that is identical in essence with [the Buddha-nature].
Furthermore, it is called "Great Compassion" because it is compassion without an object (*anālambana-karuṇā*).
Furthermore, because it possesses the three types of compassion, it is called "Great Compassion" (Mahākaruṇā).
Regarding the "practice of light," one accomplishes this practice by benefiting sentient beings with the light of compassion.
In its original Indic name, it is titled *Sarvabuddhakaruṇāguhyajñānagarbha-vimokṣa* (The Liberation of the Secret Wisdom Treasury of the Compassion of All Buddhas).
The commentary states:
This is because he skillfully and secretly gathers in sentient beings through compassion.
Second, from the section on "Teaching and Transforming" onwards, his virtues are distinguished; herein there are two parts:

First, [the Bodhisattva] never departs from the presence of the Buddha or the beings he manifests before them; second, from "Or by... onwards, it shows the benefit of gathering and transforming others through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and so forth;
third, from "Good son" onwards, it clarifies his functional activity, which is threefold:

first, establishing vows for the practice of the Dharma; second, causing others to be free from eighteen kinds of fear; third, from "Furthermore" onwards, causing their practice not to regress; fourth, from "I only... onwards, concluding with his own self-limitation.
The fifth section, "All the Great [Elements]," consists of four parts within the upward inference:

first, inferring the vows and practices of Samantabhadra; second, from "uninterrupted" onwards, the continuous flow of his activities; third, from "knowing all" onwards, clarifying the continuity of his gathering of sentient beings; and fourth, from "I shall" onwards, concluding that these are not within one's own capacity.

Having completed the dedication that accords with the equal contemplation of all sentient beings, within the eighth section on the dedication to spiritual friends according to their true nature (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), there are first two parts concerning the cultivation of internal dharma-contemplation:
first, the actual journey toward the east; second, Avalokiteśvara’s instruction; and third, his teaching on how to inquire about the Way.
At the beginning of the assembly, those who came from the east symbolized the manifestation of the *tathatā* (suchness) and the state of the illumination of realized wisdom.

They were named "Those Who Proceed Correctly" (*Samyaktva-gāmin*) because, through their supernormal powers, they swiftly reach all destinations throughout the ten directions to gather sentient beings by means of the True Dharma; hence this name was given to them.
The Indian manuscript says:
"There was a bodhisattva named Apracāra-anyamārga.
The commentary explains:
One practices only the Buddha-way and does not practice the paths of the other two vehicles; this is "rightly directed," meaning one proceeds toward what is correct.
The Sanskrit original emphasizes negation (exclusion), while the Chinese version emphasizes affirmation (manifestation).
"Abiding on the summit of Vajra Mountain" refers to this Mountain of Radiance; it symbolizes abiding in the state of suchness (*tathatā*), for it is indestructible.
The following section clarifies the shaking of the earth, its jewel-adornment, the emission of light, and the raining down of offerings.

Those who come to visit Avalokiteśvara do so because clear wisdom accords with compassion; this is also a manifestation of transformation for those with the karmic affinity, serving as a guide for Sudhana.
Second, from "At that time, Avalokiteśvara" onwards, there is the detailed instruction in response to the inquiry.
Third, the section beginning with "You should go to... instructs on how to inquire, which can be understood accordingly.
Second, the section beginning with "At that time, Sudhana... concerns entering according to the instruction, which has two parts:
first, prostration; second, mindfulness of the Dharma until reaching the subsequent stage.
Why not contemplate the gate of Avalokiteśvara’s compassion?
Because compassion is inseparable from wisdom, one must cause compassion to penetrate deeply into the ocean of wisdom; only then does it reach its ultimate consummation.
Third, from the section on “Going in Person” (*ci-yi*) onwards, we see the respectful petition.
Since this has already been seen previously, there is only the act of approaching with reverence and making a formal request.
Fourth, from "I have already accomplished" onwards, he demonstrates his own *dharmadhātu*; herein there are three parts:
first, the designation of the name; second, the elucidation of its meaning; and third, the conclusion regarding the stage.
Regarding the beginning and middle [of the text]: that which is boundless throughout the ten directions is called the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*);
that which reaches everywhere in a single thought-moment is termed Swift Movement (*javanavāhin*).
In the section following "He addressed [the Buddha] in white words," where the meaning is elucidated, there are first three questions raised, followed by three corresponding answers.
First, asking where the Dharma was obtained; second, asking how far the place of origin is; third, asking for how long he has been coming.
In the response, there are three parts: first, praising the profundity [of the teaching] to test the capacity of the recipient.
As for the phrase "only those who are diligent," this refers precisely to Sudhana;
because his faculties and conditions correspond, [the Buddha] intends to preach the Dharma for him.
Second, from "I only pray" onwards, he gives rise to a superior aspiration and joy.
Third, from "He replied" onwards is the formal explanation of the question asked.
"The World-system of Wondrous Treasury" answers the place from which [the Bodhisattva] has come.
"Where the Buddha [taught], etc. answers the place where he attained the Dharma.
The passage beginning with "having set out from there" answers the question regarding the duration of the time taken to arrive, and it also reveals whether that distance is far or near.
The second section, beginning with "in a single thought-moment," explains the extent of the practice throughout those many kalpas, precisely manifesting the meaning of swift travel.

Third, from "The various countries traversed" onwards, the meaning of accomplishing practice through swift action is elucidated. This means that while making offerings to the Buddhas above and saving sentient beings below, one does not merely avoid neglecting swift action to accomplish sublime conduct; rather, it is precisely by means of swift action that these superior practices are accomplished.
4. "Down to" [the word] "even" (乃至) concludes by extending [the principle] to the ten directions; that is, just as it is from the east, so it is in all ten directions.
3. "I only" (我唯) and below conclude one's own personal realization.
In the fifth section, "The Great Elements," within the upward inference (*ūrdhvaprasaraṇa*), first, a single line provides a general inference;

second, a specific inference [shows that] the abiding realm is immeasurable and indestructible, unlike the *Samyaktva-niyāma* (the stage of right determination) where one dwells only upon this single peak of the Vajra-mountain;
third, a specific inference regarding swift movement (*kṣipragati*), meaning that because the Dharma-body is primordially pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, it does not depend on swift movement.

4. From "Discriminating" (*vibhajya*) downward, he investigates the nature of his actions, meaning that preaching the Dharma and delivering sentient beings are all equal across the three periods of time, characterized by non-attachment and so forth;
5. From "I shall" (*ahaṃ bhaviṣyāmi*) downward, he concludes that these are not within his own domain.
The dedication according to the characteristics is concluded.

Within the ninth dedication, "Unfettered and Unattached Liberation," at the beginning of the section on exhorting practice through the presentation of the Dharma, there is a city named *Pāṭaliputra*. In its original language, it is correctly called *Vārāvatī*, which means "City with Gates. This is so named because the city possesses magnificent gates; thus, it is designated by that name.
As for Mahādeva, he is so named because he possesses unconditioned, pure retribution and excels in sovereign mastery.
Second, regarding the entry into the inner [teaching] according to the instruction, there are four parts;
first, the salutation and departure.

Within the second reflection on the Dharma, there are three parts: first, contemplating and seeking the aforementioned Dharma; second, from "giving birth" (*utpāda*) onwards, obtaining the Dharma through contemplation; third, from "attaining the inconceivable" (*acintya-prāpti*) onwards, the Dharma that has been obtained;
fourth, from "gradually" (*kramaśas*) onwards, the subsequent inquiry;
and fourth [in the structural sense], the person who provides instruction is the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who acts as a companion.
The third section, "Sudhana’s Journey," clarifies the acts of seeing, paying respect, and making a formal request.
The fourth section, beginning with "At that time, Mahādeva," demonstrates his own dharma-realm; herein there are two parts:
first, the skillful means for bestowing the dharma, and second, the actual bestowal of his own dharma.
The preceding section also has two parts:
first, bodily action (*kāyakarman*), and second, verbal action (*vākkarman*).
Within the bodily action, the phrase "having four long arms" refers to the skillful application (*upāya*) of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Taking the waters of the four oceans corresponds to the meaning of the supreme flow from the *dharmadhātu*.
Washing one’s face signifies purifying the face that responds to the capacity of sentient beings.

Traditionally, it has been said that this refers to washing the face of Sudhana; however, upon consulting the Sanskrit original, it is seen that with four long arms, he takes a portion of seawater from each of the four directions to wash his own face. Thus, having purified himself with water, he is able to approach Sudhana as the flowers are scattered toward him.
Second, from "speaking these words" onwards, the verbal karma praises the capacity of the audience; the first phrase is general.
Regarding the "extraordinary Dharma," it is because such a thing does not exist in the world.
Second, the specific praise for taking refuge summarizes [the path] by means of the Right Path.
Third, a specific praise for being a teacher who protects [beings] by means of the True Dharma.
Fourth, a specific praise for being a general who leads [them] to the city of wisdom.
Fifth, from "Endowed with" (*samanvāgata*) onwards, the conclusion regarding the departure from faults and the suitability to the capacities [of beings].
Second, "My Accomplishment" and below correctly demonstrates the three aspects within his own dharma:
first, the designation of the name and essence; second, the manifestation of functional activity; third, the conclusion regarding his own stage. Regarding the first:

as for the "cloud-net," the dharmas of the practice of the six perfections possess the meaning of moistening and benefiting, as well as the meaning of universal coverage; thus they are metaphorized as clouds.
There is the sense of straining through a filter and the sense of being obscured; when illustrated by means of a net, its essence consists of the practice of the six perfections.
In the second section, beginning with "He said," the functional activity is clarified, first by means of a question and subsequently by an answer.
The answer consists of three parts:

first, the instruction on practicing giving (*dāna*), which includes (1) the accumulation of material goods, (2) the instruction on giving itself, and (3) the extension of this to other sentient beings;
second, from "Furthermore" onwards, the instruction on practicing ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the other perfections.
Third, the section beginning with "In this manner" concludes the accomplishment of practice.
Third, the section beginning with "I only" concludes one's own personal realization.

Within the fifth section on deferential recommendation, five metaphors are used to illustrate five types of practice: the first two concern self-benefit, while the latter three concern the benefit of others.
The passage beginning with "I shall" concludes that [the merit] does not belong to oneself.
This completes the dedication free from bondage and attachment.

Within the tenth section on the immeasurable dedication of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which concerns the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), the first part raises the Dharma to encourage practice internally. While the preceding stages were all located in South India, the present reference points to Magadha in Central India.
The deity of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) intends to signify two meanings:
first, with respect to the cause, it signifies that those who have realized the truth on the stages of the path share the same status as a Buddha;
having reached the end of the stage of dedication (pariṇāmanā), they thus turn toward this place.

Secondly, regarding the fruit: this indicates that the Buddha’s manifestation of his body through skillful means (*upāya*) in response to specific circumstances is a mark of his pedagogical mastery; as this belongs to the fulfillment of the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), it is for this reason that the place where he attained enlightenment is identified here.
This is because each of the five stages culminates in the attainment of Buddhahood, and the manifestation of enlightenment beneath the tree belongs to this stage.
Furthermore, the term "divine" (*shen*) expresses the profound and subtle meaning of the virtue of wisdom.

However, regarding the deities who guard the *dōjō* (place of practice), there are tree deities of the *dōjō* and ground deities of the *dōjō*. Now, this "ground" symbolizes the mind-ground which serves as the basis; for one attains the Way within the mind, and thus the mind is taken as the site of the *dōjō*.

He is named "Abiding" because he gathers all roots of goodness and dedicates them toward enlightenment, remaining steadfastly upon the site of the ground of awakening; he maintains his resolve without loss, ensuring the attainment of the fruit, and thus this name is given to him.
Second, from "At that time, Sudhana" onwards, regarding the entry according to the instructions, there are two parts:
first, departing after paying respects; second, arriving at the subsequent location.
Third, from "The ten thousand earth goddesses each spoke these words" onwards, regarding the vision, respect, and request, there are four parts:

First, the devas of the first stage praise Sudhana’s virtues; second, from "At that time, dwelling in peace" onwards, he adorns the lands and gathers in sentient beings; third, he announces the treasury of jewels; fourth, he pays homage and expresses his intention.
The fourth section, "At that time, the earth deity then... and so forth, demonstrates her own dharma-realm; herein there are five parts: first, the demonstration of its essence;
second, the manifestation of its name; third, its functional activity; fourth, its causal conditions; and fifth, the conclusion regarding its stage.

At the beginning and middle [of this teaching], because Sudhana’s roots of goodness from past lives were all dedicated toward great bodhi, he dwells within the treasury beneath the Bodhi tree at this site of enlightenment; this, then, is the treasury of the bodhicitta.
Now, as one desires to realize the stages, they are added so that they may all manifest together; thus, all roots of goodness are contained within this place.

Second, regarding the name "The Manifestation of the Equal Dharma Accomplished by Myself": because it is maintained without loss and the attainment of Buddhahood is certain, it is called the "Indestructible Treasury."
Third, the section beginning with "I [am]" clarifies its functional activity, which consists of ten phrases.
The first phrase is general, meaning that as a constant protector, one maintains what they practice.
The final nine [verses] specifically clarify the internal [qualities]: first, the profound realization of wisdom;
second, the fulfillment of great vows;
and third, the purification of sublime conduct.
Fourth, the excellence of the fourfold emergence;
fifth, the possession of the power of virtue;
sixth, the perfection of the firm dharma.
Seventh, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, one increases the practice of protection; therefore, one hears the Dharma of the Buddha bestowing predictions.
Eighth, one transforms others below by means of the Dharma.
Ninth, one receives the Buddha’s power above.
4. From "In the past" onwards, the causes and conditions for attaining the Dharma are clarified;

this section has three parts: first, the time and place of antiquity; second, from "Cultivating" onwards, the expansion of the attainment of the Dharma; and third, from "Within that" onwards, further encounters with various Buddhas, all of whom he constantly made offerings to at the sites where they attained perfect enlightenment on the site of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because he is the principal figure associated with this gate.
5. "I alone," and so forth, concludes the section on one's own station.

Within the fifth section, which looks upward in deference, there are two parts: first, the constant attendant, because this earth goddess perceives the Buddha only at the site of the *bodhimaṇḍa* and cannot follow him constantly, she therefore looks upward in deference;
second, from "I have heard all" onwards, it expands upon the hearing [of the Dharma].
3. From "Deeply entering" onwards, it clarifies profound hearing;
4. From "In every thought-moment" onwards, it clarifies instantaneous hearing;
5. From "The reflections of all Buddhas" onwards, it clarifies that the fruit produced from the cause is indestructible, and so forth.
Sixth, from "I shall... onwards, the section concludes that [the practices] do not belong to oneself.
The ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) are thus completed.
Below this, from Vāsavadattā to Gopā, there are ten spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who clarify the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Within the first section on the "Knowledge of the Ground of Joyful Realization," there are also five parts.

In the initial exhortation to practice by citing the Dharma, it specifically states *Kapilavastu*; this is translated as "Yellow Substance City" (*Huangwu Cheng*). This is because in ancient times, the Rishi Yellow-Head (*Kapila*) previously resided in this place, and later a city was built there, hence it was given this name.
It is also called the Abode of Quiescence.
As for why he is in this city: it signifies that from the first bhūmi upward, one is born into the family of the Buddhas; therefore, he resides in the City of the Buddha’s Birth.

*Vasavatti* is correctly rendered as *Bharavasana*; this means "relying upon fearlessness," which refers to the passage below where it is extensively explained that he acts as a refuge for sentient beings who are afraid.
In the Indic language, her name is Vasanti, which here means "spring. This signifies that she can cause the myriad practices to grow, just as during the season of spring.

As for the Night Goddess (Rātridevī), she is like the Night Goddesses who preside over the first assembly; she is so named because she illuminates and saves sentient beings within the night. She symbolizes that realized wisdom is wondrously free from all marks, as it destroys the obscurations of darkness.
These nine kinds of night goddesses (rātridevatā) are all female deities according to the Sanskrit original, signifying the manifestation of compassion.
Second, from "At that time, Sudhana" onwards, regarding the entry into the teaching, there is first the expression of reverence.

The second is the recollection of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*), which consists of ten phrases: the first is general, while the remaining nine are specific; all are qualities of the indestructible dharma-gate (*dharmamukha*).
Furthermore, it is explained that one enters that dharma-gate by means of these nine practices.
That he gradually travels to that place and enters through the eastern gate signifies the beginning of illumination and the commencement of entering into realization.
His dwelling in the central city symbolizes his departure from extremes.

Third, regarding the section beginning with “At that time, Sudhana saw the sun set,” which clarifies the stage of seeing, paying respect, and making a formal request, there are first three internal points.
First, as for the inquiry into why it is said the sun has set: this symbolizes the exhaustion of all discriminative wisdom prior to the [first] bhūmi.
Furthermore, because this night deity is not seen during the daytime, one can only see them during the dark of night.
Second, the section beginning with "seeing him" clarifies the correct vision of the body.
An ancient said:
"The city" refers to the path of teaching at the first stage (bhūmi).
"Dwelling in the space above" refers to the path of realization.
That his body is like gold signifies that his true virtues are manifest.
That he wears vermilion robes symbolizes the radiance of realized wisdom (*jñāna*).
Third, regarding the section "In his body" and below, one observes his functional activity (*karmaprayoga*); herein there are three parts:
First, regarding "the body manifests starlight and so forth," this refers to gathering sentient beings during the darkness of night;
second, "manifesting dharmas from the pores" means benefiting sentient beings;
third, from "wherever they pass" onwards, it describes seeing and hearing bodhisattvas within a single pore teaching and transforming sentient beings.
Second, from "Sudhana sees and hears" downward, he pays respect;
third, from "He said" downward, he makes his request.
Regarding the phrase "the path of all-knowledge," it clarifies that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the causal path for attaining Buddhahood.
The fourth section, "The Night Goddess’s Address," below, reveals her own dharma-realm in two parts:
first, praising her resolve as it accords with the benefit of spiritual friends;
second, correctly manifesting her own dharma, which contains four sub-sections.
First, the designation of the name and essence; second, the manifestation of its activity and function; third, the causes and conditions for attaining the Dharma;
fourth, the conclusion regarding one's own stage. Regarding the first, "the light universally illuminates all phenomena" refers to the direct realization of the *dharmadhātu*.
Regarding "dispersing and so forth," this refers to destroying the obstacle of the notion of difference and eliminating the two types of delusion.
Furthermore, another interpretation states: "Universally illuminating all phenomena" clarifies its great wisdom (*mahājñāna*).
"Destroying and dispersing the ignorance of sentient beings" clarifies the function of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Another interpretation states that the former [phrase] refers to self-benefit and the latter to benefiting others.
Yet another interpretation states:

"Universally illuminating" and so forth refer to the wisdom that performs transformation; "shattering and dispersing" and so forth refer to the benefits bestowed upon those to be transformed according to their capacities.
Regarding the section beginning with "I [act] toward evil sentient beings," which clarifies the functional activity [of this wisdom], there is first the prose and subsequently the verse.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, the arousal of the mind to rescue sentient beings, which can be understood through nine types;

second, from "I am eternal" onwards, the actual responding to conditions to rescue and gather them, which contains ten gates—the first being a general explanation and the latter nine being specific manifestations.

In the preceding section, the first part clarifies the salvation of the age; this also explains the meaning of the Night Goddess (Rātridevī), as she presides over the transformation and guidance within the night of the present world, and further symbolizes the changes occurring upon the earth through her gathering of sentient beings within the darkness.
Next, "cities and towns," etc., clarifies the places of rescue.
Subsequently, regarding these sentient beings, the act of rescuing is accomplished through various means.
The passage beginning with "If there are those who encounter the sea" specifically reveals the nine gates of rescue for sentient beings in peril; each possesses two types of rescue:
First is salvation through worldly means, and second is salvation through supramundane means.
Regarding the first—salvation from perils at sea—it first clarifies the nature of the peril to be saved from, and subsequently reveals the skillful means by which one is saved.
Although he has already saved the world-ocean, he further desires to rescue and deliver sentient beings from the ocean of birth and death; this initial section briefly omits that point.
Second, regarding the salvation of sentient beings on land by providing illumination and so forth, this is worldly salvation;
second, from the passage "giving rise to such a mind" onwards, using the light of wisdom to extinguish the darkness of afflictions constitutes supramundane salvation.
The third type of rescue involves creating fruit trees and the like for sentient beings on the mountain; this is worldly rescue.
Causing sentient beings to transcend the mountain of birth and death is supramundane rescue.
First, rescuing sentient beings in the wilderness by causing them to be free from hunger, thirst, and so forth is worldly rescue;
second, as indicated by the passage "Furthermore, he thinks," causing them to enter the path of ultimate wisdom is supramundane rescue.
5. From "seeing attachment to pleasure" downward, [the text] saves sentient beings who are attached to their lands, causing them to extinguish that attachment; this is worldly salvation.
From "forming such a thought" downward, it also causes them to eliminate attachment to the five aggregates and abide in the realm of the Buddha; this is supramundane salvation.

Sixth, from "seeing attachment to the village" downward, saving sentient beings attached to the village by teaching the Dharma so they may cultivate revulsion is the mundane salvation; second, from "further forming this thought" downward, causing them to leave the empty village of the six sense bases and enter the city of omniscience is the supramundane salvation.
7. Furthermore, the section beginning with "Moreover" explains saving deluded or confused sentient beings so as to bring them liberation; this is mundane salvation.

Second, the section beginning with "Generating such a mind" clarifies supramundane salvation, which extinguishes the darkness of ignorance and halts all evils and rebellions. Within this, it first reveals the sentient beings who are to be saved, and subsequently, from "In this way" onwards, it clarifies the virtues of the one who saves.
8. From "I see their poverty and suffering" downward, the skillful means for rescuing and aiding sentient beings who are old and sick constitute worldly salvation;
from "He further thought" downward, causing them to attain the eternally abiding Dharma-body constitutes supramundane salvation.
9. From "I see various evil sentient beings" onwards, he rescues sentient beings with the false views of non-Buddhists and causes them to abide in right view; this is worldly rescue.
Second, from "He further thinks thus" onwards, he causes them to attain supramundane fruits such as Buddhahood.
Regarding these nine subsequent sections, one should understand them accordingly as they relate to the arising of nine types of minds toward the nine aforementioned types of sentient beings.
Within the twenty-one verses of the two concluding stanzas, there are four parts:
the first verse concerns the name and essence of the dharma-gate;
The second section consists of four verses clarifying the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), which are the means for saving sentient beings.

The third section consists of ten verses clarifying the excellence of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*): the first three concern the eyes, the next two the ears, the next one the nose, the next one the tongue, the next one the body, and the final two the mind.

The fourth section consists of the final six verses clarifying the vastness of its karmic functions: the first concerns the breadth of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the next three the breadth of wisdom (*prajñā*), and the final two the breadth of what is perceived.
The third section, beginning with “Sudhana said,” clarifies the causes and conditions for attaining the Dharma; it first presents two questions and subsequently provides two answers.

Within the answers, the first responds to the timing of the arousal of the bodhicitta, while the second—beginning with “Furthermore, son of good family, beyond this”—responds to the duration of time over which the Dharma was attained.

The first eight sections of the preceding [chapter] are as follows: first, a general explanation of the appearance of Buddhas throughout past kalpas; second, the manifestation of the father-king of the past; third, the initial emergence of the Buddha; fourth, the identification of his birth-body (*janma-kāya*); fifth, the praise of the Buddha’s emergence by a virtuous friend; sixth, making offerings to the Buddha and the assembly; seventh, the correlation between the present and the past; and eighth, the demonstration that the power of virtue is not in vain.
Second, the response concerning the duration since attaining the Dharma consists of five parts:
first, a general clarification of the time, place, and appearance of the Buddha;
second, the manifestation of his original birth-body; [and so forth].
3. From "That Pure Moon" onwards, it clarifies the exhortation of the spiritual friend;
4. Approaching the Buddha to hear the Dharma; 5.

Clarifying the attainment of samādhi, which contains four parts: first, the attainment of the *upāya-samādhi*; second, from "Having attained this," it clarifies the actual attainment of the dharma-gate; third, from "Emitting light," it clarifies the dharma-gate of seeing the Buddha through the illumination of light and the increase of the Dharma; fourth, from "A single body," it clarifies the expansion of the body throughout the lands to see the Buddha and increase the Dharma.
